- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

# 42Analytics

Knowledge repository built from the 42 Analytics YouTube channel (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference talks, 2012-2026), for batch ingestion into Flint's knowledge base and for applying ideas at Baylor Applied Performance.

## Layout
- `catalog/` : `channel_index_raw.tsv` (all 1,231 videos), `titles_triage.txt` (1,100 after dropping non-talks), `shortlist.tsv` (256 picked by topic, tiers A/B, with status).
- `videos/<date>_<id>_<slug>/` : `transcript.md` (YouTube captions, timestamped every 30 s), `meta.json`, `summary.md`, `applications.md`.
- `docs/` : `SELECTION_CRITERIA.md`, `SUMMARY_SPEC.md` (rules every summarizer follows, matches Flint's voice labels), `STATUS.md`.
- `scripts/` : `build_shortlist.py`, `fetch_captions.py` (captions only, throttled), `check_summary.py` (locators and numbers vs transcript).

## Not in git
Video files. The one pilot mp4 is in Google Drive: `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/04_RESEARCH/42Analytics_YouTube/`.
EOF
cat > docs/STATUS.md <<'EOF'
# 42Analytics STATUS

Last updated: 2026-09-30

## Done
- Channel triaged from titles: 1,231 videos, 256 shortlisted (A 139, B 117). See `docs/SELECTION_CRITERIA.md`.
- Caption fetcher and summary checker written. YouTube rate-limits caption requests (HTTP 429) after ~4 in a row; the fetcher backs off.
- Pilot: 11 videos have transcripts, 10 also have `summary.md` + `applications.md` (Sonnet 5.5 subagents). `check_summary.py`: 0 invented time locators; 5 numbers not found in transcript text (300, 0.8, 1000, 1940, 2017), not yet traced.
- Subagents cannot write `summary.md` (harness tells them to return text); the main session saved them. `applications.md` writes worked.

## Not verified yet
- "Eric's baseline:" claims in `applications.md` were not checked against `Flint/docs/method-baseline.md`. Sample-check before trusting.
- Pilot summaries not independently reviewed (Flint's gate: Codex or Opus falsify pass).

## Open
- Cost: each pilot video used roughly 60k subagent tokens (transcript + method-baseline re-read). Do not scale blindly; see cost options in the chat handoff.
- `2zIp6OB2XOs` (Injury Analytics 2013) still rate-limited; `2RJ-6mW_UOM` (Ivy League concussion rule) has no captions.
- Decide: which tier, which model, and whether Jev does triage and claim checks.

## Next
1. Eric picks scale and model tiers.
2. Commit pilot, then fetch captions for tier A in throttled batches (local machine).
3. Sample-verify applications against method-baseline.
EOF

content.text:
Everything is committed and pushed (`a3f4607`). Short answers to your two questions first, then where the pilot stands.

## Is Jev good for anything here?

Jev returns typed judgments (yes/no probabilities, one-of-N choices, scores). It doesn't write text, so it can't write the summaries or applications. It's a good fit for four jobs around them:

1. **Triage.** It can answer "is this about football, sports science, injury, policy, front office, decision-making?" as a yes/no per topic, plus a "useful to Baylor" score. My A/B list came from my own title reading. Jev could re-score all 1,100 titles, and later the transcripts, more consistently than keyword tags.
2. **Checking summaries against transcripts.** For each claim it would judge whether the transcript at that timestamp supports it. This is the open item in your TypeSafe `STATUS.md`: a pre-registered test of Jev checking summaries against transcripts, to run only if someone other than you reads the summaries. Flint reading them arguably meets that condition. My `scripts/check_summary.py` only covers timestamps and numbers, not whether a claim is supported.
3. **Labelling voice.** Flint's rule is that speaker claims, "Inference:" and "Eric's baseline:" stay separate. Jev could flag sentences that look like inference but aren't labelled. That was the most common failure in the Harries review.
4. **Flagging commercial bias.** It could tag whether the speaker sells the thing they discuss, for example the Sparta Science and Perry Weather talks. The ingest step then sets the confidence cap.

If you do this, I'd follow your own pattern: pre-register the bars, use my labels as the answer key, and have you blind-judge disagreements. I haven't called Jev or started this.

## Cheaper model or better model?

- **Summaries:** A mid-tier model is enough. All 10 Sonnet summaries passed `check_summary.py` with no invented time locators. Five numbers weren't found in the transcript text (300, 0.8, 1000, 1940, 2017). I haven't traced them, so I don't know if they're real errors. The agents also flagged garbled captions honestly instead of guessing. A cheaper model like Haiku could do tier B, as long as the mechanical check and a sample review gate it.
- **Applications:** This is where judgment and the "do not apply when" section matter. Sonnet's output reads well, but I haven't verified the "Eric's baseline:" quotes against `Flint/docs/method-baseline.md`. That is the main risk. I'd spot-check a sample with a stronger model before trusting any of it.
- **Cost:** Each pilot video cost roughly 60,000 subagent tokens, because every agent re-read the 6,000-word baseline and the full transcript. Scaling that to all 245 remaining videos would be around 15 million tokens. I wouldn't do that. A cheaper plan is tier A only, and writing applications from the short `summary.md` plus the baseline, not the full transcript.

## Where the pilot stands

- **Videos:** 11 have transcripts, and 10 have summaries and applications, in `videos/`.
- **Subagent limitation:** Subagents couldn't write `summary.md` (the harness says they should return text), so I saved those myself.
- **Shortlist:** The remaining ~245 videos are not fetched. The fetcher is throttled to avoid YouTube's rate limit.
- **Two bad videos:** "Injury Analytics" (2013) is still rate-limited, and the 2017 Ivy League concussion talk has no captions.

**Decisions for you:**
1. Do tier A only (139 videos) first, or all 256?
2. Which model tier for summaries (Sonnet or Haiku), and is a stronger review of a sample worth it?
3. Do you want the Jev triage and claim-check test set up?

# Drive triage: pre-registration

Tenth item measured against the capability map. Registered 2026-09-26, **before any
model call**. The registering commit is the one that adds this file. Bars approved by
Eric on 2026-09-26. Consumer: the Flint project (`erash11/Flint`), which builds Eric's
sport-science knowledge base from his Drive.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is a Drive folder path, a file name, and up to 2,000
characters of a document's first page. The documents are coaching and research
material: books, papers, course handouts and slides. No athlete data. Flint's catalog
excludes DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports before anything
reaches this test.

## Question

Can Jev put the Drive files that Flint's keyword rules cannot place into the Zotero
taxonomy (14 domains, 96 topics, `zotero_classify/taxonomy.py`), confidently enough
that Flint can route them without a person reading each one?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** Deciding a coaching PDF's domain from its folder, name and
   first page is not a join, a threshold or a lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint routes every file by domain: into Zotero, the vault,
   the book queue or the transcription queue. It also builds a per-domain shortlist
   of files to ingest in full.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Flint's keyword rules (`Flint/scripts/triage_rules.py`)
   classified 5,714 of 9,712 non-report files (59%). An md5 match against Zotero's
   Drive attachment store placed 81 more. The model pass covers only what code leaves.

## Sample (committed here: `drive_triage/sample.csv`)

200 files drawn by `Flint/scripts/draw_jev_sample.py`, seed 20260926, before any call.

- 100 from the 3,548 files the rules could not classify.
- 100 from the 5,254 files the rules did classify. These also measure the rules' own
  precision.
- Each half is stratified by source root, with proportional allocation.
- Excluded: Eric's own reports and dashboards, images, archives, and files already in
  Zotero.

## State per file

Folder path, file name, and the Zotero title where the md5 match recovered one. For
PDFs, Word files and slides, add up to 2,000 characters of first-page text. Video and
audio send path and name only. Files that are not synced locally (TB's Training Info)
are fetched with `gws` into a gitignored staging folder. State is built by code before
the answer key is written, and it is identical for every model.

## Questions

1. **Topic.** The `zotero_classify` topic Choice, unchanged (`classify.question()`),
   with the same domain fallback.
2. **Route.** One new Choice:
   - a research paper
   - a book or book chapter
   - course or lecture material
   - a coaching resource (programs, drills, templates, presentations)
   - Eric's own work
   - not sport-science material

## Answer key

Claude labels all 200 (domain, topic, route) from the same state, blind to every
model's answers, before the first Jev call. The labels are committed before Jev runs.

## Comparators (same 200, same state, same taxonomy)

- Flint's keyword rules, already run. On the unclassified half they count as misses.
- Haiku: one call per file, forced to name a topic.
- Codex: the same.

## Bars (fixed here; they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev confident: topic probability at or above the measured 0.50 cut | at least 60% of the 200 (120 files) |
| Jev domain accuracy on its confident answers, against the answer key | at least 90% |
| Jev versus Haiku: domain accuracy on Jev's confident subset | Jev at least equal to Haiku |
| Cost for the 200 | reported, no bar |

Claude labels all 200 (domain, topic, route) from the same state, blind to every

# Deliverable verifier — Research in 5

Third item in the capability map's sequence, after the skill router and the Zotero
classification. Checks a Research in 5 deck against the paper it claims to report,
before it is sent.

Built 2026-09-19 from the `citation_check` cookbook, with the aggregation rule from
`sde_cascade`. Code in `verifier/`.

**Governance: tier A.** A published paper and a deck written about it. No athlete
data, no health records.

## Why this one

The capability map called it "the one I would not have predicted". The concrete
motivation is in memory: the TOS brief was stopped on 2026-09-18 with *"3 misquotes +
bad Poisson — DO NOT SEND"*, caught by hand. Research in 5 goes out every week, to
staff, with Eric's name on it. A misquoted mean in a slide table is both easy to
produce and hard to spot by rereading your own work.

## Result

Against review 001 (Saraee et al., jumper's knee alignment), hand-checked to v4 and
marked ready to send:

| | |
|---|---|
| claims extracted | **67** — 50 numeric, 17 prose |
| verified | 59 |
| routed to a person | 8 |
| **false alarms** | **0** |
| wall time | **1.4 s** |
| cost | a fraction of a cent (17 calls) |

And against the same deck with defects planted in it, one per failure class
(`python test_verify.py`):

| planted | expected | caught |
|---|---|---|
| table mean `83.89` → `84.89` | fabricated | ✅ 2 claims |
| table source `p. 6` → `p. 4` | wrong_page | ✅ 21 claims |
| "None of the 7" → "Five of the 7 reached significance" | contradicted | ✅ 1 claim |
| sample size `22` → `93` | fabricated | ✅ 1 claim |

**4 of 4 caught, 0 false alarms on the real deck.** Finding nothing wrong with a deck
that is already correct proves very little on its own — a verifier that always says
"clear" would score the same — so the planted defects are the actual evidence.

## The design decision that matters: what counts as a claim

`review.json` is a deck, not a list of citations, so the extraction *is* the design.
It happens in `claims.py`, deterministically, in code, and sorts every claim into one
of three kinds:

**Numbers** — every table cell, chart value and numeric headline figure. Checked by
**string match only; these never go to Jev.** The capability map is explicit that the
half which catches a misquoted number is the code match, and the jaggedness page is
explicit that Jev is unreliable at arithmetic and at comparing numeric
representations. Asking a model whether 83.89 appears in a table is using the wrong
tool for a job `float()` does perfectly.

which are computed *from* the paper rather than printed in it. One Choice against the
page the deck itself cites.

overlap before any call**, then one Choice against that page. Sending all 11 pages

"""Prove the global TypeSafe API key resolves and the System One API answers.

There is deliberately no python-dotenv here. The key is meant to be available
globally from the environment (macOS Keychain -> ~/.zshenv -> every zsh), so
reading anything other than os.environ would hide a broken setup.

Run:  python smoke_test.py
"""

import os
import sys

REQUIRED_VAR = "TYPESAFE_API_KEY"


def require_key() -> None:
    if os.environ.get(REQUIRED_VAR):
        return
    print(f"{REQUIRED_VAR} is not set in this environment.\n", file=sys.stderr)
    print("Fix it in this order:", file=sys.stderr)
    print("  1. Run ./setup_global_key.sh in Terminal.app (not through Claude Code).", file=sys.stderr)
    print("  2. Restart Claude Code. A running session keeps the environment it", file=sys.stderr)
    print("     started with, so it will not see the new variable until restarted.", file=sys.stderr)
    print("  3. Check status any time with ./setup_global_key.sh --check", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)


def main() -> int:
    require_key()

    try:
        from typesafe_sdk import Noul, TypeSafeClient
    except ModuleNotFoundError:
        print("typesafe-sdk is not installed. Run:  pip install typesafe-sdk", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    # The client picks the key up from TYPESAFE_API_KEY on its own.
    with TypeSafeClient() as client:
        response = client.system_one(
            state={"document": "I was charged twice. Please fix this ASAP."},

### Answer-key audit: a required step in every pre-registered test (added 2026-09-26)

Three measurements found a bad answer key, not a bad model: the surgery count (17 by
regex, 22 under blind labels), the Evidence Library tags (the reviewed labels sided
with Jev on 5 of 8 rules-picks), and the spring notes (role words the labels missed).
The "Just Ask Jev" paper (arXiv 2609.29429) reports the same on three public
benchmarks. So every pre-registration now carries this step, written down before the
first call:

1. **Pull the confident disagreements.** Every item where Jev's probability clears the
   pre-registered confidence cut and its answer differs from the label. Fix the cut
   in the pre-registration, not after seeing results.
2. **Eric judges them blind.** Shuffle, hide which side said what, show only the input
   and the two answers. He marks label right, Jev right, or unclear.
3. **Report both scores.** The pre-registered score on the original labels decides
   pass or fail, and the bar never moves. The audited score is reported next to it,
   and the count of labels changed is a finding in its own right.
4. **Cap the audit.** At most 20 items. If there are more than 20 confident
   disagreements, audit a random 20 and report the rate. More than that is a label
   problem worth its own write-up.

What this is not: a way to rescue a failed test. A test that fails on the original
labels and passes on the audited ones is reported as FAIL, with the audit as the reason

"""Build the pre-registered sample for the video-summary claim check.

No model calls. Reads the 42Analytics repo (summary.md + transcript.md per video),
extracts the prose claims under "## Key claims", and writes video_check/sample.csv:

  real           6 real claims per video (seeded), expected label unknown: Claude labels
                 them blind in the answer key before the first Jev call.
  wrong_locator  a real claim paired with transcript text from >= 8 minutes away.
                 Expected: not supported. Label fixed by construction.
  cross_video    a real claim paired with a window from a different video.
                 Expected: not supported. Label fixed by construction.
  negation, mechanism   authored by Claude into video_check/authored_plants.csv
                 before the first call; merged in if the file exists.

Numbers are NOT in this test. They are checked by string match in code
(42Analytics/scripts/check_summary.py), per the capability map.

Usage:  python video_check/build_sample.py [path-to-42Analytics]
"""
import csv
import random
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SEED = 20260930
PER_VIDEO = 6
WRONG_LOCATOR = 20
CROSS_VIDEO = 20
PAD = 45          # seconds of transcript either side of the cited locators
MAX_CHARS = 3000  # state budget for the passage
MIN_GAP = 480     # wrong_locator must be at least this far from every cited time

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
REPO = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else HERE.parents[1] / "42Analytics"

# Video summary claim check: pre-registration

Eleventh item measured against the capability map. Drafted 2026-09-30, **before any
model call**. **Status: bars PROPOSED, not yet approved by Eric.** No Jev call runs until
Eric approves the bars below and the answer key is committed. The registering commit is
the one that adds this file; the approval is a second commit that changes this line.
Consumer: `erash11/42Analytics` (video summaries) and through it `erash11/Flint`.

This is the test the 2026-09-26 STATUS entry left open: "Jev checking course summaries
against their transcripts, only if someone other than Eric reads those summaries."
Flint reads these summaries and ingests them into the knowledge base Eric uses, so the
condition is met. Eric's call whether it counts.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is public conference transcripts (YouTube
auto-captions) and Claude-written summaries of them. No athlete data, no health records,
no Baylor data. `applications.md` files (which quote Eric's method baseline) are not in
scope and never sent.

## Question

Can Jev tell, from a short transcript passage, whether a one-sentence claim in a video
summary is supported by that passage, well enough that 42Analytics can flag unsupported
claims before they reach Flint?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** A summary claim is a paraphrase. "Does this passage say that?" is
   not a join, threshold or lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint's review gate requires that nothing reaches the vault
   without a falsify pass. Today that is a Codex or Opus read of every entry.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Numbers and time locators are checked in code
   (`42Analytics/scripts/check_summary.py`, run on 10 summaries: 0 locators past the end
   of a transcript, 0 far from a marker, 5 of ~190 numbers not found). Jev sees neither
   numbers nor locators. It sees prose only, matching the verifier's rule.

## Design (copied from `verifier/`, the Research in 5 checker)

- Deterministic extraction of claims in code: bullets under "## Key claims" with a
  locator.
- The passage is chosen in code from the cited locators (plus or minus 45 seconds,
  capped at 3,000 characters). Jev never receives the whole transcript.
- Planted defects are the real evidence. A checker that always says "supported" would
  score well on real summaries.

## Sample (`video_check/sample.csv`, built by `video_check/build_sample.py`, seed 20260930)

| Kind | n | Expected | How it is made |
|---|---|---|---|
| real | 60 | unknown, fixed by the answer key | 6 per video from the 10 pilot summaries |
| wrong_locator | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage 8 or more minutes from its cited time |
| cross_video | 20 | not supported | a real claim with a passage from a different talk |
| negation | 20 | contradicted | Claude rewrites a real claim to say the opposite (authored file, committed before any call) |
| mechanism | 20 | not supported | Claude adds a plausible reason or detail the speaker never gave, the failure Flint's reviews found most often (authored file) |

Total 140. The claims come from Sonnet-written summaries. The passages come from
captions Claude did not write. The authored plants are written once, before any call.

## Answer key

Claude (a different model instance from the summarizer, blind to every Jev answer)
labels each of the 60 real items **supported / partly / not supported** from the same
passage, and commits the labels before the first Jev call. Planted items carry their
label by construction. A real claim labelled "partly" or "not supported" is itself a
finding about the summaries.

## Questions (per item, same state for every model)

State: `claim` and `passage`. Instructions forbid judging from outside knowledge.

1. **Support.** Noul: does the passage say or directly imply the claim?
2. **Contradiction.** Noul: does the passage say the opposite of the claim?
3. **Extra detail.** Noul: does the claim include a specific detail (a reason, name, cause
   or mechanism) that the passage does not contain?

Aggregation, following `sde_cascade`: an item is **flagged** if Q2 or Q3 is at or above
the cut, or Q1 is at or below 1 minus the cut. Cut: 0.50, the measured value elsewhere
in this project, fixed here.

## Comparators (same 140, same state)

- Haiku: one call per item, forced to answer supported / partly / not supported.
- Codex: the same.
- Claude's own pass is the answer key, so it is not a comparator.

## Bars (PROPOSED, fixed on approval, they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev decisive: not in the 0.35 to 0.65 band on all three questions | at least 60% of the 140 |
| Catch rate on planted items (flagged / 80), decisive items only | at least 85% overall and at least 75% in each of the four kinds |
| False alarm rate on real items the key labels "supported" | at most 10% |
| Jev versus Haiku: catch rate at equal or lower false alarm rate | Jev at least equal |
| Cost for the 140 items | reported, no bar |

The 0.35 to 0.65 band and the 10% false-alarm bar are my proposal. Eric may change
either before approval.

## Answer-key audit (required step)

Per `JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md`: pull Jev's confident disagreements with the labels (cap 20,
random 20 if more), Eric judges them blind (label right, Jev right, unclear), and both
scores are reported. The original labels decide pass or fail.

## What each outcome changes

- **Pass:** add a Jev pre-screen to the summary pipeline: unflagged claims skip the
  expensive falsify read, flagged ones go to it. Numbers stay in code.
- **Fail:** record which kind failed and keep the Codex or Opus read as the only gate.

## Not measured here

Whether summaries capture a talk's main points (omissions); whether the auto-captions are
accurate; "Eric's baseline:" attributions (those need `method-baseline.md`, not a
transcript).

## Runtime notes

Calls need `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `typesafe-sdk`. On 2026-09-30 neither was present on
the Windows laptop, so the calls run on the Mac (key in Keychain). The sample and
answer key can be built on either machine.

## Summary

Eric Eager, introduced as Vice President of Football Analytics at the Carolina Panthers, traces football analytics from the 1970 expected points paper through decades of little progress to fast change over roughly the last five years. He credits public play-by-play data, companies that sold contextual data, and tracking data. He expects AI and transformer models to accelerate this further. He argues that data engineering remains the limiting step, and that analysts must communicate in uncertainty, meet football staff most of the way, and admit what they do not know, or the work will not be adopted.

## Key claims

- Expected points started with a 1970 paper by Virgil Carter, and football analytics then made little progress until the late 1980s. [02:34]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins, a PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, presents a causal model for crediting defenders in American football. Traditional metrics credit only the tackler, and predictive models favor high-volume tacklers. His framework models all 22 players jointly with a transformer, estimates expected points saved for each defender by comparing expected points added with and without that defender's tackle, and uses propensity weighting and doubly robust estimation. On the first 9 weeks of a 2022 season it credits set-up defenders, ranks known top players better than supervised models, and aggregates to team results. He calls it a proof of concept.

## Key claims

- Football has a defensive attribution problem: on a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler though several defenders contributed. [00:00] [00:31]
- Supervised models predict outcomes, mix correlation with causation, favor high-volume tacklers and struggle to separate skill from opportunity. [01:01] [01:31]
- Causal inference asks what would have happened without the defender; it isolates individual contributions and separates player from scheme better, but needs more assumptions and quality control and cannot be applied in every scenario. [01:31] [02:01]
- Defenders do not act independently, so the model covers coordination, interference (for example, a defensive end setting the edge so a linebacker can tackle) and substitution effects, which violate independence. [02:31] [03:01] [03:31]
- The framework, called expected points saved, treats a defender making the tackle as the treatment and expected points added as the outcome. [04:02] [04:33]
- It uses a transformer over all 22 players, a propensity score model, an outcome model and inverse propensity weighting. [04:33] [05:04] [05:35]
- On the example play, the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive credit, which the speaker says shows the model captures coordinated effort. [06:09]
- Aaron Donald's expected points saved is around 0.27. [06:40]
- The method ranks players who earned All-Pro or Pro Bowl honors better than supervised models. [07:09] [07:39]
- Mean individual values aggregate to team level and explain 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes. [07:39]
- On synthetic data the method shows higher R-squared and lower RMSE than independent models, and ranks non-rookie players better against salaries and Pro Bowl status. [08:40]
- 68% of plays show significant interference effects, and modeling them reduces bias. [08:40] [09:10]
- The speaker calls it the first multi-agent causal inference framework in professional football for defensive evaluation; it is a proof of concept using the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season. [09:10]
- Intended next steps are quarterback decision-making and defensive back evaluation; stated uses are player evaluation, contract decisions and defensive scheme optimization. [09:41] [10:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Expected points saved: expected points added on the play when the defender does not make the tackle, minus expected points added when he does (as described). [04:02]
- Expected points added: the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits on a play. [04:02]
- Treatment: a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle. [04:02]
- 6-yard loss: the example running play. [00:00]

- 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes explained at team level. [07:39] [08:10]
- 68% of plays with significant interference effects. [08:40] [09:41]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins presents a deep reinforcement learning model that learns NBA player value from game outcomes, treating basketball as a sequence of states, actions and rewards, and splits team value among players with a neural approximation of Shapley values. He argues that identical box score actions have very different win impact depending on game state, that defense and off-ball value are missed by box score metrics, and that player synergy is measurable and predictive. He reports faster stabilization than regularized adjusted plus-minus, a Rudy Gobert example, 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and better game prediction than traditional metrics, though the Vegas line remains best.

- Winning depends on context: the same made three-pointer matters more late in a close game, and value depends on teammates, opponents and interactions among the five on the floor. [00:00] [00:31]
- PER, win shares and box plus-minus aggregate box score statistics with fixed weights, overweight scoring, struggle with defense and lack context. [01:01] [01:31]
- Adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus regress possession outcomes on players on the floor but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy. [01:31]
- Sequential models such as expected possession value capture context and flow but struggle to credit individual players; the talk proposes deep reinforcement learning to combine both. [02:02] [02:32]
- In the example, a made three in the first quarter with a 15-point lead changed win probability by 2%, while one in the fourth quarter of a tied game with 1:30 left changed it by 23%; the speaker calls this a 10 times difference. [03:04]
- The model treats basketball as a Markov decision process and uses an advantage function for context-aware value. [04:05] [04:35]
- It values on-ball actions by action type, role and context, and values defense and off-ball influence by presence and constraints, not individual actions. [04:35] [05:07]
- Shapley values allocate team value by replacing each player with a learned baseline embedding; a neural approximation is used for computation. [05:38] [06:08]
- Compared with regularized adjusted plus-minus, the method needs about 67% fewer possessions for comparable accuracy and stabilizes in about 3 weeks versus 2 months. [06:38] [07:08]
- Action values peak in close clutch games, where a three-pointer can be worth more than double the traditional value, and diminish in blowouts; offensive rebounds and steals are valued significantly. [07:39]

- Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on this method; the box score missed 45% of his defensive value. [09:10]
- Defensive specialists are systematically undervalued by traditional metrics, a potential competitive advantage, and complementary skills matter in roster construction. [09:40]
- The study found 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and traditional metrics wrongly assume player values add. [10:10] [10:41]
- Two equally talented rosters can differ by five or more wins because of fit, and adding synergy explains some unexplained variance. [11:11] [11:42]
- Adding the model to a Vegas line benchmark improves prediction, and adding synergy improves it further, though the Vegas line alone is best. [11:42] [12:12]
- In a capped league, winning comes from optimizing interactions, not collecting stars. [12:43]

## Numbers and definitions

- 67% fewer possessions than regularized adjusted plus-minus for comparable accuracy. [06:38]
- 3 weeks versus 2 months to stabilize. [07:08]
- Clutch three-pointer value can exceed traditional value by "more than double." [07:39]
- Gobert: 54th traditional, 12th by the model; 45% of defensive value missed. [09:10]
- 89 positive synergies and 61 anti-synergies. [10:10]
- Five or more wins: fit difference between equally talented rosters. [11:11]
- About five seasons of play-by-play data, "thousands of games." [16:21]
- Win residual: the difference between actual results and the model's prediction. [11:11]
- Advantage function: expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation. [04:35]
- Predictive accuracy figures: shown only on a chart, not stated in the captions. [11:42]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process with states, actions, stochastic transitions and rewards in expected points and win probability. [04:05] [04:35]
- Temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model appear in the video description but are not described in the captions.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: JHgeEo3n1do
title: "SSAC26: Tackling Causality: Estimating Frame Level Defensive Impact"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [american-football, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins, a PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, presents a causal model for crediting defenders in American football. Traditional metrics credit only the tackler, and predictive models favor high-volume tacklers. His framework models all 22 players jointly with a transformer, estimates expected points saved for each defender by comparing expected points added with and without that defender's tackle, and uses propensity weighting and doubly robust estimation. On the first 9 weeks of a 2022 season it credits set-up defenders, ranks known top players better than supervised models, and aggregates to team results. He calls it a proof of concept.

## Key claims

- Football has a defensive attribution problem: on a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler though several defenders contributed. [00:00] [00:31]
- Supervised models predict outcomes, mix correlation with causation, favor high-volume tacklers and struggle to separate skill from opportunity. [01:01] [01:31]
- Causal inference asks what would have happened without the defender; it isolates individual contributions and separates player from scheme better, but needs more assumptions and quality control and cannot be applied in every scenario. [01:31] [02:01]
- Defenders do not act independently, so the model covers coordination, interference (for example, a defensive end setting the edge so a linebacker can tackle) and substitution effects, which violate independence. [02:31] [03:01] [03:31]
- The framework, called expected points saved, treats a defender making the tackle as the treatment and expected points added as the outcome. [04:02] [04:33]
- It uses a transformer over all 22 players, a propensity score model, an outcome model and inverse propensity weighting. [04:33] [05:04] [05:35]
- On the example play, the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive credit, which the speaker says shows the model captures coordinated effort. [06:09]
- Aaron Donald's expected points saved is around 0.27. [06:40]
- The method ranks players who earned All-Pro or Pro Bowl honors better than supervised models. [07:09] [07:39]
- Mean individual values aggregate to team level and explain 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes. [07:39]
- On synthetic data the method shows higher R-squared and lower RMSE than independent models, and ranks non-rookie players better against salaries and Pro Bowl status. [08:40]
- 68% of plays show significant interference effects, and modeling them reduces bias. [08:40] [09:10]
- The speaker calls it the first multi-agent causal inference framework in professional football for defensive evaluation; it is a proof of concept using the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season. [09:10]
- Intended next steps are quarterback decision-making and defensive back evaluation; stated uses are player evaluation, contract decisions and defensive scheme optimization. [09:41] [10:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Expected points saved: expected points added on the play when the defender does not make the tackle, minus expected points added when he does (as described). [04:02]
- Expected points added: the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits on a play. [04:02]
- Treatment: a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle. [04:02]
- 6-yard loss: the example running play. [00:00]
- 0.27: Aaron Donald's expected points saved; the speaker says each of his tackles prevents about 0.27 expected points. The captions describe the orange and blue distributions inconsistently (which is tackle and which is no tackle). [06:40] [07:09]
- 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes explained at team level. [07:39] [08:10]
- 68% of plays with significant interference effects. [08:40] [09:41]
- 9 weeks: the data available ("first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season"). [09:10]
- Data source named: 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl tracking data. [00:31]
- R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons: stated as better, with no values in the captions. [08:40]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Interference-aware causal framework with a multi-agent transformer over 22 players. [02:31] [04:33]
- A directed acyclic graph with features: each defender's position, speed and direction, ball carrier features, relational features, 10 teammates, opponents and game context. [04:33] [05:04]
- Propensity score model and outcome model, with inverse propensity weighting to make a pseudo-population; doubly robust estimation for protection against model misspecification. [05:04] [05:35] [09:41]
- Validation by synthetic data, team-level aggregation, Pro Bowl and All-Pro agreement and salary rank. [07:39] [08:40]

## Limits and open questions

- Proof of concept on 9 weeks of one season, as the speaker says. [09:10]
- The talk does not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model is checked, or how the treatment is defined for players who do not tackle but get credit.
- The video description mentions adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty, and sensitivity analyses; none is described in the captions.
- Validation uses synthetic data and honors; real causal effects are not observable, as the speaker notes. [08:10]
- Scheme and assignment are not in the data; a questioner raised blitzers versus droppers, and the speaker's partial answer is propensity weighting, with scheme data expected to improve estimates. [11:43] [12:43]
- Claims of being first and of better ranking are the author's own and come from a competition presentation.
- "Tackle" here is the treatment; the audience question about pass rush disruption is answered only in general terms. [11:13]

## Q&A

- Does it handle pass plays and disruption without a tackle, such as Aaron Donald in the backfield? Yes, he gets positive credit for forcing the ball carrier elsewhere or lowering the odds a pass is beneficial. [10:43] [11:13]
- How does scheme (a blitzing linebacker versus a dropping one) confound the metric, and how would a team use scheme data? Ongoing research on scheme and responsibility; propensity weighting up-weights a low-probability defender's tackle; scheme data would improve estimates. [11:43] [12:17] [12:43]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: JjeFktc4QLM
title: "SSAC26: Deep Reinforcement Learning for NBA Player Valuation"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins presents a deep reinforcement learning model that learns NBA player value from game outcomes, treating basketball as a sequence of states, actions and rewards, and splits team value among players with a neural approximation of Shapley values. He argues that identical box score actions have very different win impact depending on game state, that defense and off-ball value are missed by box score metrics, and that player synergy is measurable and predictive. He reports faster stabilization than regularized adjusted plus-minus, a Rudy Gobert example, 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and better game prediction than traditional metrics, though the Vegas line remains best.

## Key claims

- Winning depends on context: the same made three-pointer matters more late in a close game, and value depends on teammates, opponents and interactions among the five on the floor. [00:00] [00:31]
- PER, win shares and box plus-minus aggregate box score statistics with fixed weights, overweight scoring, struggle with defense and lack context. [01:01] [01:31]
- Adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus regress possession outcomes on players on the floor but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy. [01:31]
- Sequential models such as expected possession value capture context and flow but struggle to credit individual players; the talk proposes deep reinforcement learning to combine both. [02:02] [02:32]
- In the example, a made three in the first quarter with a 15-point lead changed win probability by 2%, while one in the fourth quarter of a tied game with 1:30 left changed it by 23%; the speaker calls this a 10 times difference. [03:04]
- The model treats basketball as a Markov decision process and uses an advantage function for context-aware value. [04:05] [04:35]
- It values on-ball actions by action type, role and context, and values defense and off-ball influence by presence and constraints, not individual actions. [04:35] [05:07]
- Shapley values allocate team value by replacing each player with a learned baseline embedding; a neural approximation is used for computation. [05:38] [06:08]
- Compared with regularized adjusted plus-minus, the method needs about 67% fewer possessions for comparable accuracy and stabilizes in about 3 weeks versus 2 months. [06:38] [07:08]
- Action values peak in close clutch games, where a three-pointer can be worth more than double the traditional value, and diminish in blowouts; offensive rebounds and steals are valued significantly. [07:39]
- Jokic ranks first in the top 15; the ranking agrees substantially with regularized adjusted plus-minus and worse with box plus-minus, which the speaker ties to defensive valuation. [08:09] [08:40]
- Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on this method; the box score missed 45% of his defensive value. [09:10]
- Defensive specialists are systematically undervalued by traditional metrics, a potential competitive advantage, and complementary skills matter in roster construction. [09:40]
- The study found 89 positive and 61 negative synergies, and traditional metrics wrongly assume player values add. [10:10] [10:41]
- Two equally talented rosters can differ by five or more wins because of fit, and adding synergy explains some unexplained variance. [11:11] [11:42]
- Adding the model to a Vegas line benchmark improves prediction, and adding synergy improves it further, though the Vegas line alone is best. [11:42] [12:12]
- In a capped league, winning comes from optimizing interactions, not collecting stars. [12:43]

## Numbers and definitions

- 2% versus 23%: win probability change for a low-leverage and a high-leverage made three. The speaker calls it a 10 times difference (23 divided by 2 is about 11.5, so "10 times" is approximate as spoken). [03:04]
- 67% fewer possessions than regularized adjusted plus-minus for comparable accuracy. [06:38]
- 3 weeks versus 2 months to stabilize. [07:08]
- Clutch three-pointer value can exceed traditional value by "more than double." [07:39]
- Gobert: 54th traditional, 12th by the model; 45% of defensive value missed. [09:10]
- 89 positive synergies and 61 anti-synergies. [10:10]
- Five or more wins: fit difference between equally talented rosters. [11:11]
- About five seasons of play-by-play data, "thousands of games." [16:21]
- Win residual: the difference between actual results and the model's prediction. [11:11]
- Advantage function: expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation. [04:35]
- Predictive accuracy figures: shown only on a chart, not stated in the captions. [11:42]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process with states, actions, stochastic transitions and rewards in expected points and win probability. [04:05] [04:35]
- Temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model appear in the video description but are not described in the captions.
- Neural Shapley value approximation with baseline player embeddings. [06:08]
- A comparison of synergy: on-court versus off-court pair performance, shown in a two-way quadrant plot. [10:10]
- Player dropout as a technique to swap each player for a neutral embedding and measure the change in win prediction. [14:16] [14:46]
- Benchmarks: regularized adjusted plus-minus, box plus-minus, and a Vegas line. [08:09] [11:42]
- "DRPM" appears once in the captions for the model's name (caption spelling). [15:49]

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker shows no player-level confidence intervals or exact accuracy numbers in the captions.
- A judge noted that Shapley values are contextual and not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games. The speaker agreed and pointed to synergy and player dropout as partial fixes. [13:13] [14:16]
- Sample size is a problem for new players and pairs who nearly always play together (Jokic and Murray, as captioned). [16:21]
- Predictive validation falls short of the Vegas line. [11:42]
- The defensive value claims (Gobert) rest on the model, with no independent check named.
- The claim that two equal rosters differ by five or more wins is reported without how it was computed. [11:11]
- The 67% and "3 weeks versus 2 months" figures are stated separately and not reconciled.
- Claims of market inefficiency are the author's view. [09:40]

## Q&A

- Validation sums Shapley contributions although they are contextual; how to improve? Player dropout with a neutral embedding, summed over the five on the court, is expected to do better. [13:13] [14:16] [14:46]
- How does Shapley handle two players who nearly always play together? The model accounts for who is on the court, and five seasons of play-by-play data limit the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation. [15:19] [15:49] [16:21]

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff 2026-09-30: 42 Analytics channel pipeline

Plain markdown. Any harness can resume from this.

## What this is and why

Eric wants a knowledge repository from the 42 Analytics YouTube channel (https://www.youtube.com/@42analytics, 1,231 videos, mostly MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference talks 2012-2026), batch-ingested into Flint's knowledge base (`DEV/Flint`). Topics kept: American football, basketball, sports science, analytics for those sports, policy, front-office and advanced decision-making, competitive advantage, athlete health and injury. For each kept video: transcript, summary, and applied examples for Baylor Applied Performance.

Private GitHub repo: https://github.com/erash11/42Analytics (created today; `DEV/42Analytics` was not a repo before, and the thin `DEV` repo ignores it).

## Decisions and reasoning

- **Repo holds text, Drive holds video.** `DEV/42Analytics` (git, synced by GitHub) has transcripts, summaries, scripts, docs. Video files are never in git (`.gitignore` blocks `*.mp4` etc.). The one pilot mp4 (257 MB) is in `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\04_RESEARCH\42Analytics_YouTube\2025-03-18_SSAC25_AI_and_One_Metric_NFL_Roster_Decisions\`. Reason: Drive cannot follow junctions, closeout/dev-sync work on repos, mp4s are too big for git.
- **Triage from titles only.** 1,231 videos to 1,100 (dropped hackathon, startup pitches, chess, welcome/closing) to 256 shortlisted by reading every title (A 139 strong, B 117 partial). Business topics (ticketing, sponsorship, fan engagement, betting, esports, media) and other sports are out unless about health, sport science or decision-making. Tags in the shortlist are keyword guesses.
- **Eric chose (2026-09-30): tier A only, Sonnet for summaries, set up a Jev test.**
- **Summary format** follows Flint's voice rules (`docs/SUMMARY_SPEC.md`): speaker claims plain, "Inference:" for reasoning, "Eric's baseline:" only from `Flint/docs/method-baseline.md`, every number and claim carries a transcript timestamp. Nothing goes to the vault without Flint's review gate.
- **Subagent write restriction.** Subagents may write `applications.md` but the harness refuses `summary.md` ("return findings as text"). Do not work around it. Pattern: agent writes `applications.md`, returns `summary.md` text in `=== FILE: videos/<folder>/summary.md ===` blocks, the main session saves them and runs `scripts/check_summary.py`.
- **Cost.** Pilot about 60k subagent tokens per video; wave 1 about 42k per video (4 videos per agent so the method-baseline read is amortized). Full tier A would be roughly 6M subagent tokens.
- **Jev test.** Drafted in `TypeSafe_Sandbox/docs/VIDEO_SUMMARY_CHECK_PREREG.md` (design copied from the existing deliverable verifier: numbers checked in code, prose claims to Jev, planted defects as evidence). Bars are PROPOSED and need Eric's approval before any call.

## State at closeout

- Tier A (139): 30 have captions, 15 have summary + applications, 1 has no captions (`2RJ-6mW_UOM`, Ivy League concussion rule talk), 108 still `todo`. Tier B not started (not requested).
- `scripts/check_summary.py` on all 15 summaries: 0 invented time locators, no locator far from a transcript marker; numbers not found in transcript text were derived or spelled-out values (spot-checked, not all traced).
- Caption fetcher is rate-limited by YouTube (HTTP 429 after roughly 4 requests in a row). It backs off 90 s x attempt (up to 4 tries) and leaves the video `todo`. A background run (`python scripts/fetch_captions.py --tier A --all-todo`, log `/tmp/fetchA.log`) was stalled on `sNWvAaLVS1s` at closeout. It will not survive a reboot or sleep. Rerun it; it only fetches `todo` rows.
- `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` on this Windows laptop exists but is EMPTY (saved with a blank Read-Host). `typesafe-sdk` 0.7.2 is installed. Re-set it in Eric's own terminal; do not paste the key into chat.

## Files created or changed this session

`42Analytics/` (repo root `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\42Analytics`):
- `README.md`, `.gitignore`, `docs/STATUS.md`, `docs/SELECTION_CRITERIA.md`, `docs/SUMMARY_SPEC.md`, this handoff.
- `catalog/channel_index_raw.tsv`, `catalog/titles_triage.txt`, `catalog/shortlist.tsv`.
- `scripts/build_shortlist.py`, `scripts/fetch_captions.py`, `scripts/check_summary.py`.
- `videos/<date>_<id>_<slug>/` x30: `transcript.md`, `meta.json`; 15 also `summary.md`, `applications.md` (the original pilot folder has `baylor_application.md` instead of `applications.md`).

`TypeSafe_Sandbox/` (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\TypeSafe_Sandbox`): `docs/VIDEO_SUMMARY_CHECK_PREREG.md`, `video_check/build_sample.py`, `video_check/sample.csv` (100 of 140 rows), `video_check/README.md`, `docs/STATUS.md` (new entry).

`DEV/` thin repo: `RESEARCH.md` (router row), `docs/STATUS.md` (line).

Google Drive: pilot mp4 and text copies in `04_RESEARCH\42Analytics_YouTube\2025-03-18_SSAC25_AI_and_One_Metric_NFL_Roster_Decisions\` (Drive copy of text is now stale; repo is canonical).

## Next actions, most important first

1. Rerun the caption fetch for tier A (from a network YouTube is not throttling), then run Sonnet summary waves, 4 videos per agent, following `docs/SUMMARY_SPEC.md`. Save returned summaries, run `scripts/check_summary.py`, commit, push.
2. Before anything reaches Flint: sample-check the "Eric's baseline:" lines in `applications.md` against `Flint/docs/method-baseline.md` (NOT yet verified), and run a stronger-model falsify pass on a sample of summaries (Flint's review gate).
3. Jev test: Eric re-sets the key, approves or edits the bars, then write `video_check/authored_plants.csv` (20 negations, 20 invented-detail claims), Claude's blind answer key for the 60 real rows, then calls, then Eric blind-judges up to 20 confident disagreements.
4. When tier A is summarized and reviewed: batch into Flint (`ingest-resource` / Flint atomization brief). Eric's review gate applies before costly atomization.

## Open questions for Eric

- Approve or change the proposed Jev bars (decisive >= 60%, catch rate >= 85% overall and >= 75% per kind, false alarms <= 10%, Jev >= Haiku).
- Do tier B (117 videos) later, or drop them?
- Is a cloud-scheduled version wanted (Baylor IT clearance was stated)? YouTube blocks cloud IPs more often than home ones; try one captions-only cloud run first.

## Summary

A moderated conversation between Clara Wu Tsai (owner of the New York Liberty, founder of the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance) and John Donahoe (Stanford athletic director, former Nike CEO). They describe a research alliance that studies people at peak health and aims to predict injury, personalize training, and close the data gap on female athletes. Stanford is presented as the lab for applying it. Donahoe also lays out a three-part rule set he wants for college athletics. The injury-prediction work is described by its own funder and partner, and Donahoe says it is too early to show fewer injuries.

## Key claims

- Moving the Liberty to Barclays Center in Brooklyn was the most transformative change, followed by investing in facilities, performance and player experience on the same terms as the men's team [02:06].
- Wu Tsai says owning the teams showed how much is unknown about the human body, and that most health research studies disease rather than peak performance [10:51, 11:21].
- The alliance was created to study people at peak health and ask how top performers move, adapt, fatigue and recover [11:51].
- Wu Tsai says digital twins grounded in biomechanics and physiology can predict injury, personalize training and simulate performance, using simple video from two iPhones [12:21].
- Stanford and the alliance chose ACL injuries and hamstring injuries as the two areas to push through first [13:24].
- Donahoe describes the ACL process: high-speed video of an athlete (about 10 minutes) produces a digital twin that estimates her ACL injury propensity and points to a specific weak link, shared with the athlete and trainer for targeted training [13:54, 14:24, 14:56].
- Donahoe says it is too early to show a measurable drop in injuries after about a year, but athletes, coaches and trainers like it [14:56].
- For hamstrings, researchers film football players doing a series of exercises, and the twin estimates injury or re-injury likelihood and rehab stage [15:26].
- Wu Tsai says closing the gender gap in physiology and performance knowledge is a priority, and launched a women's health institute (WHISPER) in Boston in January, run by Dr. Kate Ackerman [17:30, 18:00, 18:30].
- Donahoe says a Stanford event co-sponsored with Wu Tsai drew 400 people, and that Stanford can act as a lab with 900 student athletes [19:01, 20:32].
- Donahoe says over 200 faculty work with Wu Tsai on sports science, and gives mental wellness as an example of faculty collaborating who otherwise would not [21:33, 22:03].
- Donahoe says college athletics is in a "lawless middle" and proposes eligibility rules, transfer portal limits, and a salary cap with transparency [23:34, 24:36, 25:07].
- Donahoe says Stanford will double down on Olympic and women's sports and launch an endowment campaign [26:39, 27:09].
- Wu Tsai names three unsolved challenges: predicting injuries before they happen, individualizing training and recovery, and the data gap in women's physiology [31:46, 32:17, 32:47].
- Donahoe says all the alliance research is open and shared across institutions [38:24].
- Wu Tsai says the biggest breakthrough would come from combining league player data, academic models and private-sector mobile dashboards to tell athletes what will happen and what to do [42:58, 43:28].

## Numbers and definitions

- Only 6% of sports science studies are done exclusively on women (Wu Tsai) [17:30].
- ACL injuries are "four to six times more likely" in women; Donahoe says he looked this up on ChatGPT and that it varies by sport [13:54].
- Alliance described by the moderator: seven core institutions, hundreds of collaborations, more than 500 publications, multiple therapeutics advancing toward FDA approval [10:21].
- ACL and hamstring screens: about 10 minutes of video each [13:54, 15:26].
- Over 200 Stanford faculty involved [21:33]; 900 student athletes, 36 sports [25:38]; 400 attended the event [19:01].
- About 59 Stanford students and alumni at the Paris Olympics; Directors' Cup won 25 years straight [07:13].
- Donahoe estimates college basketball as one third professionalized and two thirds college [26:08].
- Alliance about five years old, launched 2020; teams acquired 2019 [10:21, 10:51].
- Athletes now play at most into the mid-40s, depending on sport (Wu Tsai) [44:31].
- Captions are garbled in places (for example "Wyss Institute", "Woo Sai", "Oura" for what is likely a leadership body); no number appears garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Digital twin: AI-based model of an athlete's biomechanics and physiology built from video, used for injury propensity and rehab stage [14:24, 15:26].
- Precision exercise medicine, based on molecular biology of exercise (Salk Institute) [28:10, 28:42].
- Regenerative rehabilitation (University of Oregon) [29:14].
- Open, multi-institution research network convened by the alliance [38:24].

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, sensitivity or false-positive data are shown for the ACL or hamstring twins; Donahoe says results on injury rates are too early [14:56].
- The two main speakers are the funder and the partner institution's athletic director, so benefit claims are institutional views.
- The "four to six times" figure was looked up by the speaker on a chatbot and not sourced.
- Claims that the work helps youth and everyday athletes [35:22, 41:28] were not tested in the talk.
- Claim of a "digital twin" that tells an athlete what will happen before it does is a stated goal, not a shown result [32:17].

- No audience questions were captured; the moderator asked quick-hit questions at the end.
- Liberty international games in 10 years: at least one a year [40:27].

- Biggest possible breakthrough: injury prediction with guidance, built from league data, academic models and private dashboards [42:58].
