## Summary

Emily Kraus, a sports medicine physician, argues that sports analytics tracks load, sleep and heart rate variability but almost never tracks hormonal physiology. She says the menstrual cycle should be treated as a measurable signal, not noise, and that female athletes' higher rates of ACL and bone stress injuries come from hormonal, structural and environmental factors together. She reports that average cycle-phase effects on performance are small while individual effects can be large, and that calendar counting misses anovulation and luteal phase defects. She proposes a practical framework: symptom tracking, screening, a composite score, and athlete education, with attention to data privacy.

## Key claims

- Hormonal physiology is rarely tracked in sports, unlike load, GPS, HRV and sleep [00:39].
- In an audit of top exercise science and sports medicine journals, only 6% of the research used female-specific data [04:50].
- Female athletes have higher injury rates for bone stress injuries, ACL injuries and concussions, and these are predictable patterns [05:51].
- She frames the cycle as an algorithm of dynamic hormonal signaling, not a calendar [06:22].
- Not every athlete who bleeds has a regular cycle: hormonal contraception, luteal phase defects, anovulation and irregular bleeds are possible, and calendar tracking cannot detect them [07:55].
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews conclude that average phase effects on performance are trivial or small, but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- The field is moving from phase-based prescription and "cycle syncing" toward individualized monitoring [08:59].
- Symptom burden may affect performance more than the hormonal impact itself [09:30].
- ACL fibers contain receptors for estrogen, progesterone and relaxin, and knee laxity changes across the cycle, but there is no conclusive evidence on how hormone fluctuations affect ACL injury risk [10:32].
- Anatomical and biomechanical factors (femoral notch, tibial slope, landing patterns, alignment, quad dominance) interact with hormonal ones [11:03].
- Female teams often have less medical and strength staffing and more reactive care than male teams [11:34].
- She proposes a multilevel risk framework: athlete, team, equipment, organization and society [12:04].
- Low energy availability can suppress estrogen, cause missed periods, lower bone mineral density and raise bone stress injury risk; RED-S and the female athlete triad are the clinical models [13:38], [14:08].
- Calendar counting assumes a 28-day cycle, but a normal cycle can be 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- Blood testing is invasive and expensive, urinary testing needs frequent samples, and wearables still need validation in athlete settings [15:42].
- Her implementation framework is symptom tracking, RED-S and ACL screening, wearable data, a composite score used to adjust load, recovery, nutrition and hydration, and education of athletes and staff [16:46], [17:17].
- She wants the menstrual cycle treated as a vital sign for every female athlete [17:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 6% of journal research was female-specific; 94% male or mixed [04:50].
- ACL injury annual rate "almost 4%" in certain sports versus 0.03% in the general population [10:01].
- Normal cycle length 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- "One in five of natural cycles in some populations" can have chronic or spontaneous anovulation [15:12].
- Rehabilitation after ACL surgery: 9 to 12 months [03:17].
- Bone mineral density described as accounting for 50 to 70% of variation in bone strength [14:39]. Caption reads "accounts to 4 50 to 70%", so the number is partly garbled.
- Female athlete triad: low energy availability, impaired menstrual cycle, impaired bone health [14:08].
- Eumenorrheic: a regular menstrual cycle [07:24].
- Participation remark in Q&A: "50% or less" collecting data is a poor situation [20:01]; the caption is garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Multilevel risk framework (individual, team and equipment, society and organization) [12:04].
- RED-S and female athlete triad as screening models [14:08].
- Gold-standard cycle measurement: serologic testing, quantitative urinary hormone testing, wearables [15:42].
- Proposed composite score from symptoms, screens and wearable data [16:46].

## Limits and open questions

- She says evidence on phase effects and ACL risk is limited, mixed or inconclusive [08:59], [10:32].
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or study citations are given for the performance claims.
- The composite score is proposed, not shown or validated.
- The framework has not been shown to reduce injuries; "predictable so preventable" is her stated belief [05:51], [18:19].
- Wearable validation in athletes is acknowledged as incomplete [15:42].
- The session description cites 2 to 8 times ACL rates and 2 to 4 times bone stress rates; those figures are not stated in the captions.

## Q&A

- How to convince organizations to invest: athletes are asking for it; include athletes; introduce in the off-season; low participation undermines it [19:29], [20:01].
- Advice for youth and under-resourced settings: start the conversation at the start of the season, keep it simple, use handouts and videos, have athletes track in a phone or journal [21:03], [22:03].
- Personalizing without a blanket solution: slight tweaks rather than individual programs; strength training as foundation [23:40], [24:10].
- Using data to optimize as well as prevent: tracking can show when an athlete feels best [25:12].
- Privacy and opt-in: athlete owns and controls her data; data must not be used to pull athletes from play [26:43].

## Summary

Emily Kraus, a sports medicine physician, argues that sports analytics tracks load, sleep and heart rate variability but almost never tracks hormonal physiology. She says the menstrual cycle should be treated as a measurable signal, not noise, and that female athletes' higher rates of ACL and bone stress injuries come from hormonal, structural and environmental factors together. She reports that average cycle-phase effects on performance are small while individual effects can be large, and that calendar counting misses anovulation and luteal phase defects. She proposes a practical framework: symptom tracking, screening, a composite score, and athlete education, with attention to data privacy.

## Key claims

- Hormonal physiology is rarely tracked in sports, unlike load, GPS, HRV and sleep [00:39].
- In an audit of top exercise science and sports medicine journals, only 6% of the research used female-specific data [04:50].
- Female athletes have higher injury rates for bone stress injuries, ACL injuries and concussions, and these are predictable patterns [05:51].
- She frames the cycle as an algorithm of dynamic hormonal signaling, not a calendar [06:22].
- Not every athlete who bleeds has a regular cycle: hormonal contraception, luteal phase defects, anovulation and irregular bleeds are possible, and calendar tracking cannot detect them [07:55].
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews conclude that average phase effects on performance are trivial or small, but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- The field is moving from phase-based prescription and "cycle syncing" toward individualized monitoring [08:59].
- Symptom burden may affect performance more than the hormonal impact itself [09:30].
- ACL fibers contain receptors for estrogen, progesterone and relaxin, and knee laxity changes across the cycle, but there is no conclusive evidence on how hormone fluctuations affect ACL injury risk [10:32].
- Anatomical and biomechanical factors (femoral notch, tibial slope, landing patterns, alignment, quad dominance) interact with hormonal ones [11:03].
- Female teams often have less medical and strength staffing and more reactive care than male teams [11:34].
- She proposes a multilevel risk framework: athlete, team, equipment, organization and society [12:04].
- Low energy availability can suppress estrogen, cause missed periods, lower bone mineral density and raise bone stress injury risk; RED-S and the female athlete triad are the clinical models [13:38], [14:08].
- Calendar counting assumes a 28-day cycle, but a normal cycle can be 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- Blood testing is invasive and expensive, urinary testing needs frequent samples, and wearables still need validation in athlete settings [15:42].
- Her implementation framework is symptom tracking, RED-S and ACL screening, wearable data, a composite score used to adjust load, recovery, nutrition and hydration, and education of athletes and staff [16:46], [17:17].
- She wants the menstrual cycle treated as a vital sign for every female athlete [17:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 6% of journal research was female-specific; 94% male or mixed [04:50].
- ACL injury annual rate "almost 4%" in certain sports versus 0.03% in the general population [10:01].
- Normal cycle length 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- "One in five of natural cycles in some populations" can have chronic or spontaneous anovulation [15:12].
- Rehabilitation after ACL surgery: 9 to 12 months [03:17].
- Bone mineral density described as accounting for 50 to 70% of variation in bone strength [14:39]. Caption reads "accounts to 4 50 to 70%", so the number is partly garbled.
- Female athlete triad: low energy availability, impaired menstrual cycle, impaired bone health [14:08].
- Eumenorrheic: a regular menstrual cycle [07:24].
- Participation remark in Q&A: "50% or less" collecting data is a poor situation [20:01]; the caption is garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Multilevel risk framework (individual, team and equipment, society and organization) [12:04].
- RED-S and female athlete triad as screening models [14:08].
- Gold-standard cycle measurement: serologic testing, quantitative urinary hormone testing, wearables [15:42].
- Proposed composite score from symptoms, screens and wearable data [16:46].

## Limits and open questions

- She says evidence on phase effects and ACL risk is limited, mixed or inconclusive [08:59], [10:32].
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or study citations are given for the performance claims.
- The composite score is proposed, not shown or validated.
- The framework has not been shown to reduce injuries; "predictable so preventable" is her stated belief [05:51], [18:19].
- Wearable validation in athletes is acknowledged as incomplete [15:42].
- The session description cites 2 to 8 times ACL rates and 2 to 4 times bone stress rates; those figures are not stated in the captions.

## Q&A

- How to convince organizations to invest: athletes are asking for it; include athletes; introduce in the off-season; low participation undermines it [19:29], [20:01].

- Personalizing without a blanket solution: slight tweaks rather than individual programs; strength training as foundation [23:40], [24:10].
- Using data to optimize as well as prevent: tracking can show when an athlete feels best [25:12].
- Privacy and opt-in: athlete owns and controls her data; data must not be used to pull athletes from play [26:43].

## Summary

A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.

## Key claims

- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]
- A Celtics anecdote: the team was first in defensive field goal percentage by design while packing the paint, yet tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed, and a coach answered that the point is to score baskets. [13:25]
- Tracking data changed what analysts could tell coaches, since a box score cannot say what happened and the coaches' instructions in practice are mostly not in it. [16:55] [17:56]
- The first tracking data in a real NBA game was messy (players teleporting, misidentified), yet showed how far players ran and let the team change training right away. [18:58] [19:28]
- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]
- In player development, one panelist says direct use of data with players is limited: the technology is not there yet and presenting data is not always the best coaching tool. [29:43] [30:13]

## Summary

The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. ## Summary

A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.

## Key claims

- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]

- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]

## Summary

Emily Kraus, a sports medicine physician, argues that sports analytics tracks load, sleep and heart rate variability but almost never tracks hormonal physiology. She says the menstrual cycle should be treated as a measurable signal, not noise, and that female athletes' higher rates of ACL and bone stress injuries come from hormonal, structural and environmental factors together. She reports that average cycle-phase effects on performance are small while individual effects can be large, and that calendar counting misses anovulation and luteal phase defects. She proposes a practical framework: symptom tracking, screening, a composite score, and athlete education, with attention to data privacy.

## Key claims

- Hormonal physiology is rarely tracked in sports, unlike load, GPS, HRV and sleep [00:39].
- In an audit of top exercise science and sports medicine journals, only 6% of the research used female-specific data [04:50].
- Female athletes have higher injury rates for bone stress injuries, ACL injuries and concussions, and these are predictable patterns [05:51].
- She frames the cycle as an algorithm of dynamic hormonal signaling, not a calendar [06:22].
- Not every athlete who bleeds has a regular cycle: hormonal contraception, luteal phase defects, anovulation and irregular bleeds are possible, and calendar tracking cannot detect them [07:55].
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews conclude that average phase effects on performance are trivial or small, but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- The field is moving from phase-based prescription and "cycle syncing" toward individualized monitoring [08:59].
- Symptom burden may affect performance more than the hormonal impact itself [09:30].
- ACL fibers contain receptors for estrogen, progesterone and relaxin, and knee laxity changes across the cycle, but there is no conclusive evidence on how hormone fluctuations affect ACL injury risk [10:32].
- Anatomical and biomechanical factors (femoral notch, tibial slope, landing patterns, alignment, quad dominance) interact with hormonal ones [11:03].
- Female teams often have less medical and strength staffing and more reactive care than male teams [11:34].
- She proposes a multilevel risk framework: athlete, team, equipment, organization and society [12:04].
- Low energy availability can suppress estrogen, cause missed periods, lower bone mineral density and raise bone stress injury risk; RED-S and the female athlete triad are the clinical models [13:38], [14:08].
- Calendar counting assumes a 28-day cycle, but a normal cycle can be 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- Blood testing is invasive and expensive, urinary testing needs frequent samples, and wearables still need validation in athlete settings [15:42].
- Her implementation framework is symptom tracking, RED-S and ACL screening, wearable data, a composite score used to adjust load, recovery, nutrition and hydration, and education of athletes and staff [16:46], [17:17].
- She wants the menstrual cycle treated as a vital sign for every female athlete [17:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 6% of journal research was female-specific; 94% male or mixed [04:50].
- ACL injury annual rate "almost 4%" in certain sports versus 0.03% in the general population [10:01].
- Normal cycle length 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- "One in five of natural cycles in some populations" can have chronic or spontaneous anovulation [15:12].
- Rehabilitation after ACL surgery: 9 to 12 months [03:17].
- Bone mineral density described as accounting for 50 to 70% of variation in bone strength [14:39]. Caption reads "accounts to 4 50 to 70%", so the number is partly garbled.
- Female athlete triad: low energy availability, impaired menstrual cycle, impaired bone health [14:08].
- Eumenorrheic: a regular menstrual cycle [07:24].
- Participation remark in Q&A: "50% or less" collecting data is a poor situation [20:01]; the caption is garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Multilevel risk framework (individual, team and equipment, society and organization) [12:04].
- RED-S and female athlete triad as screening models [14:08].
- Gold-standard cycle measurement: serologic testing, quantitative urinary hormone testing, wearables [15:42].
- Proposed composite score from symptoms, screens and wearable data [16:46].

## Limits and open questions

- She says evidence on phase effects and ACL risk is limited, mixed or inconclusive [08:59], [10:32].
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or study citations are given for the performance claims.
- The composite score is proposed, not shown or validated.
- The framework has not been shown to reduce injuries; "predictable so preventable" is her stated belief [05:51], [18:19].
- Wearable validation in athletes is acknowledged as incomplete [15:42].
- The session description cites 2 to 8 times ACL rates and 2 to 4 times bone stress rates; those figures are not stated in the captions.

## Q&A

- How to convince organizations to invest: athletes are asking for it; include athletes; introduce in the off-season; low participation undermines it [19:29], [20:01].
- Advice for youth and under-resourced settings: start the conversation at the start of the season, keep it simple, use handouts and videos, have athletes track in a phone or journal [21:03], [22:03].
- Personalizing without a blanket solution: slight tweaks rather than individual programs; strength training as foundation [23:40], [24:10].
- Using data to optimize as well as prevent: tracking can show when an athlete feels best [25:12].
- Privacy and opt-in: athlete owns and controls her data; data must not be used to pull athletes from play [26:43].

## Summary

A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.

## Key claims

- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]
- A Celtics anecdote: the team was first in defensive field goal percentage by design while packing the paint, yet tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed, and a coach answered that the point is to score baskets. [13:25]
- Tracking data changed what analysts could tell coaches, since a box score cannot say what happened and the coaches' instructions in practice are mostly not in it. [16:55] [17:56]
- The first tracking data in a real NBA game was messy (players teleporting, misidentified), yet showed how far players ran and let the team change training right away. [18:58] [19:28]
- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]
- In player development, one panelist says direct use of data with players is limited: the technology is not there yet and presenting data is not always the best coaching tool. [29:43] [30:13]
- The same panelist says data is better used to design the player's environment (for example plays and reads that send a player left), which is described as a bit of behavioral science. [31:15] [31:46]
- Practice data is thin, practices are few and drills are not structured enough for a computer to track. [32:16] [32:46] [37:25]
- Tracking now lets staff check many instances of a skill such as screen setting across a game instead of cutting tape for two or three. Players who sit on the bench get no game data. [36:24] [36:54]

## Summary

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. Evidence is anecdotal and no data are shown.

## Key claims

A panelist thinks draft models have not improved much in 15 years. Player development also matters to whether a player lands in the 68% or the 32%. [11:13], [11:44]

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

## Key claims

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]

- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]

- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]
- Gains are largest early, with diminishing marginal gains across seasons, and the data set does not hold enough long-tenured pairs to find a maximum. Two to three seasons together are beneficial. [19:31], [20:01]
- Practice data would be the prescriptive side, and teams hold it. [20:32], [21:03]
- Team-level integration effects and plug-and-play players are named as open, and individual pair results are noisy and biased. [21:33], [22:04]

- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]

type: video-summary
video_id: nRoPOxRWCaQ
title: "SSAC26: The Missing Variable: Menstrual Cycles, Injury Risk, and the Competitive Edge"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Emily Kraus]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Emily Kraus, a sports medicine physician, argues that sports analytics tracks load, sleep and heart rate variability but almost never tracks hormonal physiology. She says the menstrual cycle should be treated as a measurable signal, not noise, and that female athletes' higher rates of ACL and bone stress injuries come from hormonal, structural and environmental factors together. She reports that average cycle-phase effects on performance are small while individual effects can be large, and that calendar counting misses anovulation and luteal phase defects. She proposes a practical framework: symptom tracking, screening, a composite score, and athlete education, with attention to data privacy.

## Key claims

- Hormonal physiology is rarely tracked in sports, unlike load, GPS, HRV and sleep [00:39].
- In an audit of top exercise science and sports medicine journals, only 6% of the research used female-specific data [04:50].
- Female athletes have higher injury rates for bone stress injuries, ACL injuries and concussions, and these are predictable patterns [05:51].
- She frames the cycle as an algorithm of dynamic hormonal signaling, not a calendar [06:22].
- Not every athlete who bleeds has a regular cycle: hormonal contraception, luteal phase defects, anovulation and irregular bleeds are possible, and calendar tracking cannot detect them [07:55].
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews conclude that average phase effects on performance are trivial or small, but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- The field is moving from phase-based prescription and "cycle syncing" toward individualized monitoring [08:59].
- Symptom burden may affect performance more than the hormonal impact itself [09:30].
- ACL fibers contain receptors for estrogen, progesterone and relaxin, and knee laxity changes across the cycle, but there is no conclusive evidence on how hormone fluctuations affect ACL injury risk [10:32].
- Anatomical and biomechanical factors (femoral notch, tibial slope, landing patterns, alignment, quad dominance) interact with hormonal ones [11:03].
- Female teams often have less medical and strength staffing and more reactive care than male teams [11:34].
- She proposes a multilevel risk framework: athlete, team, equipment, organization and society [12:04].
- Low energy availability can suppress estrogen, cause missed periods, lower bone mineral density and raise bone stress injury risk; RED-S and the female athlete triad are the clinical models [13:38], [14:08].
- Calendar counting assumes a 28-day cycle, but a normal cycle can be 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- Blood testing is invasive and expensive, urinary testing needs frequent samples, and wearables still need validation in athlete settings [15:42].
- Her implementation framework is symptom tracking, RED-S and ACL screening, wearable data, a composite score used to adjust load, recovery, nutrition and hydration, and education of athletes and staff [16:46], [17:17].
- She wants the menstrual cycle treated as a vital sign for every female athlete [17:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 6% of journal research was female-specific; 94% male or mixed [04:50].
- ACL injury annual rate "almost 4%" in certain sports versus 0.03% in the general population [10:01].
- Normal cycle length 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- "One in five of natural cycles in some populations" can have chronic or spontaneous anovulation [15:12].
- Rehabilitation after ACL surgery: 9 to 12 months [03:17].
- Bone mineral density described as accounting for 50 to 70% of variation in bone strength [14:39]. Caption reads "accounts to 4 50 to 70%", so the number is partly garbled.
- Female athlete triad: low energy availability, impaired menstrual cycle, impaired bone health [14:08].
- Eumenorrheic: a regular menstrual cycle [07:24].
- Participation remark in Q&A: "50% or less" collecting data is a poor situation [20:01]; the caption is garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Multilevel risk framework (individual, team and equipment, society and organization) [12:04].
- RED-S and female athlete triad as screening models [14:08].
- Gold-standard cycle measurement: serologic testing, quantitative urinary hormone testing, wearables [15:42].
- Proposed composite score from symptoms, screens and wearable data [16:46].

## Limits and open questions

- She says evidence on phase effects and ACL risk is limited, mixed or inconclusive [08:59], [10:32].
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or study citations are given for the performance claims.
- The composite score is proposed, not shown or validated.
- The framework has not been shown to reduce injuries; "predictable so preventable" is her stated belief [05:51], [18:19].
- Wearable validation in athletes is acknowledged as incomplete [15:42].
- The session description cites 2 to 8 times ACL rates and 2 to 4 times bone stress rates; those figures are not stated in the captions.

## Q&A

- How to convince organizations to invest: athletes are asking for it; include athletes; introduce in the off-season; low participation undermines it [19:29], [20:01].
- Advice for youth and under-resourced settings: start the conversation at the start of the season, keep it simple, use handouts and videos, have athletes track in a phone or journal [21:03], [22:03].
- Personalizing without a blanket solution: slight tweaks rather than individual programs; strength training as foundation [23:40], [24:10].
- Using data to optimize as well as prevent: tracking can show when an athlete feels best [25:12].
- Privacy and opt-in: athlete owns and controls her data; data must not be used to pull athletes from play [26:43].

title: "SSAC26: Redefining Limits: How Elite Athletes Achieve and Sustain Peak Performance"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [David Epstein, Shane Battier, Ryan Murphy, Steve Magness, Shira Springer (moderator)]
topics: [sports-science, basketball, decision-making, other-sport:swimming, other-sport:track-and-field]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto

---

## Summary

Four athletes and coaches plus a moderator discuss how elite performers reach and keep peak performance. Panelists say they wish they had mental tools and recovery planning earlier, and that modern athletes start professional habits early. A recurring theme is the constraints-led approach: Epstein, whose book is about constraints, and others describe removing the usual solution so that athletes or teams explore new ones. The discussion is built on personal stories, with a few cited studies described from memory. Closing views are that AI will help, but the bottleneck is turning data into action.

## Key claims

- Battier says he wishes he had mental-health tools; he now teaches teenagers breathing [02:38], [03:09].
- Murphy says he wishes he had perspective, and that how he felt in warm-up did not predict race outcome [03:40].
- Magness tells of a sports psychologist who said knitting helped a driven athlete by balancing the rest of her life [05:12], [05:42].
- Epstein says he did not program recovery like training and improved when he dropped one workout a week late in his career [07:13].
- Murphy says his approach moves from working harder, to nutrition, recovery, physical therapy and mental strategies, tried well before competition [08:13], [09:15].
- Battier says top young players now have workout, basketball and mental coaches in high school and arrive already professional [10:16], [10:48].
- Magness says achieving and sustaining are different: a 15-year-old can look good on pro methods and fade by 18 to 20 because foundations were skipped [11:48], [12:20], [12:52].
- Epstein cites a Science paper on 30,000 careers, saying world-class adults were almost entirely different people from the best kids, and some predictors of youth success were negative predictors of adult success [13:54].
- Murphy says his college coach built belief step by step and he finished fourth at trials in the 200 back [16:26], [17:28].
- Battier says great coaches spent time figuring him out, and Coach K promised only the chance to earn playing time [19:00].
- Epstein describes constraints as blocking the usual solution to force exploration; brains default to the path of least resistance [24:31].
- Epstein cites a study of pass networks in 30,000 NBA games where teammates spread the ball when a star was out and kept some of it on his return [22:31], [23:01].
- Epstein says the sprint start accounts for 50% of variance in skeleton finish time, and a Canadian coach's instruction to do anything but the usual led to a one-handed start [23:31], [24:01].
- Epstein says people keep self-interrupting at their accustomed rate after distractions are removed, so focus must be trained [22:01].
- Murphy says the Olympics are not an optimal environment, so his team schedules the day in 15-minute increments to remove thinking under pressure [25:33], [26:34].
- Magness says he taped off a soccer field as a warm-up area so an athlete must adapt to a long wait; Tom Tellez had him run barefoot and use mini hurdles to change a pattern he could not feel [27:35], [29:06], [29:36].
- Battier says rebuilding his jump shot took months of one-handed shooting close to the rim [31:36], [32:06].
- Magness says Tellez switched Carl Lewis's takeoff leg and the trust built by a good reason mattered [33:38].
- Epstein tells of Sheila Taormina using a theory-of-constraints bottleneck audit to reach four Olympics in three sports [35:11], [35:42].
- Murphy says multiple sources of motivation and a strong training group help consistency [37:15], [37:45].
- Epstein says Bears GM Ryan Poles turned six draft picks into 11 by trading back; Tony Fadell advises writing the press release first as a bounding box [38:46], [39:17], [40:18].
- Magness says everyday athletes should set the bar by their actual goal, and cites a 1970s marathon study: novices used one strategy, elite marathoners about 15 [41:48], [42:18], [42:50].
- Next big thing: Epstein, AI video prediction [43:54], [44:24]; Battier, performing under pressure [44:54]; Murphy, AI spotting motivation dips [45:24]; Magness, communicating actionable insight from tracked data [45:56], [46:28].

## Numbers and definitions

- Battier played 13 years in the NBA [02:38].
- Magness ran a 4:01 mile [04:10].
- 30,000 careers in the Science paper [13:54]; 30,000 NBA games in the pass-network study [22:31].
- Murphy was about 15th in the US at 16 before the 2012 Olympics and finished fourth at trials in the 200 back (top two make the team) [15:56], [16:26], [17:28].
- Skeleton sprint start "50% of the variance" in finishing time; Canadian coach story set in 2001 [23:31].
- Day scheduled in 15-minute increments [26:34].
- Taormina: 5'2", plan to drop 3 seconds, 1996 relay gold, four summer games in three sports [35:11], [35:42]. Caption garbles details such as "management 577".
- Ryan Poles: six picks to 11, five starters including an all-pro [38:46], [39:17].
- Epstein's book: "Inside the Box", coming in May [20:31], [21:31].
- Constraints defined by the moderator as blocking what has led to an athlete's success; "preclude constraint" as precluding previous solutions [21:01], [22:31].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Constraints-led approach: preclude usual solutions so exploration happens (small-sided games, barefoot running, mini hurdles, one-handed shooting) [24:31], [29:36].
- Theory of constraints: find and fix the single bottleneck [35:11].
- Process orientation: control only one's own performance [17:58].
- Breathing tools and scheduled routines for pressure [03:09], [26:34].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost all evidence is personal story or studies cited from memory without methods.
- Panelists are athletes, coaches and an author with a book to promote; Epstein notes the book [20:31].
- No data on whether constraints outperform instruction.
- The Science paper and pass-network study are described secondhand; the sample and methods are not shown.
- Caption names are noisy ("Badier", "Shaine", "Chip England", "Jason Tatum").

## Q&A

- Training with college-age athletes at Cal: talent is talent, surround yourself with the best, use multiple sources of motivation [37:15], [37:45].
- Do innovators succeed because of imposed or self-imposed constraints: both [38:46].
- Applying the elite mindset as an everyday athlete: set the bar by your own goal; expand your toolkit of strategies [41:48], [42:50].

- Epstein says he did not program recovery like training and improved when he dropped one workout a week late in his career [07:13].
- Murphy says his approach moves from working harder, to nutrition, recovery, physical therapy and mental strategies, tried well before competition [08:13], [09:15].
- Battier says top young players now have workout, basketball and mental coaches in high school and arrive already professional [10:16], [10:48].
- Magness says achieving and sustaining are different: a 15-year-old can look good on pro methods and fade by 18 to 20 because foundations were skipped [11:48], [12:20], [12:52].
- Epstein cites a Science paper on 30,000 careers, saying world-class adults were almost entirely different people from the best kids, and some predictors of youth success were negative predictors of adult success [13:54].
- Murphy says his college coach built belief step by step and he finished fourth at trials in the 200 back [16:26], [17:28].
- Battier says great coaches spent time figuring him out, and Coach K promised only the chance to earn playing time [19:00].
- Epstein describes constraints as blocking the usual solution to force exploration; brains default to the path of least resistance [24:31].
- Epstein cites a study of pass networks in 30,000 NBA games where teammates spread the ball when a star was out and kept some of it on his return [22:31], [23:01].
- Epstein says the sprint start accounts for 50% of variance in skeleton finish time, and a Canadian coach's instruction to do anything but the usual led to a one-handed start [23:31], [24:01].
- Epstein says people keep self-interrupting at their accustomed rate after distractions are removed, so focus must be trained [22:01].
- Murphy says the Olympics are not an optimal environment, so his team schedules the day in 15-minute increments to remove thinking under pressure [25:33], [26:34].
- Magness says he taped off a soccer field as a warm-up area so an athlete must adapt to a long wait; Tom Tellez had him run barefoot and use mini hurdles to change a pattern he could not feel [27:35], [29:06], [29:36].
- Battier says rebuilding his jump shot took months of one-handed shooting close to the rim [31:36], [32:06].
- Magness says Tellez switched Carl Lewis's takeoff leg and the trust built by a good reason mattered [33:38].
- Epstein tells of Sheila Taormina using a theory-of-constraints bottleneck audit to reach four Olympics in three sports [35:11], [35:42].
- Murphy says multiple sources of motivation and a strong training group help consistency [37:15], [37:45].
- Epstein says Bears GM Ryan Poles turned six draft picks into 11 by trading back; Tony Fadell advises writing the press release first as a bounding box [38:46], [39:17], [40:18].
- Magness says everyday athletes should set the bar by their actual goal, and cites a 1970s marathon study: novices used one strategy, elite marathoners about 15 [41:48], [42:18], [42:50].

- Magness ran a 4:01 mile [04:10].
- 30,000 careers in the Science paper [13:54]; 30,000 NBA games in the pass-network study [22:31].
- Murphy was about 15th in the US at 16 before the 2012 Olympics and finished fourth at trials in the 200 back (top two make the team) [15:56], [16:26], [17:28].
- Skeleton sprint start "50% of the variance" in finishing time; Canadian coach story set in 2001 [23:31].
- Day scheduled in 15-minute increments [26:34].
- Taormina: 5'2", plan to drop 3 seconds, 1996 relay gold, four summer games in three sports [35:11], [35:42]. Caption garbles details such as "management 577".

- Almost all evidence is personal story or studies cited from memory without methods.
- Panelists are athletes, coaches and an author with a book to promote; Epstein notes the book [20:31].

- 45% click-to-open; 35% year-over-year sales [35:11], [35:41].
- 1,500 of 14,000 attendees understood; hope for 2,000 or 2,500; 10 to 15% better each year over six years [33:38], [34:08]. Caption reads "10 15%", so the range is garbled.

- Weekly revenue committee started 2015 to 2016 [18:53], [19:26].
- Annual small price increases instead of periodic large ones [19:56], [20:26].

- League and NCAA data sharing with schools and partners [12:52], [13:23].

- Does private equity belong in college sports: yes with conditions [43:17].

## Summary

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. Evidence is anecdotal and no data are shown.

## Key claims

- Analytics departments have grown. The question is where information gets throughput, so a team has to pick the highest-leverage information that can affect winning. [01:30]
- Tracking data has been available for roughly ten years and pose data is new, so teams are "behind again." Sports science also offers more information than teams know what to do with. [02:00]
- Pose data will be something teams chase for the next 5 to 10 years. [02:31]
- Players can be overloaded with information. Instincts should be built in practice, and some players tell staff they have had enough. [03:02]
- The decisions (who to play, how to improve) are the same as 20 or 40 years ago. Numbers refine them, and staff should filter before information reaches users. [03:34]
- A player on the panel accepted "the answers to the test" and said clear communication of the value to the player drives receptiveness. [04:04], [04:34]
- Staff take information to coaches, coaches pick what reaches players, and the format varies by player (a booklet for one, three clips for another). [05:04], [05:35]
- Players in their 30s grew up in the analytics generation and may be more comfortable with it than some coaches. [06:06]
- A data advantage is largely going away because the league has standardized it. Two other layers remain: how well you analyze it, and throughput into decisions and onto the floor. Getting data into the organization's mindset is called the final frontier. [08:09], [08:40], [09:11]
- The same data can support opposing arguments about one player. [09:11], [09:42]

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]

- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]

- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]

- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]

- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

## Q&A

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

## Key claims

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]
- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]
- Shot quality improves as passer-shooter pairs play together. Shorter two-point shots, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots (about 4% lower pressure score in the first 100 shots) are the measurable drivers. [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]
- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]
- The speaker (a former coach) offers confidence, rhythm and timing, and pass placement preferences as unmodeled reasons for accuracy gains. These are the speaker's explanations, not tested. [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]
- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]
- Gains are largest early, with diminishing marginal gains across seasons, and the data set does not hold enough long-tenured pairs to find a maximum. Two to three seasons together are beneficial. [19:31], [20:01]
- Practice data would be the prescriptive side, and teams hold it. [20:32], [21:03]
- Team-level integration effects and plug-and-play players are named as open, and individual pair results are noisy and biased. [21:33], [22:04]
- Positional analysis (big to big passing) was not done. [22:34]
- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]
- Chemistry here means familiarity in catch-and-shoot situations only. Lineup-level work needs care because good lineups play more together. [30:45], [31:16]
- A speaker says to study learning, first establish the normal expected curve, then see whether an intervention improves it. [30:15]
- The model has no notion of a break within a season, so decay after injury is untested. [33:19], [33:49]
- Turnover and incompletion reasons are not categorized in basketball as they are in football. [36:56], [37:28]
- An interaction between season and attempt count was statistically significant but did not change the shape much. [37:59], [38:30]
- Asked about trading for pairs of players, a speaker said no, and that trading money for talent is a bigger effect. [39:02], [39:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Data: 1600 passer-shooter combinations with between 10 and 50 catch-and-shoot attempts, averaging 1.12 points per attempt, 2023-24 season. [07:38]
- Most frequent pair: 237 catch-and-shoot attempts (captions: "Tyrese and Miles"). [07:38]
- Expected points = made-shot probability times 2 or 3. [07:08]
- Shot probability inputs: shot type, location, and NBA-supplied pressure scores (passer pressure, receiver pressure, shooter pressure, defined by defender closeness). [06:06], [06:37]
- Models tried: XGBoost (best), random forest (weird results), logistic regression (not as good). [06:37], [07:08]
- Familiarity model: a simple log-log regression with an in-season counter and a cumulative counter of passer-shooter catch-and-shoot attempts. [08:40], [09:13]
- Result: about 7% improvement in the first 50 attempts, another 4% to 200. Rarely more than 200 attempts in a season. [09:43]
- Carry-over: next season starts about 5% above where the pair started in season one, below the end of season one. [10:14]
- Accuracy analysis assumes a 1.2 expected-points baseline. [12:18]
- Phoenix trio: from 81 points per 100 shots to 93, then more up to about 200 shots (rule of thumb). [17:27]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

## Q&A

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. ## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]
- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).

- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

He says free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal leave small scouting staffs with too many players to evaluate. He describes two tracking-data models his company built: change of direction (COD) and run-game credit attribution. Both are checked against film. He presents a per-game "digital scouting report" for every FBS player as a way to narrow large candidate pools. The claims come from the vendor selling the product.

- Run-game credit is split into identifying actions and attributing them among 22 players, using a graph neural network with players as nodes and relationships as edges [12:41], [13:11], [14:12], [14:43].

## Summary

Two speakers, one from a consultancy and one from Databricks, argue that media companies and professional franchises have a coherence problem, not a data problem: metrics are defined in different places and staff spend time asking which number is right. They describe modernizing a live campaign platform for a large media organization by centralizing business definitions and governance on a lakehouse with Unity Catalog, then extend the idea to player performance, fan and sponsorship data. The talk is a vendor and consultant pitch. It shows a reference architecture and qualitative outcomes, and no measured results. There is little sport-specific content.

## Key claims

- Most media companies and franchises have a coherence problem; alignment, not data volume, decides whether analytics creates advantage [01:00], [01:32].

- They say franchises have the same pattern: coaching, scouting and commercial staff using different metrics for similar things [03:07].
- When alignment breaks, decisions slow; the speaker says the cause is architecture, not talent [03:40], [04:14].
- In the case described, audience data sat in several systems, scripts did publishing and another team owned orchestration [04:45].
- The turning point was to stop asking which tools to add and instead centralize business logic and shared semantics [06:49], [07:21], [07:55].
- The Databricks speaker says traditional catalogs cover only tables, auditing and access, while Unity Catalog governs models, agents and endpoints and can federate outside sources without copies [08:56], [09:28], [09:59], [10:30].
- Business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog can serve reports and give AI agents context; the speaker says external BI tools each use their own semantic layers with less metadata [11:33], [14:07], [14:38].
- The implementation used Delta Lake for storage, Unity Catalog for governance, Lakeflow jobs for orchestration and Databricks SQL, with campaign and audience definitions moved into governed tables [16:13], [16:45], [17:16].
- Lakebase was not implemented in this project; the speaker says the architecture now supports operational workloads without a new silo [17:16].
- Outcomes named are structural: less pipeline upkeep, clearer ownership, better cost visibility, stable definitions, and more trust [17:16], [17:47].

He describes two tracking-data models his company built: change of direction (COD) and run-game credit attribution. Both are checked against film.
