## Summary

Two speakers, one from a consultancy and one from Databricks, argue that media companies and professional franchises have a coherence problem, not a data problem: metrics are defined in different places and staff spend time asking which number is right. They describe modernizing a live campaign platform for a large media organization by centralizing business definitions and governance on a lakehouse with Unity Catalog, then extend the idea to player performance, fan and sponsorship data. The talk is a vendor and consultant pitch. It shows a reference architecture and qualitative outcomes, and no measured results. There is little sport-specific content.

## Key claims

- Most media companies and franchises have a coherence problem; alignment, not data volume, decides whether analytics creates advantage [01:00], [01:32].
- In their scenario, three days of different numbers for the same campaign shift the conversation from optimizing to reconciling [02:35], [03:07].
- They say franchises have the same pattern: coaching, scouting and commercial staff using different metrics for similar things [03:07].
- When alignment breaks, decisions slow; the speaker says the cause is architecture, not talent [03:40], [04:14].
- In the case described, audience data sat in several systems, scripts did publishing and another team owned orchestration [04:45].
- The turning point was to stop asking which tools to add and instead centralize business logic and shared semantics [06:49], [07:21], [07:55].
- The Databricks speaker says traditional catalogs cover only tables, auditing and access, while Unity Catalog governs models, agents and endpoints and can federate outside sources without copies [08:56], [09:28], [09:59], [10:30].
- Business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog can serve reports and give AI agents context; the speaker says external BI tools each use their own semantic layers with less metadata [11:33], [14:07], [14:38].
- The implementation used Delta Lake for storage, Unity Catalog for governance, Lakeflow jobs for orchestration and Databricks SQL, with campaign and audience definitions moved into governed tables [16:13], [16:45], [17:16].
- Lakebase was not implemented in this project; the speaker says the architecture now supports operational workloads without a new silo [17:16].
- Outcomes named are structural: less pipeline upkeep, clearer ownership, better cost visibility, stable definitions, and more trust [17:16], [17:47].
- Stated business effects: faster optimization cycles, consistent audience definitions, trust in metrics, and scalable governance [18:18], [18:48], [19:18], [19:50].

- Medallion gold layer: data ready for downstream use [12:36]. No quantitative performance numbers are given.

Three football executives and a moderator discuss how data has changed player evaluation, development and in-game decisions. He describes two tracking-data models his company built: change of direction (COD) and run-game credit attribution. Both are checked against film. ## Summary

Two speakers, one from a consultancy and one from Databricks, argue that media companies and professional franchises have a coherence problem, not a data problem: metrics are defined in different places and staff spend time asking which number is right. They describe modernizing a live campaign platform for a large media organization by centralizing business definitions and governance on a lakehouse with Unity Catalog, then extend the idea to player performance, fan and sponsorship data. The talk is a vendor and consultant pitch. It shows a reference architecture and qualitative outcomes, and no measured results. There is little sport-specific content.

## Key claims

- Most media companies and franchises have a coherence problem; alignment, not data volume, decides whether analytics creates advantage [01:00], [01:32].
- In their scenario, three days of different numbers for the same campaign shift the conversation from optimizing to reconciling [02:35], [03:07].
- They say franchises have the same pattern: coaching, scouting and commercial staff using different metrics for similar things [03:07].
- When alignment breaks, decisions slow; the speaker says the cause is architecture, not talent [03:40], [04:14].
- In the case described, audience data sat in several systems, scripts did publishing and another team owned orchestration [04:45].
- The turning point was to stop asking which tools to add and instead centralize business logic and shared semantics [06:49], [07:21], [07:55].
- The Databricks speaker says traditional catalogs cover only tables, auditing and access, while Unity Catalog governs models, agents and endpoints and can federate outside sources without copies [08:56], [09:28], [09:59], [10:30].
- Business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog can serve reports and give AI agents context; the speaker says external BI tools each use their own semantic layers with less metadata [11:33], [14:07], [14:38].
- The implementation used Delta Lake for storage, Unity Catalog for governance, Lakeflow jobs for orchestration and Databricks SQL, with campaign and audience definitions moved into governed tables [16:13], [16:45], [17:16].
- Lakebase was not implemented in this project; the speaker says the architecture now supports operational workloads without a new silo [17:16].
- Outcomes named are structural: less pipeline upkeep, clearer ownership, better cost visibility, stable definitions, and more trust [17:16], [17:47].
- Stated business effects: faster optimization cycles, consistent audience definitions, trust in metrics, and scalable governance [18:18], [18:48], [19:18], [19:50].

- Shared semantics are described as a basis for AI readiness [20:54], [21:25].

- One engineer architecting with four or five parallel agents writing code [23:59].
- "Business semantics": definitions of metrics and entities (audiences, yield) defined once and reused [07:21], [11:33].
- Medallion gold layer: data ready for downstream use [12:36]. No quantitative performance numbers are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Reference architecture: siloed data moved to cloud object storage, refined through layers to a gold layer, with governance and a semantic layer over it [12:04], [12:36], [15:10].

Three football executives and a moderator discuss how data has changed player evaluation, development and in-game decisions. - Kassam says football differs from baseball because roles and schemes differ, and that his metrics adjust for conference and level of competition [18:50], [19:20].

## Summary

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. Evidence is anecdotal and no data are shown.

## Key claims

- Analytics departments have grown. The question is where information gets throughput, so a team has to pick the highest-leverage information that can affect winning. [01:30]
- Tracking data has been available for roughly ten years and pose data is new, so teams are "behind again." Sports science also offers more information than teams know what to do with. [02:00]

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

## Key claims

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]
- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]
- Shot quality improves as passer-shooter pairs play together. Shorter two-point shots, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots (about 4% lower pressure score in the first 100 shots) are the measurable drivers. [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]
- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]
- The speaker (a former coach) offers confidence, rhythm and timing, and pass placement preferences as unmodeled reasons for accuracy gains. These are the speaker's explanations, not tested. [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]
- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]
- Gains are largest early, with diminishing marginal gains across seasons, and the data set does not hold enough long-tenured pairs to find a maximum. Two to three seasons together are beneficial. [19:31], [20:01]
- Practice data would be the prescriptive side, and teams hold it. [20:32], [21:03]
- Team-level integration effects and plug-and-play players are named as open, and individual pair results are noisy and biased. [21:33], [22:04]
- Positional analysis (big to big passing) was not done. [22:34]
- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]
- Chemistry here means familiarity in catch-and-shoot situations only. Lineup-level work needs care because good lineups play more together. [30:45], [31:16]
- A speaker says to study learning, first establish the normal expected curve, then see whether an intervention improves it. [30:15]
- The model has no notion of a break within a season, so decay after injury is untested. [33:19], [33:49]
- Turnover and incompletion reasons are not categorized in basketball as they are in football. [36:56], [37:28]

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

## Q&A

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

He presents a per-game "digital scouting report" for every FBS player as a way to narrow large candidate pools. The claims come from the vendor selling the product.

- College football analytics is about a decade behind the NFL, and the speaker says that gap will close [00:31].
- College evaluation is limited: in-person looks are few, and even big programs may have only three or four scouting staff, with most coaches also scouting [01:31].
- Free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal now require a few scouts and a position coach to evaluate hundreds of players and make offers within hours [02:01].
- Analytics moved from box scores, to play-by-play data, to ball and player tracking data released to all NFL teams in 2018, and each step needs more people and computing [03:32], [04:02].
- Teams get competitive advantage from the richest data and from doing the most with it, which now means tracking data and a team of people [04:02].
- Straight-line speed alone is not enough; COD matters at every position but is hard to quantify because direction data is noisy [05:34], [06:06].
- COD is measured as a deficit: the same distance run with a turn versus in a line [06:06].
- A COD is found by tracking heading angle over a play and detecting where the turn starts, ends and peaks [07:37].
- Two COD events with a similar deficit can differ in quality, so the model adds entry speed, acceleration, turn angle, rate of turn and distance as context [08:08], [08:38].

- COD is one piece of the picture and the speaker does not suggest drafting or signing from a COD list [12:10].
- Run-game credit is split into identifying actions and attributing them among 22 players, using a graph neural network with players as nodes and relationships as edges [12:41], [13:11], [14:12], [14:43].
- On one Lions at Chiefs run, the model's expected yardage rises and falls during the play as blocks and defenders act, and credit is given to the runner, blockers and defenders [15:13], [15:44], [16:15].
- The model rewards a defender who runs a long way and penalizes loafing, without being taught this; the speaker says it learned it from about 100,000 running plays [17:16], [17:46].
- Each metric took 4 to 24 months of data science and engineering; the resulting report covers every FBS player and updates after every game [19:52].
- Trait language (change of direction, burst, run blocking) is easier for staff to share than statistics like EPA per play or yards per route run [20:22].
- Teams could use the report to reduce roughly a thousand portal receivers to 20 or 30 [20:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- Decade gap between college and NFL analytics [00:31].
- Three or four scouting department members at a large SEC school [01:31].
- NFL released tracking data to teams in 2018 [03:32]. Another talk in this batch gives 2019.
- More than 70 technical staff, 25 PhDs, a dozen who led R&D departments [04:34].
- COD deficit: time with a turn compared with straight-line time over the same distance [06:36]. The 505 test is described as 15 yards one way, a 180 degree turn, five yards back (as captioned) [06:36].
- Jefferson example: two COD events with a deficit of about a second; one described as an 80 degree dig (as captioned), one a 170 degree hitch [08:08].
- Draftee: fifth round, pick 177 overall [10:09].
- Gibbs play: 18 yards on the play; expected gain about three yards at the start, about eight at its peak; percentile ratings of 96 (acceleration) and 99 (a block) [13:42], [15:13], [15:44], [16:45].
- Mike Dana (caption spelling) ran about 40 yards on the play [17:16].
- About 100,000 running plays seen by the model [17:46].
- "Two dozen models" sometimes calibrated together [18:50].
- 4 to 24 months per metric [19:52].
- Portal opens April 16th; a thousand receivers to 20 or 30 [20:52].
- Quote of 10 or 15 plays a season as the margin; the speaker thinks it underestimates [21:55].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Research first, then build on published sport-science ideas (COD deficit) [06:06].
- Signal detection on the heading angle curve (gradient to find start, end and apex of a turn) [07:37].
- Context adjustment for COD expectations [08:38].
- Graph neural network for action identification and attribution in the run game [14:12].
- Validation by a leaderboard "eye test" and by returning to film [11:09], [11:40].
- Metrics built from ball and player tracking data [09:09].

## Limits and open questions

- No validation statistics, error rates or hit rates are shown; the main evidence is single-player examples and a leaderboard eye test.
- The Nacua and Gibbs examples are chosen cases; no sample of misses is shown.
- Metric definitions, model inputs and COD noise handling are described only at a high level.
- The speaker says a COD list should not be used alone [12:10].
- Commercial source: the talk presents the speaker's own company's product.
- The speaker says high school data is not available [22:58], so the approach reaches only players with all-22 film.
- Player and team names are caption spellings and may be wrong throughout.

## Q&A

## Summary

A panel of four basketball analytics practitioners, moderated by Ben Alamar, traces the field from box-score work in the early 2000s to optical tracking, machine-learned play recognition and pose data. The panelists argue the biggest early shift was thinking per possession, that tracking and video let analysts speak a coach's language, and that data is often misused (small-sample lineups, correlations mistaken for causes). On player development they say numbers work best to design a player's environment, not as numbers handed to the player, and that practice data is still thin. They also argue that interviews and background checks are data that need their own reliability check. The session is history and opinion, with no datasets shown.

## Key claims

- The four factors came out of needing to estimate possessions per game, and the estimation formula had four inputs. [04:38]
- The biggest early change was getting people to think per possession instead of per game. [06:10]
- Adding up box score stats so a rebound, an assist and a point count the same was quickly seen as a poor way to value players. [10:16]
- Lineup data is misused most often: small samples and missing context such as matchups, actions and coverages. [12:25]
- Defensive rebounding was once called the most important stat because of its link to winning, but a panelist said it results from forcing misses. [12:55]
- A Celtics anecdote: the team was first in defensive field goal percentage by design while packing the paint, yet tenth in effective field goal percentage allowed, and a coach answered that the point is to score baskets. [13:25]
- Tracking data changed what analysts could tell coaches, since a box score cannot say what happened and the coaches' instructions in practice are mostly not in it. [16:55] [17:56]
- The first tracking data in a real NBA game was messy (players teleporting, misidentified), yet showed how far players ran and let the team change training right away. [18:58] [19:28]
- Second Spectrum taught a computer to recognize movements coaches care about, with a team member doing early quality checks on labels such as blitz and show. [20:32] [21:02]
- Tracking data is not perfect, and coaches challenge how plays are coded. Attaching video so the analyst can select and verify the plays was called a major breakthrough. [22:03]
- Players are receptive to data because they grew up in the age of analytics, though old habits are hard to change in the short term. [23:33] [24:34]
- In player development, one panelist says direct use of data with players is limited: the technology is not there yet and presenting data is not always the best coaching tool. [29:43] [30:13]
- The same panelist says data is better used to design the player's environment (for example plays and reads that send a player left), which is described as a bit of behavioral science. [31:15] [31:46]
- Practice data is thin, practices are few and drills are not structured enough for a computer to track. [32:16] [32:46] [37:25]

## Summary

A panel with Paul Tudor Jones (co-founder of Sumer Sports) and Jonathan Kraft of the Patriots, moderated by Michelle Steele. Tudor Jones argues football is the hardest strategy game ever created and that a comprehensive, transparent, model-based process for player selection adds rigor and accountability, including for intangibles, which he says can be turned into numbers. Kraft agrees models help but says coaches and personnel people hold instinct that cannot be put into zeros and ones, and doubts intangibles can be digitized soon. They also discuss Sumer as customizable software that keeps each club's data private, the limits of injury forecasting, and the Patriots' move to a younger coach. Claims about the product are the speakers' own commercial view.

## Key claims

- Kraft says the Patriots' football side was built around Bill Belichick for about a quarter century, and a new direction is needed now. [03:04] [06:11]
- Kraft says the team kept four quarterbacks on the roster in 2000 when Brady was a sixth-round pick, and notes that most teams now carry two. [08:16] [08:47]
- Tudor Jones says Sumer Sports, founded two years ago, has grown to a larger team than expected and has more resources on the NFL draft than any team by a multiple of five. [09:51] [12:57]
- Tudor Jones says football is harder than chess: more players, each with a different role, all moving at once, and about 125 plays versus about 35 chess moves. [14:34] [15:36]
- He says the search space is "virtually infinite" and expects a nonlinear evolution of football because of analytics. [16:07] [17:07]
- Kraft says coaches and personnel people have an instinctual sense of intangibles, and the real power comes from combining that with data; in-game and personnel use of analytics is at the very beginning. [19:39] [20:40]
- Kraft says the Patriots' new football operations leaders will bring more traditional analytic tools and a new grading system. [22:12] [22:43]
- Tudor Jones says everything, including leadership and smarts, can be turned into a number with rigor and process. [24:15] [24:45]
- He says a model adds three things: it is comprehensive, transparent and accurate. [25:15] [25:45] [26:47]
- He says Sumer's "Marvel" (maximize roster value) model could be a GM's, president's and owner's "best friend" by making choices explainable and cutting cost and dead cap. [28:20] [29:21] [30:23]
- He calls the current Sumer model version two and says it needs to be better by next year. [30:53] [31:24]
- Kraft says no team will match the data science staff Sumer has, so a software-as-a-service model with each club's own data in a secure environment makes sense. [32:26] [32:58]
- Kraft respectfully disagrees that intangibles can be digitized soon, citing a few thousand players a year and a couple hundred who make the league. [33:59] [34:29]
- Tudor Jones says psychographics is the hardest part of player selection because psychological tests show only small edges. [34:29] [35:01]
- He says that when two evaluators disagree on a player, each should still give a number (for example a six versus a nine) so the distinction is explicit. [36:01] [36:31]
- He says the model captures scouts' data and ranks scouts on predictive ability over time. [36:31]
- He says electronic trading in futures markets replaced human traders within a short time, and that football is on a similar path. [37:31] [38:02]
- He says the process is: the club states its offense and defense, positional weights and grades, then the model adds an injury forecast and snap counts and re-optimizes at each pick. [41:36] [42:09] [42:39]
- For injuries he says to use age curves, history and averages, because injuries are episodic and hard to forecast. [46:51]
- Kraft says the GM will not go away in his lifetime, and future GMs will be more well-rounded and understand models. [47:54] [48:26]
- Tudor Jones says the model will not replace humans in football because there are too few observations. [50:30]
- Kraft recalls football people resisting a scout-accountability review years ago, and thinks they feared the technology. [51:00] [51:31]
- Tudor Jones says a planned scenario builder will let teams optimize for win now or a two to three year horizon. [52:33] [53:03]
- Tudor Jones says Brady's leadership should get a nonlinear rating because he attracted talent, and breaks football into player selection, performance enhancement, play design and in-game play. [55:39] [56:10]

## Numbers and definitions

- Stadium built for $6 million at the start of Belichick's tenure (caption "6 million"). [06:42]
- 93 of the top 100 most-watched broadcasts were NFL games; five international games in 2024 (caption). [01:31]
- Brady: sixth-round pick in 2000; Patriots had just given Bledsoe "a 100 million" (caption). [08:47]
- Sumer team size: "20 data scientists 20 engineers 15 14 person scout team" (caption, garbled). [12:57]
- Chess: 35 moves a game; football about 125 plays; 53 by 120 yard field; 10 to the 80th possible chess games. [14:34] [15:06] [15:36]
- Player selection search space: at least 10 to the 40th, up to 10 to the 170th or 180th (Tudor Jones's own estimate). [28:51] [29:21]
- Average GM lifespan of three and a half years. [28:20]
- Claimed benefits: save "millions" per team and cut dead cap space in half (no data shown). [30:23]
- Model roles: "20 big models" with submodels and variables feeding a player selection model. [26:16]
- Casino comparison: a 5% edge at least, 5 to 15% outside craps (his description). [45:49]
- Fantasy league buy-in of "100 Grand". [44:14]

- Scout ranking by predictive ability. [36:31]
- Planned scenario builder with a chosen time horizon. [52:33]

## Summary

A panel of four sports industry data leaders (from Harris Blitzer Sports and Entertainment, Ticketmaster, ESPN and FanDuel), moderated by Katie Hodel, on building data science teams and models that get used. The recurring argument is that a model is worth little unless stakeholders adopt it, so start from the right question, ship a simple version early, iterate, and deliver outputs in the format the audience already uses. The panelists also discuss model trade-offs (explainability, runtime, accuracy), generative AI with human review at ESPN, feature bias, backlog prioritization, hiring for storytelling and problem solving, and career advice. The speakers come from business, betting and media, not athlete performance.

## Key claims

- Keith Goldner's FanDuel team builds predictive models that help set betting lines. [01:32]
- The panelists say data science is hard to define and the balance between people, software and partnerships is the challenge. [05:38] [06:09]
- Braden Moore uses an 80/20 idea: most of the value comes from the first part of the effort. [07:10]
- A model is not worth much if it does not get used and stakeholders do not give feedback. [07:40]
- In a startup a data scientist wears many hats; in a larger company a team can hire specialists. [08:11] [08:42] [09:12]
- ESPN's analytics team uses data modelers, engineers and a strong content voice. [09:43]
- Carlos Kasper interviews on hobbies because storytelling is hard to teach, while tools can be taught. [11:15] [11:45]
- Others look for problem solving, asking the right questions and thinking about edge cases after a base technical level. [12:47]
- Goldner says modeling starts with the right question, then data, features, target and delivery, and that an unused accurate model has no value. [14:50] [15:21]
- A request to export to Excel means the wrong question was asked. [15:51]
- Model type depends on trade-offs: explainability, integration, runtime, ease of maintenance and accuracy. [18:25] [19:25]
- ESPN labels generative AI content, commits to a human in the loop and keeps transparency about it. [17:24] [17:54]
- Generative AI is compared to infinite interns, to be used where errors are obvious, acceptable, or impossible. [19:25]
- Time to value matters: a game will not be delayed, so a fast decision-ready version can beat a perfect one. [19:56] [20:26]
- A model is one data point next to gut feeling and history, and model output can be stale within minutes at Ticketmaster. [20:56] [21:26]
- Goldner says analysts must be humble and treat traders as subject matter experts. [21:56]
- ESPN's public accuracy matters to its brand, and a Bubble Watch error was found by another team member. [25:02] [25:32]
- Goldner says accuracy should not be treated as the holy grail; he could not tell whether his draft models for an NBA team were accurate after a decade of drafts. [26:34]
- Moore says output should be framed so it guides strategy ("10% more likely than the average to churn" versus "10% likely"). [27:04]
- Moore's metaphor: build a bike, not a car, improving from a scooter. [28:38] [29:08]
- Single-person dependencies create a risk that a model must be scrapped when the builder leaves. [30:10]
- ESPN balances editorial voice, personalization, business revenue and representation when curating content. [31:41] [32:11] [32:42]
- For prioritization, Moore shows stakeholders the backlog and asks them to order it; an internal form asks whether a request supports an OKR. [34:14] [35:46]
- Goldner sorts projects as global models, dashboards and tools, and ad hoc requests, weighing commercial impact against effort. [36:17]
- Easier tools and AutoML allow faster failure and more people building models. [38:51] [39:24]
- Goldner says features can be biased, for example yards per game or points per game depend on schedule. [40:56]
- Meet stakeholders where they are: Excel, a table or a PDF, and build a prototype in parallel. [41:58] [42:28]
- Advice for entering the field: do a sports research project, network, stay curious, and explain what you can do for the employer. [44:00] [44:30] [46:02] [46:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length: 40 minutes plus 5 minutes of Q&A. [00:31]
- Numberfire acquired by FanDuel in 2015. [01:32]
- Goldner consulted for an NBA front office for about a decade. [02:03]
- 80/20 rule as used by Moore. [07:10]
- Churn framing: 10% likely versus 10% more likely than the average. [27:04]
- Goldner's first internship route: emails to about 30 teams, nine "no" replies and one "maybe". [44:00] [44:30]
- Model runtime and accuracy are cited as trade-offs, with no figures. [19:25]
- Ticketmaster output can be out of date in "five or 10 minutes". [21:26]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Model process: question, brainstorm data and features, target, delivery, iteration. [14:50]
- MVP approach and "bike, not car". [28:38]
- Three project levels: global models, dashboards and tools, ad hoc requests. [36:17]
- Backlog review with stakeholders and an OKR check box. [34:14] [35:46]
- ESPN's human-in-the-loop generative AI content with explainer text. [17:54]
- AutoML used for speed. [39:24]

## Limits and open questions

- No results, datasets or sample sizes; all claims are practitioner experience.
- Panelists work in betting, ticketing, media and business operations; none discuss athlete performance data.
- Speaker attribution in auto captions is unreliable; a few answers are attributed by the order of the moderator's questions.
- The Bubble Watch error and other examples were described without detail.
- Panelists are employed by the firms they describe; hiring advice reflects personal preference.
- On the youth sports poll the first answer, captioned "Bye", is probably "buy" but the caption is unclear; the rest said hold or sell. [47:33] [48:06]

## Q&A

- How do you account for data limitations and bias? Feature bias, for example schedule effects. [40:25] [40:56]
- Tools or telling the time: how do you balance outputs for stakeholders? Depends on use case; meet them where they are. [41:27] [41:58]
- Advice for breaking into the industry? Projects, networking, curiosity, learning several tools. [43:28]
- Buy, sell or hold a youth sports analytics panel at SSAC in five years? Mixed, with ethics concerns. [47:33] [48:06] [48:38]

## Summary

A panel of four sports industry data leaders (from Harris Blitzer Sports and Entertainment, Ticketmaster, ESPN and FanDuel), moderated by Katie Hodel, on building data science teams and models that get used. The recurring argument is that a model is worth little unless stakeholders adopt it, so start from the right question, ship a simple version early, iterate, and deliver outputs in the format the audience already uses. The panelists also discuss model trade-offs (explainability, runtime, accuracy), generative AI with human review at ESPN, feature bias, backlog prioritization, hiring for storytelling and problem solving, and career advice. The speakers come from business, betting and media, not athlete performance.

## Key claims

- Keith Goldner's FanDuel team builds predictive models that help set betting lines. [01:32]
- The panelists say data science is hard to define and the balance between people, software and partnerships is the challenge. [05:38] [06:09]
- Braden Moore uses an 80/20 idea: most of the value comes from the first part of the effort. [07:10]
- A model is not worth much if it does not get used and stakeholders do not give feedback. [07:40]
- In a startup a data scientist wears many hats; in a larger company a team can hire specialists. [08:11] [08:42] [09:12]
- ESPN's analytics team uses data modelers, engineers and a strong content voice. [09:43]
- Carlos Kasper interviews on hobbies because storytelling is hard to teach, while tools can be taught. [11:15] [11:45]
- Others look for problem solving, asking the right questions and thinking about edge cases after a base technical level. [12:47]
- Goldner says modeling starts with the right question, then data, features, target and delivery, and that an unused accurate model has no value. [14:50] [15:21]
- A request to export to Excel means the wrong question was asked. [15:51]
- Model type depends on trade-offs: explainability, integration, runtime, ease of maintenance and accuracy. [18:25] [19:25]
- ESPN labels generative AI content, commits to a human in the loop and keeps transparency about it. [17:24] [17:54]
- Generative AI is compared to infinite interns, to be used where errors are obvious, acceptable, or impossible. [19:25]
- Time to value matters: a game will not be delayed, so a fast decision-ready version can beat a perfect one. [19:56] [20:26]
- A model is one data point next to gut feeling and history, and model output can be stale within minutes at Ticketmaster. [20:56] [21:26]
- Goldner says analysts must be humble and treat traders as subject matter experts. [21:56]
- ESPN's public accuracy matters to its brand, and a Bubble Watch error was found by another team member. [25:02] [25:32]
- Goldner says accuracy should not be treated as the holy grail; he could not tell whether his draft models for an NBA team were accurate after a decade of drafts. [26:34]
- Moore says output should be framed so it guides strategy ("10% more likely than the average to churn" versus "10% likely"). [27:04]
- Moore's metaphor: build a bike, not a car, improving from a scooter. [28:38] [29:08]
- Single-person dependencies create a risk that a model must be scrapped when the builder leaves. [30:10]
- ESPN balances editorial voice, personalization, business revenue and representation when curating content. [31:41] [32:11] [32:42]
- For prioritization, Moore shows stakeholders the backlog and asks them to order it; an internal form asks whether a request supports an OKR. [34:14] [35:46]
- Goldner sorts projects as global models, dashboards and tools, and ad hoc requests, weighing commercial impact against effort. [36:17]
- Easier tools and AutoML allow faster failure and more people building models. [38:51] [39:24]
- Goldner says features can be biased, for example yards per game or points per game depend on schedule. [40:56]
- Meet stakeholders where they are: Excel, a table or a PDF, and build a prototype in parallel. [41:58] [42:28]
- Advice for entering the field: do a sports research project, network, stay curious, and explain what you can do for the employer. [44:00] [44:30] [46:02] [46:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length: 40 minutes plus 5 minutes of Q&A. [00:31]
- Numberfire acquired by FanDuel in 2015. [01:32]
- Goldner consulted for an NBA front office for about a decade. [02:03]
- 80/20 rule as used by Moore. [07:10]
- Churn framing: 10% likely versus 10% more likely than the average. [27:04]
- Goldner's first internship route: emails to about 30 teams, nine "no" replies and one "maybe". [44:00] [44:30]
- Model runtime and accuracy are cited as trade-offs, with no figures. [19:25]
- Ticketmaster output can be out of date in "five or 10 minutes". [21:26]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Model process: question, brainstorm data and features, target, delivery, iteration. [14:50]
- MVP approach and "bike, not car". [28:38]
- Three project levels: global models, dashboards and tools, ad hoc requests. [36:17]
- Backlog review with stakeholders and an OKR check box. [34:14] [35:46]
- ESPN's human-in-the-loop generative AI content with explainer text. [17:54]
- AutoML used for speed. [39:24]

- No results, datasets or sample sizes; all claims are practitioner experience.
- Panelists work in betting, ticketing, media and business operations; none discuss athlete performance data.
- Speaker attribution in auto captions is unreliable; a few answers are attributed by the order of the moderator's questions.
- The Bubble Watch error and other examples were described without detail.
- Panelists are employed by the firms they describe; hiring advice reflects personal preference.

- How do you account for data limitations and bias? Feature bias, for example schedule effects. [40:25] [40:56]

- Advice for breaking into the industry? Projects, networking, curiosity, learning several tools. [43:28]

## Summary

Matt Harmon, creator of Reception Perception, explains his film-charting method for wide receivers, created in 2013. He charts every route and alignment from all-22 film for 60 to 70 players a year, eight games each, to isolate receivers from quarterback, line and offensive role. The main metric is success rate against coverage, read within the receiver's alignment, and he shows examples where the numbers flagged a breakout before production (Nico Collins, caption "nicoo") and where they explained role (Smith-Schuster and Brown). He concedes the game will not be fully solved, that some calls were early or wrong, and that he does not know every player's assignment. The work is his own method and subscription product.

## Key claims

- The method aims to credit receivers for routes that are not targets: a top target leader got just over 10 targets per game while running about 40 routes. [02:01]
- Yards per route run and first downs per route run are good stats but do not isolate the receiver from quarterback, line and offensive use. [03:03] [03:33]
- Harmon charts every route and alignment from all-22 film. [03:33]
- The sample is 60 to 70 players a year, eight games each, chosen after back-testing showed eight games are representative of a season. [04:35] [05:05] [05:35]
- A percentile in the database is relative to the players he samples, not all college prospects. [04:35] [05:05]
- Everything starts with alignment and role: outside on the line faces more press and man, slot and off the line faces more zone. [07:08] [08:39] [09:09]
- In 2018 Juju Smith-Schuster (caption spelling) was weak against press (38.2%, 10th percentile) but strong against zone (84%), and as a slot player the zone number mattered more for him; Antonio Brown, an outside player, mattered more for press and man. [09:40] [10:12]
- For Puka Nacua (caption "pukan akua") in his rookie season, over 40% of routes were digs and slants and 21.3% were digs; he said the dig was his favorite route. [11:16] [11:47]
- A mystery player with dig success of 87% and slant success of 82.5%, over 80% against zone, was Amon-Ra St. Brown (caption "on ra St Brown"). [12:18] [12:52] [13:24]
- Reception Perception showed St. Brown's rookie back-half surge was not a fluke. [13:54]
- Nico Collins had under 500 receiving yards in each of his first two years yet showed 68% success against man and 71.9% against press as a rookie and 71% and 74.5% in year two. [14:25] [14:56] [15:27]
- Harmon's quick rule: an outside receiver beating man coverage above 70% and near the 75th percentile against press is worth watching in the right offense. [15:27] [15:57]
- In year three Collins had almost 1,300 yards and eight touchdowns and was second most efficient by yards per route run. [15:57]
- Football will never be fully solved, and he is fine with that. [16:28]
- He is considering a higher premium on smaller inside receivers who beat zone, get open fast against man and do something after the catch, because of two-high coverage. [17:31] [18:03]
- He wants to expand the charted player pool and find specialists for other positions. [18:03] [18:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Method created in 2013. [01:00]
- 175 targets for the league leader, just over 10 per game, about 40 routes per game (caption spelling "Jamar Chase"). [02:01]
- 60 to 70 players per year; eight games per sample. [04:35] [05:05]
- Success rate versus coverage: how often a receiver gets open against man, zone, press and double coverage, by route. [06:05]
- Nabers (caption "Malik neighbors") open on 73.7% of charted routes in the in-season rookie report. [06:05]
- Color code: green above the Reception Perception average, red below, yellow within two percentage points. [11:16]
- In-space metrics: how often a receiver is in the open field with a chance to break a tackle and how often he does. [06:37]
- Collins yards per route run 1.24 and "1.68 yards per outout run" (caption garbled, metric unclear). [14:56]
- Collins: rookie 68% man, 71.9% press; second year 71% man, 74.5% press (74th percentile). [14:56] [15:27]
- Smith-Schuster 2018: 38.2% press, 84% zone. [09:40]
- Collins third season: almost 1,300 yards, eight touchdowns. [15:57]
- Wide receivers are a "top three paid position" (his chart). [03:03]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Film charting of routes and alignment from all-22 film. [03:33]
- Metrics: route percentage, success rate versus coverage by route, targets, catches, drop rate per route, contested catches, in-space metrics and alignment. [05:35] [06:05] [06:37]
- Alignment as the starting frame (outside or slot, on or off the line). [07:08]
- Eight-game back-tested sample. [05:05] [05:35]
- Route and route-percentage charts with color coding. [11:16]

## Limits and open questions

- One person charts all data; no reliability, agreement or hit-rate statistics are shown.
- Sample of eight games per player and 60 to 70 players a year; percentiles are relative to his own sample. [04:35]
- Examples (Collins, St. Brown, Nacua) are successes he picked; one miss (Tyler Lockett, caption "Tyro lockett's") is admitted, with "never wrong, just early" conceded as not true. [20:06]
- He does not know each player's assignment and admits he may miss things. [22:40] [23:11]
- The college claim (players below the 35th percentile against man and press who became high-volume players) gives no counts. [23:41] [24:13]
- Subscription product and personal method, a commercial view.
- Caption names are garbled (Smith-Schuster, Collins, Nacua, "CJ strad", "T Higgins").

## Q&A

- Why might a player with Collins-like indicators not break out? Injuries, offensive environment, other weaknesses; patience, example Tyler Lockett (caption). [19:36] [20:06]
- How do you judge the vertical route on a dagger concept? It will likely not be open; data plus analysis. [21:08]
- How do you attribute responsibility for route success? He does not know every assignment and avoids slamming players. [22:10] [22:40]
- What are NFL teams missing in college receiver evaluations? Players below the 35th percentile against man and press who did well after moving inside; example Keon Coleman. [23:41] [24:43] [25:13]

title: "SSAC25: The Analytics Driven Franchise: Building a Modern NBA Team"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ariana andan (caption spelling), Shane Bader (caption spelling), Monty McNair, Oliver (caption spelling; data scientist at ESPN), John Hollinger (moderator)]

## Summary

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. Evidence is anecdotal and no data are shown.

## Key claims

- Analytics departments have grown. The question is where information gets throughput, so a team has to pick the highest-leverage information that can affect winning. [01:30]
- Tracking data has been available for roughly ten years and pose data is new, so teams are "behind again." Sports science also offers more information than teams know what to do with. [02:00]
- Pose data will be something teams chase for the next 5 to 10 years. [02:31]
- Players can be overloaded with information. Instincts should be built in practice, and some players tell staff they have had enough. [03:02]
- The decisions (who to play, how to improve) are the same as 20 or 40 years ago. Numbers refine them, and staff should filter before information reaches users. [03:34]
- A player on the panel accepted "the answers to the test" and said clear communication of the value to the player drives receptiveness. [04:04], [04:34]

type: video-summary
video_id: o4rMbhsdk0I
title: "SSAC25: Lessons in Chemistry: Impact of Teammate Familiarity on Shooting in the NBA"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Alamar, Dean Oliver]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

## Key claims

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]
- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]
- Shot quality improves as passer-shooter pairs play together. Shorter two-point shots, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots (about 4% lower pressure score in the first 100 shots) are the measurable drivers. [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]
- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]
- The speaker (a former coach) offers confidence, rhythm and timing, and pass placement preferences as unmodeled reasons for accuracy gains. These are the speaker's explanations, not tested. [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]
- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]
- Gains are largest early, with diminishing marginal gains across seasons, and the data set does not hold enough long-tenured pairs to find a maximum. Two to three seasons together are beneficial. [19:31], [20:01]
- Practice data would be the prescriptive side, and teams hold it. [20:32], [21:03]
- Team-level integration effects and plug-and-play players are named as open, and individual pair results are noisy and biased. [21:33], [22:04]
- Positional analysis (big to big passing) was not done. [22:34]
- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]
- Chemistry here means familiarity in catch-and-shoot situations only. Lineup-level work needs care because good lineups play more together. [30:45], [31:16]
- A speaker says to study learning, first establish the normal expected curve, then see whether an intervention improves it. [30:15]
- The model has no notion of a break within a season, so decay after injury is untested. [33:19], [33:49]
- Turnover and incompletion reasons are not categorized in basketball as they are in football. [36:56], [37:28]
- An interaction between season and attempt count was statistically significant but did not change the shape much. [37:59], [38:30]
- Asked about trading for pairs of players, a speaker said no, and that trading money for talent is a bigger effect. [39:02], [39:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Data: 1600 passer-shooter combinations with between 10 and 50 catch-and-shoot attempts, averaging 1.12 points per attempt, 2023-24 season. [07:38]
- Most frequent pair: 237 catch-and-shoot attempts (captions: "Tyrese and Miles"). [07:38]
- Expected points = made-shot probability times 2 or 3. [07:08]
- Shot probability inputs: shot type, location, and NBA-supplied pressure scores (passer pressure, receiver pressure, shooter pressure, defined by defender closeness). [06:06], [06:37]
- Models tried: XGBoost (best), random forest (weird results), logistic regression (not as good). [06:37], [07:08]
- Familiarity model: a simple log-log regression with an in-season counter and a cumulative counter of passer-shooter catch-and-shoot attempts. [08:40], [09:13]
- Result: about 7% improvement in the first 50 attempts, another 4% to 200. Rarely more than 200 attempts in a season. [09:43]
- Carry-over: next season starts about 5% above where the pair started in season one, below the end of season one. [10:14]
- Accuracy analysis assumes a 1.2 expected-points baseline. [12:18]
- Phoenix trio: from 81 points per 100 shots to 93, then more up to about 200 shots (rule of thumb). [17:27]
- Garble risk: "started off I believe it was 11 and N" and "about 40 and 20 something" [02:00], "8 low well below" [02:31], and "a 7% field goal percentage" [16:26] are garbled, and the units of the 7% and 4% gains are not stated clearly.

## Methods and frameworks named

- NBA-provided tracking and pressure data; a custom shot-quality model with gradient boosting.
- Log-log regression of shot quality and of actual minus expected points on two counters of shared attempts. [08:40]
- Decomposition of the gain into shot quality and accuracy. [15:54]

## Limits and open questions

- The speakers described the model as a first step and the numbers as rule of thumb [17:27]. They did not show controls for selection into shared playing time (shown only for lineups as a caution [31:16]).
- The explanations for accuracy are the speaker's coaching view and are not in the model. [13:52]
- Pair-level results are noisy and biased. [21:33]
- No positional, rookie-specific, break-decay, shot-frequency or role-player analysis. [22:34], [33:49], [34:49], [35:53]
- The video description quotes different figures for a Phoenix trio, which are not stated in the captions and were not checked.
- Two speakers are former or current team staff and ESPN data staff, and their coaching anecdotes are their own.

## Q&A

- Diminishing returns over more seasons? Yes, marginal gains decline and the ceiling cannot be found. [19:31]

type: video-summary
video_id: pcp9h_M6Ir8
title: "SSAC25: Causal Impact of Offensive Linemen on Pass Plays"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [american-football]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

## Q&A

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

video_id: RZNLXU2O0WM
title: "SSAC25: Minding the College Football Analytics Gap"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kim Kasam (caption spelling), vice president of product at Teamworks; introduced by Ryan smard (caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, competitive-advantage, decision-making]

caption_source: auto

## Summary

The speaker, a former first analytics hire at the Pittsburgh Steelers who now works for Teamworks Intelligence, argues that college football analytics sits about a decade behind the NFL and that the gap is about to close. He says free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal leave small scouting staffs with too many players to evaluate. He describes two tracking-data models his company built: change of direction (COD) and run-game credit attribution. Both are checked against film. He presents a per-game "digital scouting report" for every FBS player as a way to narrow large candidate pools. The claims come from the vendor selling the product.

## Key claims

- College football analytics is about a decade behind the NFL, and the speaker says that gap will close [00:31].
- College evaluation is limited: in-person looks are few, and even big programs may have only three or four scouting staff, with most coaches also scouting [01:31].
- Free agency, a salary cap and the transfer portal now require a few scouts and a position coach to evaluate hundreds of players and make offers within hours [02:01].
- Analytics moved from box scores, to play-by-play data, to ball and player tracking data released to all NFL teams in 2018, and each step needs more people and computing [03:32], [04:02].
- Teams get competitive advantage from the richest data and from doing the most with it, which now means tracking data and a team of people [04:02].
- Straight-line speed alone is not enough; COD matters at every position but is hard to quantify because direction data is noisy [05:34], [06:06].
- COD is measured as a deficit: the same distance run with a turn versus in a line [06:06].
- A COD is found by tracking heading angle over a play and detecting where the turn starts, ends and peaks [07:37].
- Two COD events with a similar deficit can differ in quality, so the model adds entry speed, acceleration, turn angle, rate of turn and distance as context [08:08], [08:38].
- For one 2023 draftee (name garbled in captions), combine 40 and three-cone looked weak while the tracking-based speed and COD looked strong; he was a fifth-round pick [09:39], [10:09], [10:39].
- The speaker treats an "eye test" of a leaderboard as the most important validation; outliers are who teams sign, retain and draft, so mistakes are costly [11:40].
- COD is one piece of the picture and the speaker does not suggest drafting or signing from a COD list [12:10].
- Run-game credit is split into identifying actions and attributing them among 22 players, using a graph neural network with players as nodes and relationships as edges [12:41], [13:11], [14:12], [14:43].
- On one Lions at Chiefs run, the model's expected yardage rises and falls during the play as blocks and defenders act, and credit is given to the runner, blockers and defenders [15:13], [15:44], [16:15].
- The model rewards a defender who runs a long way and penalizes loafing, without being taught this; the speaker says it learned it from about 100,000 running plays [17:16], [17:46].
- Each metric took 4 to 24 months of data science and engineering; the resulting report covers every FBS player and updates after every game [19:52].
- Trait language (change of direction, burst, run blocking) is easier for staff to share than statistics like EPA per play or yards per route run [20:22].
- Teams could use the report to reduce roughly a thousand portal receivers to 20 or 30 [20:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- Decade gap between college and NFL analytics [00:31].
- Three or four scouting department members at a large SEC school [01:31].
- NFL released tracking data to teams in 2018 [03:32]. Another talk in this batch gives 2019.
- More than 70 technical staff, 25 PhDs, a dozen who led R&D departments [04:34].
- COD deficit: time with a turn compared with straight-line time over the same distance [06:36]. The 505 test is described as 15 yards one way, a 180 degree turn, five yards back (as captioned) [06:36].
- Jefferson example: two COD events with a deficit of about a second; one described as an 80 degree dig (as captioned), one a 170 degree hitch [08:08].
- Draftee: fifth round, pick 177 overall [10:09].
- Gibbs play: 18 yards on the play; expected gain about three yards at the start, about eight at its peak; percentile ratings of 96 (acceleration) and 99 (a block) [13:42], [15:13], [15:44], [16:45].
- Mike Dana (caption spelling) ran about 40 yards on the play [17:16].

video_id: v-BOAaqS01c
title: "SSAC25: NCAA 2.0: What's Next?"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Oliver Luck, Mark Jackson (Northwestern athletic director), Brian Higgins (NCAA), moderator Michael mccan (caption spelling, University of New Hampshire School of Law); introduced by Ryan smard (caption spelling)]
topics: [policy, american-football]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel discusses what the pending House settlement would change in college sports: direct payments and revenue sharing, a fair-market-value clearinghouse for NIL deals, and what it leaves unresolved (employee status, transfers, eligibility). Panelists cover how money might be divided between football and other sports, private equity, conference realignment, the transfer portal and a ten-year outlook. Views are opinion and prediction from an athletic director, a former NCAA executive and an NCAA business executive. The panel is set before a court hearing on the settlement, so nothing here confirms what was approved. There is no analytics content in the sense of data or models.

## Key claims

- The settlement has two parts: back payments of about $2.8 billion over ten years for past lost NIL and broadcast revenue, and revenue sharing of up to 22% of certain revenues among opting-in schools [01:02], [01:33], [02:03].
- The moderator argues the true share is closer to 50% once scholarships and other benefits are counted [02:03].
- Objections include Title IX (most money going to men's sports, especially football) and conflicts with state NIL laws [02:33].
- NIL deals above $600 would go through a clearinghouse for a fair-market-value check [03:03].
- The settlement leaves open whether athletes are employees, transfer rules, and eligibility [03:34], [04:04], [04:36].
- Jackson says he now feels like a CEO focused on revenue, and that Northwestern has one of the smallest alumni and ticket bases in the Big 10 [06:09], [06:39].
- Luck expects a light regulatory touch on fair-market value at first, and says disclosure rules of the past three years were ignored with no penalties as far as he can tell [08:12], [08:43], [09:13].
- Higgins says a new entity separate from the NCAA will manage the cap and disclosure, so the national office will spend more on data and marketing to help schools raise revenue [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
- Luck says a paid player does not disrupt a locker room if the right players are paid [11:47].
- Jackson says large media-rights deals might be restructured so some of the money flows as NIL through the clearinghouse, pushing a school's total above the cap; Northwestern cannot do this [12:48].
- Higgins says the national office wants fair pay for athletes while keeping the field level enough that small programs can still win titles [13:48], [14:18].
- Higgins expects more scholarships post-settlement, with disproportionate growth for women's sports, and cites a new performance fund in the women's basketball championship [16:52], [17:23].
- Luck says schools are using the judge's backward-looking formula as a safe harbor, a split of 75% football, 15% men's basketball, 5% women's basketball, 5% others [19:24].
- Luck doubts private equity has a role, since the SEC and Big 10 say they can fund themselves; Jackson has been pitched and calls it expensive money; Higgins says any capital must earn more than its cost [21:56], [22:27], [22:59], [24:01].
- Luck describes the ACC arrangement sending 60% of a pool to schools with the best TV ratings, and thinks the settlement could bring five to seven stable years [25:02], [25:34].
- On the transfer portal, Luck says individual contracts (no-transfer periods, clawbacks) will matter most, and a league-wide transfer limit would be a likely antitrust problem [31:44], [32:14], [32:46].
- Higgins says many transfers are healthy and transfer rates in other sports are not much different from the general student body [30:42], [31:13].
- Luck predicts athletes in revenue sports will be found to be employees, unionize and bargain collectively, which he thinks would improve college athletics [34:47], [35:17], [35:48].
- Jackson compares today to the AFL-NFL era and expects free agency, bargaining and a cap to evolve; he hopes Congress builds a framework protecting Olympic sports [36:49], [37:19].
- Higgins wants all sports treated as commercial products, to avoid cutting sports, and to keep graduation rates [37:51], [38:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Hearing date April 7 [01:02].
- $2.8 billion over ten years, to athletes going back to about 2017 [01:02], [01:33].
- Revenue sharing up to 22% [01:33]; direct-payment cap initially about $21 million [02:03]; Jackson calls it $20 and a half million [12:18]. A later "up to 205 million" [15:20] is likely a caption error.
- Clearinghouse threshold $600 [03:03]; a later "$61" deal [09:13] is a caption problem.
- Northwestern: hundred-million organization [06:09]; $850 million stadium [18:24]; 21 sports [18:54].
- Baseball scholarship limit 11.3 going to 35 [16:52], [43:33].
- Split 75, 15, 5, 5 [19:24].
- ACC: 60% of a revenue pool to top-rated schools [25:34]. Luck says 17 members "I think" [25:34].
- Settlement is a ten-year deal; some TV contracts up in 30, 31 and 32 [25:02].
- NCAA has 91 championships, hoping for 95 [10:46], [38:22].
- Swim trials drew 35,000 versus 1500 at the NCAA championship [39:23].
- Division 2 and 3 get "4 point something" and "3 point something" percent of national office revenue (as captioned) [43:33].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fair-market-value review of NIL deals by a new entity, with Luck suggesting Deloitte builds a complex algorithm [08:12]. The moderator-cited details are not shown.
- Backward-looking allocation formula from the judge [19:24].
- Collective bargaining and the non-statutory labor exemption as a route around antitrust limits [35:17].

## Limits and open questions

- Everything is opinion or forecast; no data or analysis is shown.
- The settlement outcome is not in the talk; the hearing is still ahead.
- The moderator states that a Department of Education fact sheet on equal distribution was withdrawn [19:54].
- Panelists represent interested institutions (an athletic director, a former NCAA executive now consulting, an NCAA executive); Jackson says his general counsel told him to give no numbers [17:53].
- The 75, 15, 5, 5 split and the ACC 60% figure are Luck's secondhand descriptions.
- Names (Wilkin, Petitti, Deloitte, Kellogg) are as captioned and may be wrong.

## Q&A

- Olympic sports: Higgins says the NCAA, national governing bodies and the Olympic committee must work together, and notes the US lacks public funding for elite athletes [38:52], [39:23], [39:54].
- International athletes and NIL: visa law was not built for NIL and likely needs federal change; workarounds exist [40:25], [40:56], [41:27].
- Balancing athletes and Big 10 interests: Jackson says there is alignment so far [41:27], [41:59].
- Division 2 and 3: Higgins thinks they benefit as roster caps push players down, and notes a dedicated share of national office revenue [43:02], [43:33], [44:03].
- Should football have different rules: Luck hopes not, but says it already differs and the rest of the system would adapt [44:34], [45:04].
