## Summary

A panel discusses what the pending House settlement would change in college sports: direct payments and revenue sharing, a fair-market-value clearinghouse for NIL deals, and what it leaves unresolved (employee status, transfers, eligibility). Panelists cover how money might be divided between football and other sports, private equity, conference realignment, the transfer portal and a ten-year outlook. Views are opinion and prediction from an athletic director, a former NCAA executive and an NCAA business executive. The panel is set before a court hearing on the settlement, so nothing here confirms what was approved. There is no analytics content in the sense of data or models.

## Key claims

- The settlement has two parts: back payments of about $2.8 billion over ten years for past lost NIL and broadcast revenue, and revenue sharing of up to 22% of certain revenues among opting-in schools [01:02], [01:33], [02:03].
- The moderator argues the true share is closer to 50% once scholarships and other benefits are counted [02:03].
- Objections include Title IX (most money going to men's sports, especially football) and conflicts with state NIL laws [02:33].
- NIL deals above $600 would go through a clearinghouse for a fair-market-value check [03:03].
- The settlement leaves open whether athletes are employees, transfer rules, and eligibility [03:34], [04:04], [04:36].
- Jackson says he now feels like a CEO focused on revenue, and that Northwestern has one of the smallest alumni and ticket bases in the Big 10 [06:09], [06:39].
- Luck expects a light regulatory touch on fair-market value at first, and says disclosure rules of the past three years were ignored with no penalties as far as he can tell [08:12], [08:43], [09:13].
- Higgins says a new entity separate from the NCAA will manage the cap and disclosure, so the national office will spend more on data and marketing to help schools raise revenue [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
- Luck says a paid player does not disrupt a locker room if the right players are paid [11:47].
- Jackson says large media-rights deals might be restructured so some of the money flows as NIL through the clearinghouse, pushing a school's total above the cap; Northwestern cannot do this [12:48].
- Higgins says the national office wants fair pay for athletes while keeping the field level enough that small programs can still win titles [13:48], [14:18].
- Higgins expects more scholarships post-settlement, with disproportionate growth for women's sports, and cites a new performance fund in the women's basketball championship [16:52], [17:23].
- Luck says schools are using the judge's backward-looking formula as a safe harbor, a split of 75% football, 15% men's basketball, 5% women's basketball, 5% others [19:24].
- Luck doubts private equity has a role, since the SEC and Big 10 say they can fund themselves; Jackson has been pitched and calls it expensive money; Higgins says any capital must earn more than its cost [21:56], [22:27], [22:59], [24:01].
- Luck describes the ACC arrangement sending 60% of a pool to schools with the best TV ratings, and thinks the settlement could bring five to seven stable years [25:02], [25:34].
- On the transfer portal, Luck says individual contracts (no-transfer periods, clawbacks) will matter most, and a league-wide transfer limit would be a likely antitrust problem [31:44], [32:14], [32:46].
- Higgins says many transfers are healthy and transfer rates in other sports are not much different from the general student body [30:42], [31:13].
- Luck predicts athletes in revenue sports will be found to be employees, unionize and bargain collectively, which he thinks would improve college athletics [34:47], [35:17], [35:48].
- Jackson compares today to the AFL-NFL era and expects free agency, bargaining and a cap to evolve; he hopes Congress builds a framework protecting Olympic sports [36:49], [37:19].
- Higgins wants all sports treated as commercial products, to avoid cutting sports, and to keep graduation rates [37:51], [38:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Hearing date April 7 [01:02].
- $2.8 billion over ten years, to athletes going back to about 2017 [01:02], [01:33].
- Revenue sharing up to 22% [01:33]; direct-payment cap initially about $21 million [02:03]; Jackson calls it $20 and a half million [12:18]. A later "up to 205 million" [15:20] is likely a caption error.
- Clearinghouse threshold $600 [03:03]; a later "$61" deal [09:13] is a caption problem.
- Northwestern: hundred-million organization [06:09]; $850 million stadium [18:24]; 21 sports [18:54].
- Baseball scholarship limit 11.3 going to 35 [16:52], [43:33].
- Split 75, 15, 5, 5 [19:24].
- ACC: 60% of a revenue pool to top-rated schools [25:34]. Luck says 17 members "I think" [25:34].
- Settlement is a ten-year deal; some TV contracts up in 30, 31 and 32 [25:02].
- NCAA has 91 championships, hoping for 95 [10:46], [38:22].
- Swim trials drew 35,000 versus 1500 at the NCAA championship [39:23].
- Division 2 and 3 get "4 point something" and "3 point something" percent of national office revenue (as captioned) [43:33].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fair-market-value review of NIL deals by a new entity, with Luck suggesting Deloitte builds a complex algorithm [08:12]. The moderator-cited details are not shown.
- Backward-looking allocation formula from the judge [19:24].
- Collective bargaining and the non-statutory labor exemption as a route around antitrust limits [35:17].

## Limits and open questions

- Everything is opinion or forecast; no data or analysis is shown.
- The settlement outcome is not in the talk; the hearing is still ahead.
- The moderator states that a Department of Education fact sheet on equal distribution was withdrawn [19:54].
- Panelists represent interested institutions (an athletic director, a former NCAA executive now consulting, an NCAA executive); Jackson says his general counsel told him to give no numbers [17:53].
- The 75, 15, 5, 5 split and the ACC 60% figure are Luck's secondhand descriptions.
- Names (Wilkin, Petitti, Deloitte, Kellogg) are as captioned and may be wrong.

## Q&A

- Olympic sports: Higgins says the NCAA, national governing bodies and the Olympic committee must work together, and notes the US lacks public funding for elite athletes [38:52], [39:23], [39:54].
- International athletes and NIL: visa law was not built for NIL and likely needs federal change; workarounds exist [40:25], [40:56], [41:27].
- Balancing athletes and Big 10 interests: Jackson says there is alignment so far [41:27], [41:59].
- Division 2 and 3: Higgins thinks they benefit as roster caps push players down, and notes a dedicated share of national office revenue [43:02], [43:33], [44:03].
- Should football have different rules: Luck hopes not, but says it already differs and the rest of the system would adapt [44:34], [45:04].

## Summary

Two speakers, one from a consultancy and one from Databricks, argue that media companies and professional franchises have a coherence problem, not a data problem: metrics are defined in different places and staff spend time asking which number is right. They describe modernizing a live campaign platform for a large media organization by centralizing business definitions and governance on a lakehouse with Unity Catalog, then extend the idea to player performance, fan and sponsorship data. The talk is a vendor and consultant pitch. It shows a reference architecture and qualitative outcomes, and no measured results. There is little sport-specific content.

## Key claims

- Most media companies and franchises have a coherence problem; alignment, not data volume, decides whether analytics creates advantage [01:00], [01:32].
- In their scenario, three days of different numbers for the same campaign shift the conversation from optimizing to reconciling [02:35], [03:07].
- They say franchises have the same pattern: coaching, scouting and commercial staff using different metrics for similar things [03:07].
- When alignment breaks, decisions slow; the speaker says the cause is architecture, not talent [03:40], [04:14].
- In the case described, audience data sat in several systems, scripts did publishing and another team owned orchestration [04:45].
- The turning point was to stop asking which tools to add and instead centralize business logic and shared semantics [06:49], [07:21], [07:55].
- The Databricks speaker says traditional catalogs cover only tables, auditing and access, while Unity Catalog governs models, agents and endpoints and can federate outside sources without copies [08:56], [09:28], [09:59], [10:30].
- Business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog can serve reports and give AI agents context; the speaker says external BI tools each use their own semantic layers with less metadata [11:33], [14:07], [14:38].
- The implementation used Delta Lake for storage, Unity Catalog for governance, Lakeflow jobs for orchestration and Databricks SQL, with campaign and audience definitions moved into governed tables [16:13], [16:45], [17:16].
- Lakebase was not implemented in this project; the speaker says the architecture now supports operational workloads without a new silo [17:16].
- Outcomes named are structural: less pipeline upkeep, clearer ownership, better cost visibility, stable definitions, and more trust [17:16], [17:47].
- Stated business effects: faster optimization cycles, consistent audience definitions, trust in metrics, and scalable governance [18:18], [18:48], [19:18], [19:50].
- The same pattern is said to apply to player performance analytics, fan engagement, ticketing and sponsorship reporting [19:50], [20:22].
- Shared semantics are described as a basis for AI readiness [20:54], [21:25].

## Numbers and definitions

- Talk: 20 minutes plus 5 minutes of Q&A [00:30].
- Delivery estimate: 3 to 4 months, depending on company size and scope [24:30].
- One engineer architecting with four or five parallel agents writing code [23:59].
- "Business semantics": definitions of metrics and entities (audiences, yield) defined once and reused [07:21], [11:33].
- Medallion gold layer: data ready for downstream use [12:36]. No quantitative performance numbers are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Reference architecture: siloed data moved to cloud object storage, refined through layers to a gold layer, with governance and a semantic layer over it [12:04], [12:36], [15:10].
- Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, Lakeflow jobs, Databricks SQL, Lakebase (proposed next step) [13:06], [16:13], [17:16].
- Metric views as the semantic layer feeding agents [14:38].

## Limits and open questions

- No metrics of success (time saved, cost, error rates) are shown.
- Commercial source: a Databricks employee and a consultancy describe products and services they sell.
- The case is one media organization; sports examples are speculative ("can appear") [19:50].
- The speed claim rests on engineers working with parallel AI agents and is stated as the speaker's estimate [23:59], [24:30].
- Caption problems: the firm is spelled "Luminata" and "Lumin Alta," the lead speaker is addressed as "Jerome," and Lakebase appears as "Lake Base."

## Q&A

- How long does the process take: the speaker estimates 3 to 4 months, done with engineers directing parallel AI agents [23:29], [23:59], [24:30].

event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Karim Kassam (caption spelling "Kassam"), Teamworks; Nick Caserio, Houston Texans; Connor Barwin, Philadelphia Eagles; moderator Mina Kimes, ESPN; introduced by Quinn McCarthy]

## Summary

Three football executives and a moderator discuss how data has changed player evaluation, development and in-game decisions. Barwin recalls early performance tracking as high friction, Caserio stresses integration across departments and simple, position-specific measures, and Kassam describes tracking-derived metrics and AI models. On fourth downs, the panel says analytics points toward aggression on average but the head coach decides with game context. The panel also covers communication to coaches, players and fans, and how to handle small samples. Much of it is anecdote and opinion from people whose organizations sell or use these tools.

## Key claims

- Barwin says he had little awareness of advanced stats when he entered the league in 2009, and that the 2013 Eagles were at the forefront of performance tracking [01:33], [02:03].
- Barwin says daily HRV, hydration and survey checks created too much friction then, and that things are much better now [03:34].
- Caserio says data was once viewed as something that could be used against players; it is now more conversational and players want their measurements [04:35], [05:05].
- Caserio says more teams now build a performance area with resources and staff [05:36].
- Kassam describes data eras: box score data, play-by-play, then tracking data at 10 times a second, and says this allows measures such as change of direction and how a player affects the pocket or run game [06:36], [07:06], [07:36], [08:06].
- Kassam's get-off metric for edge rushers has a flat age curve in his analysis, which he reads as meaning players can improve it; deep speed might fall off faster [08:06], [08:36], [10:10].
- Computer vision now lets similar data be derived from all-22 film for college players [10:10].
- Barwin says at least 25 players each week get no game data, which is a chance to use data for development [11:41].
- Caserio says data use only works if analytics, coaches and scouting are integrated and communicate constantly [12:43].
- Caserio says coaches want digestible information with an application, and that one must be flexible between old and new school [13:44], [14:15].
- Caserio says the 2026 combine 40 times were fast as a group because of specific training, that about three-quarters of the drills are not real-world applicable, and that time speed and game speed can differ [15:47], [16:17].
- Barwin says combine numbers matter as an important part of a bigger puzzle [17:49].
- Kassam says football differs from baseball because roles and schemes differ, and that his metrics adjust for conference and level of competition [18:50], [19:20].
- Kassam says his pass rush metric treats the pocket as a surface to isolate one player's effect, and that such measures can be stable from college to pro [19:51], [20:21].
- Caserio says to keep measures simple and tied to what the position requires [20:52], [21:22].
- On fourth downs, Caserio says the philosophy is set before the game and the head coach decides [22:23], [22:54]; Barwin says decisions are prepared during the week, then injuries, weather and feel for the game matter [24:26], [24:56].
- Barwin says explaining the why to players builds confidence [25:26].
- Kassam says his own models showed teams should be more aggressive on average but with large error bars and many gray-zone cases [27:27], [27:57].
- Caserio says the plus-35 to 40 area is the hardest, and field position and the team's defense enter the calculus [28:28], [28:59].
- Kassam says a run-game neural network trained on a couple million plays credits hustle and penalizes loafing without being told [31:31], [32:01], [32:32].
- Caserio says AI is here and staff should experiment with use cases; his performance team uses a model to synthesize articles [33:33], [34:03].
- Kassam says tracking-based trait language (change of direction, accuracy) helps scouts, coaches and analysts speak the same language [34:33], [35:03].
- Barwin says big plays often happen because someone did not do what they were supposed to, which models would find hard to learn [35:33], [36:03].
- Barwin says analytics and coaches both overload people; show the few items you have conviction on, and say so when it is an experiment [39:06], [39:38], [40:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barwin entered the league in 2009 [01:33]; Eagles change in 2013 [02:03].
- Box score era around 2009; play-by-play by 2013 with about 100 times more data; Next Gen Stats in 2019; locations 10 times a second [07:06], [07:36]. Another talk in this batch gives 2018 and "a thousand times" for similar steps.
- Danielle Hunter (caption spelling), age 31 [09:39].
- At least 25 players not playing each week [11:41].
- Three-quarters of combine drills not applicable [15:47]; corner ran 4.65 (captions give a garbled name) [16:17].
- Plus-35 to 40 gray zone; scoring probability from minus 10 to minus 15 versus minus 40 [28:28], [28:59].
- Head coach has about two or three seconds to decide (speaker unclear in captions) [27:57].
- Run-game model trained on a couple million running plays [31:31]; Gibbs 18 yards [32:32]. Another talk in this batch gives about 100,000 plays.
- Caserio: four-week blocks, about eight to 10 games before teams are well known, 17 games [40:08], [40:39].
- Kassam: about 60 pass rush snaps for a get-off estimate, about 200 routes for receiver COD [41:09], [41:41].
- Roster: 20 offense, 22 defense and three specialists, as captioned (likely garbled) [44:45].
- Super Bowl team with three active receivers [44:45].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Get-off metric from tracking data and film [08:06], [08:36].
- Pass rush model treating the pocket as a surface [19:51].
- Run-game neural network attributing credit among 22 players [31:31].
- Projection system combining a player's history with current small samples [41:41].
- Four-week review blocks for team performance [40:39].
- Practice tracking over several years to benchmark players [43:14].
- Pre-game philosophy and a game management coordinator for fourth downs [22:23].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly anecdote; no data or results are shown on get-off aging, practice tracking or fourth-down outcomes.
- Kassam is a vendor executive describing his own company's metrics.
- Caption problems: Barwin's answer at [23:56] says "Nick wants to be aggressive" though the panel lists Caserio with the Texans and Barwin with the Eagles; the referent is unclear. Player names (Kemoko Turay, Kamari, Moro, Jobe) are unreliable.
- Kassam says the public and some commentators do not see that models know the roster, including defense [28:59], [29:30].
- The moderator asks about PFF grades; a speaker says most players do not like them, with no detail [37:04].
- Caserio says a limit of AI is that no database captures everything on the field [36:03]. The statement is in the moderator's turn and is unclear.

## Q&A

- Adjusting to small samples: Caserio says break the season into four-week blocks; Kassam says some metrics resolve quickly and uses projection; Barwin says practice tracking history gave confidence in one player [40:39], [41:09], [41:41], [43:14].
- Keeping judgment on a small-sample player: Barwin says know your own players and track practice [42:43], [43:14].
- Game-day roster decisions: Caserio says they depend on how you plan to play and who is available, with an example of three active receivers [44:45].

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

## Summary

An applied scientist from AWS presents work done with the NFL's Next Gen Stats team on measuring pass-rush pressure throughout a play instead of only counting sacks, hits, and hurries at the end. The framework has three parts: identify who is rushing and who is blocking, match each rusher to blockers, and estimate a pressure score between 0 and 1 at each moment. It uses public tracking data from the Big Data Bowl and labels from PFF. The speaker reports high F1 scores for the first two parts, picked a random forest for the pressure score because of better calibration, and shows example plays. Evaluation of the pressure score is only by proxy.

## Key claims

- Existing pass-rush statistics record only end results, so players who got close but did not finish the play get no credit [01:02].
- The aim is to measure pressure continuously across a play and give credit to players who apply it [01:34].
- Three technical problems are addressed: separating rushers from blockers, matching them, and estimating pressure over time [03:10].
- Automating blocker and rusher labeling replaces hand labeling of video clips, saving cost and labor [06:15].
- Two models were promising for the identification tasks, and the speaker went with AutoGluon-style models, spelled "Orum" and "autog glom" in the captions (caption spelling) [07:17].
- A graph neural network performed worse but was kept as a future direction because one model can handle both tasks [08:17].
- The pressure score is modeled as a probability on a 0 to 1 scale at any moment in the play [09:19].
- A random forest was chosen over neural or transformer models for better calibration [12:28].
- In sample plays, the score shows different players creating pressure early and late, and credits two players where the human label credited one [13:00, 14:04].
- Derived outputs include pressure time and a high-pressure zone above a 75 percent threshold [14:34].
- Rusher distance to the passer and the number of open rushers were the main factors the speaker gave [18:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- F1 of 0.99 for blocker and rusher identification and about 0.91 for matchups (captions: "0.99" and "close 0.91") [07:47]. The captions are rough, so the exact values may differ.
- Pressure score: instantaneous probability, on a 0 to 1 scale, of a rusher producing a hit, hurry, or sack [09:19].
- High-pressure zone: time above a 75 percent threshold [14:34].
- Blocker interference feature: count of offensive blockers within an area of interest between rusher and passer, defined by distance and angle [10:23].
- Target variables: PFF hurry, hit, sack labels, plus an engineered distance-based label [10:54]. The speaker's example: a rusher within one yard of the passer before one second [20:39] (garbled in captions, so the exact rule is uncertain).
- No accuracy figures are stated for the final pressure score. Evaluation was a proxy based on maximum pressure compared with PFF labels [11:26].
- Calibration measured with expected and maximum calibration error [12:28]; no values given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Data: Big Data Bowl tracking data (positions, velocity, acceleration, player IDs, play outcomes) from the NFL Next Gen Stats team and AWS [04:12, 04:42].
- Static features (initial positions, roles) and dynamic features (position, velocity, acceleration, direction), standardized before modeling [06:46].
- Sequential models: identify blockers and rushers, then match them [07:47].
- Random forest probability model for pressure, with the engineered blocker interference feature [09:51, 12:28].
- Ground truth for who blocks whom came from hand labels by the NFL and PFF [19:08].

## Limits and open questions

- Pressure score accuracy is not quantified in the captions; only a proxy evaluation is described [11:26].
- The speaker said model performance differed across player groups and there is room to improve [11:58]. The captions are garbled here.
- The model did not account for team scheme or blocking and rushing strategy [15:34].
- It does not attribute pressure to specific players: the speaker said they did not try to separate whose pressure it is [21:40], although the demonstration credits individual players.
- No correlation check against quarterback motion was done [23:13].
- The speaker acknowledged complex position features were not modeled [18:38].
- Several names and model names are garbled (Orum, autog glom, "Parson").

## Q&A

- Which is harder to find, a pass blocker or a pass rusher? Not answered directly; the speaker described which features drive pressure, mostly rusher distance, velocity, acceleration, and open lanes [17:37].
- What was the ground truth for who blocks whom? Hand labels from the NFL and PFF; handles double and triple teams [19:08].
- Should the metric favor how fast pressure arrives? Agreed; the target added a distance-and-time rule [20:09].
- How does it disentangle which player the pressure comes from? It does not; the target is forgiving to credit rushers in a threshold area [21:40].
- Was the score checked against quarterback motion? Not done; relative velocity features were used [23:13].

## Summary

Natalie, a faculty member in data science and a sports scientist at UVA, argues that athlete-health research needs shared, open collectives. She and a colleague reviewed GPS wearable studies in team field sports and found no conclusive evidence for injury prediction, citing inconsistent injury tracking, poor statistical framing, and overclaiming from small samples. She still uses wearables daily and describes a men's basketball monitoring day: wellness survey, countermovement jumps on force plates, barbell tracking, and GPS in practice. She proposes a collective with ACC peers sharing best practices, code, and longitudinal data. The collective is currently an idea with funding requested.

## Key claims

- Wearables spread across US teams around 2015 with promises of better performance, workload tracking, and injury prediction [02:01].
- Machine learning became easy to use, and papers confirming injury prediction with wearables followed [02:31].
- A review of GPS in team field sports found no conclusive evidence for using wearables to predict injury [03:03].
- Reasons: different injury-tracking methods across papers, treating injury as a pure prediction problem, and ambitious claims from small samples [03:33, 04:03].
- Overclaiming comes from both technology companies and researchers, partly because of publishing incentives [04:33].
- Coaches' stories that technology helps are useful for generating hypotheses [05:05].
- The program aims to optimize readiness and performance, expecting fewer fatigue and overuse injuries as a side effect [06:06].
- Countermovement jumps on force plates assess neuromuscular readiness, and strategy changes reveal fatigue that jump height hides [08:39].
- Daily data feeds coach-facing dashboards that inform lifting adjustments [09:09].
- The speaker holds that there is more signal in readiness than in injury [12:09].
- Sports research mostly sits low on the evidence hierarchy because randomized trials are hard, samples are small, and methods and data are rarely shared [13:11, 13:41].
- A collective could bring best practices, FAIR principles, multi-site research, and longitudinal tracking, including across the transfer portal and after careers [16:16, 17:48].
- Needs: funding, data architecture and agreements, oversight and consent, governance, metadata [18:19, 18:49].
- Athletic departments usually worry about giving away competitive advantage; the speaker argues the advantage is gone by the time academics publish, especially for health and safety data [19:56].
- The wellness data at her program has never made it into models, but works as a conversation starter [21:59].
- The speaker says she cares more about products people use daily than about papers [26:07].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables emerged in US teams around 2015 [02:01].
- Reviewed studies had single teams of about 15 people for one season [04:03].
- A player gained 24 pounds of muscle while lowering body fat and raising vertical jump [06:37]. Captions say "24 pounds of basically pure muscle"; this is the speaker's description.
- FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable [16:47].
- Evidence hierarchy: expert opinion at the bottom, then observational research, then cohort studies, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses; randomized trials are hard in sport [12:41, 13:11].
- She says "maybe 2%" of the room reads academic papers [15:45]; this is an offhand estimate.
- Collective idea discussed for about four years [24:02].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Review of GPS wearables in team field sports with a co-author (caption spelling "Jay hurdle") [03:03].
- UVA daily session: wellness questionnaire, optional smart ring, dashboards, countermovement jump on force plates, Perch barbell velocity camera, Catapult GPS worn between the shoulder blades, evening database for coaches [07:38 to 11:09].
- Overuse injury model credited to "koven" (caption spelling), described as open source [11:39]; a UVA model focused on optimal readiness [12:09].
- Hierarchy of evidence pyramid [12:41].
- FAIR principles, shared code instead of shared data, federated learning, a partner with data governance [16:47, 17:17, 25:05].
- UVA Sports Science and Analytics Collective, with an ACC peer effort [14:11, 14:43].

## Limits and open questions

- The review's details are not shown: how many studies, which databases, or which effect sizes. Only the conclusion is given.
- The basketball example was chosen to avoid privacy issues [05:35]; no injury results are shown.
- The claim that readiness work reduces overuse injuries is the speaker's expectation, not a tested result [06:06].
- Collective status: an idea with funding applied for, and peer schools may meet to judge feasibility [23:31, 24:02].
- Privacy and governance are unresolved [24:32].
- The speaker acknowledged she should run A/B tests on dashboards [26:07].
- Several names are caption spellings.

## Q&A

- Do coaches and athletic departments fear giving away secrets, and could pro players associations mandate this? Fear is the usual obstacle; advantage fades; pros already do league-level research [19:26].
- How does the human element fit with digital athlete data? Wellness data is a conversation starter; the speaker wants humans kept in the loop [20:58, 21:59].
- What stage is the collective at? An idea, funding requested, peer meeting planned [23:31].
- What about privacy? Plan to use a partner with governance, possibly federated learning [24:32].
- How does research return to coaches and athletes? Build daily-use products, get immediate feedback, include athletes as users [25:35].

## Summary

Natalie, a faculty member in data science and a sports scientist at UVA, argues that athlete-health research needs shared, open collectives. She and a colleague reviewed GPS wearable studies in team field sports and found no conclusive evidence for injury prediction, citing inconsistent injury tracking, poor statistical framing, and overclaiming from small samples. She still uses wearables daily and describes a men's basketball monitoring day: wellness survey, countermovement jumps on force plates, barbell tracking, and GPS in practice. She proposes a collective with ACC peers sharing best practices, code, and longitudinal data. The collective is currently an idea with funding requested.

## Key claims

- Wearables spread across US teams around 2015 with promises of better performance, workload tracking, and injury prediction [02:01].
- Machine learning became easy to use, and papers confirming injury prediction with wearables followed [02:31].
- A review of GPS in team field sports found no conclusive evidence for using wearables to predict injury [03:03].
- Reasons: different injury-tracking methods across papers, treating injury as a pure prediction problem, and ambitious claims from small samples [03:33, 04:03].
- Overclaiming comes from both technology companies and researchers, partly because of publishing incentives [04:33].
- Coaches' stories that technology helps are useful for generating hypotheses [05:05].
- The program aims to optimize readiness and performance, expecting fewer fatigue and overuse injuries as a side effect [06:06].
- Countermovement jumps on force plates assess neuromuscular readiness, and strategy changes reveal fatigue that jump height hides [08:39].
- Daily data feeds coach-facing dashboards that inform lifting adjustments [09:09].
- The speaker holds that there is more signal in readiness than in injury [12:09].
- Sports research mostly sits low on the evidence hierarchy because randomized trials are hard, samples are small, and methods and data are rarely shared [13:11, 13:41].
- A collective could bring best practices, FAIR principles, multi-site research, and longitudinal tracking, including across the transfer portal and after careers [16:16, 17:48].
- Needs: funding, data architecture and agreements, oversight and consent, governance, metadata [18:19, 18:49].
- Athletic departments usually worry about giving away competitive advantage; the speaker argues the advantage is gone by the time academics publish, especially for health and safety data [19:56].
- The wellness data at her program has never made it into models, but works as a conversation starter [21:59].
- The speaker says she cares more about products people use daily than about papers [26:07].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables emerged in US teams around 2015 [02:01].
- Reviewed studies had single teams of about 15 people for one season [04:03].
- A player gained 24 pounds of muscle while lowering body fat and raising vertical jump [06:37]. Captions say "24 pounds of basically pure muscle"; this is the speaker's description.
- FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable [16:47].
- Evidence hierarchy: expert opinion at the bottom, then observational research, then cohort studies, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses; randomized trials are hard in sport [12:41, 13:11].
- She says "maybe 2%" of the room reads academic papers [15:45]; this is an offhand estimate.
- Collective idea discussed for about four years [24:02].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Review of GPS wearables in team field sports with a co-author (caption spelling "Jay hurdle") [03:03].
- UVA daily session: wellness questionnaire, optional smart ring, dashboards, countermovement jump on force plates, Perch barbell velocity camera, Catapult GPS worn between the shoulder blades, evening database for coaches [07:38 to 11:09].
- Overuse injury model credited to "koven" (caption spelling), described as open source [11:39]; a UVA model focused on optimal readiness [12:09].
- Hierarchy of evidence pyramid [12:41].
- FAIR principles, shared code instead of shared data, federated learning, a partner with data governance [16:47, 17:17, 25:05].
- UVA Sports Science and Analytics Collective, with an ACC peer effort [14:11, 14:43].

## Limits and open questions

- The review's details are not shown: how many studies, which databases, or which effect sizes. Only the conclusion is given.

- The claim that readiness work reduces overuse injuries is the speaker's expectation, not a tested result [06:06].

## Summary

Jack Jones, co-founder and COO of SumerSports, splits football analytics into four areas: personnel selection, performance maximization, play design, and in-game decision making. He argues each is a search space too large for a person to explore, and cites estimated counts for rosters, player improvement paths, offensive plays, and game sequences. His company started with roster building. It scores a whole roster with one number, "roster value", then uses an optimizer to find the highest-value roster that fits the salary cap and player availability. The tool accepts user overrides and club-provided positional weights. The talk is a company pitch, and no accuracy results are shown.

## Key claims

- Football analytics can be split into four areas: personnel selection, performance maximization, play design, and in-game decision making [01:37].
- Personnel selection is hard because of other teams, injuries, contracts, the cap, and varying player scale [02:38].
- The speaker holds that no club or third party is seriously calculating a single measure of whole-roster strength, which his company calls roster value [11:22].
- Many metrics exist for evaluating a wide receiver, but none for a whole roster [11:54].
- Roster value is built from player grades, positional importance, and snap distribution, summed across the roster [12:55].
- The approach has three steps: define roster value, list all feasible rosters under availability and cap limits, pick the highest-value one [12:24].
- A roster that cannot fit under the cap is excluded from the feasible list [13:55].
- Signing is treated as a yes or no decision, which makes this a discrete optimization problem [14:26].
- The problem is too large to list every roster, so the team shapes it into a form that solves in seconds [15:27].
- Decision variables include "stint paths" (how a club handles a player over time, such as drafting and later cutting) and role assignments (position and depth) [15:27].
- The optimizer plans several future seasons, and users can weight them depending on whether they are contending or rebuilding [16:59].
- Users can override the system, for example by barring a signing or a draft before a given round, to cover intangibles [17:30].
- The system is meant to augment human decisions, not replace them [18:32].
- The tool uses a club's own information and tries to optimize it rather than dictate what to optimize [21:07].
- Positional importance has defaults but is adjusted using a club survey, because schemes differ [22:41].
- Cap value beyond the projection horizon is handled as assets and liabilities, such as carryover and dead money [24:47].

## Numbers and definitions

- Roster value: a single measure of overall roster strength [11:22]. Defined as the sum of player performance values, each built from grade, positional importance, and snaps [12:55].
- Roughly 150 snaps per game and 22 players on the field [01:07]. Later given as 154 plays in a game [08:17].
- 53-man roster [02:38]. Hypothetical GM fills 18 spots, with 35 under contract: 11 from free agency, 7 from the draft [03:08].
- Hypothetical pools of 100 free agents and 150 draft prospects [03:08]. The captions give "100 and 150" and the combinatorics are garbled ("1527" and "41 septillion" at [03:40]); the speaker's stated order of magnitude is 10 to the 25th rosters [03:40]. Treat the exact figure as unverified.
- About 100 trillion synapses [04:10]; roughly 600 muscles, 300 joints, four movements per joint, average 90 degrees of range [04:40]; roughly 65 million physical ways to execute a task, and 100 trillion plus 65 million combined ways to improve a player [05:12]. The captions garble part of this arithmetic.
- 36 million offensive passing plays and 17,280 running plays under the speaker's route-tree coding [06:13]. The captions garble this sentence ("36 million 17 200" at [06:45]).
- Chess comparison: 40 turns per game and about 30 moves per piece per turn, against 154 football plays [08:17]. Shannon's chess figure of 10 to the 120th, and about 10 to the 80th atoms in the observable universe [08:47].
- Average GM tenure of 2.1 years over five years, and average head coach tenure of four years [09:50].
- SumerSports formed in January 2022 [10:22].
- Over 200,000 decision variables in the optimizer [15:58].
- Projection horizon number: the captions give "25th season" [16:59]; this is likely a garbled year and should not be cited.
- Beta with two clubs, tied to the draft [20:37].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Four-quadrant framework for football analytics [01:37].
- Roster value built from player grades, positional importance, and snap distribution [12:55].
- Integer programming (a kind of discrete optimization), reformulated as a convex, linear problem to solve in seconds [14:57, 15:27].
- Stint paths and role assignments as decision variables; multi-season projection with user weighting [15:58, 16:59].
- User constraints and club-supplied positional importance via a survey [17:30, 22:41].
- A team member with ten years of club experience supplies cap knowledge [24:14].
- The product name appears in the captions as "Marvel" (caption spelling).

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, back-test, or example roster results are shown. Evidence is the speaker's description.
- How player grades are produced and combined across positions is not described.
- When asked whether linearizing and convexifying the problem loses optimality, the speaker said he was not the optimization expert and offered to follow up [21:37]. The question was not answered.
- The search-space counts are rough, partly garbled in the captions, and describe size, not quality of decisions.
- The speaker's claims about competitors and market gaps are the company's own view.
- The tool covered the draft in beta at the time, with a year-round tool in development [23:12].
- Method for market value and contract cost: only cap handling is described, not how player prices are estimated [24:14].
- The talk concerns NFL cap and roster structure and may not transfer to college.

## Q&A

- Would the company work in other leagues such as the NBA? Football focus for now, others possible later [20:04].
- Are some teams more data driven or more resistant? A beta with two clubs; interest varies; the tool uses club information [20:37].
- Does linearizing or convexifying the integer program make results suboptimal? Acknowledged a trade-off, deferred to the optimization team [21:37].
- Is positional value set by the club's scheme? Yes, defaults plus a club survey [22:11].
- Is the tool year-round? Currently draft-focused, working toward a year-round tool [23:12].
- How are market value and cap effects handled? Cap handling by a former club staffer; beyond-horizon effects via assets and liabilities [23:43].

title: "SSAC24: Research Collectives: The Call for Large-Scale, Open Science Initiatives in Sports Science"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making]

## Summary

Natalie, a faculty member in data science and a sports scientist at UVA, argues that athlete-health research needs shared, open collectives. She and a colleague reviewed GPS wearable studies in team field sports and found no conclusive evidence for injury prediction, citing inconsistent injury tracking, poor statistical framing, and overclaiming from small samples. She still uses wearables daily and describes a men's basketball monitoring day: wellness survey, countermovement jumps on force plates, barbell tracking, and GPS in practice. She proposes a collective with ACC peers sharing best practices, code, and longitudinal data. The collective is currently an idea with funding requested.

## Key claims

- Wearables spread across US teams around 2015 with promises of better performance, workload tracking, and injury prediction [02:01].
- Machine learning became easy to use, and papers confirming injury prediction with wearables followed [02:31].
- A review of GPS in team field sports found no conclusive evidence for using wearables to predict injury [03:03].
- Reasons: different injury-tracking methods across papers, treating injury as a pure prediction problem, and ambitious claims from small samples [03:33, 04:03].
- Overclaiming comes from both technology companies and researchers, partly because of publishing incentives [04:33].
- Coaches' stories that technology helps are useful for generating hypotheses [05:05].
- The program aims to optimize readiness and performance, expecting fewer fatigue and overuse injuries as a side effect [06:06].
- Countermovement jumps on force plates assess neuromuscular readiness, and strategy changes reveal fatigue that jump height hides [08:39].
- Daily data feeds coach-facing dashboards that inform lifting adjustments [09:09].
- The speaker holds that there is more signal in readiness than in injury [12:09].
- Sports research mostly sits low on the evidence hierarchy because randomized trials are hard, samples are small, and methods and data are rarely shared [13:11, 13:41].
- A collective could bring best practices, FAIR principles, multi-site research, and longitudinal tracking, including across the transfer portal and after careers [16:16, 17:48].
- Needs: funding, data architecture and agreements, oversight and consent, governance, metadata [18:19, 18:49].
- Athletic departments usually worry about giving away competitive advantage; the speaker argues the advantage is gone by the time academics publish, especially for health and safety data [19:56].
- The wellness data at her program has never made it into models, but works as a conversation starter [21:59].
- The speaker says she cares more about products people use daily than about papers [26:07].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables emerged in US teams around 2015 [02:01].
- Reviewed studies had single teams of about 15 people for one season [04:03].
- A player gained 24 pounds of muscle while lowering body fat and raising vertical jump [06:37]. Captions say "24 pounds of basically pure muscle"; this is the speaker's description.
- FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable [16:47].
- Evidence hierarchy: expert opinion at the bottom, then observational research, then cohort studies, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses; randomized trials are hard in sport [12:41, 13:11].
- She says "maybe 2%" of the room reads academic papers [15:45]; this is an offhand estimate.
- Collective idea discussed for about four years [24:02].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Review of GPS wearables in team field sports with a co-author (caption spelling "Jay hurdle") [03:03].
- UVA daily session: wellness questionnaire, optional smart ring, dashboards, countermovement jump on force plates, Perch barbell velocity camera, Catapult GPS worn between the shoulder blades, evening database for coaches [07:38 to 11:09].
- Overuse injury model credited to "koven" (caption spelling), described as open source [11:39]; a UVA model focused on optimal readiness [12:09].
- Hierarchy of evidence pyramid [12:41].
- FAIR principles, shared code instead of shared data, federated learning, a partner with data governance [16:47, 17:17, 25:05].
- UVA Sports Science and Analytics Collective, with an ACC peer effort [14:11, 14:43].

## Limits and open questions

- The review's details are not shown: how many studies, which databases, or which effect sizes. Only the conclusion is given.
- The basketball example was chosen to avoid privacy issues [05:35]; no injury results are shown.
- The claim that readiness work reduces overuse injuries is the speaker's expectation, not a tested result [06:06].
- Collective status: an idea with funding applied for, and peer schools may meet to judge feasibility [23:31, 24:02].
- Privacy and governance are unresolved [24:32].
- The speaker acknowledged she should run A/B tests on dashboards [26:07].
- Several names are caption spellings.

## Q&A

- Do coaches and athletic departments fear giving away secrets, and could pro players associations mandate this? Fear is the usual obstacle; advantage fades; pros already do league-level research [19:26].
- How does the human element fit with digital athlete data? Wellness data is a conversation starter; the speaker wants humans kept in the loop [20:58, 21:59].
- What stage is the collective at? An idea, funding requested, peer meeting planned [23:31].
- What about privacy? Plan to use a partner with governance, possibly federated learning [24:32].
- How does research return to coaches and athletes? Build daily-use products, get immediate feedback, include athletes as users [25:35].

The key idea for trades is three values: what a pick is worth historically, what a given player is worth to this team, and what the league is likely to think the pick is worth. A gap among them can justify trading up even though the conventional analytics view says trade back. All figures shown are synthetic, and no validation is presented.

## Key claims

- Margins in the NFL are thin: every Super Bowl point spread since 2009 has been five points or less, and the Chiefs, with top talent, were favored in only two of their four Super Bowls [02:06], [02:36].
- The search space is huge: roughly nine quadrillion possible draft classes from over 700 scouted players, and about 92 billion ways to fill the last 12 roster spots [03:37], [04:07], [04:40].
- Marvel (maximizing roster value) judges any proposed roster with one number, factoring in injuries and psychometrics, and then optimizes across possible rosters given player availability [06:13], [06:45], [07:16].

- Pick value $14 million; league value 19.4, against 20.2, 20.8 and 12.8 at neighboring examples; speaker cites team value near $27 million [13:54], [14:56].

Marvel roster-value framework [06:13]; roster optimization across availability [06:45]; simulation of draft scenarios [11:22]; three draft values (pick, team, league) [08:50]; a trade evaluator for break-even analysis [24:17]; SumerScout grades from former GMs, third-party licensed data, tracking-based athleticism measures [19:06], [20:09]; simulation of future seasons for future picks [20:39].

All read from slides and stated as "about". The "twoth thirs" caption is garbled.

title: "SSAC24: A New Generation: The Next Era of College Athletics"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Warren Zola (moderator), Brian Higgins, Val (caption spelling "Akerman"), Martin (caption spelling "Charmin"), Tommy Gray, Max Williams (student host)]
topics: [policy, american-football, basketball]
confidence: supported

## Summary

A panel on where college athletics goes next. Four leaders (a national-office executive, a conference commissioner, an athletic director and a sports-business adviser) discuss NIL, possible employee status, realignment and the NCAA president's proposal to separate rules for the wealthiest programs. They agree the old model is breaking and that courts may decide many outcomes. They also stress the education and life-skill benefits of college sport, and end on optimism. No data or analysis is shown. The talk matters as an account of how people running the system describe its pressure points, not as evidence about them.

## Key claims

- The NCAA strategic scan sees football and men's basketball as the revenue engine and women's sports as a fast-growing strength; the national office also needs to serve members better [06:09], [06:41], [07:12].
- Commercial pressure sits in a narrow band of programs, mainly football and some men's basketball, while most of Division I does not share it [10:13].
- Labor law, antitrust law and Title IX collide in college sport, and the commissioner worries decisions will be forced by courts [11:15], [12:19].
- The athletic director describes NIL as helping athletes pay for family travel and send money home, and calls college sport a business that must be run as one while keeping education [14:51], [15:23], [16:25].
- The adviser says the old model is effectively dead and the new one is not yet born [17:56].
- The commissioner sees the NCAA national budget as funded mainly by March Madness, so keeping the tournament together matters [22:32].
- The NCAA speaker describes the president's proposal as three parts: remove compensation caps, let schools contract directly on NIL, and allow different rules for the wealthiest conferences while keeping common standards such as academic eligibility [26:04], [26:35], [27:06].
- A school paying an athlete directly for NIL is described as the "third rail" because it moves toward employment [29:09]. Which panelist says the following employment-consequence remarks is unclear in the captions [29:09].
- The injunction in the Tennessee-Virginia case covers third parties dealing with prospects, not schools; the adviser says that activity was already happening in football and men's basketball [36:53], [37:23].
- UCLA's reasons for joining the Big Ten include competition, academic fit, exposure for NIL, and revenue to support Olympic sports [31:42], [32:12], [33:13], [33:43].
- Panelists say cost is what the public most misses (departments mostly lose money), that leaders are rational actors in a broken system, and that the education benefit is underrated [42:31], [43:02], [43:33], [44:04], [44:35].
- Worries named: separating the education goal from financial reality, a breakaway of 30 or 40 football schools, cuts to Olympic sports, and harassment of athletes tied to wagering [48:44], [49:14], [49:46], [50:17], [50:47], [51:17].

## Numbers and definitions

- Division I athletics generates about $16 billion a year, per the moderator [03:07]. About $1.25 billion goes to the NCAA, mostly from March Madness [03:37]. These are the moderator's framing figures, unsourced on stage.
- NCAA founded 1906 [02:06]; over 1,200 schools, about 65 in the power conferences [03:07] (caption garbles "NCAA" as "nle").
- 40 of the 50 highest-paid state employees are college coaches; 11 coaches earn over $9 million [03:37].
- Ohio State about a quarter billion in revenue; 40 schools over $100 million [04:07].
- Conference size changes since 2006: Big Ten 12 to 18, ACC 13 to 17, SEC 12 to 16, Pac-10 to 2 [04:07], [04:37].
- 360 Division I schools [10:13]. Big East: 11 schools, double round robin, 28 to 30 basketball games [21:01], [21:32].
- March Madness described as 16 days of ticket, media and sponsorship revenue [22:32].
- UCLA: 700 athletes, over 350 with NIL deals [32:12]; 121 national championships, second most [33:43].
- Adviser's firm: 42 Division I departments as clients [18:26].
- Post-eligibility injury insurance for all athletes in Divisions I, II and III starting in August (year not stated) [07:12].
- Number of schools in a breakaway: "30 or 40" is a figure the speaker says is "around" [49:46].
- "NIL" defined by the commissioner as college speak for endorsement deals [28:08].

## Methods and frameworks named

No data or models. Frameworks: the NCAA's strategic-scan strengths and weaknesses [05:38]; Project D1 proposal (caps removed, direct school NIL, differentiated rules) [26:04]; the adviser's interim-period framing of preparing for several possible future models [17:56].

## Limits and open questions

- Opinion panel; no data shown, and the moderator's figures are not sourced.
- Speakers have institutional or commercial stakes (a conference, a university, the NCAA, a consulting firm with clients [18:26]).
- Largely uniform optimism; the panel itself notes it deliberately pushed against doom [39:59].
- Legal facts are as of March 2024 and describe pending cases (injunction, employment status, the NCAA proposal), which the panel says could change.
- Speaker attribution is unclear in several stretches because the captions lack names.
- The panel is mostly about revenue sports and top programs; the commissioner concedes this is a narrow band [10:13].

## Q&A

No separate audience Q&A appears; the moderator folded audience questions into the "what keeps you up at night" round [48:14].

## Summary

The VP of research and development at SumerSports presents a draft decision tool built on a roster-value framework called Marvel. Starting from the thin margins and vast combinatorics of NFL roster building, he shows a dashboard that takes a club's own player grades and turns them into roster-level recommendations. The key idea for trades is three values: what a pick is worth historically, what a given player is worth to this team, and what the league is likely to think the pick is worth. A gap among them can justify trading up even though the conventional analytics view says trade back. All figures shown are synthetic, and no validation is presented.

## Key claims

- Margins in the NFL are thin: every Super Bowl point spread since 2009 has been five points or less, and the Chiefs, with top talent, were favored in only two of their four Super Bowls [02:06], [02:36].
- The search space is huge: roughly nine quadrillion possible draft classes from over 700 scouted players, and about 92 billion ways to fill the last 12 roster spots [03:37], [04:07], [04:40].
- Marvel (maximizing roster value) judges any proposed roster with one number, factoring in injuries and psychometrics, and then optimizes across possible rosters given player availability [06:13], [06:45], [07:16].
- The dashboard's design bet is that clubs grade their own players well but are not equipped to synthesize those grades into roster value, so it converts club micro-evaluations into macro recommendations [08:17], [08:50].
- Pick value is the historical value of a pick with quarterbacks removed; team value is what the projected player is worth to that team; league value is a position-weighted blend reflecting how likely each position is to go at that slot [12:53], [13:24], [13:54].
- A trade-up is signalled when team value exceeds both pick value and league value; the speaker applies this to a quarterback example and cites Mahomes as a trade-up many thought too expensive [14:25], [14:56].
- The speaker frames the standard analytics view (trade back, because trading up is negative expected value) as the loser's curse result, and says the three-value view finds exceptions [12:23], [14:25].

type: video-summary
video_id: tPgCcRc7rR0
title: "SSAC24: Using Data to Support College Athlete Mental Health"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kimberly O'Brien, Isabella Deo (student host)]
topics: [injury-health]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A therapist and founder describes the mental health situation of college athletes using a large NCAA survey, then presents a peer-support app (captioned "Endur"; the video description says NDUR) as a response. She argues that athletes often do not feel mental health is a priority or feel comfortable seeking campus help, so peer support can serve as a way in. She shows what the app's mood and forum data suggest, a pilot adoption rate and an internal satisfaction survey. The evidence is about uptake and user opinion, not about whether mental health improves, and the speaker works for the product.

## Key claims

- The NCAA 2022 to 2023 survey (over 23,000 athlete respondents) showed concerns mainly about overwhelm, sleep, mental exhaustion and anxiety, disproportionately among women [02:07], [02:38].
- Academic worries and planning for the future are major factors, and athletes carry about a 20-hour commitment that most students do not [02:38], [03:09].
- Only about half see athlete mental health as a priority, and about half feel comfortable seeking a campus professional; about two thirds know where to go [03:40], [04:10], [04:40].
- Peer support should never replace treatment but can augment it; she says research ties more social support to lower depressive symptoms (no source named) [05:41], [06:13].
- A peer model should let athletes share experiences, give access to coping content, and link to campus support [06:13], [06:43].
- The app uses mood entries to send tailored content, and aggregate mood shows overwhelm and exhaustion as the top negative emotions, matching the NCAA data [07:14], [10:20].
- A rower anecdote is offered as a case where in-the-moment coping skills might have prevented an injury [08:48], [09:18]. This is one case and her interpretation.
- Injuries are among the main topics in the anonymous forum, where athletes value talking to someone who has been through one [11:53], [12:24].
- Adoption and engagement data must be tracked alongside the app's features [12:54].
- Some athletes avoid counseling for fear a coach will find out or that it will affect play [16:00].
- Athletes must be involved in development and testing [17:03].

## Numbers and definitions

- NCAA survey: over 23,000 respondents, 2022 to 2023 [02:07].
- About two thirds know how to help a teammate and feel teammates take mental health seriously; about half feel it is a priority; about two thirds know where to go on campus; about half are comfortable seeing a campus professional [03:09], [03:40], [04:40]. All read from slides and stated as "about". The "twoth thirs" caption is garbled.
- About a quarter or less think their self-esteem would improve from therapy; less than a quarter would feel inadequate seeking services [05:10]. The captions are loose here.
- About half of logged moods are positive and half negative [10:20].
- Boston College pilot: 70 of 835 athletes on the platform, an adoption rate of 8.4%; 14 of 31 teams, 45% [13:24].
- Internal survey: about 70% very helpful; about three quarters found forum topics relevant; 82% met health and wellness needs; 90% said it enhances self-care [14:26], [14:58]. Number of respondents not given.

## Methods and frameworks named

Peer-to-peer support model with three requirements [06:13]; mood tracking with pushed content [07:14]; polling for challenges [10:50]; anonymous peer forum [11:21]; adoption and engagement tracking [12:54]; internal user-experience survey [14:26]; iterative changes with athlete involvement [17:03].

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker is affiliated with the product; no independent evaluation.
- No outcome data on mental health change, symptoms or help-seeking after use.
- Adoption was 8.4% in the pilot, and mood data come only from self-selected users.
- Survey sample size, response rate and wording are not stated.
- The injury-prevention claim rests on one anecdote.
- The research on social support and depression is cited without a source.
- Content personalization currently uses only the emotion entered [22:38].

## Q&A

- Can coaches see team-level data? Institutions can see de-identified data by sport [18:05], [18:36].
- Differences by division? Not significantly different in the NCAA data, from her memory [19:07], [19:37], [20:07].
- Barriers to adoption? App fatigue; peer interaction, in-person events and student ambassadors help [20:37], [21:07], [21:37], [22:07].
- Personalization? Based on the emotion entered [22:07], [22:38].
- Diagnosed conditions? Content on ADHD, autism, financial literacy, gambling and social media [23:10], [23:40].
- Injury versus academic stress? Loss of sport and return pressure are hard [24:13], [24:43], [25:13].

## Summary

An NHL panel with two assistant general managers (New Jersey, Florida), the head of a hockey data company, and an ESPN-affiliated former player as moderator. They discuss how a hard salary cap shapes roster building: planning a contention window around core players, structuring contracts so they stay tradeable, buying or selling at the deadline, and balancing analytics against leadership and culture. Later sections cover player tracking and sports science, how coaches and players take up data, and why amateur scouting has weak data. The views are those of executives describing their own organizations, with no data shown.

## Key claims

- A team's levers are picks, prospects, the roster and cap space, and some players who must be drafted and developed become too costly to buy later [02:34].
- Retaining talent depends on a culture and identity that gets core players to buy in [03:37].
- Rebuild or retool decisions need honesty about where the team is and discipline to the plan despite outside pressure [04:38].
- Intangibles such as leadership and veteran experience carry weight beside points and goals, as seen from the Devils' youth two years ago [06:08].
- The deadline was unusually busy and often needed a third team to retain salary [09:41]; first and second round picks were fetching less than before [10:12].
- The Presidents' Trophy winner rarely wins the Cup because playoff hockey is a different matchup style [10:43].
- A trade target has to fit on salary, culture and analytics at once, and negotiations run for days or weeks [12:16], [12:47].
- Front-loaded bonuses let large-market teams keep contracts tradeable, and a nearby minor-league affiliate adds flexibility [16:23].
- Teams build a checklist of traits (faceoffs, penalty kill, leadership) and compare it with what the roster already has; relationships with other teams and scouts fill in intangibles [17:56], [18:28].
- Alignment of core players' contract timelines with the team's window matters more than one season's push; the aim is to stay competitive for eight or nine years [22:32], [23:02].
- Opportunity is often what finds value in overlooked players [28:15].
- Goalie performance above expectation is not reliably repeatable [29:47].
- The hard cap makes building a dynasty harder, mainly because core players leave and synergy is lost [31:17], [31:47]; Megan sees both benefit (parity) and cost (pay for superstars) [25:07], [26:09].
- Teams value picks with internal and external models and a values chart, and contracts with comparables plus models [32:47], [33:18], [33:48].
- Management decides; players influence by performance; the group deliberates with differing views [34:51], [35:23].
- A pick's worth depends on whether it is the missing piece, so going all in is hard to quantify [37:24], [37:55].
- Player and puck tracking is still early (a year or so of use) and hard because hockey is fluid [38:57], [39:28]; it could support sports science and injury identification [41:00], [41:31].
- Coaches, especially assistants, are more engaged with data than five years ago [43:02], [44:02].
- A sport scientist's role is to flag deviations from baseline and propose lighter practices, not bench stars, with an "80 20" rule for plan adherence [46:05], [46:37].
- Players are interested in data; the panel describes them as year-round athletes [48:09], [50:11].
- Amateur data is thin and uneven across countries, and tracking indoors has occlusion problems [51:43], [53:16], [54:18].
- Draft logic differs by origin and age: a European project must finish by 21, a college one by 24 [55:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- Presidents' Trophy and Cup history: Bruins contenders for 13 years since the 2011 Cup [02:03].
- Devils won "13 games in a row" (Kate's words) [06:08].
- "Over 40 trades" at the deadline [09:11].
- Example of an avoided contract: "12 million dollars" [03:04].
- Brett was an agent for 15 years [14:21].
- Tampa described as having gone through it "eight nine years" [08:40]; the Devils aim to be in the same spot in eight or nine years [22:32].
- Shifts "30 seconds to 50 to a minute and a half" [38:57].
- Tracking in use "a year year and a half" [39:28].
- Draft ages 21 and 24 [55:52].
- "80 20" rule: 80 percent follow the plan, 20 percent deviate [46:37].
- Hockey player development staffs described as about three people versus about 100 at the Mets [44:32].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Pick value chart and internal asset models; contract comparables plus models [32:47], [33:48].
- Intangibles checklist against current roster gaps [17:56].
- Baseline-deviation sport science monitoring with coach communication [46:05].
- Puck and player tracking used with the team's own data [39:28].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes or outcome tests are shown; most claims are executive opinion or institutional practice.
- Kate says she cannot explain the models, which belong to her analytics group [32:47].
- The panel offers no measure of the intangibles it values.
- Megan's view of the cap is mixed and partly rhetorical.
- Several panelists' tracking remarks are unattributed in the captions; the moderator later credits Kate with the point about analytics adoption [42:31].
- Names are garbled in captions (for example players and teams around [27:13]).

## Q&A

- Methods for valuing future assets: values chart plus models [32:47].
- Do players take part in decisions: not formally, performance informs [34:20].
- Opinion on LTIR use: rule should be applied evenly [35:54].
- Can going all in be quantified: hard, picks lost signal it [36:54].
- Puck and player tracking use: early, promising for sports science [38:27].
- Coach adoption of analytics: growing, especially assistants [42:31].
- Data and hockey experience communication: scheduling and language [45:33].
- Player interest in data: high [47:07].
- Amateur data gap: large, scouting still central [51:43].
- Draft decisions by round and position: needs and ages matter [55:20].
