## Summary

A panel on high-stakes performance with a masters marathoner, a triathlon performance head, and a former Navy SEAL and astronaut. They discuss preparing for extreme conditions, treating fear as uncertainty, team culture and leadership, and the limits of data. The triathlon coach argues that measurement and physics-style thinking can push outcomes toward predictability, but that the step from world class to champion depends on human factors that are not measured. On fatigue, the astronaut stresses sleep and days off, and the runner stresses listening to the body. Most claims are personal experience and anecdote, not tested evidence.

## Key claims

- Roberta prepared for a hot midnight world marathon by slowing her goal pace, running long runs in heat in layers, and shifting her sleep to the race time zone [02:37], [03:08], [03:38].
- Olav says Kona can be made more predictable by studying conditions, ignoring myths and combining environmental data with real-time physiology and big data analysis [05:10], [05:40], [06:44].
- After Tokyo, his goal shifted from beating a rival profile to asking what is humanly possible, comparing his athletes with the fastest swimmers, cyclists and marathoners [13:56], [14:28], [14:59].
- His outsider status let him treat each athlete as a research project through monitoring and observation [16:32], [17:02].
- Chris says fear rises with uncertainty and training reduces uncertainty; the pool cannot simulate the 45 minutes of dark and light in orbit [08:49], [09:50].
- A shared training base lets a team deviate quickly within mission parameters [10:20].
- Treating the environment as the enemy helps avoid complacency [10:50], [11:21].
- "Commander's intent" lets people act on the mission's vision without constant instruction [20:35].
- Roberta says to race yourself and control your own outcome [21:37].
- Olav says reaching world class can be nearly automated, but moving to champion is an art and involves unquantifiable factors [22:38], [23:10].
- At camps, each athlete presents a competitive advantage to avoid complacency, and a coach's care and action matter ("humans first") [23:41], [25:41], [32:58].
- Chris describes leadership and followership flowing between people in space crews [29:16].
- Innate size and shape matter, and mental compartmentalizing separates performance [39:11], [39:42].
- Olav argues research is often too narrow to use and organizes performance as velocity, mechanical work, metabolic power and fuel [42:49], [43:20], [44:23].
- Data is information, not an absolute verdict; sensors can be introduced early if playful, not judgmental [49:32], [50:34], [51:05].
- Roberta advises listening to the body and taking a day off when fatigued [51:37].
- On the space station, sleep is scheduled at eight hours; long stretches without a day off raise error risk, so NASA tries to repay days off promptly [52:40], [54:11], [55:15].
- Olav says fatigue recognition comes from experience in training, and sometimes a calculated risk to push through is taken, which must be practiced [55:45], [56:49], [57:20].

## Numbers and definitions

- 2019 world marathon in Doha: midnight start, about 90 degrees, almost 80 percent humidity, and "41" dropouts, said by the moderator as a rate and as a count (unclear whether percent or runners; Roberta also says "41") [01:35], [02:07], [02:37].
- Pace changed from 5:45 to 6:15 per mile (caption) [02:37]; Roberta placed sixth [01:35].
- Roberta's age: moderator says 42 [02:07]; she says "45" at the time of speaking [34:00]; took a 10-year break [11:52].
- Kona race length described as about seven and a half hours, 7:40 for winners [04:08]; the winner's time was predicted "within a minute" per the moderator [04:38] (Olav's reply is garbled [07:15]).
- Orbit every 90 minutes, 45 minutes dark and 45 minutes light [08:49].
- SEAL training six months, hell week in the fifth week [27:43].
- Sleep scheduled eight hours [52:40]; 14 or 20 straight days without a day off [54:11].
- Free throw charity: 10 grand if made [37:35].
- Olav's four domains: velocity, work (mechanical power), metabolic power, fuel [44:23].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Input, efficiency and output (physics) view of performance [43:52].
- Meal energy measured by bomb calorimeter, with collection of waste to measure absorption [45:25], [45:55].
- Real-time in-body monitoring and big data projection [06:44].
- ISS crew experiments and sampling [47:59].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly anecdote; no sample sizes or controls.
- The "predicted within a minute" claim is made by the moderator, and Olav's response is garbled [07:15].
- Olav's methods and results reflect his own program; no outside verification.
- Astronaut and SEAL comments are not about sport athletes' physical data.
- The Apollo-versus-iPhone comparison was stated without exact numbers [06:11].
- Surname spellings garbled (Olav, Roberta).

## Q&A

- Does the military or NASA capture data to improve preparation: not in daily training; ISS crews are sampled for experiments [47:27].
- Drawbacks of relying heavily on data: treat it as information, not absolute [49:32].
- Balancing peak performance with injury or burnout risk: listen to the body, protect sleep, days off, calculated risk [51:37].

## Summary

A workshop by a former NBA analytics executive on how to combine models with expert judgment in draft decisions. He demonstrates the conjunction fallacy with an audience poll, then runs a five-player draft exercise and reveals it was his own team's first overall pick, a notable failure. He contrasts a "seat at the table" model, where data and people argue and one side wins, with a "data centered" process that starts from the model, has experts state hypotheses for why it is wrong, tests them, and updates or drops them. The Q&A covers trust, communication, time pressure and explainable models. The author cannot prove the process would have changed the pick.

## Key claims

- Judge a decision by the process across many repeated decisions, not the single outcome observed [01:31], [02:01].
- People favor a coherent story over probability; the audience repeated the conjunction fallacy [04:41].
- Cognitive biases are systematic effects of how information is framed, and data helps avoid them [06:43], [07:13].
- Humans offer narrative, creativity and deep knowledge but have bias and limited viewing; models are consistent and large-scale but miss variables and intangibles [18:41], [19:12], [19:45].
- Unlike web A/B tests with millions of data points, projecting college players leaves huge uncertainty [20:15].
- Data-centered decision making starts at the model and asks experts why it might be wrong, then tests each hypothesis and adjusts or rejects it; it differs from simply following the model [21:48], [23:25], [24:27].
- Examples: test whether the model is biased against a player type; whether injuries explain weak numbers by asking how far a metric would have to move; whether low opportunity is visible on film [24:58], [26:59], [27:30].
- The process needs analysts who accept being wrong and experts who accept dropping hypotheses [30:03], [30:34].
- He believes, without proof, that this process would have avoided the Bennett pick [31:06].
- Fit matters and can be tested, in part [31:38], [32:09].
- Trust takes time and is personal, not technical [36:41], [37:11], [41:44].
- For quick decisions, preparation of trade models is the answer [42:46].
- Keep analysts and scouts together, not separate [45:19].
- The more uncertainty in the data, the more hypothesis testing is needed; with millions of data points and an A/B test, follow the data [51:08].
- Explainable models are preferred for player projection unless a black box is much more accurate [54:15], [54:45], [55:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 percent of the audience chose "bank teller and active in liberal politics" [04:41].
- Draft exercise: five players; audience tallies given as "10 uh player B 35 player C 13 D 43 player e" (units and who got which number unclear) [13:31].
- Model estimates the probability of being a "star" (a perennial All-Star, first or second best player on a contender) and of a bust [10:47].
- Bennett's model chance of being a star: "three percent" [22:54]; two other players flagged above three percent [15:04].
- Hypothetical: a GM sees a 75 percent chance; effective field goal percentage 43 would need to rise to 47 (reasonable) versus 72 (not) [23:25], [26:59].
- Team looked at about eight players in the week before the draft [16:39].
- Westbrook decision was made about three weeks before the draft [48:27]; an intern from Stanford helped [49:00].
- Levels (star, starter, role player, bust) are labels on quantitative cut points [46:25].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Draft model from college performance predicting star and bust probabilities [10:47].
- Hypothesis, test, adjust or reject loop around the model [23:25].
- Shot probability model with passer analysis for Westbrook's move to point guard [49:30].
- "Seat at the table" versus "data centered" processes [08:45], [21:48].

## Limits and open questions

- The central example is one NBA draft, an anecdote.
- The speaker concedes he could not apply this at the time and did not have this mindset [38:42].
- The Westbrook test was rushed, crude and manually collected [50:00].
- Hustle and Mamba mentality metrics risk survivorship bias, as he says [35:41].
- Audience poll numbers are ambiguous in the captions.
- Author's commercial view: he mentions his book [48:27].

## Q&A

- Talent versus fit: testable, depends on the claim [31:38].
- Giannis not considered: lacked international data [32:39].
- Measuring hustle: use tracking data [33:39].
- Mamba mentality: ask how it shows up on court, use comparable players [34:40].
- Building trust in the model: personal trust and explanation [36:41].
- Whose pick did the model favor: Otto Porter [38:12].
- Applying the loop to model building: yes, test before the room [39:43].
- Communication with GMs: build relationships [41:14].
- Quick decisions: prepare ahead [42:46].
- Combine analyst and player-facing roles: collaborate, keep avenues open [44:18], [45:19].
- Levels of skill in models: star, starter, role, bust [46:25].
- Time allocation by pick position: less deep dive near the top [46:57].
- Westbrook 2008 [48:27].
- Business or tech transfer: depends on uncertainty [51:08].
- A player with high star and bust chance: conflicting signals or small samples [52:09].
- Revenue in draft decisions: never experienced [53:42].
- Explainable versus black box models: explainable preferred [54:15].

## Summary

ESPN analytics staff walk through how they built Receiver Tracking Metrics from NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data. The metric has three parts: open score, catch score and yards after catch, combined into an overall score on a 0 to 99 scale. They also trace the earlier history, including pass rush and pass block win rates, coverage and route classification models, and the problems of crediting receivers when they create their own context, accounting for the quarterback, and combining mixed units. The audience Q&A covers missing data, scheme, predictiveness and defender metrics. The stated goal is fan engagement, not team use.

## Key claims

- ESPN's analytics aim to tell stories and engage fans, not to help a team win [02:03].
- The receiver metric has open, catch and yards-after-catch components [04:06].
- Open score is more than distance to the nearest defender; it uses orientation, speed and trajectory, credits untargeted receivers, and looks 0.2 seconds before release [06:12], [08:19], [08:50], [09:21].
- Tracking access began in 2017, and it took almost half a season just to understand the data [11:24].
- A closest-defender script revealed who blocks whom, leading to pass rush and pass block win rates [14:59].
- On the first win-rate check, Joe Thomas ranked low on sacks allowed but third on pass block win rate, explained by the quarterback holding the ball [16:02], [16:34].
- Coverage and route classification models were built first and became components of the receiver metric [19:39], [20:41].
- Catch score uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network to estimate catch probability and credits catches over prediction [23:47], [24:17].
- The problem that receivers create their own context was solved by combining general and specific context estimates, benchmarked against a simple model [25:18], [25:49], [26:20], [26:52].
- Yards after catch uses the dots at the catch plus video-tracked ball placement [28:23], [28:55].
- The quarterback affects open score; Mahomes was average on catch score but very high on open score [29:55], [30:27].
- Seattle's receivers rated highly and Denver's lowest, which could partly explain Wilson's decline; the speakers hedge this [33:59], [34:32], [35:02].
- Component weights vary by position and were set by correlation with yards per route run [36:32], [37:03].
- Rookie receivers Olave, Wilson, Pickens and Watson ranked in the top 21; Olave in the top 10 [38:04], [38:34].
- Results are public via 538 [40:06]; the 0 to 99 scale was chosen for fan readability and the yards-after-catch scale was clipped [42:44], [43:15].
- A defender version failed because blame is unclear, especially in zone coverage [44:15].
- Open score is the most stable year to year, about as consistent as batting average, with catch and yards after catch behind; whether it predicts outcomes is still undetermined [53:28], [54:59].

## Numbers and definitions

- AJ Brown score 86, five points above the next player (Travis Kelce, caption "Kelsey") midseason [03:05].
- Release window: 0.2 seconds before release [08:50].
- Speed examples: 4.6 versus 10.3 miles per hour; 9 versus 13 [08:19], [09:21].
- Metric launched October 2022 after a six-year journey [10:23].
- Win rate: share of plays a player sustains or beats a block for 2.5 seconds [41:43].
- Catch example: 0.75 predicted probability, residual of 0.25 credited on a catch [24:17].
- Score scale: 0 to 99; Debo Samuel's yards-after-catch season would be the 99 and the next best about 60 [43:15].
- Joe Thomas: 53rd (speaker unsure whether sacks or pressures) versus third in pass block win rate [16:02].
- Orlando Brown 16th or 18th in pass block win rate [48:49].
- The "30 of the ESPN analytics team" figure is unclear in captions [01:03].

## Methods and frameworks named

- NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data (x and y only) plus ESPN video charting [11:24], [46:15].
- Position-invariant convolutional neural network [23:47].
- Expected versus predicted catch probability, combined [26:52].
- Adjusted plus-minus across seasons for quarterback and receiver effects [29:55].
- Weighting components by correlation with yards per route run [37:03].
- Year-to-year player-level correlation to test stability [54:29].

## Limits and open questions

- Predictiveness is not established; stability is stated qualitatively, with a self-correction on order of catch and yards after catch [54:59].
- No z-axis, no game-leverage context, no progression data [46:15], [47:18], [45:15].
- Scheme and quarterback cannot be separated [51:55].
- Presented by the metric's builders; ESPN's content purpose is stated [02:03].
- Garbled caption names: Diggs, Kelsey, Michael Horton, Dantzler, and the quarterback named after Joe Thomas [04:37], [16:34], [23:47].

## Q&A

- Wanted data: quarterback progression [45:15].
- Z-axis: not available [46:15].
- Time and score context: not included [47:18].
- Teammate influence: gravity credit for double teams [47:49].
- Yards after catch context: dots and blockers [50:20].
- Scheme versus quarterback: cannot be separated [51:55].
- Predictiveness: still to be determined [53:28].
- Win rate to sacks: predictive, with a finishing skill separate [55:29].
- Route types: should be accounted for; go routes inefficient, crossing and out routes efficient [57:32].

Caption problems: audience-vote tallies in the draft video [13:31], the "41" dropout figure in the Lessons video [02:07], the "30 of the analytics team" line in the ESPN video [01:03], and widespread garbled names (including the Olav and Roberta surnames and unattributed hockey tracking answers) are unverifiable as captioned.</result>

## Summary

A workshop by a former NBA analytics executive on how to combine models with expert judgment in draft decisions. He demonstrates the conjunction fallacy with an audience poll, then runs a five-player draft exercise and reveals it was his own team's first overall pick, a notable failure. He contrasts a "seat at the table" model, where data and people argue and one side wins, with a "data centered" process that starts from the model, has experts state hypotheses for why it is wrong, tests them, and updates or drops them. The Q&A covers trust, communication, time pressure and explainable models. The author cannot prove the process would have changed the pick.

## Key claims

- Judge a decision by the process across many repeated decisions, not the single outcome observed [01:31], [02:01].
- People favor a coherent story over probability; the audience repeated the conjunction fallacy [04:41].
- Cognitive biases are systematic effects of how information is framed, and data helps avoid them [06:43], [07:13].
- Humans offer narrative, creativity and deep knowledge but have bias and limited viewing; models are consistent and large-scale but miss variables and intangibles [18:41], [19:12], [19:45].
- Unlike web A/B tests with millions of data points, projecting college players leaves huge uncertainty [20:15].
- Data-centered decision making starts at the model and asks experts why it might be wrong, then tests each hypothesis and adjusts or rejects it; it differs from simply following the model [21:48], [23:25], [24:27].
- Examples: test whether the model is biased against a player type; whether injuries explain weak numbers by asking how far a metric would have to move; whether low opportunity is visible on film [24:58], [26:59], [27:30].
- The process needs analysts who accept being wrong and experts who accept dropping hypotheses [30:03], [30:34].
- He believes, without proof, that this process would have avoided the Bennett pick [31:06].
- Fit matters and can be tested, in part [31:38], [32:09].
- Trust takes time and is personal, not technical [36:41], [37:11], [41:44].
- For quick decisions, preparation of trade models is the answer [42:46].
- Keep analysts and scouts together, not separate [45:19].
- The more uncertainty in the data, the more hypothesis testing is needed; with millions of data points and an A/B test, follow the data [51:08].
- Explainable models are preferred for player projection unless a black box is much more accurate [54:15], [54:45], [55:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 percent of the audience chose "bank teller and active in liberal politics" [04:41].
- Draft exercise: five players; audience tallies given as "10 uh player B 35 player C 13 D 43 player e" (units and who got which number unclear) [13:31].
- Model estimates the probability of being a "star" (a perennial All-Star, first or second best player on a contender) and of a bust [10:47].
- Bennett's model chance of being a star: "three percent" [22:54]; two other players flagged above three percent [15:04].
- Hypothetical: a GM sees a 75 percent chance; effective field goal percentage 43 would need to rise to 47 (reasonable) versus 72 (not) [23:25], [26:59].
- Team looked at about eight players in the week before the draft [16:39].
- Westbrook decision was made about three weeks before the draft [48:27]; an intern from Stanford helped [49:00].
- Levels (star, starter, role player, bust) are labels on quantitative cut points [46:25].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Draft model from college performance predicting star and bust probabilities [10:47].
- Hypothesis, test, adjust or reject loop around the model [23:25].
- Shot probability model with passer analysis for Westbrook's move to point guard [49:30].
- "Seat at the table" versus "data centered" processes [08:45], [21:48].

## Limits and open questions

- The central example is one NBA draft, an anecdote.
- The speaker concedes he could not apply this at the time and did not have this mindset [38:42].
- The Westbrook test was rushed, crude and manually collected [50:00].
- Hustle and Mamba mentality metrics risk survivorship bias, as he says [35:41].
- Audience poll numbers are ambiguous in the captions.
- Author's commercial view: he mentions his book [48:27].

- Giannis not considered: lacked international data [32:39].
- Measuring hustle: use tracking data [33:39].
- Mamba mentality: ask how it shows up on court, use comparable players [34:40].

type: video-summary
video_id: O-EXwmHvBho
title: "SSAC23: Lessons From The Edge: Understanding Humans In The Pursuit of Peak Performance"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Danae Hirsch (host), Chris Cassidy, Olav (surname garbled in captions), Roberta Groner (caption spelling), Steve (moderator, first name only in captions)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making, competitive-advantage, other-sport:endurance]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel on high-stakes performance with a masters marathoner, a triathlon performance head, and a former Navy SEAL and astronaut. They discuss preparing for extreme conditions, treating fear as uncertainty, team culture and leadership, and the limits of data. The triathlon coach argues that measurement and physics-style thinking can push outcomes toward predictability, but that the step from world class to champion depends on human factors that are not measured. On fatigue, the astronaut stresses sleep and days off, and the runner stresses listening to the body. Most claims are personal experience and anecdote, not tested evidence.

## Key claims

- Roberta prepared for a hot midnight world marathon by slowing her goal pace, running long runs in heat in layers, and shifting her sleep to the race time zone [02:37], [03:08], [03:38].
- Olav says Kona can be made more predictable by studying conditions, ignoring myths and combining environmental data with real-time physiology and big data analysis [05:10], [05:40], [06:44].
- After Tokyo, his goal shifted from beating a rival profile to asking what is humanly possible, comparing his athletes with the fastest swimmers, cyclists and marathoners [13:56], [14:28], [14:59].
- His outsider status let him treat each athlete as a research project through monitoring and observation [16:32], [17:02].
- Chris says fear rises with uncertainty and training reduces uncertainty; the pool cannot simulate the 45 minutes of dark and light in orbit [08:49], [09:50].
- A shared training base lets a team deviate quickly within mission parameters [10:20].
- Treating the environment as the enemy helps avoid complacency [10:50], [11:21].
- "Commander's intent" lets people act on the mission's vision without constant instruction [20:35].
- Roberta says to race yourself and control your own outcome [21:37].
- Olav says reaching world class can be nearly automated, but moving to champion is an art and involves unquantifiable factors [22:38], [23:10].
- At camps, each athlete presents a competitive advantage to avoid complacency, and a coach's care and action matter ("humans first") [23:41], [25:41], [32:58].
- Chris describes leadership and followership flowing between people in space crews [29:16].
- Innate size and shape matter, and mental compartmentalizing separates performance [39:11], [39:42].
- Olav argues research is often too narrow to use and organizes performance as velocity, mechanical work, metabolic power and fuel [42:49], [43:20], [44:23].
- Data is information, not an absolute verdict; sensors can be introduced early if playful, not judgmental [49:32], [50:34], [51:05].
- Roberta advises listening to the body and taking a day off when fatigued [51:37].
- On the space station, sleep is scheduled at eight hours; long stretches without a day off raise error risk, so NASA tries to repay days off promptly [52:40], [54:11], [55:15].
- Olav says fatigue recognition comes from experience in training, and sometimes a calculated risk to push through is taken, which must be practiced [55:45], [56:49], [57:20].

## Numbers and definitions

- 2019 world marathon in Doha: midnight start, about 90 degrees, almost 80 percent humidity, and "41" dropouts, said by the moderator as a rate and as a count (unclear whether percent or runners; Roberta also says "41") [01:35], [02:07], [02:37].
- Pace changed from 5:45 to 6:15 per mile (caption) [02:37]; Roberta placed sixth [01:35].
- Roberta's age: moderator says 42 [02:07]; she says "45" at the time of speaking [34:00]; took a 10-year break [11:52].
- Kona race length described as about seven and a half hours, 7:40 for winners [04:08]; the winner's time was predicted "within a minute" per the moderator [04:38] (Olav's reply is garbled [07:15]).
- Orbit every 90 minutes, 45 minutes dark and 45 minutes light [08:49].
- SEAL training six months, hell week in the fifth week [27:43].
- Sleep scheduled eight hours [52:40]; 14 or 20 straight days without a day off [54:11].
- Free throw charity: 10 grand if made [37:35].
- Olav's four domains: velocity, work (mechanical power), metabolic power, fuel [44:23].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Input, efficiency and output (physics) view of performance [43:52].
- Meal energy measured by bomb calorimeter, with collection of waste to measure absorption [45:25], [45:55].
- Real-time in-body monitoring and big data projection [06:44].
- ISS crew experiments and sampling [47:59].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly anecdote; no sample sizes or controls.
- The "predicted within a minute" claim is made by the moderator, and Olav's response is garbled [07:15].
- Olav's methods and results reflect his own program; no outside verification.
- Astronaut and SEAL comments are not about sport athletes' physical data.
- The Apollo-versus-iPhone comparison was stated without exact numbers [06:11].
- Surname spellings garbled (Olav, Roberta).

## Q&A

- Does the military or NASA capture data to improve preparation: not in daily training; ISS crews are sampled for experiments [47:27].
- Drawbacks of relying heavily on data: treat it as information, not absolute [49:32].
- Balancing peak performance with injury or burnout risk: listen to the body, protect sleep, days off, calculated risk [51:37].
- Final advice: be kind to yourself and say yes; do your job; work equally hard and get smarter [57:51], [58:21].

## Summary

A workshop by a former NBA analytics executive on how to combine models with expert judgment in draft decisions. He demonstrates the conjunction fallacy with an audience poll, then runs a five-player draft exercise and reveals it was his own team's first overall pick, a notable failure. He contrasts a "seat at the table" model, where data and people argue and one side wins, with a "data centered" process that starts from the model, has experts state hypotheses for why it is wrong, tests them, and updates or drops them. The Q&A covers trust, communication, time pressure and explainable models. The author cannot prove the process would have changed the pick.

## Key claims

- Judge a decision by the process across many repeated decisions, not the single outcome observed [01:31], [02:01].
- People favor a coherent story over probability; the audience repeated the conjunction fallacy [04:41].
- Cognitive biases are systematic effects of how information is framed, and data helps avoid them [06:43], [07:13].
- Humans offer narrative, creativity and deep knowledge but have bias and limited viewing; models are consistent and large-scale but miss variables and intangibles [18:41], [19:12], [19:45].
- Unlike web A/B tests with millions of data points, projecting college players leaves huge uncertainty [20:15].
- Data-centered decision making starts at the model and asks experts why it might be wrong, then tests each hypothesis and adjusts or rejects it; it differs from simply following the model [21:48], [23:25], [24:27].
- Examples: test whether the model is biased against a player type; whether injuries explain weak numbers by asking how far a metric would have to move; whether low opportunity is visible on film [24:58], [26:59], [27:30].
- The process needs analysts who accept being wrong and experts who accept dropping hypotheses [30:03], [30:34].
- He believes, without proof, that this process would have avoided the Bennett pick [31:06].
- Fit matters and can be tested, in part [31:38], [32:09].
- Trust takes time and is personal, not technical [36:41], [37:11], [41:44].
- For quick decisions, preparation of trade models is the answer [42:46].
- Keep analysts and scouts together, not separate [45:19].
- The more uncertainty in the data, the more hypothesis testing is needed; with millions of data points and an A/B test, follow the data [51:08].
- Explainable models are preferred for player projection unless a black box is much more accurate [54:15], [54:45], [55:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 percent of the audience chose "bank teller and active in liberal politics" [04:41].
- Draft exercise: five players; audience tallies given as "10 uh player B 35 player C 13 D 43 player e" (units and who got which number unclear) [13:31].
- Model estimates the probability of being a "star" (a perennial All-Star, first or second best player on a contender) and of a bust [10:47].
- Bennett's model chance of being a star: "three percent" [22:54]; two other players flagged above three percent [15:04].
- Hypothetical: a GM sees a 75 percent chance; effective field goal percentage 43 would need to rise to 47 (reasonable) versus 72 (not) [23:25], [26:59].
- Team looked at about eight players in the week before the draft [16:39].
- Westbrook decision was made about three weeks before the draft [48:27]; an intern from Stanford helped [49:00].
- Levels (star, starter, role player, bust) are labels on quantitative cut points [46:25].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Draft model from college performance predicting star and bust probabilities [10:47].
- Hypothesis, test, adjust or reject loop around the model [23:25].
- Shot probability model with passer analysis for Westbrook's move to point guard [49:30].
- "Seat at the table" versus "data centered" processes [08:45], [21:48].

- The central example is one NBA draft, an anecdote.
- The speaker concedes he could not apply this at the time and did not have this mindset [38:42].
- The Westbrook test was rushed, crude and manually collected [50:00].
- Hustle and Mamba mentality metrics risk survivorship bias, as he says [35:41].
- Audience poll numbers are ambiguous in the captions.
- Author's commercial view: he mentions his book [48:27].

## Q&A

- Talent versus fit: testable, depends on the claim [31:38].
- Giannis not considered: lacked international data [32:39].
- Measuring hustle: use tracking data [33:39].
- Mamba mentality: ask how it shows up on court, use comparable players [34:40].
- Building trust in the model: personal trust and explanation [36:41].
- Whose pick did the model favor: Otto Porter [38:12].
- Applying the loop to model building: yes, test before the room [39:43].
- Communication with GMs: build relationships [41:14].
- Quick decisions: prepare ahead [42:46].
- Combine analyst and player-facing roles: collaborate, keep avenues open [44:18], [45:19].
- Levels of skill in models: star, starter, role, bust [46:25].
- Time allocation by pick position: less deep dive near the top [46:57].
- Westbrook 2008 [48:27].
- Business or tech transfer: depends on uncertainty [51:08].
- A player with high star and bust chance: conflicting signals or small samples [52:09].
- Revenue in draft decisions: never experienced [53:42].
- Explainable versus black box models: explainable preferred [54:15].

title: "SSAC23: Creating an NFL Player Tracking Metric presented by ESPN"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Max (host, first name only), Seth Walder, Brian Burke, Allison Labs (caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, other]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

ESPN analytics staff walk through how they built Receiver Tracking Metrics from NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data. The metric has three parts: open score, catch score and yards after catch, combined into an overall score on a 0 to 99 scale. They also trace the earlier history, including pass rush and pass block win rates, coverage and route classification models, and the problems of crediting receivers when they create their own context, accounting for the quarterback, and combining mixed units. The audience Q&A covers missing data, scheme, predictiveness and defender metrics. The stated goal is fan engagement, not team use.

## Key claims

- ESPN's analytics aim to tell stories and engage fans, not to help a team win [02:03].
- The receiver metric has open, catch and yards-after-catch components [04:06].
- Open score is more than distance to the nearest defender; it uses orientation, speed and trajectory, credits untargeted receivers, and looks 0.2 seconds before release [06:12], [08:19], [08:50], [09:21].
- Tracking access began in 2017, and it took almost half a season just to understand the data [11:24].
- A closest-defender script revealed who blocks whom, leading to pass rush and pass block win rates [14:59].
- On the first win-rate check, Joe Thomas ranked low on sacks allowed but third on pass block win rate, explained by the quarterback holding the ball [16:02], [16:34].
- Coverage and route classification models were built first and became components of the receiver metric [19:39], [20:41].
- Catch score uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network to estimate catch probability and credits catches over prediction [23:47], [24:17].
- The problem that receivers create their own context was solved by combining general and specific context estimates, benchmarked against a simple model [25:18], [25:49], [26:20], [26:52].
- Yards after catch uses the dots at the catch plus video-tracked ball placement [28:23], [28:55].
- The quarterback affects open score; Mahomes was average on catch score but very high on open score [29:55], [30:27].
- Seattle's receivers rated highly and Denver's lowest, which could partly explain Wilson's decline; the speakers hedge this [33:59], [34:32], [35:02].
- Component weights vary by position and were set by correlation with yards per route run [36:32], [37:03].
- Rookie receivers Olave, Wilson, Pickens and Watson ranked in the top 21; Olave in the top 10 [38:04], [38:34].
- Results are public via 538 [40:06]; the 0 to 99 scale was chosen for fan readability and the yards-after-catch scale was clipped [42:44], [43:15].
- A defender version failed because blame is unclear, especially in zone coverage [44:15].
- Open score is the most stable year to year, about as consistent as batting average, with catch and yards after catch behind; whether it predicts outcomes is still undetermined [53:28], [54:59].

## Numbers and definitions

- AJ Brown score 86, five points above the next player (Travis Kelce, caption "Kelsey") midseason [03:05].
- Release window: 0.2 seconds before release [08:50].
- Speed examples: 4.6 versus 10.3 miles per hour; 9 versus 13 [08:19], [09:21].
- Metric launched October 2022 after a six-year journey [10:23].
- Win rate: share of plays a player sustains or beats a block for 2.5 seconds [41:43].
- Catch example: 0.75 predicted probability, residual of 0.25 credited on a catch [24:17].
- Score scale: 0 to 99; Debo Samuel's yards-after-catch season would be the 99 and the next best about 60 [43:15].
- Joe Thomas: 53rd (speaker unsure whether sacks or pressures) versus third in pass block win rate [16:02].
- Orlando Brown 16th or 18th in pass block win rate [48:49].
- The "30 of the ESPN analytics team" figure is unclear in captions [01:03].

## Methods and frameworks named

- NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data (x and y only) plus ESPN video charting [11:24], [46:15].
- Position-invariant convolutional neural network [23:47].
- Expected versus predicted catch probability, combined [26:52].
- Adjusted plus-minus across seasons for quarterback and receiver effects [29:55].
- Weighting components by correlation with yards per route run [37:03].
- Year-to-year player-level correlation to test stability [54:29].

## Limits and open questions

- Predictiveness is not established; stability is stated qualitatively, with a self-correction on order of catch and yards after catch [54:59].
- No z-axis, no game-leverage context, no progression data [46:15], [47:18], [45:15].
- Scheme and quarterback cannot be separated [51:55].
- Presented by the metric's builders; ESPN's content purpose is stated [02:03].
- Garbled caption names: Diggs, Kelsey, Michael Horton, Dantzler, and the quarterback named after Joe Thomas [04:37], [16:34], [23:47].

## Q&A

- Wanted data: quarterback progression [45:15].
- Z-axis: not available [46:15].
- Time and score context: not included [47:18].
- Teammate influence: gravity credit for double teams [47:49].
- Yards after catch context: dots and blockers [50:20].
- Scheme versus quarterback: cannot be separated [51:55].
- Predictiveness: still to be determined [53:28].
- Win rate to sacks: predictive, with a finishing skill separate [55:29].
- Route types: should be accounted for; go routes inefficient, crossing and out routes efficient [57:32].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: Rn7sZ5kNsNw
title: "SSAC22: Using Technology to Monitor Workload in Elite Figure Skating"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Lindsey Slater (caption spelling: "lindsey slater")]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, other-sport:figure-skating]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker, a physical therapy professor and the sport science manager for U.S. Figure Skating, describes replacing pen-and-paper jump logs with a single hip-worn motion sensor. The first goal was to count training workload, with performance and technique feedback second, because elite athletes reject being told what to do. Three case studies show the sensor used to guide a return after puberty, to set a daily jump limit, and to test whether a skater could realistically land a triple axel by a deadline. The talk matters for athlete monitoring because it ties a device output to individual rep limits, and it shows that adoption depended on who drove the project.

## Key claims

- Vertical loading on a pop jump was found to match that of triple and quad jumps, so early monitoring counted every jump equally [01:32].
- Self-logged jump counts were unreliable: athletes skipped pop jumps and counted combinations as one [02:34].
- Priority one was tracking workload, not judging performance; telling an Olympic athlete what to do risks losing them [03:06].
- A four-sensor setup was first tested on one top athlete, and the speaker says no earlier system had captured the rotation of a triple lutz without saturating [04:38].
- Sensors on the full ice surface avoided the marker-system limit of jumping inside one circle [05:08].
- A single sensor on the hip, smaller than a smartwatch, gives immediate app feedback on jump type, revolutions, rotation speed, air time, height and timing of peak angular velocity; some outputs are estimates and loop jumps are hardest [06:40], [07:10], [07:41].
- Case 1 (post-puberty return): triple axel work was paused, rotation rose over months, peaked around May, dipped in July after a vaccination, and recovered by August [09:44], [10:16], [10:46].
- Time to peak rotation moved earlier toward a point just over halfway through the jump as she improved [11:16].
- The second jump in a combination shows angular velocity like a triple axel, so it carries heavy rotational landing load; coaches were told to track triple-triples with triple axels and quads [12:18], [12:48].
- After tracking those together, the athlete had no further hip pain flare-ups [13:50].
- Case 2: the athlete underestimated her daily jumps; rotation fell across a two-hour session, and the concern was residual fatigue the next day [14:20], [14:51].
- A 75-jump daily ceiling was set, with two recovery days required if she chose to exceed it; the ceiling was raised after progressive exposure with no fatigue [15:23], [15:54], [16:24].
- Case 3: after about four months of data the team judged a triple axel by the target date unrealistic because her rotation appeared capped at the triple; she returned the sensor [17:25], [18:25].
- Adoption pattern: coach-driven succeeded, athlete-driven succeeded, practitioner-driven did not [18:55], [19:26].
- The work was funded by the USOPC and developed with the sensor company in about a year [19:57], [20:58].

## Numbers and definitions

- Triple axel rotation needed for a woman: about 1900 to 1950 degrees per second; the speaker estimates the Russians at 2000 to 2100 (estimate) [09:14].
- Case 1 athlete rotated about 1750 degrees per second on return in February; reached the 1900s in March [09:14], [10:16].
- Setup time: about 5 minutes for sensors versus an hour or more for markers; 11 sensors about 10 minutes versus 30 to 45 minutes for a marker system [05:08], [06:09].
- Case 2: thought she did 60 to 70 jumps a day; actual close to 100 [14:20]. Limit 75; beyond it, two days around 40 jumps [15:23], [15:54]. Later limit 85 (caption is garbled around "high low days are 85") [16:24].
- Five of the six single skaters at the games wore the sensor [08:13].
- Residual fatigue: still fatigued the next day [14:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable IMU (single hip sensor, plus a four-sensor and an 11-sensor test) with app-based jump detection and an algorithm refined with more data [07:41].
- Peak angular velocity and time to peak, combined, as the two key measures [18:25].
- Individual thresholds and a progressive increase in allowed volume, compared by the speaker to progressive overload [15:54].
- Comparison of one athlete's trend against athletes who can land triple axels [17:55].

## Limits and open questions

- Three case studies, no group statistics, no accuracy figures against video.
- The speaker says the old jump-height finding (doubles versus triples) probably needs retesting with today's quads [02:03].
- Internal tension: the talk begins with "all jumps are equal" and later says not all jumps are equal [01:32], [13:19].
- The "no flare-ups" result is one athlete without a control [13:50].
- The ceiling-effect judgement in Case 3 is the speaker's belief; the athlete rejected it [17:25].
- The speaker is the sport science manager for the governing body, with an institutional interest.
- Caption problems: sensor company transcribed as "40 motion sports" and "4d sports"/"4d motion" [04:08], [06:40], [20:58]; "cheetah jump" [07:10] is probably garbled; "pear skaters" is pairs [26:18].

## Q&A

- Spins: not measured; loading is jump based; a boot sensor is planned for the next phase [22:06].
- Arms overhead: has data but keeps it private; the speaker says it reduces inertia and helps young skaters but is harder after puberty [23:10], [23:40], [24:10].
- Baseball pitch counts and volleyball jump counts are being explored with a single sensor [24:45], [25:16].
- Pairs skating: hip sensor is not workable, other locations are being discussed [26:18].

---

title: "SSAC22: How Data Journey Started for the Indianapolis Colts"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

## Summary

The Colts' vice president of data strategy and analytics describes how the club started a data program on the business side (ticketing, sponsorship, marketing), not on-field analytics. The team scored itself on a five-level maturity scale across five areas, interviewed staff, set two-year targets, and built a roadmap of initiatives, with a custom cloud data warehouse first. The speaker argues that technology alone does not fix data problems, and that people, process and clear goals matter as much. The Q&A covers team structure, a cross-department forum, and gaining leadership buy-in. The talk is useful as a method for assessing and sequencing data work, with no athlete data shown.

## Key claims

- The club began from its mission, then asked which capabilities to build or improve, with limited money and people [02:05], [02:37], [03:09].
- Having technology does not help without the right people to use it [03:09].
- A data maturity framework covered five areas (customer strategy, infrastructure, analytics, operations, performance tracking), each scored from awareness through leading [04:11], [04:42], [05:12].
- Interviews showed friction came from people, process and unclear goals, not only technology [06:13].
- Stakeholders were asked where capability needed to be in two years, which produced the gap [06:45], [07:15].
- The main infrastructure need was an integrated view of fans across touch points, not "a data warehouse" as such [10:19], [10:50].
- Designing the warehouse is partly art, since the schema must reflect strategy and use [11:20].
- The warehouse was sequenced as an immediate item because it enabled others [11:50].
- The club moved from an out-of-box solution to a custom one, and says this may not suit other organizations [12:53], [13:23].
- Four selection considerations: break silos, scale without third parties, faster insight, collaboration through self-serve tools [13:53], [14:24], [15:24], [15:54].
- Delivery: an outside firm (caption: "data climber") built it and handed over full ownership; Snowflake is the cloud warehouse; master data management gives a single view [17:57], [18:29], [19:00].
- Benefits claimed: customizable, IP owned, schema built for their needs, less duplication, speed and cost control [19:30], [20:01].
- The journey is described as never ending [20:31].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 staff interviewed across commercial departments, finance, executives and ownership [05:43].
- Five strategic areas, two components each, so 10 capabilities; five maturity levels (awareness to leading) [04:42], [08:17].
- Score of 62 out of 100 on the internal assessment [08:17].
- Blueprint spanning about two and a half years [07:47]; stakeholders were asked about two years out [06:45].
- 12 initiatives in the roadmap [11:50].
- "Center of excellence" meets weekly [24:41].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Data maturity framework with questionnaires and qualitative interviews [05:12], [06:13].
- Gap analysis (current versus target level) turned into programs and initiatives mapped to capabilities, tagged to strategy, process, organization, technology and KPIs [07:47], [09:49], [10:19].
- Roadmap with layers and timelines, warehouse first [11:50].
- Matrix of staff skills (strategy and analytics, CRM and platforms, activation of data) tied to vertical departments, plus a cross-department center of excellence [22:05], [23:07], [24:09].

title: "SSAC22: How Data Journey Started for the Indianapolis Colts"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Charlie Shin (caption spelling: "charlie shin")]
topics: [front-office, decision-making, american-football]

## Summary

The Colts' vice president of data strategy and analytics describes how the club started a data program on the business side (ticketing, sponsorship, marketing), not on-field analytics. The team scored itself on a five-level maturity scale across five areas, interviewed staff, set two-year targets, and built a roadmap of initiatives, with a custom cloud data warehouse first. The speaker argues that technology alone does not fix data problems, and that people, process and clear goals matter as much. The Q&A covers team structure, a cross-department forum, and gaining leadership buy-in. The talk is useful as a method for assessing and sequencing data work, with no athlete data shown.

## Key claims

- The club began from its mission, then asked which capabilities to build or improve, with limited money and people [02:05], [02:37], [03:09].
- Having technology does not help without the right people to use it [03:09].
- A data maturity framework covered five areas (customer strategy, infrastructure, analytics, operations, performance tracking), each scored from awareness through leading [04:11], [04:42], [05:12].
- Interviews showed friction came from people, process and unclear goals, not only technology [06:13].
- Stakeholders were asked where capability needed to be in two years, which produced the gap [06:45], [07:15].
- The main infrastructure need was an integrated view of fans across touch points, not "a data warehouse" as such [10:19], [10:50].
- Designing the warehouse is partly art, since the schema must reflect strategy and use [11:20].
- The warehouse was sequenced as an immediate item because it enabled others [11:50].
- The club moved from an out-of-box solution to a custom one, and says this may not suit other organizations [12:53], [13:23].
- Four selection considerations: break silos, scale without third parties, faster insight, collaboration through self-serve tools [13:53], [14:24], [15:24], [15:54].
- Delivery: an outside firm (caption: "data climber") built it and handed over full ownership; Snowflake is the cloud warehouse; master data management gives a single view [17:57], [18:29], [19:00].
- Benefits claimed: customizable, IP owned, schema built for their needs, less duplication, speed and cost control [19:30], [20:01].
- The journey is described as never ending [20:31].

## Numbers and definitions

- 24 staff interviewed across commercial departments, finance, executives and ownership [05:43].
- Five strategic areas, two components each, so 10 capabilities; five maturity levels (awareness to leading) [04:42], [08:17].
- Score of 62 out of 100 on the internal assessment [08:17].
- Blueprint spanning about two and a half years [07:47]; stakeholders were asked about two years out [06:45].
- 12 initiatives in the roadmap [11:50].
- "Center of excellence" meets weekly [24:41].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Data maturity framework with questionnaires and qualitative interviews [05:12], [06:13].
- Gap analysis (current versus target level) turned into programs and initiatives mapped to capabilities, tagged to strategy, process, organization, technology and KPIs [07:47], [09:49], [10:19].
- Roadmap with layers and timelines, warehouse first [11:50].
- Matrix of staff skills (strategy and analytics, CRM and platforms, activation of data) tied to vertical departments, plus a cross-department center of excellence [22:05], [23:07], [24:09].

## Limits and open questions

- Business-side data only; no athlete, performance or injury content.
- Results of the program are not reported; the work was in progress at the time [20:31].
- The speaker says he cannot share all the initiatives [09:19]; the scoring scale and per-area scores are not shown in the captions.
- 62 out of 100 is an internal measure with no external benchmark; the answer about outside-industry benchmarking gives no numbers [30:29].
- The talk was presented under a sponsor (Sigma, per the host introduction) and names vendors chosen by the club, which is institutional and commercial context [00:01].
- Caption problems: "data climber", "snowflakes", "russell scabetti" and "tan" (probably the team) may be misspelled [15:54], [18:29], [29:28].

## Q&A

- Team structure: three staff with distinct skill sets, each tied to a department, plus a weekly center of excellence [22:05], [24:09].
- Second question: the audience question is garbled; the answer covers ownership's commitment, treating the group as an internal service, and building buy-in over time [25:53], [26:24], [26:55].
- Benchmarking: teams share practices through a league community call (caption: "russell scabetti"); the club also looks outside sports for ideas [29:28], [29:58], [30:29].

## Summary

An ESPN analyst describes an early-stage project to apply 3D motion capture to basketball shooting, aiming to explain why some shooters miss more than others. He argues analytics is moving from outcomes to processes and from game data to practice and lab data. His main finding so far is that struggling free throw shooters show more joint-to-joint inconsistency than strong ones, particularly at the shoulder, elbow and wrist. He treats free throws as the easiest case and expects "shooting labs" to follow the pitching labs in baseball. He closes by saying the winners will integrate biomechanists, analysts and coaches.

## Key claims

- Three shifts in analytics: outcomes to processes, game data to game plus practice and lab data, and measurement moving toward player development rather than surveillance [02:32], [03:02], [03:32], [04:03].
- Goal: a "shot chart for the human body," asking why some shooters are better than others [06:06], [06:37].
- Free throws are a closed, repeatable task and the lowest hanging fruit; threes are contextual and harder [07:37], [08:09], [08:39].

## Summary

A four-woman panel reviews where college athletics stood in March 2022: roughly nine months into name, image and likeness (NIL) with no national rule, a patchwork of state laws, and weak NCAA enforcement. They discuss how an agency values athletes, whether athletes could become employees through labor-board charges, proposals to split fifty-bowl-subdivision football governance from the rest of the NCAA, conference realignment after Texas and Oklahoma moved, and what NIL means for women's sports. Each speaker represents an institution (a conference, a reform commission, a sports agency), so views reflect those positions. It matters for anyone whose athletes, recruits or transfers are affected by these rules.

## Key claims

- Pre-pandemic college sports revenue was about 18.9 billion dollars, mostly from Division I basketball and football (moderator's figure) [01:05].
- Without a national NIL standard the result is what was expected: a mix of state laws, and loose NCAA parameters where a state has no law [04:08] [05:09].
- Attempts at a national rule failed over legal concerns, and the appeal to Congress to override the states did not work either [05:09].
- The Supreme Court decision (caption spelling "austin") undercut the NCAA's confidence in its rule-making authority, which made it hesitant to write a framework open to legal challenge [10:17] [10:47].
- The NCAA's stated policy bars NIL as a recruiting inducement but is not enforced; the speaker compared this to pro sports, where salary caps limit such offers [07:42] [08:13].
- Congress is unlikely to act soon (election year, other priorities), and the panel said nothing "utterly chaotic" had happened yet: a patchwork but not a mess [11:17] [11:47].
- One speaker said the middle of the NIL deal distribution is small, with typical deals well below the headline figures; she hedged on the exact median pending full data [13:22].
- The agency values athletes using two data types: audience analytics and performance measurement [15:23].
- Brands often misjudge the audience: a college athlete's social following is mostly alumni and other fans of the school, not fellow students [16:25].
- The Big East has no conference NIL policy because its schools sit in different jurisdictions with differing laws [18:58].
- An NCAA working group had proposed a third-party administrator and disclosure so deals could be tracked and fair market value distinguished from recruiting inducements [19:58] [20:29].
- The NCAA does not bar schools from helping arrange NIL deals, which raises institutional involvement and Title IX questions (for example staffing for football versus Olympic sports) [21:30] [22:01].
- The Knight Commission speaker framed a choice between co-curricular sport and commercial venture, with some schools likely to pick each [22:32].
- Women athletes were described as well placed for NIL because they have had to build an off-field voice, and evidence of NIL activity extends to volleyball, soccer, swimming and women's basketball [24:34] [25:37] [26:07].
- Labor-board charges against USC, UCLA and the Pac-12 seek employee status for athletes; a September general-counsel memo opened that door [03:06] [30:46].
- Employee classification would raise open issues: Title IX, taxability of income and scholarships, overtime, termination, unionization; the speaker doubted anyone had thought these through [31:46] [38:00] [38:30].
- The Knight Commission proposes a separate body to govern football, joining revenue and rules authority and putting football athletes on the board; and a new Division I financial framework tying shared revenues to education, health and safety [33:21] [33:51] [34:55].
- Its data claim: new revenue over about 15 years flowed disproportionately to salaries and facilities [35:26].
- The 2010 realignment brought about two billion dollars in new revenue to major conferences; one speaker said football-driven alignment produces illogical travel for other sports [45:06] [45:37].
- Conference exit is mainly a notice period plus an exit fee, negotiated; the speaker expected contracts to be honored [48:11].
- The board's intent was "no harm" to Divisions II and III, and the men's basketball tournament holds Division I together [52:16] [52:47].
- A survey of college students, run for five years, finds students value an athlete's off-field voice as much as on-field performance [54:21].
- Market size matters for NIL; a bigger stage means more audience [55:25].

## Numbers and definitions

- 18.9 billion dollars revenue, year before the pandemic [01:05]. Later a speaker says "18 billion" with at least 3 billion going back as scholarships; the captions are garbled near "college boards" [28:42].
- 50,000 dollars to a Texas offensive lineman, described as for charitable purposes [12:19].
- "Under 2 3k" deal sizes for the middle of the market (garbled; likely 2 to 3 thousand dollars, speaker hedged) [13:22].
- About 500,000 college athletes, speaker's figure [28:12].
- About 6,000 dollars per student cash award said to be possible after the court decision [29:45].
- College football playoff: 500 million dollars annually, 1.5 billion if expanded to 12 teams; the NCAA makes zero revenue from FBS football [33:21] [33:51].
- Shared athletic revenue: more than 3 billion annually [34:55].
- Big East: 11 jurisdictions, 8 in states with an NIL law [18:58].
- 351 schools in Division I [52:47].
- 700,000 Instagram followers for a UConn player before college (speaker's figure, caption garbled "i think a") [54:21].
- 4 percent of media coverage for women's sports (speaker's figure) [55:25].
- "Nine schools" trying to leave Conference USA; three not following exit provisions [46:39] [47:09].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Agency valuation: audience analytics (front end) plus performance measurement (back end) [15:23].
- Knight Commission proposals for football governance and financial framework; a Knight-Newhouse college athletics database is named [34:55] [35:26].
- NCAA working-group framework: disclosure, advisors versus agents, third-party administrator, fair-market-value tracking [17:57] [19:58].

## Limits and open questions

- Every speaker has an institutional stake (conference commissioner, reform commission CEO, agency president).
- The deal-size distribution is the speaker's impression, not a shown data set; she said so [13:22].
- No data were shown for the claim that students want an off-field voice beyond the agency's own survey, which is not described.
- Employee status and national standards were left as open questions; the panel did not predict outcomes [39:31].
- Facts are as of March 2022 and mostly legal status that has since changed.
- Court names are garbled in captions ("austin decision"), and "pay for play" and recruiting inducement are used loosely.

## Q&A

- Will brands target athletes in non-revenue sports who stay four years: brands care about audience aggregation, not structure [49:13] [49:43].
- Compensation for a former kicker stripped of his scholarship over a video channel: a pending California case seeks back NIL, limited to the last few years [50:14] [50:44] [51:15].
- Effects on levels below Division I: the NCAA's new constitution aims at no harm to II and III; subdivision of Division I is undecided [51:46] [52:16] [52:47].
- NIL and female athletes: off-field voice and national television exposure help [53:51] [54:21] [54:53].
- Market size versus school brand: bigger stage, bigger opportunity [55:25].
- If football is governed separately, how do other conferences keep their relations: the NCAA would still run the other championships and governance would be rebalanced [55:55] [56:25].

## Summary

Five people look ahead from the 2012 research era of basketball analytics. Most of the first half is about biomechanics: data moving "inside the athlete's body", why current tracking only gives center-of-mass dots, and how to use movement data for skill and injury work. The sharper thread is trust. Panelists say analytics groups have often failed to build it with players, that health data raises privacy and compliance duties, and that the useful role is a conduit who answers staff questions rather than approaching players. Later topics: whether data is "maxed out", draft prediction, chemistry, causal inference, and shooting variance. Many points are panelists' opinions or anecdotes; no data are shown.

## Key claims

- The panel started from 2012 papers on skill-based chemistry, optical-tracking rebounds and spatial shooting analysis [01:32] [02:02].
- Kirk Goldsberry says the next frontier is biomechanics: the data are moving inside athletes' bodies, modeled on baseball pitching labs [02:33] [03:03].
- Each person has a unique movement strategy, so prescribing one way to shoot is wrong; the goal is to explain why a given athlete succeeds [04:04] [05:04].
- Measuring outcomes is advanced, but how a coaching change causes a better shot is not, and whether the fix repeats or transfers is open [05:35].
- Allison Feaster says players hear too many voices; analysts should equip coaches with the language and go to the head coach, not to a player [06:05] [06:36] [07:37].
- Bob Voulgaris says league tracking gives only center-of-mass blobs, so real biomechanics needs a lab with a marker suit, which is unpleasant but the only route to accurate joint centers now [08:39] [09:10] [09:40].
- Goldsberry expects computer vision to remove markers within about five years [09:40].
- Biomechanics might first flag injury risk (for example knee valgus on a Euro step, and landing asymmetry after an ACL tear) [11:41] [12:11] [12:42].
- A panelist cites a coach's view that more one-legged moves explain injuries [11:41].
- Bob says the players' association rules bar wearables during games; the risk is health data hurting contracts [13:43].
- Players are skeptical of employer collection of health data; one panelist said the analytics community has a trust problem [14:14] [14:44] [16:16].
- Goldsberry says analytics groups have more often botched than succeeded at the conduit role and need athlete buy-in, shifting from surveillance to empowerment [17:17] [17:47].
- Catherine Evans says health data at scale becomes protected health information with HIPAA-like duties, so she works through trainers and physicians who bring specific questions [18:18] [19:19].
- Predicting an ACL tear from a pile of injury data is not realistic (Evans); Goldsberry says he is not building catastrophic-injury prediction [19:50].
- Pulling a star for rest based on sports-science data creates coach-player tension, and Feaster has no ready answer; she notes star adoption of load management is uneven [20:51] [21:23] [21:53].
- Bob says tracking data and data generally are "maxed out", that a coach seeing fatigue is itself data, and that more data will not change much for elite players [22:23] [22:54] [23:25].
- Baseball is ahead partly because it is easier to analyze (closed tasks) and its smallest analytics group is larger than basketball's largest; football is expected to catch up thanks to public data [27:32] [28:03] [29:04].
- Measuring mindset: panelists do not know the brain domain, doubt players would accept it, and cite a psychologist question on traffic lights and the Celtics' earlier brain-type scouting as odd examples [30:36] [31:06] [32:39].
- A midseason surge is explained by long-season factors (new leadership, staff, switching defense gelling, an Olympics hangover); a panelist said judging analytics game by game is a small-sample mistake [34:10] [34:40] [35:10].
- The draft is hard because players are younger, experiences vary, and nobody knows what the league looks like years out [35:40] [36:10] [37:10].
- In ten years the panel expects variations on today's themes: reproducibility, shooting, and rules-of-thumb that shift as the league changes, such as post-ups and the debate on threes [38:41] [39:41] [40:11].
- Goldsberry wants the future to bring analytics to athlete development and wellness, with sleep science as a non-invasive example [41:43] [42:15].
- Feaster would like to measure how people mesh in a coaching staff or organization; Evans says chemistry measures would need data at scale [42:48] [44:21].
- Evans says teams only care about prediction as far as it tells them what to change, and wants causal inference papers [45:23] [45:53] [46:23].
- Goldsberry notes athletes and private trainers (Curry and his shooting coach is the example) use numbers teams never see [46:53] [47:23].
- Shot changes are possible (examples given are Kawhi Leonard and Tony Parker), and consistency of movement pattern is what to diagnose [48:55] [49:25].
- Bob says gamblers learn to live with game-to-game variance; the expected shot-quality metric from a tracking vendor helped show coaches a loss was luck [50:56] [51:57] [52:58].
- For slumps, one approach is to update a prior using gym numbers and past season rather than panic [55:00] [55:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Camera tracking started in 2010, full-league adoption in 2013 (Bob; caption "2010 i think") [08:39].
- 2012 papers named: three, plus Goldsberry's spatial shooting paper [01:32] [02:02].
- Heart-rate variability "gone up by 6.7" is a hypothetical example, not data [22:54].
- Five-minute bursts for a star player: a moderator scenario [20:20].
- Lucky-three-point-game counts: "three games a year maybe 10 games a year" then "30 some odd games" now, for a 2017-era coach anecdote; the captions muddle which period each number refers to [51:57] [52:27].
- "Losing 45 percent of the time" is a gambling remark [51:26].
- Expected shot quality: a number projecting points per shot or effective field goal percentage for a set of shots [52:58].
- Event panel length: 45 minutes plus 10 minutes of Q&A [00:32].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Marker-based motion capture in a lab for joint centers, with computer vision expected to replace it [09:40].

## Summary

A four-woman panel reviews where college athletics stood in March 2022: roughly nine months into name, image and likeness (NIL) with no national rule, a patchwork of state laws, and weak NCAA enforcement. They discuss how an agency values athletes, whether athletes could become employees through labor-board charges, proposals to split fifty-bowl-subdivision football governance from the rest of the NCAA, conference realignment after Texas and Oklahoma moved, and what NIL means for women's sports. Each speaker represents an institution (a conference, a reform commission, a sports agency), so views reflect those positions. It matters for anyone whose athletes, recruits or transfers are affected by these rules.

## Key claims

- Pre-pandemic college sports revenue was about 18.9 billion dollars, mostly from Division I basketball and football (moderator's figure) [01:05].
- Without a national NIL standard the result is what was expected: a mix of state laws, and loose NCAA parameters where a state has no law [04:08] [05:09].
- Attempts at a national rule failed over legal concerns, and the appeal to Congress to override the states did not work either [05:09].
- The Supreme Court decision (caption spelling "austin") undercut the NCAA's confidence in its rule-making authority, which made it hesitant to write a framework open to legal challenge [10:17] [10:47].
- The NCAA's stated policy bars NIL as a recruiting inducement but is not enforced; the speaker compared this to pro sports, where salary caps limit such offers [07:42] [08:13].
- Congress is unlikely to act soon (election year, other priorities), and the panel said nothing "utterly chaotic" had happened yet: a patchwork but not a mess [11:17] [11:47].
- One speaker said the middle of the NIL deal distribution is small, with typical deals well below the headline figures; she hedged on the exact median pending full data [13:22].
- The agency values athletes using two data types: audience analytics and performance measurement [15:23].
- Brands often misjudge the audience: a college athlete's social following is mostly alumni and other fans of the school, not fellow students [16:25].
- The Big East has no conference NIL policy because its schools sit in different jurisdictions with differing laws [18:58].
- An NCAA working group had proposed a third-party administrator and disclosure so deals could be tracked and fair market value distinguished from recruiting inducements [19:58] [20:29].
- The NCAA does not bar schools from helping arrange NIL deals, which raises institutional involvement and Title IX questions (for example staffing for football versus Olympic sports) [21:30] [22:01].
- The Knight Commission speaker framed a choice between co-curricular sport and commercial venture, with some schools likely to pick each [22:32].

- Employee status and national standards were left as open questions; the panel did not predict outcomes [39:31].

- Market size versus school brand: bigger stage, bigger opportunity [55:25].
- If football is governed separately, how do other conferences keep their relations: the NCAA would still run the other championships and governance would be rebalanced [55:55] [56:25].

title: "SSAC22: On A Finger Roll: Where the Basketball Analytics Movement Goes Next"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Catherine Evans, Kirk Goldsberry, Allison Feaster, Bob Voulgaris (caption spelling "bob vulgaris"), Kevin Arnovitz (moderator), Nahom Brahane (host, caption spelling)]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, injury-health, front-office, decision-making]

## Summary

Five people look ahead from the 2012 research era of basketball analytics. Most of the first half is about biomechanics: data moving "inside the athlete's body", why current tracking only gives center-of-mass dots, and how to use movement data for skill and injury work. The sharper thread is trust. Panelists say analytics groups have often failed to build it with players, that health data raises privacy and compliance duties, and that the useful role is a conduit who answers staff questions rather than approaching players. Later topics: whether data is "maxed out", draft prediction, chemistry, causal inference, and shooting variance. Many points are panelists' opinions or anecdotes; no data are shown.

## Key claims

- The panel started from 2012 papers on skill-based chemistry, optical-tracking rebounds and spatial shooting analysis [01:32] [02:02].
- Kirk Goldsberry says the next frontier is biomechanics: the data are moving inside athletes' bodies, modeled on baseball pitching labs [02:33] [03:03].
- Each person has a unique movement strategy, so prescribing one way to shoot is wrong; the goal is to explain why a given athlete succeeds [04:04] [05:04].
- Measuring outcomes is advanced, but how a coaching change causes a better shot is not, and whether the fix repeats or transfers is open [05:35].
- Allison Feaster says players hear too many voices; analysts should equip coaches with the language and go to the head coach, not to a player [06:05] [06:36] [07:37].
- Bob Voulgaris says league tracking gives only center-of-mass blobs, so real biomechanics needs a lab with a marker suit, which is unpleasant but the only route to accurate joint centers now [08:39] [09:10] [09:40].
- Goldsberry expects computer vision to remove markers within about five years [09:40].
- Biomechanics might first flag injury risk (for example knee valgus on a Euro step, and landing asymmetry after an ACL tear) [11:41] [12:11] [12:42].
- A panelist cites a coach's view that more one-legged moves explain injuries [11:41].
- Bob says the players' association rules bar wearables during games; the risk is health data hurting contracts [13:43].
- Players are skeptical of employer collection of health data; one panelist said the analytics community has a trust problem [14:14] [14:44] [16:16].
- Goldsberry says analytics groups have more often botched than succeeded at the conduit role and need athlete buy-in, shifting from surveillance to empowerment [17:17] [17:47].
- Catherine Evans says health data at scale becomes protected health information with HIPAA-like duties, so she works through trainers and physicians who bring specific questions [18:18] [19:19].
- Predicting an ACL tear from a pile of injury data is not realistic (Evans); Goldsberry says he is not building catastrophic-injury prediction [19:50].
- Pulling a star for rest based on sports-science data creates coach-player tension, and Feaster has no ready answer; she notes star adoption of load management is uneven [20:51] [21:23] [21:53].
- Bob says tracking data and data generally are "maxed out", that a coach seeing fatigue is itself data, and that more data will not change much for elite players [22:23] [22:54] [23:25].
- Baseball is ahead partly because it is easier to analyze (closed tasks) and its smallest analytics group is larger than basketball's largest; football is expected to catch up thanks to public data [27:32] [28:03] [29:04].
- Measuring mindset: panelists do not know the brain domain, doubt players would accept it, and cite a psychologist question on traffic lights and the Celtics' earlier brain-type scouting as odd examples [30:36] [31:06] [32:39].
- A midseason surge is explained by long-season factors (new leadership, staff, switching defense gelling, an Olympics hangover); a panelist said judging analytics game by game is a small-sample mistake [34:10] [34:40] [35:10].
- The draft is hard because players are younger, experiences vary, and nobody knows what the league looks like years out [35:40] [36:10] [37:10].
- In ten years the panel expects variations on today's themes: reproducibility, shooting, and rules-of-thumb that shift as the league changes, such as post-ups and the debate on threes [38:41] [39:41] [40:11].
- Goldsberry wants the future to bring analytics to athlete development and wellness, with sleep science as a non-invasive example [41:43] [42:15].

type: video-summary
video_id: QCewshG-Wz8
title: "SSAC22: The Next Frontier of Data Analytics in Sport: Integrating Performance Data & Video(Catapult)"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Adam Choubane (caption spelling), Mike Duke (host)]
topics: [sports-science, competitive-advantage, injury-health, american-football, other-sport:soccer, other-sport:rugby]
confidence: supported
