## Summary

A Catapult product manager demonstrates a product that places wearable physical data (sprints, impacts, heart rate, player load) inside a video and event-data platform, MatchTracker, after Catapult and its maker joined last year. He argues three benefits: context for physical numbers by syncing them to video and game state, profiling the physical demands of a style of play to design practice, and saving analyst time. Examples come from one MLS match, rugby scrums and a football tempo scenario. It is a vendor demo, so claims of benefit are commercial and not independently tested. Live use and several sports are on the roadmap, not available.

## Key claims

- Video editors let teams tag events and sync them to video, which was the start of modern analysis in soccer [00:30] [01:00].
- Positional data came separately, and the problem is data produced by different providers and analyzed in different software [02:01] [02:31].
- SBG Sports released MatchTracker in 2015 to integrate event data, video and positional data [03:01].
- Physical data come from wearables and are used for injury risk, return to play and load across a season [04:04] [04:35].
- Catapult joined SBG last year to bring physical data into MatchTracker [04:35] [05:05].
- A total like 15 sprints or 6 miles is not enough for coaching; the coach wants to know why the player was running [05:35] [06:05].
- Syncing each sprint to video lets a coach click any sprint, see the run, and share a clip with the team [06:35] [07:06].
- Impacts can be graphed by 5-minute block and sorted by force, with video behind each [07:36] [08:07].
- Physical data can be broken down by game state, such as offense versus defense, phase of play or how a sequence ended [08:38] [09:08].
- In rugby, wearables detect scrums by machine learning, giving who was involved, time to get back up, and effect on heart rate and load [09:38] [10:09].
- Physical data can quantify the toll of a style of play, such as high pressing; measuring every press in a season gives a profile of physical requirements [11:41] [12:11] [13:42].
- Because athletes wear the same device in practice, one can compare practice to game and see who practices at game speed [13:42] [14:13].
- A football tempo offense can be measured by speed, accelerations, decelerations and load per play or drive, to see who meets the requirements and for training and injury prevention [14:13] [14:44].
- The speaker presented one game in which passing accuracy dropped when heart rate was high [15:44] [16:15].
- A Division I football analyst's process for matching a physical outlier to video is manual and slow; the product removes this [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- 2015: MatchTracker release [03:01].
- 15 sprints, 6 miles: illustrative report lines, not data [05:35].
- 5-minute increments for impact graphs [07:36].
- 18th minute: example press in an MLS match [12:41].
- 150 beats per minute or more: the heart-rate cut-off "let's call it" for the passing example [15:44].
- 4 percent: passing accuracy drop when heart rates rise, one team in one game; unstated whether percentage points or relative; sample size not given [16:15].
- Physical view metrics named: work rate, player load, heart rate [13:12].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Integration of event data, video, positional data and wearable data, synced by time [03:01] [05:05].
- A "physical view" showing wearable data for a selected moment [12:41].
- Machine-learning detection of scrums by wearables [09:38].
- Bucketing impacts by time and force; splitting sprints by game state [07:36] [09:08].
- Cross-game aggregation of heart rate for presses [19:54].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker works for Catapult and is selling the integration; benefits are claimed, not tested.
- Almost all examples are one MLS match; the football content is a generic description with no numbers [14:13].
- The 4 percent result is one game, no uncertainty given, and a heart-rate cut-off set on the spot [15:44].
- Syncing is done after the match; live sync is on the roadmap [18:54].
- Pose or biomechanics: nothing to report [20:56].
- Hockey is not supported yet [20:25].
- "Ice in her veins" is framed as quantifiable, but no result is shown for it [15:14] [15:44].
- Whether football or American college workflows are supported is not stated.

## Q&A

- Live lag: data and video can be reported live, but syncing is after the match; live is on the roadmap [18:54].
- Aggregating across games for statistical weight: yes, he showed multi-game press analysis [19:54].
- Hockey video integration: not yet; will bring to as many sports as possible [20:25].
- Pose or body motion: nothing to report, an obvious next step [20:56].
- Sleep, nutrition, menstrual cycle data: wants to bring them into the fold [21:27].
- Goalkeepers: supported, including dive metrics and direction [21:27].
- Open-source data sets: unsure, nothing released right now [22:29].

## Summary

Eager argues that football analytics has used its three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, and player tracking) mostly one at a time, and that combining them gives better player evaluation. He shows three cases from Pro Football Focus (PFF): an expected pressure rate for pass rushers, a "bite distance" measure for linebackers on play action, and a speed-adjusted receiver grade for deep routes. In each case the hand-charted grade supplies the target and tracking data supplies a measure that is steadier from year to year or tracks athletic testing. The Q&A covers second-order effects, trade-offs and model context.

## Key claims

- Football analytics has advanced from a few public writers to many data sources, but each source is mostly used alone, and combining them would improve player evaluation [01:33].
- PFF charts every NFL and college game by hand, producing player grades and event labels. The NFL's tracking data comes from chips in shoulder pads and the ball [02:08, 02:40].
- For pass rushers, PFF's charted pressure and win-rate data served as training targets, and tracking data supplied the predictors, in two models (pressure and win rate) [06:16].
- The most important predictor of a pressure was the defender's vertical distance covered in the first second. The model was an XGBoost ensemble of decision trees [06:47].
- Charted position labels (nose tackle, edge defender) also entered the model, so it carries some information on player type [07:18].
- Each play yields a pressure probability, not only a yes or no [07:48].
- Pressure is treated as the process that leads to sacks. PFF pressure rate and expected pressure rate together predict sack rate better than either alone, and tracking data also adds power when predicting a player's own pressure rate [08:19, 08:49].
- Expected pressure rate tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than charted data does, which gives a time-varying athleticism measure in place of one combine number [09:19, 09:50].
- Coverage grades are unstable year to year. Linebacker "bite distance under expected" (BDU), the vertical displacement on play action adjusted for situation, is more predictive year to year than the coverage grade [10:20, 11:22, 12:23].
- Eager's reasoning for BDU: biting on a fake leaves the middle of the field open, the most valuable area to throw [10:51, 11:22].
- A receiver model using mean, median and max speed over a play found speed to be the most important variable for a positive PFF grade on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55].
- The resulting speed-adjusted grade is steadier year to year than the deep-pass grade and correlates with the 40-yard dash, with exceptions such as Landry (slow 40, good receiver) and Kupp (faster on field than his timed run) [13:55, 14:25, 14:56].
- Tracking data's promise may not be reached without combining it with charting and play-by-play [15:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Sacks take about two points on average from an offense [05:45].
- Sack rate predicting itself year to year: about 0.24 (R squared), given with "I think" and "or something" [08:19].
- BDU is described as three or four times more predictive year to year (R squared) than the coverage grade. The captions read "about four times three or four times", so the exact multiple is garbled [11:53, 12:23].
- Kupp's pro-day 40 time: 4.62 (caption "cooper cup"; the speaker was unsure of the year and said 2017) [14:56].
- Pressure: charted when a rusher moves the quarterback off his spot or gets a sack. Win rate: charted as whether the rusher won the rep. The two are correlated but can differ [05:15, 05:45].
- PFF grades are discrete steps of half a point from negative two (caption wording) [26:36].
- First-second speed was measured in the vertical (y) direction and as straight-line distance [06:47].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Charted grades as labels, tracking features as predictors (pressure, win rate, receiver grade) [06:16, 13:25].
- XGBoost classification for pressure [06:47].
- Adjusting linebacker displacement for situation (run tendencies, down and distance) and averaging over time [11:22, 11:53].
- Year-to-year R squared as the test of whether a new measure is better than the existing grade [08:19, 12:23].

## Limits and open questions

- The slides are not visible. Most R squared values, sample sizes, seasons and the number of plays are not in the captions, so only the 0.24 and the "three or four times" claims can be quoted.
- The speaker works for PFF and presents PFF tools as results, so this is an institutional and commercial view.
- The 40-yard dash question (correlation of about 0.75 raised by a questioner) concerns career averages versus one-time combine results, not within-player prediction, and the exchange is partly unclear [22:31, 23:31].
- Eager agreed in Q&A that BDU says nothing alone about whether a defender's passivity is worth what it costs against the run [18:58, 19:28].
- The linebacker examples are individual cases (Warner, Kuechly, Hewitt, Cunningham, White, David as heard in the captions); no group-level validation is shown beyond the R squared claim [11:53, 18:58, 24:31].
- Names in the captions may be misspelled (Kuechly appears as "luke lee"; Okereke as "okariki").

## Q&A

- An economist-style questioner asked about second-order effects (tired linemen, scheme and play-calling changes). Eager agreed, noting football has many columns but few rows, and that the game changes quickly, with play action as an example [16:28, 16:58, 17:28].
- Is the linebacker metric the right objective, since it measures the mean rather than variance? Eager is studying the trade-off (a good run defender may accept some middle-field plays) and wants analytics to quantify it [18:28, 18:58, 19:28].
- Do the receiver rankings match popular opinion? Eager discussed Tyreek Hill and Antonio Brown (caption spelling "tyree kill") and argued the measure captures controlled speed usable for football plays [20:28, 20:59, 21:30].
- Clarifying the 40-yard R squared table: it uses careers, because players test only once [22:31, 23:01, 23:31].
- Do defensive backs or linebackers who cushion create bias? Eager suggested team-level view of the two inside linebackers, because one may bite while the other covers [24:01, 24:31, 25:02].
- Why do context variables such as yards to go matter in the grade model? PFF does not ask graders to do context math, and the model partly adjusts for it [26:03, 26:36, 27:07].

It covers shot evaluation with context, the coming league pose data, staff composition, how players take in data, the gap between a player's skills and the role he is given, and the limits of basketball analogies to baseball biomechanics. - Evans's ideal staff: data engineers, software engineers, a design person, ML and statistics PhDs, and former players who know some SQL and Python [13:54, 14:26].
- Mike said communication is as important as insight, and few people combine statistics, basketball knowledge and communication [15:26, 15:57]. Battier advised adding a behavioral psychology course and developing emotional intelligence [16:58].

- Mike said players vary in interest in data, that small samples can mislead them, and the team wants one message across coaches and front office, so it leaves much communication to coaches [21:04, 21:34, 22:04].
- Evans said gym cameras give players immediate shot feedback, and younger players engage more [23:05, 23:35]. Panelists said data has become ordinary rather than players becoming more willing [24:36].
- Mike did not expect NBA players to buy their own data, since the team provides it, including a facility with force plates mounted separately to the ground [29:15, 29:47].
- Evans argued baseball-style biomechanics labs fit pitching more than basketball, because basketball involves constant decisions and defenders; free throws are the most mechanical case [31:18, 31:48, 32:19]. Another panelist countered that computer vision on phones will bring pose data [33:50].
- Panelists said players with more athleticism and opportunity can grow their games, and role players have less room to add skills [41:00, 41:32, 42:32]. Battier told his own move from power forward to guard as an example of opportunity [43:03].
- Evans framed development as separating who a player is from what he is asked to do, and looking for skills not used by his current team [44:36, 45:36, 46:06].

- Battier said he would listen about his shot only to someone with long credibility, and recounted fixing his own shot before Game 7 [49:39, 50:10, 51:12].

- For pass rushers, PFF's charted pressure and win-rate data served as training targets, and tracking data supplied the predictors, in two models (pressure and win rate) [06:16].
- The most important predictor of a pressure was the defender's vertical distance covered in the first second. The model was an XGBoost ensemble of decision trees [06:47].
- Charted position labels (nose tackle, edge defender) also entered the model, so it carries some information on player type [07:18].
- Each play yields a pressure probability, not only a yes or no [07:48].
- Pressure is treated as the process that leads to sacks. PFF pressure rate and expected pressure rate together predict sack rate better than either alone, and tracking data also adds power when predicting a player's own pressure rate [08:19, 08:49].
- Expected pressure rate tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than charted data does, which gives a time-varying athleticism measure in place of one combine number [09:19, 09:50].
- Coverage grades are unstable year to year. Linebacker "bite distance under expected" (BDU), the vertical displacement on play action adjusted for situation, is more predictive year to year than the coverage grade [10:20, 11:22, 12:23].
- Eager's reasoning for BDU: biting on a fake leaves the middle of the field open, the most valuable area to throw [10:51, 11:22].
- A receiver model using mean, median and max speed over a play found speed to be the most important variable for a positive PFF grade on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55].
- The resulting speed-adjusted grade is steadier year to year than the deep-pass grade and correlates with the 40-yard dash, with exceptions such as Landry (slow 40, good receiver) and Kupp (faster on field than his timed run) [13:55, 14:25, 14:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Sacks take about two points on average from an offense [05:45].
- Sack rate predicting itself year to year: about 0.24 (R squared), given with "I think" and "or something" [08:19].
- BDU is described as three or four times more predictive year to year (R squared) than the coverage grade. The captions read "about four times three or four times", so the exact multiple is garbled [11:53, 12:23].

A panel of a former NBA player turned executive, a Wizards research executive and a Celtics executive discusses how data supports player development. It covers shot evaluation with context, the coming league pose data, staff composition, how players take in data, the gap between a player's skills and the role he is given, and the limits of basketball analogies to baseball biomechanics. Most of the content is opinion and anecdote, not shown analysis.

## Key claims

- Battier said that three things matter in basketball: making open shots, finishing, and drawing fouls. A Hall of Famer does all three, most All-Stars do two elite, and he would have focused on threes and finishing [02:36, 03:06, 03:36].
- Today's players know that shots at the rim are good but not why [04:38].
- Evans said three-point percentage is the best descriptive measure of what happened, but evaluating shooting ability needs shot quality, scheme, role and gym data, and contest level [06:11, 07:15].
- A "Splash Zone" ideal shot exists in theory, but different players have different effective shots, so context about who shoots matters [08:16, 08:46].
- Mike (Celtics) said the NBA's coming camera system adds body pose, which will help judge how contested a shot is, especially farther from the rim, and teams will build better shot models [10:47, 11:18].
- Zarren-type and Evans comments agree that in-game NBA data is largely the same across teams, and advantage comes from engineering and speed of use, not access [12:20, 12:53].
- Evans's ideal staff: data engineers, software engineers, a design person, ML and statistics PhDs, and former players who know some SQL and Python [13:54, 14:26].
- Mike said communication is as important as insight, and few people combine statistics, basketball knowledge and communication [15:26, 15:57]. Battier advised adding a behavioral psychology course and developing emotional intelligence [16:58].
- Battier said he persuaded LeBron James with a scouting note about one opponent's weaker side, and that players care that it works, not how the number was made [18:30, 19:01].
- Mike said players vary in interest in data, that small samples can mislead them, and the team wants one message across coaches and front office, so it leaves much communication to coaches [21:04, 21:34, 22:04].
- Evans said gym cameras give players immediate shot feedback, and younger players engage more [23:05, 23:35]. Panelists said data has become ordinary rather than players becoming more willing [24:36].
- Mike did not expect NBA players to buy their own data, since the team provides it, including a facility with force plates mounted separately to the ground [29:15, 29:47].
- Evans argued baseball-style biomechanics labs fit pitching more than basketball, because basketball involves constant decisions and defenders; free throws are the most mechanical case [31:18, 31:48, 32:19]. Another panelist countered that computer vision on phones will bring pose data [33:50].
- Panelists said players with more athleticism and opportunity can grow their games, and role players have less room to add skills [41:00, 41:32, 42:32]. Battier told his own move from power forward to guard as an example of opportunity [43:03].
- Evans framed development as separating who a player is from what he is asked to do, and looking for skills not used by his current team [44:36, 45:36, 46:06].
- Evans said she would pass practice-data drift to the coach and ask the medical staff whether compensation or injury explains it, rather than tell the player [46:37, 47:08].
- Battier said he would listen about his shot only to someone with long credibility, and recounted fixing his own shot before Game 7 [49:39, 50:10, 51:12].
- Evans said measuring decision quality is hard because the counterfactual is unobserved, and selection bias is strong [57:22, 57:53, 58:53].

- Three numbers per Battier: open shot (no-dribble jump shot), finishing at the rim, foul drawing [03:06, 03:36].
- Shooting "Splash Zone": about 45 degrees and 10 inches back, centered on the hoop (speaker's caption wording) [08:16].
- Current data: center of mass of each player about 30 times a second plus the ball. Coming system: 19 body points per player, mentioned at about 50 hertz [08:46, 09:16, 10:47].
- Battier's Durant example: "200 bips" better over one shoulder (caption wording, unclear); LeBron guarded him twice and Durant missed both [18:30]. Battier said he left out sample size and variance [19:01].

- Half-court offense at 0.8 points per possession, from Battier's high school team, whose record the captions give as nine and fifteen [25:07, 25:38].

- Synergy tags and video platform for players [21:04].
- Drill design as steps (on air, with a coach, practice game, game) with stated goals for each [34:53, 35:24].

## Summary

A panel on AI and machine learning in sport with a basketball executive, an AWS AI director, a Stats Perform chief scientist and a bioethicist. The practical threads are large language models as productivity tools, new forecasting methods that tolerate many correlated predictors, fine-tuning a language model for NFL broadcast narratives, and health and safety applications. The cautionary threads are hallucination on sports facts, the black-box problem and the tension between explainability and predictive power, private versus public data, athlete monitoring and privacy, cheating, and whether humans stay in the loop. Panelists disagreed on how worried to be. Largely opinion, with one vendor case study.

- Morey said a deepfake highlight tape could change the case for in-person scouting [35:18].
- Black box: Liao said deep models do not explain their decisions, which matters in a fourth-quarter play call. - Visual cortex: a panelist said about 50% of the brain is associated with it [10:13].

type: video-summary
video_id: knZ8ImMzBX4
title: "SSAC23 - Leveling Up: How Basketball Teams Deploy Analytics to Develop Players"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Shane Battier, Catherine Evans (caption spelling), Mike sarin (caption spelling), Ben Cohen (moderator), Khalid McCaskill (introduction, caption spelling)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, sports-science]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel of a former NBA player turned executive, a Wizards research executive and a Celtics executive discusses how data supports player development. The panel agrees that game data is now similar across teams, so the edge lies in what teams do with it and in how it is communicated to players and coaches. It covers shot evaluation with context, the coming league pose data, staff composition, how players take in data, the gap between a player's skills and the role he is given, and the limits of basketball analogies to baseball biomechanics. Most of the content is opinion and anecdote, not shown analysis.

## Key claims

- Battier said that three things matter in basketball: making open shots, finishing, and drawing fouls. A Hall of Famer does all three, most All-Stars do two elite, and he would have focused on threes and finishing [02:36, 03:06, 03:36].
- Today's players know that shots at the rim are good but not why [04:38].
- Evans said three-point percentage is the best descriptive measure of what happened, but evaluating shooting ability needs shot quality, scheme, role and gym data, and contest level [06:11, 07:15].
- A "Splash Zone" ideal shot exists in theory, but different players have different effective shots, so context about who shoots matters [08:16, 08:46].
- Mike (Celtics) said the NBA's coming camera system adds body pose, which will help judge how contested a shot is, especially farther from the rim, and teams will build better shot models [10:47, 11:18].
- Evans and Mike agree that in-game NBA data is largely the same across teams, and advantage comes from engineering and speed of use, not access [12:20, 12:53].
- Evans's ideal staff: data engineers, software engineers, a design person, ML and statistics PhDs, and former players who know some SQL and Python [13:54, 14:26].
- Mike said communication is as important as insight, and few people combine statistics, basketball knowledge and communication [15:26, 15:57]. Battier advised adding a behavioral psychology course and developing emotional intelligence [16:58].
- Battier said he persuaded LeBron James with a scouting note about one opponent's weaker side, and that players care that it works, not how the number was made [18:30, 19:01].
- Mike said players vary in interest in data, that small samples can mislead them, and the team wants one message across coaches and front office, so it leaves much communication to coaches [21:04, 21:34, 22:04].
- Evans said gym cameras give players immediate shot feedback, and younger players engage more [23:05, 23:35]. Panelists said data has become ordinary rather than players becoming more willing [24:36].
- Mike did not expect NBA players to buy their own data, since the team provides it, including a facility with force plates mounted separately to the ground [29:15, 29:47].
- Evans argued baseball-style biomechanics labs fit pitching more than basketball, because basketball involves constant decisions and defenders; free throws are the most mechanical case [31:18, 31:48, 32:19]. Another panelist countered that computer vision on phones will bring pose data [33:50].
- Panelists said players with more athleticism and opportunity can grow their games, and role players have less room to add skills [41:00, 41:32, 42:32]. Battier told his own move from power forward to guard as an example of opportunity [43:03].
- Evans framed development as separating who a player is from what he is asked to do, and looking for skills not used by his current team [44:36, 45:36, 46:06].
- Evans said she would pass practice-data drift to the coach and ask the medical staff whether compensation or injury explains it, rather than tell the player [46:37, 47:08].
- Battier said he would listen about his shot only to someone with long credibility, and recounted fixing his own shot before Game 7 [49:39, 50:10, 51:12].
- Evans said measuring decision quality is hard because the counterfactual is unobserved, and selection bias is strong [57:22, 57:53, 58:53].

## Numbers and definitions

- Three numbers per Battier: open shot (no-dribble jump shot), finishing at the rim, foul drawing [03:06, 03:36].
- Shooting "Splash Zone": about 45 degrees and 10 inches back, centered on the hoop (speaker's caption wording) [08:16].
- Current data: center of mass of each player about 30 times a second plus the ball. Coming system: 19 body points per player, mentioned at about 50 hertz [08:46, 09:16, 10:47].
- Battier's Durant example: "200 bips" better over one shoulder (caption wording, unclear); LeBron guarded him twice and Durant missed both [18:30]. Battier said he left out sample size and variance [19:01].
- The Celtics practiced as a full team about twice in January, with 82 games in the season [44:05].
- Half-court offense at 0.8 points per possession, from Battier's high school team, whose record the captions give as nine and fifteen [25:07, 25:38].
- The moderator's Lowry example gives a shot arc dropping from 46 or 47 degrees to 41 degrees; this is the moderator's retelling of a book, not a panelist's data [46:06].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Spatial tracking and shot-quality models, in-gym shooting data and contest-level adjustment [07:15].
- Synergy tags and video platform for players [21:04].
- Drill design as steps (on air, with a coach, practice game, game) with stated goals for each [34:53, 35:24].
- Counterfactual and expected-points reasoning for decisions, acknowledged as imperfect [57:53, 58:23, 58:53].

## Limits and open questions

- Mostly opinion and personal anecdote; no model, data or sample is shown.
- Battier's Durant story rests on two possessions and he said he did not explain variance. He called the Kobe counter-analytics story unverifiable [18:30, 19:01, 27:11].
- Speakers are not labeled in the captions. Attribution above uses context (Celtics, Wizards and Battier's own history), and some lines, such as the free-throw volume argument and the comment that foul rate matters more than free-throw rate, cannot be assigned with certainty [36:25, 37:26].
- Each speaker speaks for an employer or personal experience, including claims that the team's data and facility make player-bought data unnecessary [29:47].
- Pose data accuracy was called uncertain by a panelist, and injury uses were left open [10:47, 11:18].
- Name and term problems in captions (Mike as "sarin", Evans as "Katherine"/"Kathy", Khris Middleton as "Chris Middleton", "bips").

## Q&A

- Is development data focused too much on offense? Panelists disagreed with the premise and said defense, including team rotations, gets a lot of time [51:44, 52:15, 52:47].
- What do you wish you had live in games? Evans said not much; coaches recall plays well. Challenge decisions could use spatial data. The Celtics have a staffer behind the bench for challenges [53:47, 54:17, 54:47, 55:17, 55:49].
- Does a specific defender's closeout work analytically? The sample is small, and pose data is needed [56:21, 56:52].
- What data would you want that you lack? Decision-making measures; panelists discussed the counterfactual problem [57:22, 57:53, 58:23, 58:53].
- Final prompt: what the moderator will ask in 2039; load management was the joke answer [59:25].

---

video_id: tRnkF9eTWWg
title: "SSAC23: Mind, Body, Machine: The Role of AI/ML in the Future of Sports"
event: SSAC23 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Daryl Morey, Sherry Marcus, Patrick Lucy (caption spelling), Matthew Liao, Ethan Strauss (moderator), Nick Holmes (introduction)]
topics: [american-football, basketball, injury-health, policy, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel on AI and machine learning in sport with a basketball executive, an AWS AI director, a Stats Perform chief scientist and a bioethicist. The practical threads are large language models as productivity tools, new forecasting methods that tolerate many correlated predictors, fine-tuning a language model for NFL broadcast narratives, and health and safety applications. The cautionary threads are hallucination on sports facts, the black-box problem and the tension between explainability and predictive power, private versus public data, athlete monitoring and privacy, cheating, and whether humans stay in the loop. Panelists disagreed on how worried to be. Largely opinion, with one vendor case study.

## Key claims

- A language model can write a first draft that an expert edits in a few places, which Morey said is a large productivity gain, even an order of magnitude, and removes the blank page [02:35, 03:05].
- Sherry (AWS) said health and safety excites her most, citing AWS work with the NFL on identifying helmet contact and a "digital athlete" [03:36, 04:08, 04:38].
- A Stats Perform panelist described the sweet spot for AI as assistive tools for domain experts, with an autonomous-driving analogy ("L3" versus "L5") [05:08].
- Sport is its own language: language models state sports facts wrongly with confidence, so they need to be seeded with facts, and tracking data is a visual language that needs its own models [08:42, 09:43, 10:13].
- Morey said new methods allow correlated predictors and even more parameters than observations if variance is controlled (adjusted plus-minus via ridge regression is his example). Random noise inputs still hurt, so an analyst still curates inputs [12:15, 12:47, 13:49, 14:20].
- Liao said more data is not automatically better, since it can be noisy or biased, and models are associational and do not understand objects, so they can fail on oddities [16:23, 16:53, 17:24].
- Morey said that in chess, human-plus-engine teams beat engines only briefly, and any systematic task a human does can eventually be automated; in the short term experts move up a level to curate output [22:26, 22:58, 23:30].
- Sherry said AWS fine-tuned an open-source language model for Fox Sports NFL narratives, using 58,000 statistics, and that language model plus fine-tuning beat training from scratch [25:01, 25:31, 26:01, 26:32].
- A Stats Perform panelist said public match data is only part of the picture; private team data on sleep or personality is not and should not be public, and teams can fuse public and private data [29:07, 29:38, 30:09].
- Liao raised privacy risks if teams require round-the-clock monitoring (sleep, glucose, brain interfaces) and said AI-assisted cheating (staying just under doping thresholds) and deepfakes are coming concerns [31:11, 31:42, 32:13, 32:43, 33:15, 33:45].
- Morey said a deepfake highlight tape could change the case for in-person scouting [35:18].
- Black box: Liao said deep models do not explain their decisions, which matters in a fourth-quarter play call. Sherry replied that production models are fine-tuned against historical outcomes and can reject high-variance recommendations. Liao countered with the tank-and-grass example (a model keyed on grass nearby) [36:20, 38:21, 38:52, 39:23, 40:24].
- A panelist said a coach who relies on a model at a moment of uncertainty is a bad user, and models are assistive tools [41:25].
- Liao said clinicians in a survey said they would gravitate toward the machine in a conflict, and humans may doubt themselves. He said handing over decisions is not yet appropriate [41:56, 42:26, 48:35, 49:06].
- Morey said explainability and predictive power will always be in tension, and gradients can flip because of interactions. Draft model advice is easier to defend when it is simple. His owner example: a late pick was allowed to follow the model because the stake was small [45:01, 45:31, 46:02, 47:05].
- Morey said players are pragmatic: show something useful and they listen. A panelist said weaker players are more open [51:41, 52:11].
- Morey said humans will likely not stay at the top of the stack in most fields, and curating models comes first [55:47, 56:19].
- On existential risk, Liao described the paperclip problem; the Stats Perform panelist was not worried because perception and digitization are unsolved, citing autonomous vehicles [58:54, 1:01:27, 1:03:58, 1:04:29].

## Numbers and definitions

- Talent-visa letter: three pages normally, now a draft edited in three places [02:35].
- "Order of magnitude" productivity gain (speaker's words) [03:05].
- Visual cortex: a panelist said about 50% of the brain is associated with it [10:13].
- Fox Sports fine-tuning: 58,000 statistics and hundreds of parameters [25:31].
- Sherry cited about 60% accuracy training from scratch versus about 80% with a language model plus fine-tuning, and said this figure is from science generally, not sports [26:01, 26:32].
- Fans waiting at concessions: 20 to 25 minutes (Sherry's framing for the walk-out system) [27:04].
- Chess: engines first beat top players in 1996 (caption "'96"); human-plus-engine advantage lasted about four or five years [22:58].
- A coder friend's recursive-to-iterative conversion took 2.5 days and the model did it instantly [57:53, 58:24].
- Midjourney entry won a $100 art prize (caption wording) [59:24].
- Definitions given: symbolic AI (rules), supervised, unsupervised and deep learning (Liao) [14:51, 15:23]; generative AI as predicting the next word [18:25].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Fine-tuning a general language model on domain statistics (Fox Sports case) [25:01, 25:31].
- Ridge regression and related regularization for correlated predictors [12:15, 12:47].
- Draft models with year, school and competition proxies, explainable but increasingly complex [44:31, 45:01].
- Contact detection with computer vision for helmet impacts [04:08].
- Public data plus private team data fusion [30:09].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, validation or sample sizes were shown for any sports claim; the Fox Sports result is a vendor's account, and the accuracy figures are not sport-specific.
- Speakers are not labeled in the captions. Attribution above uses context (AWS, Stats Perform, Morey's own roles); some lines (referees, marketing, sleep monitoring, forecasting additions, the 1000-times summarization claim) cannot be assigned with certainty [06:08, 07:12, 07:42, 1:04:59].
- The moderator opens with a joke where one panelist's name is misheard and blamed on hallucination [08:12].
- Panelists contradicted each other on risk and on whether black-box models are manageable [38:52, 40:24, 1:03:58].
- ChatGPT's "neuroball" invention (no concussions, a sport mixing basketball and football) was shown as a creativity example only [19:26].
- Caption problems: "Patrick Lucy", "Sherry"/"Cherry", "Peter" for Patrick, and some garbled lines (for example about explainability and the "tank" story).

## Q&A

- Will catch or touchdown probability stats be available to fans live? Sherry did not know and would follow up [50:41].
- How do you convince athletes ML helps them individually? Morey said players want to improve and listen to useful edges; weaker players are more open [51:41, 52:11].
- Does AI take authenticity out of things such as art? Panelists answered that people want instant, self-serve products, but authenticity is lost when work is synthetic, and sport will stay human [53:13, 54:46].
- Do you take existential concerns seriously? Morey said coders and designers are nervous; Liao described the paperclip problem and enhancement; the Stats Perform panelist was not worried; the close was that worry only seems to go up [57:23, 58:54, 1:03:58, 1:07:32].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: -6pe_zOKCig
title: "SSAC20: A No-Tanking Draft Allocation Policy"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Evan Monroe (caption spelling; also "Munroe"), Stefan Schmidt (host)]
topics: [basketball, policy, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A Stanford PhD student presents a research-paper talk (joint work with a fellow student the captions name "Martino") on NBA draft design. The argument: a lottery that depends only on final win-loss ranking cannot favor the worst team without giving teams some reason to lose on purpose [08:44]. The proposed alternative ties the lottery to when wins and losses happen, re-estimating each team's chance of finishing last after every game and freezing those chances at a point chosen from the season's results [11:55, 13:26]. Simulations on past NBA seasons are shown. It matters because the league's objectives (help the worst team, discourage losing on purpose) are usually treated as opposed.

## Key claims

- Tanking means losing on purpose to improve draft position, and the speaker treats it as hardest to solve in the NBA because of how much key players matter [02:39].
- The league's goals, as the speaker infers them from past rule changes, are to favor the lowest-ranked team while removing any incentive to tank [04:39, 05:09].
- Neither goal is met well today: the worst team gets the first pick with 14% probability, and tanking chatter continues [05:39, 06:10].
- A lottery based only on final ranking cannot favor the worst team at all without leaving some incentive to tank. A uniform lottery (as in 1985 to 1989) removes the incentive but does not favor the worst team [08:44].
- A lottery based on when results happen can both favor the worst team and remove the incentive, in the speaker's model [09:15].
- Once a team is eliminated, losing games that affect its ranking improves its draft odds, so under a fixed lottery that favors bad teams a rational team should try to lose [10:49, 11:20].
- Early games are better evidence of a bad team and carry weaker incentives to lose, so the policy counts them more [16:30, 21:03].
- In the 1989 example, Miami is the worst team and gets the first pick with 44 percent probability under the proposed rule, versus equal odds under the lottery used that year [15:28].
- The speaker admits the rule does worse when the pick is very valuable: in the stress case built around a star prospect (named in captions as Patrick Ewing) the top team gets only 19% [18:31, 19:01].
- In the 2019 example, the other seven non-playoff teams get 18.5% under the current lottery, versus about 5% combined under the proposed rule [20:02, 20:32].
- The speaker concedes the rule might raise the incentive to rebuild over several seasons, which the model does not cover [13:58, 23:33].

## Numbers and definitions

- Before 1985 the two conference losers had a coin flip, so the worst team had a 50% chance [03:09].
- From 1985 an equal lottery for non-playoff teams cut the worst team's chance to "between 11 and 14 percent", depending on team count (phrasing garbled in captions) [03:39].
- The captions give a 1990 figure as "70%", which looks garbled; 1994 is 25%; the most recent change (called "last year") is 14% [04:09].
- No-tanking condition: the benefit of winning a game should be at least the benefit of losing it [10:17].
- Model setup: teams value two things, making the playoffs and getting the first pick, each at a fixed value [09:46]. Results are very sensitive when the two values are near equal and flat once the playoff value is three to five times the pick's [25:06].
- Freeze point: probabilities are fixed after roughly 330 games in the 1989 simulation; the speaker says the rule adjusts "over the first 300 games" and the freeze comes "a third of the way through the season" [17:00, 17:30]. These are slightly inconsistent in the captions.
- In the star-prospect stress case only the first hundred games count [18:31]. In the 2019 case 350 games are used, "not even close to half the season" [20:32].
- Other season's second-worst team (captions say "the feet Suns") gets the highest probability in 2019 [19:31].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Game theory and mechanism design, with a mathematical setup of league objectives and team objectives [07:42].
- Re-estimating each team's probability of finishing last after every game, conditional on results so far, and setting draft odds to match [11:55, 13:26].
- A dynamically chosen stopping time, rather than a fixed date [13:26].
- Back-testing against NBA seasons: 1989 (as an unbiased case because the lottery then was uniform), a star-prospect year, and 2019 [14:28, 18:01, 19:31].
- Prior proposals named in captions: a "tombstone rule" (Adam gold, caption spelling) and a lottery set earlier in the season (Linton Smith and boys, caption spelling) [07:12].

## Limits and open questions

- The model has only two prizes and rational teams; real team goals are broader. The speaker says so [09:46].
- Only the first pick is modeled; extension to a full draft is in an appendix [02:39, 27:10].
- Results depend on a bound for the relative value of playoffs versus the pick, which would need league data to set [25:37].
- The 1989 case is called an unbiased estimate; later seasons are described as tainted because current rules already change behavior [14:58]. The 2019 results are therefore a rough indication.
- The rebuilding-over-years incentive is not modeled [13:58, 23:33].
- Forecast quality matters: if a team knows something the league's forecast does not, gaming remains possible [22:33].
- The speaker works from a paper in a competition; no independent test.

## Q&A

- Injury or late roster changes distorting early records: depends on the league's forecast including known factors; could be gamed if only the team knows [22:03].
- Incentive to lose early and rebuild: acknowledged; a frozen average rule could quantify it [23:33].
- Is the goal actually to give the worst team the pick, and how sensitive is the model to valuing playoffs versus picks: very sensitive near equal values, flat higher; estimate from pick sales and revenue; a lower bound is enough [24:35, 25:06].
- Draft classes with several top players: extend with sequential lottery; sum of terms in an appendix [26:08].

## Summary

A moderated panel on how college athletes' rights to their name, image and likeness (NIL) may work. Captions give the panelists as an investor in player-licensing (Cardinal), a current NFL running back (Salem Berkeley, caption spelling), an NCAA executive vice president (Wilcox), and a Boston College athletic director (Jarmon, caption spelling). They discuss state laws, NCAA rule changes, agents, group licensing, who speaks for athletes, recruiting effects and what college sports will look like later. Little data is shown: the panel is opinion and experience, much of it institutional. Speaker attribution below is inferred from self-descriptions because captions carry no speaker labels.

## Key claims

- The moderator says 30 to 40 states have considered NIL legislation, California's law takes effect in 2023, and Florida's may take effect this fall or a year later [01:33].
- The NCAA executive says the main hurdle is getting more than a thousand member institutions to agree and understand the changes [04:35]. He says athletes should be treated like other students who build brands online [05:36].
- He says college differs from pro sports because recruits choose a school, and the membership wants to protect that recruiting model [07:09].
- The investor says capital has rarely gone to players, and argues that teams, leagues and players are one value chain and the pie can be enlarged [09:11, 10:43].
- The player on the panel says he saw his brand grow by his sophomore year and wishes athletes could have earned something to send home [12:15, 13:15].
- The athletic director calls NIL a chance for education, with a jersey-sales example in which athletes guessed they would get more than they would [14:49, 15:50].
- The NCAA executive expects agencies of many kinds (financial advisors, brand managers, social media specialists) and says the NCAA should avoid running this in-house to prevent athletes being seen as employees [18:55, 21:03].

## Summary

A Stanford PhD student presents a research-paper talk (joint work with a fellow student the captions name "Martino") on NBA draft design. The argument: a lottery that depends only on final win-loss ranking cannot favor the worst team without giving teams some reason to lose on purpose [08:44]. The proposed alternative ties the lottery to when wins and losses happen, re-estimating each team's chance of finishing last after every game and freezing those chances at a point chosen from the season's results [11:55, 13:26]. Simulations on past NBA seasons are shown. It matters because the league's objectives (help the worst team, discourage losing on purpose) are usually treated as opposed.

## Key claims

- Tanking means losing on purpose to improve draft position, and the speaker treats it as hardest to solve in the NBA because of how much key players matter [02:39].
- The league's goals, as the speaker infers them from past rule changes, are to favor the lowest-ranked team while removing any incentive to tank [04:39, 05:09].
- Neither goal is met well today: the worst team gets the first pick with 14% probability, and tanking chatter continues [05:39, 06:10].
- A lottery based only on final ranking cannot favor the worst team at all without leaving some incentive to tank. A uniform lottery (as in 1985 to 1989) removes the incentive but does not favor the worst team [08:44].
- A lottery based on when results happen can both favor the worst team and remove the incentive, in the speaker's model [09:15].
- Once a team is eliminated, losing games that affect its ranking improves its draft odds, so under a fixed lottery that favors bad teams a rational team should try to lose [10:49, 11:20].
- Early games are better evidence of a bad team and carry weaker incentives to lose, so the policy counts them more [16:30, 21:03].
- In the 1989 example, Miami is the worst team and gets the first pick with 44 percent probability under the proposed rule, versus equal odds under the lottery used that year [15:28].
- The speaker admits the rule does worse when the pick is very valuable: in the stress case built around a star prospect (named in captions as Patrick Ewing) the top team gets only 19% [18:31, 19:01].
- In the 2019 example, the other seven non-playoff teams get 18.5% under the current lottery, versus about 5% combined under the proposed rule [20:02, 20:32].
- The speaker concedes the rule might raise the incentive to rebuild over several seasons, which the model does not cover [13:58, 23:33].

## Numbers and definitions

- Before 1985 the two conference losers had a coin flip, so the worst team had a 50% chance [03:09].
- From 1985 an equal lottery for non-playoff teams cut the worst team's chance to "between 11 and 14 percent", depending on team count (phrasing garbled in captions) [03:39].
- The captions give a 1990 figure as "70%", which looks garbled; 1994 is 25%; the most recent change (called "last year") is 14% [04:09].
- No-tanking condition: the benefit of winning a game should be at least the benefit of losing it [10:17].
- Model setup: teams value two things, making the playoffs and getting the first pick, each at a fixed value [09:46]. Results are very sensitive when the two values are near equal and flat once the playoff value is three to five times the pick's [25:06].
- Freeze point: probabilities are fixed after roughly 330 games in the 1989 simulation; the speaker says the rule adjusts "over the first 300 games" and the freeze comes "a third of the way through the season" [17:00, 17:30]. These are slightly inconsistent in the captions.
- In the star-prospect stress case only the first hundred games count [18:31]. In the 2019 case 350 games are used, "not even close to half the season" [20:32].
- Other season's second-worst team (captions say "the feet Suns") gets the highest probability in 2019 [19:31].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Game theory and mechanism design, with a mathematical setup of league objectives and team objectives [07:42].
- Re-estimating each team's probability of finishing last after every game, conditional on results so far, and setting draft odds to match [11:55, 13:26].
- A dynamically chosen stopping time, rather than a fixed date [13:26].
- Back-testing against NBA seasons: 1989 (as an unbiased case because the lottery then was uniform), a star-prospect year, and 2019 [14:28, 18:01, 19:31].
- Prior proposals named in captions: a "tombstone rule" (Adam gold, caption spelling) and a lottery set earlier in the season (Linton Smith and boys, caption spelling) [07:12].

## Limits and open questions

- The model has only two prizes and rational teams; real team goals are broader. The speaker says so [09:46].
- Only the first pick is modeled; extension to a full draft is in an appendix [02:39, 27:10].
- Results depend on a bound for the relative value of playoffs versus the pick, which would need league data to set [25:37].
- The 1989 case is called an unbiased estimate; later seasons are described as tainted because current rules already change behavior [14:58]. The 2019 results are therefore a rough indication.
- The rebuilding-over-years incentive is not modeled [13:58, 23:33].
- Forecast quality matters: if a team knows something the league's forecast does not, gaming remains possible [22:33].
- The speaker works from a paper in a competition; no independent test.

## Q&A

- Injury or late roster changes distorting early records: depends on the league's forecast including known factors; could be gamed if only the team knows [22:03].
- Incentive to lose early and rebuild: acknowledged; a frozen average rule could quantify it [23:33].
- Is the goal actually to give the worst team the pick, and how sensitive is the model to valuing playoffs versus picks: very sensitive near equal values, flat higher; estimate from pick sales and revenue; a lower bound is enough [24:35, 25:06].
- Draft classes with several top players: extend with sequential lottery; sum of terms in an appendix [26:08].

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.
- No sample sizes, no number of athletes, and no raw figures in the captions.
- The 18 percent fluctuation and the peak-power windows are the speaker's own claims with no cited source.
- Mixed signals on method: he says he no longer needs a "coach's eye" [21:13] but also modifies plans by hand for individual athletes and genetics [17:37].
- Lowering load before the biggest game and training harder before games expected to be wins is judgment, not tested [19:39].
- Resource context: he notes LSU gives him every resource. [04:11]
- Caption garbles around "coach time him off" at [05:12] (head strength coach, name unverified).

## Q&A

- Other sports? Five other sports use the weight room and the technology, including volleyball, baseball, women's soccer and beach volleyball; volleyball is trained like football. [22:17], [22:48]
- Screening before loading? Freshmen start in their own group, teach technique first, and go through screening with the medical staff before loading. [23:50], [24:21]
- Gap between regular season and bowl season? Force plate data guided adding strength work during the long break, then returned to the normal approach near competition. [24:52], [25:23]

## Summary

An ESPN analytics specialist presents a plus-minus style model that estimates a single season-level value for every football player. Plain plus-minus fails in football because players share the field nearly all the time, so the model gives each position its own variance, pulls low-snap players toward a prior based on draft rank, recruiting data or last season, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution. Results rank quarterbacks highest and put centers second in importance, which the speaker finds surprising. He shows checks (quarterback versus line, transfers) and lists planned changes. The talk gives no outcome validation beyond these plausibility checks.

## Key claims

- Football has lacked a single stat that values players across all positions, jumping from passer rating to tracking data. [03:42], [04:13]
- A standard plus-minus approach applied to 2018 college data put the top quarterback first and three offensive linemen next, which the speaker calls useless. [08:17]
- Players on the same unit were on the field together about 98 to 99 percent of plays, so the model cannot separate them without extra structure. [08:49]
- The fix: give each position a different variance, where higher variance means greater impact. [09:19]
- Low-snap players are not assumed average; the model shrinks them toward a prior from draft rank, recruiting data or the previous season. [09:49], [10:21]
- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]
- A heavy-tailed distribution lets the best players sit further from average. [11:54]
- In college data for 2019, quarterback variance is by far the highest and the center is second. [13:26]
- The speaker explains the center result by the center's role in calling blocking schemes, which film may not show. [13:56], [14:27]
- Tight end here means a player with a hand on the ground; a standing slot player counts as slot receiver. [14:27], [14:57]
- The position ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with running backs showing a lot of uncertainty. [14:57], [15:28], [15:58]
- The model rated Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson as the top players in recent NFL seasons and Derrick Henry as roughly top ten in impact. [15:58]
- The model's weakness: a strong passer on a run-heavy team may be undervalued (Russell Wilson example). [16:28]
- The previous-year prior held Joe Burrow back despite his strong season (caption: "Joe burrowed"). [17:30]
- Quarterback and line values are correlated but not tightly, so the model can separate them. [18:03], [18:34]
- Transfers in college improved on average; NFL movers declined on average. [19:05], [19:35]
- Inputs are position, on-field status, and down, distance and yard line for expected points. [20:05]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 70 offensive plays per team per game, so about 140 outcomes. [05:44]
- A college team plays about 12 of about 130 teams, described as around 10 percent (captions are muddled between "under" and "over" 10 percent). [06:16]
- Same-unit players on the field together: 98 to 99 percent of plays. [08:49]
- Student-t distribution with eight degrees of freedom, chosen for speed and thick tails, with no special justification. [11:54]
- Ridge regression parameter described as a ratio of model variance to prior variance. [07:46]
- Position scale parameter S_J, a variance multiplier by position. [09:19]
- Tight-end position is defined by alignment, not label. [14:27]
- NFL position distribution shown as a 90 percent interval. [27:15]
- NFL run: after each game window so values are ready next morning; college is slower due to manual tracking. [12:25]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Bayesian ridge-style plus-minus model fit in Stan. [12:25]
- Comparison with real plus-minus at ESPN, and a box-score prior in the planned descriptive version. [20:35], [21:06]
- Other metrics named: WAR, win shares, win probability added, Raptor, expected possession value, approximate value, an NFL scraper package, and a PFF WAR based on scout grades. [01:38], [02:10], [02:40]
- Boss named as Brian McDonald (caption). [02:10]

## Limits and open questions

- No out-of-sample test of player or position value is shown; checks are plausibility (transfer direction, quarterback versus line correlation).
- The center result is partly explained by hypothesis and the speaker admits the cause is open. [23:39]
- The caption name "Bobby Evans" at [08:17] looks wrong (caption spelling); not corrected.
- Model is built only on position, on-field status and expected points. [20:05] This excludes assignments, scheme and coaching.
- Planned changes show current gaps: separate run and pass models, predictive and descriptive versions, expected turnover points. [16:28], [20:35]
- Position importance is a posterior over variance; one questioner found the ordering unclear and the speaker clarified that these are distributions on variance. [26:45], [27:15]
- Institutional view: the author works at ESPN and frames the model for fans and storytelling. [00:37]

## Q&A

- Why does the model value centers more than draft position does? Mental and scheme-calling impact, seen in backups doing worse. [21:39], [22:09]
- Is it continuity? Part of it, but the effect differs for centers than other positions, still to be studied. [23:09], [23:39]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: -6pe_zOKCig
title: "SSAC20: A No-Tanking Draft Allocation Policy"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Evan Monroe (caption spelling; also "Munroe"), Stefan Schmidt (host)]
topics: [basketball, policy, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A Stanford PhD student presents a research-paper talk (joint work with a fellow student the captions name "Martino") on NBA draft design. The argument: a lottery that depends only on final win-loss ranking cannot favor the worst team without giving teams some reason to lose on purpose [08:44]. The proposed alternative ties the lottery to when wins and losses happen, re-estimating each team's chance of finishing last after every game and freezing those chances at a point chosen from the season's results [11:55, 13:26]. Simulations on past NBA seasons are shown. It matters because the league's objectives (help the worst team, discourage losing on purpose) are usually treated as opposed.

## Key claims

- Tanking means losing on purpose to improve draft position, and the speaker treats it as hardest to solve in the NBA because of how much key players matter [02:39].
- The league's goals, as the speaker infers them from past rule changes, are to favor the lowest-ranked team while removing any incentive to tank [04:39, 05:09].
- Neither goal is met well today: the worst team gets the first pick with 14% probability, and tanking chatter continues [05:39, 06:10].
- A lottery based only on final ranking cannot favor the worst team at all without leaving some incentive to tank. A uniform lottery (as in 1985 to 1989) removes the incentive but does not favor the worst team [08:44].
- A lottery based on when results happen can both favor the worst team and remove the incentive, in the speaker's model [09:15].
- Once a team is eliminated, losing games that affect its ranking improves its draft odds, so under a fixed lottery that favors bad teams a rational team should try to lose [10:49, 11:20].
- Early games are better evidence of a bad team and carry weaker incentives to lose, so the policy counts them more [16:30, 21:03].
- In the 1989 example, Miami is the worst team and gets the first pick with 44 percent probability under the proposed rule, versus equal odds under the lottery used that year [15:28].
- The speaker admits the rule does worse when the pick is very valuable: in the stress case built around a star prospect (named in captions as Patrick Ewing) the top team gets only 19% [18:31, 19:01].
- In the 2019 example, the other seven non-playoff teams get 18.5% under the current lottery, versus about 5% combined under the proposed rule [20:02, 20:32].
- The speaker concedes the rule might raise the incentive to rebuild over several seasons, which the model does not cover [13:58, 23:33].

## Numbers and definitions

- Before 1985 the two conference losers had a coin flip, so the worst team had a 50% chance [03:09].
- From 1985 an equal lottery for non-playoff teams cut the worst team's chance to "between 11 and 14 percent", depending on team count (phrasing garbled in captions) [03:39].
- The captions give a 1990 figure as "70%", which looks garbled; 1994 is 25%; the most recent change (called "last year") is 14% [04:09].
- No-tanking condition: the benefit of winning a game should be at least the benefit of losing it [10:17].
- Model setup: teams value two things, making the playoffs and getting the first pick, each at a fixed value [09:46]. Results are very sensitive when the two values are near equal and flat once the playoff value is three to five times the pick's [25:06].
- Freeze point: probabilities are fixed after roughly 330 games in the 1989 simulation; the speaker says the rule adjusts "over the first 300 games" and the freeze comes "a third of the way through the season" [17:00, 17:30]. These are slightly inconsistent in the captions.
- In the star-prospect stress case only the first hundred games count [18:31]. In the 2019 case 350 games are used, "not even close to half the season" [20:32].
- Other season's second-worst team (captions say "the feet Suns") gets the highest probability in 2019 [19:31].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Game theory and mechanism design, with a mathematical setup of league objectives and team objectives [07:42].
- Re-estimating each team's probability of finishing last after every game, conditional on results so far, and setting draft odds to match [11:55, 13:26].
- A dynamically chosen stopping time, rather than a fixed date [13:26].
- Back-testing against NBA seasons: 1989 (as an unbiased case because the lottery then was uniform), a star-prospect year, and 2019 [14:28, 18:01, 19:31].
- Prior proposals named in captions: a "tombstone rule" (Adam gold, caption spelling) and a lottery set earlier in the season (Linton Smith and boys, caption spelling) [07:12].

## Limits and open questions

- The model has only two prizes and rational teams; real team goals are broader. The speaker says so [09:46].
- Only the first pick is modeled; extension to a full draft is in an appendix [02:39, 27:10].
- Results depend on a bound for the relative value of playoffs versus the pick, which would need league data to set [25:37].
- The 1989 case is called an unbiased estimate; later seasons are described as tainted because current rules already change behavior [14:58]. The 2019 results are therefore a rough indication.
- The rebuilding-over-years incentive is not modeled [13:58, 23:33].
- Forecast quality matters: if a team knows something the league's forecast does not, gaming remains possible [22:33].
- The speaker works from a paper in a competition; no independent test.

## Q&A

- Injury or late roster changes distorting early records: depends on the league's forecast including known factors; could be gamed if only the team knows [22:03].
- Incentive to lose early and rebuild: acknowledged; a frozen average rule could quantify it [23:33].
- Is the goal actually to give the worst team the pick, and how sensitive is the model to valuing playoffs versus picks: very sensitive near equal values, flat higher; estimate from pick sales and revenue; a lower bound is enough [24:35, 25:06].
- Draft classes with several top players: extend with sequential lottery; sum of terms in an appendix [26:08].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: yz-O706SNck
title: "SSAC20: Tackling Name, Image, and Likeness in College Sports"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Warren Zola (moderator), Jerry Cardinal, Salem Berkeley (caption spelling), Stan Wilcox, Martin Jarmon (caption spelling)]
topics: [policy, front-office, other-sport:american-football, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel on how college athletes' rights to their name, image and likeness (NIL) may work. Captions give the panelists as an investor in player-licensing (Cardinal), a current NFL running back (Salem Berkeley, caption spelling), an NCAA executive vice president (Wilcox), and a Boston College athletic director (Jarmon, caption spelling). They discuss state laws, NCAA rule changes, agents, group licensing, who speaks for athletes, recruiting effects and what college sports will look like later. Little data is shown: the panel is opinion and experience, much of it institutional. Speaker attribution below is inferred from self-descriptions because captions carry no speaker labels.

## Key claims

- The moderator says 30 to 40 states have considered NIL legislation, California's law takes effect in 2023, and Florida's may take effect this fall or a year later [01:33].
- The NCAA executive says the main hurdle is getting more than a thousand member institutions to agree and understand the changes [04:35]. He says athletes should be treated like other students who build brands online [05:36].
- He says college differs from pro sports because recruits choose a school, and the membership wants to protect that recruiting model [07:09].
- The investor says capital has rarely gone to players, and argues that teams, leagues and players are one value chain and the pie can be enlarged [09:11, 10:43].
- The player on the panel says he saw his brand grow by his sophomore year and wishes athletes could have earned something to send home [12:15, 13:15].
- The athletic director calls NIL a chance for education, with a jersey-sales example in which athletes guessed they would get more than they would [14:49, 15:50].
- The NCAA executive expects agencies of many kinds (financial advisors, brand managers, social media specialists) and says the NCAA should avoid running this in-house to prevent athletes being seen as employees [18:55, 21:03].
- The investor argues for starting with group licensing such as video games and trading cards before individual NIL [24:37, 42:35].
- The NCAA executive says a student-athlete association built from advisory committees could represent athletes in group negotiations, but not before individual licenses come first [28:41, 29:11].
- The NCAA executive says if state laws take effect before a federal law, the NCAA could face chaos over who may compete, or would sue the states [35:20, 35:50].
- Panelists say NIL will change recruiting little for most athletes; the NCAA executive says money-focused athletes can choose pro or semi-pro routes [38:57, 40:31].
- The moderator and panelists raise women's sports: one example is elite women's ice hockey players running camps or lessons [41:34].
- Asked for five to ten years out, the NCAA executive says college sports will look much the same, within the "collegiate model", and the athletic director says the mission remains education [46:13, 47:47].

## Numbers and definitions

- 30 to 40 states considering NIL laws [01:33]; California effective 2023 [01:33]; Florida effective date as above [01:33, 34:47].
- More than a thousand NCAA member institutions [04:35].
- A $60 jersey example: athletes guessed $40 or $50 as their share [15:50].
- A social media market rate was described for an athlete with "a hundred and ten thousand followers" [19:25].
- The investor cites about two thousand NFL players and about 1,500 baseball players as constituents of the unions that anchor his company [23:35].
- The athletic director refers to 31 varsity sports, and an audience of about "800 athletes", then "750 athletes on campus" (garbled) [14:17, 29:42].
- The NCAA creates a student-athlete advisory committee in 1990-91 [27:40].
- NCAA legislative changes: phase 1 in April, phase 2 in "January 21" (captions; may be January 2021) [36:23].
- The investor says the issue has been unresolved since 1995, and the moderator says she testified before Congress in 2011 [16:21, 42:05].
- The player says he finished around third in Heisman voting (garbled) [12:45].
- Panel length: about 55 minutes with 10 minutes of audience Q&A [00:32].

## Methods and frameworks named

- No data model. The frameworks named are the NCAA's phased rule-change plan [36:23], the value-chain view of teams, leagues and players [09:43], and group licensing anchored by video games and trading cards [25:07].

## Limits and open questions

- No sample, data or evidence; opinions from people with stakes: an NCAA executive, an athletic director, an investor selling a product, and one player.
- Forecasts made in 2020 (federal pre-emption, effect on recruiting, little change by 2030) are untested here [35:20, 46:13].
- The panel does not settle who bargains for athletes; the investor and NCAA executive offer different routes [26:08, 28:41].
- Title IX is raised by the moderator and answered only with examples [41:34].
