---
type: video-summary
video_id: -nyTn7E2pKw
title: "SSAC21: Fact or Fiction: Basketball Mythbusting"
event: SSAC21 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Elton Brand, Sonia Raman (caption spelling "ramon"/"rahman"), Mike Zarin (caption spelling "sarin"), Kirk Goldsberry (moderator), Riley Foreman (student host)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, policy]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated fact-or-fiction panel with a 76ers general manager, a Grizzlies assistant coach who formerly coached MIT's women's team, and a Celtics executive, moderated by an ESPN writer. Topics: whether star players now cluster, how analytics reached players, the three-point line, mid-range shooting, an MVP race, the lottery, free throws, playoff format and tampering rules. It is mostly opinion from people who work for teams, with a few numbers from the moderator and panelists. A useful thread for sport science is how analytics is explained to players and coaches.

## Key claims

- On super teams: the Celtics executive says the talent-distribution worry is no more true than in past eras; the moderator notes final-MVP winners who switched teams rose after 2010, which suggests player choice matters more [01:34, 02:35].
- The GM attributes the change to player empowerment; the coach says markets matter less now because social media gives any player a platform [03:06, 05:36].
- The GM describes early player distrust of data, thinking staff wanted them to play a certain way, and says it is breaking down as players ask how to be effective [09:08].
- The coach says she explained numbers, showed film and asked players for their read, because analytics "never gives a cut and dry answer" [10:09, 10:41]. She adds that the NBA challenge is knowing what matters rather than what is noisy or recent, and that buy-in is the limit [11:11].
- Moving the NBA three-point line is not a priority: the Celtics executive says fans like the game and a farther line would widen the gap with the corner three [12:41, 13:44].
- The GM, a former mid-range scorer, says moving out of mid-range is the right play for efficiency [15:49, 16:19].
- The Celtics executive and moderator note that the MVP race may go to a center for the first time since 2000 to 2001, and that star centers also play in the post [25:59, 28:02].
- The moderator says current stats favor one end of the court and understate defensive anchors [29:04].
- The Celtics executive says the new flatter lottery odds are better because they remove the incentive to be extremely bad, but he dislikes perverse incentives [29:36, 31:07].
- He describes a staff idea, dubbed "draft balls", in which teams get a currency usable on lottery chances or cap exceptions; he says the league's appetite is low [31:37, 33:09].
- On free throws, the coach says drawing fouls is already prominent in scouting reports, so it is not undervalued [34:40, 35:11]. The GM says drawing contact has moved from "soft" to "smart" [36:12].
- The Celtics executive dislikes fouls where the offensive player creates the contact, but says the best foul-drawers are skilled and hard to legislate away [37:45, 38:15].
- The GM would keep conferences in the playoffs, citing rivalries and travel; the Celtics executive says one-through-sixteen seeding would add about 25,000 miles of travel [39:16, 40:48].
- On tampering rules, the Celtics executive says the enforcement changes have not been tested in a normal period, so the answer is unknown [42:20, 43:23].
- On the women's tournament weight-room controversy, the coach says it shows women are not accepting unequal treatment, and the Celtics executive notes the men and women were given different test types for the virus [18:53, 20:54].

## Numbers and definitions

- Three-point shots were 3% of NBA shots in the first year of the line (1979), close to 40% "this season", with a projection of over half by the end of the decade [11:41].
- Moderator's finals-MVP figure: "only seven of 41" between 1969 and 2010 won after switching teams (caption phrasing garbled); "eight of those 10" since 2010 [02:35].
- NBA three-point efficiency: 36.7 this season, up from 35.5 [16:19].
- Embiid, as cited by the GM: about 60% from mid-range, 50% from the field, 40% from three [23:58]. Free throws: makes 10 per game on almost 12 attempts [36:12]. The captions refer to him as "joel" or "jamal"; the second looks wrong.
- Free throw league average: 77 percent, as given in a moderator question [34:09].
- Playoff travel: about 25,000 miles added if seeded one through 16, "the circumference of the earth" [40:48].
- Women's tournament: "two to three times more fans" for men's tickets (the coach) [19:54].
- The Celtics executive says the "draft balls" idea dates to about 2011 or 2012 [32:07].
- Panel format: 35 minutes with 10 minutes of audience questions [00:32].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Analytics communication: explain, show film, then collaborate with players on coverage decisions [10:41].
- Staff-designed "draft balls" resource allocation: ping-pong balls used as a currency for lottery chances or cap exceptions [32:07].
- League tampering rules and pre-agency period [42:20].
- Travel-distance estimate for a one-to-16 playoff, done by the Celtics staff [40:48].

## Limits and open questions

- Fact-or-fiction answers are opinions from team employees, who have stakes in the league's image; the Celtics executive says he would act on fan feedback, but gives none [13:13].
- The finals-MVP claim has a garbled count in the captions; the moderator uses it to point to a trend since 2010 [02:35].
- The MVP debate is explicitly speculative at the time of the panel [24:28, 25:59].
- The "draft balls" idea is not tested; no data shown [33:09].
- The panel mentions load management only in passing [24:59].

## Q&A

- Does the ability to draw fouls deserve higher value (to the coach): not undervalued, already in scouting reports [34:40].
- Is chasing whistles soft or dirty (to the GM): now seen as smart, within limits [36:12].
- Foul legislation (Celtics executive): would remove the contact-creation fouls, not the skilled ones [37:14].
- Eliminate conferences in the playoffs: no, travel and rivalries [39:16].
- Change tampering rules: unknown until enforcement is tested [41:49, 42:20].
- Penalties severe enough (to the GM): hard to enforce, fines are large [43:53].
- Could a league official beat the GM at the game HORSE: no, per the Celtics executive and GM [44:53].

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]

The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.

- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]

- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]

- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

Plain plus-minus fails in football because players share the field nearly all the time, so the model gives each position its own variance, pulls low-snap players toward a prior based on draft rank, recruiting data or last season, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution. - Football has lacked a single stat that values players across all positions, jumping from passer rating to tracking data. [03:42], [04:13]
- A standard plus-minus approach applied to 2018 college data put the top quarterback first and three offensive linemen next, which the speaker calls useless. [08:17]
- Players on the same unit were on the field together about 98 to 99 percent of plays, so the model cannot separate them without extra structure. [08:49]
- The fix: give each position a different variance, where higher variance means greater impact. [09:19]
- Low-snap players are not assumed average; the model shrinks them toward a prior from draft rank, recruiting data or the previous season. [09:49], [10:21]
- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]
- A heavy-tailed distribution lets the best players sit further from average. [11:54]
- In college data for 2019, quarterback variance is by far the highest and the center is second. [13:26]
- The speaker explains the center result by the center's role in calling blocking schemes, which film may not show. [13:56], [14:27]
- Tight end here means a player with a hand on the ground; a standing slot player counts as slot receiver. [14:27], [14:57]
- The position ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with running backs showing a lot of uncertainty. [14:57], [15:28], [15:58]
- The model rated Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson as the top players in recent NFL seasons and Derrick Henry as roughly top ten in impact. [15:58]

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.
- No sample sizes, no number of athletes, and no raw figures in the captions.
- The 18 percent fluctuation and the peak-power windows are the speaker's own claims with no cited source.
- Mixed signals on method: he says he no longer needs a "coach's eye" [21:13] but also modifies plans by hand for individual athletes and genetics [17:37].
- Lowering load before the biggest game and training harder before games expected to be wins is judgment, not tested [19:39].
- Resource context: he notes LSU gives him every resource. [04:11]
- Caption garbles around "coach time him off" at [05:12] (head strength coach, name unverified).

## Q&A

- Other sports? Five other sports use the weight room and the technology, including volleyball, baseball, women's soccer and beach volleyball; volleyball is trained like football. [22:17], [22:48]
- Screening before loading? Freshmen start in their own group, teach technique first, and go through screening with the medical staff before loading. [23:50], [24:21]
- Gap between regular season and bowl season? Force plate data guided adding strength work during the long break, then returned to the normal approach near competition. [24:52], [25:23]

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.
- No sample sizes, no number of athletes, and no raw figures in the captions.
- The 18 percent fluctuation and the peak-power windows are the speaker's own claims with no cited source.
- Mixed signals on method: he says he no longer needs a "coach's eye" [21:13] but also modifies plans by hand for individual athletes and genetics [17:37].

- Resource context: he notes LSU gives him every resource. [04:11]
- Caption garbles around "coach time him off" at [05:12] (head strength coach, name unverified).

## Q&A

- Other sports? Five other sports use the weight room and the technology, including volleyball, baseball, women's soccer and beach volleyball; volleyball is trained like football. [22:17], [22:48]
- Screening before loading? Freshmen start in their own group, teach technique first, and go through screening with the medical staff before loading. [23:50], [24:21]

## Summary

An ESPN analytics specialist presents a plus-minus style model that estimates a single season-level value for every football player. Plain plus-minus fails in football because players share the field nearly all the time, so the model gives each position its own variance, pulls low-snap players toward a prior based on draft rank, recruiting data or last season, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution. Results rank quarterbacks highest and put centers second in importance, which the speaker finds surprising. He shows checks (quarterback versus line, transfers) and lists planned changes. The talk gives no outcome validation beyond these plausibility checks.

## Key claims

- Football has lacked a single stat that values players across all positions, jumping from passer rating to tracking data. [03:42], [04:13]
- A standard plus-minus approach applied to 2018 college data put the top quarterback first and three offensive linemen next, which the speaker calls useless. [08:17]
- Players on the same unit were on the field together about 98 to 99 percent of plays, so the model cannot separate them without extra structure. [08:49]
- The fix: give each position a different variance, where higher variance means greater impact. [09:19]
- Low-snap players are not assumed average; the model shrinks them toward a prior from draft rank, recruiting data or the previous season. [09:49], [10:21]
- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]
- A heavy-tailed distribution lets the best players sit further from average. [11:54]
- In college data for 2019, quarterback variance is by far the highest and the center is second. [13:26]
- The speaker explains the center result by the center's role in calling blocking schemes, which film may not show. [13:56], [14:27]
- Tight end here means a player with a hand on the ground; a standing slot player counts as slot receiver. [14:27], [14:57]
- The position ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with running backs showing a lot of uncertainty. [14:57], [15:28], [15:58]
- The model rated Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson as the top players in recent NFL seasons and Derrick Henry as roughly top ten in impact. [15:58]
- The model's weakness: a strong passer on a run-heavy team may be undervalued (Russell Wilson example). [16:28]
- The previous-year prior held Joe Burrow back despite his strong season (caption: "Joe burrowed"). [17:30]
- Quarterback and line values are correlated but not tightly, so the model can separate them. [18:03], [18:34]
- Transfers in college improved on average; NFL movers declined on average. [19:05], [19:35]
- Inputs are position, on-field status, and down, distance and yard line for expected points. [20:05]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 70 offensive plays per team per game, so about 140 outcomes. [05:44]
- A college team plays about 12 of about 130 teams, described as around 10 percent (captions are muddled between "under" and "over" 10 percent). [06:16]
- Same-unit players on the field together: 98 to 99 percent of plays. [08:49]
- Student-t distribution with eight degrees of freedom, chosen for speed and thick tails, with no special justification. [11:54]
- Ridge regression parameter described as a ratio of model variance to prior variance. [07:46]
- Position scale parameter S_J, a variance multiplier by position. [09:19]
- Tight-end position is defined by alignment, not label. [14:27]
- NFL position distribution shown as a 90 percent interval. [27:15]
- NFL run: after each game window so values are ready next morning; college is slower due to manual tracking. [12:25]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Bayesian ridge-style plus-minus model fit in Stan. [12:25]
- Comparison with real plus-minus at ESPN, and a box-score prior in the planned descriptive version. [20:35], [21:06]
- Other metrics named: WAR, win shares, win probability added, Raptor, expected possession value, approximate value, an NFL scraper package, and a PFF WAR based on scout grades. [01:38], [02:10], [02:40]
- Boss named as Brian McDonald (caption). [02:10]

## Limits and open questions

- No out-of-sample test of player or position value is shown; checks are plausibility (transfer direction, quarterback versus line correlation).
- The center result is partly explained by hypothesis and the speaker admits the cause is open. [23:39]
- The caption name "Bobby Evans" at [08:17] looks wrong (caption spelling); not corrected.
- Model is built only on position, on-field status and expected points. [20:05] This excludes assignments, scheme and coaching.
- Planned changes show current gaps: separate run and pass models, predictive and descriptive versions, expected turnover points. [16:28], [20:35]
- Position importance is a posterior over variance; one questioner found the ordering unclear and the speaker clarified that these are distributions on variance. [26:45], [27:15]
- Institutional view: the author works at ESPN and frames the model for fans and storytelling. [00:37]

## Q&A

- Why does the model value centers more than draft position does? Mental and scheme-calling impact, seen in backups doing worse. [21:39], [22:09]
- Is it continuity? Part of it, but the effect differs for centers than other positions, still to be studied. [23:09], [23:39]
- Should coaches be included? Possibly, especially for judging how a player transfers to a new team. [24:09]
- Do center ratings track team success? Yes, less strongly; the top-rated center going into 2019 was Clemson's. [24:42]
- Why slot cornerbacks high? The speaker does not know. [25:13]
- Outside linebackers versus defensive ends? Position is by alignment, with a weighted average for those who play both. [25:43], [26:15]
- Why only college distribution shown? NFL was shown in a different format with a 90 percent interval. [27:15]

## Summary

For the US Olympic Committee, the lab used open-source pose estimation to find the takeoff frame and launch angle and velocity in long jump video, replacing hand tagging. For Red Bull high performance in esports, it tested whether automatically adjusting game speed with finer steps raised skill acquisition. Both are short project descriptions with few reported numbers. Her closing view is that analytics is a tool whose use depends on a defined question.

## Key claims

- Training is a loop of capture, processing, coaching and repeat, and much of what is captured is not put back into the immediate loop. [02:40], [03:43]

- People are poor at judging when to make practice harder or easier, which automation can do. [13:40]
- Coaches filter what athletes hear, and a tool should give only what the coach asks for, such as launch angle and the exact frame. [20:35], [21:06]
- Analytics is a tool, not an answer; define the question and the action first. [21:36], [22:06]
- Passive collection with nothing on the athlete is where she sees the future. [23:06]

- Body locations tagged per frame: 19. [06:22]

- Pose tool identified eleven people in one frame, one being the jumper. [08:31]
- Accuracy reached: about 99 percent. [09:32]
- Adaptive rule: speed up 10 percent after a session of seven tries at 60 percent success; no change between 40 and 60; slow down below 40 percent. [11:37], [12:10]

## Limits and open questions

## Summary

A panel on how teams identify a franchise quarterback. Former NFL backup and quarterback coach Jordan Palmer says evaluation starts with confidence and maturity, then accuracy, which he argues can be trained and measured with vision testing, motion capture and an instrumented football. Kevin Mears, a football strategy fellow at Zealous Analytics, also puts accuracy first, says traditional stats hide too much, and names quarterback decision making as the open frontier. Both say fit with a team's system matters and that character, such as toughness, has no metric and was hard to read when evaluation moved to video calls. - Mears says teams can be tricked into a big arm, athleticism or charisma when the passer cannot deliver the ball on time [06:40].
- Mears says college data from companies such as PFF lets analysts see offense complexity, accurate-ball rate, and air yards versus after-catch or screen yards [07:43] [08:13].

- Palmer says Josh Allen's accuracy gain came from control (spiral efficiency on layered and touch throws) and not arm power [13:23] [13:54].
- Mears says traditional football stats are weak and newer metrics add context; the frontier is judging quarterback decision making given play design [16:28] [17:29].
- Palmer says PFF frustrates players when it assigns a missed block to someone who did not own the assignment [19:30] [20:00].
- Palmer says decision making is hard to evaluate from tape because the same concept can be read several ways and he does not know the week's plan [20:00] [20:30] [21:01].
- Palmer builds decision-making talks around game management, for example end of half and end of game situations [21:32] [22:03].
- Mears says data people need humility and trust built with scouts [24:41] [25:11].
- Mears says that for quarterbacks, a workout like Palmer's should interest the NFL more than hand size [25:42] [26:12].

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.

## Summary

An ESPN analytics specialist presents a plus-minus style model that estimates a single season-level value for every football player. Plain plus-minus fails in football because players share the field nearly all the time, so the model gives each position its own variance, pulls low-snap players toward a prior based on draft rank, recruiting data or last season, and uses a heavy-tailed distribution. Results rank quarterbacks highest and put centers second in importance, which the speaker finds surprising. He shows checks (quarterback versus line, transfers) and lists planned changes. The talk gives no outcome validation beyond these plausibility checks.

## Key claims

- Football has lacked a single stat that values players across all positions, jumping from passer rating to tracking data. [03:42], [04:13]
- A standard plus-minus approach applied to 2018 college data put the top quarterback first and three offensive linemen next, which the speaker calls useless. [08:17]
- Players on the same unit were on the field together about 98 to 99 percent of plays, so the model cannot separate them without extra structure. [08:49]
- The fix: give each position a different variance, where higher variance means greater impact. [09:19]
- Low-snap players are not assumed average; the model shrinks them toward a prior from draft rank, recruiting data or the previous season. [09:49], [10:21]
- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]
- A heavy-tailed distribution lets the best players sit further from average. [11:54]
- In college data for 2019, quarterback variance is by far the highest and the center is second. [13:26]
- The speaker explains the center result by the center's role in calling blocking schemes, which film may not show. [13:56], [14:27]
- Tight end here means a player with a hand on the ground; a standing slot player counts as slot receiver. [14:27], [14:57]
- The position ordering is stable across NFL seasons since 2007, with running backs showing a lot of uncertainty. [14:57], [15:28], [15:58]
- The model rated Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson as the top players in recent NFL seasons and Derrick Henry as roughly top ten in impact. [15:58]
- The model's weakness: a strong passer on a run-heavy team may be undervalued (Russell Wilson example). [16:28]
- The previous-year prior held Joe Burrow back despite his strong season (caption: "Joe burrowed"). [17:30]
- Quarterback and line values are correlated but not tightly, so the model can separate them. [18:03], [18:34]
- Transfers in college improved on average; NFL movers declined on average. [19:05], [19:35]
- Inputs are position, on-field status, and down, distance and yard line for expected points. [20:05]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 70 offensive plays per team per game, so about 140 outcomes. [05:44]
- A college team plays about 12 of about 130 teams, described as around 10 percent (captions are muddled between "under" and "over" 10 percent). [06:16]
- Same-unit players on the field together: 98 to 99 percent of plays. [08:49]
- Student-t distribution with eight degrees of freedom, chosen for speed and thick tails, with no special justification. [11:54]
- Ridge regression parameter described as a ratio of model variance to prior variance. [07:46]
- Position scale parameter S_J, a variance multiplier by position. [09:19]
- Tight-end position is defined by alignment, not label. [14:27]
- NFL position distribution shown as a 90 percent interval. [27:15]
- NFL run: after each game window so values are ready next morning; college is slower due to manual tracking. [12:25]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Bayesian ridge-style plus-minus model fit in Stan. [12:25]
- Comparison with real plus-minus at ESPN, and a box-score prior in the planned descriptive version. [20:35], [21:06]
- Other metrics named: WAR, win shares, win probability added, Raptor, expected possession value, approximate value, an NFL scraper package, and a PFF WAR based on scout grades. [01:38], [02:10], [02:40]
- Boss named as Brian McDonald (caption). [02:10]

## Limits and open questions

- No out-of-sample test of player or position value is shown; checks are plausibility (transfer direction, quarterback versus line correlation).
- The center result is partly explained by hypothesis and the speaker admits the cause is open. [23:39]
- The caption name "Bobby Evans" at [08:17] looks wrong (caption spelling); not corrected.
- Model is built only on position, on-field status and expected points. [20:05] This excludes assignments, scheme and coaching.
- Planned changes show current gaps: separate run and pass models, predictive and descriptive versions, expected turnover points. [16:28], [20:35]
- Position importance is a posterior over variance; one questioner found the ordering unclear and the speaker clarified that these are distributions on variance. [26:45], [27:15]
- Institutional view: the author works at ESPN and frames the model for fans and storytelling. [00:37]

## Q&A

- Why does the model value centers more than draft position does? Mental and scheme-calling impact, seen in backups doing worse. [21:39], [22:09]
- Is it continuity? Part of it, but the effect differs for centers than other positions, still to be studied. [23:09], [23:39]
- Should coaches be included? Possibly, especially for judging how a player transfers to a new team. [24:09]
- Do center ratings track team success? Yes, less strongly; the top-rated center going into 2019 was Clemson's. [24:42]
- Why slot cornerbacks high? The speaker does not know. [25:13]
- Outside linebackers versus defensive ends? Position is by alignment, with a weighted average for those who play both. [25:43], [26:15]
- Why only college distribution shown? NFL was shown in a different format with a 90 percent interval. [27:15]

For Red Bull high performance in esports, it tested whether automatically adjusting game speed with finer steps raised skill acquisition. - Detecting takeoff by the last point to leave the ground (the left toe in the example) reached about 99 percent accuracy, with small errors left. [09:32]
- Red Bull chose esports because every click is recorded. [10:33]
- Prior MIT research (Stephanie Muller, CSAIL, caption spelling) showed adaptive inputs can raise skill acquisition rate. [10:33]
- Experts gained most under the granular adaptive condition; at 10 percent adaptive most people did worse, since the change was too subtle to notice. [13:10]
- People are poor at judging when to make practice harder or easier, which automation can do. [13:40]
- Coaches filter what athletes hear, and a tool should give only what the coach asks for, such as launch angle and the exact frame. [20:35], [21:06]

- Accuracy reached: about 99 percent. [09:32]
- Adaptive rule: speed up 10 percent after a session of seven tries at 60 percent success; no change between 40 and 60; slow down below 40 percent. [11:37], [12:10]

- Task: a specific move in Super Smash Brothers (caption: "the wave -", probably a wave dash). [11:37]

- No sample sizes or statistics for the esports study, and the figure is described only by marker shape. [14:13]
- The jump accuracy figure of 99 percent has no sample size and applies to takeoff detection.

## Summary

A panel on how teams identify a franchise quarterback. Former NFL backup and quarterback coach Jordan Palmer says evaluation starts with confidence and maturity, then accuracy, which he argues can be trained and measured with vision testing, motion capture and an instrumented football. Kevin Mears, a football strategy fellow at Zealous Analytics, also puts accuracy first, says traditional stats hide too much, and names quarterback decision making as the open frontier. Both say fit with a team's system matters and that character, such as toughness, has no metric and was hard to read when evaluation moved to video calls. The panel is mostly experience and anecdote, with little data shown.

## Key claims

- Palmer says confidence and maturity are what he checks first, ahead of physical measurables [03:07].
- Palmer treats confidence as something developed, and calls confidence that depends on outside opinion a red flag, versus confidence that is self-generated [03:38] [04:08].
- Palmer defines maturity as handling brand new situations as if they were familiar [04:08].
- Mears says accuracy is the starting point and that teams can fool themselves into thinking a quarterback is accurate enough [06:10].
- Mears says teams can be tricked into a big arm, athleticism or charisma when the passer cannot deliver the ball on time [06:40].
- Mears says college data from companies such as PFF lets analysts see offense complexity, accurate-ball rate, and air yards versus after-catch or screen yards [07:43] [08:13].
- Palmer says quarterback coaching largely avoided analytics, and he disagrees that accuracy cannot be developed [09:15] [10:17].
- Palmer says vision testing can find problems that a standard 20/20 screen misses [10:48] [11:19].
- Palmer uses motion capture to assess movement and a throwing "kinematic sequence", and says some good NFL quarterbacks have an off sequence [11:52] [12:22].
- Palmer says a Wilson football with a chip measures velocity, spin rate and a spiral efficiency measure, and he tracks players weekly with goals tied to the numbers [12:22] [12:53] [13:23].
- Palmer says Josh Allen's accuracy gain came from control (spiral efficiency on layered and touch throws) and not arm power [13:23] [13:54].
- Mears says traditional football stats are weak and newer metrics add context; the frontier is judging quarterback decision making given play design [16:28] [17:29].
- Palmer says PFF frustrates players when it assigns a missed block to someone who did not own the assignment [19:30] [20:00].

title: "SSAC21: Say Goodbye to the 40 Yard Dash: The Future of NFL Roster Building"
event: SSAC21 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kevin Demoff, Nick Caserio, Brian Burke, Kevin Clark (moderator)]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, sports-science]

## Summary

A panel on how NFL teams blend tape, scouting and analytics in roster building. Rams COO Kevin Demoff, Texans GM Nick Caserio and ESPN analyst Brian Burke agree it is a hybrid model, not scouts against analysts. They say data is most useful for refining decisions retroactively, recalibrating scouts, and finding position-specific traits, and that the 40-yard dash matters little for some positions. Burke says combined metrics, such as weight with vertical jump, can show signal single metrics miss. Caserio expects growth in sports performance data used with players, such as force plates and strength asymmetry. Personality and character measurement is described as unsolved, and Burke urges caution with psychology research.

## Key claims

- Demoff says draft meetings now center on efficiency and tracking rather than raw stats, and every team now has several analytics staff [02:33] [03:03].
- Caserio says the volume of data is large, the key is application, and players benefit most when given measurable feedback, especially in the offseason [03:33] [04:05].
- Burke says player tracking plus machine learning will make X's and O's more accessible to fans [05:07].
- Caserio says growth has been largest on the player performance side, and that the test of any data is whether it helps win [06:39] [07:40].
- Demoff says teams can now look back after four or five years at decisions made on analytics and refine them [09:11] [09:42].
- Demoff says analytics grades go in without bias about a top prospect, and that analytics has most helped on later-round players seen by scouts only once or twice [10:12] [10:42].
- Demoff says character, learning and growth capacity are the unsolved piece and the source of many misses [11:12] [11:44].
- Caserio describes building a position model in New England and testing it retroactively, and says every drafted player is a developmental player and a program's structure affects growth [12:14] [12:44] [13:14] [14:15].
- Burke says a model need not give a final number; data can recalibrate scouts' grades, and scouting grades should still dominate for college players now [14:45] [15:15] [15:46].
- Burke says college tracking data will be a watershed, for example on receiver separation and safety reactions [16:17] [16:48].
- Demoff says analytics and scout grades sit side by side on the board, and that winning is the competitive advantage because it keeps staff in place to refine processes [17:49] [18:20].
- Demoff says the scouts versus analytics divide was overstated, and scouts supply information on work ethic and background [19:22] [19:52].
- Caserio says a hybrid model is where success lies, and scouts gather how a player learns and adapts, which a model cannot [20:22] [20:52] [21:22].
- Caserio says the 40 may be the least important number for some positions, and that offensive linemen's speed is useless; he calls the draft roughly 50/50, worse in later rounds [23:23] [23:53].
- Caserio says intangible traits, such as sustaining performance and mental stamina, predict more than speed or jump numbers, though the numbers are a benchmark [24:55] [25:25].
- Demoff says predictive traits differ by position and size heuristics are breaking down, citing Kyler Murray and a 10-yard burst for outside linebackers [26:26] [27:26] [27:56].
- Caserio says a study of one position found no link between length and success, which can expose beliefs scouts carry [28:58] [29:28].
- Demoff says traits that correlate with high picks may be overpriced in the fourth round, so a study can create a short-term draft edge [29:58] [30:29].
- Burke says combine results showed no correlation with pro success, but combined metrics (weight with vertical jump for linemen) do carry information [32:00] [33:02] [33:33].
- Demoff says in-game strategy will be the next area of change, held back by limits on sideline data, and that defenses adapt to whatever offenses learn [34:03] [35:05] [35:36].
- Demoff says league-wide odds from a model do not map to one decision [37:38] [38:08].
- Caserio expects growth in injury and games-lost prediction tied to training, naming force plates, strength measured by bar speed, and showing athletes imbalances, plus nutrition and sleep [38:39] [39:09] [39:40] [40:10].
- Burke warns that psychology research often fails to replicate and urges caution with it [47:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel format: 35 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions [00:31].
- Caserio began in 2001, reviewing tape on an old beta deck [06:08].
- Scouting spend: about $10 million per team, times 32 teams, $320 million [11:12] (the final "million" is split across [11:44] in captions).
- Burke's recalibration example: scout nine becomes seven, seven becomes six [15:15].
- Pro days: "100 to 125 schools" in about a month of workouts [21:22].
- Draft success: "50/50 proposition" and "coin flip" in Caserio's words [23:53].
- Speed example: "22 miles an hour" [25:25].
- Outside linebacker example: 6 feet, 230 pounds, 10-yard burst [27:56].
- Illustrative play-call odds: 28% for an out route on second and eight [34:34]; the speaker uses this as a hypothetical.
- Fourth-down model odds: 57% if done 100 times in a year [37:38].
- Strength example: 225 pounds for about 40 reps versus bar speed [38:39].
- Retest personality or psychological tests 3 to 4 years in [44:48].
- Caption error: the dash is called the "42nd dash" [15:46].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Retroactive model validation: fit a model, run past draftees through it, compare successes and misses [12:44] [13:14].
- Position-specific predictive metrics across the 40, short shuttle and three-cone [28:27].
- Converting qualitative scouting grades into quantitative data and recalibrating scouts [15:46].
- Hybrid model: analytics and scouts as equal voices in the draft room [10:42] [17:49] [20:22].
- Tracking, force plate and bar-speed feedback to players in the offseason [25:25] [38:39] [39:40].
- Retesting psychological measures after years in the program [44:48] [45:19].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes or results are shown; claims about correlations (length, combine metrics) are stated by the speakers [29:28] [32:00].
- Demoff and Caserio speak from team positions; the draft-room claims are institutional views.
- Captions attribute "our GM Tom Telesco" and the Staley and Wade Phillips remarks to the speaker introduced as the Rams COO [17:49] [18:51]; this attribution is not resolved in the captions.
- The Sean McVay anecdote cites a "wins above replacement" ranking and a claim about a fourth-and-goal call; neither is verified [36:38] [37:08].
- The talk happened in April amid a pandemic-affected draft with less information [21:52] [22:22].
- Caserio's injury and strength ideas are future goals, not results [38:39].
- Personality and learning measurement is described as unsolved; Caserio suggests a retest design, but no validated measure is named [44:48].

## Q&A

- How teams should staff analytics: Caserio says hire smart people who work in a hybrid model and ask what the department is for [41:11] [41:42].
- Analytics path to GM: Demoff says skepticism rises when analytics-minded leaders lose, and that emotional intelligence and communication matter more than raw brilliance [42:14] [43:14].
- Burke's idea: a draft for analysts [43:46].
- Using analytics to evaluate personality: Caserio proposes retesting after 3 to 4 years [44:48]; Demoff points to learning capacity and fair assessment [45:50] [46:21]; Burke urges caution [47:22].

title: "SSAC20: Numbers Don't Lie: Using Data in the Weight Room to Enhance On-Field Performance"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

## Summary

An LSU assistant strength and conditioning coach describes how his football program uses three data sources (camera-based bar velocity, force plates and GPS) to guide weekly lifting decisions. His argument is that load prescribed from a one-rep max ignores day-to-day nervous system state, whereas a velocity target adjusts to the athlete. He shows how force plate trends and practice GPS data help explain readiness dips, and claims the team's measures rose through the season, ending with its fastest practice speeds before the championship game. The talk is a single-program case study with no comparison group, so it supports a practical workflow more than a general result.

## Key claims

- A strength coach spends more time with athletes than anyone else on staff, which helps individualize training. [01:04]
- Football's fixed weekly schedule lets him plan performance week to week. [02:36]
- The program uses a camera system on every rack (22 racks), force plates and GPS units. [04:11]
- He is not interested in data that does not change what the program does, and he passes summaries to the head strength coach for programming decisions. [05:12]
- Velocity-based training lets him train the bar speed he wants rather than a fixed percentage of a tested max. [06:14]
- Newer cameras and cloud storage made velocity tracking usable every day, with data available at his desk after a session. [07:49]
- Football is a power sport, and strength gains that do not transfer to the field are questionable. [08:54]
- The aim is to move the force-velocity curve right (a heavier load moved faster), which he says correlates with field speed seen in GPS. [09:24]
- A falling eccentric braking number tells him to add strength work. [11:28]
- A tested one-rep max can swing day to day, so a fixed percentage may be too heavy or too light. [11:59]
- Everyone on the team can train at the same target velocity regardless of how they feel. [13:01]
- Accumulated data lets him build individual force-velocity profiles and set a starting load for a target velocity. [15:04]
- If the bar moves slower than expected at that load, he removes weight; if faster, he exploits the good day. [15:34]
- In season, peak power falls off at lower loads on squat, bench and deadlift than on Olympic lifts. [17:07]
- Some athletes set personal records mid-season because the velocity target was beaten before enough weight could slow them. [18:08]
- Load was adjusted by opponent (lighter and faster before the biggest game, harder before games expected to be won). [19:39]
- A dip in force plate data sends him back to bar percentages, bar velocities and practice GPS load. [20:11]
- Force plate measures rose weekly through the season, and the fastest practice GPS speeds came in the final week before the national championship game against Clemson. [20:41], [21:13]

## Numbers and definitions

- Racks with cameras: 22. [04:11]
- Force plate metrics (four): RSI modified (explained as how fast the athlete reaches peak jump height, from three jumps) [09:56]; concentric rate of power development divided by body mass [10:57]; eccentric braking rate of force development [10:57]; peak power divided by body mass [11:28]. The caption for the second metric is garbled ("rate of power development"); it may be concentric rate of force development.
- One-rep max fluctuation: 18 percent up or down per day, giving a 36 percent window. [11:59] Speaker's figure, no source given.
- Example target velocity: 0.8 m/s. [13:01]
- Example profile result: 62.5 percent of one-rep max for an athlete to reach 0.8 m/s. [15:04]
- Peak power drops between 60 and 65 percent on squat, bench and deadlift. [17:07]
- Peak power drops between 80 and 85 percent on Olympic lifts, depending on technique. [17:07]
- He says he has been at LSU five seasons. [01:34]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Perch camera velocity tracking (caption: "perch"), VALD force plates, Polar GPS and heart rate. [03:40], [04:11], [04:42]
- Velocity zones in place of percentage-only prescription; credited to Soviet origins and popularized in the US in the 1990s by Louie Simmons of Westside Barbell (caption spelling "Louise Simmons"). [07:18]
- Individual force-velocity profiles from accumulated in-season data. [15:04]
- Weekly charts of velocity, load, peak power and force plate metrics, color-coded by opponent. [16:37], [19:09]
- Head athletic trainer named as Jack Murphy (caption). [01:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Single program, single season, no comparison group. The upward trends and fast final-week GPS speeds are the speaker's reading, with no statistics shown.
- No sample sizes, no number of athletes, and no raw figures in the captions.
- The 18 percent fluctuation and the peak-power windows are the speaker's own claims with no cited source.
- Mixed signals on method: he says he no longer needs a "coach's eye" [21:13] but also modifies plans by hand for individual athletes and genetics [17:37].
- Lowering load before the biggest game and training harder before games expected to be wins is judgment, not tested [19:39].
- Resource context: he notes LSU gives him every resource. [04:11]
- Caption garbles around "coach time him off" at [05:12] (head strength coach, name unverified).

## Q&A

- Other sports? Five other sports use the weight room and the technology, including volleyball, baseball, women's soccer and beach volleyball; volleyball is trained like football. [22:17], [22:48]
- Screening before loading? Freshmen start in their own group, teach technique first, and go through screening with the medical staff before loading. [23:50], [24:21]
- Gap between regular season and bowl season? Force plate data guided adding strength work during the long break, then returned to the normal approach near competition. [24:52], [25:23]

- Players who play multiple positions get a weighted average across positions by snap share. [11:24]

title: "SSAC20: Instant Feedback: Using Real-time Data to Improve Training, Case Studies from MIT Sports Lab"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Kristina Chase]
topics: [sports-science, other-sport:track-and-field, other-sport:esports]

## Summary

The managing director of the MIT Sports Lab argues that training data is often captured and processed but rarely returned to the athlete fast enough to help. She presents two case studies. For the US Olympic Committee, the lab used open-source pose estimation to find the takeoff frame and launch angle and velocity in long jump video, replacing hand tagging. For Red Bull high performance in esports, it tested whether automatically adjusting game speed with finer steps raised skill acquisition. Both are short project descriptions with few reported numbers. Her closing view is that analytics is a tool whose use depends on a defined question.

## Key claims

- Training is a loop of capture, processing, coaching and repeat, and much of what is captured is not put back into the immediate loop. [02:40], [03:43]
- In long jump, high-speed video is tagged by hand to find launch angle and velocity, and the USOC does not allow putting devices on athletes. [04:46]
- The result must return during the session, not an hour later. [04:46]
- The team used open-source pose estimation, which labels each frame separately, so raw output had to be processed to track the jumper. [08:31], [09:01]
- Detecting takeoff by the last point to leave the ground (the left toe in the example) reached about 99 percent accuracy, with small errors left. [09:32]
- Red Bull chose esports because every click is recorded. [10:33]
- Prior MIT research (Stephanie Muller, CSAIL, caption spelling) showed adaptive inputs can raise skill acquisition rate. [10:33]
- Experts gained most under the granular adaptive condition; at 10 percent adaptive most people did worse, since the change was too subtle to notice. [13:10]
- People are poor at judging when to make practice harder or easier, which automation can do. [13:40]
- Coaches filter what athletes hear, and a tool should give only what the coach asks for, such as launch angle and the exact frame. [20:35], [21:06]
- Analytics is a tool, not an answer; define the question and the action first. [21:36], [22:06]
- Passive collection with nothing on the athlete is where she sees the future. [23:06]

## Numbers and definitions

- Body locations tagged per frame: 19. [06:22]
- Frames for the jumping motion: "50 200" in the captions (garbled, likely 50 to 200). [06:22]
- About 2,000 points per frame by hand, as captioned. [06:52] This appears to conflict with 19 points and 50 to 200 frames; the likely meaning is per jump, but the captions say per frame.
- Pose tool identified eleven people in one frame, one being the jumper. [08:31]
- Accuracy reached: about 99 percent. [09:32]
- Adaptive rule: speed up 10 percent after a session of seven tries at 60 percent success; no change between 40 and 60; slow down below 40 percent. [11:37], [12:10]
- Granular rule: larger steps both ways, with a 30 percent slowdown if the athlete struggles. [12:40] The captions here are garbled ("forty to sixty", "twenty it's a hundred percent"), so exact step sizes are unclear.
- Task: a specific move in Super Smash Brothers (caption: "the wave -", probably a wave dash). [11:37]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Feedback loop: capture, process, coach, retry. [02:40]
- Open-source pose estimation with a custom algorithm to find the largest signal and reduce error. [09:01], [09:32]
- Control, adaptive and granular groups, with beginner, intermediate and expert players. [11:37], [12:40]

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes or statistics for the esports study, and the figure is described only by marker shape. [14:13]
- The jump accuracy figure of 99 percent has no sample size and applies to takeoff detection.
- The speaker says none of them expected the expert result. [14:13]
- Esports results come from a game, not a physical task.
- Several numbers are garbled in captions (see above).
- Host names and the speaker's lab role come from the introduction. The speaker also teaches at MIT. [01:03]

## Q&A

- Eye tracking to separate experts and beginners? Useful in decision-making work, but expensive for a proof of concept. [16:23], [16:53]
- What would coaches do with the long jump analytics, and other events? Cue things like elbow and hip timing; the USOC wants to apply it widely, such as pairing synchronized divers by rotation speed. [17:55], [18:25], [18:55], [19:29]
- Does feedback risk overthinking? Coaches filter, and the tool shows only what they want. [20:02], [20:35]
- Does analytics just assist coaches or find new things? Both are possible, but define the question first. [21:36], [22:06]
- Why nothing on the athlete? Passive capture is the goal, and sensor placement, calibration and test jumps use limited training time. [23:06], [23:36]

## Summary

A panel led by an economist asks whether teams in baseball, basketball and football learn from analytics, and how fast. The opening presentation takes two long-known mistakes per sport (bunts and steals, three-point shooting, fourth downs and draft pick valuation) and shows adoption was slow, in baseball taking decades. The panelists then offer reasons: a move that usually works feels right even when it is bad value, an organization needs understanding at every level, ownership must commit, and championships speed acceptance. The later discussion covers new frontiers (spatial football data, positionless basketball, two-way baseball players) and how to communicate with athletes. It matters as a set of first-hand explanations for why good analysis changes behavior slowly.

## Key claims

- The economist opens with the view that firms are assumed smart because competition would remove poor ones, and asks whether owners, managers and coaches count among the smart minority [02:04].
- Sacrifice bunts are poor value even when they succeed, since expected runs are about the same, and steals only add value above roughly a 75% success rate [03:07] [03:38].
- Bunt rates barely moved after an influential baseball publication in 1978, rose after a 2003 book, and fell only around 2011, when a movie came out [04:08] [04:39].
- Three-point attempts rose sharply without the success rate falling much [07:22] [07:54].
- Teams punt too much on fourth down; there has been some learning, with some regression last year [09:27] [09:59].
- The long-used draft pick chart reflects observed trade prices fit by hand, not the value of picks [11:33].
- By the presenters' estimate, the chart's top pick is worth five times the first pick of round two, but the second-round pick delivers more surplus; one could trade the top pick for five picks each worth more [13:05].
- Newer trades still follow the chart as a price list, and teams rarely trade unless paid the asking price [14:12] [14:44].
- Draft ranking carries little signal: the chance that a player ranked ahead of the next one is better is 52% overall, a bit higher in round one, and 52% again when re-estimated with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- One panelist says analysis can teach something different from playing; a move that works 60 to 70 percent of the time convinces people even when its failure cost is high, which kept the sacrifice bunt alive [16:52] [17:22].
- The same panelist says a general manager is limited by the decisions scouts and coaches make, so the whole organization must understand the approach, which takes a long time [17:55] [18:27].
- Another panelist says players, coaches, GMs and owners operate on different time cycles, and sustained change needs ownership buy-in and then a long turn [18:57] [19:29].
- He describes the coach of a high-scoring Phoenix team facing resistance from media and his own players, then trading for a traditional big man that hurt the team's play; he says that only a coach plus ownership buy-in plus visible success moves others [19:59] [21:32] [22:02].
- Another panelist says organizational commitment from ownership down is missing at most places, and that how information is presented matters as much as what it says [22:33] [23:03].
- A baseball panelist says a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM would shorten acceptance, but that the growing analytics community also shifts general culture [24:03] [24:33].
- The basketball panelist says every result becomes a referendum on a novel style, and more teams fail to win playing the traditional way than the new way [25:04] [25:34].
- A counterpoint is raised: the winning team had several of the best players in the league, so players may matter more than style, though teams copy what looks successful [26:04] [26:34].
- Copying superficial features fails, as with teams trying to rebuild a championship bullpen the next year; and power offense is said to work better in the postseason despite common belief [27:05] [27:35].
- The panelist who ran a football front office says he set out in 2016 to build draft capital and ended with almost two-and-a-half extra draft classes by selling into the pick chart's pricing [29:06] [29:36].
- A panelist says one team trades this year's picks for next year's, and that successors spent the accumulated picks quickly [30:37] [31:08] [31:41].
- Analytics must be integrated into decisions, not a separate group that enters and leaves the room [32:43] [33:14].
- Football information is new, and the football panelist says it has not yet been introduced in a compelling way; owners and executives need to align patience with plan timelines [33:44] [34:14] [34:45].
- The baseball historian (by context) says an analytically strong owner and four titles during his time at one club helped acceptance, while noting luck played a part [35:49] [36:19].
- The basketball panelist says being patient is very hard, as fans and friends react nightly, and it explains why organizations swing back and forth [37:19] [37:50].
- New frontiers named: football spatial analysis with tracking data, quarterbacks adapting college styles, fourth down, the draft, and pass defense [38:52] [39:23] [39:56].
- The economist notes pro football resisted going for it on fourth down while a football video game had to change its code to stop users from always doing so [40:58] [41:28].
- Opener pitching in baseball became real only around 2017 [41:28] [41:59].
- A panelist suggests playing the five best players regardless of position, noting that very skilled players are rarely also seven feet tall [43:02] [43:33].
- Baseball culture does not tolerate two-way players, and a successful exception comes from a different culture [44:34] [45:04].
- On a question about dehumanizing players, a panelist argues that treating them as commodities is what justifies large salaries [46:36] [47:08].
- The basketball panelist asks whether position-based estimates could blind teams to creative uses of players, and the historian says yes, which keeps analysts from becoming obsolete [48:12] [48:43].
- The football panelist says communicating with players and athletes is the new frontier [49:13]. The historian says one cannot convince athletes of anything without respect [51:50].
- Free-throw shooting and other skills are selected against other traits, and the open question is what can be taught [50:46] [51:17].
- The football panelist describes a high draft pick the staff believed they could teach to run routes, which did not work out within six or seven weeks; he says commitment needs humility about what can be changed [52:52] [53:22].
- Once baseball value is measured well, edge comes from finding improvable players, since all teams working from the same chart gives no edge [54:23] [54:54].
- The economist is not optimistic about teaching and says someone should write papers on what can be improved [55:58] [56:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Steal success needed to add value: about 75% [03:38]; in no year was league success 75%, though trending up [05:12] [05:47].
- Bunt and steal turning points: 1978 baseball publication, 2003 book, 2011 movie [04:08] [04:39].
- Lifetime three-point percentage .376 for one famous player on 1.9 attempts per game; another player with the same percentage takes 10 per game [06:19] [06:52]. The speaker also says .4 times 3 exceeds .5 times 2 [06:19].
- Pick chart: top pick said to be worth five times the first pick of round two [13:05]. Second overall asking price 2,600 points (caption: "twenty six hundred points") [14:12] [14:44].
- "Better than the next guy" statistic: probability that the player ranked n is better than n+1. 52% for the full draft, 56% for the first round (caption), and 52% again with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47]. Captions around "56%" are garbled.
- Four decades for baseball to learn [16:22].
- A move that works "51 percent" of the time with failure cost "three times" the payoff, versus 60 to 70 percent success [16:52] [17:22]. Captions are muddled here.
- Football front office goal: roughly a draft and a half of additional capital in two or three years; result almost two-and-a-half [29:36].
- Four World Series during one panelist's time with a club [36:19]. Opener pitching adopted around 2017 [41:59].
- Salary examples: "thirty million" and "ten million" [46:36] [47:08]. A player offered a path to "six million a year" [53:53].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Plotting league behavior over time (bunt, steal, three-point, fourth-down rates) against key moments, to test learning speed [04:08].
- Draft pick surplus: performance value of a pick (green line), cost to acquire it (red line), and surplus as the difference (blue line) [12:03] [12:33].
- Pairwise ranking accuracy (the "better than the next guy" statistic), re-run with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- Fourth-down loss in win probability used as a measure of costly decisions, credited to a speaker named Brian [09:59].
- Explanatory factors for slow adoption, in the panelists' words: usual-success bias, organization-wide understanding, different time cycles, ownership buy-in, winning, narrative and media, presentation, and patience [17:22] [19:29] [23:03].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel is opinion and anecdote from executives and a historian; the draft figures are the economist's own work and are presented without confidence intervals or the underlying sample sizes in the captions.
- Attributions to speakers are by context only; auto-captions have no speaker labels, and the baseball and basketball panelists are not always distinguishable.
- The economist's view that the 52% result means picks are barely better than a coin flip is his; he does not test how much teams could improve the ordering.
- A counter-view is raised (players matter more than style) and is not resolved [26:04].
- The football panelist's results (extra draft classes) come from one team over a few years and cannot show how general they are [29:36].
- The closing question (what can be taught, which flaws are fatal) is called open by the speakers [55:58].
- Captions have garbled names, years ("2006 2015") and some figures, so rely on [mm:ss] to check the audio.

## Q&A

- Does a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM speed up acceptance? [24:03]
- Is the new draft chart still the asking price, and why do teams not move off it? [28:36]
- What is the role of ownership, and what would a new owner face? [32:12]
- Was an analytics-minded owner important? [34:45]
- What are the new frontiers in each sport? [38:22]
- How can analytics avoid dehumanizing players (audience question)? [46:06]
- Does data risk blinding teams to uses of players that don't fit a position box? [48:12]
- How much of the frontier is player development and teaching? [50:13]

## Summary

A moderated football panel with an ESPN analyst, a team football operations executive and a college head coach. They discuss the pass-heavy offense moving into the NFL, why quarterbacks are hard to evaluate, what player tracking data can and cannot do, and how analytical information should reach coaches and players. The coach argues accuracy and elevating teammates are the key quarterback traits and are not coachable or measurable in simple ways. The analysts say tracking data helps with play classification and separating individual contributions, but decision-making remains hard to isolate.
