## Summary

A panel led by an economist asks whether teams in baseball, basketball and football learn from analytics, and how fast. The opening presentation takes two long-known mistakes per sport (bunts and steals, three-point shooting, fourth downs and draft pick valuation) and shows adoption was slow, in baseball taking decades. The panelists then offer reasons: a move that usually works feels right even when it is bad value, an organization needs understanding at every level, ownership must commit, and championships speed acceptance. The later discussion covers new frontiers (spatial football data, positionless basketball, two-way baseball players) and how to communicate with athletes. It matters as a set of first-hand explanations for why good analysis changes behavior slowly.

## Key claims

- The economist opens with the view that firms are assumed smart because competition would remove poor ones, and asks whether owners, managers and coaches count among the smart minority [02:04].
- Sacrifice bunts are poor value even when they succeed, since expected runs are about the same, and steals only add value above roughly a 75% success rate [03:07] [03:38].
- Bunt rates barely moved after an influential baseball publication in 1978, rose after a 2003 book, and fell only around 2011, when a movie came out [04:08] [04:39].
- Three-point attempts rose sharply without the success rate falling much [07:22] [07:54].
- Teams punt too much on fourth down; there has been some learning, with some regression last year [09:27] [09:59].
- The long-used draft pick chart reflects observed trade prices fit by hand, not the value of picks [11:33].
- By the presenters' estimate, the chart's top pick is worth five times the first pick of round two, but the second-round pick delivers more surplus; one could trade the top pick for five picks each worth more [13:05].
- Newer trades still follow the chart as a price list, and teams rarely trade unless paid the asking price [14:12] [14:44].
- Draft ranking carries little signal: the chance that a player ranked ahead of the next one is better is 52% overall, a bit higher in round one, and 52% again when re-estimated with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- One panelist says analysis can teach something different from playing; a move that works 60 to 70 percent of the time convinces people even when its failure cost is high, which kept the sacrifice bunt alive [16:52] [17:22].
- The same panelist says a general manager is limited by the decisions scouts and coaches make, so the whole organization must understand the approach, which takes a long time [17:55] [18:27].
- Another panelist says players, coaches, GMs and owners operate on different time cycles, and sustained change needs ownership buy-in and then a long turn [18:57] [19:29].
- He describes the coach of a high-scoring Phoenix team facing resistance from media and his own players, then trading for a traditional big man that hurt the team's play; he says that only a coach plus ownership buy-in plus visible success moves others [19:59] [21:32] [22:02].
- Another panelist says organizational commitment from ownership down is missing at most places, and that how information is presented matters as much as what it says [22:33] [23:03].
- A baseball panelist says a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM would shorten acceptance, but that the growing analytics community also shifts general culture [24:03] [24:33].
- The basketball panelist says every result becomes a referendum on a novel style, and more teams fail to win playing the traditional way than the new way [25:04] [25:34].
- A counterpoint is raised: the winning team had several of the best players in the league, so players may matter more than style, though teams copy what looks successful [26:04] [26:34].
- Copying superficial features fails, as with teams trying to rebuild a championship bullpen the next year; and power offense is said to work better in the postseason despite common belief [27:05] [27:35].
- The panelist who ran a football front office says he set out in 2016 to build draft capital and ended with almost two-and-a-half extra draft classes by selling into the pick chart's pricing [29:06] [29:36].
- A panelist says one team trades this year's picks for next year's, and that successors spent the accumulated picks quickly [30:37] [31:08] [31:41].
- Analytics must be integrated into decisions, not a separate group that enters and leaves the room [32:43] [33:14].
- Football information is new, and the football panelist says it has not yet been introduced in a compelling way; owners and executives need to align patience with plan timelines [33:44] [34:14] [34:45].
- The baseball historian (by context) says an analytically strong owner and four titles during his time at one club helped acceptance, while noting luck played a part [35:49] [36:19].
- The basketball panelist says being patient is very hard, as fans and friends react nightly, and it explains why organizations swing back and forth [37:19] [37:50].
- New frontiers named: football spatial analysis with tracking data, quarterbacks adapting college styles, fourth down, the draft, and pass defense [38:52] [39:23] [39:56].
- The economist notes pro football resisted going for it on fourth down while a football video game had to change its code to stop users from always doing so [40:58] [41:28].
- Opener pitching in baseball became real only around 2017 [41:28] [41:59].
- A panelist suggests playing the five best players regardless of position, noting that very skilled players are rarely also seven feet tall [43:02] [43:33].
- Baseball culture does not tolerate two-way players, and a successful exception comes from a different culture [44:34] [45:04].
- On a question about dehumanizing players, a panelist argues that treating them as commodities is what justifies large salaries [46:36] [47:08].
- The basketball panelist asks whether position-based estimates could blind teams to creative uses of players, and the historian says yes, which keeps analysts from becoming obsolete [48:12] [48:43].
- The football panelist says communicating with players and athletes is the new frontier [49:13]. The historian says one cannot convince athletes of anything without respect [51:50].
- Free-throw shooting and other skills are selected against other traits, and the open question is what can be taught [50:46] [51:17].
- The football panelist describes a high draft pick the staff believed they could teach to run routes, which did not work out within six or seven weeks; he says commitment needs humility about what can be changed [52:52] [53:22].
- Once baseball value is measured well, edge comes from finding improvable players, since all teams working from the same chart gives no edge [54:23] [54:54].
- The economist is not optimistic about teaching and says someone should write papers on what can be improved [55:58] [56:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Steal success needed to add value: about 75% [03:38]; in no year was league success 75%, though trending up [05:12] [05:47].
- Bunt and steal turning points: 1978 baseball publication, 2003 book, 2011 movie [04:08] [04:39].
- Lifetime three-point percentage .376 for one famous player on 1.9 attempts per game; another player with the same percentage takes 10 per game [06:19] [06:52]. The speaker also says .4 times 3 exceeds .5 times 2 [06:19].
- Pick chart: top pick said to be worth five times the first pick of round two [13:05]. Second overall asking price 2,600 points (caption: "twenty six hundred points") [14:12] [14:44].
- "Better than the next guy" statistic: probability that the player ranked n is better than n+1. 52% for the full draft, 56% for the first round (caption), and 52% again with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47]. Captions around "56%" are garbled.
- Four decades for baseball to learn [16:22].
- A move that works "51 percent" of the time with failure cost "three times" the payoff, versus 60 to 70 percent success [16:52] [17:22]. Captions are muddled here.
- Football front office goal: roughly a draft and a half of additional capital in two or three years; result almost two-and-a-half [29:36].
- Four World Series during one panelist's time with a club [36:19]. Opener pitching adopted around 2017 [41:59].
- Salary examples: "thirty million" and "ten million" [46:36] [47:08]. A player offered a path to "six million a year" [53:53].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Plotting league behavior over time (bunt, steal, three-point, fourth-down rates) against key moments, to test learning speed [04:08].
- Draft pick surplus: performance value of a pick (green line), cost to acquire it (red line), and surplus as the difference (blue line) [12:03] [12:33].
- Pairwise ranking accuracy (the "better than the next guy" statistic), re-run with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- Fourth-down loss in win probability used as a measure of costly decisions, credited to a speaker named Brian [09:59].
- Explanatory factors for slow adoption, in the panelists' words: usual-success bias, organization-wide understanding, different time cycles, ownership buy-in, winning, narrative and media, presentation, and patience [17:22] [19:29] [23:03].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel is opinion and anecdote from executives and a historian; the draft figures are the economist's own work and are presented without confidence intervals or the underlying sample sizes in the captions.
- Attributions to speakers are by context only; auto-captions have no speaker labels, and the baseball and basketball panelists are not always distinguishable.
- The economist's view that the 52% result means picks are barely better than a coin flip is his; he does not test how much teams could improve the ordering.
- A counter-view is raised (players matter more than style) and is not resolved [26:04].
- The football panelist's results (extra draft classes) come from one team over a few years and cannot show how general they are [29:36].
- The closing question (what can be taught, which flaws are fatal) is called open by the speakers [55:58].
- Captions have garbled names, years ("2006 2015") and some figures, so rely on [mm:ss] to check the audio.

## Q&A

- Does a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM speed up acceptance? [24:03]
- Is the new draft chart still the asking price, and why do teams not move off it? [28:36]
- What is the role of ownership, and what would a new owner face? [32:12]
- Was an analytics-minded owner important? [34:45]
- What are the new frontiers in each sport? [38:22]
- How can analytics avoid dehumanizing players (audience question)? [46:06]
- Does data risk blinding teams to uses of players that don't fit a position box? [48:12]
- How much of the frontier is player development and teaching? [50:13]

event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

## Summary

Adam Douglas, an applied sport scientist at Catapult who also consults for Hockey Canada, shows how wearable load data from ice hockey practices and games was used with coaches. In one case, defensemen lost explosive output across a game and got less intensity in practice than forwards; skating was added to position drills and in-game explosive efforts rose. In the second, he plans practice duration and intensity ahead of a short tournament and plots measured load against the plan. His closing message is to use whatever you collect, and to feed objective load back to coaches while leaving tactical decisions to them.

## Key claims

- Hockey Canada's national teams target short tournaments of five or six games in about ten days, so preparation has to peak in a narrow window. [01:33]
- Hockey has little applied workload research, which was why Hockey Canada became a Catapult client about three years earlier. [02:36]
- The sensor combines an accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer worn between the shoulder plates, and it does not use GPS indoors. [03:40], [04:10]
- Coaches reported the defense could not sustain intensity across all three periods. Douglas says the athletes are fit, so he looked at the data instead of assuming a fitness problem. [05:45]
- With no comparable literature, he compared games and practices internally using player load per minute and a count of explosive efforts. [06:15], [06:47]
- Defense showed a different practice intensity from forwards, and explosive output trended down across the three periods. [07:18], [08:21]
- Defensemen got less exposure to explosive intensity than forwards, and forwards looked flatter in part because there are more of them and they get more rest. [08:51], [09:22]
- Coaches planning practice think technical and tactical first. Douglas pushed them to consider the physical content of drills, for example getting defensemen skating in position work instead of standing at the blue line for shots. [09:22], [10:23]
- After about three months, in-game explosive efforts were higher; Douglas cautions that Olympic arousal may have contributed. Coaches said the defense played better late in the season. [10:23], [10:53]
- For the men's under-20 program he calls the physical side "pillars" (a term he credits to a colleague) that support technical and tactical work. [11:56]
- He pre-plans each day on a pre-competition calendar as short or longer and medium or high intensity, then plots measured load against that plan for coaches. [12:26], [12:56], [13:27]
- In the plotted tournament, the highest-loaded day was an outdoor game against the Americans that went to a shootout, and the lowest load was the fourth game, against a weaker opponent. [15:01], [15:31]
- He combines wellness questionnaires, internal load, an HRV app and heart-rate data, but shows coaches only a pared-down summary of considerations. [15:31], [16:02]
- He frames recommendations as considerations because coaches face the media and decide how hard to push. [16:33]
- The team front-loads the tournament so athletes peak; that year's load trend went up into the medal round, but the team still lost, and he says luck and the human element are not accounted for. [17:04], [17:35]
- If you collect data, use it. He says there is a gap between how coaches rate a session's intensity and how athletes experience it, and an objective measure puts everyone on the same page. [19:07], [19:37]

## Numbers and definitions

- Player load per minute: described as intensity of work per minute in games and practices; player load is called a well-researched Catapult variable. [06:47]
- Explosive efforts: a frequency count of explosive movements on the ice. [06:47]
- 44%: increase in in-game explosive efforts "in three months." Comparison period and statistics not given. [10:23]
- Tournament: five or six games in about ten days. [01:33]
- Round-robin games on the 26th, 27th, 29th and 30th, double back-to-backs. [13:58]
- Short day: about 30 minutes or less. [12:56]
- Three years of tracking data on the athletes. [18:37]
- 25 athletes (can now be understood to individual level). [18:06]
- HRV measured from August through the January tournament. [24:26]
- Hypothetical "300 units" of load for one player, which Douglas says he is making up. [21:51]
- Caption problem: the group of players in the position comparison is garbled ("seven players" for defense). [07:18]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Inertial wearable sensor data on ice, summarized as player load per minute and explosive effort counts.
- Internal comparison of practices versus games by position group, plus simple game models for wins versus losses.
- Pre-competition calendar with planned day types, compared with measured load.
- Combined monitoring: subjective wellness, internal load, HRV, heart rate.
- Concept of tactical periodization (hard and easy days), mentioned in Q&A. [22:52]

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes for sessions or games, no statistical tests, and no control for the 44% result; the speaker flags arousal and multifactor game outcomes. [08:21], [10:23]
- Results come from national-team staff and a short-tournament setting, not a full season.
- Douglas is a vendor employee (Catapult); he says he is also a PhD student and a Hockey Canada practitioner. [01:03]
- The finite-load idea (too much load lowers explosive ratio) is described as theoretical, not shown. [21:20], [21:51]
- The slides are not visible, so the shapes of plots are only described, not verified.

## Q&A

- Wearing comfort: athletes adapt; he explains why, asks them to wear it and checks in about 15 minutes in. [20:17]
- Using the data to manage players' ice time: he has raised the finite-load concept but coaches decide who plays. [21:20]
- Applying to other sports: any sport that measures practices and games can use it; loading choices belong to the practitioner. [22:52]
- Why so little hockey research: he does not know; likely emerging applied research in North America and closed environments. [23:23]
- HRV protocol: measured from August through the tournament, kept simple for under-20 players. [24:26]

## Summary

Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

## Key claims

- The ulnar collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the throwing elbow, and a complete tear needs reconstruction with a graft. [01:36], [02:07]
- About 900 professional pitchers have had the surgery, and he says 25% of current major league pitchers have. [03:09], [03:39]
- Two causes for continued injuries: higher velocity, and early year-round single-sport play. [04:09]
- In wearable studies, faster pitches impart more elbow stress for both youth and professional pitchers, and this is pitch speed, not arm speed. [04:39], [05:10]
- In a simulated seven-inning game, fatigue ratings rose each inning and peak fastball velocity dipped around inning five, but elbow stress went up when it should have come down in fatigued pitchers. [05:10], [05:40]
- Single-sport specialization before skeletal maturity is causing burnout of muscle and tendon, and kids feel pressure to play through pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Among 140 established pitchers who had the surgery, 20% never pitched in the majors again, and about one in three returned but not at prior durability. [09:13], [09:43]
- Returning pitchers showed a statistically significant decline in numerous pitching metrics. [09:43], [10:13]
- Wins above replacement falls for three years before surgery and takes three years after return to reach pre-surgery level. [10:13], [10:43]
- Over 2004 to 2014, salary paid during rehab came to about half a billion dollars (2017 dollars), excluding medical, travel, minor leaguers and pre-surgery downtime. [12:14], [12:44], [13:14], [13:44]
- Non-operative treatment for low-grade tears works some of the time but failure means losing a second season. [14:14], [15:15]
- Expected value decision analysis can compare the two paths and show, via two-way sensitivity analysis, where each wins; he says it does not replace clinical decision-making. [15:46], [16:47], [17:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- 900 pitchers, 25% of current MLB pitchers. [03:09], [03:39]
- Youth survey: 200 healthy players; 75% admitted arm pain; 25% had symptoms suggestive of overuse injury; 50% felt pressured to play despite pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Up to 10% of drafted pitchers had already had surgery (Mayo study, speaker credits Chris Camp). [07:41], [08:11]
- Youngest patient: 12. [08:11]
- 150 MLB pitchers studied, 140 "established" (10 or more games in a season). [09:13]
- 20% of established pitchers never returned to the majors; one in three came back below the 10-game threshold. [09:43]
- Recovery to the majors: 12 to 18 months; about four to four and a half years to return to prior level. [10:43]
- Medical cost per player: about $50,000, called conservative. [11:13]
- 2004 to 2014 study: about 200 surgeries; 180 days missed on average; about half starters, half relievers. [12:14], [12:44]
- Non-operative success: 40 to 80% depending on the case; at most three months of downtime. [14:14], [14:45]
- Surgery success: "80 to 100%" in different studies; a year to a year and a half of downtime. [14:45]
- Sample model: expected WAR 1.6 non-operative versus 1.3 surgery, for one representative case. [16:47]
- Caption problem: "80 to 80 to 100%" at [14:45] is garbled. "One out of three" is ambiguous about the denominator. [09:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable elbow-stress sleeve on throwers (medial elbow torque), including a simulated game with fatigue ratings.
- Surveys of youth players; cohort analysis of public MLB data; salary and wins above replacement (WAR) measures.
- Expected value decision analysis with two-way sensitivity analysis for treatment choice.

## Limits and open questions

- The salary study was under review at the time. [11:44]
- WAR was age-matched only in the first data set; the second was not controlled, as he agrees in Q&A. [18:19]
- The salary-per-WAR figure was "back of the envelope" and not adjusted. [28:27]
- The decision example is a single sample case with chosen inputs. [16:47]
- The speaker is a clinician reporting his group's studies; the youth survey was done during his residency. [07:10]
- The speaker does not give the sample or denominator behind the relief-versus-starter injury comparison and says he does not know. [27:22]
- The fatigue study sample size is not stated.

## Q&A

- Was WAR controlled for starters versus relievers? First set age-matched, second not. [18:19]
- Recovery by age? Numbers too small, appears similar to natural age trend. [18:50]
- How to avoid the injury? Rest, pitch counts (including warm-up pitches and multiple leagues), education, wearable research on weighted balls and fatigue. [19:20], [20:21], [20:52]
- Early specialization versus remodeling of the arm in childhood? Some early throwing is needed; the problem is rest. [19:51]
- Hitters? The sleeve relies on a throwing motion so cannot measure hitters. [21:23]
- Batting after injury? He allows it if pain-free. [21:54]
- Arm slot? Next stage; slot has not shown increased elbow stress so far. [22:33]
- Coaches' attention to pitch counts? More aware now. [23:10]
- Fatigue mechanism? His hypothesis: kinetic chain fatigue makes the arm do more; core and bodyweight work suggested. [24:11]
- Does salary matter to the analysis? Depends what is measured. [25:12]
- Why research from Japan? He does not know. [25:42]
- Pitcher elbows in MRI? Pathology is common; professionals' tears are attritional. [26:13], [26:43]
- Why is the rate similar at the major league level? Elbows are what they are by then; possibly more relievers. [27:22]

type: video-summary
video_id: kEjRVwJrzl0
title: "SSAC20: The Sports Learning Curve: Why Teams Are Slow to Learn and Adapt"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Daryl Morey, Bill James, Sashi Brown, Richard Taylor (caption spelling), Kristen's Lee (caption spelling, student host)]
topics: [front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, american-football, basketball, other-sport:baseball]

## Summary

A panel led by an economist asks whether teams in baseball, basketball and football learn from analytics, and how fast. The opening presentation takes two long-known mistakes per sport (bunts and steals, three-point shooting, fourth downs and draft pick valuation) and shows adoption was slow, in baseball taking decades. The panelists then offer reasons: a move that usually works feels right even when it is bad value, an organization needs understanding at every level, ownership must commit, and championships speed acceptance. The later discussion covers new frontiers (spatial football data, positionless basketball, two-way baseball players) and how to communicate with athletes. It matters as a set of first-hand explanations for why good analysis changes behavior slowly.

## Key claims

- The economist opens with the view that firms are assumed smart because competition would remove poor ones, and asks whether owners, managers and coaches count among the smart minority [02:04].
- Sacrifice bunts are poor value even when they succeed, since expected runs are about the same, and steals only add value above roughly a 75% success rate [03:07] [03:38].
- Bunt rates barely moved after an influential baseball publication in 1978, rose after a 2003 book, and fell only around 2011, when a movie came out [04:08] [04:39].
- Three-point attempts rose sharply without the success rate falling much [07:22] [07:54].
- Teams punt too much on fourth down; there has been some learning, with some regression last year [09:27] [09:59].
- The long-used draft pick chart reflects observed trade prices fit by hand, not the value of picks [11:33].
- By the presenters' estimate, the chart's top pick is worth five times the first pick of round two, but the second-round pick delivers more surplus; one could trade the top pick for five picks each worth more [13:05].
- Newer trades still follow the chart as a price list, and teams rarely trade unless paid the asking price [14:12] [14:44].
- Draft ranking carries little signal: the chance that a player ranked ahead of the next one is better is 52% overall, a bit higher in round one, and 52% again when re-estimated with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- One panelist says analysis can teach something different from playing; a move that works 60 to 70 percent of the time convinces people even when its failure cost is high, which kept the sacrifice bunt alive [16:52] [17:22].
- The same panelist says a general manager is limited by the decisions scouts and coaches make, so the whole organization must understand the approach, which takes a long time [17:55] [18:27].
- Another panelist says players, coaches, GMs and owners operate on different time cycles, and sustained change needs ownership buy-in and then a long turn [18:57] [19:29].
- He describes the coach of a high-scoring Phoenix team facing resistance from media and his own players, then trading for a traditional big man that hurt the team's play; he says that only a coach plus ownership buy-in plus visible success moves others [19:59] [21:32] [22:02].
- Another panelist says organizational commitment from ownership down is missing at most places, and that how information is presented matters as much as what it says [22:33] [23:03].
- A baseball panelist says a championship by a prominent analytics-minded GM would shorten acceptance, but that the growing analytics community also shifts general culture [24:03] [24:33].
- The basketball panelist says every result becomes a referendum on a novel style, and more teams fail to win playing the traditional way than the new way [25:04] [25:34].
- A counterpoint is raised: the winning team had several of the best players in the league, so players may matter more than style, though teams copy what looks successful [26:04] [26:34].
- Copying superficial features fails, as with teams trying to rebuild a championship bullpen the next year; and power offense is said to work better in the postseason despite common belief [27:05] [27:35].
- The panelist who ran a football front office says he set out in 2016 to build draft capital and ended with almost two-and-a-half extra draft classes by selling into the pick chart's pricing [29:06] [29:36].
- A panelist says one team trades this year's picks for next year's, and that successors spent the accumulated picks quickly [30:37] [31:08] [31:41].
- Analytics must be integrated into decisions, not a separate group that enters and leaves the room [32:43] [33:14].
- Football information is new, and the football panelist says it has not yet been introduced in a compelling way; owners and executives need to align patience with plan timelines [33:44] [34:14] [34:45].
- The baseball historian (by context) says an analytically strong owner and four titles during his time at one club helped acceptance, while noting luck played a part [35:49] [36:19].
- The basketball panelist says being patient is very hard, as fans and friends react nightly, and it explains why organizations swing back and forth [37:19] [37:50].
- New frontiers named: football spatial analysis with tracking data, quarterbacks adapting college styles, fourth down, the draft, and pass defense [38:52] [39:23] [39:56].
- The economist notes pro football resisted going for it on fourth down while a football video game had to change its code to stop users from always doing so [40:58] [41:28].
- Opener pitching in baseball became real only around 2017 [41:28] [41:59].
- A panelist suggests playing the five best players regardless of position, noting that very skilled players are rarely also seven feet tall [43:02] [43:33].
- Baseball culture does not tolerate two-way players, and a successful exception comes from a different culture [44:34] [45:04].
- On a question about dehumanizing players, a panelist argues that treating them as commodities is what justifies large salaries [46:36] [47:08].
- The basketball panelist asks whether position-based estimates could blind teams to creative uses of players, and the historian says yes, which keeps analysts from becoming obsolete [48:12] [48:43].
- The football panelist says communicating with players and athletes is the new frontier [49:13]. The historian says one cannot convince athletes of anything without respect [51:50].
- Free-throw shooting and other skills are selected against other traits, and the open question is what can be taught [50:46] [51:17].
- The football panelist describes a high draft pick the staff believed they could teach to run routes, which did not work out within six or seven weeks; he says commitment needs humility about what can be changed [52:52] [53:22].
- Once baseball value is measured well, edge comes from finding improvable players, since all teams working from the same chart gives no edge [54:23] [54:54].
- The economist is not optimistic about teaching and says someone should write papers on what can be improved [55:58] [56:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Steal success needed to add value: about 75% [03:38]; in no year was league success 75%, though trending up [05:12] [05:47].
- Bunt and steal turning points: 1978 baseball publication, 2003 book, 2011 movie [04:08] [04:39].
- Lifetime three-point percentage .376 for one famous player on 1.9 attempts per game; another player with the same percentage takes 10 per game [06:19] [06:52]. The speaker also says .4 times 3 exceeds .5 times 2 [06:19].
- Pick chart: top pick said to be worth five times the first pick of round two [13:05]. Second overall asking price 2,600 points (caption: "twenty six hundred points") [14:12] [14:44].
- "Better than the next guy" statistic: probability that the player ranked n is better than n+1. 52% for the full draft, 56% for the first round (caption), and 52% again with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47]. Captions around "56%" are garbled.
- Four decades for baseball to learn [16:22].
- A move that works "51 percent" of the time with failure cost "three times" the payoff, versus 60 to 70 percent success [16:52] [17:22]. Captions are muddled here.
- Football front office goal: roughly a draft and a half of additional capital in two or three years; result almost two-and-a-half [29:36].
- Four World Series during one panelist's time with a club [36:19]. Opener pitching adopted around 2017 [41:59].
- Salary examples: "thirty million" and "ten million" [46:36] [47:08]. A player offered a path to "six million a year" [53:53].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Plotting league behavior over time (bunt, steal, three-point, fourth-down rates) against key moments, to test learning speed [04:08].
- Draft pick surplus: performance value of a pick (green line), cost to acquire it (red line), and surplus as the difference (blue line) [12:03] [12:33].
- Pairwise ranking accuracy (the "better than the next guy" statistic), re-run with wins over replacement [15:16] [15:47].
- Fourth-down loss in win probability used as a measure of costly decisions, credited to a speaker named Brian [09:59].

## Summary

A moderated football panel with an ESPN analyst, a team football operations executive and a college head coach. They discuss the pass-heavy offense moving into the NFL, why quarterbacks are hard to evaluate, what player tracking data can and cannot do, and how analytical information should reach coaches and players. The coach argues accuracy and elevating teammates are the key quarterback traits and are not coachable or measurable in simple ways. The analysts say tracking data helps with play classification and separating individual contributions, but decision-making remains hard to isolate. The sharpest disagreement is over fourth-down decisions and momentum. It matters as a plain view of where analytics and coaching judgment meet.

## Key claims

- The coach says a quarterback who throws accurately improves six offensive positions rather than one and a half, because the passing game spreads the ball to more players [03:04] [03:34] [05:08].
- He argues that if an offense works at the high school level it can work in any league, noting opponents are not all elite players at every position [05:38] [06:09].

- The coach says some positions are hard to manufacture (corner, defensive end, running back), while quarterback, receiver and running back can be developed [11:14] [11:46] [12:18].
- He argues accuracy cannot be coached from inaccurate to accurate, even though other quarterback traits can be improved [13:21] [14:23].
- He lists five quarterback traits (accuracy, decisions, quick feet, mobility, arm) and says most great quarterbacks had three [14:54] [15:25].
- The analyst says quantifying quarterback decision-making would be the "holy grail," and it is cognitively loaded in a way not captured by IQ [16:25] [16:55].
- Tracking shows realized decisions but not the play's intention or coached progression, so decomposing a quarterback's choices remains hard [17:26] [17:56].
- The coach says the most important quarterback skill is elevating the other eleven players, and that it can be developed at any level, citing a quarterback who came from a small program [20:36] [21:09] [21:43].
- The executive says college has historically had no player tracking data, so college quarterback evaluation differs from pro, and it is hard to tell player from system when several of one coach's quarterbacks look alike in the data [23:15] [23:45].
- He says too many players have been dismissed as products of the system [24:15], and that backup quarterback quality drops far more at the pro level than in college [24:45] [25:16].
- The coach says quarterback evaluation is heavily scrutinized yet poor, that coaches rarely make draft picks, and that teams value different things [25:46] [26:49] [28:56] [29:27].

- He describes a "sacks created" metric to credit a pass rusher whose pressure leads to someone else's sack [44:14] [44:44].
- The coach says players need applicable knowledge, not probabilities, and a panelist agrees, suggesting a person in the booth translate information into simple signals such as red, yellow and green [45:46] [46:20] [51:32] [52:02].

- The coach says he feels like a failure when he punts and uses fourth down as a "lifeline" [53:03] [53:34].
- The analyst advises making the fourth-down call on third down rather than burning a timeout, because the timeout may be worth more than the difference between a field goal and a punt [54:05].
- The coach argues collective energy and momentum are real and hard to measure, and that he does not want his offensive coordination from the booth because he loses touch with the team's emotions [54:36] [55:06] [56:09] [56:40].

## Summary

Adam Douglas, an applied sport scientist at Catapult who also consults for Hockey Canada, shows how wearable load data from ice hockey practices and games was used with coaches. In one case, defensemen lost explosive output across a game and got less intensity in practice than forwards; skating was added to position drills and in-game explosive efforts rose. In the second, he plans practice duration and intensity ahead of a short tournament and plots measured load against the plan. His closing message is to use whatever you collect, and to feed objective load back to coaches while leaving tactical decisions to them.

## Key claims

- Hockey Canada's national teams target short tournaments of five or six games in about ten days, so preparation has to peak in a narrow window. [01:33]
- Hockey has little applied workload research, which was why Hockey Canada became a Catapult client about three years earlier. [02:36]
- The sensor combines an accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer worn between the shoulder plates, and it does not use GPS indoors. [03:40], [04:10]
- Coaches reported the defense could not sustain intensity across all three periods. Douglas says the athletes are fit, so he looked at the data instead of assuming a fitness problem. [05:45]
- With no comparable literature, he compared games and practices internally using player load per minute and a count of explosive efforts. [06:15], [06:47]
- Defense showed a different practice intensity from forwards, and explosive output trended down across the three periods. [07:18], [08:21]
- Defensemen got less exposure to explosive intensity than forwards, and forwards looked flatter in part because there are more of them and they get more rest. [08:51], [09:22]
- Coaches planning practice think technical and tactical first. Douglas pushed them to consider the physical content of drills, for example getting defensemen skating in position work instead of standing at the blue line for shots. [09:22], [10:23]
- After about three months, in-game explosive efforts were higher; Douglas cautions that Olympic arousal may have contributed. Coaches said the defense played better late in the season. [10:23], [10:53]
- For the men's under-20 program he calls the physical side "pillars" (a term he credits to a colleague) that support technical and tactical work. [11:56]
- He pre-plans each day on a pre-competition calendar as short or longer and medium or high intensity, then plots measured load against that plan for coaches. [12:26], [12:56], [13:27]
- In the plotted tournament, the highest-loaded day was an outdoor game against the Americans that went to a shootout, and the lowest load was the fourth game, against a weaker opponent. [15:01], [15:31]
- He combines wellness questionnaires, internal load, an HRV app and heart-rate data, but shows coaches only a pared-down summary of considerations. [15:31], [16:02]
- He frames recommendations as considerations because coaches face the media and decide how hard to push. [16:33]
- The team front-loads the tournament so athletes peak; that year's load trend went up into the medal round, but the team still lost, and he says luck and the human element are not accounted for. [17:04], [17:35]
- If you collect data, use it. He says there is a gap between how coaches rate a session's intensity and how athletes experience it, and an objective measure puts everyone on the same page. [19:07], [19:37]

## Numbers and definitions

- Player load per minute: described as intensity of work per minute in games and practices; player load is called a well-researched Catapult variable. [06:47]
- Explosive efforts: a frequency count of explosive movements on the ice. [06:47]
- 44%: increase in in-game explosive efforts "in three months." Comparison period and statistics not given. [10:23]
- Tournament: five or six games in about ten days. [01:33]
- Round-robin games on the 26th, 27th, 29th and 30th, double back-to-backs. [13:58]
- Short day: about 30 minutes or less. [12:56]
- Three years of tracking data on the athletes. [18:37]
- 25 athletes (can now be understood to individual level). [18:06]
- HRV measured from August through the January tournament. [24:26]
- Hypothetical "300 units" of load for one player, which Douglas says he is making up. [21:51]
- Caption problem: the group of players in the position comparison is garbled ("seven players" for defense). [07:18]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Inertial wearable sensor data on ice, summarized as player load per minute and explosive effort counts.
- Internal comparison of practices versus games by position group, plus simple game models for wins versus losses.
- Pre-competition calendar with planned day types, compared with measured load.
- Combined monitoring: subjective wellness, internal load, HRV, heart rate.
- Concept of tactical periodization (hard and easy days), mentioned in Q&A. [22:52]

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes for sessions or games, no statistical tests, and no control for the 44% result; the speaker flags arousal and multifactor game outcomes. [08:21], [10:23]
- Results come from national-team staff and a short-tournament setting, not a full season.
- Douglas is a vendor employee (Catapult); he says he is also a PhD student and a Hockey Canada practitioner. [01:03]
- The finite-load idea (too much load lowers explosive ratio) is described as theoretical, not shown. [21:20], [21:51]
- The slides are not visible, so the shapes of plots are only described, not verified.

## Q&A

- Wearing comfort: athletes adapt; he explains why, asks them to wear it and checks in about 15 minutes in. [20:17]
- Using the data to manage players' ice time: he has raised the finite-load concept but coaches decide who plays. [21:20]
- Applying to other sports: any sport that measures practices and games can use it; loading choices belong to the practitioner. [22:52]
- Why so little hockey research: he does not know; likely emerging applied research in North America and closed environments. [23:23]
- HRV protocol: measured from August through the tournament, kept simple for under-20 players. [24:26]

## Summary

Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

## Key claims

- The ulnar collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the throwing elbow, and a complete tear needs reconstruction with a graft. [01:36], [02:07]
- About 900 professional pitchers have had the surgery, and he says 25% of current major league pitchers have. [03:09], [03:39]
- Two causes for continued injuries: higher velocity, and early year-round single-sport play. [04:09]
- In wearable studies, faster pitches impart more elbow stress for both youth and professional pitchers, and this is pitch speed, not arm speed. [04:39], [05:10]
- In a simulated seven-inning game, fatigue ratings rose each inning and peak fastball velocity dipped around inning five, but elbow stress went up when it should have come down in fatigued pitchers. [05:10], [05:40]
- Single-sport specialization before skeletal maturity is causing burnout of muscle and tendon, and kids feel pressure to play through pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Among 140 established pitchers who had the surgery, 20% never pitched in the majors again, and about one in three returned but not at prior durability. [09:13], [09:43]
- Returning pitchers showed a statistically significant decline in numerous pitching metrics. [09:43], [10:13]
- Wins above replacement falls for three years before surgery and takes three years after return to reach pre-surgery level. [10:13], [10:43]

In one case, defensemen lost explosive output across a game and got less intensity in practice than forwards; skating was added to position drills and in-game explosive efforts rose. In the second, he plans practice duration and intensity ahead of a short tournament and plots measured load against the plan. His closing message is to use whatever you collect, and to feed objective load back to coaches while leaving tactical decisions to them.

## Summary

Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

## Key claims

- The ulnar collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the throwing elbow, and a complete tear needs reconstruction with a graft. [01:36], [02:07]
- About 900 professional pitchers have had the surgery, and he says 25% of current major league pitchers have. [03:09], [03:39]
- Two causes for continued injuries: higher velocity, and early year-round single-sport play. [04:09]
- In wearable studies, faster pitches impart more elbow stress for both youth and professional pitchers, and this is pitch speed, not arm speed. [04:39], [05:10]
- In a simulated seven-inning game, fatigue ratings rose each inning and peak fastball velocity dipped around inning five, but elbow stress went up when it should have come down in fatigued pitchers. [05:10], [05:40]
- Single-sport specialization before skeletal maturity is causing burnout of muscle and tendon, and kids feel pressure to play through pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Among 140 established pitchers who had the surgery, 20% never pitched in the majors again, and about one in three returned but not at prior durability. [09:13], [09:43]
- Returning pitchers showed a statistically significant decline in numerous pitching metrics. [09:43], [10:13]
- Wins above replacement falls for three years before surgery and takes three years after return to reach pre-surgery level. [10:13], [10:43]
- Over 2004 to 2014, salary paid during rehab came to about half a billion dollars (2017 dollars), excluding medical, travel, minor leaguers and pre-surgery downtime. [12:14], [12:44], [13:14], [13:44]
- Non-operative treatment for low-grade tears works some of the time but failure means losing a second season. [14:14], [15:15]
- Expected value decision analysis can compare the two paths and show, via two-way sensitivity analysis, where each wins; he says it does not replace clinical decision-making. [15:46], [16:47], [17:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- 900 pitchers, 25% of current MLB pitchers. [03:09], [03:39]
- Youth survey: 200 healthy players; 75% admitted arm pain; 25% had symptoms suggestive of overuse injury; 50% felt pressured to play despite pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Up to 10% of drafted pitchers had already had surgery (Mayo study, speaker credits Chris Camp). [07:41], [08:11]
- Youngest patient: 12. [08:11]
- 150 MLB pitchers studied, 140 "established" (10 or more games in a season). [09:13]
- 20% of established pitchers never returned to the majors; one in three came back below the 10-game threshold. [09:43]
- Recovery to the majors: 12 to 18 months; about four to four and a half years to return to prior level. [10:43]
- Medical cost per player: about $50,000, called conservative. [11:13]
- 2004 to 2014 study: about 200 surgeries; 180 days missed on average; about half starters, half relievers. [12:14], [12:44]
- Non-operative success: 40 to 80% depending on the case; at most three months of downtime. [14:14], [14:45]
- Surgery success: "80 to 100%" in different studies; a year to a year and a half of downtime. [14:45]
- Sample model: expected WAR 1.6 non-operative versus 1.3 surgery, for one representative case. [16:47]
- Caption problem: "80 to 80 to 100%" at [14:45] is garbled. "One out of three" is ambiguous about the denominator. [09:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable elbow-stress sleeve on throwers (medial elbow torque), including a simulated game with fatigue ratings.
- Surveys of youth players; cohort analysis of public MLB data; salary and wins above replacement (WAR) measures.
- Expected value decision analysis with two-way sensitivity analysis for treatment choice.

## Limits and open questions

- The salary study was under review at the time. [11:44]
- WAR was age-matched only in the first data set; the second was not controlled, as he agrees in Q&A. [18:19]
- The salary-per-WAR figure was "back of the envelope" and not adjusted. [28:27]
- The decision example is a single sample case with chosen inputs. [16:47]
- The speaker is a clinician reporting his group's studies; the youth survey was done during his residency. [07:10]
- The speaker does not give the sample or denominator behind the relief-versus-starter injury comparison and says he does not know. [27:22]
- The fatigue study sample size is not stated.

## Q&A

- Was WAR controlled for starters versus relievers? First set age-matched, second not. [18:19]
- Recovery by age? Numbers too small, appears similar to natural age trend. [18:50]
- How to avoid the injury? Rest, pitch counts (including warm-up pitches and multiple leagues), education, wearable research on weighted balls and fatigue. [19:20], [20:21], [20:52]
- Early specialization versus remodeling of the arm in childhood? Some early throwing is needed; the problem is rest. [19:51]
- Hitters? The sleeve relies on a throwing motion so cannot measure hitters. [21:23]
- Batting after injury? He allows it if pain-free. [21:54]
- Arm slot? Next stage; slot has not shown increased elbow stress so far. [22:33]
- Coaches' attention to pitch counts? More aware now. [23:10]
- Fatigue mechanism? His hypothesis: kinetic chain fatigue makes the arm do more; core and bodyweight work suggested. [24:11]
- Does salary matter to the analysis? Depends what is measured. [25:12]
- Why research from Japan? He does not know. [25:42]
- Pitcher elbows in MRI? Pathology is common; professionals' tears are attritional. [26:13], [26:43]
- Why is the rate similar at the major league level? Elbows are what they are by then; possibly more relievers. [27:22]

## Summary

Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

## Key claims

- The ulnar collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the throwing elbow, and a complete tear needs reconstruction with a graft. [01:36], [02:07]
- About 900 professional pitchers have had the surgery, and he says 25% of current major league pitchers have. [03:09], [03:39]
- Two causes for continued injuries: higher velocity, and early year-round single-sport play. [04:09]
- In wearable studies, faster pitches impart more elbow stress for both youth and professional pitchers, and this is pitch speed, not arm speed. [04:39], [05:10]
- In a simulated seven-inning game, fatigue ratings rose each inning and peak fastball velocity dipped around inning five, but elbow stress went up when it should have come down in fatigued pitchers. [05:10], [05:40]
- Single-sport specialization before skeletal maturity is causing burnout of muscle and tendon, and kids feel pressure to play through pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Among 140 established pitchers who had the surgery, 20% never pitched in the majors again, and about one in three returned but not at prior durability. [09:13], [09:43]
- Returning pitchers showed a statistically significant decline in numerous pitching metrics. [09:43], [10:13]
- Wins above replacement falls for three years before surgery and takes three years after return to reach pre-surgery level. [10:13], [10:43]
- Over 2004 to 2014, salary paid during rehab came to about half a billion dollars (2017 dollars), excluding medical, travel, minor leaguers and pre-surgery downtime. [12:14], [12:44], [13:14], [13:44]
- Non-operative treatment for low-grade tears works some of the time but failure means losing a second season. [14:14], [15:15]
- Expected value decision analysis can compare the two paths and show, via two-way sensitivity analysis, where each wins; he says it does not replace clinical decision-making. [15:46], [16:47], [17:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- 900 pitchers, 25% of current MLB pitchers. [03:09], [03:39]
- Youth survey: 200 healthy players; 75% admitted arm pain; 25% had symptoms suggestive of overuse injury; 50% felt pressured to play despite pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Up to 10% of drafted pitchers had already had surgery (Mayo study, speaker credits Chris Camp). [07:41], [08:11]
- Youngest patient: 12. [08:11]
- 150 MLB pitchers studied, 140 "established" (10 or more games in a season). [09:13]
- 20% of established pitchers never returned to the majors; one in three came back below the 10-game threshold. [09:43]
- Recovery to the majors: 12 to 18 months; about four to four and a half years to return to prior level. [10:43]
- Medical cost per player: about $50,000, called conservative. [11:13]
- 2004 to 2014 study: about 200 surgeries; 180 days missed on average; about half starters, half relievers. [12:14], [12:44]
- Non-operative success: 40 to 80% depending on the case; at most three months of downtime. [14:14], [14:45]
- Surgery success: "80 to 100%" in different studies; a year to a year and a half of downtime. [14:45]
- Sample model: expected WAR 1.6 non-operative versus 1.3 surgery, for one representative case. [16:47]
- Caption problem: "80 to 80 to 100%" at [14:45] is garbled. "One out of three" is ambiguous about the denominator. [09:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable elbow-stress sleeve on throwers (medial elbow torque), including a simulated game with fatigue ratings.
- Surveys of youth players; cohort analysis of public MLB data; salary and wins above replacement (WAR) measures.
- Expected value decision analysis with two-way sensitivity analysis for treatment choice.

## Limits and open questions

- The salary study was under review at the time. [11:44]
- WAR was age-matched only in the first data set; the second was not controlled, as he agrees in Q&A. [18:19]
- The salary-per-WAR figure was "back of the envelope" and not adjusted. [28:27]
- The decision example is a single sample case with chosen inputs. [16:47]
- The speaker is a clinician reporting his group's studies; the youth survey was done during his residency. [07:10]
- The speaker does not give the sample or denominator behind the relief-versus-starter injury comparison and says he does not know. [27:22]
- The fatigue study sample size is not stated.

## Q&A

- Was WAR controlled for starters versus relievers? First set age-matched, second not. [18:19]
- Recovery by age? Numbers too small, appears similar to natural age trend. [18:50]
- How to avoid the injury? Rest, pitch counts (including warm-up pitches and multiple leagues), education, wearable research on weighted balls and fatigue. [19:20], [20:21], [20:52]
- Early specialization versus remodeling of the arm in childhood? Some early throwing is needed; the problem is rest. [19:51]
- Hitters? The sleeve relies on a throwing motion so cannot measure hitters. [21:23]
- Batting after injury? He allows it if pain-free. [21:54]
- Arm slot? Next stage; slot has not shown increased elbow stress so far. [22:33]
- Coaches' attention to pitch counts? More aware now. [23:10]
- Fatigue mechanism? His hypothesis: kinetic chain fatigue makes the arm do more; core and bodyweight work suggested. [24:11]
- Does salary matter to the analysis? Depends what is measured. [25:12]
- Why research from Japan? He does not know. [25:42]
- Pitcher elbows in MRI? Pathology is common; professionals' tears are attritional. [26:13], [26:43]
- Why is the rate similar at the major league level? Elbows are what they are by then; possibly more relievers. [27:22]

## Summary

A moderator, a former NFL quarterback turned analyst, a congressman who is a Marine veteran, and the head of an addiction treatment company discuss opioids in sports and in society. They argue that addiction is a chronic condition often tied to untreated trauma, depression or anxiety, that short rehab stays have little evidence behind them, and that stigma keeps athletes and veterans from asking for help. They disagree in part on blame: one panelist stresses personal responsibility, another says prescribing played a role. The panel closes on harm reduction and on testing treatments through data. It is a personal and policy discussion, with few worked analytics.

## Key claims

- Overdose deaths have risen steadily, and the moderator frames them through her own brother's death [01:00], [02:03].
- Addiction should be treated as a chronic condition with relapse and genetic risk, not as a one-time 28-day event [08:10].
- Substance use often sits on top of another psychiatric condition, with depression, anxiety and trauma the most common [08:43].
- Risk comes from three sources: biology, life experience such as trauma, and access to the substance [09:13].
- Veterans meet both trauma and painkillers, which raises overdose risk [09:44].
- Leaf says an opioid given for injury pain became his way of coping with emotional pain, and that competition was his first dependence [13:20].
- Leaf says locker-room culture offered no example of a man asking for help [13:51].
- Moulton says veterans seeking therapy are often sent home with a prescription because the VA lacks therapists [11:47].
- The treatment field is called a cottage industry built on individual recovery stories rather than evidence [16:27].
- Corbin says 28-day luxury rehab has nothing in evidence behind it [16:58].
- The evidence-based model is medication, therapy for co-occurring conditions, and recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Moulton proposes routine mental health check-ups, first for the military and then for high schoolers, and a three-digit hotline [22:42], [23:43].
- Corbin says payment models reward service volume, not outcomes, which favors repeated short stays [29:20], [29:54].
- Corbin says pharmaceutical companies deserve some blame but blaming the substance undercuts the disease model [35:00]. Moulton says fentanyl from China is a policy problem but that sufferers must take personal responsibility [37:05]. Corbin replies that responsibility is hard when a doctor prescribed the drug [37:35].
- Leaf says dosing beyond the prescription may be the first symptom of trouble [39:09].
- Telling personal stories reduces stigma and lets others come forward [41:13], [43:45].
- Corbin says analytics can flag people who have not been diagnosed, such as those seeking drugs across several providers [44:47].
- Harm reduction means accepting patients as they arrive, and supervised injection sites and naloxone access are defended as life-saving [49:18], [51:19], [51:50].
- Moulton supports studying cannabis and psychedelics for post-traumatic stress and says the data should decide [54:26], [54:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Opioid overdose deaths since 1999: 400,000 (moderator) [01:00].
- Drug overdose deaths in 2017: 72,000, compared to the size of an NFL stadium, with 50,000 opioid related [01:00], [01:31].
- Leaf's brother's addiction reached $4,000 a month before a switch to heroin; he died in 2015 at 30 [02:03]. (The moderator says her own brother.)
- Veterans are twice as likely as non-veterans to die of an opioid overdose (Moulton) [04:34].
- Leaf describes a $31 million opportunity at the draft, second overall [06:04].
- 80 percent of people with a substance use disorder have an underlying co-occurring psychiatric condition (Corbin) [08:43].
- 28-day rehab: described as having single-digit success rates; a Malibu stay cited at $45,000 for 30 days [16:58].
- Relapse risk falls after one year in recovery and becomes that of the general public after five years [18:01].
- 51 percent of former NFL players said they used opioids, and 70 percent of those said they abused them (Corbin) [25:15].
- Chinese supply: the claim is that China provides 90 percent of US fentanyl, and a 2014 agreement was followed by US Customs stopping 1207 shipments. The Chinese customs figure in the sentence is cut off in the captions [36:33], [37:05].
- 20 million people diagnosed with a substance use disorder, with an 80 percent treatment gap, meaning 20 percent seek treatment [44:16], [44:47].
- Treatment cost: several years in outpatient care at Corbin's company costs about the same as one month of resort rehab [29:54].
- Leaf: nearly eight years sober [26:45]; stayed 90 days at rehab while three years sober [31:26]; same therapist five years [32:57].
- Moulton: hotline number is "nine eight eight" [23:43].
- Caption problems: "Corbin pho" and "Stephanie widdled wacks" are garbled names; the company is spelled Eleonora, Ellenor and Eleanor in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Biopsychosocial model of addiction (biological, psychological, social) [08:43], [09:13].
- Evidence-based treatment: medication, therapy, recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Claims analytics to flag undiagnosed patients, including multiple prescribers and emergency room visits [44:47].
- Harm reduction, including supervised injection sites and naloxone [49:18], [51:19].
- Moulton's three-part legislative plan: annual check-ups for veterans and service members, extension to high schoolers, and a national hotline [22:42], [23:43].

## Limits and open questions

- Most claims are personal experience, opinion or policy advocacy; no study is cited by name.
- The 51 and 70 percent figures for former NFL players are not sourced in the talk.
- Corbin leads a treatment company, and Moulton is a legislator promoting his own bills; both have an institutional stake.
- Panelists disagree on blame (Moulton and Leaf stress accountability; Corbin points to prescribing). Not resolved.
- Leaf's statement that studies prove injection sites make communities safer is not backed by named studies [51:50].

## Summary

An ESPN-hosted panel shows how a data analyst and a former cornerback work together on tracking data, then thinks aloud about how to build an individual metric for pass defenders. They stress that metrics need film knowledge and that the work is a cycle of question, data, model and plain-language story. The panel walks through press coverage, coverage responsibility (with an audience poll) and anticipation, and names what tracking data cannot capture. No finished defender metric is presented, and the panel says it is brainstorming. They close with questions on the Ravens' quarterback and other industries.

## Key claims

- Before tracking data, defensive back analysis was hard because play-by-play data covers few defenders and broadcast video often omits them [01:34].
- Using tracking data amounts to teaching a computer to watch film, which needs deep game knowledge (Burke) [05:12], [05:44].
- A former player says the software does what he did when he watched film but faster and at scale [07:48], [53:42].
- A former front office researcher says the goal is a partnership in which the analyst learns enough football to work alone [11:26], [11:56].
- Kaplan describes three steps: give feedback on metric names, find stories in current league events, and meet analysts to match data with film [12:26], [13:26].
- Kaplan says coverage metrics let a TV analyst confirm that a team used man coverage on every drop back in one half of a championship game [13:57], [14:27].
- The moderator frames the process as words into numbers into words, a data science cycle with collaboration at each step [17:00], [17:30].
- For press coverage, Foxworth stresses leverage, keeping a receiver at the line, and reputation affecting where the quarterback throws [19:04], [21:36].
- Burke says the tracking provider supplies clean data with tagged snap and release events [22:39], [23:10].
- Alignment at the snap does not prove press, since bail technique can start close to the line [23:41], [24:11].
- Tracking data lacks some body detail such as hip position, and a film expert will be richer, but the data applies one rule set to every player at scale [24:42], [25:13].
- Candidate press measures: how far a receiver is moved off the expected route and how long to get three yards downfield [25:45]; distance plus velocity, since a defender can be close and losing [26:15].
- Re-routing a receiver at the line buys safeties time in zone coverage [27:47].
- Outside observers do not know the call, so some mistakes cannot be assigned [28:17], [28:49].
- For responsibility, steps are coverage identification, defender roles, route identification, then comparing where the defender should be to where he was [35:06], [35:38], [36:08].
- Foxworth says a defender is graded at fault in the shown clip, even if the play might have been completed regardless [38:10].
- For anticipation, one idea is to group plays with similar concepts and coverages and compare a defender's path to the average [41:47], [42:19]. The baseline is hard to establish [43:21].
- Anticipation may also be the precursor to reaction time, such as when a safety breaks on the ball [44:54].
- Pass denial is hard to see in statistics; a defender who prevents a throw leaves no box-score trace [46:55], [47:25].
- Ravens opponents are seen using single-high man or cover three coverages more than other teams, and the quarterback's scrambles averaged high yards against man [48:57], [49:30], [50:30].
- Football is called harder to analyze than baseball because player interactions are tangled, and tracking data helps isolate one player [52:05].

## Numbers and definitions

- Clip 3.9 seconds: a quarterback holds the ball because he beats a blitzer [03:08].
- 500 double-teams: a pass rusher doubled more than 500 times since the start of the previous season [08:19].
- 17.6 percent: catch chance given on one play by next-gen stats [08:52]; expected completion percentage of 63 percent, and plus 10 over expected [08:52], [09:22].
- 84 percent catch rate, 15 percent above expectation [09:22]; 40 percent catch probability on one throw [09:22].
- 2.2 seconds to throw, and under 2.5 seconds as the league average time [09:52].
- Pass rush win rate: beating a blocker within 2.5 seconds [10:54].
- Man coverage on 100 percent of drop backs in the first half of a 2018 conference championship game, the only team to do so in a half all season [13:57], [14:27].
- Poll on responsibility: 30 percent chose number 54, 46 percent chose number 20, 24 percent chose number 27 [33:02], [33:32].
- About 13 yards per scramble when defenses played man at one point in the season [50:30].
- Press coverage is defined for the exercise by proximity to the line at and just after the snap [23:41], [24:11].
- Clip numbers come from short TV narration, so units and exact subjects may be garbled in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Next-gen stats and Zebra as tracking providers [22:39].
- Coverage classification, route classification, and route tree labels [12:26], [35:06].
- Pass rush win rate and double-team rate [10:54].
- Calling the model's role definitions per defender (hook, flat, deep thirds) in cover three [35:06].
- Average-player comparison for anticipation [41:47].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel produces no validated metric and says it is hypothesizing.
- Tracking data lacks hip position, and the call or assignment is unknown to outsiders [24:42], [28:17].
- The poll vote is not a ground truth, and Foxworth's judgement on one play is one expert's view.
- The panelists work at or came from ESPN or the NFL; ESPN products are the subject of the opening clips.
- Establishing the average baseline for anticipation is described as hard [43:21].
- Caption problems: "Bryan Burk Seger," "Mathieu" spelled "Matthew," and the opening video failed to play on the first attempt [03:39].

- How do players like Lamar Jackson change strategy? Defenses play more predictable coverage, and scramble results can be separated by coverage [48:57], [50:30].
- Are other industries faster to adopt analytics? Football is hard because of interacting players; firms face the same problem isolating employees but segment customers well [51:32], [53:06].
- Would this data have helped Foxworth as a player? Yes, he did by hand what the data does across thousands of plays [53:42].

## Summary

Adam Douglas, an applied sport scientist at Catapult who also consults for Hockey Canada, shows how wearable load data from ice hockey practices and games was used with coaches. In one case, defensemen lost explosive output across a game and got less intensity in practice than forwards; skating was added to position drills and in-game explosive efforts rose. In the second, he plans practice duration and intensity ahead of a short tournament and plots measured load against the plan. His closing message is to use whatever you collect, and to feed objective load back to coaches while leaving tactical decisions to them.

## Key claims

- Hockey Canada's national teams target short tournaments of five or six games in about ten days, so preparation has to peak in a narrow window. [01:33]
- Hockey has little applied workload research, which was why Hockey Canada became a Catapult client about three years earlier. [02:36]
- The sensor combines an accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer worn between the shoulder plates, and it does not use GPS indoors. [03:40], [04:10]
- Coaches reported the defense could not sustain intensity across all three periods. Douglas says the athletes are fit, so he looked at the data instead of assuming a fitness problem. [05:45]
- With no comparable literature, he compared games and practices internally using player load per minute and a count of explosive efforts. [06:15], [06:47]
- Defense showed a different practice intensity from forwards, and explosive output trended down across the three periods. [07:18], [08:21]
- Defensemen got less exposure to explosive intensity than forwards, and forwards looked flatter in part because there are more of them and they get more rest. [08:51], [09:22]
- Coaches planning practice think technical and tactical first. Douglas pushed them to consider the physical content of drills, for example getting defensemen skating in position work instead of standing at the blue line for shots. [09:22], [10:23]
- After about three months, in-game explosive efforts were higher; Douglas cautions that Olympic arousal may have contributed. Coaches said the defense played better late in the season. [10:23], [10:53]
- For the men's under-20 program he calls the physical side "pillars" (a term he credits to a colleague) that support technical and tactical work. [11:56]
- He pre-plans each day on a pre-competition calendar as short or longer and medium or high intensity, then plots measured load against that plan for coaches. [12:26], [12:56], [13:27]
- In the plotted tournament, the highest-loaded day was an outdoor game against the Americans that went to a shootout, and the lowest load was the fourth game, against a weaker opponent. [15:01], [15:31]
- He combines wellness questionnaires, internal load, an HRV app and heart-rate data, but shows coaches only a pared-down summary of considerations. [15:31], [16:02]
- He frames recommendations as considerations because coaches face the media and decide how hard to push. [16:33]
- The team front-loads the tournament so athletes peak; that year's load trend went up into the medal round, but the team still lost, and he says luck and the human element are not accounted for. [17:04], [17:35]
- If you collect data, use it. He says there is a gap between how coaches rate a session's intensity and how athletes experience it, and an objective measure puts everyone on the same page. [19:07], [19:37]

## Numbers and definitions

- Player load per minute: described as intensity of work per minute in games and practices; player load is called a well-researched Catapult variable. [06:47]
- Explosive efforts: a frequency count of explosive movements on the ice. [06:47]
- 44%: increase in in-game explosive efforts "in three months." Comparison period and statistics not given. [10:23]
- Tournament: five or six games in about ten days. [01:33]
- Round-robin games on the 26th, 27th, 29th and 30th, double back-to-backs. [13:58]
- Short day: about 30 minutes or less. [12:56]
- Three years of tracking data on the athletes. [18:37]
- 25 athletes (can now be understood to individual level). [18:06]
- HRV measured from August through the January tournament. [24:26]
- Hypothetical "300 units" of load for one player, which Douglas says he is making up. [21:51]
- Caption problem: the group of players in the position comparison is garbled ("seven players" for defense). [07:18]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Inertial wearable sensor data on ice, summarized as player load per minute and explosive effort counts.
- Internal comparison of practices versus games by position group, plus simple game models for wins versus losses.
- Pre-competition calendar with planned day types, compared with measured load.
- Combined monitoring: subjective wellness, internal load, HRV, heart rate.
- Concept of tactical periodization (hard and easy days), mentioned in Q&A. [22:52]

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes for sessions or games, no statistical tests, and no control for the 44% result; the speaker flags arousal and multifactor game outcomes. [08:21], [10:23]
- Results come from national-team staff and a short-tournament setting, not a full season.
- Douglas is a vendor employee (Catapult); he says he is also a PhD student and a Hockey Canada practitioner. [01:03]
- The finite-load idea (too much load lowers explosive ratio) is described as theoretical, not shown. [21:20], [21:51]
- The slides are not visible, so the shapes of plots are only described, not verified.

## Q&A

- Wearing comfort: athletes adapt; he explains why, asks them to wear it and checks in about 15 minutes in. [20:17]
- Using the data to manage players' ice time: he has raised the finite-load concept but coaches decide who plays. [21:20]
- Applying to other sports: any sport that measures practices and games can use it; loading choices belong to the practitioner. [22:52]
- Why so little hockey research: he does not know; likely emerging applied research in North America and closed environments. [23:23]
- HRV protocol: measured from August through the tournament, kept simple for under-20 players. [24:26]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: z_6M5r7031A
title: "SSAC19: The True Cost of Tommy John Surgery in Major League Baseball"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Eric McNally]
topics: [injury-health, policy, decision-making, other-sport:baseball]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Dr. Eric McNally, an orthopedic surgeon, argues that elbow ligament injuries in baseball keep rising because pitches are faster and young players specialize and pitch year-round. He presents wearable-sleeve findings that faster pitches load the elbow more and that the velocity-stress link breaks down with fatigue. Using public data, he shows that many pitchers who have the surgery do not return to prior durability or value, and that salary paid during recovery adds up to about half a billion dollars over a decade. He closes by proposing expected value decision analysis as an adjunct for choosing surgery versus non-operative treatment.

## Key claims

- The ulnar collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the throwing elbow, and a complete tear needs reconstruction with a graft. [01:36], [02:07]
- About 900 professional pitchers have had the surgery, and he says 25% of current major league pitchers have. [03:09], [03:39]
- Two causes for continued injuries: higher velocity, and early year-round single-sport play. [04:09]
- In wearable studies, faster pitches impart more elbow stress for both youth and professional pitchers, and this is pitch speed, not arm speed. [04:39], [05:10]
- In a simulated seven-inning game, fatigue ratings rose each inning and peak fastball velocity dipped around inning five, but elbow stress went up when it should have come down in fatigued pitchers. [05:10], [05:40]
- Single-sport specialization before skeletal maturity is causing burnout of muscle and tendon, and kids feel pressure to play through pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Among 140 established pitchers who had the surgery, 20% never pitched in the majors again, and about one in three returned but not at prior durability. [09:13], [09:43]
- Returning pitchers showed a statistically significant decline in numerous pitching metrics. [09:43], [10:13]
- Wins above replacement falls for three years before surgery and takes three years after return to reach pre-surgery level. [10:13], [10:43]
- Over 2004 to 2014, salary paid during rehab came to about half a billion dollars (2017 dollars), excluding medical, travel, minor leaguers and pre-surgery downtime. [12:14], [12:44], [13:14], [13:44]
- Non-operative treatment for low-grade tears works some of the time but failure means losing a second season. [14:14], [15:15]
- Expected value decision analysis can compare the two paths and show, via two-way sensitivity analysis, where each wins; he says it does not replace clinical decision-making. [15:46], [16:47], [17:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- 900 pitchers, 25% of current MLB pitchers. [03:09], [03:39]
- Youth survey: 200 healthy players; 75% admitted arm pain; 25% had symptoms suggestive of overuse injury; 50% felt pressured to play despite pain. [07:10], [07:41]
- Up to 10% of drafted pitchers had already had surgery (Mayo study, speaker credits Chris Camp). [07:41], [08:11]
- Youngest patient: 12. [08:11]
