## Summary

A moderated panel of league, team and player-side voices treats the NBA season as a design problem: 1,230 games, many of them low-stakes. Panelists discuss a December start, a play-in for seeds seven through ten, an in-season tournament, dividing the season into legs with points, and a points-based "octopus" format, always with the constraint that changes be revenue neutral. They stress that parts interact (calendar, tournament, draft, TV windows) and that league owners, broadcasters and players must align. The session is opinion and brainstorming; no data analysis is shown.

## Key claims

- The moderator's premise is that the 82-game season with the top teams advancing is boring and that viewership shows it; Evan (caption spelling) disputes that framing, saying the league does not see the schedule as ill-suited. [01:34], [04:11]
- Evan says the goal is a better product, which could mean fewer games, new tournaments or a rethought season, and not cutting games for its own sake. [05:11], [05:41]
- Steve Koonin says relevance equals revenue, and the NBA gets crushed at the season's start by a prime football game. [06:41], [07:11]
- Gerson Rose says lost practice days hurt a young team's development and a contending team's recovery. [08:44], [09:14]
- Shane Battier says players' first concern is money, and the season is grueling. [11:15], [11:47]
- Steve argues the season calendar follows the ad market rather than the consumer, and that the gap between second and third quarter ad dollars is 3 percent. [14:22]
- Evan says the league is open to moving the calendar, with network partners needing to get comfortable with a later finals. [15:55], [16:25]
- Panelists favor a play-in with seeds seven through ten competing for the last two spots, calling it a fairly easy change. [18:55], [19:25]
- Evan wants more "spikes" like Christmas Day through tradition and mini-seasons with something at stake. [19:25], [19:55], [20:26]
- Shane says coaches create artificial motivators and a structurally measurable stake would help. [21:28], [21:59]
- A reset-style structure raises a tanking and draft concern. [23:00]
- Evan credits the All-Star game change with near-unanimous praise but says luck played a part, and argues tournaments take time to build tradition. [24:32], [25:04], [25:35]
- Shane says European soccer cups changed his mind about an in-season tournament. [26:38], [27:10]
- Evan argues that cutting games may not raise the value of each one proportionally; bigger events matter more. [33:53], [34:23]
- Panelists warn that changing one piece (calendar, tournament, draft) affects others. [39:31], [40:03], [40:33]
- Revenue must be at least neutral because players receive a share of basketball related income. [41:34], [42:36]
- Alignment among teams, broadcast partners and players is the route to adoption, and the player and broadcast contracts expire at about the same time. [51:23], [52:24]

## Numbers and definitions

- 1,230 regular season games. [03:40]
- Reset after 40 or 41 games, top four teams per conference into half one (moderator's example). [09:14], [09:44]
- 66-game season during the lockout year, per Shane. [12:17]
- Games that feel meaningless: about 10 or 12 for bottom teams, 5 or 6 for top teams (Shane's estimate). [12:17]
- Ad revenue variance between second and third quarter: 3 percent; an Olympics drawing over 1.25 billion dollars in ad revenue. [14:22]
- Octopus: eight legs, ten-game legs; first win worth one point, tenth worth five, max 25 points a leg. [35:28], [35:58]
- Players receive 50.1% of basketball related income. [42:36]
- Cable homes: 102 million then, "under 80 million" now. [43:07]
- Caption problems: speaker attribution is often unclear; "262 games for 154" is garbled [39:00]; moderator and Evan surnames garbled in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- No data model or analysis is shown. The panel runs a "constitutional convention" thought exercise under a revenue-neutral constraint [01:34], [03:10].
- Proposals named: December start, a play-in, an in-season tournament, season split into legs with points, the octopus format, three-game series, a different ending rule. [17:25], [19:55], [35:28], [48:20]

## Limits and open questions

- Opinion and brainstorming; the speakers say these are not contingencies or plans. [17:55]
- The moderator's boring-season premise is disputed by the league representative. [04:11]
- Panelists are stakeholders (league, team, player) with institutional interests; the Hawks CEO draws on past broadcast work.
- No viewership, revenue or injury data shown for any proposal.
- The "fan" segment is a single volunteer. [31:18]

## Q&A

- Q&A begins near [44:09] (announced as ten minutes at [00:32]).
- Could the all-star ending be used beyond the all-star game? Everything is on the table; the G League tests rule changes. [44:42], [45:12]
- Would players resist changes? Shane thinks the game will always win out; competition is valued. [46:46], [47:17]
- Does it change how players are valued? Not addressed beyond "basketball is basketball." [47:48]
- Three-game series? Cuts travel; selling it is a challenge. [48:20], [48:50]
- Biggest hurdle? Shane says broadcasters. [49:21]
- How does it become real? Alignment of three groups, easy wins first. [51:23], [51:54]

## Summary

An ESPN-hosted panel shows how a data analyst and a former cornerback work together on tracking data, then thinks aloud about how to build an individual metric for pass defenders. They stress that metrics need film knowledge and that the work is a cycle of question, data, model and plain-language story. The panel walks through press coverage, coverage responsibility (with an audience poll) and anticipation, and names what tracking data cannot capture. - A former front office researcher says the goal is a partnership in which the analyst learns enough football to work alone [11:26], [11:56].
- Kaplan describes three steps: give feedback on metric names, find stories in current league events, and meet analysts to match data with film [12:26], [13:26].
- Kaplan says coverage metrics let a TV analyst confirm that a team used man coverage on every drop back in one half of a championship game [13:57], [14:27].
- The moderator frames the process as words into numbers into words, a data science cycle with collaboration at each step [17:00], [17:30].
- For press coverage, Foxworth stresses leverage, keeping a receiver at the line, and reputation affecting where the quarterback throws [19:04], [21:36].
- Burke says the tracking provider supplies clean data with tagged snap and release events [22:39], [23:10].
- Alignment at the snap does not prove press, since bail technique can start close to the line [23:41], [24:11].
- Tracking data lacks some body detail such as hip position, and a film expert will be richer, but the data applies one rule set to every player at scale [24:42], [25:13].
- Candidate press measures: how far a receiver is moved off the expected route and how long to get three yards downfield [25:45]; distance plus velocity, since a defender can be close and losing [26:15].
- Re-routing a receiver at the line buys safeties time in zone coverage [27:47].
- Outside observers do not know the call, so some mistakes cannot be assigned [28:17], [28:49].
- For responsibility, steps are coverage identification, defender roles, route identification, then comparing where the defender should be to where he was [35:06], [35:38], [36:08].
- Foxworth says a defender is graded at fault in the shown clip, even if the play might have been completed regardless [38:10].
- For anticipation, one idea is to group plays with similar concepts and coverages and compare a defender's path to the average [41:47], [42:19]. The baseline is hard to establish [43:21].
- Anticipation may also be the precursor to reaction time, such as when a safety breaks on the ball [44:54].
- Pass denial is hard to see in statistics; a defender who prevents a throw leaves no box-score trace [46:55], [47:25].
- Ravens opponents are seen using single-high man or cover three coverages more than other teams, and the quarterback's scrambles averaged high yards against man [48:57], [49:30], [50:30].

- 500 double-teams: a pass rusher doubled more than 500 times since the start of the previous season [08:19].
- 17.6 percent: catch chance given on one play by next-gen stats [08:52]; expected completion percentage of 63 percent, and plus 10 over expected [08:52], [09:22].
- 84 percent catch rate, 15 percent above expectation [09:22]; 40 percent catch probability on one throw [09:22].
- 2.2 seconds to throw, and under 2.5 seconds as the league average time [09:52].
- Pass rush win rate: beating a blocker within 2.5 seconds [10:54].
- Man coverage on 100 percent of drop backs in the first half of a 2018 conference championship game, the only team to do so in a half all season [13:57], [14:27].
- Poll on responsibility: 30 percent chose number 54, 46 percent chose number 20, 24 percent chose number 27 [33:02], [33:32].
- About 13 yards per scramble when defenses played man at one point in the season [50:30].
- Press coverage is defined for the exercise by proximity to the line at and just after the snap [23:41], [24:11].
- Clip numbers come from short TV narration, so units and exact subjects may be garbled in captions.

- Next-gen stats and Zebra as tracking providers [22:39].
- Coverage classification, route classification, and route tree labels [12:26], [35:06].
- Pass rush win rate and double-team rate [10:54].
- Calling the model's role definitions per defender (hook, flat, deep thirds) in cover three [35:06].
- Average-player comparison for anticipation [41:47].

- The panel produces no validated metric and says it is hypothesizing.
- Tracking data lacks hip position, and the call or assignment is unknown to outsiders [24:42], [28:17].
- The poll vote is not a ground truth, and Foxworth's judgement on one play is one expert's view.
- The panelists work at or came from ESPN or the NFL; ESPN products are the subject of the opening clips.

- Caption problems: "Bryan Burk Seger," "Mathieu" spelled "Matthew," and the opening video failed to play on the first attempt [03:39].

They stress that metrics need film knowledge and that the work is a cycle of question, data, model and plain-language story. The panel walks through press coverage, coverage responsibility (with an audience poll) and anticipation, and names what tracking data cannot capture. No finished defender metric is presented, and the panel says it is brainstorming. They close with questions on the Ravens' quarterback and other industries.

## Key claims

- Before tracking data, defensive back analysis was hard because play-by-play data covers few defenders and broadcast video often omits them [01:34].

- A former front office researcher says the goal is a partnership in which the analyst learns enough football to work alone [11:26], [11:56].
- Kaplan describes three steps: give feedback on metric names, find stories in current league events, and meet analysts to match data with film [12:26], [13:26].
- Kaplan says coverage metrics let a TV analyst confirm that a team used man coverage on every drop back in one half of a championship game [13:57], [14:27].
- The moderator frames the process as words into numbers into words, a data science cycle with collaboration at each step [17:00], [17:30].
- For press coverage, Foxworth stresses leverage, keeping a receiver at the line, and reputation affecting where the quarterback throws [19:04], [21:36].
- Burke says the tracking provider supplies clean data with tagged snap and release events [22:39], [23:10].
- Alignment at the snap does not prove press, since bail technique can start close to the line [23:41], [24:11].
- Tracking data lacks some body detail such as hip position, and a film expert will be richer, but the data applies one rule set to every player at scale [24:42], [25:13].
- Candidate press measures: how far a receiver is moved off the expected route and how long to get three yards downfield [25:45]; distance plus velocity, since a defender can be close and losing [26:15].
- Re-routing a receiver at the line buys safeties time in zone coverage [27:47].
- Outside observers do not know the call, so some mistakes cannot be assigned [28:17], [28:49].
- For responsibility, steps are coverage identification, defender roles, route identification, then comparing where the defender should be to where he was [35:06], [35:38], [36:08].

## Summary

A moderator, a former NFL quarterback turned analyst, a congressman who is a Marine veteran, and the head of an addiction treatment company discuss opioids in sports and in society. They argue that addiction is a chronic condition often tied to untreated trauma, depression or anxiety, that short rehab stays have little evidence behind them, and that stigma keeps athletes and veterans from asking for help. They disagree in part on blame: one panelist stresses personal responsibility, another says prescribing played a role. The panel closes on harm reduction and on testing treatments through data. It is a personal and policy discussion, with few worked analytics.

## Key claims

- Overdose deaths have risen steadily, and the moderator frames them through her own brother's death [01:00], [02:03].
- Addiction should be treated as a chronic condition with relapse and genetic risk, not as a one-time 28-day event [08:10].
- Substance use often sits on top of another psychiatric condition, with depression, anxiety and trauma the most common [08:43].
- Risk comes from three sources: biology, life experience such as trauma, and access to the substance [09:13].
- Veterans meet both trauma and painkillers, which raises overdose risk [09:44].
- Leaf says an opioid given for injury pain became his way of coping with emotional pain, and that competition was his first dependence [13:20].
- Leaf says locker-room culture offered no example of a man asking for help [13:51].
- Moulton says veterans seeking therapy are often sent home with a prescription because the VA lacks therapists [11:47].
- The treatment field is called a cottage industry built on individual recovery stories rather than evidence [16:27].
- Corbin says 28-day luxury rehab has nothing in evidence behind it [16:58].
- The evidence-based model is medication, therapy for co-occurring conditions, and recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Moulton proposes routine mental health check-ups, first for the military and then for high schoolers, and a three-digit hotline [22:42], [23:43].
- Corbin says payment models reward service volume, not outcomes, which favors repeated short stays [29:20], [29:54].
- Corbin says pharmaceutical companies deserve some blame but blaming the substance undercuts the disease model [35:00]. Moulton says fentanyl from China is a policy problem but that sufferers must take personal responsibility [37:05]. Corbin replies that responsibility is hard when a doctor prescribed the drug [37:35].
- Leaf says dosing beyond the prescription may be the first symptom of trouble [39:09].
- Telling personal stories reduces stigma and lets others come forward [41:13], [43:45].
- Corbin says analytics can flag people who have not been diagnosed, such as those seeking drugs across several providers [44:47].
- Harm reduction means accepting patients as they arrive, and supervised injection sites and naloxone access are defended as life-saving [49:18], [51:19], [51:50].
- Moulton supports studying cannabis and psychedelics for post-traumatic stress and says the data should decide [54:26], [54:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Opioid overdose deaths since 1999: 400,000 (moderator) [01:00].
- Drug overdose deaths in 2017: 72,000, compared to the size of an NFL stadium, with 50,000 opioid related [01:00], [01:31].
- Leaf's brother's addiction reached $4,000 a month before a switch to heroin; he died in 2015 at 30 [02:03]. (The moderator says her own brother.)
- Veterans are twice as likely as non-veterans to die of an opioid overdose (Moulton) [04:34].
- Leaf describes a $31 million opportunity at the draft, second overall [06:04].
- 80 percent of people with a substance use disorder have an underlying co-occurring psychiatric condition (Corbin) [08:43].
- 28-day rehab: described as having single-digit success rates; a Malibu stay cited at $45,000 for 30 days [16:58].
- Relapse risk falls after one year in recovery and becomes that of the general public after five years [18:01].
- 51 percent of former NFL players said they used opioids, and 70 percent of those said they abused them (Corbin) [25:15].
- Chinese supply: the claim is that China provides 90 percent of US fentanyl, and a 2014 agreement was followed by US Customs stopping 1207 shipments. The Chinese customs figure in the sentence is cut off in the captions [36:33], [37:05].
- 20 million people diagnosed with a substance use disorder, with an 80 percent treatment gap, meaning 20 percent seek treatment [44:16], [44:47].
- Treatment cost: several years in outpatient care at Corbin's company costs about the same as one month of resort rehab [29:54].
- Leaf: nearly eight years sober [26:45]; stayed 90 days at rehab while three years sober [31:26]; same therapist five years [32:57].
- Moulton: hotline number is "nine eight eight" [23:43].
- Caption problems: "Corbin pho" and "Stephanie widdled wacks" are garbled names; the company is spelled Eleonora, Ellenor and Eleanor in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Biopsychosocial model of addiction (biological, psychological, social) [08:43], [09:13].
- Evidence-based treatment: medication, therapy, recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Claims analytics to flag undiagnosed patients, including multiple prescribers and emergency room visits [44:47].
- Harm reduction, including supervised injection sites and naloxone [49:18], [51:19].
- Moulton's three-part legislative plan: annual check-ups for veterans and service members, extension to high schoolers, and a national hotline [22:42], [23:43].

## Limits and open questions

- Most claims are personal experience, opinion or policy advocacy; no study is cited by name.
- The 51 and 70 percent figures for former NFL players are not sourced in the talk.
- Corbin leads a treatment company, and Moulton is a legislator promoting his own bills; both have an institutional stake.
- Panelists disagree on blame (Moulton and Leaf stress accountability; Corbin points to prescribing). Not resolved.
- Leaf's statement that studies prove injection sites make communities safer is not backed by named studies [51:50].
- A mid-talk comment that "if it wasn't opioids it would be meth" is speculation [36:02].
- Several numbers may be garbled in the captions (see above).

## Q&A

- Is every addiction unhealthy, such as addiction to competition or work? Panelists say the difference lies in consequences, with positive addictions rewarded by society [46:17].
- Is the problem international? Yes; other countries handle mental health with less stigma and more harm reduction [48:48].
- What are supervised injection sites? A safe place for people not yet willing to seek help; defended as lowering deaths and exposing people to treatment [49:48], [51:19].
- What about psychedelics for post-traumatic stress? Moulton says data should lead; Leaf defers to clinicians; Corbin says approaches need personalizing [53:24], [54:26], [55:27].

## Summary

A moderator, a former NFL quarterback turned analyst, a congressman who is a Marine veteran, and the head of an addiction treatment company discuss opioids in sports and in society. They argue that addiction is a chronic condition often tied to untreated trauma, depression or anxiety, that short rehab stays have little evidence behind them, and that stigma keeps athletes and veterans from asking for help. They disagree in part on blame: one panelist stresses personal responsibility, another says prescribing played a role. The panel closes on harm reduction and on testing treatments through data. It is a personal and policy discussion, with few worked analytics.

## Key claims

- Overdose deaths have risen steadily, and the moderator frames them through her own brother's death [01:00], [02:03].
- Addiction should be treated as a chronic condition with relapse and genetic risk, not as a one-time 28-day event [08:10].
- Substance use often sits on top of another psychiatric condition, with depression, anxiety and trauma the most common [08:43].
- Risk comes from three sources: biology, life experience such as trauma, and access to the substance [09:13].
- Veterans meet both trauma and painkillers, which raises overdose risk [09:44].
- Leaf says an opioid given for injury pain became his way of coping with emotional pain, and that competition was his first dependence [13:20].
- Leaf says locker-room culture offered no example of a man asking for help [13:51].
- Moulton says veterans seeking therapy are often sent home with a prescription because the VA lacks therapists [11:47].
- The treatment field is called a cottage industry built on individual recovery stories rather than evidence [16:27].
- Corbin says 28-day luxury rehab has nothing in evidence behind it [16:58].
- The evidence-based model is medication, therapy for co-occurring conditions, and recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Moulton proposes routine mental health check-ups, first for the military and then for high schoolers, and a three-digit hotline [22:42], [23:43].
- Corbin says payment models reward service volume, not outcomes, which favors repeated short stays [29:20], [29:54].
- Corbin says pharmaceutical companies deserve some blame but blaming the substance undercuts the disease model [35:00]. Moulton says fentanyl from China is a policy problem but that sufferers must take personal responsibility [37:05]. Corbin replies that responsibility is hard when a doctor prescribed the drug [37:35].
- Leaf says dosing beyond the prescription may be the first symptom of trouble [39:09].
- Telling personal stories reduces stigma and lets others come forward [41:13], [43:45].
- Corbin says analytics can flag people who have not been diagnosed, such as those seeking drugs across several providers [44:47].
- Harm reduction means accepting patients as they arrive, and supervised injection sites and naloxone access are defended as life-saving [49:18], [51:19], [51:50].
- Moulton supports studying cannabis and psychedelics for post-traumatic stress and says the data should decide [54:26], [54:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Opioid overdose deaths since 1999: 400,000 (moderator) [01:00].
- Drug overdose deaths in 2017: 72,000, compared to the size of an NFL stadium, with 50,000 opioid related [01:00], [01:31].
- Leaf's brother's addiction reached $4,000 a month before a switch to heroin; he died in 2015 at 30 [02:03]. (The moderator says her own brother.)
- Veterans are twice as likely as non-veterans to die of an opioid overdose (Moulton) [04:34].
- Leaf describes a $31 million opportunity at the draft, second overall [06:04].
- 80 percent of people with a substance use disorder have an underlying co-occurring psychiatric condition (Corbin) [08:43].
- 28-day rehab: described as having single-digit success rates; a Malibu stay cited at $45,000 for 30 days [16:58].
- Relapse risk falls after one year in recovery and becomes that of the general public after five years [18:01].
- 51 percent of former NFL players said they used opioids, and 70 percent of those said they abused them (Corbin) [25:15].
- Chinese supply: the claim is that China provides 90 percent of US fentanyl, and a 2014 agreement was followed by US Customs stopping 1207 shipments. The Chinese customs figure in the sentence is cut off in the captions [36:33], [37:05].
- 20 million people diagnosed with a substance use disorder, with an 80 percent treatment gap, meaning 20 percent seek treatment [44:16], [44:47].
- Treatment cost: several years in outpatient care at Corbin's company costs about the same as one month of resort rehab [29:54].
- Leaf: nearly eight years sober [26:45]; stayed 90 days at rehab while three years sober [31:26]; same therapist five years [32:57].
- Moulton: hotline number is "nine eight eight" [23:43].
- Caption problems: "Corbin pho" and "Stephanie widdled wacks" are garbled names; the company is spelled Eleonora, Ellenor and Eleanor in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Biopsychosocial model of addiction (biological, psychological, social) [08:43], [09:13].
- Evidence-based treatment: medication, therapy, recovery services [17:30], [18:01].
- Claims analytics to flag undiagnosed patients, including multiple prescribers and emergency room visits [44:47].
- Harm reduction, including supervised injection sites and naloxone [49:18], [51:19].
- Moulton's three-part legislative plan: annual check-ups for veterans and service members, extension to high schoolers, and a national hotline [22:42], [23:43].

## Limits and open questions

- Most claims are personal experience, opinion or policy advocacy; no study is cited by name.
- The 51 and 70 percent figures for former NFL players are not sourced in the talk.
- Corbin leads a treatment company, and Moulton is a legislator promoting his own bills; both have an institutional stake.
- Panelists disagree on blame (Moulton and Leaf stress accountability; Corbin points to prescribing). Not resolved.
- Leaf's statement that studies prove injection sites make communities safer is not backed by named studies [51:50].
- A mid-talk comment that "if it wasn't opioids it would be meth" is speculation [36:02].
- Several numbers may be garbled in the captions (see above).

## Q&A

- Is every addiction unhealthy, such as addiction to competition or work? Panelists say the difference lies in consequences, with positive addictions rewarded by society [46:17].
- Is the problem international? Yes; other countries handle mental health with less stigma and more harm reduction [48:48].
- What are supervised injection sites? A safe place for people not yet willing to seek help; defended as lowering deaths and exposing people to treatment [49:48], [51:19].
- What about psychedelics for post-traumatic stress? Moulton says data should lead; Leaf defers to clinicians; Corbin says approaches need personalizing [53:24], [54:26], [55:27].

video_id: _rPWvkmRvRY
title: "SSAC20: Basketball Analytics: Nothin’ but Net...Rating"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Cohen (moderator), Bob (caption spelling "vulgaris"), Mike (caption spelling "Zarin"), Tom Thibodeau, Zach Lowe]
topics: [basketball, front-office, sports-science, decision-making]
confidence: supported

## Summary

A five-person NBA panel (two team analytics executives, a former head coach, a writer, and a moderator) discusses how the three-point shot has changed the game and how teams mix data with scouting. They agree three-point volume may keep growing but say playoff success needs variety in the offense. They disagree on how far to trust catch-all defensive numbers versus watching film, and they admit load management for the playoffs is unsettled, with wearables limited by the players' union agreement and by player trust. The panel ends with rule changes and a stated view that team data work is mostly about context and role.

## Key claims

- Three-point volume has not stopped growing, and teams have different ways of getting them [01:30], [02:00].
- One executive thinks diminishing returns would begin around 60 to 65 percent of shots from three, and most teams are far below that [04:01].
- Thibodeau says shot value matters most and that being fouled on a three has the highest value [05:34].
- Thibodeau says winning a playoff series needs offensive variety, because opponents can prepare for one pattern [06:35], [07:07].
- A panelist says shot profiles and efficiency in the playoffs look similar to the regular season, and that the best players matter most in the playoffs [22:02], [23:03].
- Thibodeau says rule changes have favored offense and officials should clean up traveling and carrying [10:41], [11:11].
- The guests lean differently on evaluation: one executive prefers large samples and data, another wants to see a player live once, and Thibodeau uses eyes, ears and numbers together [12:46], [14:20], [16:23].
- An executive says an archived numbers approach lets a team review its misses, while some organizations do not hold scouts accountable for predictions [16:53].
- Lowe says he trusts no catch-all individual defense number over his eyes; an executive replies that those numbers are contextual but beat the average analyst [17:23], [18:25].
- Non-numeric information such as work habits can be turned into usable ratings [38:54].
- A panelist says prospects may simply tell a team what it wants to hear on personality surveys [39:55].
- Thibodeau says steals and rebounding rate show how a player anticipates but that how he sees the game needs film [41:57], [42:28].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: 9rh-AScDN8k
title: "SSAC20: Defending the Pass: Using Player Tracking Data to Gain New Insights"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Brian McDonald (moderator), Kevin Beers (caption spelling), Evan Kaplan, Brian Burke (caption spelling; introduced as "Bryan Burk Seger"), Dominique Foxworth]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

An ESPN-hosted panel shows how a data analyst and a former cornerback work together on tracking data, then thinks aloud about how to build an individual metric for pass defenders. They stress that metrics need film knowledge and that the work is a cycle of question, data, model and plain-language story. The panel walks through press coverage, coverage responsibility (with an audience poll) and anticipation, and names what tracking data cannot capture. No finished defender metric is presented, and the panel says it is brainstorming. They close with questions on the Ravens' quarterback and other industries.

## Key claims

- Before tracking data, defensive back analysis was hard because play-by-play data covers few defenders and broadcast video often omits them [01:34].
- Using tracking data amounts to teaching a computer to watch film, which needs deep game knowledge (Burke) [05:12], [05:44].
- A former player says the software does what he did when he watched film but faster and at scale [07:48], [53:42].
- A former front office researcher says the goal is a partnership in which the analyst learns enough football to work alone [11:26], [11:56].
- Kaplan describes three steps: give feedback on metric names, find stories in current league events, and meet analysts to match data with film [12:26], [13:26].
- Kaplan says coverage metrics let a TV analyst confirm that a team used man coverage on every drop back in one half of a championship game [13:57], [14:27].
- The moderator frames the process as words into numbers into words, a data science cycle with collaboration at each step [17:00], [17:30].
- For press coverage, Foxworth stresses leverage, keeping a receiver at the line, and reputation affecting where the quarterback throws [19:04], [21:36].
- Burke says the tracking provider supplies clean data with tagged snap and release events [22:39], [23:10].
- Alignment at the snap does not prove press, since bail technique can start close to the line [23:41], [24:11].
- Tracking data lacks some body detail such as hip position, and a film expert will be richer, but the data applies one rule set to every player at scale [24:42], [25:13].
- Candidate press measures: how far a receiver is moved off the expected route and how long to get three yards downfield [25:45]; distance plus velocity, since a defender can be close and losing [26:15].
- Re-routing a receiver at the line buys safeties time in zone coverage [27:47].
- Outside observers do not know the call, so some mistakes cannot be assigned [28:17], [28:49].
- For responsibility, steps are coverage identification, defender roles, route identification, then comparing where the defender should be to where he was [35:06], [35:38], [36:08].
- Foxworth says a defender is graded at fault in the shown clip, even if the play might have been completed regardless [38:10].
- For anticipation, one idea is to group plays with similar concepts and coverages and compare a defender's path to the average [41:47], [42:19]. The baseline is hard to establish [43:21].
- Anticipation may also be the precursor to reaction time, such as when a safety breaks on the ball [44:54].
- Pass denial is hard to see in statistics; a defender who prevents a throw leaves no box-score trace [46:55], [47:25].
- Ravens opponents are seen using single-high man or cover three coverages more than other teams, and the quarterback's scrambles averaged high yards against man [48:57], [49:30], [50:30].
- Football is called harder to analyze than baseball because player interactions are tangled, and tracking data helps isolate one player [52:05].

## Numbers and definitions

- Clip 3.9 seconds: a quarterback holds the ball because he beats a blitzer [03:08].
- 500 double-teams: a pass rusher doubled more than 500 times since the start of the previous season [08:19].
- 17.6 percent: catch chance given on one play by next-gen stats [08:52]; expected completion percentage of 63 percent, and plus 10 over expected [08:52], [09:22].
- 84 percent catch rate, 15 percent above expectation [09:22]; 40 percent catch probability on one throw [09:22].
- 2.2 seconds to throw, and under 2.5 seconds as the league average time [09:52].
- Pass rush win rate: beating a blocker within 2.5 seconds [10:54].
- Man coverage on 100 percent of drop backs in the first half of a 2018 conference championship game, the only team to do so in a half all season [13:57], [14:27].
- Poll on responsibility: 30 percent chose number 54, 46 percent chose number 20, 24 percent chose number 27 [33:02], [33:32].
- About 13 yards per scramble when defenses played man at one point in the season [50:30].
- Press coverage is defined for the exercise by proximity to the line at and just after the snap [23:41], [24:11].
- Clip numbers come from short TV narration, so units and exact subjects may be garbled in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Next-gen stats and Zebra as tracking providers [22:39].
- Coverage classification, route classification, and route tree labels [12:26], [35:06].
- Pass rush win rate and double-team rate [10:54].
- Calling the model's role definitions per defender (hook, flat, deep thirds) in cover three [35:06].
- Average-player comparison for anticipation [41:47].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel produces no validated metric and says it is hypothesizing.
- Tracking data lacks hip position, and the call or assignment is unknown to outsiders [24:42], [28:17].
- The poll vote is not a ground truth, and Foxworth's judgement on one play is one expert's view.
- The panelists work at or came from ESPN or the NFL; ESPN products are the subject of the opening clips.
- Establishing the average baseline for anticipation is described as hard [43:21].
- Caption problems: "Bryan Burk Seger," "Mathieu" spelled "Matthew," and the opening video failed to play on the first attempt [03:39].

## Q&A

- How do players like Lamar Jackson change strategy? Defenses play more predictable coverage, and scramble results can be separated by coverage [48:57], [50:30].
- Are other industries faster to adopt analytics? Football is hard because of interacting players; firms face the same problem isolating employees but segment customers well [51:32], [53:06].
- Would this data have helped Foxworth as a player? Yes, he did by hand what the data does across thousands of plays [53:42].

---
type: video-summary
video_id: 9rh-AScDN8k
title: "SSAC20: Defending the Pass: Using Player Tracking Data to Gain New Insights"
event: SSAC20 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Brian McDonald (moderator), Kevin Beers (caption spelling), Evan Kaplan, Brian Burke (caption spelling; introduced as "Bryan Burk Seger"), Dominique Foxworth]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

An ESPN-hosted panel shows how a data analyst and a former cornerback work together on tracking data, then thinks aloud about how to build an individual metric for pass defenders. They stress that metrics need film knowledge and that the work is a cycle of question, data, model and plain-language story. The panel walks through press coverage, coverage responsibility (with an audience poll) and anticipation, and names what tracking data cannot capture. No finished defender metric is presented, and the panel says it is brainstorming. They close with questions on the Ravens' quarterback and other industries.

## Key claims

- Before tracking data, defensive back analysis was hard because play-by-play data covers few defenders and broadcast video often omits them [01:34].
- Using tracking data amounts to teaching a computer to watch film, which needs deep game knowledge (Burke) [05:12], [05:44].
- A former player says the software does what he did when he watched film but faster and at scale [07:48], [53:42].
- A former front office researcher says the goal is a partnership in which the analyst learns enough football to work alone [11:26], [11:56].
- Kaplan describes three steps: give feedback on metric names, find stories in current league events, and meet analysts to match data with film [12:26], [13:26].
- Kaplan says coverage metrics let a TV analyst confirm that a team used man coverage on every drop back in one half of a championship game [13:57], [14:27].
- The moderator frames the process as words into numbers into words, a data science cycle with collaboration at each step [17:00], [17:30].
- For press coverage, Foxworth stresses leverage, keeping a receiver at the line, and reputation affecting where the quarterback throws [19:04], [21:36].
- Burke says the tracking provider supplies clean data with tagged snap and release events [22:39], [23:10].
- Alignment at the snap does not prove press, since bail technique can start close to the line [23:41], [24:11].
- Tracking data lacks some body detail such as hip position, and a film expert will be richer, but the data applies one rule set to every player at scale [24:42], [25:13].
- Candidate press measures: how far a receiver is moved off the expected route and how long to get three yards downfield [25:45]; distance plus velocity, since a defender can be close and losing [26:15].
- Re-routing a receiver at the line buys safeties time in zone coverage [27:47].
- Outside observers do not know the call, so some mistakes cannot be assigned [28:17], [28:49].
- For responsibility, steps are coverage identification, defender roles, route identification, then comparing where the defender should be to where he was [35:06], [35:38], [36:08].
- Foxworth says a defender is graded at fault in the shown clip, even if the play might have been completed regardless [38:10].
- For anticipation, one idea is to group plays with similar concepts and coverages and compare a defender's path to the average [41:47], [42:19]. The baseline is hard to establish [43:21].
- Anticipation may also be the precursor to reaction time, such as when a safety breaks on the ball [44:54].
- Pass denial is hard to see in statistics; a defender who prevents a throw leaves no box-score trace [46:55], [47:25].
- Ravens opponents are seen using single-high man or cover three coverages more than other teams, and the quarterback's scrambles averaged high yards against man [48:57], [49:30], [50:30].
- Football is called harder to analyze than baseball because player interactions are tangled, and tracking data helps isolate one player [52:05].

## Numbers and definitions

- Clip 3.9 seconds: a quarterback holds the ball because he beats a blitzer [03:08].
- 500 double-teams: a pass rusher doubled more than 500 times since the start of the previous season [08:19].
- 17.6 percent: catch chance given on one play by next-gen stats [08:52]; expected completion percentage of 63 percent, and plus 10 over expected [08:52], [09:22].
- 84 percent catch rate, 15 percent above expectation [09:22]; 40 percent catch probability on one throw [09:22].
- 2.2 seconds to throw, and under 2.5 seconds as the league average time [09:52].
- Pass rush win rate: beating a blocker within 2.5 seconds [10:54].
- Man coverage on 100 percent of drop backs in the first half of a 2018 conference championship game, the only team to do so in a half all season [13:57], [14:27].
- Poll on responsibility: 30 percent chose number 54, 46 percent chose number 20, 24 percent chose number 27 [33:02], [33:32].
- About 13 yards per scramble when defenses played man at one point in the season [50:30].
- Press coverage is defined for the exercise by proximity to the line at and just after the snap [23:41], [24:11].
- Clip numbers come from short TV narration, so units and exact subjects may be garbled in captions.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Next-gen stats and Zebra as tracking providers [22:39].
- Coverage classification, route classification, and route tree labels [12:26], [35:06].
- Pass rush win rate and double-team rate [10:54].
- Calling the model's role definitions per defender (hook, flat, deep thirds) in cover three [35:06].
- Average-player comparison for anticipation [41:47].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel produces no validated metric and says it is hypothesizing.
- Tracking data lacks hip position, and the call or assignment is unknown to outsiders [24:42], [28:17].
- The poll vote is not a ground truth, and Foxworth's judgement on one play is one expert's view.
- The panelists work at or came from ESPN or the NFL; ESPN products are the subject of the opening clips.
- Establishing the average baseline for anticipation is described as hard [43:21].
- Caption problems: "Bryan Burk Seger," "Mathieu" spelled "Matthew," and the opening video failed to play on the first attempt [03:39].

- Are other industries faster to adopt analytics? Football is hard because of interacting players; firms face the same problem isolating employees but segment customers well [51:32], [53:06].

title: "SSAC19: DeepQB Deep Learning with Player Tracking to Quantify Quarterback Decision Makin Performance"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

topics: [american-football, decision-making, sports-science]

## Summary

Brian Burke presents DeepQB, a neural network applied to NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data, built to measure quarterback decision-making apart from teammates and opponents. It predicts which of five eligible receivers the passer will target, the expected yardage, and whether the pass is completed, incomplete or intercepted. He argues earlier uses of tracking data amounted to a "fancy radar gun" [02:08]. The model picks the right target about 60 percent of the time, and he uses the gap between expected and observed yards per attempt as a performance measure. A fourth, quarterback-specific variant did not work well. He calls the work a proof of concept [23:32].

## Key claims

- Quarterback performance is hard to project, which he attributes to the position being cognitive and decision-driven [00:33].
- His past as a Navy fighter pilot shaped his interest in decisions under time pressure; he says a pilot has about three seconds and a quarterback about two and a half [01:38].
- Earlier tracking-data applications were limited to maximum speed and total distance [02:08].
- DeepQB uses a feed-forward neural network, described as a fairly standard deep learning type, with the same architecture reused for four variants [04:12].
- The model predicts the targeted receiver correctly about 60 percent of the time, which he frames as triple a one-in-five chance baseline [07:48].
- Completion rate is higher when the passer throws to the model's recommended receiver than when he does not [08:50].
- Proximity of a defender alone does not tell whether a receiver is targeted; one example showed a covered receiver the model and quarterback both chose [11:23].
- Yards above expectation can be credited to the quarterback as isolated performance [12:23].
- Rookies appear low on production relative to expectation and highly predictable [14:05].
- Agreement with the model shows a slight negative correlation with production, which he did not expect and attributes to selection bias, not tested in the talk [14:38].
- Aggregated decision-making explained little of interception differences; he judged most of one high-interception passer's rate came from inaccurate throws rather than poor decisions [17:43].
- The quarterback-specific variant, built with transfer learning, did not work as hoped [19:51].
- He says the approach can be run in reverse, aggregating by receiving corps or secondary [20:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- More than 45,000 targeted passes; training, validation and test sets drawn from the 2016 through 2018 seasons, test set is 2018 through week 12 [04:43], [05:13].
- Tracking data supplies position, speed, direction, acceleration and orientation, available about 10 seconds after a play [05:44].
- Chance baseline for target selection: one in five, or 20 percent; model accuracy about 60 percent [07:48].
- Completion percentage 74 percent when the quarterback throws to the recommended receiver, 55 percent otherwise, a factor of 1.4 [08:50].
- Example target probabilities: 80 percent [09:50], 15 percent [10:21], 8 percent and 77 percent [10:52].
- Goff example: model-expected 7.8 yards per attempt, actual 9.9 on targeted passes, difference +2.1 [12:54].
- Average predicted completion probability 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions [15:40].
- Yards per attempt above expected: the talk reports it for the top five and bottom five 2018 quarterbacks [12:54].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Feed-forward neural network with four variants: receiver target probability, expected yards, outcome probability, and a quarterback-tailored version of the first [04:43].
- Feature vector arranged by five eligible receivers: absolute and relative positions, velocities, orientations, receiver type, the nearest two defenders, game state, down, distance, yard line, play action, a binary duress flag, and quarterback velocity at release [06:15], [06:46].
- Mirror-image augmentation of each play to teach symmetry; he notes handedness is a flaw [07:16].
- Expected yards computed two ways: whole play configuration, or assuming each receiver is the target [12:23].
- Transfer learning: train all layers on all quarterbacks, freeze base layers, retrain on one quarterback [18:50].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker calls this a proof of concept built on choices made to get a result [23:32].
- Model agreement correlated slightly negatively with production; the selection-bias explanation is offered without a test [14:38].
- The quarterback-specific variant gave odd similarity results, with a best performer least similar to others; his explanation involves running back targets and is unverified [19:51].
- Not isolated from receivers or scheme [20:52]; no hands, height or vertical information [22:01].
- Class imbalance for interceptions was not corrected [24:36].
- Results are from one test period, and 60 percent accuracy is his own framing of what counts as good [07:48].

## Q&A

- Asked whether he had reviewed results with quarterbacks: answer is garbled in captions [22:01].
- Asked about receiver quality: largely captured through velocity and separation, but hands and height are not [22:01].
- Asked about snapshots versus progressions: model can assume release at any time after the snap to find open receivers a quarterback missed [23:02].
- Asked about linemen and pressure: he says the project was a proof of concept and later work adds alignments and passing lanes [24:02].
- Asked about class imbalance: he did not rebalance interceptions because of time [24:36].

## Summary

Benjamin Foster, a PhD student in environmental sciences and engineering, presents a method for valuing NBA draft picks that carry protections, conditions that let a trading team keep a pick if it falls in a protected range. He treats a protected pick like a financial option and prices it in basketball terms (five-year win shares), not money. The system simulates team standings, builds outcome distributions by pick position, runs a Monte Carlo simulation, and adjusts for market risk with the Wang transform. A worked example on one traded pick shows protections removing about half its value. The goal is to help teams choose protections.

## Key claims

- Draft picks are trade assets, and protections change the distribution of outcomes the receiving team gets [03:36].
- Millions of protection schemes are possible, so one base pick can have millions of trade values [04:07].
- The NBA trade market is illiquid, and protections can help teams assemble trades they otherwise could not [04:37], [05:07].
- Traded protections cluster at top five, top 10 and top 14, which the authors read as psychological anchors on round numbers [05:38], [06:08].
- Protected picks parallel financial options, where volatility of the underlying value matters [07:40].
- Risk preference differs by pick: the first pick is priced risk-seeking, and picks 25 and 30 risk-averse [14:48].
- In the worked example, protections removed about half the value of the base pick [16:20].
- The model's findings lined up with what the Suns general manager said at the time of the trade, per the speaker [16:51], [17:22].
- Applications named: reviewing past trades, private negotiation of protections, possibly spotting mispriced assets, and pricing other assets such as Bird rights [20:25], [20:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Player value metric: win shares summed over a player's first five years [11:45].
- Team standings simulated 10,000 times for roughly 20 remaining games [09:40]; Monte Carlo simulation also run 10,000 times [11:14].
- Seven asset classes from K-means clustering of pick outcome distributions [14:18].
- One bar in the output: a 16.8 percent chance of a player producing between 17 and a half and 21 and a half win shares [11:45], [12:16].
- Priced values: 43.1 win shares per five years unprotected, 21.0 protected [15:49]. Implied annual 8.6 unprotected, compared to a named player's 2018 season [15:49].
- Protections subtracted about 51 percent of the base pick's value [16:20].
- A 78 percent chance the pick would be protected in the first year [16:51].
- Next-year outcome range for the fourth-worst team: first worst to 24th worst, median eight [17:22].
- Protected pick priced at 4.2 (annual win shares, as spoken), against 4.5 for the player received in the prior year [17:52]. Caption note: 4.2 matches 21.0 divided by five; the unit is not stated in the captions.
- Market price of risk (gamma) is the single Wang-transform assumption, read generally as the market's risk preference [13:47], [14:18].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Three principles: characterize volatility of the underlying asset, assess contractual conditions, account for market risk [08:40].
- Module one: Elo-based season simulation giving a probability distribution of finishing position [09:10].
- Module two: cumulative distributions of win shares by pick position from historical Basketball-Reference data, for first-round picks [10:42].
- Monte Carlo combining lottery probabilities and protection schemes [11:14].
- Wang transform, with market price of risk calibrated on pick-for-pick trades and interpolated where needed [13:17], [14:48].

## Limits and open questions

- Calibration of risk parameters rests on few pick-for-pick trades; the speaker says more work is needed [14:48].
- Simulation does not account for player movement, and the work was done on personal computers with limited time [19:23].
- The example comparison omits team-building considerations such as an expiring contract [18:22].
- Time discounting and option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled [22:26].
- Win shares was chosen for simplicity; other metrics could be swapped in [10:11].
- The explanation for round-number clustering is a hypothesis [06:08].

## Q&A

- Asked about discounting for player performance and the future option value of rolling over picks: the speaker said time considerations are hard to frame in a market sense and are not explicitly handled [22:26].</result>

---
type: video-summary
video_id: SIn6IyYQEVI
title: "SSAC19: Analytics for the Front Office: Valuing Protections on NBA Draft Picks"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Benjamin Foster; Michael Bins (co-author, caption spelling); Jonah (host)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Benjamin Foster, a PhD student in environmental sciences and engineering, presents a method for valuing NBA draft picks that carry protections, conditions that let a trading team keep a pick if it falls in a protected range. He treats a protected pick like a financial option and prices it in basketball terms (five-year win shares), not money. The system simulates team standings, builds outcome distributions by pick position, runs a Monte Carlo simulation, and adjusts for market risk with the Wang transform. A worked example on one traded pick shows protections removing about half its value. The goal is to help teams choose protections.

## Key claims

- Draft picks are trade assets, and protections change the distribution of outcomes the receiving team gets [03:36].
- Millions of protection schemes are possible, so one base pick can have millions of trade values [04:07].
- The NBA trade market is illiquid, and protections can help teams assemble trades they otherwise could not [04:37], [05:07].
- Traded protections cluster at top five, top 10 and top 14, which the authors read as psychological anchors on round numbers [05:38], [06:08].
- Protected picks parallel financial options, where volatility of the underlying value matters [07:40].
- Risk preference differs by pick: the first pick is priced risk-seeking, and picks 25 and 30 risk-averse [14:48].
- In the worked example, protections removed about half the value of the base pick [16:20].
- The model's findings lined up with what the Suns general manager said at the time of the trade, per the speaker [16:51], [17:22].
- Applications named: reviewing past trades, private negotiation of protections, possibly spotting mispriced assets, and pricing other assets such as Bird rights [20:25], [20:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Player value metric: win shares summed over a player's first five years [11:45].
- Team standings simulated 10,000 times for roughly 20 remaining games [09:40]; Monte Carlo simulation also run 10,000 times [11:14].
- Seven asset classes from K-means clustering of pick outcome distributions [14:18].
- One bar in the output: a 16.8 percent chance of a player producing between 17 and a half and 21 and a half win shares [11:45], [12:16].
- Priced values: 43.1 win shares per five years unprotected, 21.0 protected [15:49]. Implied annual 8.6 unprotected, compared to a named player's 2018 season [15:49].
- Protections subtracted about 51 percent of the base pick's value [16:20].
- A 78 percent chance the pick would be protected in the first year [16:51].
- Next-year outcome range for the fourth-worst team: first worst to 24th worst, median eight [17:22].
- Protected pick priced at 4.2 (annual win shares, as spoken), against 4.5 for the player received in the prior year [17:52]. Caption note: 4.2 matches 21.0 divided by five; the unit is not stated in the captions.
- Market price of risk (gamma) is the single Wang-transform assumption, read generally as the market's risk preference [13:47], [14:18].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Three principles: characterize volatility of the underlying asset, assess contractual conditions, account for market risk [08:40].
- Module one: Elo-based season simulation giving a probability distribution of finishing position [09:10].
- Module two: cumulative distributions of win shares by pick position from historical Basketball-Reference data, for first-round picks [10:42].
- Monte Carlo combining lottery probabilities and protection schemes [11:14].
- Wang transform, with market price of risk calibrated on pick-for-pick trades and interpolated where needed [13:17], [14:48].

## Limits and open questions

- Calibration of risk parameters rests on few pick-for-pick trades; the speaker says more work is needed [14:48].
- Simulation does not account for player movement, and the work was done on personal computers with limited time [19:23].
- The example comparison omits team-building considerations such as an expiring contract [18:22].
- Time discounting and option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled [22:26].
- Win shares was chosen for simplicity; other metrics could be swapped in [10:11].
- The explanation for round-number clustering is a hypothesis [06:08].

## Q&A

- Asked about discounting for player performance and the future option value of rolling over picks: the speaker said time considerations are hard to frame in a market sense and are not explicitly handled [22:26].

## Summary

A sleep physician from the Henry Ford sleep disorder center argues that circadian timing is an under-used performance lever. # SSAC19: Built to Outlast: Youth Athlete Development for Performance and Durability

## Summary

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. She describes adolescence as a period of peak growth and change, falling and unequal sports participation, and a booming youth sports market that pushes early specialization, overload and under-built movement foundations. Her recommendation is "smart specialization": multi-sport, athlete-centered, skill-driven activity with foundational strength and movement first. The talk is a conceptual argument with few data points, and the complex-systems framework is her stated hypothesis.

## Key claims

- Injury and performance states lie on the same health continuum, and the goal is to keep athletes on the healthy, adaptive side [00:35] [01:39] [02:09].
- Health should be assessed across four domains: physiologic, biomechanic, behavioral and mental, and environmental [02:09].
- The transition into adolescence brings peak growth velocity and major brain and social change, so health determinants become performance determinants [02:42] [03:12] [03:45].
- Training load is system stress, and the aim is to raise capacity for it; youth athletes are often overloaded without enough recovery, which erodes capacity [04:15] [04:46] [05:17].
- Sports participation overall is falling, and the speaker ties access to socioeconomic status: lower-status athletes face sedentary-behavior risk, higher-status athletes face early specialization and injury risk [05:48] [06:18] [06:48].
- Youth athletes are over-scheduled, over-coached and spend less time on foundational strength and movement skills, which the speaker links to injury and attrition [08:22] [08:53] [09:26].
- Athletes who reach elite levels tend to specialize later, and highly specialized high school athletes are at higher injury risk [09:56]. Among NBA players, multi-sport athletes tended to miss fewer games, last longer and be less likely to be injured [10:26].
- The American development model has five stages; stage one, discover, learn and play, runs from age zero to twelve [10:57] [11:27].
- Studying loading, recovery and fueling one factor at a time misses their interactions; performance is a pattern emerging from relationships among determinants, whose influence changes over time [14:40] [16:13] [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].
- Because of this, models should be continuously reassessed, and the speaker holds that this approach yields more predictable outcomes [18:45] [19:48].
- Recommended approach is smart specialization: structured, supervised, multi-sport, athlete-centered, readiness- and skill-focused activity [20:48]. Practical steps include calibrating to physiologic and cognitive stage, mixing quantitative and "fuzzy" data, sport sampling, athlete engagement, and linking performance goals to health goals [21:18] [21:48].
- Future directions: cluster sports by shared physical demands, refine the language of training load, find protective or enhancing sport clusters, and focus on dissemination [22:18] [22:49].

## Numbers and definitions

- Youth sports market: twenty-two billion dollars worldwide, projected near sixty billion by 2024 [07:51].
- Stage one of the development model: ages 0 to 12; the model's activities are shown across ages 0 to 20 [11:27] [11:57].
- "Fuzzy data": elements that cannot easily be quantified but influence other parts of the system [16:44].
- Complex system: multifactorial web of related determinants that is iterative, recursive, self-organizing, decentralized and adaptive [16:44] [17:15].
- Training load: defined as system stress [04:15].
- Participation decline and the market projection are attributed to an Aspen Institute report and, for the market, no named source [05:48] [07:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Performance-health-disease continuum (credited to Dr. Fran O'Connor, military sports medicine) [01:39].
- Four-domain health assessment [02:09].
- Load and recovery continuum [04:46].
- American development model, five stages [10:57].
- Complex-systems approach with "fuzzy data" [16:44].
- Smart specialization and sport sampling (John O'Sullivan, Changing the Game Project, is cited on athlete engagement) [21:18] [21:48].
- Youth basketball is named as an example of a sport adopting this approach, with lacrosse and tennis also mentioned; another speaker ("Dr. D Fury", caption spelling) is referenced [21:48] [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost no sample sizes or effect sizes are given; the specialization and NBA findings are stated briefly without sources.
- The complex-systems model is described as the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15] and she says it is unclear whether 10,000 hours, intrinsic ability or load quality drives elite performance [14:40].
- The recommendation to play multiple sports collides with ranking and selection of ten-year-olds, which the speaker names but does not resolve [12:59].
- Population-level youth framing; no measures or thresholds for individual athletes are offered.
- Her view as a sports medicine physician and the speaker's institutional position shape the injury emphasis.

## Q&A

- How is recovery determined? Athlete-specific, using readiness, physical status, soreness and pain, on a scale of days for games and varying by activity [23:20] [23:51] [24:21].
- What about aesthetic sports such as dance, where early specialization is needed? Balance early specialization for physical parameters with strength and aerobic work, which has not been shown to harm those pursuits; understand the athlete's goals and find lower-stress activities [24:21] [24:51] [25:22] [25:52].
- Which injuries concern her most? ACL tears because of post-traumatic arthritis later; the most modifiable factor is healthy participation and giving athletes perspective on their lives beyond sport [26:33] [27:03] [27:37].

# SSAC19: Performance Optimization Strategies that Helped Win a Championship

## Summary

The West Coast Eagles' high performance manager describes four guiding principles and four "big rocks" that he credits with preparing the club for its 2018 Grand Final win. The principles are levels of perspective, the Hedgehog principle, start with why, and big rocks before small marginal gains. The big rocks are a strategic plan with objectives and key results, having the best players available, a high chronic running load, and training that matches or exceeds the hardest running in a game. The evidence is one club's data presented by its own staff, and the talk is sponsored by a data platform vendor.

## Key claims

- The speaker's department has medical, strength and conditioning, and sports science branches, with a research arm that always has a student working on a club question [05:39].
- Single events such as one hamstring or ACL are not worried over; a run of events signals the systems and structures are not working [06:40].
- Doing one or two things very well (the Hedgehog principle, from Jim Collins's work) and documenting the reason behind each plan (start with why) guide decisions [07:11] [07:41] [08:43].
- Teams are distracted by small one-percent gains; the big rocks should be placed first, and sand added after [09:14]. The example given is altitude camps for a small aerobic gain while kicking effectiveness stayed poor; he would rather fund kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Big rock one: a strategic plan following vision, mission, objectives, strategies and tactics, with key results per objective, which aligns all staff and is described as a competitive advantage [10:45] [11:15].
- Big rock two: get the best players on the field. The club's data led it to target nine or more of its top 10 players each week [12:18] [12:49].
- Few clubs can field their best players often; the club exceeded the league average for this last season [13:20] [13:52].
- A star young player's development is shown with official provider points to argue best players must play [14:23] [14:53].
- Big rock three: chronic load, defined as a rolling four-week average of work done; high chronic load is needed so that game spikes are not excessive [15:55] [16:26] [16:57].
- A mandated two-week Christmas break drops chronic load enough that returning to the same session lands in very high risk, so players must train in off periods [17:58] [18:30].
- Big rock four: hard running. Being fit does not mean being conditioned, so the club identified the hardest 15 minutes of running in five years and built drills matching or exceeding it, with a belief effect on players [19:02] [19:33] [20:06] [20:38].
- Message: align staff and coaches with one plan, put big rocks before one-percenters, ignore what other clubs or one paper do, and keep data simple but not simpler [21:39] [22:10].

## Numbers and definitions

- Collins study: over 1,400 companies, 11 that made the leap from good to great [07:11].
- Altitude trip: 200,000 to 300,000 dollars, 2 percent gain in aerobic capacity, about 50 percent kicking effectiveness; he would prefer to spend 400,000 dollars on two kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Example key result: no more than 15 percent of injuries should be recurrences of a previous injury [11:46].
- Top-10 availability objective: nine or more of the top 10 each week [12:18]. With all 10, win rate 80 percent (four of five); with nine, two-thirds [12:49].
- League average: 10 of 10 available only 15 percent of the time, nine of 10 about 25 percent (the caption mentions 18 as the competition's club count) [13:20].
- Club season: average 8.7 of 10 over 25 games, nine or more on 15 occasions [14:53]. Eight of 10 by season end and seven in the Grand Final [15:24].
- Chronic load: rolling four-week average [15:55]. Risk bands: green "sweet spot", pink two times risk, dark red three to five times risk [17:27].
- Weekly running about 30 km plus, tackled about 10 times (caption wording) [16:26].
- Midfielder covers 15 to 16 km in a game; hardest block was one midfielder running about 180 m per minute on a rolling five-minute average over the first 15 minutes [18:30] [19:33].
- Field 170 m long by 130 m wide [20:06].
- Drills at the hardest running duration: four occasions of 12 minutes or more, the captions for the 9-to-12 and 6-to-9 minute counts are garbled (eight times each is the likeliest reading) [21:08].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Levels of perspective (Daniel Kim) [06:09].
- Hedgehog principle (Jim Collins) [07:11].
- Start with why (Simon Sinek, caption spelling "Simon syic") [08:43].
- Big rocks metaphor [09:14].
- Vision, mission, objectives, strategies, tactics with key results [10:45].
- Official statistics provider player points (called "Champion data" in captions) [14:23].
- Rolling four-week chronic load from GPS with risk bands [16:26] [17:27].
- Rolling five-minute distance-per-minute to find the hardest 15 minutes [19:33].
- Data entered by players in a vendor platform (smartabase) and a vendor dashboard produced many of the shown graphs [22:42] [26:08].

## Limits and open questions

- One club, one season, with the club's own staff reporting outcomes; no control or comparison is shown for the load and drill choices.
- Source and sample for the risk bands (two times, three to five times) are not given.
- The speaker says other research links squad-wide injury count to performance but his club's data points to the best players mattering [12:18].

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
- Hard-interval average 179 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10 beats (caption wording unclear about which) [24:40].
- Subjective measure: a 1 to 10 satisfaction score for each workout [13:41].
- Context: program started in 2007 [05:05]; only one quarter of the studied masters athletes were risk-factor free [03:35].

## Methods and frameworks named

- A four-step sequence for suboptimal performance: medical evaluation, physiology evaluation, training evaluation, then planning, reassessment and implementation [07:07].
- Lab measures: max heart rate, aerobic efficiency (slope of oxygen against work), ventilatory threshold [12:11].
- Field data: 90 days of untouched training with a heart-rate monitor and a satisfaction rating [13:41].
- Training plan: individualize physiology, set a calendar working back from the goal event, assess the support structure (coach, nutrition, family), and run a longitudinal reassessment loop [16:46] [18:18].
- Sub-doldrum sessions are aerobic base, technique and active recovery. Supra-doldrum sessions include steady state, short and long intervals [17:17] [17:47].

## Limits and open questions

- One athlete, no control and no group data. Other changes during the eleven months are not shown.
- The speaker states his program has financial relationships with local and national groups (disclosed at [01:02]).
- Some figures are hard to verify due to captions (see Numbers).
- The oxygen-uptake threshold is described as "the single most important measurement" without data beyond the case.
- Heart rate variability skepticism is opinion, no data shown.
- Whether the same split works in team sports is not shown; he says the lab suits endurance components [26:27].

## Q&A

- Heart rate variability: promising in theory, many confounders, useful only as a backup to how the athlete feels [22:23] [22:54].
- Did the volume drop explain the gain: no, the key change was two clearly different kinds of days [23:33].
- Race-day intensity and the variance in hard sessions: hard sessions varied in effort to mimic race conditions, and he says most athletes improve when forced to rest after injury [24:10] [24:40].
- Power meters: pair power with heart rate, a rise in power at a given heart rate signals adaptation [25:26].
- Anaerobic power testing: Wingate is limited, better to use the sport's own exercises as benchmarks [25:56] [26:27].

A university football performance staff member uses Catapult data, sliced play by play in OpenField, to compare what offensive linemen do in games with what they do in practice. He argues that total player load looks alike for linemen and wide receivers, but the make-up differs: linemen have contacts, short work bouts and little high-speed running. - Training should start from game demands and work backwards [02:02].
- A published group study reported what linemen cover in a game, but the speaker argues it reports load, not the actual demands [03:04].

- A line coach ignored his report until the data were reframed in terms the coach cared about [04:04] [04:34].
- A gyroscope-based line metric detects when a lineman drops into a stance, then counts contacts and load per contact [05:38].
- Runs bring more contact and passes bring more force absorption [07:13].
- Practice was far below game intensity in contact load, even on the most intense practice day [08:16] [08:47].
