## Summary

A 76ers performance-research director argues that wearables can improve return-to-play by adding two things: a surrogate for the load an injured limb actually receives, and a profile of what a game will demand. He says the process matters more than the product. He links rehab load to tissue-loading research, uses shin-mounted accelerometers as a rough bone-load proxy, and uses game tracking and publicly available data to define the bursts and transitions an athlete must be ready for. He also says trust matters: athletes accept devices that give insight and reject ones that feel like policing. No outcome data are shown, so it is a conceptual framework.

## Key claims

- Return to play is a negotiation between agents (reinjury risk), front office and coaches (missed games), and the athlete [02:02] [02:33].
- Wearables fall into two types, what the athlete does and how the body responds, and both together are most informative [03:34].
- The market is unregulated, so data reliability must be checked or artifacts can mislead [04:05] [04:35].
- Devices used to police athletes get pushed back, while devices that provide insight are welcomed [05:06].
- Injury databases are contaminated because some absences are strategic, but are accurate enough for trends [06:06].
- Accurate diagnosis comes first, and no wearable fixes a misdiagnosis [06:37].
- Rehab should follow criterion-based progressions grounded in how tendons, ligaments and bone respond to load [07:08].
- Practice style can differ from game style, so a player who scrimmaged may still face an unaccustomed high-intensity exposure [07:38].
- Tissue has a loading sweet spot: too much stress stalls or breaks down, too little gives no collagen resynthesis [08:08] [08:38].
- A tibia-mounted accelerometer can give a rough low, moderate or severe bone-load proxy and a daily cumulative load, to be read alongside clinical signs [10:15] [10:45].
- If imaging shows poor response, loads can be stepped back to a previously tolerated level [11:48].
- Sensors can show ground-contact loading and left-right symmetry during water running and anti-gravity treadmill work [12:19] [12:49].
- Game demands should be profiled before clearing a player, and the fundamentals of basketball running distance were measured as early as 1931 [15:22] [15:53].
- Matching skill actions (catches, passes, shots, defensive slides, contacts) gives the athlete confidence and a way to communicate readiness to owners, general managers and coaches [20:27].
- Athletes in rehab welcome devices that help them build a bridge back, but are suspicious if data could leak into trades or sales [21:29] [22:01].

## Numbers and definitions

- About 1 in 4 NBA athletes will have an ankle injury that costs at least one game [05:36].
- A progression of six to eight weeks of monitored load, with no pain, swelling or stiffness, before the athlete returns to full practice [13:49].
- Loading range from under one times body weight to about seven and a half or eight times body weight per footstrike [13:19].
- 1931 study: a guard ran about two to two and a half miles, against public guesses of 5 to 10 [15:53]; running bursts of about two minutes at three to four miles per hour [15:53].
- 2016-17: a high-minute player averaged about 36 minutes, the 1931 player about 40, covering similar distance and speeds [16:24] [16:54].
- Tracking data: 1.2 to 1.5 million data points, mostly 6 to 10 mph, with some runs at 13 to 14 and up to 17 mph [17:25].
- Running bursts of 90 to 120 seconds are common, often under 30 seconds, sometimes three minutes without a break (the captions say three to four minutes) [17:55].
- Rehab profile targets: segments of three to six minutes, transitions every ten to twenty seconds, continuous play up to three minutes, six to eight full-court transitions [20:58].
- Caption trouble: company names, co-author first names and the cited bone study author are garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- A pathway: diagnosis, medical treatment, load-based rehab, demand-matched practice, game return [06:37] [07:08] [07:38].
- Mechanobiological approach: link sensor-derived load to tissue-loading research (rodent bone and ligament work cited) [09:42].
- Shank-mounted accelerometers, waterproofed sensors for pool and anti-gravity work, and RFID-style player tracking for games [10:15] [12:49] [14:20].
- Publicly available tracking data used to build speed distribution, burst length and recovery profiles [17:25] [17:55].
- Symmetry patterns by intensity band from a New Zealand pro team across a season [19:26].

## Limits and open questions

- No return-to-play outcomes, reinjury rates or sample sizes are shown. Bone proxies are described as not super precise [10:15].
- Load-response evidence cited is largely rodent and laboratory work [08:38].
- The speaker discloses his team's involvement with two companies and says no one receives money from them [01:02] [01:32]. One device was approved by the league's wearables committee and another was in process [01:02].

title: "SSAC18: Sleep Science Hacking your Biological Clock to Win"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Nita Singh (caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, american-football, basketball, other-sport:baseball]

## Summary

A sleep physician from the Henry Ford sleep disorder center argues that circadian timing is an under-used performance lever. She explains how the body clock sets alertness, when performance peaks, and why a chronotype (morning or night person) shifts that peak. She then covers jet lag in travelling teams and the two tools that move the clock, light and melatonin, with timing that matters. Three case examples follow (an NFL team going to London, an East Coast baseball team going west, a West Coast NBA team going east). The point is that travel plans should be built around body-clock time, not local time.

## Key claims

- More than half of genes and gene functions are driven by the biological clock [02:02].
- The master clock in the brain is set by light, which suppresses melatonin; at night melatonin is released and dampens the alerting signal [02:34].
- Two independent processes set sleepiness: a sleep drive that builds with time awake, and a clock-driven alerting signal; the afternoon dip is the clock, not the audience [04:09].
- Alerting signal and body temperature are lowest between 3:00 and 6:00 in the morning, which matters when shifting the clock [05:11].
- Coordination, reaction time, cardiovascular efficiency and strength peak in the evening, about 4:00 to 7:00 [06:11].
- Over 40 years of NFL night games, West Coast teams in 9:00 night games beat the point spread and won twice as often as the opposing side [07:12]; the speaker says this was replicated in the NBA and that more time zones crossed in baseball lowers win chance [07:42].
- A 20-year MLB study found East Coast teams returning from the West Coast lose the first home game because they are jet-lagged [07:42].
- Chronotype is inherited; in a study of competitive athletes the group peaked between 4 and 7 p.m., but night owls peaked later and morning types earlier [09:47], [10:19].
- Jet lag arises from crossing three or more time zones quickly and affects sleep, alertness, concentration, motivation and stomach [10:49].
- Light and melatonin are the two effective clock shifters: morning light advances the clock, night light delays it, and melatonin acts in the opposite direction to light [12:21], [13:21].
- Brighter light and blue-green wavelengths shift the clock more [13:51].
- Timing relative to body temperature minimum decides direction of shift; wrong-timed light makes things worse [14:21], [14:52].
- For the Saints London trip, players avoided light with UV-blocking sunglasses until about noon London time for three days, took supervised melatonin, banked sleep beforehand and switched to London time on the plane [16:23], [17:25], [18:28].
- Acclimatization normally takes about one day per time zone, and targeted steps can shift in a day [19:00].
- For the baseball team the aim was aligning peak performance to game time, using education, pre-shifting, light boxes and caffeine [20:31], [21:34].
- For the NBA team the advice was to not shift: stay on West Coast time, no morning practices, and stay overnight after the game instead of a red-eye [22:05], [22:36].
- Jet lag and sleep loss may leave athletes more open to the common cold, because immune cells have a rhythm and sleep loss lowers immunity [23:06].

## Numbers and definitions

- More than 50% of genes driven by the clock [02:02].
- Alerting signal and temperature minimum between 3:00 and 6:00 a.m. [05:11].
- Performance peak 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. [06:11].
- NFL: 40 years of data, West Coast teams win twice as often against the spread in night games [07:12].
- MLB: 20 years of data [07:42].
- Jet lag: three or more time zones [10:49].
- Light: 10,000 lux versus 1,500 lux, brighter is better [13:51].
- Saints game time about 2:30 p.m. London time; suggested bedtime about 11 p.m. and wake about 7:00 a.m. [14:52], [15:23]; sunglasses until about noon for the first three days [16:23].
- About one day per time zone to acclimatize [19:00].
- Caption garbles: "2:30" and the Saints sleep-time mapping (4:00 to 5:00 p.m. New Orleans time) are as captioned [15:53]; "red-eye" and "4:00 in the morning" for NBA are as captioned [22:36]. Chronotype study sample size not given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Two-process model of sleep (sleep drive and circadian alerting signal) [04:09].
- Light and melatonin timing relative to the temperature minimum [14:21].
- Chronotype assessment, shown by audience hand-raise on bedtime [08:43].
- Team travel protocols: pre-flight sleep banking, setting watches to destination time, plane sleep rules, sunglasses, strict bedtime, cold dark room [17:25], [19:00].

## Limits and open questions

- Case studies have no outcome data beyond reported better sleep and feeling refreshed for the Saints [19:30]; wins are mentioned but not attributed to the program.
- The speaker says light and melatonin are 100% effective in a sleep lab but travel adds many uncontrolled variables [16:54].
- The 40-year NFL and 20-year MLB findings are stated without sample sizes or effect estimates beyond "twice as often".
- Baseball and NBA teams are unnamed; interventions differ and are not compared.
- Presenter is a clinician describing her own practice, a professional view.
- Caption errors likely (for example "ear" for eye [02:34]).

## Q&A

No Q&A in the captions; the speaker invites questions after the talk [13:21], [25:07].

type: video-summary
video_id: TbYgc6_qQzo
title: "SSAC18: Volume and Intensity in Injury Incidence in Football Athletes"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward"), John Kendall (host)]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, injury-health]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A research-paper-competition talk that relates inertial sensor training load to non-contact time-loss injuries in football. It starts with the limits of earlier load and injury papers (binary injury coding, no censoring, small samples, thresholds that vary by team, retrospective rather than predictive) and cites work finding single-club models predict poorly on unseen data. The study followed 101 players for one season with 29 non-contact injuries. The best model combined total player load, low player load and high impacts: higher volume and higher physical intensity went with higher risk, and the speaker frames this as risk context for practitioners, not prediction.

## Key claims

- Non-contact injuries matter because they are thought to be partly due to training errors: too much too soon, too much for too long, or too little [03:03].
- Earlier papers often merge contact and non-contact injuries, mix time loss and non-time loss, skip censoring, give thresholds that differ across papers, and are retrospective [03:33], [04:04], [05:06], [06:08].
- A cited Australian football study found single-club injury models predicted poorly on unseen data [06:39], [07:10].
- The aim was to find associations between training load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, not to predict before a session [07:41].
- Metrics used were total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts (three thresholds) and IMA (three thresholds) [08:12], [08:42], [09:12].
- The speaker argues IMA helps with linemen because GPS-type measures are less reliable for high-intensity work in spaces under 20 meters [09:44].
- The joint model (total player load, player load low, impacts high) fit best; total player load and impacts high carried the highest added risk, and player load low was inversely related [14:20], [14:51], [15:22].
- Position group did not add explanatory value, possibly because of too few injuries per group [15:22], [15:53].
- Volume and intensity are risk factors to be combined with coaches' own judgment [15:53], [16:23].
- Injury is multifactorial; intrinsic and extrinsic factors and their change over a season would be needed for prediction [17:24], [17:54].

## Numbers and definitions

- Hundreds of millions: about 200 million dollars per year paid to players on injured reserve, in "some articles" [01:02].
- Knee injuries 3.1 per 1000 athlete exposures; hip and hamstring 2.2 per 1000 (ten years of NFL training camp data, cited work by "feely and colleagues", caption spelling) [02:03].
- Athlete exposure: one athlete in one game or training session [02:33].
- Season length: 16 NFL games, 9 to 13 in college [01:32].
- Sample: 101 football athletes, one full season preseason through regular season [11:14].
- Definition: non-contact injury that caused missed later sessions or games, coded by a medical professional [11:14], [11:45].
- Training load normalized per minute and standardized by position group [11:45], [12:15].
- Models: logistic regression, compared with Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood, with leave-one-out-style cross validation [12:47], [13:18]. Caption reads "four logistic regression models" as "for"; model count is ambiguous (one per variable group plus a joint model).
- 29 non-contact injuries [13:18].
- Caption problems: the figure "200 million dollars" at [01:02] appears as captioned; "Bayesian information criterion" is clear; effect sizes (odds ratios) are not given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Catapult-type inertial sensors with player load, effort bands, impacts and IMA (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer) [08:12], [09:12].
- Censoring of athletes removed from a session by injury [12:15].
- Logistic regression and leave-one-out style validation on one season [12:47], [13:18].

## Limits and open questions

- One team, one season; 29 injuries is small and no position-group effect was found [13:18], [15:22].
- No game load, so no games injuries [16:53].
- Association only; the speaker says prediction would need intrinsic and extrinsic factors [17:24].
- Effect sizes and thresholds were not shown, and several injury types were pooled [16:23].
- Most injuries occurred in training camp, per Q&A [22:05].
- Underreporting of pain is a recognized limit [24:10].

## Q&A

- Is the problem data or random assignment, and could effort drive both load and injury? Random assignment would help if a coach agreed; effort perception data exist but were not in this paper [18:24], [19:27].
- A panelist said a full picture needs internal load, HRV, hydration, hip mobility asymmetry and pain, and RPE; the speaker said no research shows joint range or posture predicts injury, and measures would change during a season [19:59], [20:29].
- Did the 101 players include roster cuts and did the final 53 differ? Most injuries were in camp and effort looks similar across players, with starters managed more [21:35], [22:05].
- Medical-attention and contact injuries? They looked at time loss and non-time loss; underreporting is a big limit; contact injury and over-exertion link is plausible but hard to model [23:09], [24:10], [24:41].

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. ## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].

## Summary

A 76ers performance-research director argues that wearables can improve return-to-play by adding two things: a surrogate for the load an injured limb actually receives, and a profile of what a game will demand. He says the process matters more than the product. He links rehab load to tissue-loading research, uses shin-mounted accelerometers as a rough bone-load proxy, and uses game tracking and publicly available data to define the bursts and transitions an athlete must be ready for. He also says trust matters: athletes accept devices that give insight and reject ones that feel like policing. No outcome data are shown, so it is a conceptual framework.

## Key claims

- Return to play is a negotiation between agents (reinjury risk), front office and coaches (missed games), and the athlete [02:02] [02:33].
- Wearables fall into two types, what the athlete does and how the body responds, and both together are most informative [03:34].
- The market is unregulated, so data reliability must be checked or artifacts can mislead [04:05] [04:35].
- Devices used to police athletes get pushed back, while devices that provide insight are welcomed [05:06].
- Injury databases are contaminated because some absences are strategic, but are accurate enough for trends [06:06].

- Symmetry patterns by intensity band from a New Zealand pro team across a season [19:26].

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
- Hard-interval average 179 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10 beats (caption wording unclear about which) [24:40].
- Subjective measure: a 1 to 10 satisfaction score for each workout [13:41].
- Context: program started in 2007 [05:05]; only one quarter of the studied masters athletes were risk-factor free [03:35].

## Methods and frameworks named

- A four-step sequence for suboptimal performance: medical evaluation, physiology evaluation, training evaluation, then planning, reassessment and implementation [07:07].
- Lab measures: max heart rate, aerobic efficiency (slope of oxygen against work), ventilatory threshold [12:11].
- Field data: 90 days of untouched training with a heart-rate monitor and a satisfaction rating [13:41].
- Training plan: individualize physiology, set a calendar working back from the goal event, assess the support structure (coach, nutrition, family), and run a longitudinal reassessment loop [16:46] [18:18].
- Sub-doldrum sessions are aerobic base, technique and active recovery. Supra-doldrum sessions include steady state, short and long intervals [17:17] [17:47].

## Limits and open questions

- One athlete, no control and no group data. Other changes during the eleven months are not shown.
- The speaker states his program has financial relationships with local and national groups (disclosed at [01:02]).
- Some figures are hard to verify due to captions (see Numbers).
- The oxygen-uptake threshold is described as "the single most important measurement" without data beyond the case.
- Heart rate variability skepticism is opinion, no data shown.
- Whether the same split works in team sports is not shown; he says the lab suits endurance components [26:27].

## Q&A

- Heart rate variability: promising in theory, many confounders, useful only as a backup to how the athlete feels [22:23] [22:54].
- Did the volume drop explain the gain: no, the key change was two clearly different kinds of days [23:33].
- Race-day intensity and the variance in hard sessions: hard sessions varied in effort to mimic race conditions, and he says most athletes improve when forced to rest after injury [24:10] [24:40].
- Power meters: pair power with heart rate, a rise in power at a given heart rate signals adaptation [25:26].
- Anaerobic power testing: Wingate is limited, better to use the sport's own exercises as benchmarks [25:56] [26:27].

# SSAC19: Built to Outlast: Youth Athlete Development for Performance and Durability

## Summary

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. She describes adolescence as a period of peak growth and change, falling and unequal sports participation, and a booming youth sports market that pushes early specialization, overload and under-built movement foundations. Her recommendation is "smart specialization": multi-sport, athlete-centered, skill-driven activity with foundational strength and movement first. The talk is a conceptual argument with few data points, and the complex-systems framework is her stated hypothesis.

## Key claims

- Injury and performance states lie on the same health continuum, and the goal is to keep athletes on the healthy, adaptive side [00:35] [01:39] [02:09].
- Health should be assessed across four domains: physiologic, biomechanic, behavioral and mental, and environmental [02:09].
- The transition into adolescence brings peak growth velocity and major brain and social change, so health determinants become performance determinants [02:42] [03:12] [03:45].
- Training load is system stress, and the aim is to raise capacity for it; youth athletes are often overloaded without enough recovery, which erodes capacity [04:15] [04:46] [05:17].
- Sports participation overall is falling, and the speaker ties access to socioeconomic status: lower-status athletes face sedentary-behavior risk, higher-status athletes face early specialization and injury risk [05:48] [06:18] [06:48].
- Youth athletes are over-scheduled, over-coached and spend less time on foundational strength and movement skills, which the speaker links to injury and attrition [08:22] [08:53] [09:26].
- Athletes who reach elite levels tend to specialize later, and highly specialized high school athletes are at higher injury risk [09:56]. Among NBA players, multi-sport athletes tended to miss fewer games, last longer and be less likely to be injured [10:26].
- The American development model has five stages; stage one, discover, learn and play, runs from age zero to twelve [10:57] [11:27].
- Studying loading, recovery and fueling one factor at a time misses their interactions; performance is a pattern emerging from relationships among determinants, whose influence changes over time [14:40] [16:13] [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].
- Because of this, models should be continuously reassessed, and the speaker holds that this approach yields more predictable outcomes [18:45] [19:48].
- Recommended approach is smart specialization: structured, supervised, multi-sport, athlete-centered, readiness- and skill-focused activity [20:48]. Practical steps include calibrating to physiologic and cognitive stage, mixing quantitative and "fuzzy" data, sport sampling, athlete engagement, and linking performance goals to health goals [21:18] [21:48].
- Future directions: cluster sports by shared physical demands, refine the language of training load, find protective or enhancing sport clusters, and focus on dissemination [22:18] [22:49].

## Numbers and definitions

- Youth sports market: twenty-two billion dollars worldwide, projected near sixty billion by 2024 [07:51].
- Stage one of the development model: ages 0 to 12; the model's activities are shown across ages 0 to 20 [11:27] [11:57].
- "Fuzzy data": elements that cannot easily be quantified but influence other parts of the system [16:44].
- Complex system: multifactorial web of related determinants that is iterative, recursive, self-organizing, decentralized and adaptive [16:44] [17:15].
- Training load: defined as system stress [04:15].
- Participation decline and the market projection are attributed to an Aspen Institute report and, for the market, no named source [05:48] [07:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Performance-health-disease continuum (credited to Dr. Fran O'Connor, military sports medicine) [01:39].
- Four-domain health assessment [02:09].
- Load and recovery continuum [04:46].
- American development model, five stages [10:57].
- Complex-systems approach with "fuzzy data" [16:44].
- Smart specialization and sport sampling (John O'Sullivan, Changing the Game Project, is cited on athlete engagement) [21:18] [21:48].
- Youth basketball is named as an example of a sport adopting this approach, with lacrosse and tennis also mentioned; another speaker ("Dr. D Fury", caption spelling) is referenced [21:48] [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost no sample sizes or effect sizes are given; the specialization and NBA findings are stated briefly without sources.
- The complex-systems model is described as the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15] and she says it is unclear whether 10,000 hours, intrinsic ability or load quality drives elite performance [14:40].
- The recommendation to play multiple sports collides with ranking and selection of ten-year-olds, which the speaker names but does not resolve [12:59].
- Population-level youth framing; no measures or thresholds for individual athletes are offered.
- Her view as a sports medicine physician and the speaker's institutional position shape the injury emphasis.

Balance early specialization for physical parameters with strength and aerobic work, which has not been shown to harm those pursuits; understand the athlete's goals and find lower-stress activities [24:21] [24:51] [25:22] [25:52].

# SSAC19: Performance Optimization Strategies that Helped Win a Championship

## Summary

The West Coast Eagles' high performance manager describes four guiding principles and four "big rocks" that he credits with preparing the club for its 2018 Grand Final win. The principles are levels of perspective, the Hedgehog principle, start with why, and big rocks before small marginal gains. The big rocks are a strategic plan with objectives and key results, having the best players available, a high chronic running load, and training that matches or exceeds the hardest running in a game. The evidence is one club's data presented by its own staff, and the talk is sponsored by a data platform vendor.

## Key claims

- The speaker's department has medical, strength and conditioning, and sports science branches, with a research arm that always has a student working on a club question [05:39].
- Single events such as one hamstring or ACL are not worried over; a run of events signals the systems and structures are not working [06:40].
- Doing one or two things very well (the Hedgehog principle, from Jim Collins's work) and documenting the reason behind each plan (start with why) guide decisions [07:11] [07:41] [08:43].
- Teams are distracted by small one-percent gains; the big rocks should be placed first, and sand added after [09:14]. The example given is altitude camps for a small aerobic gain while kicking effectiveness stayed poor; he would rather fund kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Big rock one: a strategic plan following vision, mission, objectives, strategies and tactics, with key results per objective, which aligns all staff and is described as a competitive advantage [10:45] [11:15].
- Big rock two: get the best players on the field. The club's data led it to target nine or more of its top 10 players each week [12:18] [12:49].
- Few clubs can field their best players often; the club exceeded the league average for this last season [13:20] [13:52].
- A star young player's development is shown with official provider points to argue best players must play [14:23] [14:53].
- Big rock three: chronic load, defined as a rolling four-week average of work done; high chronic load is needed so that game spikes are not excessive [15:55] [16:26] [16:57].
- A mandated two-week Christmas break drops chronic load enough that returning to the same session lands in very high risk, so players must train in off periods [17:58] [18:30].
- Big rock four: hard running. Being fit does not mean being conditioned, so the club identified the hardest 15 minutes of running in five years and built drills matching or exceeding it, with a belief effect on players [19:02] [19:33] [20:06] [20:38].
- Message: align staff and coaches with one plan, put big rocks before one-percenters, ignore what other clubs or one paper do, and keep data simple but not simpler [21:39] [22:10].

## Numbers and definitions

- Collins study: over 1,400 companies, 11 that made the leap from good to great [07:11].
- Altitude trip: 200,000 to 300,000 dollars, 2 percent gain in aerobic capacity, about 50 percent kicking effectiveness; he would prefer to spend 400,000 dollars on two kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Example key result: no more than 15 percent of injuries should be recurrences of a previous injury [11:46].
- Top-10 availability objective: nine or more of the top 10 each week [12:18]. With all 10, win rate 80 percent (four of five); with nine, two-thirds [12:49].
- League average: 10 of 10 available only 15 percent of the time, nine of 10 about 25 percent (the caption mentions 18 as the competition's club count) [13:20].
- Club season: average 8.7 of 10 over 25 games, nine or more on 15 occasions [14:53]. Eight of 10 by season end and seven in the Grand Final [15:24].
- Chronic load: rolling four-week average [15:55]. Risk bands: green "sweet spot", pink two times risk, dark red three to five times risk [17:27].
- Weekly running about 30 km plus, tackled about 10 times (caption wording) [16:26].
- Midfielder covers 15 to 16 km in a game; hardest block was one midfielder running about 180 m per minute on a rolling five-minute average over the first 15 minutes [18:30] [19:33].
- Field 170 m long by 130 m wide [20:06].
- Drills at the hardest running duration: four occasions of 12 minutes or more, the captions for the 9-to-12 and 6-to-9 minute counts are garbled (eight times each is the likeliest reading) [21:08].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Levels of perspective (Daniel Kim) [06:09].
- Hedgehog principle (Jim Collins) [07:11].
- Start with why (Simon Sinek, caption spelling "Simon syic") [08:43].
- Big rocks metaphor [09:14].
- Vision, mission, objectives, strategies, tactics with key results [10:45].
- Official statistics provider player points (called "Champion data" in captions) [14:23].
- Rolling four-week chronic load from GPS with risk bands [16:26] [17:27].

## Limits and open questions

- Source and sample for the risk bands (two times, three to five times) are not given.
- The speaker says other research links squad-wide injury count to performance but his club's data points to the best players mattering [12:18].

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
- Hard-interval average 179 with a standard deviation of 8 to 10 beats (caption wording unclear about which) [24:40].
- Subjective measure: a 1 to 10 satisfaction score for each workout [13:41].
- Context: program started in 2007 [05:05]; only one quarter of the studied masters athletes were risk-factor free [03:35].

## Methods and frameworks named

- A four-step sequence for suboptimal performance: medical evaluation, physiology evaluation, training evaluation, then planning, reassessment and implementation [07:07].
- Lab measures: max heart rate, aerobic efficiency (slope of oxygen against work), ventilatory threshold [12:11].
- Field data: 90 days of untouched training with a heart-rate monitor and a satisfaction rating [13:41].
- Training plan: individualize physiology, set a calendar working back from the goal event, assess the support structure (coach, nutrition, family), and run a longitudinal reassessment loop [16:46] [18:18].
- Sub-doldrum sessions are aerobic base, technique and active recovery. Supra-doldrum sessions include steady state, short and long intervals [17:17] [17:47].

## Limits and open questions

- One athlete, no control and no group data. Other changes during the eleven months are not shown.
- The speaker states his program has financial relationships with local and national groups (disclosed at [01:02]).
- Some figures are hard to verify due to captions (see Numbers).
- The oxygen-uptake threshold is described as "the single most important measurement" without data beyond the case.
- Heart rate variability skepticism is opinion, no data shown.
- Whether the same split works in team sports is not shown; he says the lab suits endurance components [26:27].

## Q&A

- Heart rate variability: promising in theory, many confounders, useful only as a backup to how the athlete feels [22:23] [22:54].
- Did the volume drop explain the gain: no, the key change was two clearly different kinds of days [23:33].
- Race-day intensity and the variance in hard sessions: hard sessions varied in effort to mimic race conditions, and he says most athletes improve when forced to rest after injury [24:10] [24:40].
- Power meters: pair power with heart rate, a rise in power at a given heart rate signals adaptation [25:26].
- Anaerobic power testing: Wingate is limited, better to use the sport's own exercises as benchmarks [25:56] [26:27].

## Summary

A university football performance staff member uses Catapult data, sliced play by play in OpenField, to compare what offensive linemen do in games with what they do in practice. He argues that total player load looks alike for linemen and wide receivers, but the make-up differs: linemen have contacts, short work bouts and little high-speed running. Practice contact load was far below game level, which he says risked detraining and a spike on Saturday. The talk also covers how he gained coach buy-in, a sprint-speed myth, and a practice-schedule change moving intensity to Friday. The evidence is one team and one season, with no controlled outcome.

## Key claims

- Coaches rely on subjective grading, and objective data reduce opinion-versus-opinion conflict [01:02] [01:32].
- Training should start from game demands and work backwards [02:02].
- A published group study reported what linemen cover in a game, but the speaker argues it reports load, not the actual demands [03:04].
- Linemen and wide receivers have similar total player load, but very different composition (explosive yardage, high-speed distance, max speed) [03:34].
- A line coach ignored his report until the data were reframed in terms the coach cared about [04:04] [04:34].
- A gyroscope-based line metric detects when a lineman drops into a stance, then counts contacts and load per contact [05:38].
- Runs bring more contact and passes bring more force absorption [07:13].
- Practice was far below game intensity in contact load, even on the most intense practice day [08:16] [08:47].
- Energy-system detraining may occur if the alactic system is only stimulated on game day [08:47].
- Even contact periods in practice (first-team offense versus first-team defense, scout team) gave few game-like reps [09:18] [09:48].
- Speed is overrated for football: very few plays reach 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Intensity should rise while volume holds, because raising both creates fatigue [15:35].
- Moving the fast session to Friday (instead of a walkthrough) raised subjective and objective readiness on game day in his program [16:05] [16:36].
- Athletes must be shown their own data to get buy-in, or they feel like "lab rats" [17:38].
- A compromise with receivers: trim low-value periods and ask for full speed in the remaining ones, with load unchanged [18:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Lineman game distance from the cited study: about 3,600 yards [01:32].
- Player load: summed movement from the unit, described as a more elaborate step counter [03:34].
- Average play duration: about 8 seconds, 7 for a run and 8 for a pass [06:10].
- Time between plays: about 30 seconds for his team, not up-tempo; some teams aim for under 18 seconds [06:42].
- Average load per contact: about 2.12 for pass, 2.32 for run, 2.22 combined [06:42] [07:13] [07:45].
- Contacts per game for a lineman: about 45 [07:13].
- Most intense practice: load per contact 1.54 against 2.22 in games [08:47].
- Alactic stimulus guideline: lose it if not stimulated every five to eight days [08:47].
- Game-like reps in practice: about 3.5 in one period and 1.5 in another, around five total [09:48].
- Contacts as a share of game player load: caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", so likely 66% (caption garbled) [10:19].
- Contact load rises by over 100% from practice to game [10:19].
- Work-to-rest ratio about 1 to 3.75 [10:50].
- Fewer than 1% of more than 1,000 plays reached 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Average lineman travel per play: 13.5 yards, with direction split about 25% left and 25% right [11:52].
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance in practice [13:27].
- Three-hour camp practice example: about 7,000 yards for a skill player, pacing at 17 to 18 mph [15:05].
- Eight-second work bouts fall under ten seconds all-out, treated as alactic [10:50].

## Methods and frameworks named

- OpenField used to slice each play in the game files [04:04].
- Offensive-line metric from the gyroscope: stance detection, contacts, load per contact, percent contact load [05:38].
- Practice versus game comparison by period type (individual, seven on seven, team versus scout) [09:18].
- Bioenergetic profile (work, rest) plus a movement profile to define what a lineman needs [12:22].
- Tapered week with a Friday fast session, tracked with wellness questionnaires and heart rate variability from a wearable [16:05].

## Limits and open questions

- One program and one season, no sample size given for contacts or practice periods.
- No evidence that closing the gap changes performance or injury. A question on this was asked and answered with his current approach, not outcomes [14:35] [15:05].
- Adding contact is limited by concussion risk, and the speaker had not yet solved this [12:22] [12:52].
- Heart rate variability is described as mixed: good and bad signals [16:05].
- The "Fast Friday" result is his team's own change, no controls.
- The speaker presents on behalf of Kentucky and the sponsor Catapult, who supply the units, and the caption suggests a company-sponsored session.
- Garbled captions: contacts-share percentage, and some wording in [05:06] and [10:50].

## Q&A

## Summary

A 76ers performance-research director argues that wearables can improve return-to-play by adding two things: a surrogate for the load an injured limb actually receives, and a profile of what a game will demand. He says the process matters more than the product. He links rehab load to tissue-loading research, uses shin-mounted accelerometers as a rough bone-load proxy, and uses game tracking and publicly available data to define the bursts and transitions an athlete must be ready for. He also says trust matters: athletes accept devices that give insight and reject ones that feel like policing. No outcome data are shown, so it is a conceptual framework.

## Key claims

- Return to play is a negotiation between agents (reinjury risk), front office and coaches (missed games), and the athlete [02:02] [02:33].
- Wearables fall into two types, what the athlete does and how the body responds, and both together are most informative [03:34].
- The market is unregulated, so data reliability must be checked or artifacts can mislead [04:05] [04:35].
- Devices used to police athletes get pushed back, while devices that provide insight are welcomed [05:06].
- Injury databases are contaminated because some absences are strategic, but are accurate enough for trends [06:06].
- Accurate diagnosis comes first, and no wearable fixes a misdiagnosis [06:37].
- Rehab should follow criterion-based progressions grounded in how tendons, ligaments and bone respond to load [07:08].
- Practice style can differ from game style, so a player who scrimmaged may still face an unaccustomed high-intensity exposure [07:38].
- Tissue has a loading sweet spot: too much stress stalls or breaks down, too little gives no collagen resynthesis [08:08] [08:38].
- A tibia-mounted accelerometer can give a rough low, moderate or severe bone-load proxy and a daily cumulative load, to be read alongside clinical signs [10:15] [10:45].
- If imaging shows poor response, loads can be stepped back to a previously tolerated level [11:48].
- Sensors can show ground-contact loading and left-right symmetry during water running and anti-gravity treadmill work [12:19] [12:49].
- Game demands should be profiled before clearing a player, and the fundamentals of basketball running distance were measured as early as 1931 [15:22] [15:53].
- Matching skill actions (catches, passes, shots, defensive slides, contacts) gives the athlete confidence and a way to communicate readiness to owners, general managers and coaches [20:27].
- Athletes in rehab welcome devices that help them build a bridge back, but are suspicious if data could leak into trades or sales [21:29] [22:01].

## Numbers and definitions

- About 1 in 4 NBA athletes will have an ankle injury that costs at least one game [05:36].
- A progression of six to eight weeks of monitored load, with no pain, swelling or stiffness, before the athlete returns to full practice [13:49].
- Loading range from under one times body weight to about seven and a half or eight times body weight per footstrike [13:19].
- 1931 study: a guard ran about two to two and a half miles, against public guesses of 5 to 10 [15:53]; running bursts of about two minutes at three to four miles per hour [15:53].
- 2016-17: a high-minute player averaged about 36 minutes, the 1931 player about 40, covering similar distance and speeds [16:24] [16:54].
- Tracking data: 1.2 to 1.5 million data points, mostly 6 to 10 mph, with some runs at 13 to 14 and up to 17 mph [17:25].
- Running bursts of 90 to 120 seconds are common, often under 30 seconds, sometimes three minutes without a break (the captions say three to four minutes) [17:55].
- Rehab profile targets: segments of three to six minutes, transitions every ten to twenty seconds, continuous play up to three minutes, six to eight full-court transitions [20:58].

- A pathway: diagnosis, medical treatment, load-based rehab, demand-matched practice, game return [06:37] [07:08] [07:38].
- Mechanobiological approach: link sensor-derived load to tissue-loading research (rodent bone and ligament work cited) [09:42].
- Shank-mounted accelerometers, waterproofed sensors for pool and anti-gravity work, and RFID-style player tracking for games [10:15] [12:49] [14:20].
- Publicly available tracking data used to build speed distribution, burst length and recovery profiles [17:25] [17:55].
- Symmetry patterns by intensity band from a New Zealand pro team across a season [19:26].

- No return-to-play outcomes, reinjury rates or sample sizes are shown. Bone proxies are described as not super precise [10:15].
- Load-response evidence cited is largely rodent and laboratory work [08:38].

## Summary

A short vendor-sponsored talk (title names Fusion Sport) on integrating the data streams a university athletic program collects, so that decisions are centralized and tied to a shared performance model. The speaker describes pushing data from a programming tool, GPS units and an electronic medical record into one system without double entry, then showing it back to coaches, athletes and medical staff as dashboards, automatic reports and role-based reports. The captions are heavily garbled, so details are uncertain and no outcome evidence is presented. The talk reads as a capability demonstration for a product, not a study.

## Key claims

- The aim is to use data for corrective purposes with centralized decision-making, which first requires agreeing on what is monitored and defining a performance model everyone understands [00:00].
- The program aggregates many technologies across training, recovery, practice and injury identification and feeds the data back into that model [01:01].
- A strength-programming tool (captions: "Bridge Athletic") connects through an API so athlete data entered on gym iPads flows into the system without further handling [01:32] [02:03] [02:34].
- GPS units used across several sports (captions name American football, soccer and volleyball) upload automatically, so no one enters data twice [02:34] [03:05].
- Injury data from an electronic medical record is visualized for coaches and medical staff on phones, tablets, PCs and facility TVs, including injuries within seven days [03:36] [04:07].
- Weekly musculoskeletal screening (dorsiflexion is named) is shown against position and team ranges, with outliers flagged and drill-down to injury history [04:38] [05:11].
- Reports for coaches are generated automatically after GPS data processes, and wellness and injury information is summarized by group [05:44] [06:14].
- A Microsoft visualization tool (caption spelling garbled) provides access at different security levels, including season summaries, availability, cross-team comparison and individual athlete progress [06:48] [07:19].

## Numbers and definitions

- Seven days: injury highlighting window ("injuries within seven days") [04:07]. Captions are garbled around this.
- "90 sport" and "two years in the process" appear in the answer on rollout [09:23]. Caption likely garbled; do not rely on either figure.
- No performance or injury outcome numbers are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- A performance model used to identify discrepancies in athlete development and decide what to test [00:00] [00:30].
- Integration by API and automatic upload from three source types: programming tool, GPS, electronic medical record [01:32] to [03:36].
- Dashboards and hubs for individual case conferences covering items such as hydration, body composition and past injuries [06:14].

## Limits and open questions

- Captions are too garbled to confirm product names, the sport list, or the access-control description.
- Speaker is not named in the captions. The institution is described only as a university.
- Commercial context: the talk is presented by Fusion Sport. No evidence of benefit to athletes or outcomes was shown.
- Does not address data quality, athlete privacy for medical data on shared displays, or the cost of integration.

## Q&A

- Do athletes use the data to help recovery? Answer (partly garbled): medical staff and coaches inform the athletes, and it becomes a conversation and an intervention [08:21].
- Is coach buy-in mandatory? Answer (garbled): mandating it would be the fastest way to ensure no one does it; some coaches are more interested than others, and the system takes their own inputs and makes them meaningful to them [08:51] [09:23].

type: video-summary
video_id: OhyCbBfJpJA
title: "SSAC19: Built to Outlast: Youth Athlete Development for Performance and Durability"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: ["Siddiqui (caption spelling; assistant professor of rehabilitation and regenerative medicine, Columbia University Medical Center)"]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, policy, basketball]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. She describes adolescence as a period of peak growth and change, falling and unequal sports participation, and a booming youth sports market that pushes early specialization, overload and under-built movement foundations. Her recommendation is "smart specialization": multi-sport, athlete-centered, skill-driven activity with foundational strength and movement first. The talk is a conceptual argument with few data points, and the complex-systems framework is her stated hypothesis.

## Key claims

- Injury and performance states lie on the same health continuum, and the goal is to keep athletes on the healthy, adaptive side [00:35] [01:39] [02:09].
- Health should be assessed across four domains: physiologic, biomechanic, behavioral and mental, and environmental [02:09].
- The transition into adolescence brings peak growth velocity and major brain and social change, so health determinants become performance determinants [02:42] [03:12] [03:45].
- Training load is system stress, and the aim is to raise capacity for it; youth athletes are often overloaded without enough recovery, which erodes capacity [04:15] [04:46] [05:17].
- Sports participation overall is falling, and the speaker ties access to socioeconomic status: lower-status athletes face sedentary-behavior risk, higher-status athletes face early specialization and injury risk [05:48] [06:18] [06:48].
- Youth athletes are over-scheduled, over-coached and spend less time on foundational strength and movement skills, which the speaker links to injury and attrition [08:22] [08:53] [09:26].
- Athletes who reach elite levels tend to specialize later, and highly specialized high school athletes are at higher injury risk [09:56]. Among NBA players, multi-sport athletes tended to miss fewer games, last longer and be less likely to be injured [10:26].
- The American development model has five stages; stage one, discover, learn and play, runs from age zero to twelve [10:57] [11:27].
- Studying loading, recovery and fueling one factor at a time misses their interactions; performance is a pattern emerging from relationships among determinants, whose influence changes over time [14:40] [16:13] [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].
- Because of this, models should be continuously reassessed, and the speaker holds that this approach yields more predictable outcomes [18:45] [19:48].
- Recommended approach is smart specialization: structured, supervised, multi-sport, athlete-centered, readiness- and skill-focused activity [20:48]. Practical steps include calibrating to physiologic and cognitive stage, mixing quantitative and "fuzzy" data, sport sampling, athlete engagement, and linking performance goals to health goals [21:18] [21:48].
- Future directions: cluster sports by shared physical demands, refine the language of training load, find protective or enhancing sport clusters, and focus on dissemination [22:18] [22:49].

## Numbers and definitions

- Youth sports market: twenty-two billion dollars worldwide, projected near sixty billion by 2024 [07:51].
- Stage one of the development model: ages 0 to 12; the model's activities are shown across ages 0 to 20 [11:27] [11:57].
- "Fuzzy data": elements that cannot easily be quantified but influence other parts of the system [16:44].
- Complex system: multifactorial web of related determinants that is iterative, recursive, self-organizing, decentralized and adaptive [16:44] [17:15].
- Training load: defined as system stress [04:15].
- Participation decline and the market projection are attributed to an Aspen Institute report and, for the market, no named source [05:48] [07:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Performance-health-disease continuum (credited to Dr. Fran O'Connor, military sports medicine) [01:39].
- Four-domain health assessment [02:09].
- Load and recovery continuum [04:46].
- American development model, five stages [10:57].
- Complex-systems approach with "fuzzy data" [16:44].
- Smart specialization and sport sampling (John O'Sullivan, Changing the Game Project, is cited on athlete engagement) [21:18] [21:48].
- Youth basketball is named as an example of a sport adopting this approach, with lacrosse and tennis also mentioned; another speaker ("Dr. D Fury", caption spelling) is referenced [21:48] [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost no sample sizes or effect sizes are given; the specialization and NBA findings are stated briefly without sources.
- The complex-systems model is described as the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15] and she says it is unclear whether 10,000 hours, intrinsic ability or load quality drives elite performance [14:40].
- The recommendation to play multiple sports collides with ranking and selection of ten-year-olds, which the speaker names but does not resolve [12:59].
- Population-level youth framing; no measures or thresholds for individual athletes are offered.
- Her view as a sports medicine physician and the speaker's institutional position shape the injury emphasis.

## Q&A

- How is recovery determined? Athlete-specific, using readiness, physical status, soreness and pain, on a scale of days for games and varying by activity [23:20] [23:51] [24:21].
- What about aesthetic sports such as dance, where early specialization is needed? Balance early specialization for physical parameters with strength and aerobic work, which has not been shown to harm those pursuits; understand the athlete's goals and find lower-stress activities [24:21] [24:51] [25:22] [25:52].
- Which injuries concern her most? ACL tears because of post-traumatic arthritis later; the most modifiable factor is healthy participation and giving athletes perspective on their lives beyond sport [26:33] [27:03] [27:37].

## Summary

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. She describes adolescence as a period of peak growth and change, falling and unequal sports participation, and a booming youth sports market that pushes early specialization, overload and under-built movement foundations. Her recommendation is "smart specialization": multi-sport, athlete-centered, skill-driven activity with foundational strength and movement first. The talk is a conceptual argument with few data points, and the complex-systems framework is her stated hypothesis.

## Key claims

- Injury and performance states lie on the same health continuum, and the goal is to keep athletes on the healthy, adaptive side [00:35] [01:39] [02:09].
- Health should be assessed across four domains: physiologic, biomechanic, behavioral and mental, and environmental [02:09].
- The transition into adolescence brings peak growth velocity and major brain and social change, so health determinants become performance determinants [02:42] [03:12] [03:45].
- Training load is system stress, and the aim is to raise capacity for it; youth athletes are often overloaded without enough recovery, which erodes capacity [04:15] [04:46] [05:17].
- Sports participation overall is falling, and the speaker ties access to socioeconomic status: lower-status athletes face sedentary-behavior risk, higher-status athletes face early specialization and injury risk [05:48] [06:18] [06:48].
- Youth athletes are over-scheduled, over-coached and spend less time on foundational strength and movement skills, which the speaker links to injury and attrition [08:22] [08:53] [09:26].
- Athletes who reach elite levels tend to specialize later, and highly specialized high school athletes are at higher injury risk [09:56]. Among NBA players, multi-sport athletes tended to miss fewer games, last longer and be less likely to be injured [10:26].
- The American development model has five stages; stage one, discover, learn and play, runs from age zero to twelve [10:57] [11:27].
- Studying loading, recovery and fueling one factor at a time misses their interactions; performance is a pattern emerging from relationships among determinants, whose influence changes over time [14:40] [16:13] [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].
- Because of this, models should be continuously reassessed, and the speaker holds that this approach yields more predictable outcomes [18:45] [19:48].
- Recommended approach is smart specialization: structured, supervised, multi-sport, athlete-centered, readiness- and skill-focused activity [20:48]. Practical steps include calibrating to physiologic and cognitive stage, mixing quantitative and "fuzzy" data, sport sampling, athlete engagement, and linking performance goals to health goals [21:18] [21:48].
- Future directions: cluster sports by shared physical demands, refine the language of training load, find protective or enhancing sport clusters, and focus on dissemination [22:18] [22:49].

## Numbers and definitions

- Youth sports market: twenty-two billion dollars worldwide, projected near sixty billion by 2024 [07:51].
- Stage one of the development model: ages 0 to 12; the model's activities are shown across ages 0 to 20 [11:27] [11:57].
- "Fuzzy data": elements that cannot easily be quantified but influence other parts of the system [16:44].
- Complex system: multifactorial web of related determinants that is iterative, recursive, self-organizing, decentralized and adaptive [16:44] [17:15].
- Training load: defined as system stress [04:15].
- Participation decline and the market projection are attributed to an Aspen Institute report and, for the market, no named source [05:48] [07:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Performance-health-disease continuum (credited to Dr. Fran O'Connor, military sports medicine) [01:39].
- Four-domain health assessment [02:09].
- Load and recovery continuum [04:46].
- American development model, five stages [10:57].
- Complex-systems approach with "fuzzy data" [16:44].
- Smart specialization and sport sampling (John O'Sullivan, Changing the Game Project, is cited on athlete engagement) [21:18] [21:48].
- Youth basketball is named as an example of a sport adopting this approach, with lacrosse and tennis also mentioned; another speaker ("Dr. D Fury", caption spelling) is referenced [21:48] [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost no sample sizes or effect sizes are given; the specialization and NBA findings are stated briefly without sources.
- The complex-systems model is described as the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15] and she says it is unclear whether 10,000 hours, intrinsic ability or load quality drives elite performance [14:40].
- The recommendation to play multiple sports collides with ranking and selection of ten-year-olds, which the speaker names but does not resolve [12:59].
- Population-level youth framing; no measures or thresholds for individual athletes are offered.
- Her view as a sports medicine physician and the speaker's institutional position shape the injury emphasis.

## Q&A

- How is recovery determined? Athlete-specific, using readiness, physical status, soreness and pain, on a scale of days for games and varying by activity [23:20] [23:51] [24:21].
- What about aesthetic sports such as dance, where early specialization is needed? Balance early specialization for physical parameters with strength and aerobic work, which has not been shown to harm those pursuits; understand the athlete's goals and find lower-stress activities [24:21] [24:51] [25:22] [25:52].
- Which injuries concern her most? ACL tears because of post-traumatic arthritis later; the most modifiable factor is healthy participation and giving athletes perspective on their lives beyond sport [26:33] [27:03] [27:37].

## Summary

The West Coast Eagles' high performance manager describes four guiding principles and four "big rocks" that he credits with preparing the club for its 2018 Grand Final win. The principles are levels of perspective, the Hedgehog principle, start with why, and big rocks before small marginal gains. The big rocks are a strategic plan with objectives and key results, having the best players available, a high chronic running load, and training that matches or exceeds the hardest running in a game. The evidence is one club's data presented by its own staff, and the talk is sponsored by a data platform vendor.

## Key claims

- The speaker's department has medical, strength and conditioning, and sports science branches, with a research arm that always has a student working on a club question [05:39].
- Single events such as one hamstring or ACL are not worried over; a run of events signals the systems and structures are not working [06:40].
- Doing one or two things very well (the Hedgehog principle, from Jim Collins's work) and documenting the reason behind each plan (start with why) guide decisions [07:11] [07:41] [08:43].
- Teams are distracted by small one-percent gains; the big rocks should be placed first, and sand added after [09:14]. The example given is altitude camps for a small aerobic gain while kicking effectiveness stayed poor; he would rather fund kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Big rock one: a strategic plan following vision, mission, objectives, strategies and tactics, with key results per objective, which aligns all staff and is described as a competitive advantage [10:45] [11:15].
- Big rock two: get the best players on the field. The club's data led it to target nine or more of its top 10 players each week [12:18] [12:49].
- Few clubs can field their best players often; the club exceeded the league average for this last season [13:20] [13:52].
- A star young player's development is shown with official provider points to argue best players must play [14:23] [14:53].
- Big rock three: chronic load, defined as a rolling four-week average of work done; high chronic load is needed so that game spikes are not excessive [15:55] [16:26] [16:57].
- A mandated two-week Christmas break drops chronic load enough that returning to the same session lands in very high risk, so players must train in off periods [17:58] [18:30].
- Big rock four: hard running. Being fit does not mean being conditioned, so the club identified the hardest 15 minutes of running in five years and built drills matching or exceeding it, with a belief effect on players [19:02] [19:33] [20:06] [20:38].
- Message: align staff and coaches with one plan, put big rocks before one-percenters, ignore what other clubs or one paper do, and keep data simple but not simpler [21:39] [22:10].

## Numbers and definitions

- Collins study: over 1,400 companies, 11 that made the leap from good to great [07:11].
- Altitude trip: 200,000 to 300,000 dollars, 2 percent gain in aerobic capacity, about 50 percent kicking effectiveness; he would prefer to spend 400,000 dollars on two kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Example key result: no more than 15 percent of injuries should be recurrences of a previous injury [11:46].
- Top-10 availability objective: nine or more of the top 10 each week [12:18]. With all 10, win rate 80 percent (four of five); with nine, two-thirds [12:49].
- League average: 10 of 10 available only 15 percent of the time, nine of 10 about 25 percent (the caption mentions 18 as the competition's club count) [13:20].
- Club season: average 8.7 of 10 over 25 games, nine or more on 15 occasions [14:53]. Eight of 10 by season end and seven in the Grand Final [15:24].
- Chronic load: rolling four-week average [15:55]. Risk bands: green "sweet spot", pink two times risk, dark red three to five times risk [17:27].
- Weekly running about 30 km plus, tackled about 10 times (caption wording) [16:26].
- Midfielder covers 15 to 16 km in a game; hardest block was one midfielder running about 180 m per minute on a rolling five-minute average over the first 15 minutes [18:30] [19:33].
- Field 170 m long by 130 m wide [20:06].
- Drills at the hardest running duration: four occasions of 12 minutes or more, the captions for the 9-to-12 and 6-to-9 minute counts are garbled (eight times each is the likeliest reading) [21:08].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Levels of perspective (Daniel Kim) [06:09].
- Hedgehog principle (Jim Collins) [07:11].
- Start with why (Simon Sinek, caption spelling "Simon syic") [08:43].
- Big rocks metaphor [09:14].
- Vision, mission, objectives, strategies, tactics with key results [10:45].
- Official statistics provider player points (called "Champion data" in captions) [14:23].
- Rolling four-week chronic load from GPS with risk bands [16:26] [17:27].
- Rolling five-minute distance-per-minute to find the hardest 15 minutes [19:33].
- Data entered by players in a vendor platform (smartabase) and a vendor dashboard produced many of the shown graphs [22:42] [26:08].

## Limits and open questions

- One club, one season, with the club's own staff reporting outcomes; no control or comparison is shown for the load and drill choices.
- Source and sample for the risk bands (two times, three to five times) are not given.
- The speaker says other research links squad-wide injury count to performance but his club's data points to the best players mattering [12:18].
- The Grand Final win is not attributed to a tested cause; he lists things they did.
- Two caption problems: the opposition's count of available top players is cut off [15:55], and the drill duration counts are garbled [21:08].
- The talk is sponsored by Fusion Sport and the speaker praises their platform [01:06] [22:42].

## Q&A

- Can cycling-style performance modeling be used? The game is too chaotic and random, fields vary, so the club models only a little in training [23:14] [23:47] [24:17].
- Biggest marginal gain? The mental side; the club has a part-time performance psychologist and added mindfulness before meetings [24:59] [25:30].
- How is load tracked when players are away? Players log their program in the platform, and the staff manage the group whose chronic load dropped [26:08].
- Data over time? Long, clean data allows slow increases in group load across years while staying in the sweet spot [26:41] [27:12].

title: "SSAC18: Using Lab Science and Field Analytics to Maximize Performance"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Aaron Bagga (caption spelling; host introduces him as "Dr." and a clinical cardiologist), Sam Feder (host)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, competitive-advantage, other-sport:rowing]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft

## Summary

A sports cardiologist argues that endurance athletes stall when they train in a narrow band of heart rate right around their ventilatory threshold, which he calls the physiologic doldrums. He says the fix is to combine laboratory measurements (measured max heart rate, oxygen uptake, and threshold) with the athlete's own field data, then split training into clearly easy and clearly hard work. He illustrates this with one 26-year-old elite rower who trained 13 sessions a week, clustered at threshold, and improved his threshold heart rate over about eleven months while training less. The talk matters because it challenges formula-based heart-rate zones and flat zone charts on consumer devices. The evidence is one case plus the speaker's program experience.

## Key claims

- Performance work rests on basic exercise physiology, and athletes differ, so each one has to be measured and re-measured [01:33].
- Lab physiology without field analytics, or the reverse, leads to the doldrums [02:03].
- Roughly 40% of athletic adults over 40 in one local study felt dismissed by their doctors because they were athletes [03:35].
- About half of elite athletes who arrive with a performance decline have an undetected medical cause (the speaker notes selection bias), so medical causes should be ruled out first [07:38].
- Oxygen flows lung to heart and circulation to muscle, and all three links are trainable (the speaker hints lungs are not the one that changed here) [09:10].
- Heart rate, oxygen uptake and work rate are linear in a healthy person, while carbon dioxide output steepens above a point called the ventilatory threshold [10:10].
- That threshold is, in his view, the single most important measurement for elite athletes, and physiologically there are only two zones, below it (sustainable for hours with fuel and fluids) and above it (effort-dependent fatigue) [10:40] [11:10].
- Equations for max heart rate are unreliable and should be replaced by measurement [11:40].
- Easy days must sit clearly below the threshold and hard days clearly above it, with little to gain in between [17:17] [17:47].
- Coaches who apply physiology tend to win and those who ignore it lose, in his experience [18:48].
- A reassessment cycle in the lab, about every four months in this case, keeps the plan honest [19:19].
- Heart rate variability is a fickle measure and he has not seen it work alone at the elite level, though he accepts it as a backup to subjective recovery [22:54].
- Changes in the power-to-heart-rate relationship are the best sign of fitness change for athletes with power meters [25:26].
- The lab fits endurance-heavy athletes best, because anaerobic lab tests such as the Wingate engage different machinery from the sport [26:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Max heart rate prediction error: the true standard deviation is on the order of 15 to 20 beats per minute [12:11].
- Case athlete at baseline: measured max heart rate 208, peak oxygen uptake 71 mL per kg, threshold at 78% of max oxygen uptake at a heart rate of about 162 [12:41].
- Tracking period requested before any change: 90 days [13:11].
- Training before intervention: 13 sessions per week, about 18 hours, 11 base-building and 2 higher-intensity [13:41].
- Field heart rate: base sessions about 160 plus or minus 2, hard sessions about 12 beats higher, resting about 52, felt recovered 50% of the time [14:12]. Caption at [15:14] gives 180 and 172 for these sessions, which conflicts with 160 and +12; probably garbled.
- Doldrums: roughly 5 beats above and 5 below the threshold heart rate [16:46].
- Goal horizon: an 18-month periodized plan toward an Olympic team [18:18].
- Reassessment every four months, and the third reassessment came roughly eleven months later [19:19].
- After the program: threshold heart rate 162 to 176 (a 10 to 15% rise), peak heart rate unchanged, peak oxygen uptake only slightly higher [19:49].
- Field after: base heart rates in the 150s, hard intervals close to 180, resting heart rate lower [20:20]; felt recovered 70% of the time, up from 50% [20:51].
