---
type: video-summary
video_id: QLdbKUiNadg
title: "SSAC18: Preparing for the Game Optimizing Player Performance"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Chris Morris (University of Kentucky, per the speaker and host)]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A university football performance staff member uses Catapult data, sliced play by play in OpenField, to compare what offensive linemen do in games with what they do in practice. He argues that total player load looks alike for linemen and wide receivers, but the make-up differs: linemen have contacts, short work bouts and little high-speed running. Practice contact load was far below game level, which he says risked detraining and a spike on Saturday. The talk also covers how he gained coach buy-in, a sprint-speed myth, and a practice-schedule change moving intensity to Friday. The evidence is one team and one season, with no controlled outcome.

## Key claims

- Coaches rely on subjective grading, and objective data reduce opinion-versus-opinion conflict [01:02] [01:32].
- Training should start from game demands and work backwards [02:02].
- A published group study reported what linemen cover in a game, but the speaker argues it reports load, not the actual demands [03:04].
- Linemen and wide receivers have similar total player load, but very different composition (explosive yardage, high-speed distance, max speed) [03:34].
- A line coach ignored his report until the data were reframed in terms the coach cared about [04:04] [04:34].
- A gyroscope-based line metric detects when a lineman drops into a stance, then counts contacts and load per contact [05:38].
- Runs bring more contact and passes bring more force absorption [07:13].
- Practice was far below game intensity in contact load, even on the most intense practice day [08:16] [08:47].
- Energy-system detraining may occur if the alactic system is only stimulated on game day [08:47].
- Even contact periods in practice (first-team offense versus first-team defense, scout team) gave few game-like reps [09:18] [09:48].
- Speed is overrated for football: very few plays reach 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Intensity should rise while volume holds, because raising both creates fatigue [15:35].
- Moving the fast session to Friday (instead of a walkthrough) raised subjective and objective readiness on game day in his program [16:05] [16:36].
- Athletes must be shown their own data to get buy-in, or they feel like "lab rats" [17:38].
- A compromise with receivers: trim low-value periods and ask for full speed in the remaining ones, with load unchanged [18:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- Lineman game distance from the cited study: about 3,600 yards [01:32].
- Player load: summed movement from the unit, described as a more elaborate step counter [03:34].
- Average play duration: about 8 seconds, 7 for a run and 8 for a pass [06:10].
- Time between plays: about 30 seconds for his team, not up-tempo; some teams aim for under 18 seconds [06:42].
- Average load per contact: about 2.12 for pass, 2.32 for run, 2.22 combined [06:42] [07:13] [07:45].
- Contacts per game for a lineman: about 45 [07:13].
- Most intense practice: load per contact 1.54 against 2.22 in games [08:47].
- Alactic stimulus guideline: lose it if not stimulated every five to eight days [08:47].
- Game-like reps in practice: about 3.5 in one period and 1.5 in another, around five total [09:48].
- Contacts as a share of game player load: caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", so likely 66% (caption garbled) [10:19].
- Contact load rises by over 100% from practice to game [10:19].
- Work-to-rest ratio about 1 to 3.75 [10:50].
- Fewer than 1% of more than 1,000 plays reached 90% of max speed [11:21].
- Average lineman travel per play: 13.5 yards, with direction split about 25% left and 25% right [11:52].
- Target for skill players: about 75% of game high-speed distance in practice [13:27].
- Three-hour camp practice example: about 7,000 yards for a skill player, pacing at 17 to 18 mph [15:05].
- Eight-second work bouts fall under ten seconds all-out, treated as alactic [10:50].

## Methods and frameworks named

- OpenField used to slice each play in the game files [04:04].
- Offensive-line metric from the gyroscope: stance detection, contacts, load per contact, percent contact load [05:38].
- Practice versus game comparison by period type (individual, seven on seven, team versus scout) [09:18].
- Bioenergetic profile (work, rest) plus a movement profile to define what a lineman needs [12:22].
- Tapered week with a Friday fast session, tracked with wellness questionnaires and heart rate variability from a wearable [16:05].

## Limits and open questions

- One program and one season, no sample size given for contacts or practice periods.
- No evidence that closing the gap changes performance or injury. A question on this was asked and answered with his current approach, not outcomes [14:35] [15:05].
- Adding contact is limited by concussion risk, and the speaker had not yet solved this [12:22] [12:52].
- Heart rate variability is described as mixed: good and bad signals [16:05].
- The "Fast Friday" result is his team's own change, no controls.
- The speaker presents on behalf of Kentucky and the sponsor Catapult, who supply the units, and the caption suggests a company-sponsored session.
- Garbled captions: contacts-share percentage, and some wording in [05:06] and [10:50].

## Q&A

- Evidence that raising practice intensity helps game performance or fatigue: keep load constant and raise intensity, shorter sharper practices, and the Friday change [14:35] [15:05].
- Heart rate variability and wellness use: used, mixed results, Friday intensity improved readiness [16:05] [16:36].
- Player pushback (the Eagles with Chip Kelly were cited as an earlier case): show athletes their data and trim wasted periods so intensity is high in the remaining ones [17:38] [18:08].
- Contact: the speaker invites email and Twitter follow-up [18:38].

## Summary

A four-person NBA panel describes how front offices combine analytics, scouting, medical work and background research when drafting. The panelists reject the idea that analytics and scouting compete, and say the hard parts are prospects who change quickly, small or mismatched samples, and a league whose style keeps shifting. They use named players as examples, discuss how teams review their own process, and name psychological data as the missing piece. The talk is useful as a description of how decision groups weigh conflicting evidence, though the examples are anecdotes and the panel itself says prediction is poor.

## Key claims

- The split between analytics and scouting is called a myth; all sources are used together, including box score numbers, medical information and background research. [01:32]
- A panelist objects to calling traditional scouting "gut," saying it is done systematically. [02:03]
- It helps to read both the most positive and most negative evaluator on a prospect, because that shows blind spots. [03:06]
- Being right can be for the wrong reasons, and being wrong can come from team situation or injury. [03:36]
- Information overload is a challenge, so teams must decide what matters. [04:06]
- Teams now tolerate less character or background risk than 10 to 15 years ago. [05:09]
- A draft pick is a three or four year decision, so no playing time in year one is not automatically a failure. [05:39]
- Defining value is hard because the league changes; a back-to-the-basket center prized earlier now has little value. [08:15]
- Versatility and switching defense are valued now, with one panelist's example of a player once out of the league for lacking a position. [09:18, 10:19]
- A prospect can look worse in college or overseas because he is used poorly there, so context matters. [10:49]
- One panelist describes weighing a player's non-contact workouts against a weak college stretch; the player later shot over 40% as a rookie. [11:51, 12:22, 12:54]
- Another prospect was judged by the panelist as poorly fit to his college team, so the college snapshot was discounted. [13:24, 13:54]
- Interviews and workouts do not get a player drafted but can address concerns. [14:56]
- Even with a lot of information on one prospect, the panel says outcomes were unclear; one panelist says prediction of human behavior is hard in any field. [15:26, 15:57]
- Panelists wish NBA teams could watch high school competition; one notes some outside tracking data now exists. [16:28, 17:00]
- A network of contacts abroad is what led one panelist to see a foreign prospect early. [19:02, 19:33]
- One panelist would throw out one league's stats entirely; international leagues change year to year, so stats need current context. [20:37, 22:11]
- Too much data needs processes about what you value; experience teaches not to overreact to a short stretch. [22:42, 23:14, 23:45]
- Experience with analytical tools and with medical information makes the evidence easier to weigh. [24:47, 25:18]
- Teams should review the whole draft, not just one pick, and adjust method if a good result came from luck. [25:49, 26:20]
- Some boards are shaped by ownership or the GM through red flags, so a decision may be about culture or health more than talent. [26:20, 26:50]
- Most teams hold similar boards, so surprises are rare. [27:20, 27:50]
- Trade offers add a comparison between a pick and a player under contract, plus cap questions. [28:21]
- The missing data is mental: how players handle money, attention and lifestyle. [29:53, 30:23]
- Need breaks ties among similar players; a team that is resetting takes bets on talent. [34:57, 35:28, 36:00]
- A panelist predicts a return of defensive innovation; star outliers force other teams to adjust. [38:02, 38:34]
- Panelists do not look forward to scouting high school players if one-and-done ends, and think teams oppose removal of the rule. [40:05, 40:36]
- One drafted player was dropped after a year of work on one skill with no improvement. [42:39, 43:10]
- A panelist says teams are moving quickly on young players. [43:44, 44:16]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Three or four year decision" for a draft pick. [05:39]
- Roughly 300 three-point attempts in each of two workouts, made "almost all." [12:22]
- Shot "over 40%" from three as a rookie. [12:54]
- A caption reading "20g honest calls a year ... 19 of those turned out to be nothing" is garbled; the intent is about 20 tips and 19 duds. [24:15]
- Studying a prospect "4 to 6 years," and teams spending "16 hours a day for three months" before the draft. [30:53]
- "14 or 15" big players drafted in picks 10 through 30 last year. [36:30]
- A prospect described at six foot six and about 160 pounds, later six foot nine playing point guard. [19:33, 20:04]
- No metric definitions are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Group process: scouting, analytics, medical, psychological and background streams are combined and discussed. [03:06, 06:42]
- Heuristics and bias reading (Kahneman is named in the captions). [07:13]
- Review of own decisions against the top 100 prospects. [25:49]
- Trade evaluation: expected outcome of a pick versus a player under contract, with cap effects. [28:21]
- Fit to team style and development environment. [07:44, 41:06]

## Limits and open questions

- No data or model is shown; every claim is anecdote from the panelists.
- Captions have no speaker labels, so who said what is often unclear.
- Examples are hits the panel can name; misses are discussed less.
- Panelists speak for their own organizations, and several claims are institutional views (for example, on the one-and-done rule).
- Several names and details are garbled in the captions.

## Q&A

- Best available versus need. [34:57]
- Next trend. [37:31]
- Effect of ending one-and-done. [39:05]
- What can be taught after the draft. [41:06]
- When to cut bait. [42:07]

## Summary

A panel of a players' association researcher, a sports technology adviser, a former NFL player with a neck injury and an anatomist discusses why sports science has not made injuries disappear. The panel stresses trust, communication and athlete access to their own data over technology alone. They discuss the tension between player health and contract risk, the role of independent medical opinions, personalized protection and care, and why adoption of sports science varies. It is a discussion of practice and culture, with one personal injury account, and offers no data analysis.

## Key claims

- Football's anatomy (head leaning forward, weak neck) means higher injury risk by sport design. [02:02, 02:35]
- Team doctors work for the team, so concussions may not reach independent care; a panelist wants doctors inside locker rooms. [03:07, 03:37]
- Communication and trust are the most integral part of a program. [04:09, 05:09]
- Technology is an enabler; experts must give context and explain to athletes why they are doing it. [05:40, 06:10]
- The aim is to mitigate risk, not eliminate injuries; in key games the best players still play. [06:10, 06:40]
- Next steps for data are sport, then position, then individual context. [08:11, 08:42]
- One player says a daily check on sleep and eating, with a readiness percentage, helped him. [09:45, 10:16]
- A wearables committee was set up under the latest collective bargaining agreement to vet products for reliability and validity, with privacy and legal layers. [11:18]
- A new ligament in the front of the neck has been described recently. [12:24]
- The player describes a neck fracture and spinal cord contusion; he says he does not know if it was preventable. [13:56, 16:32, 21:09]
- The panel says the mental side of injury is large, and the union finds former players with similar injuries to talk to current players. [22:44, 23:14]
- A retired-player health screening program and research on retirees are in place. [24:18, 24:48]
- Parties in an injury (GM, medical director, athlete, agent, owner) need different framing. [26:21]
- Open organizations without silos tend to do best, as seen by one panelist. [27:23, 28:24]
- Athletes may not be honest about sleep or soreness if they fear consequences, and injury history affects contracts. [30:30, 31:01, 32:04]
- Giving athletes more medical options and giving both parties access to the same data may help. [33:07, 34:09]
- Athletes are treated too similarly; a panelist wants personalized imaging and equipment. [35:11, 36:12]
- Meals at team facilities are now standard, unlike in 2005. [38:18, 38:49]
- Sports science took longer to take hold in the US for reasons including athlete numbers abroad, framing of the tool to coaches, and strong unions. [40:24, 40:54, 42:28]
- Teams now add performance staff instead of handing technology to a strength coach. [41:56]

## Numbers and definitions

- Head about "five kilos." [02:02]
- Player injury date given as "November 1st 2015." [13:56]
- Readiness percentages of 70% and 90% in the daily check. [10:16]
- A caption about a speed of "25 and 1/2 miles per hour" for a player is garbled. [07:10]

- Access to collected data for both sides. [34:09]

## Summary

A speaker from a sports analytics company argues the field has plenty of data but too few insights, and that analysis must be dynamic and explainable to practitioners. He presents Premier League examples: win-rate splits based on a few match metrics, position-specific profiles, links from weekly training load to match mistakes, and hamstring injury thresholds that combine several measures. He says acute to chronic ratio alone showed no relationship with injury but did in combination with others. ## Summary

Brandon Payne, who says he owns Accelerate Basketball, describes a ten-point training philosophy built over roughly eight or nine years and used with Stephen Curry. He says the philosophy came first and technology was added where it fit without slowing sessions. The argument is that a less explosive player can close the gap by training the brain along with the body, and that drills double as readiness assessments. Conditioning is redefined as keeping decision accuracy and speed when tired, tested by repeating a light-based decision drill after simulated quarters. The talk is a practitioner description with video clips. No data, sample sizes or outcomes are shown.

## Key claims

- Technology was added to a philosophy built in 2008 and 2009, not the other way round. [02:10]
- Curry would not top an NFL-style combine of explosive athletes, so the gap to more athletic players has to be closed another way. [05:44]
- Technology should not replace the player's own work, and overloading a player with it makes them shut it out. [08:20]
- The same philosophy is scaled from age three or four up to NBA players. Drill speed and implementation change, but the elements stay the same. [09:53]
- The tennis-ball and dribbling overload drill is an assessment, not a ball-handling drill. The coach watches for held breath, shoulders rocking (core not engaged) and knees buckling in. [10:55] [11:56]
- If any of those signs appear, the speaker concludes the brain-body link is not ready for accelerated learning that day. [12:26]
- Everyone has a physical ceiling. The aim is to reach it, then use the brain (decisions, efficiency) to operate past it. [13:27] [13:58]
- A headphone brain-stimulation product was added to physical activation in the past 18 months. The speaker says it looks good after reading the literature and cites no study. [14:28] [14:59]
- An oxygen mask is used to produce a winded state in stationary drills, not to build conditioning, so the offseason body is not stressed further. [16:31] [17:04]
- Light discs flash colours that map to assigned moves, and players sometimes freeze when several flash at once. The tool is used for decision-making and for grading conditioning. [18:06] [19:08]
- Every drill trains three movement elements: acceleration, deceleration and dynamic stability. Video is important for this. [19:40] [20:10]
- Conditioning tests that players must pass are not used. The aim is the same decision at the same speed at minute 48 as at minute one. [21:11] [21:42]
- Conditioning is graded by repeating a baseline decision drill after each simulated quarter. If fourth-quarter scores match pregame scores, the speaker says he knows the player is ready for 82 games. [23:15] [23:48]

## Summary

Four sports executives and a Wharton moderator talk about how cognitive bias affects front-office decisions. They agree that people are poor decision makers and discuss luck versus process, anchoring, loss aversion, regret, group think and owner influence. Practical tools they describe include writing a thesis and rereading it, reversing a trade, treating each decision as independent, and asking scouts to explain their weighting. They debate blending quantitative models with subjective scouting, how to judge scouts, and whether team chemistry causes winning. The panel is mostly anecdote from the speakers' own experience.

## Key claims

- A panelist said people are very poor at decisions and that even knowing about biases such as anchoring and loss aversion does not remove them. [02:34]
- Each decision should be treated as independent of earlier ones; a prior assumption about a college or region can mislead. [06:39]
- Good outcomes involve luck, and a right process can still produce a bad outcome. [07:41]
- Leaders should act as a corrective against over-praising good moves and over-grieving bad ones. [08:11]
- Over-correcting by thinking too much about bias can stifle a decision. [09:11]
- A secret grading ballot may give a false sense of independence because staff share the same training. [10:12]
- Model-versus-expert studies in other fields suggest added expertise can make a model worse; whether sports models are good enough to be improved is open. [11:46]
- Hands stay on the knobs because data is thin and does not know the future of a young player. [12:46]
- The first Moneyball-style draft was purely objective, and a panelist said he would not recommend that. [15:18]
- Subjective scouting became a data point in decisions once a quantitative colleague pushed for balance. [16:49]
- Some of the best analysts weigh analytics lower because they have seen where it misleads. [18:21]
- Predicting a young player's course is like predicting a stranger, so gather many data points about the person. [19:54]
- Scouts cannot be expected to predict a 17-year-old's ten-year result; ground-level information adds value. [20:56]
- A draftee's early performance in instruction or practice may reveal a lower pick as better, and a team should accept that. [22:28]
- Ordinal ranking of subjective qualities can aid decisions (a panelist cited Kahneman and a paper). [23:29]
- A firefighter example in the captions is used to argue that "gut" is accumulated information. [24:29]
- Ask scouts to explain how they weight things; share of an evaluation resting on one data point matters. [27:01]
- Test a strong claim as a hypothesis: the panelist had ten staff rate a player's ball handling on random video. [28:03]
- Passionate advocates are useful because they expose reasoning. [28:34]
- A panelist described clearing the slate with a new strategy, citing a 2011 trade of three players. [30:09]
- Write the argument down and reread it, or have someone else poke holes. [30:39]
- Write an investment thesis with confidence, set it aside two weeks, and reread. [31:10]
- Reverse every trade: would you do the other side? [31:41]
- A panelist described a hypothetical removal of a player to test whether regret was driving resistance to a trade. [32:44]
- Owners' hints shift staff decisions quickly, and a panelist said hunkering down is common in sports organizations. [34:49], [35:50]
- Transparency with the owner was the lesson one panelist took from his first year as GM. [39:26]
- Panelists said they mostly took accepted ideas to their logical conclusion (more threes, drafting stars). [40:58]
- A team without a singular edge that it resources is not differentiated. [43:04]
- Baseball is becoming a more efficient market, in a panelist's view, and football is not. [47:09]
- Panelists thought a GM could switch sports if the job is leadership and building a rational organization. [48:40]
- Chemistry: one panelist has never seen a winning team without it; the panel debated causal direction and suggested a virtuous or vicious cycle. [50:43], [54:49]
- Prediction of who will improve chemistry should carry low confidence. [55:49]
- Fans and owners can react negatively when a traded player does well elsewhere, which a panelist linked to loss aversion. [1:00:24]

- Group grading on a 1 to 10 scale by secret ballot. [09:42]
- A drafted player projected over about a 10-year period. [19:23]
- A team drafts about 50 players in baseball. [21:58]

## Summary

A four-person NBA panel describes how front offices combine analytics, scouting, medical work and background research when drafting. - A panelist objects to calling traditional scouting "gut," saying it is done systematically. [02:03]
- It helps to read both the most positive and most negative evaluator on a prospect, because that shows blind spots. [03:06]
- Being right can be for the wrong reasons, and being wrong can come from team situation or injury. [03:36]
- Information overload is a challenge, so teams must decide what matters. [04:06]
- Teams now tolerate less character or background risk than 10 to 15 years ago. [05:09]
- A draft pick is a three or four year decision, so no playing time in year one is not automatically a failure. [05:39]
- Defining value is hard because the league changes; a back-to-the-basket center prized earlier now has little value. [08:15]
- Versatility and switching defense are valued now, with one panelist's example of a player once out of the league for lacking a position. [09:18, 10:19]
- A prospect can look worse in college or overseas because he is used poorly there, so context matters. [10:49]
- One panelist describes weighing a player's non-contact workouts against a weak college stretch; the player later shot over 40% as a rookie. [11:51, 12:22, 12:54]
- Another prospect was judged by the panelist as poorly fit to his college team, so the college snapshot was discounted. [13:24, 13:54]
- Interviews and workouts do not get a player drafted but can address concerns. [14:56]
- Even with a lot of information on one prospect, the panel says outcomes were unclear; one panelist says prediction of human behavior is hard in any field. [15:26, 15:57]
- Panelists wish NBA teams could watch high school competition; one notes some outside tracking data now exists. [16:28, 17:00]
- A network of contacts abroad is what led one panelist to see a foreign prospect early. [19:02, 19:33]
- One panelist would throw out one league's stats entirely; international leagues change year to year, so stats need current context. [20:37, 22:11]
- Too much data needs processes about what you value; experience teaches not to overreact to a short stretch. [22:42, 23:14, 23:45]
- Experience with analytical tools and with medical information makes the evidence easier to weigh. [24:47, 25:18]
- Teams should review the whole draft, not just one pick, and adjust method if a good result came from luck. [25:49, 26:20]
- Some boards are shaped by ownership or the GM through red flags, so a decision may be about culture or health more than talent. [26:20, 26:50]
- Most teams hold similar boards, so surprises are rare. [27:20, 27:50]
- Trade offers add a comparison between a pick and a player under contract, plus cap questions. [28:21]
- The missing data is mental: how players handle money, attention and lifestyle. [29:53, 30:23]
- Need breaks ties among similar players; a team that is resetting takes bets on talent. [34:57, 35:28, 36:00]
- A panelist predicts a return of defensive innovation; star outliers force other teams to adjust. [38:02, 38:34]
- Panelists do not look forward to scouting high school players if one-and-done ends, and think teams oppose removal of the rule. [40:05, 40:36]
- One drafted player was dropped after a year of work on one skill with no improvement. [42:39, 43:10]
- A panelist says teams are moving quickly on young players. [43:44, 44:16]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Three or four year decision" for a draft pick. [05:39]
- Roughly 300 three-point attempts in each of two workouts, made "almost all." [12:22]
- Shot "over 40%" from three as a rookie. [12:54]
- A caption reading "20g honest calls a year ... 19 of those turned out to be nothing" is garbled; the intent is about 20 tips and 19 duds. [24:15]
- Studying a prospect "4 to 6 years," and teams spending "16 hours a day for three months" before the draft. [30:53]
- "14 or 15" big players drafted in picks 10 through 30 last year. [36:30]
- A prospect described at six foot six and about 160 pounds, later six foot nine playing point guard. [19:33, 20:04]
- No metric definitions are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Group process: scouting, analytics, medical, psychological and background streams are combined and discussed. [03:06, 06:42]
- Heuristics and bias reading (Kahneman is named in the captions). [07:13]
- Review of own decisions against the top 100 prospects. [25:49]
- Trade evaluation: expected outcome of a pick versus a player under contract, with cap effects. [28:21]
- Fit to team style and development environment. [07:44, 41:06]

## Limits and open questions

- No data or model is shown; every claim is anecdote from the panelists.
- Captions have no speaker labels, so who said what is often unclear.
- Examples are hits the panel can name; misses are discussed less.
- Panelists speak for their own organizations, and several claims are institutional views (for example, on the one-and-done rule).
- Several names and details are garbled in the captions.

## Q&A

- Favorite drafting moment: getting your guy after years of study. [30:53]
- Best available versus need. [34:57]
- Next trend. [37:31]
- Effect of ending one-and-done. [39:05]
- What can be taught after the draft. [41:06]
- When to cut bait. [42:07]

## Summary

A panel of a players' association researcher, a sports technology adviser, a former NFL player with a neck injury and an anatomist discusses why sports science has not made injuries disappear. The panel stresses trust, communication and athlete access to their own data over technology alone. They discuss the tension between player health and contract risk, the role of independent medical opinions, personalized protection and care, and why adoption of sports science varies. It is a discussion of practice and culture, with one personal injury account, and offers no data analysis.

## Key claims

- Football's anatomy (head leaning forward, weak neck) means higher injury risk by sport design. [02:02, 02:35]
- Team doctors work for the team, so concussions may not reach independent care; a panelist wants doctors inside locker rooms. [03:07, 03:37]
- Communication and trust are the most integral part of a program. [04:09, 05:09]
- Technology is an enabler; experts must give context and explain to athletes why they are doing it. [05:40, 06:10]
- The aim is to mitigate risk, not eliminate injuries; in key games the best players still play. [06:10, 06:40]
- Next steps for data are sport, then position, then individual context. [08:11, 08:42]
- One player says a daily check on sleep and eating, with a readiness percentage, helped him. [09:45, 10:16]
- A wearables committee was set up under the latest collective bargaining agreement to vet products for reliability and validity, with privacy and legal layers. [11:18]
- A new ligament in the front of the neck has been described recently. [12:24]
- The player describes a neck fracture and spinal cord contusion; he says he does not know if it was preventable. [13:56, 16:32, 21:09]
- The panel says the mental side of injury is large, and the union finds former players with similar injuries to talk to current players. [22:44, 23:14]
- A retired-player health screening program and research on retirees are in place. [24:18, 24:48]
- Parties in an injury (GM, medical director, athlete, agent, owner) need different framing. [26:21]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: _HqxMC9h938
title: "SSAC18: Machine Learning in Performance Analytics"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [not stated]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, competitive-advantage, other-sport:soccer]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft

## Summary

A speaker from a sports analytics company argues the field has plenty of data but too few insights, and that analysis must be dynamic and explainable to practitioners. He presents Premier League examples: win-rate splits based on a few match metrics, position-specific profiles, links from weekly training load to match mistakes, and hamstring injury thresholds that combine several measures. He says acute to chronic ratio alone showed no relationship with injury but did in combination with others. He cautions that injury counts per team are small, so output should be descriptive, not a predictive formula. The work is a commercial product demonstration.

## Key claims

- Sport science has had too much data and too little insight, and teams do not want more. [00:00, 00:31]
- Performance and injuries are not binary, and differ across players and teams. [01:02]
- Humans cannot process the combinations involved, but computers alone cannot be trusted with decisions; both are needed. [02:34, 03:04]
- Analysis has to be dynamic, and unexplained "secret formula" risk scores are unusable for practitioners. [03:34, 04:04]
- Performance is the sum of individual performance and individual health. [04:34]
- Winning patterns differ by team and by opposing team type, with several routes to winning in the league data. [06:07, 06:41, 07:43]
- One team's strongest factor was avoiding "grave mistakes," not shots on target. [08:14, 08:44]
- Position profiles differ; for attacking midfielders, involvement in scoring attacks was most influential and winning aerial challenges was not helpful. [09:46, 10:16]
- For one team, two central defenders played most games while performing poorly; a loan signing performed better and was later signed for 20 million pounds. [12:19, 12:50]
- Lower weekly meters per minute linked to more mistakes; too much high-speed running, accelerating and decelerating linked to more than one mistake. [13:51]
- More sleep linked to more successful tackles; acute to chronic ratio between 1.5 and 2 improved tackles. [14:23]
- Larger swings in weekly meters per minute linked to many more lost balls for central defenders; the two poor-performing defenders were beyond that swing in poor weeks. [14:55, 15:56]
- The speaker asks if the signed defender was better or just better managed. [16:27]
- Injuries differ even within a diagnosis; medical records, mechanism, time in game, position, age, injury history and training load all matter. [17:27, 17:58, 18:29, 19:00]
- Hamstring example: hip mobility, acute to chronic ratio and a groin measure combined to define a higher-risk pattern; acute to chronic ratio alone showed no relationship. [21:03, 21:34]
- Workload may not be the problem; the response is, so the pattern should guide fixes, not a go or no-go. [21:34, 22:04]
- Game injuries should be analyzed separately from training injuries. [22:35]
- Teams set their own risk threshold, and the tool alerts them with reasons. [20:31, 21:03]

## Numbers and definitions

- 33 metrics, nine calculations and eight timelines yield 2376 univariate possibilities (33 times 9 times 8 matches this). [01:33, 02:03]
- 2.8 million multivariate possibilities (derivation not given). [02:34]
- Premier League tool: above 1.5 million metrics, over 1 billion multivariate possibilities in seconds. [05:37]
- 38 games for each team in the season analyzed. [05:37]
- Six or more shots on target: 78% wins; two or fewer: 11%. [06:07]
- More than 67 interceptions raises 11% to 42%. [06:41]
- Bottom bucket 7%; more than 15 counter-attacks gives 15%. [07:13]
- One team: 32% average win rate; more than one grave mistake gives 12%, none gives 69%; more than 18 successful tackles gives 75%. [08:14, 08:44]
- Grave mistake: giving the ball away to the opposition with a clear chance to score. [08:14]
- Attacking midfielders: more than one scoring attack gives 80%, otherwise 38%; passing accuracy above 81% moves 38% to 52%. [09:46, 10:16]
- Central defenders: more than three lost balls gives 3%, otherwise 46%; more than one grave mistake gives 0%. [11:49]
- Two standard deviations change in weekly meters per minute linked to a 6x increase in lost balls. [14:55, 15:56]
- Acute to chronic ratio between 1.5 and 2 on distance and high-speed running. [14:23]
- 47% of injuries are thigh injuries. [20:01]
- Hamstring: hip mobility above 41 degrees, acute to chronic ratio above 1.38 and groin squeeze above 293 gives 25% injury; the 0% claim for below 41 degrees is garbled in captions. [21:03]
- Game injuries about 15 times as frequent as training injuries. [22:35]
- 20 to 30 injuries per team in the data. [24:39]
- Captions are garbled for "more than twenty eight extra attacks in key passes" and the 68% figure. [06:41, 07:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Machine learning on Premier League match and tracking data with outcome KPIs per team and position. [05:37]
- Training load to KPI links using weekly aggregates. [13:51]
- Joined medical record, load and wellness data with four steps: choose injury type, set risk threshold, alerts, descriptive reasons. [20:01, 22:35]
- Aggregate league data from one optical tracking vendor for early slides; a single team's own data for team slides. [25:40]

## Limits and open questions

- Product demonstration; no method, validation or error rates shown, and the company is not named in captions.
- Thresholds come from one season or one league; the speaker says season-to-season results were "generally" similar, but the caption is unclear and no data is shown. [26:13]
- Only 20 to 30 injuries per team, so the speaker says this is descriptive, not predictive. [24:39]
- A questioner raises correlation versus causation; the caption of the answer ("certainly not correlation") is unclear. [24:09]
- Anecdotes about specific players and a transfer fee are not tested.
- The speaker says computers cannot be trusted, then markets automated alerts; the two are not reconciled.

## Q&A

- Correlation versus causation. [24:09]
- Data sources and vendor dependence. [25:10]
- Whether data is combined across teams. [25:40]
- Whether results hold season to season. [26:13]

## Summary

Four sports executives and a Wharton moderator talk about how cognitive bias affects front-office decisions. They agree that people are poor decision makers and discuss luck versus process, anchoring, loss aversion, regret, group think and owner influence. Practical tools they describe include writing a thesis and rereading it, reversing a trade, treating each decision as independent, and asking scouts to explain their weighting. They debate blending quantitative models with subjective scouting, how to judge scouts, and whether team chemistry causes winning. The panel is mostly anecdote from the speakers' own experience.

## Key claims

- A panelist said people are very poor at decisions and that even knowing about biases such as anchoring and loss aversion does not remove them. [02:34]
- Each decision should be treated as independent of earlier ones; a prior assumption about a college or region can mislead. [06:39]
- Good outcomes involve luck, and a right process can still produce a bad outcome. [07:41]
- Leaders should act as a corrective against over-praising good moves and over-grieving bad ones. [08:11]
- Over-correcting by thinking too much about bias can stifle a decision. [09:11]
- A secret grading ballot may give a false sense of independence because staff share the same training. [10:12]
- Model-versus-expert studies in other fields suggest added expertise can make a model worse; whether sports models are good enough to be improved is open. [11:46]
- Hands stay on the knobs because data is thin and does not know the future of a young player. [12:46]
- The first Moneyball-style draft was purely objective, and a panelist said he would not recommend that. [15:18]
- Subjective scouting became a data point in decisions once a quantitative colleague pushed for balance. [16:49]
- Some of the best analysts weigh analytics lower because they have seen where it misleads. [18:21]
- Predicting a young player's course is like predicting a stranger, so gather many data points about the person. [19:54]
- Scouts cannot be expected to predict a 17-year-old's ten-year result; ground-level information adds value. [20:56]
- A draftee's early performance in instruction or practice may reveal a lower pick as better, and a team should accept that. [22:28]
- Ordinal ranking of subjective qualities can aid decisions (a panelist cited Kahneman and a paper). [23:29]
- A firefighter example in the captions is used to argue that "gut" is accumulated information. [24:29]
- Ask scouts to explain how they weight things; share of an evaluation resting on one data point matters. [27:01]
- Test a strong claim as a hypothesis: the panelist had ten staff rate a player's ball handling on random video. [28:03]
- Passionate advocates are useful because they expose reasoning. [28:34]
- A panelist described clearing the slate with a new strategy, citing a 2011 trade of three players. [30:09]
- Write the argument down and reread it, or have someone else poke holes. [30:39]
- Write an investment thesis with confidence, set it aside two weeks, and reread. [31:10]
- Reverse every trade: would you do the other side? [31:41]
- A panelist described a hypothetical removal of a player to test whether regret was driving resistance to a trade. [32:44]
- Owners' hints shift staff decisions quickly, and a panelist said hunkering down is common in sports organizations. [34:49], [35:50]
- Transparency with the owner was the lesson one panelist took from his first year as GM. [39:26]
- Panelists said they mostly took accepted ideas to their logical conclusion (more threes, drafting stars). [40:58]
- A team without a singular edge that it resources is not differentiated. [43:04]
- Baseball is becoming a more efficient market, in a panelist's view, and football is not. [47:09]
- Panelists thought a GM could switch sports if the job is leadership and building a rational organization. [48:40]
- Chemistry: one panelist has never seen a winning team without it; the panel debated causal direction and suggested a virtuous or vicious cycle. [50:43], [54:49]
- Prediction of who will improve chemistry should carry low confidence. [55:49]
- Fans and owners can react negatively when a traded player does well elsewhere, which a panelist linked to loss aversion. [1:00:24]

- Group grading on a 1 to 10 scale by secret ballot. [09:42]
- A drafted player projected over about a 10-year period. [19:23]

## Summary

Four sports executives and a Wharton moderator talk about how cognitive bias affects front-office decisions. Practical tools they describe include writing a thesis and rereading it, reversing a trade, treating each decision as independent, and asking scouts to explain their weighting. ## Summary

Brandon Payne, who says he owns Accelerate Basketball, describes a ten-point training philosophy built over roughly eight or nine years and used with Stephen Curry. He says the philosophy came first and technology was added where it fit without slowing sessions. The argument is that a less explosive player can close the gap by training the brain along with the body, and that drills double as readiness assessments. Conditioning is redefined as keeping decision accuracy and speed when tired, tested by repeating a light-based decision drill after simulated quarters. The talk is a practitioner description with video clips. No data, sample sizes or outcomes are shown.

## Key claims

- Technology was added to a philosophy built in 2008 and 2009, not the other way round. [02:10]
- Curry would not top an NFL-style combine of explosive athletes, so the gap to more athletic players has to be closed another way. [05:44]
- Technology should not replace the player's own work, and overloading a player with it makes them shut it out. [08:20]
- The same philosophy is scaled from age three or four up to NBA players. Drill speed and implementation change, but the elements stay the same. [09:53]
- The tennis-ball and dribbling overload drill is an assessment, not a ball-handling drill. The coach watches for held breath, shoulders rocking (core not engaged) and knees buckling in. [10:55] [11:56]
- If any of those signs appear, the speaker concludes the brain-body link is not ready for accelerated learning that day. [12:26]
- Everyone has a physical ceiling. The aim is to reach it, then use the brain (decisions, efficiency) to operate past it. [13:27] [13:58]
- A headphone brain-stimulation product was added to physical activation in the past 18 months. The speaker says it looks good after reading the literature and cites no study. [14:28] [14:59]
- An oxygen mask is used to produce a winded state in stationary drills, not to build conditioning, so the offseason body is not stressed further. [16:31] [17:04]
- Light discs flash colours that map to assigned moves, and players sometimes freeze when several flash at once. The tool is used for decision-making and for grading conditioning. [18:06] [19:08]
- Every drill trains three movement elements: acceleration, deceleration and dynamic stability. Video is important for this. [19:40] [20:10]
- Conditioning tests that players must pass are not used. The aim is the same decision at the same speed at minute 48 as at minute one. [21:11] [21:42]
- Conditioning is graded by repeating a baseline decision drill after each simulated quarter. If fourth-quarter scores match pregame scores, the speaker says he knows the player is ready for 82 games. [23:15] [23:48]
- Overload and contrast (bands, heavy balls, accelerometers) is used to teach new movements. [24:19]
- Video and a shot-tracking product are used to see whether fatigue changes mechanics and shot arc, depth and location. [24:51] [25:21]
- Each drill is meant to serve several purposes, and a more body-aware player gets more from it. The drills also serve as feedback on readiness. [26:24] [26:57]

## Summary

Chris Collinssworth (caption spelling) and Neil Hornsby, founder of Pro Football Focus, present how PFF grades football players. Collinssworth argues that analysts are taking over decisions once left to veteran coaches. Hornsby explains that grades come from analysts watching every play, and that raw grades are then adjusted for the quality of each opportunity, such as time to throw, step drop, down and distance and alignment. He says grades score what should have happened on a play, not its result, and are a production measure that ignores injury and talent. - PFF was working with 25 teams, expecting 28 or 30, and the speakers say data analysts now make decisions once left to coaches. [01:16] [01:46]
- Raw grades are a blunt instrument. They must be turned into player grades by adjusting for the opportunity behind them. [13:05]

- Screens and rollouts are removed from the pass-rush set because they limit the chance to get pressure. [16:43] [17:14]
- Alignment matters: chance of pressure rises as a rusher lines up further from the centre. [17:14]
- Step drop matters: a rusher against a quarterback who takes many seven-step drops has more chance than one against a quarterback taking many three-step drops. [18:16] [18:46]

- The data go back ten years, and old seasons are graded too (2006 last year). [16:43] [38:37] [39:08]

He explains that NFL rules come from the collective bargaining agreement, not state law, outlines the league's staged testing and penalties, and notes a raised positive threshold. Four sports executives and a Wharton moderator talk about how cognitive bias affects front-office decisions. Practical tools they describe include writing a thesis and rereading it, reversing a trade, treating each decision as independent, and asking scouts to explain their weighting. - Good outcomes involve luck, and a right process can still produce a bad outcome. [07:41]
- Leaders should act as a corrective against over-praising good moves and over-grieving bad ones. [08:11]
- Over-correcting by thinking too much about bias can stifle a decision. [09:11]

title: "SSAC17: Player Grades: The Competitive Advantage in Football Performance"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Chris Collinssworth (caption spelling), Neil Hornsby; introduced by Barry Brney (caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]

## Summary

Chris Collinssworth (caption spelling) and Neil Hornsby, founder of Pro Football Focus, present how PFF grades football players. Collinssworth argues that analysts are taking over decisions once left to veteran coaches. Hornsby explains that grades come from analysts watching every play, and that raw grades are then adjusted for the quality of each opportunity, such as time to throw, step drop, down and distance and alignment. He says grades score what should have happened on a play, not its result, and are a production measure that ignores injury and talent. A coach is shown saying he disagreed with about a dozen of about 600 plays. A Q&A follows.

## Key claims

- PFF was working with 25 teams, expecting 28 or 30, and the speakers say data analysts now make decisions once left to coaches. [01:16] [01:46]
- Raw grades are a blunt instrument. They must be turned into player grades by adjusting for the opportunity behind them. [13:05]
- Counting opportunities is not enough. A tackle with 450 pass blocks can have faced more total time than one with 550, because the quarterback holds the ball longer. [14:07] [14:39]
- Factors named: time to throw, step drop, help or chips, slide protection, down and distance, opponent technique. [15:09] [15:40]
- Each player has a raw grade plus a normalization factor that compares the player with average. [16:11]
- Screens and rollouts are removed from the pass-rush set because they limit the chance to get pressure. [16:43] [17:14]
- Alignment matters: chance of pressure rises as a rusher lines up further from the centre. [17:14]
- Step drop matters: a rusher against a quarterback who takes many seven-step drops has more chance than one against a quarterback taking many three-step drops. [18:16] [18:46]
- Down and distance matters: a situational third-down rusher has more chance than a rusher who must also play the run. [19:16]
- Fatigue (number of rush attempts) showed noise over ten years, so it is left out. [19:49]
- A new process planned for 2017 will record matchup, block type, block location, how well it was done and the pass-rush move, to test whether assignment difficulty matters. The speaker does not know the answer. [21:51] [22:22] [22:53]
- An offensive line coach says he disagreed with about a dozen of about 600 negative plays and that the grades are close to what the players are. [24:25] [25:28]
- Grades are by position. Ranking across positions needs separate maths. [27:30] [28:02]
- Grading is done by about 350 people on a cloud system, with a second pass, a coach-network pass, then adjustment. [29:44] [30:15]
- Grades score what should have happened, not the result. The example is a game with five touchdown passes and no interceptions graded near zero. [31:17] [31:47] [32:17]
- Opponent-quality adjustment is done after grades are published, by looking at who a player faced. Matchup data will allow it directly. [32:56] [33:27] [33:58]
- PFF Ultimate is a tool to ask football questions and send answers to video or charts. [26:28]
- The data go back ten years, and old seasons are graded too (2006 last year). [16:43] [38:37] [39:08]
- The grade is a production metric for how a player is playing now. It ignores injury, talent and, at the moment, who was faced. [39:40]
- One speaker is less enamoured with red-zone statistics and says the game between the 20s differs from the game inside the 20. [37:05] [37:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- 25 teams now; 28 or 30 expected; about 20 teams met. [01:16]
- 300 to 350 people; 350 analysts. [02:16] [08:54]
- 30 quarterback disruptions in 450 or 550 pass blocks. [13:37]
- Seven-step drop, quarterback at 10 yards, rusher taken to 11 yards. [18:16]
- About 600 plays (two thirds of the season; caption garbled), disagreement with about a dozen. [24:25]
- Grade of 84 said to mean nothing to viewers; ranking instead, for example "number 117 of 117". [27:30]
- About 15 years average NFL coaching in the coach network; about 20 people can input at once. [29:44] [30:15]
- Ten years of data. [16:43]
- Definition: production metric = how the player is playing now, excluding injury, talent and opponent strength. [39:40]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Analysts grade every play, with multiple passes and coach review, producing raw grades.
- Opportunity normalization: adjust raw grade for time to throw, step drop, down and distance, alignment, help, and exclusions (screens, rollouts).
- Point-of-attack tapes built from raw grades for each player. [12:34]
- Grade by what should have happened on the play, not the outcome.
- 2017 matchup and block-type data project to test assignment difficulty.

## Limits and open questions

- Accuracy evidence shown is one coach's disagreement count (about a dozen of about 600), reported as small.
- Neither speaker gives the grade scale or the weights in the normalization.
- Collinssworth says he bought the company [08:54], and Hornsby sells the grades, so claims about accuracy are the vendors' view.
- Opponent strength is not yet in the grade, which the speaker admits. [39:40]
- Whether assignment difficulty matters is stated as unknown. [22:53]
- The captions garble parts of the Q&A, notably [30:45]. A talk about wide-receiver or evaluation (question) cannot be recovered.
- Mostly NFL examples; the FBS level is mentioned but no college results are shown.

## Q&A

- How is grading done by hand, and can it be automated? Answer: cloud input, multiple passes, coach network, then maths. [29:44]
- Question from a wide receiver (garbled caption). The answer says PFF grades should-have-happened, unlike league statistics. [30:45] [31:17]
- Why not adjust for above-average opposition in the grade? Answer: done after publication; matchup data will do it. [32:56]
- Value of the data set and uses beyond football (partly garbled). Answer: ten years of depth, possibly other sports. [34:29] [36:03]
- Red-zone statistics. Answer: personal scepticism; and a view that the game differs inside the 20. [36:34] [37:05]
- Grading history (Hall of Fame debates) and training new analysts. [38:37]

Andrew Brant (caption spelling), a former agent who says he worked for the Green Bay Packers for ten years, argues that growing public acceptance of marijuana is unlikely to reach the NFL through recreational use but may through pain management. - Eugene Monroe is described as a former lineman who says he was handed opioids early, had problems from overuse, and found marijuana better for pain. [19:53] [20:26]
- Concussion concern may be the route to getting owners to listen, and Monroe has donated to Johns Hopkins and Pennsylvania for study. [20:58] [21:30]
- The NFL has followed the science on concussions, and the speaker expects kickoff returns to disappear within five years. [23:34]
- The NFL tends to follow other leagues and avoid being a first mover on taboo subjects. [24:05]
- Change would need a bargaining trade, or a framing as health and safety, which he calls a tough sell. [26:41] [27:43]
- He does not expect another revision before the agreement ends in 2021. [26:41]

## Numbers and definitions

- 2016 ballot measures; 21 states allowing medicinal use, nine allowing recreational use including DC, and 21 illegal (caption ambiguous). [05:12]
- Positive threshold raised from 15 to 35 nanograms per millilitre; MLB at 15; the world anti-doping body at 115 (caption names are garbled: "anagrams", "water world anti-doping Association"). [09:23]
- Testing window April 20th to August 9th. [10:55] [11:26]
- Stage 1: 90-day treatment plan; violation fine of three of 17 weeks' pay (caption reads "317"). [12:28] [12:59]
- Stage 2: up to 10 tests a month, four hours to give a sample, 12 to 24 months; first violation a two-week fine versus four weeks for performance-enhancing drugs; second violation leads to a four-to-six-game suspension. [12:59] [13:30] [14:01] [14:35]
- Stage 3: ten-game suspension, then one-year banishment with reapplication; the stage 2 testing regime continues for the rest of the career. [15:06] [15:38] (caption says "in Italy", likely garbled)
- Opioid study: 25 percent felt pressure; "7%" taking them at three times the national rate (caption ambiguous). [16:44]
- Collective bargaining agreement ends 2021. [26:41]
- Fourteen padded practices in season. [28:14]
- About 95 percent of brains tested for CTE at BU (caption says "95%"), a sample he calls slanted. [31:09] [31:39]

- The staged NFL testing and penalty system.
- A bargaining frame: marijuana as a trade item versus a health-and-safety issue like concussions.
- The "follow the science" frame borrowed from concussion policy.

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker repeatedly says he is not a scientist [09:23] [28:14]; claims on cannabis for pain and CTE cite no study, and the Washington Post study is not shown.
- He is a former agent and team executive, so his bargaining views are his own.
- Anecdotes: Packers Toradol, Eugene Monroe's account, and players he says he knows.

- Monroe's quotes are advocacy and the talk does not test them.
- Captions garble league names and units at [09:23] and [15:06].

---

video_id: 81CC-uLrOtE
title: "SSAC17: Ball Don't Lie: The Future of Basketball Analytics"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Barry brudney (host, caption spelling), Zach low (moderator, caption spelling), Luis skola (caption spelling), Mike Zaron (caption spelling), Vin Alro (caption spelling), Dean Oliver, Sue (first name only, [59:29])]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel of a current player, a front-office executive, a former player and coach, a WNBA guard and an analytics executive discusses where basketball analytics goes next. The recurring argument is that tracking data is most useful when it produces small, specific, coachable findings (who gets hung up on screens, how often hands go up) and when it reaches players in a form they can use. The panel also covers wearables, tests that players can train for, how to judge coaches, and officiating data. The speakers repeatedly stress that human judgment and communication decide whether a number gets used.

## Key claims

- Camera tracking data is most valuable for small defensive details (screen handling, closeouts, hand position), not for confirming large strategic trends. [02:44]
- Every screen can now be identified and reviewed, which lets analysts speak in coaches' terms. [03:15]
- Giving a coach the percentage of ways an opponent creates a shot lets a staff decide which version to concede. [04:17]
- A panelist argued that a small fix, such as one high hand, can decide a game because runs happen fast. [05:19]
- Data is a way to build a relationship with a player, but it has to be delivered simply; the panel says players are far behind coaches and analysts in understanding numbers. [09:24]
- Seeing percentages about yourself can become a mental problem (a player described being told which direction she shoots better and then overthinking it). [10:25]
- Some panelists said numbers help a team know the opponent better than they help a player know himself. [11:25]
- Some players can take many items and others only one or two, so staff must know the individual. [11:56]
- A panelist told young players they will have to understand analytics eventually, so they should start early. [12:27]
- For acquisitions, the useful question is fit: whether a player's skills overlap with or add to existing players. [19:36]
- A panelist argued against combining skill metrics into one good-or-bad score; instead, keep the skill metrics and weigh them by the team's system. [20:06]
- Fit analysis can be done quickly if the groundwork is built before the deadline. [21:08]
- Psychological or neurological tests should be tested against on-court results before being trusted; vendors who say they can quantify them need checking. [25:12]
- Physical numbers need context: compare a strong, high-jumping player with another who rebounds more. [25:42]
- A team's hand-coordination test matched its deflection chart, but players who trained for the test rose in the rankings without rising in deflections. [28:15]
- Training for a test exclusively changes the result without translating to the game. [28:45]
- Some teams are growing skeptical of wearables and asking whether a device is worth its cost. [29:45]
- One panelist trusts sport scientists by default but wants to confirm they cause no harm and keep looking. [31:16]
- A practice described as a "light" half-court session was tracked as much harder than a full-court one, and the player said this kind of information is crucial. [32:48]
- Perceived exertion compared with tracking data could indicate whether a player is getting hurt, if one player's rating drifts from the group. [33:50]
- A panelist is willing to wear a device in games and argued analytics tools only need to be a little better than what came before, not perfect. [35:21]
- Players who dismiss a mismatch between feel and data are common, and some may use the data as an excuse. [36:53]
- A panelist said team and player interests are nearly always aligned on this data, so the excuse problem is not a reason to withhold it. [37:23]
- Wearable data identified a drill coaches had called a throwaway as very tiring. [38:26]
- One panelist said most "new" ideas from outsiders were tried and discarded earlier. [39:30]
- A panelist proposed game-format practices with tracked stats scaled up to build bigger samples for lineup analysis. [41:02]
- A shoot-around is disliked by some panelists, who said sleep matters more. [42:34]
- Wide-open three-point range extension is described as becoming common in the league. [44:07]
- Coaching quality is hard to measure; indirect measures such as player development under a coach do not say why. [48:47]
- Coaching is a bundle of skills, some measurable (lineups) and some human (teaching). [50:49]
- The league's openness with teams about officiating process was praised, though calls will still anger teams. [56:56]
- Coaches track short-term patterns well, with a staff and bench computer; longer-term patterns are harder for human brains. [58:58]

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length 45 minutes plus 15 minutes of Q&A. [00:42]
- A coach was told high hands were happening 10 percent of the time (an illustrative example). [04:48]
- The "80" and "2 minutes" in the run discussion are garbled in the captions; do not rely on them. [04:48]
- One panelist is 36. [10:55]
- Information can be pulled up within 5 minutes for most fit questions. [21:08]
- The draft-combine example questions: 90 cents in five coins, and how many balloons fit in a room (10,000 cited). [22:10]
- One player's team in Russia did tests for 30 seconds each; he played there 10 years. [26:13]
- Perceived exertion example: players rate a practice eight or nine while the coach thinks two. [33:19]
- 440 NBA players next year (as stated). [34:21]
- A panelist said team and player interests align 98 percent of the time. [37:23]
- Multiply tracked stats by four for a one-quarter scrimmage, by two for two quarters. [41:02]
- Shoot-around: the speaker said she believed the other 11 teams in her league have one. [42:04]
- Three-point range: 28 to 30 footers cited for two named players. [44:07]
- Russell Westbrook triple-double streak described as something not done in 50 years. [46:43]
- Of the 30 NBA coaches, a hypothetical person might class three as good, three as bad and not know 24. [51:20]
- Win Share and adjusted plus-minus per minute were suggested for MVP. [45:41]
- Perceived exertion (RPE) is defined by the panel as the player's rating of how hard a practice was. [33:19]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Optical player tracking (SportVU/camera data, "sport view" in the captions) for possessions and screens.
- Pick-and-roll coverage and screen quality analysis from tracking data.
- Wearable tracking (Zephyr, caption spelling) compared with perceived exertion.
- Test-the-test: validate non-basketball tests against on-court outcomes.
- Game-format practice to enlarge samples.
- Indirect coach evaluation via player development with and without a coach.
- Points per possession for youth-level video tracking.

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker attribution is unclear in the auto captions; many statements cannot be tied to a named panelist.
- Most evidence is anecdote; no sample sizes or results were shown for wearables, tests or practice formats.
- The panel did not resolve whether wearables improve outcomes; skepticism was acknowledged.
- A panelist's contractual limit prevented discussion of one team's front office. [16:05]
- Claims about player-team interest alignment (98 percent) are one panelist's view, not data.
- No research evidence was named for the coach-evaluation approach.

## Q&A

- MVP analytics: panelists named Win Share and adjusted plus-minus, and noted award voting is often based on a stat. [45:41]
- Analytics for youth and high school coaches: cheap video tools and points per possession. [47:47]
- How to measure coaches: indirect development measures and lineups; much remains unmeasured. [48:47]
- Officiating data: panelists praised league transparency and discussed adding a fourth referee. [55:55]
- Real-time data to coaches: staff track plays by hand or bench computer; coaches remember short-term patterns. [58:28]

## Summary

A presentation from a company that combines athlete tracking data with coaching video. The main speaker, a former college football graduate assistant, argues that data only matters if coaches understand it and believe it. He uses a personal story about missing bowl-game stats to show that analysts must know the limits of their data. He describes observed versus laboratory metrics, the value of consistent third-party data, and the need to validate new tracked metrics against film. He says staff should set thresholds, and analysts should earn trust by checking current decisions. The talk is a vendor presentation.

## Key claims

- The company's data pairs with coaching video, since coaches work in video. [02:06]
- Analysts must know the boundaries of their data; a missed bowl-game stat in a report cost the speaker and a colleague credibility with the head coach. [05:41]
- Metrics have long come in two kinds: observed (video, practice) and laboratory. [06:42]
- Some fields are empirical (down, distance) and others subjective (formation, personnel), and verbiage differs by staff. [08:14]
- Third-party data gives consistent definitions across teams. [09:46]
- A defined metric such as burn defender can save coaches large amounts of review time, at the cost of some false positives. [10:18]
- Coaches grew willing to use third-party data after comparing it with their own for about a year. [10:49]
- Staff buy-in decides whether findings are used. [12:23]
- Metrics must be accurate and precise, and must help win a game. [14:28]
- A researcher whose results cannot be explained to a coach does not matter to the coach. [15:30]
- Wearables allow metrics from practice and games rather than the laboratory. [16:01]
- Staff must decide the threshold that matters for a given sport and metric. [18:03]
- Coaches often get spreadsheets of tracking numbers that do not relate to their coaching points. [18:33]
- Load metrics can address within-game, weekly and seasonal preparation and injury risk, but coaches often do not understand them. [19:03]
- Players may resist if they fear the data shows they are out of shape. [19:34]
- The company validated a repeat-effort movement metric against hours of video. [20:35]
- A radar view overlays tracked speed on practice film, letting coaches pick color thresholds. [22:06]
- Specific film examples (a cut one way versus the other) make the data usable with athletes. [22:38]
- Buy-in needs to run from head coach to players. [23:09]
- Build the relationship by checking how the staff decides today and validating or invalidating it. [24:11]
- Many research papers will go unused if no team relates to them. [24:41]

## Numbers and definitions

- The speaker's story is dated 1996 (first year as graduate assistant), with a call in 2000. [02:36], [04:40]
- Report: a three-ring binder about an inch thick, several hundred pages. [03:38]
- The captions for the player's bowl-game line are garbled: five catches and a figure that reads "another hundred 38 yards." [03:38]
- Burn defender: defined as a receiver within two yards of the person who caught the ball. [10:18]
- 256 games and 40,000 plays for an NFL season; the captions say 87 results with "eight full false positives" (garbled). [10:18]
- Hockey example: heart rate above 165 beats per minute, a shift of 25 seconds, recovery in under 20 seconds versus two minutes on the bench. [17:32]
- Coaches and scouts watch video 10 to 14 hours a day. [20:35]
- The movement metric was developed over a year. [20:35]
- Radar-view example threshold of 12 miles an hour; the second figure ("80 miles hour") is garbled. [22:06]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Observed versus laboratory metrics.
- Peer-review test: accurate, precise, understandable to coaches, helps win.
- Validation of tracked metrics against video by staff.
- Radar view: tracked speed over practice film with staff-chosen thresholds.
- Third-party event data (a named provider appears in captions as "ProFootballFocus").

## Limits and open questions

- The talk is a vendor presentation; claims about the value of combining video and wearable data are the speaker's commercial view.
- No data, sample sizes or results were shown for any validation.
- Captions are very garbled in several passages (speed thresholds, false-positive counts, statistics).
- Names in the story may be misspelled. Adam "gay" in the captions was named as a former student and later a head coach of the Dolphins (caption spelling).
- Smart-ball and heart-rate examples are described as examples, not results.
- No Q&A was captured; the talk ends with applause. [25:11]

## Q&A

No Q&A in the captions.

## Summary

The speaker argues that sports data scientists need subject matter knowledge, including basic physiology, because athletes differ by sport and by position, and so should the way they are measured. She compares NFL and NBA combine results by position, questions whether single tests (the bench press especially) suit every position, and presents a measurement model with physical, physiological, psychological, behavioral and environmental variables. She briefly describes a tennis pilot on narcissism and calls for individualized "precision athleticism" using wearables, borrowed from precision medicine. The talk is a broad survey drawn from her new book, with few numbers and no validation data.

## Key claims

- Data scientists in sport should be able to discuss their sport as a fan would, not only the numbers [02:05].
- Muscle fiber type is partly genetic and partly trained; type one fibers resist fatigue but give less power and force, type two the reverse [04:37].
- The three energy systems are phosphagen, glycogen and oxidative; a maximal sprint relies on the first only briefly before speed drops [06:42, 07:14].
- Between sports, and between positions within a sport, athletes should be assessed and trained differently [10:16].
- NFL combine results differ by position, shown with a simple ANOVA on public data [13:52].
- The bench press may not suit some positions; she asked whether a quarterback should be tested on it at all and said she was only posing questions [13:52].
- Height is not the best predictor in basketball; wingspan and hand size are better [17:00].
- Psychological variables are often neglected and should be measured, but available scales are self-reported and biased [19:34, 20:05].
- Outliers should be studied, not just removed [23:07].
- Treatment should be individualized ("n of one") using wearables, as in precision medicine [27:13].
- Psychological variables can be trained, with some harder to change than others [30:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- Seven to eight muscle fiber types exist, simplified to type one and type two [03:36].
- Phosphagen system dominates the first five to 10 seconds of a maximal effort [06:42].
- Work to rest ratios of "1:3, 1:2, 1:20" are mentioned [08:15]; the captions are garbled and the intended ratios cannot be confirmed.
- NFL combine bench press is at 225 pounds; centers reached about 35 to 40 reps [13:21].
- NBA draft bench press is at 185 pounds, with results up to five, 10 or 15 reps [15:27, 15:59].
- "Load" here means resistance weight, not wearable load [15:59].
- Muscular strength is maximum force in one repetition; muscular endurance is maximum repetitions [13:21].
- Brady is cited as winning four out of six Super Bowls, as an outlier example [23:07].

## Methods and frameworks named

- ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests (normality assumed) on public combine data, in R [11:18, 13:52].

- Implicit association task to probe confidence versus narcissism by reaction time latency [21:05, 22:05].
- Precision medicine framing, "n of one" trials, time varying covariates [27:13, 27:44].

- The tennis pilot gave no sample size, results or validation [20:35 to 22:05].
- Combine position comparisons are not tied to game performance or to injury.
- Self-report measures are acknowledged as biased [20:05]; the implicit task was shown only as a similar example.

## Summary

The founder of a jump-measuring wearable describes his company's path from a waist-worn device that reports jump height and jump count to broadcast use (VERT Cast) and a new device that adds g-force and acceleration. He argues the same data serve fans, motivation, performance and injury prevention. Examples come mostly from volleyball: televised jump numbers, a 30 inch club for motivation, and a jump count cap in USA Volleyball practice. This is a company pitch with testimonials, not a study; no validity, reliability or injury data are shown.

## Key claims

- A waist-worn device logs jump height and count and syncs to an app [01:46].
- Jump count is an unmeasured load in volleyball and basketball, comparable to pitch count in baseball [06:21].
- Real-time jump data on Jumbotron and TV can drive fan engagement [07:54, 12:31].
- Public milestones (the 30 inch club) motivate athletes [13:01, 13:32].
- Coaches can set a jump count limit per practice; USA Volleyball players stop at a certain number to avoid overdoing it [16:07].
- Players have written to him saying they stayed healthy because of the product [16:38]; no data were shown.
- Step counts say little; measuring g-force of each movement says more about effort [19:12, 19:42].
- Combining jump, g-force and heart rate gives an idea of an athlete's condition [20:43].
- Future focus is recovery, looking at surges and jerk [22:16].
- A private mode keeps team data on the team's own servers [21:44].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables market expected to reach "$40 billion" by "20121" (garbled year) [04:49].
- Coaches notice jumps of 35 or 40 inches [05:51].
- Example in-game jumps of 32 inches [08:26] and 28.6 inches with seven kills [08:56]; top tournament jump 34 inches, later 34 and a half [10:59, 12:00].
- A player averaging 27 inches with best of 38 [10:29].
- 103 jumps shown on a coach screen; a practice cap of about 100 suggested; pitch count example of 58 [15:05, 15:36].
- Example g-force readings: 8.3 g peak; cycling example 3.2 rising to 4.1 [20:12].
- Heart rate of 110 during a convention [20:43].
- First NBA client the Miami Heat; first used in a game the week before [21:13, 21:44].
- Built "in about two years" [24:49]; USA men's team win after 30 years [24:19].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable jump and g-force sensor with app, team system (VERT Coach) for multiple sensors, VERT Cast broadcast feed [15:05, 02:18].
- Jump count thresholds per position and drill [15:36].

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, reliability or validity data for jump height or g-force.
- Injury prevention is supported by testimonials only [16:38]; no outcome data.
- The USA volleyball medal results are credited loosely and are not evidence of a product effect [24:19].
- Speaker is the company founder; all claims are commercial.
- Several names (players, coaches) are garbled in captions and not repeated here.

## Q&A

- None; the talk ends at [24:49] with a closing remark and applause.

## Summary

Two vendor presenters introduce a near-field indoor tracking system for hockey and basketball, built after a team owner asked why GPS could not be used indoors. The system records position and speed and merges them with video and physiology monitors into video-centric reports, shown on screens or a Jumbotron as motivation. Most of the talk is the engineering pitch and a long Q&A on accuracy, subject limits, league approval and football fields. No team data are shown. It is a product description, with vendor-stated precision and no independent validation.

## Key claims

- Athlete monitoring makes workload and fatigue visible and may help prevent injury [04:29].
- Injury prediction is hard because of luck and missing covariates, in the lead speaker's view [04:59].
- Outdoor GPS companies struggle indoors with accuracy and obstruction [07:03].
- Near-field technology is not affected by line of sight, bunching or head position [09:08].
- Coaches already study video, so metrics should appear synchronized with video [05:29, 10:42].
- Live display of speed and velocity motivates players in training [13:17, 17:24].
- A virtual private network can let offsite clinicians review a player's metrics, but cloud servers are not recommended [14:48].
- The system is not approved for league games [23:05].

## Numbers and definitions

- Introduced in 2012; tested at The Edge Sports Center and at Boston University in 2013; system at the Honda Center from September [05:59, 06:31].
- 13 direct measurements [09:39, 10:11].
- Tag size of a pack of wooden matches, 3 to four hour duty cycle [11:15].
- Precision of 30 cm at 10 Hz [18:59].
- Limits of 20 subjects for hockey and 15 for basketball; a marching band test tracked 400 subjects at five Hertz [22:03, 22:34].
- Range: about a hockey rink of 200 by 95; a thousand yard track tried the previous week [24:36, 25:08].
- 2D capture currently, 3D planned [16:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Near-field electromagnetic tag with three-axis antenna, claimed to work through walls [19:59, 20:30].
- Synchronized capture of video, computer-generated animation, biometrics from third-party monitors, and a metrics panel [08:35, 12:16].
- Reports by line, shift, time in zone [13:47].

## Limits and open questions

- No team results shown (the speaker explained a team's data could not be shared) [12:47].
- Accuracy claim is the vendor's; no validation study cited.
- Claim of superiority to accelerometer-based systems is unsupported [20:30].
- Football fields and indoor football were still under test [25:08, 25:38].
- Only one team can be tracked; whether both sides could be is a league decision [23:05].
- Caption inconsistency: company named "bioamp" at [00:22] and "biocam" later.

## Q&A

- Hardware dimensions: 2D capture now [16:51].
- Sport psychology use: motivation and feedback plus practice for learning [17:24, 17:55].
- Precision and sampling: 30 cm at 10 Hz [18:59].
- How it differs from competitors: near-field shortwave, video combined with workload [19:59, 20:30, 21:01].
- Only tagged subjects tracked [21:01].
- How many subjects: 20 hockey, 15 basketball [22:03].
- Both teams in games: league decision [23:05].
- Tag type: shown against a coin [24:05].
- Venue size: rink sized, football fields planned [24:36, 25:08].
- Puck tracking: not practical, but grip and EMG were put in a stick [26:12, 26:44].
