---
type: video-summary
video_id: LkNYHpC82yc
title: "SSAC16: Sports Performance  Measurement and Analytics"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Dr Lorena Martin (caption spelling, named by the host)]
topics: [sports-science, american-football, basketball, injury-health, other-sport:tennis]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker argues that sports data scientists need subject matter knowledge, including basic physiology, because athletes differ by sport and by position, and so should the way they are measured. She compares NFL and NBA combine results by position, questions whether single tests (the bench press especially) suit every position, and presents a measurement model with physical, physiological, psychological, behavioral and environmental variables. She briefly describes a tennis pilot on narcissism and calls for individualized "precision athleticism" using wearables, borrowed from precision medicine. The talk is a broad survey drawn from her new book, with few numbers and no validation data.

## Key claims

- Data scientists in sport should be able to discuss their sport as a fan would, not only the numbers [02:05].
- Muscle fiber type is partly genetic and partly trained; type one fibers resist fatigue but give less power and force, type two the reverse [04:37].
- The three energy systems are phosphagen, glycogen and oxidative; a maximal sprint relies on the first only briefly before speed drops [06:42, 07:14].
- Between sports, and between positions within a sport, athletes should be assessed and trained differently [10:16].
- NFL combine results differ by position, shown with a simple ANOVA on public data [13:52].
- The bench press may not suit some positions; she asked whether a quarterback should be tested on it at all and said she was only posing questions [13:52].
- Height is not the best predictor in basketball; wingspan and hand size are better [17:00].
- Psychological variables are often neglected and should be measured, but available scales are self-reported and biased [19:34, 20:05].
- Outliers should be studied, not just removed [23:07].
- Treatment should be individualized ("n of one") using wearables, as in precision medicine [27:13].
- Psychological variables can be trained, with some harder to change than others [30:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- Seven to eight muscle fiber types exist, simplified to type one and type two [03:36].
- Phosphagen system dominates the first five to 10 seconds of a maximal effort [06:42].
- Work to rest ratios of "1:3, 1:2, 1:20" are mentioned [08:15]; the captions are garbled and the intended ratios cannot be confirmed.
- NFL combine bench press is at 225 pounds; centers reached about 35 to 40 reps [13:21].
- NBA draft bench press is at 185 pounds, with results up to five, 10 or 15 reps [15:27, 15:59].
- "Load" here means resistance weight, not wearable load [15:59].
- Muscular strength is maximum force in one repetition; muscular endurance is maximum repetitions [13:21].
- Brady is cited as winning four out of six Super Bowls, as an outlier example [23:07].

## Methods and frameworks named

- ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests (normality assumed) on public combine data, in R [11:18, 13:52].
- A measurement model with her colleague: physical variables (strength, power, endurance, flexibility, reaction time, coordination, body composition, specific skills), physiological (lactate threshold, resting heart rate, blood pressure, VO2 max, glucose and insulin, injury history, telomere length, methylome), psychological, behavioral and environmental [17:31, 18:31, 19:03].
- Implicit association task to probe confidence versus narcissism by reaction time latency [21:05, 22:05].
- Precision medicine framing, "n of one" trials, time varying covariates [27:13, 27:44].

## Limits and open questions

- The tennis pilot gave no sample size, results or validation [20:35 to 22:05].
- Combine position comparisons are not tied to game performance or to injury.
- Self-report measures are acknowledged as biased [20:05]; the implicit task was shown only as a similar example.
- The cryotherapy, stem cell and gene editing remarks are loose and not evidenced [24:39, 26:43].
- Claim that the injury risk of a quarterback tested on the bench press is raised is explicitly not asserted [13:52].
- Book promotion and commercial thanks to a sponsor appear at [28:14].

## Q&A

- A question on how the data would be used: she would use it for injury prevention, baselines and response to training [29:14].
- Can psychological variables be modified: yes, with willingness, though some are harder [29:44, 30:15].
- Self-reports and big data: patterns may become clearer, and self-efficacy, confidence and narcissism need better objective models, which she called a call to action [31:19, 31:50].

## Summary

The founder of a jump-measuring wearable describes his company's path from a waist-worn device that reports jump height and jump count to broadcast use (VERT Cast) and a new device that adds g-force and acceleration. He argues the same data serve fans, motivation, performance and injury prevention. Examples come mostly from volleyball: televised jump numbers, a 30 inch club for motivation, and a jump count cap in USA Volleyball practice. This is a company pitch with testimonials, not a study; no validity, reliability or injury data are shown.

## Key claims

- A waist-worn device logs jump height and count and syncs to an app [01:46].
- Jump count is an unmeasured load in volleyball and basketball, comparable to pitch count in baseball [06:21].
- Real-time jump data on Jumbotron and TV can drive fan engagement [07:54, 12:31].
- Public milestones (the 30 inch club) motivate athletes [13:01, 13:32].
- Coaches can set a jump count limit per practice; USA Volleyball players stop at a certain number to avoid overdoing it [16:07].
- Players have written to him saying they stayed healthy because of the product [16:38]; no data were shown.
- Step counts say little; measuring g-force of each movement says more about effort [19:12, 19:42].
- Combining jump, g-force and heart rate gives an idea of an athlete's condition [20:43].
- Future focus is recovery, looking at surges and jerk [22:16].
- A private mode keeps team data on the team's own servers [21:44].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables market expected to reach "$40 billion" by "20121" (garbled year) [04:49].
- Coaches notice jumps of 35 or 40 inches [05:51].
- Example in-game jumps of 32 inches [08:26] and 28.6 inches with seven kills [08:56]; top tournament jump 34 inches, later 34 and a half [10:59, 12:00].
- A player averaging 27 inches with best of 38 [10:29].
- 103 jumps shown on a coach screen; a practice cap of about 100 suggested; pitch count example of 58 [15:05, 15:36].
- Example g-force readings: 8.3 g peak; cycling example 3.2 rising to 4.1 [20:12].
- Heart rate of 110 during a convention [20:43].
- First NBA client the Miami Heat; first used in a game the week before [21:13, 21:44].
- Built "in about two years" [24:49]; USA men's team win after 30 years [24:19].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable jump and g-force sensor with app, team system (VERT Coach) for multiple sensors, VERT Cast broadcast feed [15:05, 02:18].
- Jump count thresholds per position and drill [15:36].

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, reliability or validity data for jump height or g-force.
- Injury prevention is supported by testimonials only [16:38]; no outcome data.
- The USA volleyball medal results are credited loosely and are not evidence of a product effect [24:19].
- Speaker is the company founder; all claims are commercial.
- Several names (players, coaches) are garbled in captions and not repeated here.

## Q&A

- None; the talk ends at [24:49] with a closing remark and applause.

title: "SSAC17: Truths and Myths of the Three Point Revolution in Basketball"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

## Summary

The speaker argues that how analysts frame a finding decides whether it is adopted, and tests that idea against four common complaints about the rise of the three-point shot: that the league has become a jump shooting league, that long shots cause long rebounds and fast breaks, that the mid-range game is lost, and that defenses can control three-point percentage. In each case he grants a grain of truth, shows what the data says, and offers a replacement story. He closes with the causes he sees behind the rise in threes and calls his account a theory to be improved. He says his work for the team is private, so the talk avoids team specifics.

## Key claims

- The meta point: statistics have to be tied to a story and a mechanism to be accepted, because fans, coaches and front-office people hold strong prior beliefs [01:30], [02:00], [02:30].
- The goal of framing is to give people permission to accept a new narrative [03:00].
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season [04:00].
- The league has always taken many jump shots: the share of shots from beyond ten feet was the same in 1999-2000 and last year, so the change is in distance, not in jump shooting [04:32].
- Taking more long jump shots can be described as settling or as using the geometry of the court, and the description changes how it is heard [06:03].
- Long misses do produce longer rebounds, but they do not produce more fast breaks than other misses [06:35].
- Shots rebounded from around the rim lead to fast breaks more often than rebounded above-the-break threes [07:07].
- His explanation is that a three usually follows good execution and balanced spacing, so a defender is already back; this is his own account [08:10].
- The mid-range share has fallen, but the self-created (unassisted) mid-range shots by star players have held roughly steady [08:43], [09:44].
- Among high-usage players, long two-pointers rose as a share of made shots over about fifteen years [10:44].
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by star players have risen sharply in four years, driven by a small number of players [11:16], [11:47].
- Baseball analogies hold for rate stats and efficiency, but basketball has no batting order, and a possession has a third outcome besides made or missed: not shooting [13:18], [13:48], [14:18].
- A well-contested shot often means the player did not shoot at all [15:18].
- Defensive three-point percentage looks like a coin flip at the individual level, and the speaker says it is not necessarily luck [16:18], [16:48].
- Defenders can affect a shot in known ways: distance to the shooter, avoiding fouls on a jump shooter, and late-clock or end-game contests [16:48], [17:18], [17:48].
- Defending the three therefore means avoiding it, since a three-point shot at lower than a certain accuracy is not taken [18:19].
- Four factors behind more threes: player skill development, teams permitting players to shoot from farther, downsizing, and strategies that move where the ball is caught [18:50], [19:20], [19:50].
- Power forwards' three-point rates have risen in four years and teams more often play four or five shooters [20:20].
- He calls all this a theory and invites better ones, aiming to be "less wrong" [21:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump shot (his definition): a shot from outside ten feet. Share was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year [04:32].
- Shots from outside fifteen feet: began at 42%, peaked at 48%, about 46% now [04:32], [05:02].
- Mid-range (his definition): outside the paint, inside the three-point arc [08:43].
- High-usage player (his definition, "arbitrary"): usage of 27% or higher [10:44].
- Share of made shots that are long twos for that group: from 7% to 11.5%, which he calls over a 50% increase, over fifteen years [10:44].
- Extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate: about 340, of which two players accounted for 308 [11:47]. He said he may have done the math wrong.
- Rim-area rebound versus above-the-break three fast-break likelihood: one and a half to two times, over 15 to 20 years of data [07:07].
- Four feet away on a catch-and-shoot: about 34%; ten feet away: about 40% [16:48], [17:18].
- Fouling a jump shooter turns a 35% shot into 75 or 80% [17:18].
- A 34% three is a 51% effective shot [18:19].
- Caption problem: "worth 50% less" at twenty feet [19:50] reads unclearly; do not rely on it.
- Ten of the last twelve finalists in the top ten for three-point rate [04:00].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Shot-location data, described as reliable from about 1999-2000 [04:32].
- Assisted versus unassisted split of shots, and density plots of assisted share by location [09:44], [10:14].
- Usage-based grouping of star players [10:44].
- A graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") treating individual defensive three-point percentage against a coin-flip pattern [16:18].
- Baseball's batting average on balls in play as an analogy for what the defense controls [15:18].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker said his team's work is proprietary and the talk draws on public work from his earlier site [01:00].
- The mechanism for the fast-break finding is his hypothesis, not tested in the talk [08:10].
- The coin-flip claim rests on one graph by another writer, with no detail shown; the speaker did not claim luck, only similarity [16:48].
- Star-player trends rest on a small group of players, and he said two players drive the unassisted three increase [11:47].
- The talk is built around framing, and most numbers are shown on slides the captions do not describe.

## Q&A

- A question about how teams measure the chains of actions that lead to a shot and how advanced teams are; the speaker declined to answer [21:52], [22:25], [22:55].
- A question whether star shots are still inefficient; he said shot clock and the need for someone to be open limit alternatives, and that there is probably a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor [23:25], [23:56]. The question text is garbled.

## Summary

The speaker, a sleep scientist who says she works with athletes and teams (and refers to a lab at Henry Ford), argues that sleep and circadian rhythm are the most ignored performance factor and touch every other one. She presents three things: why sleep matters (reaction time, judgment, injury, hormones, pain, glucose), how much athletes need (9 to 10 hours, based on extension studies), and how the body clock affects performance (travel across time zones, evening games, and individual chronotype). Her take-home points are that deficits accumulate, that regular sleep matters more than sleep before a game, and that circadian timing is an unexplored, manageable advantage. A long Q&A covers quality, individual need, naps and clock shifting.

## Key claims

- Sleep and recovery are integral to performance and the most ignored aspect; sleep and circadian rhythm affect diet, hydration, training, cognition, mental preparation and coaching [00:00], [00:32].
- The function of sleep is not known, but the effects of too little are [01:03].
- Getting six to seven hours instead of eight doubles or triples reaction time [01:33].
- Deficits accumulate over days, and three days of recovery sleep do not bring people to the level of those who sleep nine hours regularly [02:05], [02:36].
- Sleep regularly, not only before the game; athletes tend to sleep poorly just before games [03:07].
- Sleep loss impairs the prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and decision-making, while emotional brain activity rises; fouls increase [03:37], [04:08].
- Hours of sleep was the strongest predictor of injury in a study of high school athletes followed for about 22 months [04:38], [05:08].
- Growth hormone is released in deep sleep and testosterone while sleeping; five lost hours lowered testosterone [05:40], [06:12].
- Sleep loss raises hormones that break down muscle [06:42].
- Less sleep increases pain sensitivity [06:42], [07:12].
- Sleep deprivation reduced glucose tolerance in college students [07:12], [07:42].
- Impairment from lost sleep was compared to impairment from drinking [07:42], [08:12].
- Adults need seven to eight hours but athletes need nine to ten [08:42].
- In Stanford sleep-extension studies (six weeks, ten hours in bed), basketball players sprinted faster and shot better, were less sleepy, and had better mood [09:12], [09:42], [10:13].
- Football players improved in the 40-yard dash and shuttle; swimmers improved turn times; tennis players improved serve accuracy [10:44], [11:14].
- Sleepiness depends on a homeostatic drive (time awake) and on a circadian alerting signal, with an afternoon dip [11:45], [12:18], [13:19].
- Coordination, reaction time, cardiovascular efficiency and strength tend to peak in the evening [13:49].
- In forty years of evening NFL games, West Coast teams beat the spread and won twice as often against East Coast teams; there was no difference in daytime games [14:19], [14:49].
- In baseball data, East Coast teams lost their home advantage when returning home, and crossing three time zones raised the chance of losing the first game [15:50], [16:20].
- Chronotype (night owl, morning lark) shifts the time of peak performance, and teams of mostly late chronotypes peak later than teams of early ones [16:51], [18:55], [21:00].
- Peak performance occurred six to seven hours after waking for early and intermediate chronotypes, and eleven or more hours after for late [20:30].
- Take-homes: elite sport is a 24-hour commitment, deficits are cumulative, sleep touches all performance factors, and circadian advantage is unexplored [22:03], [22:33], [23:03].
- She suggests sleep loss was once masked by amphetamines and steroids in sport [23:03].

## Numbers and definitions

- Normal reaction time: about a quarter of a second; six to seven hours of sleep doubles or triples it [01:33].
- Study design: seven days at reduced time in bed (the captions give "7 five versus 3 hours", garbled), then three days of nine hours [02:05], [02:36].
- Injury: sleeping under eight hours raised injury likelihood by "1.7%" in the captions [05:08]. This may be garbled (a ratio versus a percent); do not rely on it.
- Testosterone: down 10 to 12% after five hours of lost sleep (caption "increased... decreased" is inconsistent) [06:12]. Normal aging loss: 1 to 2% per year; she says a 20-year-old would look 31 [06:12].
- Glucose tolerance: reduced by 40% after a week or ten days [07:42].
- Alcohol comparison: six hours of sleep like two to three beers; four hours like about six beers [07:42], [08:12].
- Stanford extension: ten hours in bed for six weeks; basketball free throws and three-pointers each up 9% [09:12], [09:42].
- Football 40-yard dash improvement is garbled in the captions ("1 point1 2 seconds") [10:44]; swimmers added "five kicks" [11:14].
- NFL: West Coast evening teams won and beat the spread "twice" as often, forty years of data [14:19].
- Baseball: first-game loss "60% or more" after crossing three time zones; home field advantage 3.9% [15:50], [16:20]. The 60% caption is unclear.
- Chronotype peaks: early, noon to 2; intermediate, mid-afternoon; late, 7 to 8 in the evening [18:55]. The group-level peak "between four and seven" has no am or pm in the captions [18:24].
- Naps described: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 90 minutes [29:33], [30:03].
- Twelve teams were used in the team chronotype analysis [20:30].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Sleep-deprivation and recovery experiments with repeated performance tests [02:05].
- Stanford sleep-extension studies using actigraphs and sleep diaries, measuring performance at the end of six weeks [09:12].
- Forty years of NFL evening-game results compared to the Las Vegas spread, with controls for team quality and travel [14:19], [14:49].
- Multi-year baseball game data on time zones and home advantage [15:50], [16:20].
- The morning-evening questionnaire to classify chronotype, with performance tests six times across the day (bleep test, sprint times) [17:52], [18:24].
- Light and melatonin to shift the body clock [29:02].

## Limits and open questions

- Sample sizes are not stated for most studies; the high school injury study, Stanford extension and chronotype studies are cited without numbers of athletes, except twelve teams [20:30].
- The extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep, as she acknowledged [25:57].
- The 40-year NFL study is called robust by the speaker [14:49]; the authors are named in captions only as "Smith and motra" (caption spelling).
- The 9 to 10 hour recommendation is the speaker's synthesis of those extension studies [11:14].
- Her claim that a third of teams are not interested is her own experience [28:31].
- Several numbers (injury, football dash, baseball first-game loss) are garbled in the captions.

## Q&A

- Facility-limited sports such as swimming and hockey are hit hardest; swimmer studies showed gains from more sleep [23:55], [24:25].
- Whether to get extra sleep before a long event: yes [24:55].
- Training at peak time is better, and sleep consolidates learning; nap after training [25:25].
- Sleep quality: the extension studies did not measure sleep itself; both quality (reaching deep sleep) and quantity matter [25:57], [26:28].
- Individual need: those who "get by" tolerate deprivation better, not need less; chronic deprivation erases the reference for feeling alert; sleeping in on days off signals a deficit [26:58], [27:29], [28:00].
- Team interest: about a third already do this, a third want to try, a third are not interested [28:31].
- Shifting the clock earlier: possible with light boxes and melatonin; she mentions a trip to London for a team [29:02].
- Naps: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, or 90 minutes; a nap is not advised if night sleep is a problem; falling-asleep trouble usually comes from time zones or late caffeine [29:33], [30:03], [30:35].

## Summary

The speaker argues that how analysts frame a finding decides whether it is adopted, and tests that idea against four common complaints about the rise of the three-point shot: that the league has become a jump shooting league, that long shots cause long rebounds and fast breaks, that the mid-range game is lost, and that defenses can control three-point percentage. In each case he grants a grain of truth, shows what the data says, and offers a replacement story. He closes with the causes he sees behind the rise in threes and calls his account a theory to be improved. He says his work for the team is private, so the talk avoids team specifics.

## Key claims

- The meta point: statistics have to be tied to a story and a mechanism to be accepted, because fans, coaches and front-office people hold strong prior beliefs [01:30], [02:00], [02:30].
- The goal of framing is to give people permission to accept a new narrative [03:00].
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season [04:00].
- The league has always taken many jump shots: the share of shots from beyond ten feet was the same in 1999-2000 and last year, so the change is in distance, not in jump shooting [04:32].
- Taking more long jump shots can be described as settling or as using the geometry of the court, and the description changes how it is heard [06:03].
- Long misses do produce longer rebounds, but they do not produce more fast breaks than other misses [06:35].
- Shots rebounded from around the rim lead to fast breaks more often than rebounded above-the-break threes [07:07].
- His explanation is that a three usually follows good execution and balanced spacing, so a defender is already back; this is his own account [08:10].
- The mid-range share has fallen, but the self-created (unassisted) mid-range shots by star players have held roughly steady [08:43], [09:44].
- Among high-usage players, long two-pointers rose as a share of made shots over about fifteen years [10:44].
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by star players have risen sharply in four years, driven by a small number of players [11:16], [11:47].
- Baseball analogies hold for rate stats and efficiency, but basketball has no batting order, and a possession has a third outcome besides made or missed: not shooting [13:18], [13:48], [14:18].
- A well-contested shot often means the player did not shoot at all [15:18].
- Defensive three-point percentage looks like a coin flip at the individual level, and the speaker says it is not necessarily luck [16:18], [16:48].
- Defenders can affect a shot in known ways: distance to the shooter, avoiding fouls on a jump shooter, and late-clock or end-game contests [16:48], [17:18], [17:48].
- Defending the three therefore means avoiding it, since a three-point shot at lower than a certain accuracy is not taken [18:19].
- Four factors behind more threes: player skill development, teams permitting players to shoot from farther, downsizing, and strategies that move where the ball is caught [18:50], [19:20], [19:50].
- Power forwards' three-point rates have risen in four years and teams more often play four or five shooters [20:20].
- He calls all this a theory and invites better ones, aiming to be "less wrong" [21:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump shot (his definition): a shot from outside ten feet. Share was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year [04:32].
- Shots from outside fifteen feet: began at 42%, peaked at 48%, about 46% now [04:32], [05:02].
- Mid-range (his definition): outside the paint, inside the three-point arc [08:43].
- High-usage player (his definition, "arbitrary"): usage of 27% or higher [10:44].
- Share of made shots that are long twos for that group: from 7% to 11.5%, which he calls over a 50% increase, over fifteen years [10:44].
- Extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate: about 340, of which two players accounted for 308 [11:47]. He said he may have done the math wrong.
- Rim-area rebound versus above-the-break three fast-break likelihood: one and a half to two times, over 15 to 20 years of data [07:07].
- Four feet away on a catch-and-shoot: about 34%; ten feet away: about 40% [16:48], [17:18].
- Fouling a jump shooter turns a 35% shot into 75 or 80% [17:18].
- A 34% three is a 51% effective shot [18:19].
- Caption problem: "worth 50% less" at twenty feet [19:50] reads unclearly; do not rely on it.
- Ten of the last twelve finalists in the top ten for three-point rate [04:00].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Shot-location data, described as reliable from about 1999-2000 [04:32].
- Assisted versus unassisted split of shots, and density plots of assisted share by location [09:44], [10:14].
- Usage-based grouping of star players [10:44].
- A graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") treating individual defensive three-point percentage against a coin-flip pattern [16:18].
- Baseball's batting average on balls in play as an analogy for what the defense controls [15:18].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker said his team's work is proprietary and the talk draws on public work from his earlier site [01:00].
- The mechanism for the fast-break finding is his hypothesis, not tested in the talk [08:10].
- The coin-flip claim rests on one graph by another writer, with no detail shown; the speaker did not claim luck, only similarity [16:48].
- Star-player trends rest on a small group of players, and he said two players drive the unassisted three increase [11:47].
- The talk is built around framing, and most numbers are shown on slides the captions do not describe.

## Q&A

- A question about how teams measure the chains of actions that lead to a shot and how advanced teams are; the speaker declined to answer [21:52], [22:25], [22:55].
- A question whether star shots are still inefficient; he said shot clock and the need for someone to be open limit alternatives, and that there is probably a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor [23:25], [23:56]. The question text is garbled.

## Summary

The speaker, a sleep scientist who says she works with athletes and teams (and refers to a lab at Henry Ford), argues that sleep and circadian rhythm are the most ignored performance factor and touch every other one. She presents three things: why sleep matters (reaction time, judgment, injury, hormones, pain, glucose), how much athletes need (9 to 10 hours, based on extension studies), and how the body clock affects performance (travel across time zones, evening games, and individual chronotype). Her take-home points are that deficits accumulate, that regular sleep matters more than sleep before a game, and that circadian timing is an unexplored, manageable advantage. A long Q&A covers quality, individual need, naps and clock shifting.

## Key claims

- Sleep and recovery are integral to performance and the most ignored aspect; sleep and circadian rhythm affect diet, hydration, training, cognition, mental preparation and coaching [00:00], [00:32].
- The function of sleep is not known, but the effects of too little are [01:03].
- Getting six to seven hours instead of eight doubles or triples reaction time [01:33].
- Deficits accumulate over days, and three days of recovery sleep do not bring people to the level of those who sleep nine hours regularly [02:05], [02:36].
- Sleep regularly, not only before the game; athletes tend to sleep poorly just before games [03:07].
- Sleep loss impairs the prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and decision-making, while emotional brain activity rises; fouls increase [03:37], [04:08].
- Hours of sleep was the strongest predictor of injury in a study of high school athletes followed for about 22 months [04:38], [05:08].
- Growth hormone is released in deep sleep and testosterone while sleeping; five lost hours lowered testosterone [05:40], [06:12].
- Sleep loss raises hormones that break down muscle [06:42].
- Less sleep increases pain sensitivity [06:42], [07:12].
- Sleep deprivation reduced glucose tolerance in college students [07:12], [07:42].
- Impairment from lost sleep was compared to impairment from drinking [07:42], [08:12].
- Adults need seven to eight hours but athletes need nine to ten [08:42].
- In Stanford sleep-extension studies (six weeks, ten hours in bed), basketball players sprinted faster and shot better, were less sleepy, and had better mood [09:12], [09:42], [10:13].
- Football players improved in the 40-yard dash and shuttle; swimmers improved turn times; tennis players improved serve accuracy [10:44], [11:14].
- Sleepiness depends on a homeostatic drive (time awake) and on a circadian alerting signal, with an afternoon dip [11:45], [12:18], [13:19].
- Coordination, reaction time, cardiovascular efficiency and strength tend to peak in the evening [13:49].
- In forty years of evening NFL games, West Coast teams beat the spread and won twice as often against East Coast teams; there was no difference in daytime games [14:19], [14:49].
- In baseball data, East Coast teams lost their home advantage when returning home, and crossing three time zones raised the chance of losing the first game [15:50], [16:20].
- Chronotype (night owl, morning lark) shifts the time of peak performance, and teams of mostly late chronotypes peak later than teams of early ones [16:51], [18:55], [21:00].
- Peak performance occurred six to seven hours after waking for early and intermediate chronotypes, and eleven or more hours after for late [20:30].
- Take-homes: elite sport is a 24-hour commitment, deficits are cumulative, sleep touches all performance factors, and circadian advantage is unexplored [22:03], [22:33], [23:03].
- She suggests sleep loss was once masked by amphetamines and steroids in sport [23:03].

## Numbers and definitions

- Normal reaction time: about a quarter of a second; six to seven hours of sleep doubles or triples it [01:33].
- Study design: seven days at reduced time in bed (the captions give "7 five versus 3 hours", garbled), then three days of nine hours [02:05], [02:36].
- Injury: sleeping under eight hours raised injury likelihood by "1.7%" in the captions [05:08]. This may be garbled (a ratio versus a percent); do not rely on it.
- Testosterone: down 10 to 12% after five hours of lost sleep (caption "increased... decreased" is inconsistent) [06:12]. Normal aging loss: 1 to 2% per year; she says a 20-year-old would look 31 [06:12].
- Glucose tolerance: reduced by 40% after a week or ten days [07:42].
- Alcohol comparison: six hours of sleep like two to three beers; four hours like about six beers [07:42], [08:12].
- Stanford extension: ten hours in bed for six weeks; basketball free throws and three-pointers each up 9% [09:12], [09:42].
- Football 40-yard dash improvement is garbled in the captions ("1 point1 2 seconds") [10:44]; swimmers added "five kicks" [11:14].
- NFL: West Coast evening teams won and beat the spread "twice" as often, forty years of data [14:19].
- Baseball: first-game loss "60% or more" after crossing three time zones; home field advantage 3.9% [15:50], [16:20]. The 60% caption is unclear.
- Chronotype peaks: early, noon to 2; intermediate, mid-afternoon; late, 7 to 8 in the evening [18:55]. The group-level peak "between four and seven" has no am or pm in the captions [18:24].
- Naps described: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 90 minutes [29:33], [30:03].
- Twelve teams were used in the team chronotype analysis [20:30].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Sleep-deprivation and recovery experiments with repeated performance tests [02:05].
- Stanford sleep-extension studies using actigraphs and sleep diaries, measuring performance at the end of six weeks [09:12].
- Forty years of NFL evening-game results compared to the Las Vegas spread, with controls for team quality and travel [14:19], [14:49].
- Multi-year baseball game data on time zones and home advantage [15:50], [16:20].
- The morning-evening questionnaire to classify chronotype, with performance tests six times across the day (bleep test, sprint times) [17:52], [18:24].
- Light and melatonin to shift the body clock [29:02].

## Limits and open questions

- Sample sizes are not stated for most studies; the high school injury study, Stanford extension and chronotype studies are cited without numbers of athletes, except twelve teams [20:30].
- The extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep, as she acknowledged [25:57].
- The 40-year NFL study is called robust by the speaker [14:49]; the authors are named in captions only as "Smith and motra" (caption spelling).
- The 9 to 10 hour recommendation is the speaker's synthesis of those extension studies [11:14].
- Her claim that a third of teams are not interested is her own experience [28:31].
- Several numbers (injury, football dash, baseball first-game loss) are garbled in the captions.

## Q&A

- Facility-limited sports such as swimming and hockey are hit hardest; swimmer studies showed gains from more sleep [23:55], [24:25].
- Whether to get extra sleep before a long event: yes [24:55].
- Training at peak time is better, and sleep consolidates learning; nap after training [25:25].
- Sleep quality: the extension studies did not measure sleep itself; both quality (reaching deep sleep) and quantity matter [25:57], [26:28].
- Individual need: those who "get by" tolerate deprivation better, not need less; chronic deprivation erases the reference for feeling alert; sleeping in on days off signals a deficit [26:58], [27:29], [28:00].
- Team interest: about a third already do this, a third want to try, a third are not interested [28:31].
- Shifting the clock earlier: possible with light boxes and melatonin; she mentions a trip to London for a team [29:02].
- Naps: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, or 90 minutes; a nap is not advised if night sleep is a problem; falling-asleep trouble usually comes from time zones or late caffeine [29:33], [30:03], [30:35].

## Summary

Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013. It measures cognitive ability and personality traits tied to football, and is meant as an addition to physical and film evidence. A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. The second half describes player-type clusters, a bust-rate comparison using a public value metric, and planned longitudinal modeling of second contracts.

## Key claims

- The goal was to add a standardized psychological measure alongside combine physical tests, not to replace them [04:13], [06:17].
- A league study with team executives produced 16 factors, with intelligence and personality as the two key areas [05:46].
- Intelligence items cover learning, thinking quickly and avoiding mental errors; personality items cover leadership, teamwork, self-control, dependability, preparedness and team fit [06:50].
- The test has run at the combine since 2013 with full participation, and the data were also turned into a coaching report [07:20], [07:51].
- The validation compared pre-draft scores with coach ratings after the players had been on a team for at least a year [09:54].
- The speaker calls correlations of this size good for behavioral science and says they are uncorrected [10:24].
- High, middle and low test scores matched coach rating bands; coaches were more straightforward than expected [12:27], [12:59].
- Low scorers on intelligence were about three times as likely to be rated poor as star; high scorers about three times as likely rated star [13:30].
- Personality: low scorers were about four times as likely to be rated low, high scorers about four and a half times as likely rated high [14:32].
- Intelligence and personality together predicted some ratings better, such as decisions under stress [15:33], [16:03].
- Decisions under stress also correlated with penalties per play and yards per penalty, and the result held in a larger sample [16:35], [17:07].
- Personality variables relate to injuries only weakly, with significance, in an early study; injury type has not been examined [17:37], [18:07].
- Cluster analysis found nine player types combining coach-rated physical talent and the psychological scores [22:16].
- A "whole package" cluster had a lower bust rate than a low-on-everything cluster, and two clusters with opposite strengths had the same failure rate [24:19], [25:20].
- The speakers argue this approach can find undervalued players and de-risk draft and contract decisions [25:51].
- Planned work: longitudinal models for second-contract decisions [26:53], [27:24].

- Test length: one hour [07:20]. Almost 100 players tested the morning of the talk [28:26].
- Validation: three years, 1,500 player scores, about 330 combine participants per year (plus a Super Regional), about 70 percent team participation across all 32 teams [08:52], [09:22].
- Coach ratings on about 24 dimensions after at least a year; about 500 players with performance data [09:54].
- Coaches' scale of about seven points [12:59].

The captions garble the decimal points; these are the likeliest readings.
- Top and bottom groups each about 25 percent of the sample [12:27].
- Rated low by coaches 13 percent of the time, good to great 87 percent (high intelligence scorers) [14:01]; 91 percent good to great (strong personality scorers) [15:02].
- Larger penalty sample about 400 players [17:07].
- Clusters: nine profiles from 2014 to 2016 data, shown as z-scores [22:16].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Competency model from a team-executive study; subscale items built from intelligence and personality dimensions [05:46], [06:50].
- Criterion validation against coach ratings, penalties, yards per penalty and injuries [09:54], [17:07], [17:37].

No Q&A in the recording; the speakers invite questions afterward [28:57].

topics: [injury-health, sports-science, american-football, basketball, decision-making]

## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

## Key claims

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].
- More data has meant more decisions but not better ones; people are disillusioned, as with fitness bands [05:40], [06:11].
- A soccer team's higher exposure to high-speed running and explosive efforts coincided with no injuries, and lower exposure with more; the team had been holding athletes back [06:42], [07:13], [07:43].
- Two NFL examples showed more risk with doing less, and for one team the degree of change mattered, not the total [08:13], [08:43].
- Another NFL chart showed the reverse for accelerations: above 200 in a week, injuries were frequent [08:43].
- The common baseball view that a small change in range of motion sharply raises risk is challenged; the speaker says it varies by person, and an increase in hip internal rotation was linked to elbow ligament strain more than the opposite [09:13], [09:43], [10:13].
- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].
- Each team and each person has a different load signature, including phenotypes that break from too much load, too little, or both [14:15], [14:46].
- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].
- Teams should keep a few core metrics and review them yearly rather than manage a hundred variables [18:51].
- He claims the company helps teams cut days lost to injury by 42 percent [19:21].

## Numbers and definitions

- Correlation of salary-adjusted spending with wins: 0.76 NBA, 0.89 NFL [03:08].
- NBA average spend on injured players: 12.9 million dollars a year; 8.1 million dollars of that avoidable [03:08], [03:39].
- 46.6 million dollars of athlete on court: 40 wins West, 36 East, 0 percent playoff chance; 52 million dollars: 49 or 43 wins, 100 percent chance [03:39], [04:10].
- Share of wins set by health: NFL 25 percent, MLB 9 percent, NHL 12, MLS 15 [04:40]; NBA said as nine wins, "20%" of wins needed for the playoffs [04:10]. The captions say "NFL or NBA" at [04:10], so the 20 percent is likely NBA.
- Soccer team: "above 30 150 meters" of high-speed running over seven days (garbled; the figure is unclear) and more than 390 explosive multi-directional efforts, with no injuries [06:42], [07:13]. A one standard deviation increase was treated as risky [07:43].
- NFL team: above 200 accelerations in seven days, 33 or 34 percent injured (phrase unclear) [08:43].
- Baseball: 180 degrees of motion; a five degree change claimed to raise risk six to seven times [09:13].
- Acute to chronic ratio: 150 percent said to raise risk six or seven times; the speaker's four teams would have lost 8, (garbled), 15 and 26 percent of training [10:43], [11:13]. The top-right value is garbled in the captions.
- Premier League team: 23 injuries a year of 14 days or more; 8 to 12 of the same type [11:44], [12:14].
- Company claims: 42 percent fewer days lost; 25 leagues, five continents; over four years, first annual report last year [19:21], [19:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Salary-weighted availability as a proxy for performance [02:38], [03:08].
- Dose-response charts of weekly load against injury risk, per team [06:42].
- Electronic medical record at the center, every data point statistically related to injury [11:13], [11:44].
- Anonymized aggregation across athletes, split by sport, position and team [12:14].
- Phenotypes of athletes by load response [14:15].
- Annual review of metrics [18:51].

## Limits and open questions

- Chart samples and statistics are not stated; many numbers are partly garbled.
- The salary link is correlational, and using salary as a stand-in for performance is the speaker's assumption.
- Results cover a few teams; the speaker says each team differs, which limits any general rule.
- It is a company presentation; claims such as 42 percent fewer days lost and being the "proven global leader" are the speaker's own [19:21].
- "Infinitely higher" game injury rate is a figure of speech, not a number [16:48], [17:18].
- Captions garble "Kitman," "Tommy John" context and some terms.

## Q&A

No Q&A in the recording.

Caption problems: speaker names are caption-spelled throughout (Mary wise, adieu schiffman, Abe matkour, Ken yuso, Charles sheram, "Kidman labs"/Stephen Smith, Cyrus "Mary"); garbled figures flagged inline (Catapult "70" at [54:45], correlation decimals at [10:24]/[10:56]/[11:26]/[15:33]/[16:03] in 40NV3, the "0%" at [24:50] in 40NV3, "30 150 meters" at [06:42], "33 or 34 percent" at [08:43] and the missing top-right value at [11:13] in AO1Q9); I did not verify any caption-external fact.</result>

---
type: video-summary
video_id: BJkCqf6Fj2w
title: "SSAC17: Truths and Myths of the Three Point Revolution in Basketball"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Seth part now (caption spelling; director of basketball research, Milwaukee Bucks), introduced by Justin gold (caption spelling; student organizer)]
topics: [basketball, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker argues that how analysts frame a finding decides whether it is adopted, and tests that idea against four common complaints about the rise of the three-point shot: that the league has become a jump shooting league, that long shots cause long rebounds and fast breaks, that the mid-range game is lost, and that defenses can control three-point percentage. In each case he grants a grain of truth, shows what the data says, and offers a replacement story. He closes with the causes he sees behind the rise in threes and calls his account a theory to be improved. He says his work for the team is private, so the talk avoids team specifics.

## Key claims

- The meta point: statistics have to be tied to a story and a mechanism to be accepted, because fans, coaches and front-office people hold strong prior beliefs [01:30], [02:00], [02:30].
- The goal of framing is to give people permission to accept a new narrative [03:00].
- Ten of the last twelve NBA finalists ranked in the top ten in three-point rate that season [04:00].
- The league has always taken many jump shots: the share of shots from beyond ten feet was the same in 1999-2000 and last year, so the change is in distance, not in jump shooting [04:32].
- Taking more long jump shots can be described as settling or as using the geometry of the court, and the description changes how it is heard [06:03].
- Long misses do produce longer rebounds, but they do not produce more fast breaks than other misses [06:35].
- Shots rebounded from around the rim lead to fast breaks more often than rebounded above-the-break threes [07:07].
- His explanation is that a three usually follows good execution and balanced spacing, so a defender is already back; this is his own account [08:10].
- The mid-range share has fallen, but the self-created (unassisted) mid-range shots by star players have held roughly steady [08:43], [09:44].
- Among high-usage players, long two-pointers rose as a share of made shots over about fifteen years [10:44].
- Unassisted above-the-break threes by star players have risen sharply in four years, driven by a small number of players [11:16], [11:47].
- Baseball analogies hold for rate stats and efficiency, but basketball has no batting order, and a possession has a third outcome besides made or missed: not shooting [13:18], [13:48], [14:18].
- A well-contested shot often means the player did not shoot at all [15:18].
- Defensive three-point percentage looks like a coin flip at the individual level, and the speaker says it is not necessarily luck [16:18], [16:48].
- Defenders can affect a shot in known ways: distance to the shooter, avoiding fouls on a jump shooter, and late-clock or end-game contests [16:48], [17:18], [17:48].
- Defending the three therefore means avoiding it, since a three-point shot at lower than a certain accuracy is not taken [18:19].
- Four factors behind more threes: player skill development, teams permitting players to shoot from farther, downsizing, and strategies that move where the ball is caught [18:50], [19:20], [19:50].
- Power forwards' three-point rates have risen in four years and teams more often play four or five shooters [20:20].
- He calls all this a theory and invites better ones, aiming to be "less wrong" [21:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump shot (his definition): a shot from outside ten feet. Share was 55% in 1999-2000 and 55% last year [04:32].
- Shots from outside fifteen feet: began at 42%, peaked at 48%, about 46% now [04:32], [05:02].
- Mid-range (his definition): outside the paint, inside the three-point arc [08:43].
- High-usage player (his definition, "arbitrary"): usage of 27% or higher [10:44].
- Share of made shots that are long twos for that group: from 7% to 11.5%, which he calls over a 50% increase, over fifteen years [10:44].
- Extra unassisted threes last year versus the 2000 rate: about 340, of which two players accounted for 308 [11:47]. He said he may have done the math wrong.
- Rim-area rebound versus above-the-break three fast-break likelihood: one and a half to two times, over 15 to 20 years of data [07:07].
- Four feet away on a catch-and-shoot: about 34%; ten feet away: about 40% [16:48], [17:18].
- Fouling a jump shooter turns a 35% shot into 75 or 80% [17:18].
- A 34% three is a 51% effective shot [18:19].
- Caption problem: "worth 50% less" at twenty feet [19:50] reads unclearly; do not rely on it.
- Ten of the last twelve finalists in the top ten for three-point rate [04:00].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Shot-location data, described as reliable from about 1999-2000 [04:32].
- Assisted versus unassisted split of shots, and density plots of assisted share by location [09:44], [10:14].
- Usage-based grouping of star players [10:44].
- A graph by another writer (caption spelling "Hest Becker") treating individual defensive three-point percentage against a coin-flip pattern [16:18].
- Baseball's batting average on balls in play as an analogy for what the defense controls [15:18].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker said his team's work is proprietary and the talk draws on public work from his earlier site [01:00].
- The mechanism for the fast-break finding is his hypothesis, not tested in the talk [08:10].
- The coin-flip claim rests on one graph by another writer, with no detail shown; the speaker did not claim luck, only similarity [16:48].
- Star-player trends rest on a small group of players, and he said two players drive the unassisted three increase [11:47].
- The talk is built around framing, and most numbers are shown on slides the captions do not describe.

## Q&A

- A question about how teams measure the chains of actions that lead to a shot and how advanced teams are; the speaker declined to answer [21:52], [22:25], [22:55].
- A question whether star shots are still inefficient; he said shot clock and the need for someone to be open limit alternatives, and that there is probably a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor [23:25], [23:56]. The question text is garbled.

- The mechanism for the fast-break finding is his hypothesis, not tested in the talk [08:10].
- The coin-flip claim rests on one graph by another writer, with no detail shown; the speaker did not claim luck, only similarity [16:48].
- Star-player trends rest on a small group of players, and he said two players drive the unassisted three increase [11:47].
- The talk is built around framing, and most numbers are shown on slides the captions do not describe.

- A question about how teams measure the chains of actions that lead to a shot and how advanced teams are; the speaker declined to answer [21:52], [22:25], [22:55].
- A question whether star shots are still inefficient; he said shot clock and the need for someone to be open limit alternatives, and that there is probably a ceiling on how many players have the skill to space the floor [23:25], [23:56]. The question text is garbled.

## Summary

The speaker, a sleep scientist who says she works with athletes and teams (and refers to a lab at Henry Ford), argues that sleep and circadian rhythm are the most ignored performance factor and touch every other one. She presents three things: why sleep matters (reaction time, judgment, injury, hormones, pain, glucose), how much athletes need (9 to 10 hours, based on extension studies), and how the body clock affects performance (travel across time zones, evening games, and individual chronotype). Her take-home points are that deficits accumulate, that regular sleep matters more than sleep before a game, and that circadian timing is an unexplored, manageable advantage. A long Q&A covers quality, individual need, naps and clock shifting.

## Key claims

- Sleep and recovery are integral to performance and the most ignored aspect; sleep and circadian rhythm affect diet, hydration, training, cognition, mental preparation and coaching [00:00], [00:32].
- The function of sleep is not known, but the effects of too little are [01:03].
- Getting six to seven hours instead of eight doubles or triples reaction time [01:33].
- Deficits accumulate over days, and three days of recovery sleep do not bring people to the level of those who sleep nine hours regularly [02:05], [02:36].
- Sleep regularly, not only before the game; athletes tend to sleep poorly just before games [03:07].
- Sleep loss impairs the prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and decision-making, while emotional brain activity rises; fouls increase [03:37], [04:08].
- Hours of sleep was the strongest predictor of injury in a study of high school athletes followed for about 22 months [04:38], [05:08].
- Growth hormone is released in deep sleep and testosterone while sleeping; five lost hours lowered testosterone [05:40], [06:12].
- Sleep loss raises hormones that break down muscle [06:42].
- Less sleep increases pain sensitivity [06:42], [07:12].
- Sleep deprivation reduced glucose tolerance in college students [07:12], [07:42].
- Impairment from lost sleep was compared to impairment from drinking [07:42], [08:12].
- Adults need seven to eight hours but athletes need nine to ten [08:42].
- In Stanford sleep-extension studies (six weeks, ten hours in bed), basketball players sprinted faster and shot better, were less sleepy, and had better mood [09:12], [09:42], [10:13].
- Football players improved in the 40-yard dash and shuttle; swimmers improved turn times; tennis players improved serve accuracy [10:44], [11:14].
- Sleepiness depends on a homeostatic drive (time awake) and on a circadian alerting signal, with an afternoon dip [11:45], [12:18], [13:19].
- Coordination, reaction time, cardiovascular efficiency and strength tend to peak in the evening [13:49].
- In forty years of evening NFL games, West Coast teams beat the spread and won twice as often against East Coast teams; there was no difference in daytime games [14:19], [14:49].
- In baseball data, East Coast teams lost their home advantage when returning home, and crossing three time zones raised the chance of losing the first game [15:50], [16:20].
- Chronotype (night owl, morning lark) shifts the time of peak performance, and teams of mostly late chronotypes peak later than teams of early ones [16:51], [18:55], [21:00].
- Peak performance occurred six to seven hours after waking for early and intermediate chronotypes, and eleven or more hours after for late [20:30].
- Take-homes: elite sport is a 24-hour commitment, deficits are cumulative, sleep touches all performance factors, and circadian advantage is unexplored [22:03], [22:33], [23:03].
- She suggests sleep loss was once masked by amphetamines and steroids in sport [23:03].

## Numbers and definitions

- Normal reaction time: about a quarter of a second; six to seven hours of sleep doubles or triples it [01:33].
- Study design: seven days at reduced time in bed (the captions give "7 five versus 3 hours", garbled), then three days of nine hours [02:05], [02:36].
- Injury: sleeping under eight hours raised injury likelihood by "1.7%" in the captions [05:08]. This may be garbled (a ratio versus a percent); do not rely on it.
- Testosterone: down 10 to 12% after five hours of lost sleep (caption "increased... decreased" is inconsistent) [06:12]. Normal aging loss: 1 to 2% per year; she says a 20-year-old would look 31 [06:12].
- Glucose tolerance: reduced by 40% after a week or ten days [07:42].
- Alcohol comparison: six hours of sleep like two to three beers; four hours like about six beers [07:42], [08:12].
- Stanford extension: ten hours in bed for six weeks; basketball free throws and three-pointers each up 9% [09:12], [09:42].
- Football 40-yard dash improvement is garbled in the captions ("1 point1 2 seconds") [10:44]; swimmers added "five kicks" [11:14].
- NFL: West Coast evening teams won and beat the spread "twice" as often, forty years of data [14:19].
- Baseball: first-game loss "60% or more" after crossing three time zones; home field advantage 3.9% [15:50], [16:20]. The 60% caption is unclear.
- Chronotype peaks: early, noon to 2; intermediate, mid-afternoon; late, 7 to 8 in the evening [18:55]. The group-level peak "between four and seven" has no am or pm in the captions [18:24].
- Naps described: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 90 minutes [29:33], [30:03].
- Twelve teams were used in the team chronotype analysis [20:30].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Sleep-deprivation and recovery experiments with repeated performance tests [02:05].
- Stanford sleep-extension studies using actigraphs and sleep diaries, measuring performance at the end of six weeks [09:12].
- Forty years of NFL evening-game results compared to the Las Vegas spread, with controls for team quality and travel [14:19], [14:49].
- Multi-year baseball game data on time zones and home advantage [15:50], [16:20].
- The morning-evening questionnaire to classify chronotype, with performance tests six times across the day (bleep test, sprint times) [17:52], [18:24].
- Light and melatonin to shift the body clock [29:02].

## Limits and open questions

- Sample sizes are not stated for most studies; the high school injury study, Stanford extension and chronotype studies are cited without numbers of athletes, except twelve teams [20:30].
- The extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep, as she acknowledged [25:57].
- The 40-year NFL study is called robust by the speaker [14:49]; the authors are named in captions only as "Smith and motra" (caption spelling).
- The 9 to 10 hour recommendation is the speaker's synthesis of those extension studies [11:14].
- Her claim that a third of teams are not interested is her own experience [28:31].
- Several numbers (injury, football dash, baseball first-game loss) are garbled in the captions.

## Q&A

- Facility-limited sports such as swimming and hockey are hit hardest; swimmer studies showed gains from more sleep [23:55], [24:25].
- Whether to get extra sleep before a long event: yes [24:55].
- Training at peak time is better, and sleep consolidates learning; nap after training [25:25].
- Sleep quality: the extension studies did not measure sleep itself; both quality (reaching deep sleep) and quantity matter [25:57], [26:28].
- Individual need: those who "get by" tolerate deprivation better, not need less; chronic deprivation erases the reference for feeling alert; sleeping in on days off signals a deficit [26:58], [27:29], [28:00].
- Team interest: about a third already do this, a third want to try, a third are not interested [28:31].
- Shifting the clock earlier: possible with light boxes and melatonin; she mentions a trip to London for a team [29:02].
- Naps: 15 to 20 minutes, 30 minutes, or 90 minutes; a nap is not advised if night sleep is a problem; falling-asleep trouble usually comes from time zones or late caffeine [29:33], [30:03], [30:35].

title: "SSAC17: Avoiding Tommy John: How the MLB has Used Better Data and Training Methods"

## Summary

A Major League Baseball league-office official describes the league's response to a spike in Tommy John (UCL reconstruction) surgeries that came to a head in 2014. He lays out four concerns (more surgeries at MLB level, more repeat surgeries, more at youth and high school level, and widespread misperceptions) and the three-part Pitch Smart program built with a medical committee and USA Baseball: pitch count and rest limits, plain-language research, and accurate surgery information. He reports adoption by youth and high school bodies, a leveling off of MLB surgeries, a long-term prospective study, early results on rest-based care and orthobiologics, and new repair and training approaches, stressing that evidence on the newer methods is thin.

## Key claims

- MLB clubs have been required to use a league-wide electronic medical record since 2010, and the league does not share the data publicly until it is ready for peer review; the talk therefore draws on public data [01:09], [01:39].
- The league's 2014 concerns were more MLB surgeries, more second surgeries, more surgery at youth and high school levels, and misperceptions [02:10].

A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. - The goal was to add a standardized psychological measure alongside combine physical tests, not to replace them [04:13], [06:17].
- A league study with team executives produced 16 factors, with intelligence and personality as the two key areas [05:46].

- The test has run at the combine since 2013 with full participation, and the data were also turned into a coaching report [07:20], [07:51].
- The validation compared pre-draft scores with coach ratings after the players had been on a team for at least a year [09:54].

## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

## Key claims

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].
- More data has meant more decisions but not better ones; people are disillusioned, as with fitness bands [05:40], [06:11].
- A soccer team's higher exposure to high-speed running and explosive efforts coincided with no injuries, and lower exposure with more; the team had been holding athletes back [06:42], [07:13], [07:43].
- Two NFL examples showed more risk with doing less, and for one team the degree of change mattered, not the total [08:13], [08:43].
- Another NFL chart showed the reverse for accelerations: above 200 in a week, injuries were frequent [08:43].
- The common baseball view that a small change in range of motion sharply raises risk is challenged; the speaker says it varies by person, and an increase in hip internal rotation was linked to elbow ligament strain more than the opposite [09:13], [09:43], [10:13].
- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].
- Each team and each person has a different load signature, including phenotypes that break from too much load, too little, or both [14:15], [14:46].
- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].
- Teams should keep a few core metrics and review them yearly rather than manage a hundred variables [18:51].
- He claims the company helps teams cut days lost to injury by 42 percent [19:21].

## Numbers and definitions

- Correlation of salary-adjusted spending with wins: 0.76 NBA, 0.89 NFL [03:08].
- NBA average spend on injured players: 12.9 million dollars a year; 8.1 million dollars of that avoidable [03:08], [03:39].
- 46.6 million dollars of athlete on court: 40 wins West, 36 East, 0 percent playoff chance; 52 million dollars: 49 or 43 wins, 100 percent chance [03:39], [04:10].
- Share of wins set by health: NFL 25 percent, MLB 9 percent, NHL 12, MLS 15 [04:40]; NBA said as nine wins, "20%" of wins needed for the playoffs [04:10]. The captions say "NFL or NBA" at [04:10], so the 20 percent is likely NBA.
- Soccer team: "above 30 150 meters" of high-speed running over seven days (garbled; the figure is unclear) and more than 390 explosive multi-directional efforts, with no injuries [06:42], [07:13]. A one standard deviation increase was treated as risky [07:43].
- NFL team: above 200 accelerations in seven days, 33 or 34 percent injured (phrase unclear) [08:43].
- Baseball: 180 degrees of motion; a five degree change claimed to raise risk six to seven times [09:13].
- Acute to chronic ratio: 150 percent said to raise risk six or seven times; the speaker's four teams would have lost 8, (garbled), 15 and 26 percent of training [10:43], [11:13]. The top-right value is garbled in the captions.
- Premier League team: 23 injuries a year of 14 days or more; 8 to 12 of the same type [11:44], [12:14].
- Company claims: 42 percent fewer days lost; 25 leagues, five continents; over four years, first annual report last year [19:21], [19:51].

- Salary-weighted availability as a proxy for performance [02:38], [03:08].
- Dose-response charts of weekly load against injury risk, per team [06:42].
- Electronic medical record at the center, every data point statistically related to injury [11:13], [11:44].
- Anonymized aggregation across athletes, split by sport, position and team [12:14].
- Phenotypes of athletes by load response [14:15].

- "Infinitely higher" game injury rate is a figure of speech, not a number [16:48], [17:18].
- Captions garble "Kitman," "Tommy John" context and some terms.

## Summary

A moderated panel with a college volleyball coach, an Intel manager, an NFL receiver, a Catapult executive and a neurostimulation founder on wearables in team sport. The panelists argue that player welfare comes first and that performance, fan engagement and broadcast value follow from it. Practical examples include jump counts for volleyball, a hamstring "pitch count" for a Browns player, and an Australian rule change tied to late-game velocity. The recurring cautions are that data needs context, should not drive cut decisions alone, and raises unresolved questions about who owns player data in collective bargaining. Claims are mostly anecdotes and company views.

- Hawkins says a Browns player with hamstring trouble was put on a "pitch count" and then played all 16 games [08:42], [09:13].
- Hawkins says scaled-back weekly work lets athletes peak on Sunday, supported by data rather than by his own report of tired legs [09:44].
- The Catapult speaker says soft tissue injuries should not be treated as acceptable and that welfare is the base of the whole ecosystem [10:16].
- Training personalization is named as a major opportunity, since a uniform workload suits one athlete and overloads another [11:50].
- Hawkins expects resistance once data feeds evaluation, because it may shorten some careers while extending others [13:22], [13:53].
- The Catapult speaker says the worst use is policing effort, and says he has seen no evidence of players cut for falling scores [14:25], [14:55]. Hawkins disagrees from experience of players cut despite good play [15:25].
- Data should be contextualized and complementary to human judgment [16:55].
- A panelist notes that volleyball has little research on how many jumps are too many, and that research has mostly been on men [22:03], [22:35].
- For fan engagement, the Catapult speaker says people want stories, not raw data [24:07].
- Next-level analytics should say what to do next, not only report what happened [25:08], [25:38].
- Catapult speaker: Australian football used wearable data to test a substitution rule change; late-quarter velocity and soft tissue injuries fell together [30:45], [31:17].
- On concussion, the Halo founder says prevention is best and that stimulation after concussion would need a clinical trial [31:48], [32:18].
- The coach says concussion removal belongs to medical staff [33:21].

Two industrial and organizational psychologists describe a one-hour psychological assessment given to every player at the NFL combine since 2013. It measures cognitive ability and personality traits tied to football, and is meant as an addition to physical and film evidence. A three-year validation study compared combine scores with coach ratings of players after at least a year, plus penalties and injuries. Correlations are modest (about 0.22 to 0.35) but the speakers show that top and bottom scorers are rated very differently. ## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].

- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].

- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].

## Summary

A media talk (no slides) by the co-founder of The Cauldron, drawn from his new book on how the NBA uses technology and analytics. He argues that biometric and health data is now where on-court analytics was five or six years earlier. He treats keeping players healthy as the most protectable edge, because a rival can see a playing style but not how a team keeps players on the floor. His main concern is not the technology but data ownership, privacy and what players should give up in the coming collective bargaining talks. He also flags known error in tracking data.

## Key claims

- Biometric ideas are not new: diet changes by one star, and a team being fined for resting players in 2012, came before resting became fashionable. [01:39]
- A Warriors assistant general manager said that having two named players healthy for 75 games would tell him all he needed about the team. [02:40]
- A 2013-14 Spurs rotation outproduced peers at every slot, and strategic rest produced no drop-off in performance. [03:42] [04:13]
- Health and rest strategy is the most protectable secret, because a team's draft and playing style can be dissected but its method of keeping players healthy is hard to see. [05:14] [05:44]
- A quoted bioethics attorney says employer control of employee health care is a conflict of interest, and monitoring aimed at predicting performance is an economic purpose rather than a health one. [06:46]
- The reopened collective bargaining agreement is where this fight will be settled, and a cynic reads monitoring as a team benefit. [07:16] [07:46]
- Tools are improving but how to apply, collect and interpret the data on human actors is unresolved. [09:18] [09:48]
- Raw tracking data has an established error rate, including misidentified players and plays. [10:18] [10:48]
- Players cannot wear tracking devices in games until the agreement is reopened, so teams use practice and camera-based data to approximate load and fatigue. [11:18] [11:49]
- A Marquette program was said to be using wearables in college this year. [12:19]
- Who owns testing data (the testing company, the player, the team as employer) is unsettled; agents want it but may not want teams to have equal access. [12:49] [14:24] [14:54]
- The speaker says the larger question is ethics and privacy law, not technical limits. [15:56]
- The players union faces the problem of deciding what to give up while the technology and its uses keep changing. [16:26]
- Teams adopt what other teams adopt, and no one is sure of efficacy yet; some teams ask for raw data without a plan or staff to use it. [17:27] [17:57] [18:27]
- Teams should look for small actionable steps, such as rest and sleep, where the speaker says there is evidence (days of rest, travel). [18:57] [19:27]
- Flexibility loss across a game and then travel is substantial, per the Suns research head. [19:27] [19:58]

## Numbers and definitions

- Raw data error "as much as 15 to 20%" for play differentiation on court, told to the speaker by team personnel; he does not know the figure for force, speed or power. [10:48]
- Dietary change by one star in 2008 and 2009; Spurs resting fine in 2012. [01:39]
- Warriors condition: two named players healthy for 75 games; one played 77 games and the other 67; the team went 83 and 20 (caption wording "83 and 20", likely 83 wins including playoffs, not stated). [02:40] [03:10]
- Dean Oliver's book is dated 2002 or 2003 (caption "2002 2003"). [08:47]
- Season labels such as "20145" and "20134" are caption garbles (likely 2014-15 and 2013-14). [01:09] [03:10]
- A "7,000" injury reports remark is a joke, not a count. [15:24]
- Flexibility: the Suns research head estimates 25% lost across a game and another 10 to 15% after a flight. [19:27] [19:58]
- Adoption timeline for the union answer: next 6 to 12 to 18 months; "six to 12 months" for the story. [17:27] [20:29]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Interpolation: teams combine practice wearable data, off-court training and camera tracking data to estimate game load and fatigue because in-game wearables are barred. [11:49]
- Baseline testing at a pre-draft combine (P3, caption spelling "p 3") and independent testing by the Suns research head. [12:49] [13:21]
- No model, algorithm or formal evaluation is described.

## Limits and open questions

- A media perspective; the speaker also promotes his book. [00:38] [20:29]
- The rookie-class injury story is told without numbers, and he says no player-level prediction was given to him. [13:53]
- The 15 to 20% error comes from unnamed team personnel and refers to basketball camera data, not wearables. [10:48]
- The speaker says no one is sure of efficacy of the data. [17:57]
- Spurs rest and the Warriors anecdote support a view; no controls or sample are shown.

## Summary

A moderated panel (presented by Catapult) of a football high performance coach, a 76ers research head, a rugby and Australian sport veteran, a science writer and a Catapult executive. The theme is that sport science fails when it ignores people: buy-in, trust and culture matter more than any single metric. Panelists argue for individualized load, recovery as part of adaptation, caution against over-reading risk data and against pulling athletes back, and tying measures to performance outcomes players care about. The close covers nutrition monitoring, doping incentives and whether players trust wearables.

## Key claims

- Poor results are usually a mismatch between the scientist and the coach and athlete, and sport science should not be judged by a team's win-loss record. [02:32] [03:02]
- A rugby culture reset had the team write the articles they wanted written about them. [04:34] [05:06]
- At a football program, buy-in follows winning and meeting a need; it is a service role. [06:36] [07:37]
- Do not import "what worked here"; learn the culture before offering solutions. [08:08]

- Scientists should question assumed answers and fit into the existing culture. [12:43]
