- Without trust, athletes may say they feel fine to stay in the game. [17:19]
- Coaches can confuse talent and readiness; a talented freshman may lack work capacity. [18:20]
- A fluid plan that adjusts dose up or down by the athlete's daily state is reported to beat a static plan. [19:20] [19:51]
- Sport science has gone too far toward rest; every pull-back limits overload, so respond to modifiable risk factors by changing training. [20:22] [20:52] [21:22]
- Monitoring something not understood can create self-fulfilling beliefs; the panelist describes a fetal monitoring example and sleep feedback studies. [22:22] [22:52] [23:23]
- Published thresholds do not hold for real athletes; ask a performance question, collect broad data, then see what it says. [23:54] [24:24]
- An NBA coach wanted to know "where the cliff is" to push to the edge safely. [24:54]
- Smart periodization allows harder camps with more players ready. [25:24]
- NCAA rules limiting football in practice, and acclimatization rules, are criticized as counterproductive. [25:56] [26:26] [26:57]
- All stress counts, including academic and social. [27:59] [28:29]
- A one-week sleep change (no console after 10) was followed by a higher game grade for one player. [29:31] [30:03]
- The relationship between practitioner and athlete may matter more than the method. [30:33] [31:05]
- Black-box monitoring breeds suspicion; feed results back to players. [32:38] [33:08]

- Garbled: "Al Duz is a 35 minute sufferfest" (caption). [35:44]

- At a football program, buy-in follows winning and meeting a need; it is a service role. [06:36] [07:37]

- The "sports science" label can read as a lab and be unwelcome; blame follows losses and credit goes to the people involved. [08:39] [09:40]

- Scientists should question assumed answers and fit into the existing culture. [12:43]
- Recovery is part of adaptation, and athletes differ in how they recover. [14:14] [14:44] [15:14]
- Data and talking to the athlete both matter; no single recovery number exists, and asking the athlete is the best current tool if they are paying attention. [15:46] [16:47]
- Without trust, athletes may say they feel fine to stay in the game. [17:19]
- Coaches can confuse talent and readiness; a talented freshman may lack work capacity. [18:20]
- A fluid plan that adjusts dose up or down by the athlete's daily state is reported to beat a static plan. [19:20] [19:51]
- Sport science has gone too far toward rest; every pull-back limits overload, so respond to modifiable risk factors by changing training. [20:22] [20:52] [21:22]

- Published thresholds do not hold for real athletes; ask a performance question, collect broad data, then see what it says. [23:54] [24:24]
- An NBA coach wanted to know "where the cliff is" to push to the edge safely. [24:54]
- Smart periodization allows harder camps with more players ready. [25:24]

- All stress counts, including academic and social. [27:59] [28:29]

## Summary

A moderated panel with a college volleyball coach, an Intel manager, an NFL receiver, a Catapult executive and a neurostimulation founder on wearables in team sport. The panelists argue that player welfare comes first and that performance, fan engagement and broadcast value follow from it. Practical examples include jump counts for volleyball, a hamstring "pitch count" for a Browns player, and an Australian rule change tied to late-game velocity. The recurring cautions are that data needs context, should not drive cut decisions alone, and raises unresolved questions about who owns player data in collective bargaining. Claims are mostly anecdotes and company views.

## Key claims

- The Catapult speaker frames practice and game day as one continuum, with wearables serving player welfare, tactics, broadcast and fans [03:35].
- Florida's volleyball staff turned to a jump-measuring wearable after a hand-tracked jump limit for an injured player worked poorly [06:06].
- The coach uses it daily to see when front-row players reach diminishing returns and to adjust drills; she says it confirms her judgment and adds objective feedback [07:39], [08:11].
- Hawkins says a Browns player with hamstring trouble was put on a "pitch count" and then played all 16 games [08:42], [09:13].
- Hawkins says scaled-back weekly work lets athletes peak on Sunday, supported by data rather than by his own report of tired legs [09:44].
- The Catapult speaker says soft tissue injuries should not be treated as acceptable and that welfare is the base of the whole ecosystem [10:16].
- Training personalization is named as a major opportunity, since a uniform workload suits one athlete and overloads another [11:50].
- Hawkins expects resistance once data feeds evaluation, because it may shorten some careers while extending others [13:22], [13:53].
- The Catapult speaker says the worst use is policing effort, and says he has seen no evidence of players cut for falling scores [14:25], [14:55]. Hawkins disagrees from experience of players cut despite good play [15:25].
- Data should be contextualized and complementary to human judgment [16:55].
- A panelist notes that volleyball has little research on how many jumps are too many, and that research has mostly been on men [22:03], [22:35].
- For fan engagement, the Catapult speaker says people want stories, not raw data [24:07].
- Next-level analytics should say what to do next, not only report what happened [25:08], [25:38].
- Catapult speaker: Australian football used wearable data to test a substitution rule change; late-quarter velocity and soft tissue injuries fell together [30:45], [31:17].
- On concussion, the Halo founder says prevention is best and that stimulation after concussion would need a clinical trial [31:48], [32:18].
- The coach says concussion removal belongs to medical staff [33:21].
- The panel disagrees on collective bargaining: Hawkins expects data access and public disclosure to come up in the next agreement; the Catapult speaker says unions should be involved [36:56], [37:57].
- In Australia, a player's data follows a trade; Hawkins expects NFL workload history to follow players and affect draft and signing outcomes [38:58], [39:58].
- A Catapult speaker says wearable data is handled much like medical data (HIPAA compliance), with gaps in athlete access [49:10]; another panelist says performance and medical data should be blended [50:44].
- A closing criterion offered: data should connect to value, be non-obvious and be actionable [57:19].
- Hawkins predicts a new talent pool of people who translate data [58:22].

## Numbers and definitions

- Jump count limit for the injured player: 40 jumps in a week, set by doctors [06:06].
- A volleyball player jumps over 11 feet 3 inches and averages over 30 inches in practice [07:08].
- Browns hamstring case: 16 games played; three or four earlier seasons with large missed time [09:13].
- Catapult works with 800 to 900 teams ("eight or nine hundred") [14:25].
- Catapult business size: from 50 or 60 million dollars to 300 million dollars in a year [17:58].
- Elite-market penetration: seven, eight or nine percent, and "under 10" percent [17:58], [18:30]. Forecast of near-universal use in three to five years [18:30].
- Claimed 83 percent drop in soft tissue injuries credited to a college coach (caption spelling "Jimbo official FSU") [17:58].
- Average NFL career: three years, which wearables could help extend to six (Hawkins) [13:22].
- Catapult high school clients: under two dozen [21:02].
- Snowboarding landings of 10 G's versus 20 G's shown on a broadcast [20:02].
- Softball and volleyball serve speeds of 55 to 65 miles an hour mentioned as a wearable target [27:40].
- Catapult future focus "70" on predictive analytics (caption is garbled; unit not stated) [54:45].
- Hawkins: NFL workload tracked for the eight years since high school [39:58].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable accelerometer-based tracking (Catapult, the vert jump sensor); tackle identification through algorithms from sensor data, since no single sensor flags a tackle [29:14].
- Load limits by count (jumps, hamstring reps) set with trainers.
- Australian football rule test: measure velocity and soft tissue injury frequency over a season of use [30:45], [31:17].
- Biometric data used to see different performance and injury risk in wet and dry weather [42:30].
- Active (neurostimulation) versus passive (sensing) wearables [46:06].
- Virtual reality for quarterback reps without physical load [47:07].

## Limits and open questions

- No sample sizes, controls or data are shown. Injury-reduction claims are single stories or vendor statements.
- Four of six speakers have a commercial stake (Catapult, Intel, Halo, plus the sport-technology framing).
- The Australian rule-change result is called a direct correlation over a year; cause is the speaker's reading.
- Speakers disagree on whether data is used to cut players; no evidence is shown either way.
- Captions do not reliably separate speakers in places; "Mary wise," "adieu schiffman," "Abe matkour," the introducer's name and several product names are probably misspelled.
- The caption at [56:17] reads "will not be solid" where the intended word may be different.

## Q&A

- High school adoption: Catapult sees uptake starting; challenge is simplification, not hardware [21:02], [24:37].
- Past data for data's sake: stories and "what next" recommendations [24:07], [25:38].
- Wanted wearable: ball speed on the wrist (coach); concussion detection and a first-down ball sensor (Hawkins) [27:10], [28:12].
- Concussion prevention and treatment [31:48].
- Pulling a player at the end of a final game on wearable data [32:50].
- Accuracy, battery life and security [34:23], [34:54].
- Collective bargaining and data ownership [35:56].
- Licensing heart rate for broadcast [40:29].
- Weather as data [41:30].
- Protecting college and high school athletes' data, and treating it as medical information [48:40], [49:10].
- Fashion and consumer wearables [51:14], [53:15].
- Where things stand in two years [55:15].

title: "SSAC17: Quantifying Injury Risk presented by Kitman Labs"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Stephen Smith (caption spelling; CEO of "Kidman labs" as captioned), Ronan Parisi (introducer)]
topics: [injury-health, sports-science, american-football, basketball, decision-making]
confidence: supported

## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

## Key claims

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].
- More data has meant more decisions but not better ones; people are disillusioned, as with fitness bands [05:40], [06:11].
- A soccer team's higher exposure to high-speed running and explosive efforts coincided with no injuries, and lower exposure with more; the team had been holding athletes back [06:42], [07:13], [07:43].
- Two NFL examples showed more risk with doing less, and for one team the degree of change mattered, not the total [08:13], [08:43].
- Another NFL chart showed the reverse for accelerations: above 200 in a week, injuries were frequent [08:43].
- The common baseball view that a small change in range of motion sharply raises risk is challenged; the speaker says it varies by person, and an increase in hip internal rotation was linked to elbow ligament strain more than the opposite [09:13], [09:43], [10:13].
- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].
- Each team and each person has a different load signature, including phenotypes that break from too much load, too little, or both [14:15], [14:46].
- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].
- Teams should keep a few core metrics and review them yearly rather than manage a hundred variables [18:51].
- He claims the company helps teams cut days lost to injury by 42 percent [19:21].

## Numbers and definitions

- Correlation of salary-adjusted spending with wins: 0.76 NBA, 0.89 NFL [03:08].
- NBA average spend on injured players: 12.9 million dollars a year; 8.1 million dollars of that avoidable [03:08], [03:39].
- 46.6 million dollars of athlete on court: 40 wins West, 36 East, 0 percent playoff chance; 52 million dollars: 49 or 43 wins, 100 percent chance [03:39], [04:10].
- Share of wins set by health: NFL 25 percent, MLB 9 percent, NHL 12, MLS 15 [04:40]; NBA said as nine wins, "20%" of wins needed for the playoffs [04:10]. The captions say "NFL or NBA" at [04:10], so the 20 percent is likely NBA.
- Soccer team: "above 30 150 meters" of high-speed running over seven days (garbled; the figure is unclear) and more than 390 explosive multi-directional efforts, with no injuries [06:42], [07:13]. A one standard deviation increase was treated as risky [07:43].
- NFL team: above 200 accelerations in seven days, 33 or 34 percent injured (phrase unclear) [08:43].
- Baseball: 180 degrees of motion; a five degree change claimed to raise risk six to seven times [09:13].
- Acute to chronic ratio: 150 percent said to raise risk six or seven times; the speaker's four teams would have lost 8, (garbled), 15 and 26 percent of training [10:43], [11:13]. The top-right value is garbled in the captions.
- Premier League team: 23 injuries a year of 14 days or more; 8 to 12 of the same type [11:44], [12:14].
- Company claims: 42 percent fewer days lost; 25 leagues, five continents; over four years, first annual report last year [19:21], [19:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Salary-weighted availability as a proxy for performance [02:38], [03:08].
- Dose-response charts of weekly load against injury risk, per team [06:42].
- Electronic medical record at the center, every data point statistically related to injury [11:13], [11:44].
- Anonymized aggregation across athletes, split by sport, position and team [12:14].
- Phenotypes of athletes by load response [14:15].
- Annual review of metrics [18:51].

## Limits and open questions

- Chart samples and statistics are not stated; many numbers are partly garbled.
- The salary link is correlational, and using salary as a stand-in for performance is the speaker's assumption.
- Results cover a few teams; the speaker says each team differs, which limits any general rule.
- It is a company presentation; claims such as 42 percent fewer days lost and being the "proven global leader" are the speaker's own [19:21].
- "Infinitely higher" game injury rate is a figure of speech, not a number [16:48], [17:18].
- Captions garble "Kitman," "Tommy John" context and some terms.

## Q&A

No Q&A in the recording.

Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. - A panelist relays that communication is about 70 percent of the battle and the data about 30. [17:54]

- How does injury prevention push the field forward? Days lost and return-from-injury signals. [57:35] [59:07]

## Summary

A 2015 panel of NCAA, university, law and NBA voices debates how college sports should change as money, lawsuits and the Power 5 split reshape the amateur model. Panelists discuss whether athletes are employees under labor law, an antitrust challenge to scholarship caps, Title IX limits on paying revenue-sport athletes, the NBA age rule, and the role of agents. Most speakers favor gradual recalibration over abolition, with more weight on academics and athlete health and welfare. No analytics or data models are shown. The value for a performance staff is the policy context that shapes eligibility, time demands and what athlete data collection could mean legally.

## Summary

A 2015 panel with a Browns receiver, Catapult, the Warriors, Zebra and Zephyr discusses how wearable tracking is used in pro sport. Speakers agree that hardware matters less than turning data into simple, trusted guidance for coaches and athletes. Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. Evidence is anecdotal and several speakers sell the technology.

## Key claims

- Zebra's speaker separates player tracking from consumer wearables, expecting consumer wearables to be dominated by large apparel and tech brands. [04:07]
- Catapult's speaker says the value is in the data and in showing teams value, not in new hardware, and that the US is early in adopting sports science. [04:37] [05:08]
- The Warriors use Catapult, previously used Zephyr, and are trying Zebra with their minor league team. [06:08]
- Hawkins says a teammate with hamstring problems in prior seasons was shut down once his calculated workload reached a set level, and had no hamstring issues that season. [07:10]
- Australian clubs use the devices in games and practice (no pads), and the league uses longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations. [08:13] [08:44]
- Hawkins says the data confirmed that his workload after a coaching change was high, and he was scaled back. [10:47] [11:19]
- Lacob says the front office trusts coaches and trainers to manage players day to day and looks at long-term effects; use is still in its infancy. [11:49] [12:20] [12:50]
- The technology touches the whole organization and coaches must be shown why a change is needed. [13:20]
- Hawkins says a pre-combine analysis found slower 40 times came from coasting through the second step, and sharing video and acceleration data gave a way to fix it, so the technology is not only for restricting athletes. [15:21]
- A simplified load number gives head coaches a shared language, for example asking for a light mechanical day. [16:23]
- Measuring load individually could replace fixed rules like a flat pitch count. [17:23]
- A panelist relays that communication is about 70 percent of the battle and the data about 30. [17:54]
- Data is a tool that often confirms coaches' intuition; the quants-versus-subjective split is a false dichotomy. [18:24] [18:55]
- Zebra's speaker says everything should connect to game day, then to the rest of the week. [20:59]
- Metrics must be explained to fans; physiology is harder to explain than speed and distance. [23:03] [23:33]
- Hawkins expects that after about five years of data the numbers will show decline, and this may affect releases. [25:36]
- Lacob says anything placed on an athlete will be part of labor negotiations, and that data looks backward while management must project. [31:43] [32:13]

- Barriers to adoption include safety of a battery-powered device, and the need for smaller washable units. [40:21] [40:51]
- Hawkins says the hardware is cheap but the service around it costs money; Zephyr's speaker says college engineering students can do analysis as projects. [48:31] [49:01]

- Sleep and nutrition are named as the two biggest drivers of performance. [52:33]
- Lacob speculates, and says it is not a fact, that more pick and rolls could relate to knee injuries. [54:34]
- Zebra's system can pass heart-rate data from other vendors' devices over Bluetooth; the panel does not want 18 devices on an athlete. [55:34] [56:04]
- Days lost to injury is a simple metric teams use. [57:35]
- Injury prevention is the clearest way to show dollars of value and reach mass adoption. [1:01:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Catapult has done this "over eight years". [04:37]
- Hawkins' 16-game season; the capped player had hamstring-derailed seasons for the last three years. [07:10] [07:41]
- Pittsburgh pitchers stop at 120 as an example of a fixed rule; others could go 150 or need to stop at 100. [17:23]
- Communication 70 percent, data 30 percent (relayed remark). [17:54]

- Simplified load or intensity scores for coaches.
- Live dashboards and Australian dynamic substitution.
- Days lost as an outcome metric.
- Data integration over Bluetooth.

## Limits and open questions

- Three of the five panelists work for vendors; claims are commercial and anecdotal. No data, sample sizes or studies were shown.
- The hamstring example is one player; the ACL example [59:07] and Bryant example are single cases.

- How has wearable data helped basketball coaching? Still learning; load capacity and movement types are being studied. [53:34] [54:04]
- Could wearables talk to each other? Yes through integration, but how much is too much. [55:34] [56:04]
- How does injury prevention push the field forward? Days lost and return-from-injury signals. [57:35] [59:07]

Two Baylor Applied Performance staff describe how they package GPS, heart-rate and questionnaire data for football coaches. They frame athlete stress with general versus specific adaptation, stacking of risk factors, and use it or lose it. They report that mood, nutrition, soreness, sleep and body weight changed how hard practice felt or how fast athletes ran, separate preparedness (recent exposure) from readiness, use position-specific load metrics, and set weekday loads as a percent of game load. The talk stresses relationships, storytelling and the 22 hours outside practice. Despite the title, it shows little in-game data, no predictive model, and no sample sizes.

## Summary

A 2015 panel with a Browns receiver, Catapult, the Warriors, Zebra and Zephyr discusses how wearable tracking is used in pro sport. Speakers agree that hardware matters less than turning data into simple, trusted guidance for coaches and athletes. Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. ## Summary

Two Baylor Applied Performance staff describe how they package GPS, heart-rate and questionnaire data for football coaches. They frame athlete stress with general versus specific adaptation, stacking of risk factors, and use it or lose it. They report that mood, nutrition, soreness, sleep and body weight changed how hard practice felt or how fast athletes ran, separate preparedness (recent exposure) from readiness, use position-specific load metrics, and set weekday loads as a percent of game load. The talk stresses relationships, storytelling and the 22 hours outside practice. Despite the title, it shows little in-game data, no predictive model, and no sample sizes.

- The speakers say their job is to package information so coaches with decades of experience do not need to handle the analytics, and the coaches should trust them to compartmentalize. [02:01] [02:31] [03:01] [07:35]
- Athletes adapt generally to general stress, so high-level athletes need specific stressors. [04:33]
- Injuries come from stacking factors (sleep, nutrition, body weight), not single causes, compared to comorbidity in disease. [05:33] [06:04]
- Qualities fade if not worked: speed needs work every 7 to 10 days and strength about weekly. [06:04]
- They found athletes in a good mood tolerate higher load, and bad mood can make an easy GPS session feel hard. [08:37] [09:07]
- Preparedness should be based on the last three or four weeks of exposure, not on last year's camp. [10:38]
- Readiness covers what the athlete can handle today given recent load; they say a spike is manageable if the athlete is ready. [11:08]
- A wide receiver's speed was half a mile an hour faster at a heavier body weight, which they share with nutrition staff. [11:08]
- Poor daytime nutrition led to soreness, worse sleep and lower body weight the next day, seen over three years. [11:38] [12:08]
- Player load is divided by distance for linemen; high-velocity distance is not used for them; accelerations, decelerations and low-velocity IMA are. [12:38] [13:08] [13:38]
- Left tackles turn outside 70 percent of the time; whether to balance this is debated. [14:10] [14:42]
- Weekly practice load is set as a percent of game load: Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70, Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- Training is a dose of stress, and both too little and too much fail. [18:20]
- The week is split into the first 48 hours (recovery), the middle 72 (push, and get ahead on schoolwork) and the final 48 (ramp up). [18:52] [19:22]
- They use Catapult and wellness questionnaire data to find habits of the fastest and most powerful athletes, since they have athletes about two hours a day and the other 22 matter. [20:54] [21:24]
- They do not monitor sleep objectively; they use self-report as a way to start conversations. [21:54]
- A well-developed aerobic system helps the body handle load spikes. [23:25]
- Information does not automatically change behavior; stories and relationships do. [23:55] [24:27]
- They look for 1 percent improvements through outside partners. [25:29]
- Takeaways: stress pairing, the psychological side, better storytelling (monster truck and Prius analogy), and a buffer so athletes and the organization never stop. [26:00] [27:32] [28:34]

- Speed every 7 to 10 days; strength about once a week. [06:04]
- Example optimal body weight between 198 and 202 (one athlete). [06:04]

- Spike tolerance: caption reads "within 25 or 50%" then "spike of 25%"; ambiguous. [11:08]

- Left tackle turns outside 70 percent. [14:10]
- Saturday game is 100 percent; Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70; Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- First 48, middle 72, final 48 hours. [18:52] [19:22]
- Athletes seen about two hours a day, 22 hours otherwise. [21:24]
- Fall camp averaged over two to three years as a reference. [09:37]
- Practice rating example: athlete gave 4 and then 2 on 1 to 5 scales against GPS. [08:37] [09:07]

## Methods and frameworks named

- General adaptation and specific adaptation to imposed demands. [04:03]
- Stress pairing (comorbidity). [05:33]
- Use it or lose it. [06:04]
- Catapult GPS (player load, high-velocity distance, IMA, accelerations), heart rate, "a mega wave" (caption spelling, device unclear), wellness questionnaire. [09:07] [21:24]
- Preparedness versus readiness. [10:38] [11:08]

- Calendar notes covering loading and meals. [16:15]
- Stories and analogies for behavior change. [24:27]

video_id: NReHfiYxxS4
title: "SSAC15: Wearable Technology: Athlete Analytics (Presented by Zebra Technologies)"
event: SSAC15 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Andrew Hawkins (Cleveland Browns), Brian Kopp (Catapult Sports), Kirk Lacob (Golden State Warriors; caption spelling), Eric Petrotinelli (Zebra Technologies; caption spelling), Brian Russell (Zephyr Technologies), Mark McCloskey (moderator, Wired), Amanda Lurie (student host; caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, basketball, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested

## Summary

A 2015 panel with a Browns receiver, Catapult, the Warriors, Zebra and Zephyr discusses how wearable tracking is used in pro sport. Speakers agree that hardware matters less than turning data into simple, trusted guidance for coaches and athletes. Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. Evidence is anecdotal and several speakers sell the technology.

## Key claims

- Zebra's speaker separates player tracking from consumer wearables, expecting consumer wearables to be dominated by large apparel and tech brands. [04:07]
- Catapult's speaker says the value is in the data and in showing teams value, not in new hardware, and that the US is early in adopting sports science. [04:37] [05:08]
- The Warriors use Catapult, previously used Zephyr, and are trying Zebra with their minor league team. [06:08]
- Hawkins says a teammate with hamstring problems in prior seasons was shut down once his calculated workload reached a set level, and had no hamstring issues that season. [07:10]
- Australian clubs use the devices in games and practice (no pads), and the league uses longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations. [08:13] [08:44]
- Hawkins says the data confirmed that his workload after a coaching change was high, and he was scaled back. [10:47] [11:19]
- Lacob says the front office trusts coaches and trainers to manage players day to day and looks at long-term effects; use is still in its infancy. [11:49] [12:20] [12:50]
- The technology touches the whole organization and coaches must be shown why a change is needed. [13:20]
- Hawkins says a pre-combine analysis found slower 40 times came from coasting through the second step, and sharing video and acceleration data gave a way to fix it, so the technology is not only for restricting athletes. [15:21]
- A simplified load number gives head coaches a shared language, for example asking for a light mechanical day. [16:23]
- Measuring load individually could replace fixed rules like a flat pitch count. [17:23]
- A panelist relays that communication is about 70 percent of the battle and the data about 30. [17:54]
- Data is a tool that often confirms coaches' intuition; the quants-versus-subjective split is a false dichotomy. [18:24] [18:55]
- Zebra's speaker says everything should connect to game day, then to the rest of the week. [20:59]
- Metrics must be explained to fans; physiology is harder to explain than speed and distance. [23:03] [23:33]
- Hawkins expects that after about five years of data the numbers will show decline, and this may affect releases. [25:36]
- Lacob says anything placed on an athlete will be part of labor negotiations, and that data looks backward while management must project. [31:43] [32:13]
- The technology can be delivered live; Australian football makes substitutions from live data, while US college teams view it live without acting on it. [34:16] [34:47] [35:17]
- The NFL plans to have systems in all 31 stadiums the next year, with data kept central for competitive equality, and offensive and defensive coaches differ on who should see it. [37:48] [38:49] [39:49]
- Barriers to adoption include safety of a battery-powered device, and the need for smaller washable units. [40:21] [40:51]
- Hawkins says the hardware is cheap but the service around it costs money; Zephyr's speaker says college engineering students can do analysis as projects. [48:31] [49:01]
- On withholding data, one panelist says athletes do not need to know everything because the data are not always conclusive; others say transparency matters for buy-in, and timing matters. [50:02] [51:32] [52:33]
- Sleep and nutrition are named as the two biggest drivers of performance. [52:33]
- Lacob speculates, and says it is not a fact, that more pick and rolls could relate to knee injuries. [54:34]
- Zebra's system can pass heart-rate data from other vendors' devices over Bluetooth; the panel does not want 18 devices on an athlete. [55:34] [56:04]
- Days lost to injury is a simple metric teams use. [57:35]
- Injury prevention is the clearest way to show dollars of value and reach mass adoption. [1:01:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Catapult has done this "over eight years". [04:37]
- Hawkins' 16-game season; the capped player had hamstring-derailed seasons for the last three years. [07:10] [07:41]
- Pittsburgh pitchers stop at 120 as an example of a fixed rule; others could go 150 or need to stop at 100. [17:23]
- Communication 70 percent, data 30 percent (relayed remark). [17:54]
- Olympic track: up to three percent speed increase for an 800 meter runner. [44:24]
- Team Oracle catamaran: 72 feet, 40 knots, 30 feet in the air. [44:24]
- A receiver lined up 15 times on the left and three times on the right; every right-side snap was a run. [38:18]
- NFL systems in 31 stadiums next year. [37:48]
- Antonio Bryant story: about 10 million guaranteed, cut within a month or two; panelist says tracking could have saved 8 to 10 million. Hedged ("I think") and unverified. [59:37] [1:00:09]
- Anquan Boldin (caption "bolden") reportedly ran 4.85 (caption "485") at age 21, now 34. Unverified. [28:41]

## Methods and frameworks named

- RFID player tracking and GPS wearables (Zebra, Catapult), remote physiological monitoring (Zephyr).
- Workload thresholds per player; longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations.
- Simplified load or intensity scores for coaches.
- Live dashboards and Australian dynamic substitution.
- Days lost as an outcome metric.
- Data integration over Bluetooth.

## Limits and open questions

- Three of the five panelists work for vendors; claims are commercial and anecdotal. No data, sample sizes or studies were shown.
- The hamstring example is one player; the ACL example [59:07] and Bryant example are single cases.
- Panelists disagree on withholding data: one says some data should not be told, another says if denied he would not wear it. [50:02] [51:02]
- Hawkins says players' feel and data matched, but he did not show a comparison. [10:47]
- Real-time data was not available to North American decision makers at the time. [33:46]
- Auto-captions do not mark speakers; first answers at [03:07] could not be attributed to one panelist. Names garbled in places (Petrotinelli spelled two ways).

## Q&A

- Are these tools affordable for high schools and colleges? Eventually yes; pricing, packaging and service are the barrier. [45:25] [46:27]
- Is there data you would not tell an athlete? Some; timing and transparency matter. [50:02] [52:33]
- How has wearable data helped basketball coaching? Still learning; load capacity and movement types are being studied. [53:34] [54:04]
- Could wearables talk to each other? Yes through integration, but how much is too much. [55:34] [56:04]
- How does injury prevention push the field forward? Days lost and return-from-injury signals. [57:35] [59:07]

This is Baylor's own department speaking in 2016, so it is relevant as an institutional record of earlier practice.

- They found athletes in a good mood tolerate higher load, and bad mood can make an easy GPS session feel hard. [08:37] [09:07]
- Preparedness should be based on the last three or four weeks of exposure, not on last year's camp. [10:38]
- Readiness covers what the athlete can handle today given recent load; they say a spike is manageable if the athlete is ready. [11:08]
- A wide receiver's speed was half a mile an hour faster at a heavier body weight, which they share with nutrition staff. [11:08]
- Poor daytime nutrition led to soreness, worse sleep and lower body weight the next day, seen over three years. [11:38] [12:08]
- Player load is divided by distance for linemen; high-velocity distance is not used for them; accelerations, decelerations and low-velocity IMA are. [12:38] [13:08] [13:38]
- Left tackles turn outside 70 percent of the time; whether to balance this is debated. [14:10] [14:42]
- Weekly practice load is set as a percent of game load: Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70, Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- Training is a dose of stress, and both too little and too much fail. [18:20]
- The week is split into the first 48 hours (recovery), the middle 72 (push, and get ahead on schoolwork) and the final 48 (ramp up). [18:52] [19:22]
- They use Catapult and wellness questionnaire data to find habits of the fastest and most powerful athletes, since they have athletes about two hours a day and the other 22 matter. [20:54] [21:24]
- They do not monitor sleep objectively; they use self-report as a way to start conversations. [21:54]
- A well-developed aerobic system helps the body handle load spikes. [23:25]
- Information does not automatically change behavior; stories and relationships do. [23:55] [24:27]
- They look for 1 percent improvements through outside partners. [25:29]
- Takeaways: stress pairing, the psychological side, better storytelling (monster truck and Prius analogy), and a buffer so athletes and the organization never stop. [26:00] [27:32] [28:34]

- Player load per yard: player load divided by distance. [13:08]
- Speed every 7 to 10 days; strength about once a week. [06:04]
- Example optimal body weight between 198 and 202 (one athlete). [06:04]
- Wide receiver about half a mile an hour faster at 220 pounds or heavier. [11:08]
- Spike tolerance: caption reads "within 25 or 50%" then "spike of 25%"; ambiguous. [11:08]
- Linemen cover about 60 percent of a skill player's distance. [12:38]
- Left tackle turns outside 70 percent. [14:10]
- Saturday game is 100 percent; Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70; Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- First 48, middle 72, final 48 hours. [18:52] [19:22]
- Athletes seen about two hours a day, 22 hours otherwise. [21:24]
- Fall camp averaged over two to three years as a reference. [09:37]
- Practice rating example: athlete gave 4 and then 2 on 1 to 5 scales against GPS. [08:37] [09:07]

- Stress pairing (comorbidity). [05:33]
- Use it or lose it. [06:04]

- Stories and analogies for behavior change. [24:27]

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive.

**Session routine.** When working inside a project repo, follow the Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` and read `docs/STATUS.md` at the start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, and `git push` at the end. This is what keeps the two machines in step.

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), finish with the produced file in hand. Check what exists first, then build the file even when a similar one already exists.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools: invoke one when it clearly fits the task.

# Session Startup

The `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, a summary of `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot. Work from the injected copy.

- If hook failures appear, surface them once on the first response, then continue. Entries mean a hook or scheduled job failed.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- The injection is a frozen snapshot: mid-session writes take effect next session. Load anything further only when a question needs it.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are written only by `claude-memory-compiler`. Read one only when a question needs that day.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

---

Maintainer note: `AGENTS.md` diverges from this file on purpose (Codex has no Skill tool, so it spells out the memory rules). Keep them as separate files; the memory procedure's one home is the `memory-write` skill.

# Shell / Environment (Windows)

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.
- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows-MCP when both could do the job.
- Tool paths: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md` is Mac-centric; on this machine verify with `Get-Command <tool>` / `where.exe <tool>`.
- Traps:
  - `uv` lives at `~/.local/bin/uv.exe`. Hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not relocate it.
  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
  - Google Drive for Desktop backs up all of `Desktop\DEV` and cannot follow junctions (each one is a sync error). So renv project libraries live outside DEV: user env var `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY_ROOT` = `%LOCALAPPDATA%\R\renv-library` (set 2026-09-22). Do not undo it; restart RStudio after env changes. `DEV\_DRIVE` and `LibraryProject\ZoteroInjestion` are junctions kept on purpose (2 expected Drive errors).
  - R is at `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.3\bin\Rscript.exe` (not on PATH).
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.
- Paths that differ from the Mac:
  - SecondBrain vault: `~/Desktop/SecondBrain` (Mac: `~/SecondBrain`).
  - Workspace memory (Tier A for `DEV`): `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV/memory/`.
  - Printing-press CLIs: `~/go/bin/*.exe`.

# ~/DEV — workspace map

Eric Rash — Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Sport science and
football analytics, plus the agent system that runs them.

This file is a **map, not a rulebook**. Behavior rules live in
`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Read only the index you need.

## Areas

| Area | Index | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| Football | `FOOTBALL.md` | Game film, player analytics, CFB prediction. ~39k files — about two thirds of DEV. |
| Performance | `PERFORMANCE.md` | Athlete monitoring, testing, load, risk. GPS, force plate, VALD, DEXA, S2. |
| Research | `RESEARCH.md` | Literature, Zotero, book library, reading pipelines. |
| Platform | `PLATFORM.md` | KeystoneOS, dashboards, CLIs, scheduled jobs. |
| Program | `PROGRAM.md` | Staff reporting, curriculum, proposals, vetting, brand. |
| Personal | `PERSONAL.md` | Side projects. Not Baylor work. |
| Commands | `COMMANDS.md` | Desk reference: every report/project command Eric can run himself. |

## Elsewhere on disk

`~/DEV` in this file means the workspace root: `~/DEV` on the Mac,
`~/Desktop/DEV` on Windows. Paths that differ per machine are in `~/.claude/machine.md`.

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/` | Parked projects. Not a git repo, so the consolidation sweep skips it. Has its own `README.md`. |
| `~/DEV/_INBOX/` | Loose files from the `~/DEV` root. Own repo. |
| SecondBrain vault | Obsidian vault, ~850 notes. Own `CLAUDE.md`. Mac `~/SecondBrain`, Windows `~/Desktop/SecondBrain`. |
| `~/.claude/skills/` | ~155 skills |
| `~/go/bin/` | ~8 custom CLIs built with `cli-printing-press` |
| `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/knowledge/` | ~230 compiled articles |

## Layout rules

Full rules — grouping depth, the depth-2 discovery limit, and the gitignored-subtree
trap — live in project memory: `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md`.

- 23 projects carry their own `CLAUDE.md`. Read it before working in one.

## Handling care

- `DexaProject/` holds identifiable health data. It lives on Google Drive, not in
  `~/DEV`, on **both** machines — one copy, reached by each machine's own path:
  - Mac: `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/DexaProject`
  - Windows: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject`

  See `PERFORMANCE.md`.
  Never paste its contents into chat, an artifact, or an external service.

## Keeping this true

When a file moves or a new project starts, **update the router in the same
turn**. A stale pointer is worse than no pointer.

The counts above are approximate on purpose — they convey scale, not state, and
a `~` keeps ordinary growth from making this file wrong. Re-measure them only
when one is off by enough to change a decision. Counts last checked 2026-09-05.

Memory files named in these indexes (`project_*.md`, `user_*.md`) live in the
workspace's Tier A folder: Mac `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/`,
Windows `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV/memory/`. They auto-load
only when cwd is the workspace root itself — from inside a sub-project, open them by path.

Search everything with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`.

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), finish with the produced file in hand. Check what exists first, then build the file even when a similar one already exists.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools: invoke one when it clearly fits the task.

# Session Startup

The `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, a summary of `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot. Work from the injected copy.

- If hook failures appear, surface them once on the first response, then continue. Entries mean a hook or scheduled job failed.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- The injection is a frozen snapshot: mid-session writes take effect next session. Load anything further only when a question needs it.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are written only by `claude-memory-compiler`. Read one only when a question needs that day.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

---

Topics to keep: American football, basketball, sports science, analytics for those sports, policymaking, front-office decision-making, advanced decision-making, competitive advantage, athlete health and injury.

   - yt-dlp caption-only fetching (`--write-subs --write-auto-subs --skip-download --convert-subs srt`), YouTube HTTP 429 throttling with backoff; rolling-caption dedupe.

event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Josh Nelson (Baylor University), Andrew alov (caption spelling; Baylor University; later "coach alof")]
topics: [american-football, sports-science, injury-health]
confidence: untested

status: draft

## Summary

Two Baylor Applied Performance staff (the host introduces them as speakers "from Baylor University") describe how they package GPS, heart-rate and questionnaire data for football coaches. They frame athlete stress with general versus specific adaptation, stacking of risk factors, and use it or lose it. They report that mood, nutrition, soreness, sleep and body weight changed how hard practice felt or how fast athletes ran, separate preparedness (recent exposure) from readiness, use position-specific load metrics, and set weekday loads as a percent of game load. The talk stresses relationships, storytelling and the 22 hours outside practice. Despite the title, it shows little in-game data, no predictive model, and no sample sizes. This is Baylor's own department speaking in 2016, so it is relevant as an institutional record of earlier practice.

## Key claims

- The speakers say their job is to package information so coaches with decades of experience do not need to handle the analytics, and the coaches should trust them to compartmentalize. [02:01] [02:31] [03:01] [07:35]
- Athletes adapt generally to general stress, so high-level athletes need specific stressors. [04:33]
- Injuries come from stacking factors (sleep, nutrition, body weight), not single causes, compared to comorbidity in disease. [05:33] [06:04]
- Qualities fade if not worked: speed needs work every 7 to 10 days and strength about weekly. [06:04]
- They found athletes in a good mood tolerate higher load, and bad mood can make an easy GPS session feel hard. [08:37] [09:07]
- Preparedness should be based on the last three or four weeks of exposure, not on last year's camp. [10:38]
- Readiness covers what the athlete can handle today given recent load; they say a spike is manageable if the athlete is ready. [11:08]
- A wide receiver's speed was half a mile an hour faster at a heavier body weight, which they share with nutrition staff. [11:08]
- Poor daytime nutrition led to soreness, worse sleep and lower body weight the next day, seen over three years. [11:38] [12:08]
- Player load is divided by distance for linemen; high-velocity distance is not used for them; accelerations, decelerations and low-velocity IMA are. [12:38] [13:08] [13:38]
- Left tackles turn outside 70 percent of the time; whether to balance this is debated. [14:10] [14:42]
- Weekly practice load is set as a percent of game load: Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70, Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- Training is a dose of stress, and both too little and too much fail. [18:20]
- The week is split into the first 48 hours (recovery), the middle 72 (push, and get ahead on schoolwork) and the final 48 (ramp up). [18:52] [19:22]
- They use Catapult and wellness questionnaire data to find habits of the fastest and most powerful athletes, since they have athletes about two hours a day and the other 22 matter. [20:54] [21:24]
- They do not monitor sleep objectively; they use self-report as a way to start conversations. [21:54]
- A well-developed aerobic system helps the body handle load spikes. [23:25]
- Information does not automatically change behavior; stories and relationships do. [23:55] [24:27]
- They look for 1 percent improvements through outside partners. [25:29]
- Takeaways: stress pairing, the psychological side, better storytelling (monster truck and Prius analogy), and a buffer so athletes and the organization never stop. [26:00] [27:32] [28:34]

## Numbers and definitions

- Player load per yard: player load divided by distance. [13:08]
- Speed every 7 to 10 days; strength about once a week. [06:04]
- Example optimal body weight between 198 and 202 (one athlete). [06:04]
- Wide receiver about half a mile an hour faster at 220 pounds or heavier. [11:08]
- Spike tolerance: caption reads "within 25 or 50%" then "spike of 25%"; ambiguous. [11:08]
- Linemen cover about 60 percent of a skill player's distance. [12:38]
- Left tackle turns outside 70 percent. [14:10]
- Saturday game is 100 percent; Tuesday and Wednesday 60 to 70; Thursday 50 to 55. [17:16] [17:48]
- First 48, middle 72, final 48 hours. [18:52] [19:22]
- Athletes seen about two hours a day, 22 hours otherwise. [21:24]
- Fall camp averaged over two to three years as a reference. [09:37]
- Practice rating example: athlete gave 4 and then 2 on 1 to 5 scales against GPS. [08:37] [09:07]

## Methods and frameworks named

- General adaptation and specific adaptation to imposed demands. [04:03]
- Stress pairing (comorbidity). [05:33]
- Use it or lose it. [06:04]
- Catapult GPS (player load, high-velocity distance, IMA, accelerations), heart rate, "a mega wave" (caption spelling, device unclear), wellness questionnaire. [09:07] [21:24]
- Preparedness versus readiness. [10:38] [11:08]
- Weekly load as percent of game load. [17:16]
- Calendar notes covering loading and meals. [16:15]
- Stories and analogies for behavior change. [24:27]

## Limits and open questions

- No numbers, sample sizes, effect sizes or comparison groups; observations are described as seen over three years. [12:08]
- Despite the title, no in-game wearable results or predictive injury model are shown; game load is only the 100 percent reference. [17:16]
- Cannot tell which speaker said what; claims are the Baylor program's own view from 2016.
- Mood and nutrition findings could be correlation with other factors; the speakers describe the mechanisms without testing.
- Spike tolerance claim is garbled in the captions. [11:08]
- Speakers acknowledge two schools of thought on balancing turn direction. [14:42]
- Names of other staff are garbled in captions and are not used here.

## Q&A

No Q&A; the speakers say they are out of time. [29:05]

---
type: video-summary
video_id: NReHfiYxxS4
title: "SSAC15: Wearable Technology: Athlete Analytics (Presented by Zebra Technologies)"
event: SSAC15 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Andrew Hawkins (Cleveland Browns), Brian Kopp (Catapult Sports), Kirk Lacob (Golden State Warriors; caption spelling), Eric Petrotinelli (Zebra Technologies; caption spelling), Brian Russell (Zephyr Technologies), Mark McCloskey (moderator, Wired), Amanda Lurie (student host; caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, american-football, basketball, front-office, decision-making]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A 2015 panel with a Browns receiver, Catapult, the Warriors, Zebra and Zephyr discusses how wearable tracking is used in pro sport. Speakers agree that hardware matters less than turning data into simple, trusted guidance for coaches and athletes. Examples include a hamstring-history player held to a workload ceiling, individualized limits in place of fixed pitch counts, and live substitutions in Australian football. The panel also covers adoption barriers (league equality, device safety, size), contract and labor worries, whether to tell athletes everything, and days lost to injury as the clearest value case. Evidence is anecdotal and several speakers sell the technology.

## Key claims

- Zebra's speaker separates player tracking from consumer wearables, expecting consumer wearables to be dominated by large apparel and tech brands. [04:07]
- Catapult's speaker says the value is in the data and in showing teams value, not in new hardware, and that the US is early in adopting sports science. [04:37] [05:08]
- The Warriors use Catapult, previously used Zephyr, and are trying Zebra with their minor league team. [06:08]
- Hawkins says a teammate with hamstring problems in prior seasons was shut down once his calculated workload reached a set level, and had no hamstring issues that season. [07:10]
- Australian clubs use the devices in games and practice (no pads), and the league uses longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations. [08:13] [08:44]
- Hawkins says the data confirmed that his workload after a coaching change was high, and he was scaled back. [10:47] [11:19]
- Lacob says the front office trusts coaches and trainers to manage players day to day and looks at long-term effects; use is still in its infancy. [11:49] [12:20] [12:50]
- The technology touches the whole organization and coaches must be shown why a change is needed. [13:20]
- Hawkins says a pre-combine analysis found slower 40 times came from coasting through the second step, and sharing video and acceleration data gave a way to fix it, so the technology is not only for restricting athletes. [15:21]
- A simplified load number gives head coaches a shared language, for example asking for a light mechanical day. [16:23]
- Measuring load individually could replace fixed rules like a flat pitch count. [17:23]
- A panelist relays that communication is about 70 percent of the battle and the data about 30. [17:54]
- Data is a tool that often confirms coaches' intuition; the quants-versus-subjective split is a false dichotomy. [18:24] [18:55]
- Zebra's speaker says everything should connect to game day, then to the rest of the week. [20:59]
- Metrics must be explained to fans; physiology is harder to explain than speed and distance. [23:03] [23:33]
- Hawkins expects that after about five years of data the numbers will show decline, and this may affect releases. [25:36]
- Lacob says anything placed on an athlete will be part of labor negotiations, and that data looks backward while management must project. [31:43] [32:13]
- The technology can be delivered live; Australian football makes substitutions from live data, while US college teams view it live without acting on it. [34:16] [34:47] [35:17]
- The NFL plans to have systems in all 31 stadiums the next year, with data kept central for competitive equality, and offensive and defensive coaches differ on who should see it. [37:48] [38:49] [39:49]
- Barriers to adoption include safety of a battery-powered device, and the need for smaller washable units. [40:21] [40:51]
- Hawkins says the hardware is cheap but the service around it costs money; Zephyr's speaker says college engineering students can do analysis as projects. [48:31] [49:01]
- On withholding data, one panelist says athletes do not need to know everything because the data are not always conclusive; others say transparency matters for buy-in, and timing matters. [50:02] [51:32] [52:33]
- Sleep and nutrition are named as the two biggest drivers of performance. [52:33]
- Lacob speculates, and says it is not a fact, that more pick and rolls could relate to knee injuries. [54:34]
- Zebra's system can pass heart-rate data from other vendors' devices over Bluetooth; the panel does not want 18 devices on an athlete. [55:34] [56:04]
- Days lost to injury is a simple metric teams use. [57:35]
- Injury prevention is the clearest way to show dollars of value and reach mass adoption. [1:01:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Catapult has done this "over eight years". [04:37]
- Hawkins' 16-game season; the capped player had hamstring-derailed seasons for the last three years. [07:10] [07:41]
- Pittsburgh pitchers stop at 120 as an example of a fixed rule; others could go 150 or need to stop at 100. [17:23]
- Communication 70 percent, data 30 percent (relayed remark). [17:54]
- Olympic track: up to three percent speed increase for an 800 meter runner. [44:24]
- Team Oracle catamaran: 72 feet, 40 knots, 30 feet in the air. [44:24]
- A receiver lined up 15 times on the left and three times on the right; every right-side snap was a run. [38:18]
- NFL systems in 31 stadiums next year. [37:48]
- Antonio Bryant story: about 10 million guaranteed, cut within a month or two; panelist says tracking could have saved 8 to 10 million. Hedged ("I think") and unverified. [59:37] [1:00:09]
- Anquan Boldin (caption "bolden") reportedly ran 4.85 (caption "485") at age 21, now 34. Unverified. [28:41]

## Methods and frameworks named

- RFID player tracking and GPS wearables (Zebra, Catapult), remote physiological monitoring (Zephyr).
- Workload thresholds per player; longitudinal data to find injury-prone situations.
- Simplified load or intensity scores for coaches.
- Live dashboards and Australian dynamic substitution.
- Days lost as an outcome metric.
- Data integration over Bluetooth.

## Limits and open questions

- Three of the five panelists work for vendors; claims are commercial and anecdotal. No data, sample sizes or studies were shown.
- The hamstring example is one player; the ACL example [59:07] and Bryant example are single cases.
- Panelists disagree on withholding data: one says some data should not be told, another says if denied he would not wear it. [50:02] [51:02]
- Hawkins says players' feel and data matched, but he did not show a comparison. [10:47]
- Real-time data was not available to North American decision makers at the time. [33:46]
- Auto-captions do not mark speakers; first answers at [03:07] could not be attributed to one panelist. Names garbled in places (Petrotinelli spelled two ways).

## Q&A

- Are these tools affordable for high schools and colleges? Eventually yes; pricing, packaging and service are the barrier. [45:25] [46:27]
- Is there data you would not tell an athlete? Some; timing and transparency matter. [50:02] [52:33]
- How has wearable data helped basketball coaching? Still learning; load capacity and movement types are being studied. [53:34] [54:04]
- Could wearables talk to each other? Yes through integration, but how much is too much. [55:34] [56:04]
- How does injury prevention push the field forward? Days lost and return-from-injury signals. [57:35] [59:07]

## Summary

A 2015 panel of NCAA, university, law and NBA voices debates how college sports should change as money, lawsuits and the Power 5 split reshape the amateur model. Panelists discuss whether athletes are employees under labor law, an antitrust challenge to scholarship caps, Title IX limits on paying revenue-sport athletes, the NBA age rule, and the role of agents. Most speakers favor gradual recalibration over abolition, with more weight on academics and athlete health and welfare. No analytics or data models are shown. The value for a performance staff is the policy context that shapes eligibility, time demands and what athlete data collection could mean legally.

## Key claims

- Jim Phillips (Northwestern) says campus athletics exists to teach skills such as teamwork that a classroom does not, and that academics must be the base of any reform. [03:37]
- Oliver Luck says he joined the NCAA because he thinks the college model is unique in the world and worth saving while reforming what is broken. [06:11]
- Rod Thorne (NBA, caption spelling) says the league's concern is player health, including very dense schedules, and that the injury level is no higher than in recent years. [08:15]
- Mike mccan (caption spelling) explains that if football players are declared employees, a separate vote is still needed to unionize, and a ruling could let athletes at other private schools rely on it. [10:17] [10:47]
- Mike notes the employee question is tricky because only some athletes (football) might unionize, leaving others unclear. [11:17]
- Jim lists recent reforms: unlimited meals, full cost of attendance, four-year grants. [13:19]
- Jim asks whether seasons are too long and time demands too high, and mentions a "year of readiness" idea that needs study. [13:51] [14:21]
- A panelist, citing a former NCAA president, says amateurism is a social construct that changes by era. [16:23]
- A panelist says cost of attendance is a federal calculation done by each school's financial aid office and that athletes have been under-resourced for decades. [18:26] [19:29]
- Rod says the NBA one-year rule is a disaster for colleges but better for the NBA than drafting from high school; the league would prefer two years but needs the Players Association. [22:31] [23:03] [23:35]
- Mike says those hurt by eligibility rules have no seat at the bargaining table, and a legal challenge to the age rule would likely also name the union. [24:05] [25:07]
- Oliver says rules on agents may be liberalized so athletes get better information, with a warning that some advice would be self-serving. [27:38] [28:39]
- Jim says realignment was partly driven by finances, and that nearly all programs lose money without institutional subsidy. [30:42] [31:11]
- Mike expects Title IX litigation if men's basketball and football players are paid. [33:14]
- Mike says the Jenkins antitrust case could be a game changer, but stars would gain while many athletes might not exceed the value of a scholarship. [35:48] [36:19]
- Schools are budgeting for a trust fund per year under a judge's order (caption: "oanon" case, judge "wilin"). [34:16] [34:46]
- Predictions: Oliver sees a healthy enterprise with more liberalization and academic emphasis [38:24]; Mike sees a trust-fund compromise and a capped, group-negotiated name and likeness model [39:24] [40:28]; Jim hopes pro-bound athletes get non-college options such as training academies [42:32]; Rod says the NBA's minor league could play a larger role [44:35].
- Jim says schools made decisions that were not in athletes' interest, and that graduation rates and academic standards either matter or they do not. [53:51] [54:53]
- A panelist says a single national academic cutoff is hard because campuses differ in mission. [55:24]
- Mike says coaches, not presidents or athletic directors, often hold the decision power, unlike in pro leagues. [56:55] [57:27]

## Numbers and definitions

- About 2.7 to 2.8 billion dollars in scholarships a year. [05:40]
- Over a thousand NCAA institutions, about 300 in Division I, 65 in the Power 5 (moderator's figures). [15:21] 351 Division I schools. [15:52]
- At one panelist's former campus, 141 athletes had Pell grants (caption "pill Grant"; the count may be garbled). [16:54]
- Cost of attendance adds 2 to 4,000 beyond the athletic scholarship. [17:56]
- NBA 2005 negotiation set the one-year-after-high-school rule. [22:00]
- Developmental league salary mentioned as "I think 25,000". [25:37]
- 1100 schools play college athletics and 23 turn a profit without subsidy. [31:11]
- 23 coaches paid more than 2.5 million (moderator, "I think it was 23"). [32:11]
- Trust fund of 5,000 dollars per year. [34:46] Caption at [39:56] reads "$55,000", probably garbled.
- Northwestern: 492 athletes, 19 sports (11 female, 8 male); the spending figure "over $800,000" is ambiguous in the captions. [47:40]
- Hypothetical: student body graduation rate of 65 percent used as an example. [56:25]
- NLRB vote described as five votes, possibly three to two. [10:47]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Labor law: employee status under the National Labor Relations Act, then a separate union vote. [10:17]
- Antitrust: the Jenkins case argues scholarship caps restrain trade. [35:48]
- Title IX parity. [33:14]
- Collective bargaining as the route for league age rules. [22:00]
- Federal cost-of-attendance calculation. [18:26]
- Academic Progress Rate (APR) called better than before but a weak standard. [52:50]
- Proposed graduation-rate proportionality: compare athlete rates to the school's own student body. [56:25]

## Limits and open questions

- No data, analytics or models were presented; this is opinion and legal commentary.
- Speakers represent the NCAA, a university, the NBA and a law school; each speaks from an institutional position.
- Outcomes were pending in 2015 (labor board decision, appeal of the antitrust case).
- Captions do not mark speaker changes; some attributions above are by context. Several names, case names ("oanon", "Kesler") and figures are garbled.
- Claim that coaches are the highest paid public employee in 40 of 50 states is garbled ("40 of the highest paid employees and 40 of the 50 states") and unverified. [57:27]
- Predictions at [38:24] to [44:35] are untested.

## Q&A

- Does UAB dropping football signal more schools doing so? Panelists say probably not; it was a unique situation. [46:39]
- Why keep athletic scholarships rather than need-based aid? A panelist says the experience seems similar either way and need-based aid may be discussed. [48:40] [49:12]
- What does reform mean for Olympic sports? Mike says they are on the sidelines now and could be the next phase of legal challenges. [50:15] [50:47]
- How to handle academic standards and the North Carolina lawsuit? Jim says institutions must be accountable; another panelist says one cutoff would hit campuses differently. [51:49] [53:51] [55:24]
- Could graduation targets be proportional to the school's student body rate? Panelists say it has merit. [56:25] [56:55]

title: "SSAC17: Quantifying Injury Risk presented by Kitman Labs"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Stephen Smith (caption spelling; CEO of "Kidman labs" as captioned), Ronan Parisi (introducer)]
topics: [injury-health, sports-science, american-football, basketball, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The CEO of an athlete-management and analytics company argues that injuries drive wins, and that most teams use load data wrongly. Using base salary as a stand-in for performance, he links lost salary from injuries to wins in the NBA and NFL. He then presents team-level charts where less load, not more, coincided with more injuries, and argues that common thresholds (a one standard deviation change, the 1.5 acute to chronic ratio) fail when checked against a team's own data. He says risk models need pooled, anonymized data and specific questions about pathology, timing and mechanism. Many results are shown only as charts, and the speaker's company is the source.

## Key claims

- Earlier attempts to link injuries to wins failed because counts of injuries or days lost assume every athlete matters equally [01:36], [02:06].
- Base salary is used as a stand-in for contribution because the speaker believes the best talent is paid the most in a salary cap market [02:38].
- Days lost are priced by deducting a day of salary per missed day, then correlated with wins [03:08].
- The speaker says 63 percent of NBA injury spending is on avoidable injuries (ruptures, strains and sprains) [03:39].
- In the NBA, health alone is said to decide about nine wins a year [04:10].
- Injury rates are rising across leagues while time lost shrinks, and prevention spending is not working [05:10].
- More data has meant more decisions but not better ones; people are disillusioned, as with fitness bands [05:40], [06:11].
- A soccer team's higher exposure to high-speed running and explosive efforts coincided with no injuries, and lower exposure with more; the team had been holding athletes back [06:42], [07:13], [07:43].
- Two NFL examples showed more risk with doing less, and for one team the degree of change mattered, not the total [08:13], [08:43].
- Another NFL chart showed the reverse for accelerations: above 200 in a week, injuries were frequent [08:43].
- The common baseball view that a small change in range of motion sharply raises risk is challenged; the speaker says it varies by person, and an increase in hip internal rotation was linked to elbow ligament strain more than the opposite [09:13], [09:43], [10:13].
- A published acute to chronic ratio threshold did not fit any of four rugby teams in one league [10:13], [10:43].
- Each team and each person has a different load signature, including phenotypes that break from too much load, too little, or both [14:15], [14:46].
- Risk tolerance should change with roster and opponent [13:14].
- Good injury models need specific questions about pathology, season phase, practice versus game, and injury mechanism [16:48], [17:18], [17:49].
- The speaker says no one is truly doing injury prediction with machine learning [15:46], [16:17].
- Teams should keep a few core metrics and review them yearly rather than manage a hundred variables [18:51].
- He claims the company helps teams cut days lost to injury by 42 percent [19:21].

## Numbers and definitions

- Correlation of salary-adjusted spending with wins: 0.76 NBA, 0.89 NFL [03:08].
- NBA average spend on injured players: 12.9 million dollars a year; 8.1 million dollars of that avoidable [03:08], [03:39].
- 46.6 million dollars of athlete on court: 40 wins West, 36 East, 0 percent playoff chance; 52 million dollars: 49 or 43 wins, 100 percent chance [03:39], [04:10].
- Share of wins set by health: NFL 25 percent, MLB 9 percent, NHL 12, MLS 15 [04:40]; NBA said as nine wins, "20%" of wins needed for the playoffs [04:10]. The captions say "NFL or NBA" at [04:10], so the 20 percent is likely NBA.
- Soccer team: "above 30 150 meters" of high-speed running over seven days (garbled; the figure is unclear) and more than 390 explosive multi-directional efforts, with no injuries [06:42], [07:13]. A one standard deviation increase was treated as risky [07:43].
- NFL team: above 200 accelerations in seven days, 33 or 34 percent injured (phrase unclear) [08:43].
- Baseball: 180 degrees of motion; a five degree change claimed to raise risk six to seven times [09:13].
- Acute to chronic ratio: 150 percent said to raise risk six or seven times; the speaker's four teams would have lost 8, (garbled), 15 and 26 percent of training [10:43], [11:13]. The top-right value is garbled in the captions.
- Premier League team: 23 injuries a year of 14 days or more; 8 to 12 of the same type [11:44], [12:14].
- Company claims: 42 percent fewer days lost; 25 leagues, five continents; over four years, first annual report last year [19:21], [19:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Salary-weighted availability as a proxy for performance [02:38], [03:08].
- Dose-response charts of weekly load against injury risk, per team [06:42].
- Electronic medical record at the center, every data point statistically related to injury [11:13], [11:44].
- Anonymized aggregation across athletes, split by sport, position and team [12:14].
- Phenotypes of athletes by load response [14:15].
- Annual review of metrics [18:51].

## Limits and open questions

- Chart samples and statistics are not stated; many numbers are partly garbled.
- The salary link is correlational, and using salary as a stand-in for performance is the speaker's assumption.
- Results cover a few teams; the speaker says each team differs, which limits any general rule.
- It is a company presentation; claims such as 42 percent fewer days lost and being the "proven global leader" are the speaker's own [19:21].
- "Infinitely higher" game injury rate is a figure of speech, not a number [16:48], [17:18].
- Captions garble "Kitman," "Tommy John" context and some terms.

## Q&A

No Q&A in the recording.
