tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

## Summary

A panel with the Falcons' general manager and head coach on how the two of them stay aligned. Both describe a close, near-daily working relationship, and say analytics informs player, coach and contract decisions but a small group at the top makes the final call. They walk through the 2008 start, a quarterback pick and a trade for a receiver, the shift from 13-3 to 4-12, and the rise of technology for teaching and tracking players. The talk is first-person accounts from two decision makers, so it shows how they describe their process, not whether the process works.

## Key claims

- The two leaders met daily at first and still rarely go a day without talking [07:11].
- The coach lives week to week while the GM works on a longer timeline; they treat the difference as a check and balance [09:45].
- Many people feed a decision, but the final choice is made by the GM and head coach [11:17].
- The GM evaluated the coach with a statistical look at past defenses (sacks, tackles, rankings) alongside interviews with five or six other candidates [03:34] [04:06].
- The staff was built with a mix of former college coaches, former NFL players and coaches with head coaching experience [14:51] [15:21].
- Culture work began with the support staff (film, video, IT) and a first week of meeting everyone in the building [16:22] [17:54].
- Roster evaluation compared contracts by position to the rest of the league for cap and value reasons [19:56].
- Players are evaluated on the human side first, then biomechanical and statistical study, and the decision is ultimately human [28:38] [29:40].
- The coach says watching every pass thrown by the quarterback prospect changed the reading of the interception total: only a handful were throws to regret [31:44] [32:16].
- The coach says numbers point you toward more information and are not the end-all [32:46].
- The trade for the receiver was studied for what the extra picks historically produced [35:19].
- The GM says he is learning to study how a free agent fits with position coaches and scheme before signing [38:53] [39:54].
- After a 4-12 season, the GM says he practiced "productive vulnerability," examining everything including himself [42:00].
- The coach describes player-made film cut-ups and devices replacing paper playbooks, and teaching to different development stages instead of the lowest level [44:34] [46:08].
- The GM describes heart rate and GPS tracking in practice to decide whom to draw back, without dictating practice [47:10].
- Analytics sets the practice plan using expected plays by situation; game planning includes score, wind and temperature [52:53] [53:55].
- The coach expects the next wave to use positional plotting data to set where players line up [57:31] [58:03].
- Disagreement between the two is healthy and best kept private, and the GM says the coach should be able to bring any concern to him [1:00:04] [1:00:34].

## Numbers and definitions

- Record together: 60 and 36, four playoff appearances [01:01].
- First meeting: scheduled for an hour, lasted about two and a half hours [05:06].
- Staff size: over 150 employees [17:54].
- Cap: potentially 130 million plus [20:57]. The quarterback signed a 104 million contract [21:27]. Two players making over a quarter of the cap [21:27].
- The "middle class" of salary is described as five or six million and shrinking [21:58].
- Records: 13 and 3 last year, 4 and 12 this past year [27:05].
- Quarterback prospect: third overall pick [28:07]; threw almost 650 passes, 19 interceptions as a senior [30:43].
- Receiver trade (2011): moved from the mid 20s to number six; gave a first the next year plus a second and two fourths [36:19]. The GM says fewer than 50% of those fourth-rounders were active and fewer than 14% were starters [35:19].
- "Fifteen 230 million" on a free agent [38:53]: garbled in captions, likely a range; do not rely on it.
- A defensive end expected to produce 15 to 20 sacks [39:54].
- The coach was second to one other coach in wins over the last five years before this season [40:57].
- Play data: 250 plus characters per play for player-made cut-ups [45:36].
- Player tracking involvement: four plus years [47:10].
- Over 20 teams attending the conference [54:56].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Contract and salary comparison by position across the league [19:56].
- Biomechanical assessment of a player compared with other quarterbacks and receivers [28:38] [33:48].
- Analysis of how draft picks of a given round have produced (active and starter rates) [35:19].
- Review of the quarterback's full pass history, play by play [31:14].
- Fit check: whether a defense has produced the output (sacks versus pressures) the new player is bought for [39:54].
- Practice plan built on play counts by down and distance [52:53].
- Heart rate and GPS tracking of practices [47:10]; a sports science partner (Sparta Sports Science) announced [51:48].
- Decision model: many contributors, two final decision makers [11:17].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, model or sample sizes are shown; claims are recollections by the two decision makers.
- Both describe outcomes of their own decisions positively; each decision reviewed has a known result, and failures are only discussed generally [36:50] [37:20].
- The GM's interpretation of the receiver's draft-pick study is his own; the method (population, years) is not stated.
- The analytics head is named only at the end, with no description of what the group produces [50:16].
- Claims that tracking will keep a named player healthy [47:41] are not supported by anything shown.
- Caption names: "Mike Ree", "Thomas demitro", "Carl piber" and "Scott Pei" are caption spellings.
- The panel's front-office, salary cap setting is professional football, not college.

## Q&A

- Does the GM draw on other industries to improve football analytics? Yes, particularly basketball, and the team recently announced a sports science partner [51:17] [51:48].
- How much of the team's analytics is about the salary cap versus football? The coach says everything is built on breaking down plays, and it is used for practice plans and game planning [52:53] [53:23].
- How important is gut instinct? The GM says it is important and built from experience, and expects future head coaches to be steeped in analysis; the coach says it ends up a gut decision [54:56] [55:27] [57:00].
- How important is respectful tension? The coach says disagreement is needed and best kept private; the GM says eliminating the divide between coaching and personnel is key [59:34] [1:00:34].

## Summary

A book talk arguing that football behaves like a system in which a small change can have large downstream effects. The speaker gives examples (helmet and face mask, a quarterback injury leading to a new offense, size, tempo, a trick formation), then describes how science is being applied: a decision flowchart framed as digital thinking, gene and protein research on concussions, and a multiple-object tracking test of brain performance. It is storytelling with a few figures; the causal claims are the authors' interpretation, not tested.

## Key claims

- The speakers describe football as a system where poking one spot gives an unpredictable response elsewhere [01:08].
- The helmet was introduced to prevent skull fractures [02:40].
- The authors argue that adding the face mask changed the game because players began to tackle with their heads [03:10] [03:41].
- The authors argue helmets in their current form do not reduce concussions because the brain still moves inside the skull [04:12].
- Chaos theory and the butterfly effect are used to explain small changes with big results [05:14] [05:44].
- A quarterback's career-ending injury led his coach to reuse plays built for his arm in a shorter form, leading to the West Coast offense [06:44] [07:14].
- Coaches gain advantages through size, conditioning and surprise [07:44].
- The no-huddle offense is described as denying defenders rest, and early adopters benefit until others copy it [09:18] [09:48].
- A small high school used a rule loophole to disguise who would receive the ball [10:48].
- The authors suggest the age of science may have started with a coach who taught chemistry and physics [11:51].
- The speaker argues the quarterback read moved from analog to digital by using a short yes-or-no flowchart, linked to Boolean algebra and Shannon's telephone work [12:52] [13:23] [13:54].
- Genetic profiles may show concussion susceptibility, and a protein tied to muscle twitch speed may relate to performance [14:56] [15:26].
- The combine measures speed, explosiveness and strength; the brain is the untested part [15:56] [16:28].
- A tracking test of four balls over eight seconds was developed by colleagues at the University of Montreal, and athletes do better than non-athletes [17:29] [19:00].
- The ability is both innate and trained, and regular training improves reading the game [19:31].

## Numbers and definitions

- Players of 300 pounds: three in 1980, 461 at the last count in 2012 [07:44] [08:16].
- Lorenz example: captions give two input numbers as "0 5 50627" and "0506" and a difference of 0.127; the captions are garbled and the numbers do not reconcile, so do not rely on them [05:14] [05:44].
- Greg Cook played three games [06:44].
- Formation: 16,634 possible receivers [10:48].
- The tracking test: four of the balls are designated, then all move, then the person identifies the four; eight seconds [17:29] [17:59].
- Decision flowchart: option one, option two, option three, then the "guarantee" [13:23].
- Talk length 25 minutes with five for questions [00:06].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Chaos theory (sensitivity to initial conditions) [09:18].
- Boolean algebra and its use in telephone systems and computers [13:54].
- Genetic and protein analysis for concussion and muscle twitch [14:56] [15:26].
- Multiple-object tracking test, "neurot Tracker" in captions [16:58] [17:29].
- Wonderlic test, mentioned critically [16:28].

## Limits and open questions

- Causal stories (face mask, injury, no-huddle) are presented as the authors' view with no data.
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or references for the tracking test findings; the attributed conclusions are summarized in a sentence [19:00].
- The authors say the genetic and protein work is early and the final outcome unknown [15:56] [20:01].
- The speaker names the 1-2-3 flowchart coach as "Sam wsh" in the captions; later text says Bill Walsh at [06:14], so the garble is in the captions.

- The audience test result is not reported [19:00].

## Summary

A sleep researcher and an ESPN writer discuss how sleep deficiency, travel and schedule design affect NBA performance. The researcher describes persuading teams to change flight times, practice times and time-zone handling. He argues that lost sleep slows reaction, raises injury and illness risk, weakens learning and memory, and worsens emotional control. The main point is that sleep and travel are controllable performance factors that teams mostly ignored. The speakers admit the basketball-specific evidence is early and rests on small player numbers, and they lean on research from other occupations and on team anecdotes.

## Key claims

- A common team routine was a late night, then an early-morning flight, so players arrived sleep deprived. This was defended as a way to tough out jet lag. [02:43] [03:46]
- After one trip moved to an afternoon flight, the plane reportedly ran out of food because players were so alert. [04:16]
- Teams can stay on home-clock time and practice at the hour they would normally play, which moved a curfew to about 3 a.m. [04:46] [05:17]
- Players questioned the speaker for far longer than the briefing planned, and buy-in from players and coaches was seen as essential. [06:53] [07:24]
- A missed night of sleep slows average reaction time sharply, which matters for read-and-react and help-defense decisions. [09:56]
- Sleep loss increases missed signals in the visual field and raises injury risk. [10:56] [11:26]
- A week of short sleep is said to lower testosterone by the equivalent of many years of aging. [11:26]
- Sleep deficiency raises inflammation and infection risk and lengthens injury recovery. [12:26]
- Baseball data from a colleague showed the home team's results depend on the direction of the visitor's cross-country travel. [12:56]
- Learning needs adequate sleep before (attention) and after (memory consolidation), shown with animal maze studies. [15:02] [15:33]
- Sleep loss impairs integrating lessons from a loss into next-game adjustments. [16:35]
- The speaker hopes the league eliminates road back-to-backs because teams cannot structurally secure enough sleep on such trips. [17:07] [17:37]
- Sleep deprivation heightens emotional-brain reactivity and weakens judgment control, which he links to getting a technical foul. [18:09] [18:42]

## Numbers and definitions

- Average reaction time: about a quarter of a second (250 milliseconds) normally; after a missed night it jumps to about 750 to 900 milliseconds. [09:25] [09:56]
- Missed signals: those who had not slept had 10 times as many as those who had. [10:56]
- Testosterone: four hours of sleep a night for a week equals the drop of 11 years of aging; he says this takes a 25-year-old to a 36-year-old's level. [11:26] [11:56]
- Garbled: a caption line about a west-to-east team being "a 6337 dog" cannot be read. [11:56]
- Baseball: the visitor having completed eastward travel is associated with 1.24 more runs per game for the home team. [12:56]
- Amygdala firing is about 10 times higher after a night awake when shown disturbing images. [18:09]
- Sleep need: about 8.2 or 8.3 hours per 24 hours for the average person, more than two sleep bouts being less efficient. [22:16]
- Brain clearing: some support cells shrink so debris clears about 20 times more rapidly during sleep. [23:18]
- Aging: total sleep duration changes by only about 20 or 30 minutes in someone without a sleep disorder. [25:22]
- Sample framing: the host notes about 15 players and eight or nine regular ones, and asks whether this equals "one and a half two two and a half three wins a season". The speaker does not give a win figure. [12:56] [13:29]
- Other occupations studied: 5,000 policemen and 7,000 firefighters. [13:59]
- Schedule: baseball season is called about 182 games in the captions. [20:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Consulting on shootaround and practice schedules and on how teams fly. [01:41]
- Matching physiology to occupation: the speaker argues that findings from pilots, firefighters and police transfer to athletes because the physiology is the same. [13:59]
- Experiments with electrodes on hippocampal place cells in animals. [15:33]
- fMRI studies of the amygdala. [18:42]
- A "baby steps" negotiation with teams, one trip at a time. [04:16]
- Screening players for sleep disorders, including sleep apnea. [25:53]

## Limits and open questions

- No basketball dataset is shown. The host says there is no basketball data for the testosterone claim. [11:56]

## Summary

A hockey front-office member reflects on bringing analytics into a junior team and then an NHL club. He argues analytics did not so much build his roster as teach him that his eyes and mind mislead him. He walks through recency bias, sample-size bias and a bias toward players who "keep it simple", and says the real lesson is the difference between knowing a fact and valuing it in decisions. He also stresses that analytics takes time and needs organization-wide buy-in, including the coach. The evidence is his own experience, mostly one team and one coaching change.

## Key claims

- Collecting data is different from valuing and using it in a team process. [05:16]
- After a coaching change on the same roster, the team's shot share rose. [06:47]
- Buy-in across the organization (president, general manager, coach, scouts) gives more success than one person pushing analytics. [07:18]
- Analytics served him as a teacher more than as a builder. [07:49]
- "Eyeballs business" thinking is wrong: eyes and mind can fool you if you allow it. [08:20]
- Recency bias: one scouted game can override hundreds of games and many data points. [09:51]
- A World Juniors appearance inflated a draft list. [10:21]
- A hot training camp can displace a player who has proven himself over years, including losing him on waivers. [10:51]
- Simplicity bias: scouts favor safe players who "keep it simple", which he distrusts. [11:51] [12:22]
- A playoff sweep can be driven by an unsustainably low shooting percentage and a hot opposing goalie. [13:22]
- Putting a value on drawing a penalty helps staff care about a known fact. [14:23]
- Analytics is a process, not magic, and takes time. [15:25]
- Showing results visually works better than raw numbers for coaches and players. [21:08]
- The cap creates a chance to find market inefficiencies, which disappear as others catch on. [18:33]
- Analytics and coaching must work together. [23:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Year-one trade: the captions say nine things, "seven draft picks two players", for a goaltender; the caption is garbled after "goendale". [03:42]
- Shot share (called "Cory" in the captions) in the first 30 games was 47 percent and in the remaining 38 games 57 percent, which he calls a "21%" difference. The captions do not reconcile 47 to 57 with 21. [06:47]
- Greyhounds record: caption reads "369 and2", garbled. [07:18]
- Playoff sweep: four straight games; opposing goalie save percentage "970" against his goalie's "910"; his team scored on about 2.5 percent of shots. [13:22]
- Defined PDO: the name of an internet commenter; a team in R&D suggested "percentage driven outcome", meaning the part of results driven by percentages. [13:52]
- Penalty value: each penalty drawn gives 18 percent (.18 goals), "five penalties drawn equals one goal". The caption arithmetic is rounded, as five times .18 is .9. [14:23]
- Scouting began at age 17; draft-list example involves players aged 17. [10:21] [11:21]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Cumulative shot differential or possession percentage as the team-quality measure. [06:17]
- Naming specific biases (recency, sample size, simplicity) as a personnel-decision checklist. [09:20]
- Using the farm team to test whether a training-camp improvement is sustained. [17:28]
- Finding market inefficiencies under a cap. [18:33]
- Telling players which turnovers are acceptable so they feel free to be creative. [19:35] [20:05]

## Limits and open questions

- The central evidence is a single coaching change. He says his sample size is one. [22:10]
- Year-one result was a failure after a large trade, and no measure of later success is given. [03:42] [04:14]
- He does not test whether his scouts' judgments were less accurate than the stats.
- Whether the shot-share gain was due to the coach or other factors is not shown.
- Claims about "simple" defensemen are the speaker's inference from analytics. [12:52]
- He works for an NHL club, so his view is institutional.

## Q&A

- Recency vs real improvement: training camp is a small sample, so test the player in the minor league. [16:56] [17:28]
- Salary cap effect: it creates inefficiency opportunities. [18:03] [18:33]
- Breaking simplicity bias in coaching: educate players and set accepted turnovers. [19:04] [19:35]
- Communicating complex analysis: use visuals, photos or video. [20:36] [21:08]
- Personnel vs coaching: they must work together. [22:10] [22:40] [23:11]

## Summary

He covers variation in a single athlete's performance, the "aggregation of marginal gains" idea from British cycling, how different bodies and genes make athletes individual, measurement effects, consumer and team technology, and sleep. He closes by saying the only sustainable advantage is learning faster than the competition. Much of the evidence is illustration and anecdote, and some figures are the speaker's retelling of other people's work.

## Key claims

- Margins at the elite level are tiny, so even a blowout can sit inside normal day-to-day variation. [05:09] [05:40]

## Summary

A sponsored lunchtime panel on the NFL's first season of league-wide RFID player tracking, supplied by Zebra. After a promotional opening, an NFL media executive, an NFL football-development executive, a head coach and a former running back and broadcaster discuss what the data changed in year one. The coach's first use was practice workload by position, aimed at fewer soft tissue injuries. Other uses discussed were player wellness, officials, combine testing, quarterback training, and fan products. The panel is mostly forward-looking and anecdotal: no accuracy figures or injury outcomes are shown.

## Key claims

- Zebra says its system was in 18 stadiums and worn by every player in 2014 [02:42].
- The league says it collected more data this season than in its entire history, and expects that trend to continue [22:49].
- The league chose RFID after evaluating dozens of technologies, on three grounds: right technology, right partner, and a five-year road map [24:19] [24:50].
- The coach's first use was workload by position: distance by speed band, with an aim of keeping players healthy and cutting soft tissue injuries [28:24] [28:54].
- Tracking let the coach see one receiver doing much more than the other receivers on a given day, which could change the next day's practice [29:25].
- Early on, linemen reportedly walked in circles to avoid low distance numbers [29:56].

- Data that confirms a coach's read (for example where a receiver aligns) makes a play caller more confident [41:50].
- A former player says the data could change "does he still have it" conversations in contracts and evaluation, though what it means for a slower or faster player is unknown [42:53].
- The league is considering whether in-game speed and distance could change combine testing, as a project for this offseason [47:26] [47:57].
- The coach sees possible quarterback "simulator" use for rep-starved positions [49:29].
- Panelists say knowing exactly how hard a game was could help recovery and might extend careers [50:32].
- The coach says one year of practice data will shape practice scheduling in May, training camp and season [54:39].

## Summary

A panel with the Falcons' general manager and head coach on how the two of them stay aligned. Both describe a close, near-daily working relationship, and say analytics informs player, coach and contract decisions but a small group at the top makes the final call. They walk through the 2008 start, a quarterback pick and a trade for a receiver, the shift from 13-3 to 4-12, and the rise of technology for teaching and tracking players. The talk is first-person accounts from two decision makers, so it shows how they describe their process, not whether the process works.

## Key claims

- The two leaders met daily at first and still rarely go a day without talking [07:11].
- The coach lives week to week while the GM works on a longer timeline; they treat the difference as a check and balance [09:45].
- Many people feed a decision, but the final choice is made by the GM and head coach [11:17].
- The GM evaluated the coach with a statistical look at past defenses (sacks, tackles, rankings) alongside interviews with five or six other candidates [03:34] [04:06].
- The staff was built with a mix of former college coaches, former NFL players and coaches with head coaching experience [14:51] [15:21].
- Culture work began with the support staff (film, video, IT) and a first week of meeting everyone in the building [16:22] [17:54].
- Roster evaluation compared contracts by position to the rest of the league for cap and value reasons [19:56].
- Players are evaluated on the human side first, then biomechanical and statistical study, and the decision is ultimately human [28:38] [29:40].
- The coach says watching every pass thrown by the quarterback prospect changed the reading of the interception total: only a handful were throws to regret [31:44] [32:16].
- The coach says numbers point you toward more information and are not the end-all [32:46].
- The trade for the receiver was studied for what the extra picks historically produced [35:19].
- The GM says he is learning to study how a free agent fits with position coaches and scheme before signing [38:53] [39:54].
- After a 4-12 season, the GM says he practiced "productive vulnerability," examining everything including himself [42:00].
- The coach describes player-made film cut-ups and devices replacing paper playbooks, and teaching to different development stages instead of the lowest level [44:34] [46:08].
- The GM describes heart rate and GPS tracking in practice to decide whom to draw back, without dictating practice [47:10].
- Analytics sets the practice plan using expected plays by situation; game planning includes score, wind and temperature [52:53] [53:55].
- The coach expects the next wave to use positional plotting data to set where players line up [57:31] [58:03].
- Disagreement between the two is healthy and best kept private, and the GM says the coach should be able to bring any concern to him [1:00:04] [1:00:34].

## Numbers and definitions

- Record together: 60 and 36, four playoff appearances [01:01].
- First meeting: scheduled for an hour, lasted about two and a half hours [05:06].
- Staff size: over 150 employees [17:54].
- Cap: potentially 130 million plus [20:57]. The quarterback signed a 104 million contract [21:27]. Two players making over a quarter of the cap [21:27].
- The "middle class" of salary is described as five or six million and shrinking [21:58].
- Records: 13 and 3 last year, 4 and 12 this past year [27:05].
- Quarterback prospect: third overall pick [28:07]; threw almost 650 passes, 19 interceptions as a senior [30:43].
- Receiver trade (2011): moved from the mid 20s to number six; gave a first the next year plus a second and two fourths [36:19]. The GM says fewer than 50% of those fourth-rounders were active and fewer than 14% were starters [35:19].
- "Fifteen 230 million" on a free agent [38:53]: garbled in captions, likely a range; do not rely on it.
- A defensive end expected to produce 15 to 20 sacks [39:54].
- The coach was second to one other coach in wins over the last five years before this season [40:57].
- Play data: 250 plus characters per play for player-made cut-ups [45:36].
- Player tracking involvement: four plus years [47:10].
- Over 20 teams attending the conference [54:56].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Contract and salary comparison by position across the league [19:56].
- Biomechanical assessment of a player compared with other quarterbacks and receivers [28:38] [33:48].
- Analysis of how draft picks of a given round have produced (active and starter rates) [35:19].
- Review of the quarterback's full pass history, play by play [31:14].
- Fit check: whether a defense has produced the output (sacks versus pressures) the new player is bought for [39:54].
- Practice plan built on play counts by down and distance [52:53].
- Heart rate and GPS tracking of practices [47:10]; a sports science partner (Sparta Sports Science) announced [51:48].
- Decision model: many contributors, two final decision makers [11:17].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, model or sample sizes are shown; claims are recollections by the two decision makers.
- Both describe outcomes of their own decisions positively; each decision reviewed has a known result, and failures are only discussed generally [36:50] [37:20].
- The GM's interpretation of the receiver's draft-pick study is his own; the method (population, years) is not stated.
- The analytics head is named only at the end, with no description of what the group produces [50:16].
- Claims that tracking will keep a named player healthy [47:41] are not supported by anything shown.
- Caption names: "Mike Ree", "Thomas demitro", "Carl piber" and "Scott Pei" are caption spellings.
- The panel's front-office, salary cap setting is professional football, not college.

## Q&A

- Does the GM draw on other industries to improve football analytics? Yes, particularly basketball, and the team recently announced a sports science partner [51:17] [51:48].
- How much of the team's analytics is about the salary cap versus football? The coach says everything is built on breaking down plays, and it is used for practice plans and game planning [52:53] [53:23].
- How important is gut instinct? The GM says it is important and built from experience, and expects future head coaches to be steeped in analysis; the coach says it ends up a gut decision [54:56] [55:27] [57:00].
- How important is respectful tension? The coach says disagreement is needed and best kept private; the GM says eliminating the divide between coaching and personnel is key [59:34] [1:00:34].

## Summary

A book talk arguing that football behaves like a system in which a small change can have large downstream effects. The speaker gives examples (helmet and face mask, a quarterback injury leading to a new offense, size, tempo, a trick formation), then describes how science is being applied: a decision flowchart framed as digital thinking, gene and protein research on concussions, and a multiple-object tracking test of brain performance. It is storytelling with a few figures; the causal claims are the authors' interpretation, not tested.

## Key claims

- The speakers describe football as a system where poking one spot gives an unpredictable response elsewhere [01:08].
- The helmet was introduced to prevent skull fractures [02:40].
- The authors argue that adding the face mask changed the game because players began to tackle with their heads [03:10] [03:41].
- The authors argue helmets in their current form do not reduce concussions because the brain still moves inside the skull [04:12].
- Chaos theory and the butterfly effect are used to explain small changes with big results [05:14] [05:44].
- A quarterback's career-ending injury led his coach to reuse plays built for his arm in a shorter form, leading to the West Coast offense [06:44] [07:14].
- Coaches gain advantages through size, conditioning and surprise [07:44].
- The no-huddle offense is described as denying defenders rest, and early adopters benefit until others copy it [09:18] [09:48].
- A small high school used a rule loophole to disguise who would receive the ball [10:48].
- The authors suggest the age of science may have started with a coach who taught chemistry and physics [11:51].
- The speaker argues the quarterback read moved from analog to digital by using a short yes-or-no flowchart, linked to Boolean algebra and Shannon's telephone work [12:52] [13:23] [13:54].
- Genetic profiles may show concussion susceptibility, and a protein tied to muscle twitch speed may relate to performance [14:56] [15:26].
- The combine measures speed, explosiveness and strength; the brain is the untested part [15:56] [16:28].
- A tracking test of four balls over eight seconds was developed by colleagues at the University of Montreal, and athletes do better than non-athletes [17:29] [19:00].
- The ability is both innate and trained, and regular training improves reading the game [19:31].

## Numbers and definitions

- Players of 300 pounds: three in 1980, 461 at the last count in 2012 [07:44] [08:16].
- Lorenz example: captions give two input numbers as "0 5 50627" and "0506" and a difference of 0.127; the captions are garbled and the numbers do not reconcile, so do not rely on them [05:14] [05:44].
- Greg Cook played three games [06:44].
- Formation: 16,634 possible receivers [10:48].
- The tracking test: four of the balls are designated, then all move, then the person identifies the four; eight seconds [17:29] [17:59].
- Decision flowchart: option one, option two, option three, then the "guarantee" [13:23].
- Talk length 25 minutes with five for questions [00:06].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Chaos theory (sensitivity to initial conditions) [09:18].
- Boolean algebra and its use in telephone systems and computers [13:54].
- Genetic and protein analysis for concussion and muscle twitch [14:56] [15:26].
- Multiple-object tracking test, "neurot Tracker" in captions [16:58] [17:29].
- Wonderlic test, mentioned critically [16:28].

## Limits and open questions

- Causal stories (face mask, injury, no-huddle) are presented as the authors' view with no data.
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or references for the tracking test findings; the attributed conclusions are summarized in a sentence [19:00].
- The authors say the genetic and protein work is early and the final outcome unknown [15:56] [20:01].
- The speaker names the 1-2-3 flowchart coach as "Sam wsh" in the captions; later text says Bill Walsh at [06:14], so the garble is in the captions.
- A coach named "Vince l" is cut off in the captions [11:51].
- The audience test result is not reported [19:00].

## Q&A

- The host asked for questions; none were taken [20:01].

## Summary

Two people from the league office's analytics and data products group demonstrate a platform that all 32 teams can use, built about three years ago. The talk opens with a short league network segment on two quarterbacks, then walks through filterable reports (passer rating, personnel groupings, success rate, a scorecard, player similarity, combine similarity, passing charts) linked to video. The stated lesson is that making data easy to use matters most. The talk is a product demonstration; it does not test whether the reports improve decisions.

## Key claims

- The platform was built so the business can get information directly, without depending on other departments [06:08].
- The system holds every NFL stat; nothing was selected out [23:16].
- Personnel groupings are known for every play, so stats can be filtered by grouping, defense, down, quarter and others [06:39] [09:43].
- The success definition is configurable by the user [09:43].
- Video is integrated with the analytics so filtered plays can be watched [10:46] [11:17].
- A scorecard of keys to winning is set up ahead of time, with green, red and yellow by game [11:48].
- Player similarity compares players on a standardized year in the league, so players from different entry years line up [12:54].
- Combine similarity matches players on measurements within a percentage range [15:28] [15:59].
- Passing charts use zones measured in air yards and can be color-customized by the team [16:30] [17:02].
- Data enters at the stadium during play, goes to the league office, then the warehouse [18:35] [19:05].
- The most important lesson is making data easy for people to use, otherwise it becomes a mess [20:07].
- The speakers do not know everything teams do with it, and some teams still use their own systems [20:44] [24:18].

## Summary

A sleep researcher and an ESPN writer discuss how sleep deficiency, travel and schedule design affect NBA performance. The researcher describes persuading teams to change flight times, practice times and time-zone handling. He argues that lost sleep slows reaction, raises injury and illness risk, weakens learning and memory, and worsens emotional control. The main point is that sleep and travel are controllable performance factors that teams mostly ignored. The speakers admit the basketball-specific evidence is early and rests on small player numbers, and they lean on research from other occupations and on team anecdotes.

## Key claims

- A common team routine was a late night, then an early-morning flight, so players arrived sleep deprived. This was defended as a way to tough out jet lag. [02:43] [03:46]
- After one trip moved to an afternoon flight, the plane reportedly ran out of food because players were so alert. [04:16]
- Teams can stay on home-clock time and practice at the hour they would normally play, which moved a curfew to about 3 a.m. [04:46] [05:17]
- Players questioned the speaker for far longer than the briefing planned, and buy-in from players and coaches was seen as essential. [06:53] [07:24]
- A missed night of sleep slows average reaction time sharply, which matters for read-and-react and help-defense decisions. [09:56]
- Sleep loss increases missed signals in the visual field and raises injury risk. [10:56] [11:26]
- A week of short sleep is said to lower testosterone by the equivalent of many years of aging. [11:26]
- Sleep deficiency raises inflammation and infection risk and lengthens injury recovery. [12:26]
- Baseball data from a colleague showed the home team's results depend on the direction of the visitor's cross-country travel. [12:56]
- Learning needs adequate sleep before (attention) and after (memory consolidation), shown with animal maze studies. [15:02] [15:33]
- Sleep loss impairs integrating lessons from a loss into next-game adjustments. [16:35]
- The speaker hopes the league eliminates road back-to-backs because teams cannot structurally secure enough sleep on such trips. [17:07] [17:37]
- Sleep deprivation heightens emotional-brain reactivity and weakens judgment control, which he links to getting a technical foul. [18:09] [18:42]

## Numbers and definitions

- Average reaction time: about a quarter of a second (250 milliseconds) normally; after a missed night it jumps to about 750 to 900 milliseconds. [09:25] [09:56]
- Missed signals: those who had not slept had 10 times as many as those who had. [10:56]
- Testosterone: four hours of sleep a night for a week equals the drop of 11 years of aging; he says this takes a 25-year-old to a 36-year-old's level. [11:26] [11:56]
- Garbled: a caption line about a west-to-east team being "a 6337 dog" cannot be read. [11:56]
- Baseball: the visitor having completed eastward travel is associated with 1.24 more runs per game for the home team. [12:56]
- Amygdala firing is about 10 times higher after a night awake when shown disturbing images. [18:09]
- Sleep need: about 8.2 or 8.3 hours per 24 hours for the average person, more than two sleep bouts being less efficient. [22:16]
- Brain clearing: some support cells shrink so debris clears about 20 times more rapidly during sleep. [23:18]
- Aging: total sleep duration changes by only about 20 or 30 minutes in someone without a sleep disorder. [25:22]
- Sample framing: the host notes about 15 players and eight or nine regular ones, and asks whether this equals "one and a half two two and a half three wins a season". The speaker does not give a win figure. [12:56] [13:29]
- Other occupations studied: 5,000 policemen and 7,000 firefighters. [13:59]
- Schedule: baseball season is called about 182 games in the captions. [20:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Consulting on shootaround and practice schedules and on how teams fly. [01:41]
- Matching physiology to occupation: the speaker argues that findings from pilots, firefighters and police transfer to athletes because the physiology is the same. [13:59]
- Experiments with electrodes on hippocampal place cells in animals. [15:33]
- fMRI studies of the amygdala. [18:42]
- A "baby steps" negotiation with teams, one trip at a time. [04:16]
- Screening players for sleep disorders, including sleep apnea. [25:53]

## Summary

A hockey front-office member reflects on bringing analytics into a junior team and then an NHL club. He argues analytics did not so much build his roster as teach him that his eyes and mind mislead him. He walks through recency bias, sample-size bias and a bias toward players who "keep it simple", and says the real lesson is the difference between knowing a fact and valuing it in decisions. He also stresses that analytics takes time and needs organization-wide buy-in, including the coach. The evidence is his own experience, mostly one team and one coaching change.

## Key claims

- Collecting data is different from valuing and using it in a team process. [05:16]
- After a coaching change on the same roster, the team's shot share rose. [06:47]
- Buy-in across the organization (president, general manager, coach, scouts) gives more success than one person pushing analytics. [07:18]
- Analytics served him as a teacher more than as a builder. [07:49]
- "Eyeballs business" thinking is wrong: eyes and mind can fool you if you allow it. [08:20]
- Recency bias: one scouted game can override hundreds of games and many data points. [09:51]
- A World Juniors appearance inflated a draft list. [10:21]
- A hot training camp can displace a player who has proven himself over years, including losing him on waivers. [10:51]
- Simplicity bias: scouts favor safe players who "keep it simple", which he distrusts. [11:51] [12:22]
- A playoff sweep can be driven by an unsustainably low shooting percentage and a hot opposing goalie. [13:22]
- Putting a value on drawing a penalty helps staff care about a known fact. [14:23]
- Analytics is a process, not magic, and takes time. [15:25]
- Showing results visually works better than raw numbers for coaches and players. [21:08]
- The cap creates a chance to find market inefficiencies, which disappear as others catch on. [18:33]
- Analytics and coaching must work together. [23:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Year-one trade: the captions say nine things, "seven draft picks two players", for a goaltender; the caption is garbled after "goendale". [03:42]
- Shot share (called "Cory" in the captions) in the first 30 games was 47 percent and in the remaining 38 games 57 percent, which he calls a "21%" difference. The captions do not reconcile 47 to 57 with 21. [06:47]
- Greyhounds record: caption reads "369 and2", garbled. [07:18]
- Playoff sweep: four straight games; opposing goalie save percentage "970" against his goalie's "910"; his team scored on about 2.5 percent of shots. [13:22]
- Defined PDO: the name of an internet commenter; a team in R&D suggested "percentage driven outcome", meaning the part of results driven by percentages. [13:52]
- Penalty value: each penalty drawn gives 18 percent (.18 goals), "five penalties drawn equals one goal". The caption arithmetic is rounded, as five times .18 is .9. [14:23]
- Scouting began at age 17; draft-list example involves players aged 17. [10:21] [11:21]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Cumulative shot differential or possession percentage as the team-quality measure. [06:17]
- Naming specific biases (recency, sample size, simplicity) as a personnel-decision checklist. [09:20]
- Using the farm team to test whether a training-camp improvement is sustained. [17:28]
- Finding market inefficiencies under a cap. [18:33]
- Telling players which turnovers are acceptable so they feel free to be creative. [19:35] [20:05]

## Limits and open questions

- The central evidence is a single coaching change. He says his sample size is one. [22:10]
- Year-one result was a failure after a large trade, and no measure of later success is given. [03:42] [04:14]
- He does not test whether his scouts' judgments were less accurate than the stats.
- Whether the shot-share gain was due to the coach or other factors is not shown.
- Claims about "simple" defensemen are the speaker's inference from analytics. [12:52]
- He works for an NHL club, so his view is institutional.

## Q&A

- Recency vs real improvement: training camp is a small sample, so test the player in the minor league. [16:56] [17:28]
- Salary cap effect: it creates inefficiency opportunities. [18:03] [18:33]
- Breaking simplicity bias in coaching: educate players and set accepted turnovers. [19:04] [19:35]
- Communicating complex analysis: use visuals, photos or video. [20:36] [21:08]
- Personnel vs coaching: they must work together. [22:10] [22:40] [23:11]

## Summary

A Wired editor and author of a sports-science book argues that elite results turn on tiny margins and that the high-performance world offers lessons for any field. He covers variation in a single athlete's performance, the "aggregation of marginal gains" idea from British cycling, how different bodies and genes make athletes individual, measurement effects, consumer and team technology, and sleep. He closes by saying the only sustainable advantage is learning faster than the competition. Much of the evidence is illustration and anecdote, and some figures are the speaker's retelling of other people's work.

## Key claims

- Margins at the elite level are tiny, so even a blowout can sit inside normal day-to-day variation. [05:09] [05:40]
- Variation is about one percent in short events and larger in long and technical events. [06:11] [06:41]
- British cycling improved by finding many small gains instead of one large one. [09:15] [09:45]
- Small items (own pillows, hand washing, beet juice, wiping tires, heated pants) were used for small edges. [11:46] [12:16] [14:19] [14:50]
- Elite athletes are physically individual, and bodies match their sports. [16:51] [19:26]
- Early specialization is argued against, because sampling sports helps find the right fit. [19:56]
- Trainability varies by genetics, and few people combine a high baseline with a strong training response. [21:58] [23:29]
- Genes set the size of the "bucket" and environment decides how much is poured in. [24:30]
- Being measured may change performance (Hawthorne effect), though the speaker says this is disputed. [26:32] [27:04]
- Cheap sensors and data are now widespread. [27:37] [29:40] [30:11]
- Data is a starting point, and the gap between analyst and decision maker matters. [32:14] [32:45]
- Teams neglect basics while chasing new things, and nutrition response is individual ("n equals one"). [33:17] [33:47]

A hockey front-office member reflects on bringing analytics into a junior team and then an NHL club. He walks through recency bias, sample-size bias and a bias toward players who "keep it simple", and says the real lesson is the difference between knowing a fact and valuing it in decisions. ## Summary

A hockey front-office member reflects on bringing analytics into a junior team and then an NHL club. He argues analytics did not so much build his roster as teach him that his eyes and mind mislead him. He walks through recency bias, sample-size bias and a bias toward players who "keep it simple", and says the real lesson is the difference between knowing a fact and valuing it in decisions. He also stresses that analytics takes time and needs organization-wide buy-in, including the coach. The evidence is his own experience, mostly one team and one coaching change.

## Key claims

- Collecting data is different from valuing and using it in a team process. [05:16]
- After a coaching change on the same roster, the team's shot share rose. [06:47]
- Buy-in across the organization (president, general manager, coach, scouts) gives more success than one person pushing analytics. [07:18]
- Analytics served him as a teacher more than as a builder. [07:49]
- "Eyeballs business" thinking is wrong: eyes and mind can fool you if you allow it. [08:20]
- Recency bias: one scouted game can override hundreds of games and many data points. [09:51]
- A World Juniors appearance inflated a draft list. [10:21]
- A hot training camp can displace a player who has proven himself over years, including losing him on waivers. [10:51]
- Simplicity bias: scouts favor safe players who "keep it simple", which he distrusts. [11:51] [12:22]
- A playoff sweep can be driven by an unsustainably low shooting percentage and a hot opposing goalie. [13:22]
- Putting a value on drawing a penalty helps staff care about a known fact. [14:23]
- Analytics is a process, not magic, and takes time. [15:25]
- Showing results visually works better than raw numbers for coaches and players. [21:08]
- The cap creates a chance to find market inefficiencies, which disappear as others catch on. [18:33]
- Analytics and coaching must work together. [23:11]

## Summary

A sleep researcher and an ESPN writer discuss how sleep deficiency, travel and schedule design affect NBA performance. The researcher describes persuading teams to change flight times, practice times and time-zone handling. He argues that lost sleep slows reaction, raises injury and illness risk, weakens learning and memory, and worsens emotional control. The main point is that sleep and travel are controllable performance factors that teams mostly ignored. The speakers admit the basketball-specific evidence is early and rests on small player numbers, and they lean on research from other occupations and on team anecdotes.

## Key claims

- A common team routine was a late night, then an early-morning flight, so players arrived sleep deprived. This was defended as a way to tough out jet lag. [02:43] [03:46]
- After one trip moved to an afternoon flight, the plane reportedly ran out of food because players were so alert. [04:16]
- Teams can stay on home-clock time and practice at the hour they would normally play, which moved a curfew to about 3 a.m. [04:46] [05:17]
- Players questioned the speaker for far longer than the briefing planned, and buy-in from players and coaches was seen as essential. [06:53] [07:24]
- A missed night of sleep slows average reaction time sharply, which matters for read-and-react and help-defense decisions. [09:56]
- Sleep loss increases missed signals in the visual field and raises injury risk. [10:56] [11:26]
- A week of short sleep is said to lower testosterone by the equivalent of many years of aging. [11:26]
- Sleep deficiency raises inflammation and infection risk and lengthens injury recovery. [12:26]
- Baseball data from a colleague showed the home team's results depend on the direction of the visitor's cross-country travel. [12:56]
- Learning needs adequate sleep before (attention) and after (memory consolidation), shown with animal maze studies. [15:02] [15:33]
- Sleep loss impairs integrating lessons from a loss into next-game adjustments. [16:35]
- The speaker hopes the league eliminates road back-to-backs because teams cannot structurally secure enough sleep on such trips. [17:07] [17:37]
- Sleep deprivation heightens emotional-brain reactivity and weakens judgment control, which he links to getting a technical foul. [18:09] [18:42]

## Numbers and definitions

- Average reaction time: about a quarter of a second (250 milliseconds) normally; after a missed night it jumps to about 750 to 900 milliseconds. [09:25] [09:56]
- Missed signals: those who had not slept had 10 times as many as those who had. [10:56]
- Testosterone: four hours of sleep a night for a week equals the drop of 11 years of aging; he says this takes a 25-year-old to a 36-year-old's level. [11:26] [11:56]
- Garbled: a caption line about a west-to-east team being "a 6337 dog" cannot be read. [11:56]
- Baseball: the visitor having completed eastward travel is associated with 1.24 more runs per game for the home team. [12:56]
- Amygdala firing is about 10 times higher after a night awake when shown disturbing images. [18:09]
- Sleep need: about 8.2 or 8.3 hours per 24 hours for the average person, more than two sleep bouts being less efficient. [22:16]
- Brain clearing: some support cells shrink so debris clears about 20 times more rapidly during sleep. [23:18]
- Aging: total sleep duration changes by only about 20 or 30 minutes in someone without a sleep disorder. [25:22]
- Sample framing: the host notes about 15 players and eight or nine regular ones, and asks whether this equals "one and a half two two and a half three wins a season". The speaker does not give a win figure. [12:56] [13:29]
- Other occupations studied: 5,000 policemen and 7,000 firefighters. [13:59]
- Schedule: baseball season is called about 182 games in the captions. [20:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Consulting on shootaround and practice schedules and on how teams fly. [01:41]
- Matching physiology to occupation: the speaker argues that findings from pilots, firefighters and police transfer to athletes because the physiology is the same. [13:59]
- Experiments with electrodes on hippocampal place cells in animals. [15:33]
- fMRI studies of the amygdala. [18:42]
- A "baby steps" negotiation with teams, one trip at a time. [04:16]
- Screening players for sleep disorders, including sleep apnea. [25:53]

## Limits and open questions

- No basketball dataset is shown. The host says there is no basketball data for the testosterone claim. [11:56]
- The speaker acknowledges the evidence is early and that only about 15 players per team are available. [12:56]
- The opening story (a predicted loss) comes from a coach's retelling, and the researcher says the coach "embellishes". [17:37]
- Whether the testosterone effect is reversible is unknown. [24:18]
- The speaker consults for teams, so his enthusiasm is an institutional view.
- No measured win effect is given.
- Slides were hard to read in the room, and captions reference graphs we cannot see. [09:25]

## Q&A

- Interest from soccer or rugby: none heard; hockey and baseball have asked. [19:13] [19:43]
- Naps: supports them, with caution only for insomnia patients; some players rent a hotel room before games. [20:13]
- Baseball reaction time and nap logistics: reaction time is a big issue and a long schedule makes it harder. [20:43] [21:15]
- Efficiency of sleep: no known way to get more from less; average need about 8.2 or 8.3 hours. [22:16]
- Sleep medication: newer drugs are being developed but none rival sleep without medication. [22:48]
- Reversibility of testosterone drop: unknown. [24:18]
- Sending reserves ahead: no team has done it, he calls it a good idea. [24:49]
- Aging and sleep, then sleep apnea in muscular athletes. [25:22] [25:53] [26:23]

## Summary

A hockey front-office member reflects on bringing analytics into a junior team and then an NHL club. He argues analytics did not so much build his roster as teach him that his eyes and mind mislead him. He walks through recency bias, sample-size bias and a bias toward players who "keep it simple", and says the real lesson is the difference between knowing a fact and valuing it in decisions. He also stresses that analytics takes time and needs organization-wide buy-in, including the coach. The evidence is his own experience, mostly one team and one coaching change.

## Key claims

- Collecting data is different from valuing and using it in a team process. [05:16]
- After a coaching change on the same roster, the team's shot share rose. [06:47]
- Buy-in across the organization (president, general manager, coach, scouts) gives more success than one person pushing analytics. [07:18]
- Analytics served him as a teacher more than as a builder. [07:49]
- "Eyeballs business" thinking is wrong: eyes and mind can fool you if you allow it. [08:20]
- Recency bias: one scouted game can override hundreds of games and many data points. [09:51]
- A World Juniors appearance inflated a draft list. [10:21]
- A hot training camp can displace a player who has proven himself over years, including losing him on waivers. [10:51]
- Simplicity bias: scouts favor safe players who "keep it simple", which he distrusts. [11:51] [12:22]
- A playoff sweep can be driven by an unsustainably low shooting percentage and a hot opposing goalie. [13:22]
- Putting a value on drawing a penalty helps staff care about a known fact. [14:23]
- Analytics is a process, not magic, and takes time. [15:25]
- Showing results visually works better than raw numbers for coaches and players. [21:08]
- The cap creates a chance to find market inefficiencies, which disappear as others catch on. [18:33]
- Analytics and coaching must work together. [23:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Year-one trade: the captions say nine things, "seven draft picks two players", for a goaltender; the caption is garbled after "goendale". [03:42]
- Shot share (called "Cory" in the captions) in the first 30 games was 47 percent and in the remaining 38 games 57 percent, which he calls a "21%" difference. The captions do not reconcile 47 to 57 with 21. [06:47]
- Greyhounds record: caption reads "369 and2", garbled. [07:18]
- Playoff sweep: four straight games; opposing goalie save percentage "970" against his goalie's "910"; his team scored on about 2.5 percent of shots. [13:22]
- Defined PDO: the name of an internet commenter; a team in R&D suggested "percentage driven outcome", meaning the part of results driven by percentages. [13:52]
- Penalty value: each penalty drawn gives 18 percent (.18 goals), "five penalties drawn equals one goal". The caption arithmetic is rounded, as five times .18 is .9. [14:23]
- Scouting began at age 17; draft-list example involves players aged 17. [10:21] [11:21]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Cumulative shot differential or possession percentage as the team-quality measure. [06:17]
- Naming specific biases (recency, sample size, simplicity) as a personnel-decision checklist. [09:20]
- Using the farm team to test whether a training-camp improvement is sustained. [17:28]
- Finding market inefficiencies under a cap. [18:33]
- Telling players which turnovers are acceptable so they feel free to be creative. [19:35] [20:05]

## Limits and open questions

- The central evidence is a single coaching change. He says his sample size is one. [22:10]
- Year-one result was a failure after a large trade, and no measure of later success is given. [03:42] [04:14]
- He does not test whether his scouts' judgments were less accurate than the stats.
- Whether the shot-share gain was due to the coach or other factors is not shown.
- Claims about "simple" defensemen are the speaker's inference from analytics. [12:52]
- He works for an NHL club, so his view is institutional.

## Q&A

- Recency vs real improvement: training camp is a small sample, so test the player in the minor league. [16:56] [17:28]
- Salary cap effect: it creates inefficiency opportunities. [18:03] [18:33]
- Breaking simplicity bias in coaching: educate players and set accepted turnovers. [19:04] [19:35]
- Communicating complex analysis: use visuals, photos or video. [20:36] [21:08]
- Personnel vs coaching: they must work together. [22:10] [22:40] [23:11]

Much of the evidence is illustration and anecdote, and some figures are the speaker's retelling of other people's work.

## Summary

A moderated panel of NFL front-office and analytics people and a high school coach discusses where analytics help football and where they stop. The panel covers how much information a quarterback can carry to the line, what the combine is still good for, why speed numbers miss reaction and vision, and why fourth-down and other in-game decisions are the easiest gains. A recurring theme is that a small edge in the odds is hard to sell to coaches and owners whose jobs depend on short-term results. The panelists also say communication matters more than data volume, and that player performance, hydration and injury prevention are underused areas.

## Key claims

- A quarterback should be given a distilled set of situational tendencies, because too much analytics makes players think instead of react [04:08].
- The NFL does not allow computers or technology in the coach's booth, so context has to be carried by people [05:38].
- Coach decision-making in games (such as fourth-down choices) is described as low-hanging fruit for analytics [06:39].
- It is not currently possible to measure how a quarterback decides under duress, and the panel says the physical punishment a quarterback takes cannot be replicated in training [08:45], [12:19].
- One panelist says clutch performance exists but is mostly a mirage, and that players are already selected for handling pressure [13:53].
- The combine is still useful for medical checks, interviews, and a standardized comparison of players, and physical traits matter more in later rounds [17:58].
- Speed and playing speed differ; times are flags that film and intelligence work must confirm [26:07].
- Analytics helps by making assumptions explicit so they can be questioned (the running back and offensive line example) [28:41].
- Good data and analysis are useless without communication a coach can use [34:17].
- Analytics moves the odds, not the outcome, so a good process can give a bad result and people blame the process [36:22].
- Owners and front offices push coaches toward comfortable choices because of fan and finance pressure, though a panelist says analytics-friendly owners may have an edge [48:13], [51:14].
- A panelist says injury prevention, nutrition, recovery and hydration measurement are underused, and the league lags Europe and Olympic sports [38:55], [58:27].

- "Moving the odds from 48% to 52%" is the example of a small analytic edge [35:49].
