## Summary

A former college football player and wrestler who now runs a concussion research group argues that technology is about to improve four things: impact indicators, sideline assessment, return-to-play testing and "hit counts." He says concussions are badly under-diagnosed, return to play is poorly timed, and subconcussive blows may also damage the brain. He does rough math to show that perfect detection and cautious return would sideline a fifth of players, so the sports themselves would have to change, starting with less contact in practice. He also discusses helmets, informed consent, and genetics. He discloses ties to a test and a company.

## Key claims

- Technology is improving assessment, removal from play, return to play and hit counts [00:30].
- Concussions do not show on standard imaging; diagnosis relies on signs and symptoms [05:04].
- Diagnosed concussions run about 5% a year in contact sports, but anonymous athlete surveys give numbers more like 50% [06:04].
- In a hockey study, putting a doctor in the stands to pull players liberally found seven times as many concussions: 5% versus 35% [06:34], [07:04].
- Impact thresholds are a problem: risk is an S-curve, no known concussion at 10 G, and certain concussion at 300 G, so any red-light threshold is arbitrary [08:04], [08:35].
- The current 20-minute sideline evaluation has not been validated and its parts cannot decide return to play alone [09:36].
- Substitution rules in rugby and soccer make it hard to remove and evaluate players, and a "brain bin" 20-minute window has been proposed [10:38].
- A less-than-one-minute test is described as promising, based on two published papers [11:41].
- The vulnerability window after a concussion is longer than believed; in 2008 players were still returning within 15 minutes [12:43].
- Research tests suggest no one recovers to baseline within 30 days [13:13].
- If athletes were held out for 60 days, about one in five would be out at any time [14:14].
- Over 90% of brains of those who played collision sports for more than 10 years show the disease, in a biased sample [15:15].
- Subconcussive hits matter, and the speaker wants hit counts modeled on baseball pitch counts [16:16], [16:48].
- Up to 75% of football brain trauma exposure occurs in practice, so reducing contact in practice is the top lever [19:23].
- The NFL players' union negotiated fewer contact practice days, and the Ivy League and Pop Warner followed with limits [19:23], [19:54].
- Helmets mainly prevent skull fractures and the bigger gains are rule changes [24:03].
- Athletes should not play while symptomatic for at least ten years until the culture changes [26:37].

- Hockey study ages "16 to 21"; 5% versus 35%, "seven times as many" [06:34], [07:04].

## Summary

A panel of a player, a writer, two former head coaches and a basketball front-office moderator argues about how analytics meets real coaching decisions. They test a famous fourth-down call and a late-game foul-or-not decision against the numbers, then move to adjusting a plan mid-game, hiring coaches, team culture, minutes for players, and judging a game beyond the score. The recurring point is that a decision's quality is not its result, and that a sound choice still fails if the players have not been sold on it in practice. Several panelists say culture and character resist measurement.

## Key claims

- Going for it on fourth down is praised when it works and criticized for a long time when it fails, so coaches feel pressure to punt [02:09].
- One panelist argues the football play call itself was weak because the opponent had stacked the line, so an average yards-per-carry figure did not apply [04:48].
- Another argues any play that worked would have been called great and any that failed poor, so judging the call by the result is unfair [05:18].
- On a three-point lead with the other team in possession, the panel splits on fouling; the moderator says fouling is slightly better in the data but few coaches do it [19:14].
- A coach says a decision like fouling must be practiced and sold to the team, and that his own loss came partly because he had not sold it hard enough [17:41].
- A panelist says the best players must be in lockstep with the plan, otherwise results diminish for the rest of the team [15:08].
- Corrections must be consistent: what you would not tolerate in defeat you cannot tolerate in victory [20:14].
- Offenses script early plays to gather information about the opponent, and that information shapes the rest of the plan [21:15].
- Players expect plan B to be prepared in advance and presented as just as good as plan A [23:50].
- A coach says to first decide whether the problem is effort or plan, since changing the plan does nothing if effort is lacking [25:21].
- Panelists say owners and general managers should get more scrutiny when teams cycle through coaches [30:30], and one proposes mandatory meetings among owner, general manager and coach [32:03].
- Hiring should match the coach to the team's character and culture, and wins follow if players buy in [33:37].
- One panelist says team chemistry shows up in body language during timeouts and free throws, and says he does not know how analytics would measure it [37:15].
- A coach says playing a star center a full game made the team win more even when he was tired, but the larger picture made that impossible [45:56].
- Bench players can help immediately and become detrimental if kept in too long, and coaches should decide how valuable those minutes are [46:56].
- Teams are trimming a star's minutes to save him for the playoffs [48:28].
- After a game the staff wrote a report: things done well, things done poorly, suggestions; the value of a loss is whether the team can be better next time [49:32].
- Players want coaches accountable to the plan they described before the game [52:39].
- A panelist says the media reaction to a statistically favored fourth-down call shows coaches are not yet in a world where non-traditional calls are easy [55:48].
- A panelist suggests a heuristic: choose the action that the other team's fans would be scared of [57:18].

## Numbers and definitions

- Fourth-down example: Atlanta, caption says "third and one" at one point [03:15] and "fourth and two" later [57:18]; the captions are inconsistent. Field position cited as the 29 [03:15] and later the 28 yard line [08:21].
- Run strength: "four and a half yards a carry," against a "10- man line" [04:48].
- Basketball clip: up three, about 10 seconds left [10:29]; one coach says he would feel comfortable fouling at "six or seven" seconds [11:30].
- A three-point shot at that point is described as a "32 or 33% shot" [12:33].
- Moderator says "way more than 90% of the time" the team wins either way, with no source or sample shown [16:39].
- First 15 plays scripted [21:15].
- Panelist says a general manager hires "two usually three" head coaches and states he does not know the figure [31:02].
- A new coach has to change "50 to 60" players' viewpoints [32:35].
- A team went "5 and 11" in a first year [42:21].
- Star center played at 48 minutes in the discussion [45:56].
- A team won "61 wins" last year [48:28].
- A star guard came out at the "six minute Mark" of first and third quarters [47:56]. The caption says he "played till he was 75"; this is almost certainly garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Probability-of-winning reasoning for fourth down and fouling, described qualitatively, no model shown [03:15], [09:25].
- Scripted opening plays used to gather information, followed by adjustment [21:15].
- Tiered contingency plans for defending a star player (trap, force to baseline, go under) [24:20].
- Post-game "after Action Report" by phase [49:32].
- Informal "sniff test" of team behavior at games [36:43].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes or sources are shown; the 90% and 3-point-shot figures are asserted by panelists.
- The panel is mostly opinion; one participant says the analytics panel turned into a "sniff test" topic [36:43].
- The fouling question is not resolved; the moderator says the data lean slightly toward fouling while coaches disagree [19:14].
- Several statements about general managers and coaches (hire counts, recycled coaches) are admitted guesses [31:02].
- Caption problems: names are garbled (moderator "Daryl Mory"; "Eric manini"), the clip descriptions are unclear (team names and players mixed), and the Atlanta down and distance is inconsistent.

## Q&A

- How do you judge a game besides win or loss, and what does the head coach emphasize afterward? Answers at [49:32] to [52:39].
- Are there ways to tell whether coaches are consistently good at percentages? The question is unclear in the captions; no real answer [53:09].
- Did media backlash ever affect decisions? A coach says criticism is part of the job and he hopes it did not, but subconscious effect is likely [54:11], [55:17].
- Does a more analytical environment make non-traditional calls easier? Answer: not yet [55:48].
- What do you wish you could know? Which later-round draft pick becomes a star; the right minutes for each player; when media will judge players on production; the ceiling for a particular player [58:21], [59:21], [59:52].

type: video-summary
video_id: npgdKKdJSww
title: "2012 SSAC - EOS Concussion Technology.m4v"
event: SSAC12 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Chris nowinsky (caption spelling)]
topics: [injury-health, policy, american-football, other-sport:ice-hockey, other-sport:soccer]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A former college football player and wrestler who now runs a concussion research group argues that technology is about to improve four things: impact indicators, sideline assessment, return-to-play testing and "hit counts." He says concussions are badly under-diagnosed, return to play is poorly timed, and subconcussive blows may also damage the brain. He does rough math to show that perfect detection and cautious return would sideline a fifth of players, so the sports themselves would have to change, starting with less contact in practice. He also discusses helmets, informed consent, and genetics. He discloses ties to a test and a company.

## Key claims

- Technology is improving assessment, removal from play, return to play and hit counts [00:30].
- Concussions do not show on standard imaging; diagnosis relies on signs and symptoms [05:04].
- Diagnosed concussions run about 5% a year in contact sports, but anonymous athlete surveys give numbers more like 50% [06:04].
- In a hockey study, putting a doctor in the stands to pull players liberally found seven times as many concussions: 5% versus 35% [06:34], [07:04].
- Impact thresholds are a problem: risk is an S-curve, no known concussion at 10 G, and certain concussion at 300 G, so any red-light threshold is arbitrary [08:04], [08:35].
- The current 20-minute sideline evaluation has not been validated and its parts cannot decide return to play alone [09:36].
- Substitution rules in rugby and soccer make it hard to remove and evaluate players, and a "brain bin" 20-minute window has been proposed [10:38].
- A less-than-one-minute test is described as promising, based on two published papers [11:41].
- The vulnerability window after a concussion is longer than believed; in 2008 players were still returning within 15 minutes [12:43].
- Research tests suggest no one recovers to baseline within 30 days [13:13].
- If athletes were held out for 60 days, about one in five would be out at any time [14:14].
- Over 90% of brains of those who played collision sports for more than 10 years show the disease, in a biased sample [15:15].
- Subconcussive hits matter, and the speaker wants hit counts modeled on baseball pitch counts [16:16], [16:48].
- Up to 75% of football brain trauma exposure occurs in practice, so reducing contact in practice is the top lever [19:23].
- The NFL players' union negotiated fewer contact practice days, and the Ivy League and Pop Warner followed with limits [19:23], [19:54].
- Helmets mainly prevent skull fractures and the bigger gains are rule changes [24:03].
- Athletes should not play while symptomatic for at least ten years until the culture changes [26:37].
- Genetic risk is unknown and unlikely to be one gene [27:37], [28:09].

## Numbers and definitions

- Brain bank: "500" living pledges, "105 brains", over 35 former NFL players [01:30].
- Diagnosed 5% (one out of 20) versus "more like 50%" by survey [06:04].
- A cited study: average of "three dings per season" [06:34].
- Hockey study ages "16 to 21"; 5% versus 35%, "seven times as many" [06:34], [07:04].
- Observer study: observers thought they saw 33, athletes reported 54 [07:04]; speaker estimates two to 10% of concussions get diagnosed [07:34].
- Rough math: 50-person team, half concussed, 10 days each, 250 days, about 4% of playing days [12:12]; with 60 days out, 21% [14:14]. Speaker says the math was done "on the plane" [12:12].
- Vulnerability window: rats 7 to 10 days [12:43], [13:13]; 30 days for tests [13:13].
- Brain bank sample: over 90% with disease, "N of 50" [15:15]; first 25 college and pro players: 19 pro, six college, all but one with pathology [15:46].
- Pitch counts example: 75 at age 10, 85 at 11, three days of rest after 61 pitches [17:19].
- Sensors: 500 to 1,000 blows in college football; a high school player 2,235 blows in three months above 10 G [18:20].
- Position totals: receivers under 400; linemen "near a th000 or well over" (garbled) [18:51].
- Practice limits: NFL players' union asked 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks; NCAA allows five days a week and Ivy League chose two; Pop Warner from six hours to two [19:23], [19:54].
- Headers: up to 5,000 a year; those over 1300 more likely abnormal (unpublished study, caption "Lipton") [20:55].
- Informed athletes: "less than 1%" of professionals; "four professional athletes" visited the brain bank [25:36].
- APOE4 (caption "ape4"): two to four times greater risk, small sample; "four for four" players exceeding any threshold [27:37], [28:09].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Window of vulnerability concept [04:34].
- Hit indicator (helmet, headband or mouthpiece) with red-light and green-light alerts [08:04].
- Fast sideline test compared with a baseline [11:41].
- Hit count modeled on baseball pitch count [16:48].
- Practice-contact limits and limits on multi-sport exposure [19:23], [20:24].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker discloses a consultant role and a financial tie to a test's owner [00:30].
- The 21% and 4% figures are his back-of-envelope math using assumed recovery times, with "the science is iffy" on the 10-day figure [12:12].
- Brain-bank findings are a self-selected, biased sample, as he says [15:15].
- Header study is unpublished; a threshold for safe hit counts is unknown [18:51].
- Caption problems: names and organizations garbled (sports legacy institute, "SC stat too" likely SCAT2, "King devic" likely King-Devick, "ape4"); the "5 Point score" phrase at [10:06] is unclear; "th000" at [18:51] is garbled.
- Personal case described at [02:30] to [03:03] is used as an illustration, not data.

## Q&A

- Does protective equipment make play more dangerous? Helmets mostly prevent skull fractures; rule changes matter more [24:03], [24:33].
- Should athletes choose to play after a concussion? Not until athletes are informed and the culture changes [25:36], [26:37].
- Any breakthrough in predicting who gets the disease? Genetics unknown; no magic gene expected [27:37], [28:09].

## Summary

A former college football player and wrestler who now runs a concussion research group argues that technology is about to improve four things: impact indicators, sideline assessment, return-to-play testing and "hit counts." He says concussions are badly under-diagnosed, return to play is poorly timed, and subconcussive blows may also damage the brain. He does rough math to show that perfect detection and cautious return would sideline a fifth of players, so the sports themselves would have to change, starting with less contact in practice. He also discusses helmets, informed consent, and genetics. He discloses ties to a test and a company.

## Key claims

- Technology is improving assessment, removal from play, return to play and hit counts [00:30].
- Concussions do not show on standard imaging; diagnosis relies on signs and symptoms [05:04].
- Diagnosed concussions run about 5% a year in contact sports, but anonymous athlete surveys give numbers more like 50% [06:04].
- In a hockey study, putting a doctor in the stands to pull players liberally found seven times as many concussions: 5% versus 35% [06:34], [07:04].
- Impact thresholds are a problem: risk is an S-curve, no known concussion at 10 G, and certain concussion at 300 G, so any red-light threshold is arbitrary [08:04], [08:35].
- The current 20-minute sideline evaluation has not been validated and its parts cannot decide return to play alone [09:36].
- Substitution rules in rugby and soccer make it hard to remove and evaluate players, and a "brain bin" 20-minute window has been proposed [10:38].
- A less-than-one-minute test is described as promising, based on two published papers [11:41].
- The vulnerability window after a concussion is longer than believed; in 2008 players were still returning within 15 minutes [12:43].
- Research tests suggest no one recovers to baseline within 30 days [13:13].
- If athletes were held out for 60 days, about one in five would be out at any time [14:14].
- Over 90% of brains of those who played collision sports for more than 10 years show the disease, in a biased sample [15:15].
- Subconcussive hits matter, and the speaker wants hit counts modeled on baseball pitch counts [16:16], [16:48].
- Up to 75% of football brain trauma exposure occurs in practice, so reducing contact in practice is the top lever [19:23].
- The NFL players' union negotiated fewer contact practice days, and the Ivy League and Pop Warner followed with limits [19:23], [19:54].
- Helmets mainly prevent skull fractures and the bigger gains are rule changes [24:03].
- Athletes should not play while symptomatic for at least ten years until the culture changes [26:37].
- Genetic risk is unknown and unlikely to be one gene [27:37], [28:09].

## Numbers and definitions

- Brain bank: "500" living pledges, "105 brains", over 35 former NFL players [01:30].
- Diagnosed 5% (one out of 20) versus "more like 50%" by survey [06:04].
- A cited study: average of "three dings per season" [06:34].
- Hockey study ages "16 to 21"; 5% versus 35%, "seven times as many" [06:34], [07:04].
- Observer study: observers thought they saw 33, athletes reported 54 [07:04]; speaker estimates two to 10% of concussions get diagnosed [07:34].
- Rough math: 50-person team, half concussed, 10 days each, 250 days, about 4% of playing days [12:12]; with 60 days out, 21% [14:14]. Speaker says the math was done "on the plane" [12:12].
- Vulnerability window: rats 7 to 10 days [12:43], [13:13]; 30 days for tests [13:13].
- Brain bank sample: over 90% with disease, "N of 50" [15:15]; first 25 college and pro players: 19 pro, six college, all but one with pathology [15:46].
- Pitch counts example: 75 at age 10, 85 at 11, three days of rest after 61 pitches [17:19].
- Sensors: 500 to 1,000 blows in college football; a high school player 2,235 blows in three months above 10 G [18:20].
- Position totals: receivers under 400; linemen "near a th000 or well over" (garbled) [18:51].
- Practice limits: NFL players' union asked 14 practice days with contact in 18 weeks; NCAA allows five days a week and Ivy League chose two; Pop Warner from six hours to two [19:23], [19:54].
- Headers: up to 5,000 a year; those over 1300 more likely abnormal (unpublished study, caption "Lipton") [20:55].
- Informed athletes: "less than 1%" of professionals; "four professional athletes" visited the brain bank [25:36].
- APOE4 (caption "ape4"): two to four times greater risk, small sample; "four for four" players exceeding any threshold [27:37], [28:09].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Window of vulnerability concept [04:34].
- Hit indicator (helmet, headband or mouthpiece) with red-light and green-light alerts [08:04].
- Fast sideline test compared with a baseline [11:41].
- Hit count modeled on baseball pitch count [16:48].
- Practice-contact limits and limits on multi-sport exposure [19:23], [20:24].

## Limits and open questions

- Should athletes choose to play after a concussion? Not until athletes are informed and the culture changes [25:36], [26:37].

## Summary

A 2012 SSAC panel on the creation of the modern athlete and performance analytics. The moderator opens by asking whether any team is truly optimizing player performance. Panelists from the NBA, the IOC and Team USA, sports law and media, and a performance company cover concussion and league rule changes, who gets to see an athlete's medical and genetic data, performance-enhancing drugs and where the legal line sits, sleep tracking, and how a general manager weighs injury risk in the draft. A recurring theme is that data matters only if it changes what someone does, and that daily habits, sleep and behavior hold more untapped performance than extra technology. Most of it is opinion and anecdote, not data.

## Key claims

- The moderator says last year's panel found professional teams doing little to optimize performance, with little centralized injury data and little use of medical information in contracts. [00:30] [01:30]
- A panelist who played in the NBA says player care 20 years ago was mostly recovery after injury, and that athletes now want as much information as possible. [02:31] [03:01]
- In the NBA, the athlete, the agent and the team have to come together on recovery, and a general manager has to know the athlete's body. [03:31]
- One panelist argues the private sector outperforms the public sector, and treats leagues as a framework that the private sector fills. [05:02] [06:02]
- The new NFL agreement reduced contact drills, which that panelist calls overdue because so many injuries happen in practice. [05:32]
- Concussion should not be thought of as one hit. [07:32]
- A panelist says counting impacts and G-loads in light gear shows that limiting contact saves an athlete a large number of blows. [08:02]
- An athlete's awareness and proper diagnosis come first; an athlete trusts clinicians to say whether they may compete. [09:02] [09:32]
- Doctors are not always as educated as assumed, and concussions do not show up on CT or MRI, so families can follow advice and still return too early. [14:32] [15:02]
- Medical protocols sit inside collective bargaining, so concussion rules can end up traded against minimum wage. [15:32] [16:02]
- Unions in some sports may not want health-risk information because it could hurt a player's contract chances. [13:02] [13:32]
- A manager would want genetic information before a long contract, but a former athlete may not want it shared; the IOC panelist wants the athlete to control who sees it. [16:32] [17:02] [17:32]
- If you cannot turn data into something actionable, sometimes it is better not to know; ask what you would do with the result. [19:32]
- A genetic predisposition says little to a general manager, and testing children to pick a sport is called madness. [21:04] [22:05]
- Athletes differ: some want all the data, others a few basic facts, plus an actionable plan. [20:33]
- There is no magic number; the mental side is underrated and cannot be given a numerical value. [22:35] [23:05]
- The line between legal and banned enhancement is described as a gray area, with enough money at stake that some will always cheat. [26:08] [30:41]
- A panelist says most athletes they see have more performance available through coordination, "kinetic connection" and behavior, and that bigger muscle is mostly irrelevant outside combat sports. [31:41] [32:11]
- Doping's main benefit is described as faster recovery. [33:41]
- Feeling better is not enough; athletes and teams want real change in specific indicators. [34:11]
- An Olympian describes a food sensitivity test, heart rate zones set for her rather than her team, and comparing recovery with her partner to inform pairings. [37:41] [38:11] [38:42]
- A general manager draws on scouting, doctors and psychologists, and can buy injury-risk players cheaply if the organization has strong support staff. [40:12] [42:13] [42:44]
- Players with the least bargaining leverage, such as draft prospects, are the most likely to be forced to disclose medical information. [44:15]
- A panelist says society undervalues sleep and that sleep research needs to change. [45:15] [45:45]
- One organization bought sleep monitors and made the scores a competition, which made sleep part of the culture. [46:15] [46:45]
- The IOC panelist says contaminated supplements make clean athletes unsure what to trust, and teams and leagues should provide a trusted safe harbor. [51:46] [52:16] [53:17]
- A panelist says to fix the basics first, meals, sleep and training, before talking about stem cells. [49:46]

## Numbers and definitions

- NBA player care compared "20 years ago", early 1990s. [02:31]
- Practice injuries: a panelist says 70% of all NFL injuries happen in practice; no source is given. [05:32]
- Impact blows: a panelist says limiting contact saves 10 to 15 thousand blows per year, and 60 to 100 thousand overall; the captions are garbled and the basis is unclear. [08:02]
- A baseball example: a 25-year-old left-hander who pitched 180 innings. [13:02]
- A player refused a DNA test but would accept "12 other types of tests". [12:32]
- "90%" of athletes have more performance left through coordination and behavior; "90%" of daily organization is subconscious; "90% of the time" you do not know what you are doing. Rough speaker figures, no source. [31:41] [36:41]
- Kinetic connection: the ability to transfer energy from one segment to another. [32:11]
- Workload: 162 games and over 100,000 miles a year in flights. [33:11]
- A heart rate or wearable example: 42 sprints; a device that stays in a cleat seven months. [35:11]
- Sleep: "a hundred Zeos" bought; a "ZQ score"; athletes boast of "104" and "70" (units and scale not explained). [46:15] [46:45] [47:15]
- A story about data scoring "seven or eight" out of 10, speaker unclear in the captions. [44:15]
- A "62 recovery score" with three of six meals missed; "98%" efficiency. [49:16] [49:46]
- A "90-something percent" of needs met by ethical recovery products. [53:17]
- "$10 million" at stake in the ethics example. [30:11]

## Methods and frameworks named

- The athlete, agent and team triangle for recovery decisions in the NBA. [03:31]
- Decision test for any assessment: what will I do with this result. [19:32]
- Individualized profiles built from sport, head coach philosophy and position analysis. [23:35]
- Ethics ordering from a panelist: is it illegal, is it banned by the governing body, is it the right conversation with the athlete, where does it rank among performance factors. [48:16] [48:46]
- Heart rate monitoring with personal zones, and comparison of recovery between partners. [38:11] [38:42]
- Sleep monitors with scores treated as a team competition. [46:15]
- Team data from medical exams, MRIs, scouts and psychologists in the draft. [40:12] [41:42]

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker labels are missing in the captions, so most lines cannot be tied to a named panelist with confidence.
- Most numbers are rough or garbled and have no source.
- Some panelists speak from their commercial interest (a performance company, a sleep-monitor program).
- Examples (Eddie Curry, Greg Oden, a 15-year-old with a concussion) are single cases.
- A panelist says it is impossible to predict the future from medical data; the panel did not test any predictive model. [41:42]
- The IOC commission name appears as "Entourage" and "Environmental" in the captions. [17:32] [18:32]
- Conflicting views on disclosure: some want more medical data, some see it as an invasion of privacy. [13:02] [14:02]

## Q&A

- Which medical information do you weigh in the draft, for an injury-prone player? A general manager says they use all sources, with scouts, doctors and psychologists. [39:42] [40:12]
- Does health-focused league policy risk alienating fans? A panelist says no, unless the game changes radically. [43:44]
- How do you measure return on a performance program? A panelist says athletes need real change in specific indicators. [34:11]

## Summary

A 2013 SSAC panel of NFL front-office and analytics people on how numbers fit into player evaluation, free agency, trades, the draft and coaching. The panelists treat analytics as one input beside scouting and film, argue that football's interdependent roles and schemes make clean predictors rare, and describe draft picks as currency under the salary cap and the new rookie wage scale. They also discuss combine testing and its limits, psychological testing, injury and character risk, how an analyst should get a head coach to listen, and a closing round on overrated and underrated players. The evidence is anecdote and each speaker's own organizational view, not data shown on screen.

## Key claims

- Analytics plays an important role in player evaluation but is one tool, and strong teams marry scouting and analytics. [04:35] [05:38]
- Statistics see every play while memory favors the best and worst, and statistics place a player on the continuum of his position. [05:38] [06:09]
- Quality control coaches have long done analytics, in the form of opponent tendency reports. [03:34] [04:04]
- One organization graded players on the combine tests before they ran, and looked again only at big outliers. [07:10] [07:40]
- Playing speed differs from pure speed, and 40 times can mislead. [08:40] [09:10]
- A panelist found the 20 to 40 yard portion of the 40 correlates with receiver performance, as separation speed. [10:43] [11:14]
- Another panelist found receiver projections depend only on the early part of the run. [11:14] [11:44]
- Speed score, built on 40 time and weight, was described as a good way to spot running backs who will do well. [12:14] [12:44]
- No test measures reactive quickness well, and watching a player against air tells less. [14:18]
- Workouts up close and drills built around routes told one team more than the combine, with one panelist saying that part is more gut than analytics. [14:48] [15:50] [16:21]
- No unified theory links measurables to performance, because of team system and the other players. [16:52] [17:23]
- Football's interdependence makes trades and free agency hard: a player may not travel from one system to another. [17:53] [18:25]
- In free agency, a team that thinks a player is worth twice what the market says should ask what the other side knows. [22:31]
- Knowing your own players is the most important part of free agency. [23:02]
- Draft picks are wholesale and veterans are retail under the salary cap. [24:33]
- Draft picks work as currency, and more picks mean more chances. [26:35] [27:06]
- The Jimmy Johnson draft value chart overrates the top picks, and many successful teams trade down. [28:07] [28:37]
- The time horizon of a coach and general manager changes whether trading down makes sense. [29:38] [30:08]
- Teams chase undervalued positions and schemes, and market inefficiencies move as others copy them. [31:40] [32:11] [32:43] [33:14]
- Spending is shifting toward fewer star players, and cheap rookie contracts fund the rest. [36:50] [37:22] [37:53]
- Injuries should be analyzed in groups, but recoveries from major injuries now seem faster, which weakens past comparisons. [41:25] [41:56] [42:26]
- Combine psychological testing has long used the Wonderlic and a new player assessment tool was mandated; panelists raised bias concerns about the old test. [43:26] [43:56] [44:26]
- A panelist separates work ethic from work habits and sees personality as an untapped area for analytics. [44:58] [45:28] [47:32]
- Consistency between coach, general manager and system is called the most important thing in the NFL. [49:37] [50:08]
- Analysts should communicate clearly, solve something real, and learn how coaches and scouts see the game. [51:10] [51:40] [52:11] [52:43]
- A panelist uses analytics to track coach tendencies (fourth downs, run or pass, timeouts) and to explain rules, not on game day. [53:14] [53:44] [54:15]

## Numbers and definitions

- 18 NFL teams represented at the conference. [00:00]
- A hiring history: one team has had an analytics hire since 2001, 12 years. [02:32]
- Quality control: watching the last four or five games of the next opponent. [04:04]
- A scouting example of "112 defensive ends" in the league. [06:09]
- Flying 20: time between the 20 and 40 of the 40-yard dash; the cornerback starts "five to nine yards" behind. [10:43]
- Receiver projections use the "first 10 seconds" of the run; the unit is probably yards, caption error. [11:14]
- A safety is described as a "43 guy", probably 4.3 seconds, caption error. [09:10]
- Speed score: based on 40 time and weight rather than 40 time alone. [12:14]
- 11 picks and three compensatory picks as a hypothetical haul. [25:04]
- A 15% discount on every veteran's market value would still leave a veteran team over the cap. [25:34]
- A trade chain from a seventh round pick to a sixth, a fifth and eventually a third. [26:35] [27:06]
- Nose tackles worth "$12 million". [31:40]
- Eight million in free agency: seven million on one player and one million on another versus two players at four million. [37:22]
- 12 first or second round picks costing less than $25 million combined in 2014. [37:53]
- Combine order examples: fifth overall twice and third overall once on one defense. [39:25]
- Overrated rankings: a speaker says there is no difference between 10th and 20th but 89th is a problem. [56:22]
- A game that took "149 minutes and 45 seconds" to win. [31:10]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Grading expected combine performance before the test and flagging outliers. [07:10]
- Flying 20 and first 10 splits for receivers; speed score for running backs. [10:43] [12:14]
- Comparing a player to similar players for aging and rebounds. [20:27] [20:58]
- Wholesale versus retail framing under the salary cap. [24:33]
- Market efficiency search across positions and schemes. [31:40] [32:43]
- Group-based injury comparison. [41:25]
- Psychological testing, including the Wonderlic and the player assessment tool. [43:26] [43:56]
- Game charting for coverages, with admitted errors. [56:22]

## Limits and open questions

- Speaker labels are missing, so most claims cannot be tied to a named panelist.
- Mostly anecdote: a few named players are used as examples with no sample sizes.
- Panelists gave opposite findings on receivers' speed. [10:43] [11:14]
- Reasons for early separation were not explained. [11:44]
- The panel concedes quick free agency decisions are made with no information. [20:27]
- The injury recovery trend is the speaker's impression, not shown with data. [41:25]

- A panelist admits the game charting statistics have mistakes. [56:22]

## Q&A

- How do you convince a head coach to listen to an analytics person who never played? A panelist says it takes mutual respect, an open-minded coach and a clear delivery. [50:08] [50:40] [51:10]
- How do you use analytics with coaches during the week? Tendency tracking, rules help and review, but not on game day. [53:14] [53:44]
- Who is most overrated and underrated? Rams free agents (as a joke), D'Angelo Hall, Levante David, and Tony Romo. [54:48] [55:50] [56:54]

## Summary

A short SSAC13 talk previewing a book called Newton's Football, due the following fall. The speaker, a scientist by training, presents three "falling apples": the shape of the football and the chaos it brings to loose balls, Vince Lombardi's run-heavy approach explained through game theory, and the helmet, whose face mask may have led players to tackle with their heads. The talk uses two NFL teams' fumble recoveries as an example of chaos. The helmet section uses a robust-and-fragile design idea to say a safety change can shift behavior in unplanned ways. The material is illustrative and the speakers' own framing, and the Q&A pushes back on it in places.

## Key claims

- The modern football is a prolate spheroid that gives control in the air but erratic bounces on the ground. [02:03] [02:33]
- Loose-ball randomness is a hidden force worth controlling for those seeking championships. [03:36] [04:06]
- Vince Lombardi was methodical, studied tape, gave players grades, and had taught science. [04:37] [05:07]
- After a 1960 loss that came from risky fourth-down decisions, Lombardi settled on a low-risk approach. [05:07] [05:38]
- Game theory is described as interpersonal decision-making, where each choice has a payoff depending on the other side's response. [06:08] [06:39]
- Lombardi ran the same plays with great precision rather than randomizing, which the speaker calls a dominant strategy. [08:11] [08:41]
- Modern game theory says a team should randomize its run and pass choices. [21:50]
- The helmet was designed to prevent skull fractures, not to stop the brain from moving inside the skull. [09:42]
- The face mask began after Otto Graham took an elbow to the face in 1953, and false confidence led players to lead with the head. [10:12] [10:43] [11:13]
- The speaker calls the helmet robust against skull fractures but fragile against concussion. [11:43]
- A technology can change behavior in ways its designers did not expect; the LED traffic light that does not melt snow is the example. [12:15] [12:45] [13:15]
- The next step for the helmet is unclear because fans, coaches and general managers pull in different directions. [13:15] [13:45] [14:45]
- In Q&A the speaker favors a new helmet with better impact-absorbing materials, and the co-speaker adds that tackling with the body is safer. [15:46] [20:49] [21:19]
- On fumbles, the co-speaker says forcing and avoiding fumbles is a skill, but recovery looks mostly random. [16:48]
- The co-speaker says holding on to the ball is controllable once, but not recovery after it is out. [19:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- Two teams, the 49ers and the Rams (2011 to 2012 season), each had forced fumbles "on the order of 20". [03:36]
- The 49ers recovered "75%" and the Rams "30%" of those balls; the captions also say "about 75 of them", so the unit is garbled. [04:06]
- Lombardi taught science for eight years at St. Cecilia's high school. [04:37]
- The loss that changed his approach came in 1960. [05:07]
- Payoff table (yards): run when a run is anticipated, 4; run when a pass is anticipated, 7; pass when a run is anticipated, 9; pass when a pass is anticipated, no yards. [07:09]
- More than two-thirds of Lombardi's plays were runs. [08:41]
- An audience member says the optimal mix from the chart is three-quarters runs. [18:19]
- Otto Graham's injury: 1953. [10:12]
- Incandescent bulbs: about 70% of the energy goes to waste heat; the bulb has been around for over a hundred years. [12:15]
- Helmet analogy: skull as egg shell, brain as yolk. [09:42]
- Robust: protects against the designed threat; fragile: fails against an unplanned one. [11:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Chaos theory applied to loose balls. [03:36]
- Game theory with a two-by-two payoff matrix of run or pass against anticipated run or pass. [06:39] [07:09]
- A dominant strategy label for Lombardi's repeated approach. [08:41]
- Robustness and fragility, and a technology-behavior design cycle. [11:43] [12:15]
- A fumble comparison drawn from data "provided from one source". [18:49]

## Limits and open questions

- The fumble example is one season for two teams, and the co-speaker calls recovery "very much random" and the data "kind of inconclusive". [18:19] [18:49]

## Summary

A 2013 SSAC panel of NFL front-office and analytics people on how numbers fit into player evaluation, free agency, trades, the draft and coaching. The panelists treat analytics as one input beside scouting and film, argue that football's interdependent roles and schemes make clean predictors rare, and describe draft picks as currency under the salary cap and the new rookie wage scale. They also discuss combine testing and its limits, psychological testing, injury and character risk, how an analyst should get a head coach to listen, and a closing round on overrated and underrated players. The evidence is anecdote and each speaker's own organizational view, not data shown on screen.

## Key claims

- Analytics plays an important role in player evaluation but is one tool, and strong teams marry scouting and analytics. [04:35] [05:38]
- Statistics see every play while memory favors the best and worst, and statistics place a player on the continuum of his position. [05:38] [06:09]
- Quality control coaches have long done analytics, in the form of opponent tendency reports. [03:34] [04:04]
- One organization graded players on the combine tests before they ran, and looked again only at big outliers. [07:10] [07:40]
- Playing speed differs from pure speed, and 40 times can mislead. [08:40] [09:10]
- A panelist found the 20 to 40 yard portion of the 40 correlates with receiver performance, as separation speed. [10:43] [11:14]
- Another panelist found receiver projections depend only on the early part of the run. [11:14] [11:44]
- Speed score, built on 40 time and weight, was described as a good way to spot running backs who will do well. [12:14] [12:44]
- No test measures reactive quickness well, and watching a player against air tells less. [14:18]
- Workouts up close and drills built around routes told one team more than the combine, with one panelist saying that part is more gut than analytics. [14:48] [15:50] [16:21]
- No unified theory links measurables to performance, because of team system and the other players. [16:52] [17:23]
- Football's interdependence makes trades and free agency hard: a player may not travel from one system to another. [17:53] [18:25]
- In free agency, a team that thinks a player is worth twice what the market says should ask what the other side knows. [22:31]
- Knowing your own players is the most important part of free agency. [23:02]
- Draft picks are wholesale and veterans are retail under the salary cap. [24:33]
- Draft picks work as currency, and more picks mean more chances. [26:35] [27:06]
- The Jimmy Johnson draft value chart overrates the top picks, and many successful teams trade down. [28:07] [28:37]
- The time horizon of a coach and general manager changes whether trading down makes sense. [29:38] [30:08]
- Teams chase undervalued positions and schemes, and market inefficiencies move as others copy them. [31:40] [32:11] [32:43] [33:14]
- Spending is shifting toward fewer star players, and cheap rookie contracts fund the rest. [36:50] [37:22] [37:53]
- Injuries should be analyzed in groups, but recoveries from major injuries now seem faster, which weakens past comparisons. [41:25] [41:56] [42:26]
- Combine psychological testing has long used the Wonderlic and a new player assessment tool was mandated; panelists raised bias concerns about the old test. [43:26] [43:56] [44:26]

- Consistency between coach, general manager and system is called the most important thing in the NFL. [49:37] [50:08]
- Analysts should communicate clearly, solve something real, and learn how coaches and scouts see the game. [51:10] [51:40] [52:11] [52:43]
- A panelist uses analytics to track coach tendencies (fourth downs, run or pass, timeouts) and to explain rules, not on game day. [53:14] [53:44] [54:15]

## Numbers and definitions

- 18 NFL teams represented at the conference. [00:00]

- A scouting example of "112 defensive ends" in the league. [06:09]

- Nose tackles worth "$12 million". [31:40]
- Eight million in free agency: seven million on one player and one million on another versus two players at four million. [37:22]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Grading expected combine performance before the test and flagging outliers. [07:10]
- Flying 20 and first 10 splits for receivers; speed score for running backs. [10:43] [12:14]
- Comparing a player to similar players for aging and rebounds. [20:27] [20:58]
- Wholesale versus retail framing under the salary cap. [24:33]

## Summary

A short SSAC13 talk previewing a book called Newton's Football, due the following fall. The speaker, a scientist by training, presents three "falling apples": the shape of the football and the chaos it brings to loose balls, Vince Lombardi's run-heavy approach explained through game theory, and the helmet, whose face mask may have led players to tackle with their heads. The talk uses two NFL teams' fumble recoveries as an example of chaos. The helmet section uses a robust-and-fragile design idea to say a safety change can shift behavior in unplanned ways. The material is illustrative and the speakers' own framing, and the Q&A pushes back on it in places.

## Key claims

- The modern football is a prolate spheroid that gives control in the air but erratic bounces on the ground. [02:03] [02:33]
- Loose-ball randomness is a hidden force worth controlling for those seeking championships. [03:36] [04:06]
- Vince Lombardi was methodical, studied tape, gave players grades, and had taught science. [04:37] [05:07]
- After a 1960 loss that came from risky fourth-down decisions, Lombardi settled on a low-risk approach. [05:07] [05:38]
- Game theory is described as interpersonal decision-making, where each choice has a payoff depending on the other side's response. [06:08] [06:39]
- Lombardi ran the same plays with great precision rather than randomizing, which the speaker calls a dominant strategy. [08:11] [08:41]
- Modern game theory says a team should randomize its run and pass choices. [21:50]
- The helmet was designed to prevent skull fractures, not to stop the brain from moving inside the skull. [09:42]
- The face mask began after Otto Graham took an elbow to the face in 1953, and false confidence led players to lead with the head. [10:12] [10:43] [11:13]
- The speaker calls the helmet robust against skull fractures but fragile against concussion. [11:43]
- A technology can change behavior in ways its designers did not expect; the LED traffic light that does not melt snow is the example. [12:15] [12:45] [13:15]
- The next step for the helmet is unclear because fans, coaches and general managers pull in different directions. [13:15] [13:45] [14:45]
- In Q&A the speaker favors a new helmet with better impact-absorbing materials, and the co-speaker adds that tackling with the body is safer. [15:46] [20:49] [21:19]
- On fumbles, the co-speaker says forcing and avoiding fumbles is a skill, but recovery looks mostly random. [16:48]
- The co-speaker says holding on to the ball is controllable once, but not recovery after it is out. [19:19]

## Numbers and definitions

- Two teams, the 49ers and the Rams (2011 to 2012 season), each had forced fumbles "on the order of 20". [03:36]
- The 49ers recovered "75%" and the Rams "30%" of those balls; the captions also say "about 75 of them", so the unit is garbled. [04:06]
- Lombardi taught science for eight years at St. Cecilia's high school. [04:37]
- The loss that changed his approach came in 1960. [05:07]
- Payoff table (yards): run when a run is anticipated, 4; run when a pass is anticipated, 7; pass when a run is anticipated, 9; pass when a pass is anticipated, no yards. [07:09]
- More than two-thirds of Lombardi's plays were runs. [08:41]
- An audience member says the optimal mix from the chart is three-quarters runs. [18:19]
- Otto Graham's injury: 1953. [10:12]
- Incandescent bulbs: about 70% of the energy goes to waste heat; the bulb has been around for over a hundred years. [12:15]
- Helmet analogy: skull as egg shell, brain as yolk. [09:42]
- Robust: protects against the designed threat; fragile: fails against an unplanned one. [11:43]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Chaos theory applied to loose balls. [03:36]
- Game theory with a two-by-two payoff matrix of run or pass against anticipated run or pass. [06:39] [07:09]
- A dominant strategy label for Lombardi's repeated approach. [08:41]
- Robustness and fragility, and a technology-behavior design cycle. [11:43] [12:15]
- A fumble comparison drawn from data "provided from one source". [18:49]

## Limits and open questions

- The fumble example is one season for two teams, and the co-speaker calls recovery "very much random" and the data "kind of inconclusive". [18:19] [18:49]
- The speaker said the data on when fumbles occur still needed to be sorted. [18:49]
- The helmet and Otto Graham account is the speakers' own proposal, not shown with injury data. [10:12]
- Inference: with the payoffs shown, neither run nor pass is the better choice against both defensive guesses, so the "dominant strategy" label does not match the table. The audience member's three-quarters figure does match the table.
- Inference: the 4, 7, 9 and 0 payoffs look illustrative; the captions do not say they are measured.
- A former player's view in Q&A is that the problem is how the helmet is used, not the equipment. [19:49] [20:19]
- The talk is a promotion for a forthcoming book. [14:45] [15:15]
- Captions garble some names ("Packards", "Schroinger") and the speaker's surname.

## Q&A

- Would replacing the face mask solve concussions? The speaker says the helmet itself needs better impact-absorbing materials. [15:15] [15:46]
- Could teams control chaos and recover fumbles more reliably? The co-speaker says recovery is mostly random, though forcing and avoiding fumbles is a skill. [16:18] [16:48]
- Lombardi ran two-thirds, but the optimal mix is three-quarters? The speakers agree it is useful to know. [18:19]
- When do fumbles occur and does it affect recovery? Not yet analyzed; the co-speaker spoke with EA Sports about how hard the bounce is to model. [18:49] [19:19] [19:49]
- Is it the player's evolution rather than the helmet? The speaker says materials should still absorb impact and behavior should change too. [19:49] [20:19] [20:49]
- How has game theory evolved? Randomize, to keep the other team guessing. [21:50]

A short SSAC13 talk previewing a book called Newton's Football, due the following fall. The talk uses two NFL teams' fumble recoveries as an example of chaos. The helmet section uses a robust-and-fragile design idea to say a safety change can shift behavior in unplanned ways. - The speaker calls the helmet robust against skull fractures but fragile against concussion. [11:43]

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

## Summary

The presenters propose a team-selection model for soccer that tries to cut injuries without giving up points. Each player gets a skill rating and a next-match injury probability. A Monte Carlo tree search then simulates the coming weeks to choose the starting eleven, treating the coach's job as a sequential decision problem. Tested on open Premier League data against a greedy pick-the-best-team-each-week baseline, the model reduced simulated injuries while keeping expected points similar, and the speakers argue real managers lean toward short-term choices. They state the work is a decision framework built on public data, not a clinical prediction tool.

## Key claims

- The work was motivated by crowded schedules; after the winter World Cup, injury severity rose and injury costs reached very large figures [01:01].
- Each player has a skill rating and an injury probability, and a search over team selections balances winning now against injury risk later [02:01].
- Resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, but the coach has to pick the right moment [03:02].
- Short-term and long-term workload and detailed injury history contributed most to the injury model, ahead of travel, rain, days since last injury, temperature and age [04:33].
- The team-level scoring model was modified to use player skill values and matched the original model within margins of error over two seasons [06:06].
- Compared with a greedy selection, the search model kept similar expected points while lowering injuries for the squad and the ideal starting eleven [11:14].
- Real managers' selections were more similar to the greedy model than to the search model; the speakers suggest short-term pressure as the reason [10:43].
- In higher injury-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy one on season points, while the margin of injury reduction shrank [12:15].
- Real technical directors often decide for short-term gains rather than long-term athlete protection [14:48].
- The presenters conclude teams can rest athletes and reduce injury risk without sacrificing results [14:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup [01:01].
- Almost $770 million in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season [01:01]. The Q&A-adjacent conclusion later says "nearly $800 million" [12:46]; the two spoken figures differ and the captions do not reconcile them.
- 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season [01:01].
- Injury model: gradient-boosted trees (caption spelling "XG boost") on 2017-18 Premier League data plus a career injury dataset [03:02]; injury durations sampled from a Gaussian distribution fitted to real injury data [03:32].
- Expected points come from an adapted Maher model, which assumes scoring rates follow a Poisson distribution [05:05]; team identity features were replaced with player skill values from a contribution model captioned "VAPE" [05:36].
- Data: StatsBomb event data for the 17/18 and 18/19 Premier League seasons, Transfermarkt for injury history, Capology for salary [09:11].
- Injury model test: 70/30 split with cross-validation (captioned "five-block"), log loss 0.16 [09:11]; Pearson correlation 0.77 with observed 18/19 outcomes [09:42].
- Selection similarity to real coaches: about 76% for the search model, 82% for the greedy model [10:12].
- Brighton: 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least benefited at 7.5% for the ideal eleven [11:14].
- Average across Premier League teams: 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal eleven [11:44].
- Risk multipliers of two and three times; 1.8% more expected points at three times [12:15].
- Salary cost tied to predicted injuries: 22% reduction for Brighton, about 11% on average [13:16].
- Headline: approximately 13% fewer injuries and an 11% reduction in injury-related costs [14:18]. Inference: the 13% matches the ideal-eleven average, not the 4.6% squad figure; the speaker did not say which. The captions may also garble "five-block."

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process framing of the coach's selection problem, solved approximately with Monte Carlo tree search using an upper-confidence heuristic and progressive broadening [06:37, 07:38, 08:09].
- Simulation assumes the coach picks the most qualified team in the rolled-out season; values are propagated back to the root [08:09].
- Feature attribution with SHAP values for the injury model [04:03].
- Greedy baseline that maximizes expected points for each match only [10:12].
- Salary data used to translate injuries into wages spent on unavailable players [12:46].

## Limits and open questions

- Built only on free and open data; no club medical or GPS training data [13:48]. Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model [17:53].
- Substitutions are not modeled; rest is all or nothing for a full match [13:48].
- Tested on Premier League only; other leagues, women's sports, rugby and American football are future work [14:18, 19:54].
- Results are simulated; no club has used the recommendations, and the Q&A notes a team would have to be convinced to follow it [18:54].
- Speaker's own framing: it is a decision framework, not a medical prediction model [18:54].
- Sample sizes beyond two seasons are not stated. The company affiliation of the presenter (a startup) is an institutional interest.
- Spoken cost figures conflict ($770 million versus nearly $800 million).

## Q&A

- A questioner proposed optimizing only the next several games, like a survivor pool, and re-optimizing as injuries occur [15:49]; the presenter said the model has a setting for how many games ahead to simulate, including a five-game window [16:51].
- Does the model rely on a reliable injury probability from load and history? Yes [17:22].
- How was load estimated from public data? From event counts, with a separate model imputing physical metrics, since tracking data is not open [17:53].
- Is training load included? No; the aim was a framework, and club medical and training data would improve it [18:24, 18:54].
- Other leagues? Not yet; the design allows other event data and women's sports would be interesting [19:54, 20:24].

## Summary

The presenters propose a team-selection model for soccer that tries to cut injuries without giving up points. Each player gets a skill rating and a next-match injury probability. A Monte Carlo tree search then simulates the coming weeks to choose the starting eleven, treating the coach's job as a sequential decision problem. Tested on open Premier League data against a greedy pick-the-best-team-each-week baseline, the model reduced simulated injuries while keeping expected points similar, and the speakers argue real managers lean toward short-term choices. They state the work is a decision framework built on public data, not a clinical prediction tool.

## Key claims

- The work was motivated by crowded schedules; after the winter World Cup, injury severity rose and injury costs reached very large figures [01:01].
- Each player has a skill rating and an injury probability, and a search over team selections balances winning now against injury risk later [02:01].
- Resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, but the coach has to pick the right moment [03:02].
- Short-term and long-term workload and detailed injury history contributed most to the injury model, ahead of travel, rain, days since last injury, temperature and age [04:33].
- The team-level scoring model was modified to use player skill values and matched the original model within margins of error over two seasons [06:06].
- Compared with a greedy selection, the search model kept similar expected points while lowering injuries for the squad and the ideal starting eleven [11:14].
- Real managers' selections were more similar to the greedy model than to the search model; the speakers suggest short-term pressure as the reason [10:43].
- In higher injury-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy one on season points, while the margin of injury reduction shrank [12:15].
- Real technical directors often decide for short-term gains rather than long-term athlete protection [14:48].
- The presenters conclude teams can rest athletes and reduce injury risk without sacrificing results [14:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup [01:01].
- Almost $770 million in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season [01:01]. The conclusion later says "nearly $800 million" [12:46]; the two spoken figures differ and the captions do not reconcile them.
- 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season [01:01].
- Injury model: gradient-boosted trees (caption spelling "XG boost") on 2017-18 Premier League data plus a career injury dataset [03:02]; injury durations sampled from a Gaussian distribution fitted to real injury data [03:32].
- Expected points come from an adapted Maher model, which assumes scoring rates follow a Poisson distribution [05:05]; team identity features were replaced with player skill values from a contribution model captioned "VAPE" [05:36].
- Data: StatsBomb event data for the 17/18 and 18/19 Premier League seasons, Transfermarkt for injury history, Capology for salary [09:11].
- Injury model test: 70/30 split with cross-validation (captioned "five-block"), log loss 0.16 [09:11]; Pearson correlation 0.77 with observed 18/19 outcomes [09:42].
- Selection similarity to real coaches: about 76% for the search model, 82% for the greedy model [10:12].
- Brighton: 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least benefited at 7.5% for the ideal eleven [11:14].
- Average across Premier League teams: 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal eleven [11:44].
- Risk multipliers of two and three times; 1.8% more expected points at three times [12:15].
- Salary cost tied to predicted injuries: 22% reduction for Brighton, about 11% on average [13:16].
- Headline: approximately 13% fewer injuries and an 11% reduction in injury-related costs [14:18]. Inference: the 13% matches the ideal-eleven average, not the 4.6% squad figure; the speaker did not say which. The captions may also garble "five-block."

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process framing of the coach's selection problem, solved approximately with Monte Carlo tree search using an upper-confidence heuristic and progressive broadening [06:37] [07:38] [08:09].
- Simulation assumes the coach picks the most qualified team in the rolled-out season; values are propagated back to the root [08:09].
- Feature attribution with SHAP values for the injury model [04:03].
- Greedy baseline that maximizes expected points for each match only [10:12].
- Salary data used to translate injuries into wages spent on unavailable players [12:46].

## Limits and open questions

- Built only on free and open data; no club medical or GPS training data [13:48]. Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model [17:53].
- Substitutions are not modeled; rest is all or nothing for a full match [13:48].
- Tested on Premier League only; other leagues, women's sports, rugby and American football are future work [14:18] [19:54].
- Results are simulated; no club has used the recommendations, and the Q&A notes a team would have to be convinced to follow it [18:54].
- Speaker's own framing: it is a decision framework, not a medical prediction model [18:54].
- Sample sizes beyond two seasons are not stated. The company affiliation of the presenter (a startup) is an institutional interest.
- Spoken cost figures conflict ($770 million versus nearly $800 million).

## Q&A

- A questioner proposed optimizing only the next several games, like a survivor pool, and re-optimizing as injuries occur [15:49]; the presenter said the model has a setting for how many games ahead to simulate, including a five-game window [16:51].
- Does the model rely on a reliable injury probability from load and history? Yes [17:22].
- How was load estimated from public data? From event counts, with a separate model imputing physical metrics, since tracking data is not open [17:53].
- Is training load included? No; the aim was a framework, and club medical and training data would improve it [18:24] [18:54].
- Other leagues? Not yet; the design allows other event data and women's sports would be interesting [19:54] [20:24].

## Summary

A moderated panel debates whether analytics-driven optimization, especially the rise of three-point shooting, has hurt basketball. One executive argues the three-point value is too large and the league office should adjust design as teams optimize. A league-office panelist says the only test is whether fans like the resulting product and that the league acts when data show harm, citing a transition-foul rule. Others argue play styles remain varied and that media narrative is the bigger problem. The panel also covers how much weight fan input deserves, public data access, rule-change ideas, and AI. It is opinion and debate, with few verifiable figures.

## Key claims

- The shift in shot locations came from avoiding inefficient two-pointers, since a three is worth 50% more [02:03].
- One panelist says the three-point value is too large and the league should step in as teams optimize [03:04] [03:37].
- The league-office panelist says a rule is a problem only if the resulting playstyle is not exciting, and that fans like the three-point era overall [05:09] [05:40].
- A team executive says the claim that all teams play one style is untrue, citing varied styles and open three-point looks [09:47].
- The same side says the spread of play styles between teams is about as wide as before [10:17].
- Fan engagement and a large media deal are cited as evidence the product is healthy [11:18].
- The narrative about the three-point revolution, not the game itself, is described as a problem that shapes fan opinion, and players dislike being told to do the same thing every possession [12:19] [12:49].
- Panelists place low to middling weight on what fans say they want; behavioral data count for more [14:20] [14:50].
- The league office tests fan reaction with lab studies using physiological monitors [15:20].
- Public data access has narrowed: team-held player-pose data are not public, which limits what a young analyst can do [19:57] [20:28].
- A former player says missing WNBA data left gaps in the history and stories of the game [18:55].
- Rules set incentives that push well-run teams in one direction, and whether that direction is better or worse is not known in advance [22:29].
- The league says it has acted where the optimal play hurt the game, for example transition fouls and the draft lottery [24:30] [25:00].
- Most fan rule-change suggestions are easier to voice than to implement because of second-order effects [26:31] [33:34].
- Panelists expect AI to change on-court play less than analytics already has, with bigger effects off the court [37:06] [37:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- 100 most common shooting spots in 2001-2002 shown against about 15 years later [01:32] [02:03].
- Three-pointers worth 50% more than other shots [02:03].
- About 15% of an NBA game is shooting [04:38].
- Over 60% of one team's three-pointers are open [09:47].
- Gap between the lowest and highest three-point-shooting teams: something like 18% in 2012, now 15 or 16 [10:47]. The captions are garbled here; do not rely on it.
- Fan-weight scale of 1 to 10: answers of three, about six or seven, and five [14:20] [14:50]; speaker attribution is unclear in the captions.
- Roughly 1,500 plays a season affected by transition fouls before the rule [24:30].
- WNBA season length: 40 games last season, 44 next season; Sue Bird played 32, 34 and 36 in different stretches [18:24].
- Tracking data described as 29 pose points at 60 frames per second [19:57].
- Hiring exercise: 100 points across analytical ability, interpersonal skills and passion; one answer was 40, 40 and 20 [35:05] [36:06]; other answers are garbled.

- Decision rule from the league: act when data are clear, and consider stakeholder views as a proxy for fans [25:00].
- Informal survey of conference registrants for rule ideas, read aloud [28:31].

- Panel of executives and a former player speaking from institutional positions (league office, teams); no data were shown beyond images and spoken figures, and no sample sizes are given.
- The captions have no speaker labels and several passages are garbled, so some attributions and figures are uncertain.
- The panelists disagree and do not resolve whether the three-point value is too high [03:04] [05:09] [24:00].
- Claims that fan satisfaction did not change during the season rest on the league's own survey and social data, which were not shown [12:19].

# SSAC18: Life Behind the Curtain An Inside Look at Working NFL Front Office

## Summary

A former sports agent who became the Green Bay Packers' contract and business executive describes how an NFL front office works from the inside. He recounts building a team abroad from nothing, then explains his role as a link between long-term business planning and the urgent needs of the football side. His stories cover contract talks, the decision to draft Aaron Rodgers while holding a long-time starting quarterback, the cost of negotiating directly with players, and weighing talent against character. The talk is anecdotal: it offers no data, no model and no Q&A, and the captions are noisy.

## Key claims

- The speaker describes his job as a fulcrum between the business side, which thinks long term, and the football side, which wants answers now [08:35].
- He says he was sometimes the voice of caution toward football staff and sometimes the voice of aggression toward the business side [09:05].
- He argues every team needs someone in that role so the organization does not split into isolated structures [09:40].
- Players mostly want to know they are getting a bit more than the other guy, not a particular dollar figure [11:12]; he calls insecurity and ego dominant in the business [11:42].
- He says a free-agent signing took over a month because the team's was the only offer, so he had to keep pushing [12:12] [12:43].
- Having no owner above him gave him freedom, and he let personnel evaluators do their jobs while he did his [13:43] [14:13].
- He says combining personnel work with payroll could be called Moneyball or analytics, and he thinks the team was ahead of its time [14:43].
- He says the team did not need a second quarterback behind a starter who never missed a game, and the pick was a present-versus-future balancing act [15:47] [16:22].
- Coaches were frustrated because the player might not help for years, or ever, and the room's mantra was to trust the board [19:59] [20:30].
- He says he expects no team to let a first-round quarterback wait three years again, because of pressure from fans [23:03] [23:33].
- Negotiating directly with players, which some offered because he was a former agent, was the worst experience, and he came to see an agent as a buffer [24:33] [25:03].
- On character, he says every player is a mix of talent and character, and that more talent brings more tolerance [26:35].
- He recounts opposing a position coach who wanted to sign a player with a long record of off-field problems, winning that argument and losing others [27:06] [27:36].
- He describes forcing a coach and a player into his office to talk, with four minutes of silence, ending with no firing and no agreement that they understood each other [29:06] [29:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barcelona team: 80 players selected, 40 told they could not travel, built in about 10 days [02:32].
- Opening-day ticket sales of 173 in a stadium he says holds 40,000 [02:32].
- The next night, 18,000 attended, with roughly 6,000 tickets given away by his own estimate [03:33].
- Food ordered for 60 people was eaten after 20 [05:03]; the team lasted two seasons [05:03].
- Seven contracts were waiting while he tried to reach a star quarterback [10:10].
- That quarterback's deal was described as the first hundred million dollar contract in the NFL [11:12].
- Free agent contact around March 15th, signing around April 26th [12:12].
- In the 2005 draft room, he says about 19 or 20 players were rated as first-rounders [17:55].
- The choice between two quarterbacks was "51 to 49 percent" by his recollection [18:29].
- The team reached the 24th pick with one first-round-rated name on the board [20:30].
- He kept the player's agent on hold for 15 minutes [21:31], with 13 minutes elapsed in the room [22:01] and two minutes left on the clock [22:32].
- He had three cases of direct negotiation before refusing to do it again [25:03].
- A coach's line about a player being asked to win "75 street fights a day" [27:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- The draft board with first-round ratings, and the rule to trust the board [20:30].
- A business-versus-football time-horizon split in roster and contract decisions [08:35].
- Using an agent as a buffer in contract talks [25:03].
- No quantitative model or data set is described.

## Limits and open questions

- The talk is a first-person set of stories with no data, no outcomes tracking and no comparison group, so none of it shows a method works.
- The Moneyball or analytics description of the team's approach [14:43] is the speaker's own claim; no metric or example is given.
- Probabilities such as 51 to 49 [18:29] are recollections, not documented model outputs.

- The talk touches on a former player's later criminal conviction as an example that character is hard to judge [26:04]; no process for judging character is offered.

- None: the speaker says he did not plan time for questions [29:36].

# SSAC22: In the Trenches of Football Analytics

## Summary

A moderated panel with an ESPN analyst, a former NFL offensive lineman, a Ravens analytics staffer and a Rams panelist discusses where football analytics works and where it strains. The central tension is season-long efficiency and tracking-based line grades against the on-field view that technique, coaching and teammates shape every play. The panelists describe how analysts earn trust from scouts and coaches, why grading individuals in a team game is hard, how fourth-down attitudes have shifted, and what data they want next, such as college tracking data. The captions are heavily garbled, so turn attribution and many details need checking against the video.

## Key claims

- The moderator opens by saying analytics is no longer a novelty or a rising phenomenon [01:01].
- The Rams panelist says football analytics lagged partly because revenue sharing under the cap lowers the need for innovation in small markets [02:32].
- He adds that on-field analyses are easy to copy, so teams look for edges others cannot easily reproduce [02:32] [03:02].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts and scouts process information differently but can reach the same conclusions, and that open dialogue helps when they disagree [03:33] [04:06].
- She frames modeling as having unknowns where coach and scout expertise enters, so the two views do not clash [05:06] [05:37].
- Mitch Schwartz says crude stats such as blitz rate mislead, giving examples of one team counted as a 50% blitz team and another as an 8% blitz team [06:08] [06:38].
- He prefers to study each opponent's tendencies on film, because knowing what a defender does most often matters more than his signature move [06:38] [07:08] [07:38].
- Bryan Burke describes building block identification from the separation between all players at each time step, then adding orientation and later win and loss on blocks [08:39] [09:09].
- The Rams panelist says tracking data reduces human bias in evaluation, for example liking a well-run team and discounting a mysterious one [10:09] [10:40].
- Schwartz says the ESPN line metric looked too simple (is your player between you and the quarterback at 2.5 seconds), and that a coached vertical set can make a blocker look worse on distance [11:41] [12:11] [12:41].
- He says a tackle was second in pass block wins while leading the league in sacks allowed, which he attributes partly to quarterbacks holding the ball [14:13] [14:43].
- The Ravens panelist says her view of running backs changed: value shows up in beating second-level tacklers, vision, and speed against an unblocked edge defender [15:45] [16:15] [16:45] [17:15].
- She argues run defense and pass defense merge: solid interior linemen mean fewer defenders in the box and more help in coverage [17:48] [18:23].
- Schwartz says the running game builds toughness and that tiring defensive linemen is a real but unquantified effect, and that he would not stop running with a large late lead [19:54] [21:25] [24:00].
- He says the best way to tire a defensive line is a fast-paced passing game [21:55].
- An analytics panelist says efficiency data favor passing, and that the question is how much to sacrifice for physicality, not whether the running game matters [22:56].
- A panelist notes the NFL is results-oriented while analytics focuses on process [25:32].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts must learn what coaches and scouts value, and tests a finding by asking what she would tell a coordinator [27:37] [28:08].
- She gives an example where a play's high passer rating looked like old news to senior scouts and coaches [29:12] [29:42].
- The Rams panelist says coaches are data processors without realizing it, use information differently from each other, and should be free to succeed or fail with or without analytics [30:12] [31:42] [32:44].
- A panelist says the share of teams going for it on fourth down rose a lot, raising what counts as conservative [33:44] [34:16].
- Schwartz says tracking could show how pre-snap depth off the ball affects a lineman's reach at contact [35:16] [35:47].
