- A panelist defends tracking metrics as objective and rule-consistent, noting two scouts in a room will disagree [37:47] [38:19] [38:51].
- A panelist says players picked high get more chances regardless of results and suggests quantifying that [39:21] [39:52].
- The Rams panelist says defensive line results depend on who plays next to you, using examples of players who changed teams [40:52] [41:23].
- A panelist says the aim is to understand interdependencies, not assign individual values, and doubts whether isolating individual plays works for paying or drafting [41:53] [42:23].
- Burke says tracking data work requires studying the sport at a deeper level and that analytics and film communities must merge [43:25] [43:55].
- The Ravens panelist wants better ways to value positions in roster construction and says left tackle pay, once about double right tackle pay, is now close to even [45:27] [45:57].

# SSAC24: The Numbers Game: Football Analytics from Combines to Championships

## Summary

A panel with a Pro Football Focus product chief, a Washington Commanders football-strategy executive, an analytics executive at a sports-analytics firm (captions: "Summer Sports") and a StatsBomb moderator covers analytics in drafting, tracking data, roster depth, in-game management, college football and analytical failures. Recurring themes: draft models are only as good as the scouting input, tracking data moves evaluation from outcomes toward traits, expectation models can misassign credit, and the hardest skill is communicating probability to decision makers. They also discuss the transfer portal, NIL, and language-model tools for coaches. Panelists speak from their own employers' viewpoints.

## Key claims

- The moderator says football's complexity far exceeds chess, so decisions still come down to humans even with a data-driven approach [03:34] [04:05].
- Palazzolo says the 2018 first overall pick of Baker Mayfield was analytically driven and did not pan out, while Josh Allen, picked seventh, became the best quarterback of the generation [04:36] [05:06].
- He says Aiden Hutchinson (caption spelling) was the clear analytical favorite over the player the Jaguars chose in the top two [05:06] [05:37].
- Clement says an offensive lineman from a small college (caption: Zack Tom of Wake Forest) was rated highly by analytics, played all five line positions, was hard to sell to scouts, and became a successful starter after being drafted by Green Bay [06:08].
- Palazzolo says PFF data covers every action, and calls the grading subjective but applied objectively [07:39].
- He values a player's whole college career, early years included, plus age adjustments [08:09], and says PFF detail is especially valuable for edge, defensive line and offensive line [08:39].
- Clement says it is hard to predict pro position from college position, and trait ratings from scouts can differ from performance under coaching assignments [09:10] [09:40].
- Shen says a draft model is only as good as the scouting data fed into it, and that he values scouts' input [11:13].
- He says data can make scouts more productive, so they stop spending time on poor players, and this earns their trust [11:43].
- The moderator says teams increasingly want to insulate scouts from analytics bias, with analysts synthesizing both views afterward [12:15].
- Before tracking data, most analytics measured outcomes, even PFF grades; tracking lets analysts estimate traits such as speed and field control [13:15] [13:45].
- Examples of teams using game speed rather than combine data are named as Rams wide receivers, and one panelist says the team may not attend the combine [13:45] [14:15].
- Teams are building their own athleticism metrics from data, which matter most for late-round picks, and combine participation is declining [14:45] [15:15].
- Panelists argue combine drills can be redesigned using tracking data to see what actually predicts game performance [15:45] [16:15].
- A panelist says medical problems found around the combine are a common reason a player falls, and risk appetite is a team's call [17:16] [17:47].
- A panelist says NFL teams are never honest about injuries [18:18], and that a quarterback's difficult stretch included eight head coaches in six years [18:49].
- Shen says the Ravens succeed partly on depth, using later-round and unsigned players [20:52] [21:22].
- A panelist says smart teams know where their system is strong-link or weak-link and add premium depth in weak-link spots such as quarterback, safety and linebacker [21:22] [21:52].

## Summary

A former sports agent who became the Green Bay Packers' contract and business executive describes how an NFL front office works from the inside. He recounts building a team abroad from nothing, then explains his role as a link between long-term business planning and the urgent needs of the football side. His stories cover contract talks, the decision to draft Aaron Rodgers while holding a long-time starting quarterback, the cost of negotiating directly with players, and weighing talent against character. The talk is anecdotal: it offers no data, no model and no Q&A, and the captions are noisy.

## Key claims

- The speaker describes his job as a fulcrum between the business side, which thinks long term, and the football side, which wants answers now [08:35].
- He says he was sometimes the voice of caution toward football staff and sometimes the voice of aggression toward the business side [09:05].
- He argues every team needs someone in that role so the organization does not split into isolated structures [09:40].
- Players mostly want to know they are getting a bit more than the other guy, not a particular dollar figure [11:12]; he calls insecurity and ego dominant in the business [11:42].
- He says a free-agent signing took over a month because the team's was the only offer, so he had to keep pushing [12:12] [12:43].
- Having no owner above him gave him freedom, and he let personnel evaluators do their jobs while he did his [13:43] [14:13].
- He says combining personnel work with payroll could be called Moneyball or analytics, and he thinks the team was ahead of its time [14:43].
- He says the team did not need a second quarterback behind a starter who never missed a game, and the pick was a present-versus-future balancing act [15:47] [16:22].
- Coaches were frustrated because the player might not help for years, or ever, and the room's mantra was to trust the board [19:59] [20:30].
- He says he expects no team to let a first-round quarterback wait three years again, because of pressure from fans [23:03] [23:33].
- Negotiating directly with players, which some offered because he was a former agent, was the worst experience, and he came to see an agent as a buffer [24:33] [25:03].
- On character, he says every player is a mix of talent and character, and that more talent brings more tolerance [26:35].
- He recounts opposing a position coach who wanted to sign a player with a long record of off-field problems, winning that argument and losing others [27:06] [27:36].
- He describes forcing a coach and a player into his office to talk, with four minutes of silence, ending with no firing and no agreement that they understood each other [29:06] [29:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barcelona team: 80 players selected, 40 told they could not travel, built in about 10 days [02:32].
- Opening-day ticket sales of 173 in a stadium he says holds 40,000 [02:32].
- The next night, 18,000 attended, with roughly 6,000 tickets given away by his own estimate [03:33].
- Food ordered for 60 people was eaten after 20 [05:03]; the team lasted two seasons [05:03].
- Seven contracts were waiting while he tried to reach a star quarterback [10:10].
- That quarterback's deal was described as the first hundred million dollar contract in the NFL [11:12].
- Free agent contact around March 15th, signing around April 26th [12:12].
- In the 2005 draft room, he says about 19 or 20 players were rated as first-rounders [17:55].
- The choice between two quarterbacks was "51 to 49 percent" by his recollection [18:29].
- The team reached the 24th pick with one first-round-rated name on the board [20:30].
- He kept the player's agent on hold for 15 minutes [21:31], with 13 minutes elapsed in the room [22:01] and two minutes left on the clock [22:32].
- He had three cases of direct negotiation before refusing to do it again [25:03].
- A coach's line about a player being asked to win "75 street fights a day" [27:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- The draft board with first-round ratings, and the rule to trust the board [20:30].
- A business-versus-football time-horizon split in roster and contract decisions [08:35].
- Using an agent as a buffer in contract talks [25:03].
- No quantitative model or data set is described.

## Limits and open questions

- The talk is a first-person set of stories with no data, no outcomes tracking and no comparison group, so none of it shows a method works.
- The Moneyball or analytics description of the team's approach [14:43] is the speaker's own claim; no metric or example is given.
- Probabilities such as 51 to 49 [18:29] are recollections, not documented model outputs.
- Captions are machine text and garble many names and phrases (the Barcelona opening, the agent names, the draft sequence); treat spellings as unreliable.
- The speaker had an institutional view as a team executive with no owner above him [13:43], which may not apply to teams that do have one.
- The talk touches on a former player's later criminal conviction as an example that character is hard to judge [26:04]; no process for judging character is offered.

## Q&A

- None: the speaker says he did not plan time for questions [29:36].

## Summary

A moderated panel with an ESPN analyst, a former NFL offensive lineman, a Ravens analytics staffer and a Rams panelist discusses where football analytics works and where it strains. The central tension is season-long efficiency and tracking-based line grades against the on-field view that technique, coaching and teammates shape every play. The panelists describe how analysts earn trust from scouts and coaches, why grading individuals in a team game is hard, how fourth-down attitudes have shifted, and what data they want next, such as college tracking data. The captions are heavily garbled, so turn attribution and many details need checking against the video.

## Key claims

- The moderator opens by saying analytics is no longer a novelty or a rising phenomenon [01:01].
- The Rams panelist says football analytics lagged partly because revenue sharing under the cap lowers the need for innovation in small markets [02:32].
- He adds that on-field analyses are easy to copy, so teams look for edges others cannot easily reproduce [02:32] [03:02].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts and scouts process information differently but can reach the same conclusions, and that open dialogue helps when they disagree [03:33] [04:06].
- She frames modeling as having unknowns where coach and scout expertise enters, so the two views do not clash [05:06] [05:37].
- Mitch Schwartz says crude stats such as blitz rate mislead, giving examples of one team counted as a 50% blitz team and another as an 8% blitz team [06:08] [06:38].
- He prefers to study each opponent's tendencies on film, because knowing what a defender does most often matters more than his signature move [06:38] [07:08] [07:38].
- Bryan Burke describes building block identification from the separation between all players at each time step, then adding orientation and later win and loss on blocks [08:39] [09:09].
- The Rams panelist says tracking data reduces human bias in evaluation, for example liking a well-run team and discounting a mysterious one [10:09] [10:40].
- Schwartz says the ESPN line metric looked too simple (is your player between you and the quarterback at 2.5 seconds), and that a coached vertical set can make a blocker look worse on distance [11:41] [12:11] [12:41].
- He says a tackle was second in pass block wins while leading the league in sacks allowed, which he attributes partly to quarterbacks holding the ball [14:13] [14:43].
- The Ravens panelist says her view of running backs changed: value shows up in beating second-level tacklers, vision, and speed against an unblocked edge defender [15:45] [16:15] [16:45] [17:15].
- She argues run defense and pass defense merge: solid interior linemen mean fewer defenders in the box and more help in coverage [17:48] [18:23].
- Schwartz says the running game builds toughness and that tiring defensive linemen is a real but unquantified effect, and that he would not stop running with a large late lead [19:54] [21:25] [24:00].
- He says the best way to tire a defensive line is a fast-paced passing game [21:55].
- An analytics panelist says efficiency data favor passing, and that the question is how much to sacrifice for physicality, not whether the running game matters [22:56].
- A panelist notes the NFL is results-oriented while analytics focuses on process [25:32].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts must learn what coaches and scouts value, and tests a finding by asking what she would tell a coordinator [27:37] [28:08].
- She gives an example where a play's high passer rating looked like old news to senior scouts and coaches [29:12] [29:42].
- The Rams panelist says coaches are data processors without realizing it, use information differently from each other, and should be free to succeed or fail with or without analytics [30:12] [31:42] [32:44].
- A panelist says the share of teams going for it on fourth down rose a lot, raising what counts as conservative [33:44] [34:16].
- Schwartz says tracking could show how pre-snap depth off the ball affects a lineman's reach at contact [35:16] [35:47].
- He is skeptical of ranking individual linemen from tracking data because technique and blame assignment (lineman or running back) are subjective [35:47] [36:17] [36:47] [37:17].
- A panelist defends tracking metrics as objective and rule-consistent, noting two scouts in a room will disagree [37:47] [38:19] [38:51].
- A panelist says players picked high get more chances regardless of results and suggests quantifying that [39:21] [39:52].
- The Rams panelist says defensive line results depend on who plays next to you, using examples of players who changed teams [40:52] [41:23].
- A panelist says the aim is to understand interdependencies, not assign individual values, and doubts whether isolating individual plays works for paying or drafting [41:53] [42:23].
- Burke says tracking data work requires studying the sport at a deeper level and that analytics and film communities must merge [43:25] [43:55].
- The Ravens panelist wants better ways to value positions in roster construction and says left tackle pay, once about double right tackle pay, is now close to even [45:27] [45:57].
- The Rams panelist says a talented quarterback on a rookie contract has been the biggest team-building advantage [47:57].
- Burke wants college and high school tracking data to see win rates of every lineman and pass rusher [47:57] [48:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length 45 minutes with 10 minutes of Q&A, per the opening [00:30].
- The moderator recalls one NFL official in the audience at his first visit in 2012 [01:01].
- The Rams panelist cites six or seven years of analytics effort [02:02].
- Blitz-rate example: one team called a 50% blitz team versus another at 8% when counting differently [06:08] [06:38].
- Schwartz's example: an opponent likely goes inside 80% of the time and outside 20% [06:38] [07:08].
- Block metric: is the blocker between the rusher and the quarterback at 2.5 seconds, as Schwartz describes it [11:41].
- Pre-snap depth example: 1.5 feet of space [35:16].
- Garbled number: the captions say PFF treats 10 or 15 odd plays out of over 1000 as too small a sample to move a group rating [36:47]; the exact claim is unclear.
- Passer rating example: about 70 average, about 70 against one coverage, about 80 for one called play, and about 110 for that play against that coverage, with the play name garbled in the captions [28:42] [29:12].
- Rams EPA example: 150 EPA total and -50 from running, described as giving up a third of productivity; the captions are unclear on what scale or system [22:56].
- Schwartz's hypothetical: a team passing 70% of the time with a 24-point lead [21:25].
- Roster count: 256 drafted players per year; combine attendance of about 290 other athletes [48:58] [49:30].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Separation-based block identification and block win rates from player tracking [08:39] [09:09].
- GPS and tracking data as a reduced-bias evaluation source [10:09].
- EPA and win probability as abstractions from down, distance and score [43:25].
- A scout-analyst bridge test: what would you tell the coordinator? [28:08].
- Film study of opponent tendencies, as practised by Schwartz [06:38] [07:08].

## Limits and open questions

- The captions are heavily garbled, with turns often unlabeled, play names wrong ("Forbert"), and "combine harvesters" appearing for the combine [49:30]. Attribution of some claims to a specific panelist is a best guess.
- The captions call two panelists "players", but some of their statements sound like club staff; their roles are unverified.
- Examples (one tackle's pass block wins versus sacks, one coach's fourth-down call) are single cases, not samples.
- The first-in-history fourth-down claim and the margin of victory are garbled [31:12] and unverified.
- The panelists' views reflect their institutions (ESPN's metrics, club preferences); no validation data is shown for the block metric.
- The panel says body blows are not quantified [24:00], so those arguments rest on experience.

## Q&A

- Will tracking data change the combine, and could it go away? Rams panelist: it will not disappear, top-10 picks are unaffected, others benefit, and meaningless drills will be replaced by ones closer to game demands [49:30] [50:02].
- Have coaches used analytics more in game planning over a career? Schwartz: yes, his team gave players data on strengths and weaknesses, such as weaker third-and-long pass protection, framed as not subjective [50:32] [51:02].

title: "SSAC24: The Numbers Game: Football Analytics from Combines to Championships"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ted Knutson (moderator), Steve Palazzolo (caption spelling), Eugene Shen, Shawn Clement (caption spelling), Isabella Dillio (caption spelling, student host)]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, policy]

## Summary

A panel with a Pro Football Focus product chief, a Washington Commanders football-strategy executive, an analytics executive at a sports-analytics firm (captions: "Summer Sports") and a StatsBomb moderator covers analytics in drafting, tracking data, roster depth, in-game management, college football and analytical failures. Recurring themes: draft models are only as good as the scouting input, tracking data moves evaluation from outcomes toward traits, expectation models can misassign credit, and the hardest skill is communicating probability to decision makers. They also discuss the transfer portal, NIL, and language-model tools for coaches. Panelists speak from their own employers' viewpoints.

## Key claims

- The moderator says football's complexity far exceeds chess, so decisions still come down to humans even with a data-driven approach [03:34] [04:05].
- Palazzolo says the 2018 first overall pick of Baker Mayfield was analytically driven and did not pan out, while Josh Allen, picked seventh, became the best quarterback of the generation [04:36] [05:06].
- He says Aiden Hutchinson (caption spelling) was the clear analytical favorite over the player the Jaguars chose in the top two [05:06] [05:37].
- Clement says an offensive lineman from a small college (caption: Zack Tom of Wake Forest) was rated highly by analytics, played all five line positions, was hard to sell to scouts, and became a successful starter after being drafted by Green Bay [06:08].
- Palazzolo says PFF data covers every action, and calls the grading subjective but applied objectively [07:39].
- He values a player's whole college career, early years included, plus age adjustments [08:09], and says PFF detail is especially valuable for edge, defensive line and offensive line [08:39].
- Clement says it is hard to predict pro position from college position, and trait ratings from scouts can differ from performance under coaching assignments [09:10] [09:40].
- Shen says a draft model is only as good as the scouting data fed into it, and that he values scouts' input [11:13].
- He says data can make scouts more productive, so they stop spending time on poor players, and this earns their trust [11:43].
- The moderator says teams increasingly want to insulate scouts from analytics bias, with analysts synthesizing both views afterward [12:15].
- Before tracking data, most analytics measured outcomes, even PFF grades; tracking lets analysts estimate traits such as speed and field control [13:15] [13:45].
- Examples of teams using game speed rather than combine data are named as Rams wide receivers, and one panelist says the team may not attend the combine [13:45] [14:15].
- Teams are building their own athleticism metrics from data, which matter most for late-round picks, and combine participation is declining [14:45] [15:15].
- Panelists argue combine drills can be redesigned using tracking data to see what actually predicts game performance [15:45] [16:15].
- A panelist says medical problems found around the combine are a common reason a player falls, and risk appetite is a team's call [17:16] [17:47].
- A panelist says NFL teams are never honest about injuries [18:18], and that a quarterback's difficult stretch included eight head coaches in six years [18:49].
- Shen says the Ravens succeed partly on depth, using later-round and unsigned players [20:52] [21:22].
- A panelist says smart teams know where their system is strong-link or weak-link and add premium depth in weak-link spots such as quarterback, safety and linebacker [21:22] [21:52].
- A panelist credits the Ravens with many small good decisions and with paying for a linebacker with less positional value because he held the system together [22:22] [22:52].
- The panel describes a dedicated game manager role, which one panelist calls analytics-driven and part of weekly coaching staff meetings [23:23] [23:53] [24:30].
- A panelist says the head coach has too many jobs, so a specialist should focus on in-game decisions [25:00].
- On the Super Bowl overtime coin toss, the panelist says analyses (including one by the NFL) show receiving still gives a slight edge, and he does not think the choice was a huge mistake [26:01] [26:32].
- He credits a Chiefs game manager with educating players on the new overtime rules before every playoff game [26:32] [27:03].
- College football differs because there is no salary cap, resources differ widely, and the transfer portal creates a free-agency-like decision each year with little advance notice [28:37] [29:07] [29:37].
- Power Five teams often lack data scientists and rely on vendor material and student interns [33:44] [34:14].
- NIL and transfers change draft classes, which are getting older, and previous observations may no longer hold, so analysts should seek leading indicators [32:11] [32:42].
- A panelist says the rushing yards over expected family of metrics has a flaw: speed belongs to the player yet is built into the expectation, so a fast receiver or runner is penalized [36:15] [36:46].
- He says a model that does not check its assumptions can be extremely precise but wrong [37:16].
- Palazzolo says that over about ten years the best quarterbacks were not the analysts' favorites, and data work better for finding starters at tackle, safety or cornerback than a top-eight quarterback [37:16] [37:47] [38:18].
- A panelist stresses process over outcome and recalls a coach who wanted an 80 percent conversion chance before calling it a trend [38:48] [39:19].
- Panelists say analysts must communicate probabilities in the language of football people, even when that feels like overclaiming, because hedging with margins of error does not land [39:49] [40:20] [40:50].
- Credit for a rushing play is shared among at least six players, and a defense can matter as much as the line [41:51] [42:22] [43:53].
- Pass rusher is easier than offensive line to evaluate for the draft, and the running game is harder still [45:23] [45:54] [46:24].
- A panelist says language-model tools for coaches could answer midnight questions, especially if the NCAA allows tablets on the sideline [46:55] [47:28].
- College scheme differences complicate scouting (some defenses use one edge rusher), and NFL needs shift with offenses, which one panelist calls non-stationarity [48:29] [49:29].
- One panelist says running backs matter though they peak early, so a second contract may not be worth it [51:31].
- Another panelist argues pass-catching runners and pre-snap motion add value by making defenses think [52:32] [53:03] [53:34].

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length about 45 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions [00:32].
- A PFF tenure since 2011 [02:33]; Shen's first conference visit in 2011 [10:42]; another panelist blogging from 2017 and working for teams from 2019 [03:03].
- 2018 first overall pick; the seventh overall pick [04:36].
- Eight head coaches in six years [18:49]; a quoted $40 million contract for an average quarterback [19:19].
- A Ravens game manager hired in 2016 [23:53]; fourth-down increase after 2014 [24:30].
- More than 3,000 players entered the transfer portal the previous year [29:37]; a 25-person recruiting group [30:07]; 120 leagues in the StatsBomb dataset [30:39]; four interns tracking the portal [31:10].
- Fourth-down conversion chance of 65 percent versus a coach's 80 percent threshold [38:48] [39:19]; a 70 percent chance a player is better [39:49].
- Top-64 cornerback and top-eight quarterback as examples of thresholds [37:47].
- At least six players contribute to a run [41:51]; a game of 200 rushing yards with a 50-yard play [43:23] [43:53].
- The captions say a quarterback had 800 passing yards in one game [50:29]; possibly garbled and not verified.
- PFF began collecting quarterback data in 2014 [37:16].
- Rushing yards over expected: named by a panelist as a metric with a flaw; the captions give no formal definition [36:15].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Draft models combining combine metrics, PFF grades and scouting input [11:13].
- Tracking-derived estimates of speed, field control, pressure and quarterback decisions [13:45].
- Team-built athleticism metrics from data [14:45].
- Strong-link versus weak-link roster thinking [21:22].
- Fourth-down and overtime decision analyses by a game manager [26:01].
- Expectation models with a check on who owns the residual [36:46].
- Keeping scouts blind to analytics, then synthesizing [12:15].

## Limits and open questions

- Captions are auto-generated and garble names and phrases (names spelled as "Trayvon Walker", "Aiden Hutchinson", "Zack Tom", "Mike Frasier", "Summer Sports"); turn attribution is often unlabeled.
- The panelists work for PFF, a club, a vendor and a data provider, so statements about data value and club choices reflect their employers.
- Examples are single cases (a few quarterbacks, one lineman); no sample sizes or validation numbers are given.
- The claim that analysts' favorite quarterbacks have not been the best ones is not quantified; no list of models or hit rates is shown [37:16] [37:47].
- Contradiction: one view says insulate scouts from analytics [12:15], another says data should raise scout productivity [11:43]; the panel does not reconcile them.
- The panelists acknowledge the chess comparison is dated for current engines [25:30].

## Q&A

- Elite offensive lineman or elite pass rusher, which is harder to project? Pass rusher is easier, since it is closer to a one-on-one outcome [45:23] [45:54].
- What about the running game? Harder, because credit is shared and defensive tackles' double-team roles needed better data [46:24].
- Role of AI and language models? Near-term tool for coaches' questions, including on the sideline at college [46:55] [47:28].
- How do college systems affect scouting? Scheme differences mean less direct comparison, and offseason training before the draft can help [48:29] [48:59].
- More confident drafting system fits? One panelist says quarterback development is hard to predict, using a spread-offense passer who fell in the draft [50:29].
- Do running backs matter again? Yes, they matter though they peak early; a versatile back adds value in a multi-threat offense [51:31] [52:02] [52:32].

The speaker, who says he works for the Texas A&M football team and earlier at Florida State, argues that football tracking data (GPS, heart rate, sensors) is incomplete unless it is read alongside film. He describes practice-level grading reports, time-to-contact for linemen, play-tendency "cheat sheets" for defensive coordinators, a computer vision system that pulls tracking data from broadcast video, and acceleration-based matchups and recruiting. The point is that coaches trust and act on data that is tied to what they see on film and that is presented in the form they prefer. The evidence is a set of anecdotes from one program plus one prediction accuracy figure.

- Game data was too thin in college football (few big games, substitutes in the second half, players leaving each year), so the staff built a PFF-style report for every practice. [03:47] [04:17]

- Tracking data can be tied to skill, for example whether a fast receiver runs the right route. [05:19] [05:49]
- For linemen, a key measure is time from the ball being thrown to first contact. [05:49] [06:19]
- A rookie quarterback's heart rate spiked before each snap in spring practice. The head coach attributed it to not knowing the plays, the focus became learning the playbook, and he returned a different quarterback and won the competition. [06:49] [07:20] [07:50]
- A center's time to contact rose only against one particular opponent. The line coach, after watching film, attributed it to fear. [09:20]
- Coaches understand time metrics more readily than acceleration numbers. [09:50]
- Single-variable and multivariable trends serve three purposes for a defensive coordinator: spotting play-combination choices, building training scenarios, and building cheat sheets, since iPads and computers are not allowed in the boxes. [10:20] [10:50]
- The coordinator rejected a filter interface and asked for Excel, so an Excel-based system was built. [12:22]
- Coach trust in the data was described as extremely valuable. [12:52]

# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]

## Department model and roles

- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Inferred (author uncertain — see Testing tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Rehab and return to play

- Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization — a support/advisory role, not a stated final-decision role. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (principle) / gap (no criteria stated)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Daily wellness-style subjective monitoring, dropped for general roster use, is explicitly kept in return-to-play scenarios specifically because subjective context still fills a gap objective testing can't. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- NordBord hamstring testing, dropped for roster-wide use, is explicitly retained for smaller, targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style). **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

*This is the thinnest discipline in the corpus — see Interview prep.*

## Injury risk and prevention

- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice.
127 files, 574 baseline lines
## Eric's baseline
Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's stated role is to supply information that supports decisions made by Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine, and to help the team answer and ask better questions rather than hand down answers. The panel extends this: coaches want analysts to arrive with context and a plan that can be communicated, and the panel's skepticism of "the result leads to the analysis" ([41:21]) matches Eric's baseline caution about judging a method by one outcome. Eric's baseline also says the annual plan is a flexible roadmap that gets adapted; the panel's scripted opening plays used to gather information ([21:15]) is a similar adapt-as-you-learn idea, but the corpus gives no matching football decision rule.
## Eric's baseline
Eric's baseline: Daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent answers that carried no signal, and objective measures (daily CMJ with mRSI) replaced them. The talk agrees on the weakness of self-report: the speaker says food diaries underreport and he tracks no intake. Eric's baseline also says data collection must justify its cost in time, compliance and staff attention, and that a valid test is worthless without consistent collection at scale (the NordBord decision). The talk leaves this open: the speaker describes morning fasted draws and a few days for results ([13:35]), which is a logistics cost he does not weigh against benefit. The Playbook also places body composition and nutrition with a separate unit, so this is a link to be routed through them, not a new Applied Performance data stream.
## Eric's baseline
- Eric's baseline: a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories beats an exhaustive battery, and data collection is judged on cost versus insight (method-baseline, Testing and Philosophy sections). The talk agrees with cutting to the few items that matter.

- **Main problem:** Claims the baseline tags as Inferred were written as plain "Eric's baseline", without the course-team or speaker-unconfirmed tag. The commonest were "injury risk is reduced, not eliminated", "a small number of valid tests", "testing must be exactly repeatable", "recovery has to be earned / culture of fear", "preparedness vs readiness", and "coach's eye". They now carry the course-team Inferred tag, since the transcripts can't confirm which instructor said them.
- **Not in the baseline (4 claims):** These were relabeled "Inference:". An example is a "caution about judging a method by one outcome", which the baseline never states. The other three:
  - "Eric's operations-first view" in `ghrWAiUb9zk`
  - "monitoring should not overwhelm coaches" in `f3HTL6XOmw4`
  - "no documented Baylor decision protocol" in `m7vJ7ozZj3U`
- **Softened:** Two claims said Applied Performance "does not make the final call". They now say it has a support/advisory role, which is what the Playbook says.
- **Still to do:** The stronger-model review of a sample before Flint ingest, which I haven't done. The baseline itself says its transcript bullets are shared course-team positions until you claim them.
